2026 elections: What you need to know about LA County's state Senate, Assembly races

By Linh Tat

Pasadena Star-News · 2026-10-24 · Section: California Politics · Page 14 · 2238 words

There are 32 legislative races – eight state Senate and 24 Assembly seats – on the Nov. 3 ballot where Los Angeles County voters will help decide the winner during this year's general election.

Eight of these races have no incumbent running.

In the state Senate, they include the 24th and 34th districts, where outgoing Sens. Ben Allen and Tom Umberg are facing term limits. Also, in the 26th District, Sen. María Elena Durazo did not seek reelection but instead ran for, and won, a seat on the L.A. County Board of Supervisors in June.

In the Assembly, five races feature no incumbent. That's because Assemblymembers Tom Lackey (District 34), Jacqui Irwin (District 42), Mike Gipson (District 65), Al Muratsuchi (District 66) and Sharon Quirk-Silva (District 67) are termed out.

There are also two races where the incumbent is running unopposed: Assemblymembers Mark Gonzalez and Tina McKinnor, who represent the 54th and 61st districts, respectively. Both are Democrats.

In many of these races, a candidate captured more than 50% of the vote in the June primary election. But for state legislative races, the top two vote-getters, regardless of political party, move on to the general election, even if one candidate received the majority of the vote in the primary.

Below is a breakdown of L.A. County's legislative races.

20th State Senate District Sen. Caroline Menjivar, a Democrat seeking a second term, is running against Republican Tony Rodriguez, a construction recruitment manager.

SD-20 spans an area roughly bordered by Burbank, Sunland/Tujunga, Sylmar and Canoga Park in the northern and eastern portions of the San Fernando Valley.

22nd State Senate District Democratic Sen. Susan Rubio, going for a third term, is facing Republican Mike Netter, a small business owner. This district mostly represents communities in eastern San Gabriel Valley, including El Monte, Covina and Pomona. But it also includes parts of San Bernardino County, including Ontario and Chino.

24th State Senate District West Hollywood Councilmember John Erickson and media consultant Brian Goldsmith are embroiled in one of the most expensive legislative races this cycle to see which Democrat will succeed term-limited Sen. Ben Allen, D-Santa Monica.

This largely coastal district stretches from the Santa Monica Mountains – including Agoura Hills, Calabasas and Malibu – to L.A.'s Westside and Hollywood area, and on down to the South Bay, taking in Redondo Beach, Torrance and Rancho Palos Verdes.

Erickson, who is chief of staff at Alliance for a Better Community, an L.A.-based organization whose mission is to advance social, economic and racial equity and justice, was first elected to the West Hollywood City Council in 2020.

Goldsmith, a Beverly Hills resident, has never been elected to office, though he worked on Hillary Clinton's 2000 U.S. Senate campaign and advised Pete Buttigieg during his 2020 presidential run.

Since the June primary election and up through mid-October the two candidates raised more than $3.2 million combined while outside "independent expenditure" groups poured at least another $5.8 million into the race. 26th State Senate District This race pits Sara Hernandez, an affordable housing advocate and president of the Los Angeles Community College District board, against environmental advocate Sarah Rascón to see who will replace Sen. María Elena Durazo, who is moving on to serve on the L.A. County Board of Supervisors.

SD-26 stretches from L.A.'s Eagle Rock and Highland Park neighborhoods in the north, toward Los Feliz and Koreatown in the west, and Boyle Heights, East L.A. and the city of Vernon in the southeastern part of the district. It's one of just two L.A. County state Senate races — the other being SD-24 — where both candidates on the ballot are Democrats.

They're also the only two Senate races in which the California Democratic Party did not endorse a candidate because the members of its endorsement caucus couldn't reach consensus.

And like the 24th District, the race in SD-26 is also among the more expensive legislative races in L.A. County this year.

Between the primary election and mid-October, more than $4.5 million have been spent by outside "independent expenditure" groups on ads, mailers and other expenses in hopes of influencing the outcome of this race. 28th State Senate District Democratic Sen. Lola Smallwood-Cuevas, who is seeking a second term, is running against Republican businessman Joe Lisuzzo.

This district stretches from downtown L.A. west toward Mar Vista and Westchester and takes in most of South Central L.A., including Florence at its southeastern edge.

30th State Senate District Sen. Bob Archuleta, a Democrat, wants a third and final term. To do that, he must fend off Republican challenger Araceli Martinez, a small business owner.

This district represents a portion of southeastern L.A. County and includes Downey, Norwalk and Whittier. It also dips into Orange County, picking up the community of Brea.

34th State Senate District Democratic Assemblymember Avelino Valencia and former Placentia City Councilmember Rhonda Shader, a Republican, are vying to replace termed-out Sen. Tom Umberg, D-Santa Ana.

This district represents a portion of L.A. County, including South Whittier, but is mostly located in Orange County,

and includes the communities of Anaheim, Buena Park, Fullerton, La Habra and Santa Ana.

36th State Senate District Republican Sen. Tony Strickland is facing off against former San Clemente City Councilmember Chris Duncan, a Democrat.

This largely coastal district includes Artesia, Cerritos and Hawaiian Gardens in Los Angeles County and a larger portion of Orange County, including Garden Grove, Westminster, Fountain Valley, Huntington Beach, Newport Beach, Dana Point and San Clemente.

34th Assembly District Big Bear Lake Mayor Randall Putz, a Democrat, is in a runoff with Charles Frederick Hughes, a Republican, after the two advanced from a four-person primary race.

The winner will replace Assemblymember Tom Lackey, R-Palmdale, who is termed out.

The 34th District spans three counties: Los Angeles, San Bernardino and Kern, and includes the communities of Palmdale, Lancaster, Barstow, Lake Arrowhead, Big Bear Lake, and Twentynine Palms.

39th Assembly District Assemblymember Juan Carrillo, D-Palmdale, faces Republican challenger Paul Andre Marsh as he seeks a third term. This district takes in parts of Los Angeles and San Bernardino counties. It includes parts of northern Antelope Valley and stretches into the San Bernardino communities of Adelanto, Hesperia and Victorville.

40th Assembly District Assemblymember Pilar Schiavo, D-Chatsworth, and Ricky Tracy Hayes II, a Republican entrepreneur and businessman, are facing off after advancing out of a four-person primary race.

Schiavo was first elected in 2022 and is seeking a third term.

The 40th District is entirely within L.A. County and represents communities in Santa Clarita Valley and northwestern San Fernando Valley.

41st Assembly District First-term Democratic Assemblymember John Harabedian is up against Republican Adam Christopher Vena, a sanitation employee. The two automatically advanced to the general election since they were the only two to run in the primary.

This district represents voters in Pasadena, Altadena, La Cañada Flintridge, Monrovia and Sierra Madre in Los Angeles County and Rancho Cucamonga, Wrightwood and San Antonio Heights in San Bernardino County. 42nd Assembly District Agoura Hills Councilmember Deborah Klein Lopez, a Democrat, and small business owner Ted Nordblum, a Republican, are running against each other after advancing out of a three-person primary race.

The winner will replace termed out Assemblymember Jacqui Irwin, D-Thousand Oaks, who is running for a U.S. House seat being vacated by retiring Rep. Julia Brownley.

The district includes portions of Ventura and Los Angeles counties, including Simi Valley, Thousand Oaks, Calabasas and Pacific Palisades.

43rd Assembly District Democratic Assemblymember Celeste Rodriguez faces off again against Republican Ricardo Benitez, a plumber and electrical contractor, who was her lone challenger in the primary.

This San Fernando Valley district represents Pacoima, Mission Hills, Sylmar, Arleta, Sun Valley, Panorama City, Lake View Terrace, Valley Glen, Van Nuys and San Fernando.

44th Assembly District Assemblymember Nick Schultz, a Democrat, seeks a second term as he goes toe-to-toe with Republican Carolyn Daniels, an independent contractor. The two advanced from a three-person primary contest.

The district represents residents in the San Fernando Valley and stretches from Sherman Oaks east through North Hollywood and Burbank and north to La Crescenta.

46th Assembly District Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, who is seeking a fifth term, will go toe-to-toe again with his only challenger in the primary, Republican Tracey Schroeder, who is a teacher.

The two also squared off two years ago.

The winner will represent western San Fernando Valley in Los Angeles County and a small portion of Ventura County. Communities include Encino and Van Nuys near its eastern border and West Hills and Woodland Hills further west.

48th Assembly District Assemblymember Blanca Rubio, a Democrat first elected in 2016, wants a sixth and final term. She faces off again against her sole challenger in the primary, Republican Dan Tran, a real estate businessman whom Rubio beat two years ago.

The winner will represent a swath of the San Gabriel Valley, including West Covina, Baldwin Park, Glendora, Covina, Azusa, Duarte and Monrovia.

49th Assembly District Assemblymember Mike Fong, a Democrat first elected in a special election in February 2022, is up against Republican Long "David" Liu, the chief executive of The Liu Law Firm. The two also ran against each other two years ago.

Whoever wins will represent communities in the San Gabriel Valley, including Alhambra, Arcadia, El Monte, Monterey Park, Rosemead, San Gabriel, San Marino, South Pasadena and Temple City.

51st Assembly District Assemblymember Rick Chavez Zbur, who was first elected in 2022, and challenger Colin Hernandez, a digital communications strategist and fellow Democrat, will go head-to-head after advancing from a five-person primary race.

This district represents Hollywood, West Hollywood, Beverly Hills and Santa Monica.

52nd Assembly District Democratic Assemblymember Jessica Caloza seeks a second term in this rematch with musician Andrea Lee Anderson, a Republican and the only person to challenge the incumbent in the primary.

The winner will represent East Los Angeles, including the neighborhoods of Lincoln Heights, Highland Park, Glassell Park, Eagle Rock, Los Feliz, Silver Lake and Echo Park.

53rd Assembly District Assemblymember Michelle Rodriguez, a Democrat seeking a second term, faces off again against her only challenger in the primary, Republican Rafaela Romero, a special education aide.

The district includes parts of Los Angeles and San Bernardino counties, including Pomona, Ontario, Chino, Upland and Montclair.

54th Assembly District Assemblymember Mark Gonzalez, a Democrat seeking a second term, is running unopposed.

He represents a district that includes L.A.'s Koreatown, Westlake, Chinatown, Little Tokyo and Boyle Heights, as well as the cities of Vernon and Montebello.

55th Assembly District Democratic Assemblymember Isaac Bryan, first elected in 2021, faces school social worker Ashley Brown, a fellow Democrat, after the two advanced from a four-person primary race.

This district represents Crenshaw, Culver City, Ladera Heights, Mar Vista, Del Rey, Palms, Pico-Robertson, Beverly Grove and Mid-Wilshire.

56th Assembly District Democratic Assemblymember Lisa Calderon, who was first elected in 2020, faces off again against her only challenger in the primary, Republican Jessica Martinez, a retired teacher.

The winner will represent the southeastern parts of Los Angeles County and the San Gabriel Valley, including El Monte, Hacienda Heights, La Habra Heights, La Puente, Pico Rivera and Whittier.

57th Assembly District Democratic Assemblymember Sade Elhawary, hoping for a second term, will face off against Republican Constance Jewel Menzies, an in-home care provider who was also Elhawary's only challenger in the primary.

The district represents South Central and downtown Los Angeles and includes the area around Exposition Park, Florence and Firestone Park.

61st Assembly District Assemblymember Tina McKinnor, a Democrat first elected in 2022, is running unopposed.

Her district includes Inglewood, Venice, Westchester, Hawthorne, Westmont and Lawndale.

62nd Assembly District Democratic Assemblymember José Luis Solache, who is seeking a second term, is up against Republican Paul Irving Jones, a retired Marine. The two also ran against each other two years ago.

This district represents voters in Bellflower, Huntington Park, Lakewood, Lynwood, Maywood, Paramount, South Gate and Walnut Park.

64th Assembly District Assemblymember Blanca Pacheco, a Democrat, is being challenged by Republican Raul Ortiz Jr., a pest control manager.

Just like in 2024, the two will battle it out to represent Southeast L.A. and a small portion of Orange County, including Bell, Bell Gardens, Cudahy, Downey, East Whittier, La Mirada, Norwalk, Santa Fe Springs, South Whittier and La Habra.

65th Assembly District Compton school board member Ayanna Davis, a Democrat, is facing off against public school teacher Lydia Gutiérrez, a Republican, after the two advanced from a six-person primary race.

The winner will replace termed-out Assemblymember Mike Gipson, D-Carson, who is running for a seat on the state Board of Equalization.

The district stretches from the Port of Los Angeles up to Compton and includes parts of Carson and Long Beach. 66th Assembly District Rancho Palos Verdes Mayor Paul Seo and Palos Verdes Peninsula Unified school board President Sara Deen are going toe-to-toe after the two advanced from a six-person primary race.

The winner will succeed termed-out Assemblymember Al Muratsuchi, D-Torrance.

With no incumbent running, this year's Democrat-versus-Democrat race has turned what has typically been a sleepy race for this district into one where voters are being inundated with television or digital ads, mailers or text messages on a daily basis.

The 66th Assembly District includes many of Los Angeles County's South Bay communities, from El Segundo and Manhattan Beach and on down through Redondo Beach Torrance, Rancho Palos Verdes and San Pedro.

67th Assembly District Republican Paulo Morales, a U.S. Marshals Service special deputy, and Cerritos City Councilmember Mark Pulido, a Democrat, are facing off after advancing from the primary, where six candidates ran to replace termed-out Assemblymember Sharon Quirk-Silva, D-Fullerton.

Pulido edged out Ada Briceño, co-president of Unite Here Local 11 and the former chair of the Orange County Democratic Party, to secure his spot in the runoff.

This district includes Artesia, Cerritos and Hawaiian Gardens in southeastern Los Angeles County, plus Buena Park, Fullerton and Cypress in northern Orange County.

69th Assembly District Assemblymember Josh Lowenthal, who is seeking a third term, is running again against fellow Democrat Carolyn Essex, a policy analyst, and Lowenthal's only challenger in the primary.

The winner will represent parts of southern Los Angeles County, including Avalon, Carson and Long Beach.

California has more revenue than expected thanks to AI. Should the state save it?

By Yue Stella Yu, CalMatters · October 23, 2026

In summary

Proponents say Prop. 2 would allow the state to shore up its reserves for an economic downturn. Critics say it would only allow state leaders to spend more in the future.

The question Proposition 2 poses to California voters is simple: Should the state be able to save more money when its economy is booming?

The ballot measure, dubbed the Save for California’s Future Act, seeks to shore up California’s rainy day fund by allowing state lawmakers to sock away up to 20% of the state’s general fund tax revenue — double the current ceiling of 10%.

It would also require the state to save a bigger share of the gains when revenue is growing faster.

Proponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and Democratic lawmakers, say the state needs a bigger savings account to weather its volatile economy.

Because California’s tax revenue depends so much on wealthy residents’ stock earnings, the state budget is often caught in a boom-or-bust cycle at the mercy of the market. In recent years, the state has seen robust tax revenue from an AI-fueled economy, which has helped state leaders avoid or delay painful cuts to social services even when they projected significant deficits. But economists have consistently warned the boom may not last, and the federal budget cuts to healthcare and welfare programs this year deepened that uncertainty.

Supporters pitched Prop. 2 as a common sense solution, noting the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, which advises state lawmakers, has long recommended the state set aside funding for downturns. The measure is endorsed by a bipartisan coalition of groups, including labor unions, hospital associations and chambers of commerce.

“It doubles the size of the state’s rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we’re not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits,” wrote Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel, an Encino Democrat, and Assembly Appropriations Vice Chair Josh Hoover, a Folsom Republican and the only GOP lawmaker to vote for the measure.

Most Republican lawmakers opposed Prop. 2, stating that the state should use its excess revenue to give taxpayers refunds instead of saving it. They argue that state government already spends too much and that a bigger reserve would merely give state leaders more to spend.

“When they say we’re here for fiscal responsibility, it’s like the devil offering a Bible study. Don’t buy it,” said Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a San Diego Republican.

How long have we had a rainy day fund?

Before 2014, California leaders and voters established reserve funds several times to weather financial storms, but ended up quickly withdrawing most of those funds, leaving the state with very little savings on hand, according to the legislative analyst.

In 2004, following the dot-com bust, voters overwhelmingly supported Prop. 58, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to establish a budget stabilization account and make annual deposits into the fund.

But lawmakers swiftly depleted the fund during the early months of the Great Recession and were forced to make steep spending cuts, borrow money at expensive rates and use accounting gimmicks to weather the rest of the crisis. Under then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, the state Legislature slashed health and welfare funding, scrapped tax credits, furloughed state employees and delayed payments to schools and local governments.

In 2014, as the state’s economy rebounded, then-Gov. Jerry Brown, a Democrat, urged that the state save more. He and the Legislature championed Prop. 2, a bipartisan ballot measure that required the state to save more aggressively and limited when lawmakers could withdraw from the reserves. Nearly 70% of voters approved it.

“When the pendulum swings again, we won’t be forced to raise taxes or make the kinds of harsh cuts that were all too common in recent years,” Brown said in a 2014 op-ed stumping for the reform.

The law requires the state to set aside 1.5% of its general fund revenue and any spikes in capital gains tax revenue each year, with half deposited into the reserves and the other half to pay down state debts. It also made it harder for the state to spend the reserves and carved out portions of the savings for schools.

Under the law, state lawmakers can withdraw from the reserves only when the governor declares a budget emergency and decides that the state is not expected to collect enough revenue in the upcoming fiscal year to match the spending in the three previous budget years.

A majority of state lawmakers must vote to ratify the budget emergency. If approved, they are allowed to withdraw up to half of the rainy day fund balance at once, unless they already withdrew half the balance in the previous budget year and still need to take out more. There are no limits on what lawmakers can use the funds for.

Bigger reserve = more to spend?

Prop. 2 would maintain those withdrawal rules, which critics say would give future governors broad authority to spend down the reserves instead of reining in spending.

“The rainy day fund can be invaded even when it’s not raining, simply because spending isn’t as high as it was within the prior three years,” wrote David Crane, a former economic adviser to Schwarzenegger and founder of Govern for California, a nonprofit fundraising powerhouse that aims to “counter special interest influence.”

“Unless the withdrawal rules change, a larger reserve just lets governors bake in spending based on optimistic forecasts, knowing they can always dip into reserves if revenue falls short.”

In an interview with CalMatters, Gabriel stressed that voters approved those rules in 2014 and emphasized that the measure has bipartisan support. He also dismissed the criticism that the state should just spend less during downturns, likening it to telling families to eat less or downsize instead of dipping into their savings when they fall on hard times.

“I think (the concern) is very misplaced,” he said. “(Prop. 2) is recommended by the experts, because it matches the common-sense wisdom of California families.”

ANCA-WR Announces 2026 General Election Endorsements

by Contributor October 20, 2026

in Community, Featured Story, Latest, News, Top Stories

0

Slate of 61 candidates spans Congress, Governor and California statewide offices, the State Legislature and local offices in Los Angeles

LOS ANGELES—The Armenian National Committee of America, Western Region on Tuesday announced its slate of endorsed candidates for the November 3, General Elections. The 61-candidate slate spans the U.S. House of Representatives, Governor and California’s statewide constitutional offices, the California State Legislature and local offices in Los Angeles. It reflects a careful review of each candidate’s record, public statements, and engagement with the Armenian-American community.

The endorsed candidates are best positioned to advance the Armenian-American community’s most pressing priorities: the right of return for the Armenians of Artsakh who were forcibly displaced by Azerbaijan, accountability for Azerbaijan’s aggression against the Armenian people, the unconditional release of the Armenian prisoners of war and hostages held illegally in Baku, the security and sovereignty of the Republic of Armenia, recognition of and education about the Armenian Genocide, and the safety and prosperity of Armenian Americans in their own communities. The Armenian National Committee of America endorsed the U.S. House and backed its merit-based 2026 Congressional Report Cards, available at anca.org/report-card.

“Our sole measure in deciding whether to support a candidate is his or her commitment to the Armenian Cause, shown not only in words but in real-world actions,” said ANCA-WR Chair Oshin Harootoonian.

“The candidates on this slate have demonstrated that commitment on the issues that matter most to our community, from confronting denial of the Armenian Genocide, building bridges with their Armenian-American constituents, to holding Azerbaijan accountable for its crimes against the Armenian people. We encourage every Armenian-American across the country to make their voice heard and continue their civic duty at the ballot box on November 3,” added Harootoonian.

Community members are encouraged to visit ancawr.org/elect26 for more information about the endorsed candidates. Members are also encouraged to visit hyevotes.org for nonpartisan voter information, including key dates and deadlines, how to confirm or update voter registration, find the nearest vote center, and return a mail ballot on time. All community members across the region are encouraged to take part in the November 3 general election.

Community News Battle between business owner Timothy Gaspar and government employee Barri Worth Girvan in LA City Council’s District 3 race Sara C. Lemon, UT Community News Audio Editor October 20, 2026 LA City Council District 3 Candidates: Barri Worth Girvan (left) and Tim Gaspar (right). Barri Worth Girvan photo by: Yauna Olmstead and Tim Gaspar photo by: Robyn Richardson Business owner Timothy Gaspar and longtime government worker Barri Worth Girvan are vying for the Los Angeles City Council District 3 seat.

After serving three terms, council member Bob Blumenfield will be termed out of the district, which includes a large chunk of the West San Fernando Valley, including the Canoga Park, Reseda, Tarzana, Winnetka, and Woodland Hills neighborhoods.

Both candidates support fully-funded police departments, addressing the homelessness crisis in the area, and have taken stands against state mandates, saying they want what’s best for the existing community and to ensure the community has a voice.

Barri Worth Girvan The candidates differ in a few areas. Worth Girvan’s policy platform emphasizes more interim housing and treatment beds for people who need them, wraparound mental health services and a transparent system to track outcomes of programs that serve people experiencing homelessness actually need them.

Girvan has held staff positions in the California State Legislature, the office of former Los Angeles Mayor Antonio Villaraigosa and local county offices, according to the Los Angeles Times.

“My years of experience in the public sector will ensure that I can best navigate City Hall to advocate for the district’s interests. Delivering core city services is my bread and butter,” Worth Girvan told the Times. “Delivering core city services is my bread and butter…If your trash isn’t picked up, if your trees aren’t trimmed, if your street lights aren’t working, if you pick up the phone to call 911 and nobody responds, then not only is your neighborhood not safe, but your city is not working for you.”

Working in the state Senate, Worth Girvan said on her website that she organized Valley-wide efforts to successfully secure funding for transportation infrastructure and helped lead efforts to rebuild organizations affected by wildfires.

She has strong support from environmental advocates and major labor unions, according to the L.A. Times. Her endorsements include more than one dozen labor unions, including SEIU Local 721, International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 11, National Union of Healthcare Workers , American Federation of Teachers (AFT Local 1521 Faculty Guild) and the Communications Workers of America , according to her website. Other supporters include the National Women‘s Political Caucus - San Fernando Valley, Women‘s Political Committee of Los Angeles, Abundant Housing LA and Sierra Club. She is also supported by the Democratic Party in Los Angeles County and the San Fernando Valley and the Democratic group for the LGBTQ community, called the Stonewell Democratic Club, the Los Angeles County Young Democrats and the Democrats for Israel Los Angeles group. Other supporters include Los Angeles County District 3 Supervisor Lindsey Horvath; and California State Assembly Majority Whip Mark

González, Assembly Democratic Caucus Chair Rick Chavez Zbur and California Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel, Nick Schultz, Celeste Rodriguez, Jacqui Irwin, Mike Fong and Pilar Schiavo.

Timothy Gaspar Timothy Gaspar, who started his own independent insurance firm, has worked with several local nonprofit and civic organizations, including the Metropolitan YMCA of Los Angeles, the Woodland Hills/Warner Center Chamber of Commerce and on the board of trustees of a private school in Calabasas, according to his campaign website. Gaspar also said he supports encampment cleanups, saying that they need to be cleaned up “swiftly and humanely.”

Gaspar said the city council could benefit from his business experience to counter members whose backgrounds are mostly in public policy or community organizing.

“They’re missing the business perspective,” he told the L.A. Times.

Sergei Goldstein, a Valley resident and a security guard at a Los Angeles Public Library, said he supports Gaspar partly because he knows him personally.

“He helps out. He goes around checking with the homeless and makes sure there‘s a place for them to go and, health-wise, if they‘re OK [since they’re on] the streets,” said Goldstein, who met Gaspar in high school through a mutual friend. “That can help a lot for a community.”

Gaspar has a huge lead in fundraising, reporting more than $180,000 in donations to his runoff campaign through June 30, compared with about $31,000 for Worth Girvan.

Gasper is endorsed by Blumenfield and LA City Councilmember Monica Rodriguez, Tim McOsker and John Lee, as well as California Assemblymember Jacqui Irwin, D-Thousand Oaks, and U.S. Rep. Luz Rivas, D-North Hollywood, Los Angeles County Supervisor Kathryn Barger, Former Los Angeles City Controller Laura Chick, who previously served as an LA City Councilmember for District 3, and former State Senator Robert Hertzberg, according to Ballotpedia. Gaspar is also backed by groups including the Apartment Association of Greater Los Angeles, Southland Regional Association of Realtors, IBEW Local 18, IBEW Local 40, UA250, Painters and Allied Trades DC36, LASPMA and ILWU13, according to his website. Other supporters include law enforcement groups such as the Los Angeles Police Protective League, Los Angeles County Professional Peace Officers’ Association, Los Angeles Airport Peace Officers Association and the Association for Los Angeles Deputy Sheriffs, and Democratic groups such as Avance Democratic Club, Democratic Municipal Officials, and Blue Wave Democratic Club. VICA, the Valley Industry & Commerce Association, and the Israeli-American Civic Action Network also support him.

Endorsement: Prop 2 could help California be more fiscally responsible — if our politicians bother to use it

By Chronicle Editorial Board

San Francisco Chronicle · 2026-10-15 · Section: Opinion · 1044 words

What would you do if you suddenly found yourself flush with an unexpected cash windfall?

Would you run out and treat yourself to something expensive and irresponsible? Or would you pay off your debts and sock the extra money away for a rainy day?

Proposition 2, which Democratic state lawmakers (and one Republican) placed on California's November ballot, would encourage California to take the latter approach with its budget.

Understanding how requires a bit of backstory.

California's budget relies heavily on a progressive tax structure; 1% of the richest taxpayers account for 50% of the state's income taxes.

But this structure is volatile. If the stock market takes a hit, so do California's tax revenues and the critical programs they fund — including schools, which account for a huge portion of the state's budget since the passage of Proposition 13, the 1978 measure that limited local governments' ability to raise property taxes. When revenues nosedive, lawmakers at all levels of government typically ask voters to approve tax increases at the ballot box — when they can least afford them.

On the flip side, when the stock market is booming, California is constrained by the Gann Limit, an obscure rule that prevents the state from spending more per taxpayer than it did in 1979 — the year voters approved the measure — once adjusted for inflation. Any money the state collects over the limit must be refunded to taxpayers or spent on certain purposes, such as infrastructure or education.

In 2014, voters approved a ballot measure that stabilized this budget chaos. It did three main things: First, it required the state to set aside 1.5% of general fund tax revenue each year. Second, whenever the state collected especially high capital gains tax revenue, it required some of that money to be set aside. Third, it directed the state to put half the combined funds in a rainy-day savings account and use the other half to make additional payments on long-term retiree healthcare and pension debt through 2030.

These rules "substantially improved" California's reserve policy, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office, permitting the state's savings account to go from basically zilch to $23 billion.

But it wasn't nearly sufficient to smooth out the state's budget volatility.

The 2014 measure capped the rainy-day fund at 10% of the general fund — only enough to cover about one-third of likely shortfalls during the next 50 years, the Legislative Analyst's Office concluded after running thousands of simulations.

To make up the difference, California would have to cut core services during every economic downturn or raise taxes.

Neither are good options.

Prop 2, which was inspired by the Legislative Analyst's Office research, is designed to create conditions for a stabler budget.

The measure would double California's reserve cap to 20% of general fund dollars and direct the state to save an even larger share of capital gains windfalls. It would also require California to keep making additional debt payments through 2040 and permit funds set aside for this purpose to be spent on a wider variety of debts, including repaying loans from the federal government and state special funds that backfilled holes in the general fund.

These provisions aren't particularly controversial. Even Republican Assembly Member David Tangipa of Fresno, a Prop 2 opponent, acknowledged to the editorial board that "I supported quite a bit of the measure." The sticking point for him and others who oppose Prop 2 centers on the Gann Limit.

Currently, depositing money into the rainy-day fund counts as "spending" under the Gann Limit. Ironically, this can discourage lawmakers from putting money into reserves in good budget years — which is precisely when they should be socking funds away.

Prop 2 would change that calculus by counting withdrawals from the account as spending under the Gann Limit — leaving lawmakers with fewer excuses for not filling the rainy-day fund during boom years.

Tangipa argued that this "takes away the ability to actually reimburse the taxpayers money that belongs to them." But padding the rainy-day fund in flush budget years arguably saves taxpayers money in the long run by increasing stability and decreasing the likelihood of taxes in down years. The Legislative Analyst's Office described the proposed accounting tweak as "reasonable."

If used to the fullest extent, Prop 2 could improve California's budget stability, permitting the state to cover about 50% of funding shortfalls in the next 50 years.

That's better than the 30% it can cover now. Still, Prop 2 is a far cry from the model the Legislative Analyst's Office recommended: raising California's reserve cap to 50% by 2055, either by establishing more robust deposit rules or setting aside much more capital gains tax revenue in especially flush years.

This framework, the analyst's office found, would allow the state to absorb 75% of funding shortfalls in the next 50 years.

Lawmakers considered the 50% cap, but "we realized that was not going to be an achievable level, both politically and from a policy perspective," Assembly Member Jesse Gabriel, D-Encino (Los Angeles County), and Prop 2's author, told the editorial board.

Nevertheless, he said, Prop 2 is one of the most "concrete and achievable" things "we can do in the near term that would put California on stronger financial footing."

The catch, Gabriel acknowledged: "You still need responsible decision-makers."

In other words, Prop 2 is effectively useless if politicians don't exercise fiscal prudence.

Prop 2's deposit and withdrawal rules can be waived during a natural disaster or if the governor and Legislature declare a fiscal emergency — and the state's criteria for one are farcical.

Case in point: California's revenue is currently booming amid an overheated stock market, but Gov. Gavin Newsom and the Legislature have declared multiple fiscal emergencies in recent years — postponing deposits into the rainy-

day fund, pulling billions of dollars out of reserves and raising taxes on everyday Californians to maintain $100 billion in spending growth.

"There are natural political incentives to spend when you have a lot of money," Gabriel admitted. Prop 2 won't necessarily curb those, but if used appropriately, it could improve California's budget resilience and make it harder for lawmakers to justify reckless spending during good years — and then beg voters for more money when the economy turns south.

Voters should pass Prop 2 and hold lawmakers accountable to their promise to be more responsible stewards of taxpayer money.

Reach the Chronicle editorial board with a letter to the editor:www.sfchronicle.com/submit-your-opinion.

At Alcatraz, Native advocates criticize Newsom’s vetoes of tribal bills

Roughly a mile north of San Francisco, on Alcatraz Island, thousands gathered in the early hours of Monday to celebrate Native American resilience, reports CalMatters’ Melanie Henshaw.

The event, which took place on Indigenous Peoples Day, commemorates the 19-month occupation of Alcatraz from 1969 to 1971 by the Indigenous advocacy group, Indians of All Tribes. At one point, as many as 400 people lived on the island and ran their own basic services to protest federal policies targeting Native American communities and religions.

During the observance, organizers and attendees highlighted the challenges facing California Native people. Several criticized Gov. Gavin Newsom’s recent vetoes of bills that would have required state agencies to address tribal water shortages, and strengthened protections for tribal religious practices and sacred sites.

  • Morning Star Gali, executive director of the advocacy group Indigenous Justice and a citizen of the Pit River Tribe: “I’ve gone into state parks with all of our relatives to go in to be able to gather medicine and to be able to pray, to be able to pray at the sacred waters — I’ve been kicked out of those spaces.”

Sixty-two tribes in California lack federal recognition, which among other things would provide protections for sacred sites. Tribal leaders have argued that without additional protections, they are limited in their ability to safeguard sacred sites that could be damaged as a result of state and federal policies.

Attendees also criticized Newsom’s veto of a bill that would have established a Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons Justice Program within the California Department of Justice. In his veto message, Newsom said existing efforts rendered the proposal “unnecessary.”

  • Teyana Viscarra, co-founder of Way of the Sacred Mountain, an advocacy group focused on missing and murdered Indigenous women: “It’s ridiculous, our sisters continue to be ignored even as they go missing and die.”

CalMatters and the UC Student and Policy Center are hosting a lunchtime conversation today in Sacramento on the ballot propositions shaping California’s future. We will break down what each measure would do and what’s at stake before you vote. Register here.

Other Stories You Should Know

Grappling with ICE in Central Valley and college campuses

As federal agents continue to crack down on immigrants, CalMatters’ reporters examine how Immigration and Customs Enforcement is rattling two different California communities:

  • Central Valley: In California’s agricultural heartland, residents are reporting a surge of ICE arrests. Unconfirmed social media videos in recent days appear to show uniformed agents in Madera and Chowchilla, as well as cars with missing drivers and smashed windows parked alongside the region’s farmlands. Workers in Mendota are carrying immigration documents in case they’re stopped. Democratic Assemblymember Esmeralda Soria, whose district covers Fresno and Madera, said her office heard about a family whose parent was detained on his way to cash his work check, leaving them unable to pay their rent. Said Soria: “They’re out there terrorizing our families.” Read more from Wendy Fry.
  • Community colleges: ICE agents have been making arrests near community college campuses, including at parking lots and public streets, inciting panic among students. Though college presidents say they’re doing everything to keep students safe, they admit that they have limited power. Some colleges have installed or plan to install signs outside building entrances telling agents they need approval to enter. In Santa Barbara, one college has partnered with a local immigration advocacy organization to help alert the college of ICE agents. Read more from Adam Echelman.

Where do CA gubernatorial hopefuls stand on water?

California’s next governor will have to grapple with the state’s thirst for water, including groundwater overuse, lack of access to safe drinking water and ongoing water usage conflicts involving farmers, tribes, water districts and environmentalists. 

So what would the candidates, Republican Steve Hilton or Democrat Xavier Becerra, do to address these challenges?

As CalMatters’ Rachel Becker explains, Hilton is outspoken about his plans to build more ways to store and move water to farms and cities. He supports the Sites Reservoir to store Sacramento River water and the Trump administration’s controversial proposal to build Shasta Dam higher. 

Meanwhile, Becerra offers no specific proposals, but his record as former California attorney general can be telling: His lawsuits halted an effort to raise Shasta Dam, and he contested President Donald Trump’s proposal affecting water delivery systems that state officials feared would harm salmon and other species.

And lastly: Fallout from $600K travel scandal

The board that oversees the California High-Speed Rail Authority voted to restrict the spending power of the agency’s chief executive, after a state investigation found that consultants billed the agency $600,000 in travel expenses that were unauthorized or poorly justified. Some consultants flew first class, hailed luxury rides and traveled to night clubs. Read more from CalMatters’ Yue Stella Yu.

California Voices

Proposition 2 is about fiscal responsibility, and would double the size of the state’s rainy day fund so we’re not caught flat-footed when the next economic downturn hits, write Jesse Gabriel and Josh Hoover, Democratic and Republican California assemblymembers, respectively.

Opinion | One area Democrats, GOP agree: California needs a larger rainy day fund

Guest Commentary

Guest Commentary written by

Jesse Gabriel

Jesse Gabriel, a Democrat from Encino, represents California’s 46th Assembly District and chairs the Assembly Budget Committee.

Josh Hoover

Josh Hoover, a Republican from Folsom, represents California’s 7th Assembly District and is vice chair of the Assembly Appropriations Committee.

At a moment when Californians can’t agree on much, we’ve found common ground on something that matters: how the state saves for hard times.

One of us is a Democrat. The other is a Republican. We are united about Proposition 2, because this measure isn’t about partisan politics. It’s about basic fiscal responsibility, and it was developed by the people who understand California’s budget best.

California has one of the largest and most dynamic economies in the world. It’s also one of the most volatile. The state ranks fifth in the nation in revenue volatility because of our tax structure, but only 29th in the size of its budget reserves.

When the good times roll, state revenue pours in. When the economy faces challenges, the state is often forced into abrupt, painful cuts to programs Californians rely on: healthcare, higher education, public safety and safety net services.

Seniors, students and working families bear the brunt, often with little warning.

Prop. 2 fixes that imbalance. It doubles the size of the state’s rainy day fund and requires California to save more during strong budget years, so we’re not caught flat-footed when the next downturn hits. 

This is a structural budget fix without raising taxes to save more. It’s the type of budgetary planning we need to protect our future.

This isn’t a new or radical idea. It builds directly on a framework voters approved in 2014. And it reflects more than a decade of experience with how that fund has actually worked. 

Prop. 2 didn’t start with politicians. It was born from budget experts, not special interests. 

The Legislative Analyst’s Office, California’s nonpartisan fiscal watchdog, recommended its reforms, which developed during legislative hearings with input from the Department of Finance, independent fiscal experts and business leaders.

But its earliest supporters were firefighters, small business advocates, healthcare providers and education leaders — people who see firsthand what happens when reserves run dry and cuts land on hospitals, schools and emergency response. 

That list has since grown because state leaders and fiscal experts from across the political spectrum have lived through what happens when California doesn’t save enough.

A stronger rainy day fund would make California more fiscally credible to taxpayers. States that save responsibly don’t just weather downturns better; they also borrow more cheaply and give families and businesses more confidence that the state can keep its commitments, even when the economy turns. 

That’s the real case for Prop 2. California is safer, steadier and more trustworthy when it saves like it means it.

Saving responsibly is not a partisan value. It’s common sense. California’s budget shouldn’t lurch from boom to bust. Prop. 2 gives us a better way forward.

Newsom Signs Safe Worship Act, Ira Gershwin Initiative, Technion Society Names Board President

Jewish Journal Staff

Less than a year after a protest outside Wilshire Blvd. Temple turned violent, California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) returned to that same sanctuary to sign the law it inspired.

Newsom signed AB 2664, the Safe Worship Zone Act, in a ceremony at the historic LA synagogue, joined by Jewish California CEO David Bocarsly; Board Chair Debi Graboff; clergy and leadership of Wilshire Boulevard Temple; six members of the California Legislative Jewish Caucus – Asms. Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), Rebecca Bauer-Kahan (D-Orinda), Josh Lowenthal (D-Long Beach) and Rick Chavez Zbur (D-Hollywood) and State Sens. Ben Allen (D-El Segundo) and Henry Stern (D-Sherman Oaks) – and leaders of the bill’s cosponsoring organizations: Tye Gregory of JCRC Bay Area, Rabbi Noah Farkas and Joanna Mendelson of Jewish Federation Los Angeles, and David Englin of ADL LA.

AB 2664 establishes a 100-foot zone around the entrances of houses of worship, inside which no one may approach a congregant within eight feet without consent to hand out literature, display a sign, or otherwise obstruct, harass, or intimidate them. It is modeled on Colorado’s buffer-zone law protecting reproductive health clinics, upheld by the U.S. Supreme Court, and balances two co-equal First Amendment protections: right to worship and right to protest.

“Every Californian, no matter their faith, will now be able to walk to their place of worship without fear of being surrounded or intimidated,” Bocarsly said. “Governor Newsom signing this bill alongside Jewish California and our partners speaks to the depth of the relationship we have built together, and to how seriously he takes the safety of every Californian who gathers to practice their faith. We’re grateful to Assemblymember Bauer-Kahan, the Jewish Caucus, and our interfaith partners for standing behind this effort.”

At the signing ceremony, Newsom also signed Assembly Bill 1836, authored by Gabriel and sponsored by Jewish California and Equality California. The bill expands the California State Nonprofit Security Grant Program to cover offsite community events – menorah lightings, Pride celebrations, cultural festivals – closing a gap that had limited funding to a nonprofit’s own physical building. It passed the Senate unanimously and the Assembly 78-0, with one abstention.

“California is stepping up to protect our communities, so that Californians of all faiths and backgrounds can gather together and celebrate without fear,” Gabriel, chair of the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, said. “This bill sends a powerful message that California will continue to stand with the LGBTQ+ community and all others targeted by hate. We will never let hate win.” Both laws take effect Jan. 1, 2027.

The Ira and Leonore S. Gershwin Philanthropic Fund is the new named sponsor of Creative Community for Peace’s (CCFP) Vanguard Initiative, now the Ira Gershwin Vanguard Initiative. Ira Gershwin wrote lyrics that helped define the Great American Songbook, which makes him a fitting namesake for a program that trains the next generation of entertainment leaders. Vanguard gives young entertainment professionals the knowledge and connections to understand the challenges facing the Jewish people, how to confront antisemitism and anti-Israel bigotry, and lead in their industry.

The program held its inaugural event under the new name on Sept. 17. About 150 industry leaders and young professionals turned out to the Beverly Hills home of Blair and David Kohan for a WGA Jewish affinity group panel. The speakers were David Kohan (“Will and Grace”), Jamie Denbo (“Grey’s Anatomy”), Leslie Schapira (“Creature Commandos”), and Jeff Astrof (“Friends”). They discussed what pitching Jewish or Israeli stories means for writers’ careers in today’s environment.

The American Technion Society (ATS), a community of donors and alumni across the United States that supports the Technion – Israel Institute of Technology, announced that Janet Shatz has begun her term as national board president. Shatz was elected by the organization’s national board of directors.

“Janet has been a valued member of the ATS family for decades, and her determination, vision, and deep personal knowledge of the Technion make her the ideal leader for the board at this moment,” Mark Gaines, former national board president and current chair of the ATS board of directors, said.

Shatz will work alongside ATS and Technion leadership to grow giving at a time when the university’s scientific innovation is more critical than ever to global progress and the future of the State of Israel. A second-generation supporter, her connection to the Technion runs deep — from her first visit to the Haifa campus in her 20s, through years of regional leadership, national board service, financial governance and investment stewardship. She has served on the national board of directors for 12 years and was president of ATS – Washington, D.C. from 2019-22. As national board president, she plans to focus particularly on strengthening multi-generational connections to the Technion, drawn from her own family’s history with the institution.

California General Election: Key Dates and Statewide Propositions

By ANGELINA PARISI and ADENIYI LATINWO Record Gazette Staff

Record Gazette · 2026-10-06 · Section: News · 3011 words

California General Election: Key Dates and Statewide Propositions By ANGELINA PARISI and ADENIYI LATINWO California's general election is approaching, with voters set to cast their ballots Nov. 3. As Election Day draws closer, several important dates, deadlines and Statewide ballot propositions are on the calendars and minds for voters.

Proposition 1: Housing Bond What it would do: Proposition 1 would authorize the state to issue $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing programs. The money would be divided among multifamily rental housing, affordable housing preservation and supportive housing, veterans' mortgages, homeownership and down-payment assistance, farmworker, tribal and student housing, housing infrastructure and local housing programs. The measure would cost the state an estimated $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the bonds.

Support Supporters, including US Vets, the California Federation of Teachers, Habitat for Humanity California and Self-Help for the Elderly, say the measure would expand affordable housing for veterans, seniors, people with disabilities and working families. They also argue that the bond would help expand homeownership and prevent homelessness while providing funding without raising taxes.

Opposition No argument against Proposition 1 was submitted for the official voter guide.

Supporters:

US VetsCA Federation of TeachersSelf-Help for the ElderlyHabitat for Humanity CACA Alliance of Child & Family Services No opponents were listed.

Proposition 2: Rainy Day Fund What it would do: Proposition 2 would change California's rules for saving money during periods of strong state revenue. It would require the state to continue making deposits into its main rainy day fund until the fund reaches 20% of General Fund tax revenue, compared with the current 10% threshold. It also would require additional debt payments through 2040, extending the current requirement that is scheduled to end in 2030. Deposits into the rainy day fund and a separate account used to set aside money during revenue surges would not count toward the state's constitutional spending limit until the money is withdrawn.

Support Supporters, including the California Professional Firefighters, Los Angeles Area Chamber of Commerce and Gov.

Gavin Newsom, say the measure would strengthen the state's financial reserves and help protect funding for education, health care, public safety and other services during economic downturns. Supporters also argue that increasing the reserve would help the state avoid sharp spending cuts when revenue falls.

Opposition Opponents argue that the measure would effectively allow the state to set aside more money outside the constitutional spending limit and could make taxpayer rebates less likely. They also say the measure does not directly provide new funding for education, health care or public safety.

Supporters:

CA Professional Firefighters LA Chamber of Commerce Gavin Newsom Xavier Becerra Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel No opponents were listed.

Proposition 3: High-Income Tax What it would do: Proposition 3 would make permanent existing voter-approved higher income tax rates for Californians earning more than $371,000, with the income threshold adjusted annually for inflation. The tax rates were approved in 2012 and are scheduled to expire in 2031. The measure is estimated to maintain between $5 billion and $15 billion in annual state income tax revenue. Roughly 40% of the revenue would go to schools and community colleges, with the remainder supporting other state programs.

Support Supporters, including the California Teachers Association, California School Nurses Organization and California State PTA, say keeping the higher tax rates would protect funding for schools and health care. They argue the measure would prevent a tax reduction for the state's highest-income earners while maintaining money for public services.

Opposition Opponents, including the California Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association of California and California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, argue that California already has high taxes and a high cost of living. They say the state should address spending and government programs before making the higher income tax rates permanent.

Supporters:

California Teachers AssociationCA School Nurses Organization California State PTA Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA Opponents:

California Taxpayers AssociationFamily Business Association of California California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce Proposition 4: Public Campaign Financing What it would do:

PROP 4 would allow California state and local governments to establish public campaign-financing programs for candidates if they choose to do so. The measure would reverse a 1988 ban on such systems for the state and most

local governments. Currently, five California cities, including Berkeley and San Francisco, have public financing for local offices.

Support Supporters say public campaign financing could reduce the influence of private money in politics, arguing that publicly funded campaigns could encourage candidates without significant financial backing to run for office and give small-dollar donors a greater role.

Opposition:

Opponents say the measure could require taxpayers to subsidize candidates they do not support and could direct public money to fraudulent candidates. They also argue that establishing public-financing systems could be costly for state and local governments.

Supporters:

Laurel Plimier, co-president, League of Women Voters of CaliforniaTom Umberg, California state senator Opponents:

Dan Schnur, Former Chair Fair Political Practices Commission Colleen McAndrews, Former Commissioner Fair Political Practices Commission Proposition 5: Recall Elections What it would do: Proposition 5 would change the process for replacing statewide elected officials who are recalled.

Under current law, recall elections ask voters two questions: whether an official should be removed and who should replace the official. Proposition 5 would remove the second question. If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would become governor for the remainder of the term or until a successor is elected, depending on when the recall occurs. For other recalled state officials, the vacancy would generally be filled through a subsequent special election or appointment under existing vacancy rules.

Support Supporters argue that the measure would return the recall process to its primary purpose of deciding whether an elected official should be removed. They say the current replacement system can allow a candidate to win with only a small share of the vote because multiple candidates can divide the vote in a recall election. Supporters also argue that a separate process for selecting replacements would reduce the political component of recalls.

Opposition Opponents argue that the measure would remove voters' ability to select a replacement at the same time they decide whether to recall an official. They say the proposal could result in politicians selecting replacements for some statewide offices or require an additional taxpayer-funded election for other offices.

No supporters or opponents were listed.

Proposition 37: Middle-Income Homebuyers What it would do: Proposition 37 would authorize the California Housing Finance Agency to issue up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to create a homeownership assistance program. Eligible buyers could receive a loan covering up to 17% of the purchase price of a qualifying newly constructed home. Buyers would need to provide at least 3% of the purchase price as a down payment, be California residents, occupy the home and meet income requirements. The

home also would have to meet specified price requirements. The bonds would be repaid through homeowners' loan payments rather than state tax revenue, and the Legislative Analyst's Office estimates there would be no direct state or local government costs.

Support Supporters, including the United Nurses Associations of California, California Conference of Carpenters and state Treasurer Fiona Ma, say the measure would make homeownership more attainable for middle-income Californians.

They argue that down-payment requirements are a major barrier to homeownership and that the program could also encourage new home construction.

Opposition No argument against Proposition 37 was submitted for the official voter guide.

Supporters United Nurses Associations of CaliforniaCalifornia Conference of Carpenters Fiona Ma, California State Treasurer No opponents were listed.

Proposition 38: Research Bond What it would do:

PROP38 would authorize an $8.4 billion bond primarily for research into cancer, heart disease, Alzheimer's and other conditions that can be treated through immunotherapies. Half of the funding would go to a research institute affiliated with the University of California. The remaining half would be distributed among select public universities and nonprofits. Drugs developed through this research would have to be discounted by 20% for Californians, and 10% of revenue from those drugs would go to the state general fund.

Support Supporters say immunotherapy research has significant potential because the immune system is involved in many diseases. They argue that additional funding is needed as the Trump administration has sought to reduce federal funding for health science research.

Opposition:

Critics say the measure focuses too narrowly on one area of biomedical research instead of a broader range of health research. They question whether research funded by the bond would ultimately produce commercial drugs, given the difficulty of bringing new drugs through the approval process and onto the market. Opponents also question why one nonprofit would receive half of the funding and say the bond would add an estimated $500 million to $600 million annually in debt payments for 20 years.

Supporters:

California Democratic Party Susan Disney Lord, Board Chair Alzheimers Los Angeles Opponents:

Robert Kaplan, senior scholar at StanfordLeague of Women Voters Proposition 39: Voter Identification

What it would do:

PROP39 would require voters to show government-issued identification at polling places and would require election officials to verify that registered voters are U.S. citizens. Voters casting mail-in ballots would have to provide the last four digits of a government-issued identification document, such as a driver's license number. California currently requires residents to provide identification and a Social Security number when registering to vote but does not require identification at polling places.

Support Supporters argue that requiring ID at polling sites would strengthen public trust in California's election system. They point to the number of states that require some form of identification to vote.

Opposition Opponents say requiring ID could make it more difficult for eligible voters who do not have a drivers license or other qualifying documents. They argue that the requirement could disproportionately affect people with disabilities, low incomes and people who have recently moved.

Supporters:

California Republican PartyMargit Whitlock, Democratic Coalition Chair Californians for Voter ID Opponents:

California Democratic Party Darius Kemp, California State Director Common Cause Proposition 40: Billionaire Tax What it would do:

PROP40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on an estimated 200 Californians whose net worth exceeded $1 billion at the beginning of the year. The Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which sponsors the measure, projects that the tax would raise approximately $100 billion over five years. The money would be earmarked primarily for health care, with some funding reserved for food assistance and education.

If Proposition 41 or Proposition 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, Proposition 40 would be nullified.

Support Supporters argue that the people subject to the tax benefitted the most financially from recent federal tax changes.

They point to federal cuts to Medicaid (Medi-Cal), which provides health coverage to low income residents. SEIUUHW argues those cuts could lead to hospital and clinic closures, the loss of thousands of jobs and reduced access to health care.

Opposition:

Opponents include Silicon Valley entrepreneurs, business interests, and some health and labor organizations. They argued that the measure could cause billionaires to leave California, reducing tax revenue over the long term.

Health organizations opposing the measure state they were not consulted in its development and argue that it does not address the long-term fiscal challenges facing health care. The same groups support Propositions 41 and 42, competing measures that would limit new special taxes.

Supporters:

California Democratic PartySuzanne Jimenez, Chief of Staff SEIU-United HealthCare Workers West Opponents:

Planned ParenthoodFrancisco Silva, CEO California Primary Care Association Proposition 41: Tax Audits and Spending Limits What it would do: Proposition 41 would require the California State Auditor to review programs funded by new special taxes before certain voter-initiated tax measures appear on the ballot. It also would require recurring audits of programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature after Jan. 1, 2026. The measure also would nullify state taxes enacted after Jan. 1, 2026, if those taxes exclude their revenue from the voter-approved state spending limit. The overall fiscal effect is unknown and would depend on future decisions by voters, lawmakers and other policymakers.

Support Supporters, including the California Society of Certified Public Accountants, CalAsian Chamber of Commerce and California Taxpayers Association, say the measure would increase transparency and accountability for programs funded by new taxes. They argue that independent audits would allow taxpayers to track how tax revenue is being used and evaluate whether publicly funded programs are producing results.

Opposition Opponents, including U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, argue that the measure is connected to efforts to prevent a proposed tax on wealthy Californians. They say the measure could restrict the state's ability to raise revenue for health care and other services.

Supporters:

CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs)CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax)

Opponents:

US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West Proposition 42: Property Taxes What it would do:

Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on the ownership of assets such as investment accounts, business interests and personal property. Those assets are typically taxed when they are sold or generate income. Like Proposition 41, Proposition 42 would seek to block Proposition 40, the proposed wealth tax on billionaires. If Proposition 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, Proposition 40 would be nullified, even if the billionaire tax receives a majority of votes.

Support Those who back the measure argue that California should not tax people simply for owning or controlling retirement accounts, financial portfolios or valuable personal property such as art. They want to prevent taxes on unrealized gains, increases in the value of assets that have not been sold or generated taxable income, and warn that pensions

and retirement accounts could eventually be subject to taxes based on future value.

Opposition:

SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, the sponsor of Proposition 40, is the chief opponent of Proposition 42. The union argues that PROP42 is intended to prevent California from imposing a wealth tax on billionaires. The union says the measure is not primarily about protecting everyday Californians from new taxes but about preventing a one-time tax on the wealth of billionaires.

Supporters:

Michael Hedes, President California Small Business Association Jennifer Yoder, Board Members California Senior Alliance Opponents:

California Democratic PartySuzanne Jimenez, Chief of Staff SEIU-United HealthCare Workers West Proposition 43: Local Taxes What it would do: Proposition 43 would change the approval threshold for certain local special taxes proposed by voters. Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, new, increased or extended local special taxes placed on the ballot through voter signature gathering would require approval from at least two-thirds of voters instead of a simple majority. The measure would apply to taxes dedicated to specific purposes, such as certain taxes used to fund local services. The Legislative Analyst's Office says local government tax revenues could be lower in the future because of the higher approval threshold.

Support Supporters, including the California Taxpayers Association, Family Business Association of California and California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, say the measure would restore a two-thirds voter approval requirement for local special taxes and strengthen taxpayer protections. They argue that recent court decisions have allowed certain voter-proposed tax increases to pass with less than two-thirds approval.

Opposition Opponents, including California Professional Firefighters, the California Federation of Teachers and the Nurse Alliance of SEIU California, argue that Proposition 43 would make it more difficult for communities to raise money for services such as fire protection, emergency response, roads, schools, hospitals and affordable housing. They say increasing the threshold would allow a minority of voters to block tax measures approved by a majority.

Supporters:

California Taxpayers AssociationFamily Business Association of CaliforniaCalifornia Hispanic Chambers of Commerce Opponents:

California Professional FirefightersCalifornia Federation of TeachersNurse Alliance of SEIU CA.

Proposition 44: Clinic funding What it would do:

Proposition 44 would require community clinics that serve low-income patients to spend 90% of their annual revenue on patient care. The measure would direct the attorney general to publish guidance defining which expenses qualify as patient-care spending and would allow the state to fine clinics that fail to meet the 90% requirement. The labor union SEIU-UHW supported a similar bill last year, but it failed. Clinics also unsuccessfully sought to keep the measure off the ballot through a lawsuit earlier this year.

Support Supporters, led by SEIU-UHW, argue that community clinics should devote more money to direct patient care and less to executive compensation and overhead. With federal cuts under H.R.1 expected to leave more people uninsured, supporters say it is important for clinics to prioritize patient care.

Opposition:

Opponents say the measure is unnecessary because community clinics are already subject to extensive state and federal regulation. They argue that the measure could result in more than $1.7 billion in noncompliance fees during its first year, potentially forcing clinics to reduce services or close.

Supporters:

Shawna Brown, Initiative Proponent Brisa J. Barrera, Community Clinic Worker Opponents:

California Hospital Association Eric Ball, MD, FAAP, President American Academy of Pediatrics, California Proposition 45: Environmental review What it would do:

PROP45 would overhaul the California Environmental Quality Act, the state's landmark environmental review law.

Sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, the measure would allow developers to seek expedited review for projects designated as "essential." It would establish a 365-day limit for environmental reviews of those projects, including roads and bridges, housing, schools, broadband infrastructure and wildfire mitigation projects.

The measure also would require courts to rule within 270 days on lawsuits involving the environmental review law.

Support:

The California Chamber of Commerce says the state's environmental review law is outdated and allows costly bureaucracy and frivolous litigation to delay development. The organization argues that those delays increase costs for taxpayers and consumers. Supporters say Proposition 45 would accelerate development while maintaining essential environmental protections.

Opposition:

Opponents argue that the state's environmental review law protects people and the environment from potentially harmful development. They say weakening the requirements would reduce agencies' ability to protect communities, increase costly litigation and limit their ability to enforce environmental protections. Opponents also argue that the long-term costs of poor planning would ultimately fall on agencies and taxpayers.

Affordable housing law expected to prevent foreclosures

By Madeline Shannon

(The Center Square) – A new law taking effect next year will give affordable housing owners more options in avoiding foreclosure.

Assembly Bill 2020, authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, D-Encino, will allow the California Department of Housing and Community Development to permit owners to transfer money produced by their affordable housing units to another property to prevent the latter's foreclosure.

Editor's Note This story has been updated with comments from economist Wayne Winegarden of the Pacific Research Institute. The law is meant to keep affordable housing units on the market in California and protect taxpayers’ investment in the state’s affordable housing market, according to the bill analysis.

“California’s affordable housing developments currently operate on razor-thin margins,” Gabriel told The Center Square via email on Tuesday. “We cannot afford to lose units that took years and significant public investment to create – especially to a foreclosure that could have been prevented. Preserving what we’ve built is far more cost-effective than starting over.” According to supporting statements submitted as part of the bill analysis, affordable housing developments in California operated with very narrow margins, and they're dependent on carefully structured financial reserves and operating income to stay viable. Insurance costs, the cost of maintaining the property and other operating expenses created financial strains for many of these properties, according to supporters of AB 2020.

“When these developments experience operating deficits, the risk of financial distress or foreclosure increases, putting critical affordable housing units, and the residents who call them home, at risk,” Enterprise Community Partners Inc. wrote in comments supporting the bill earlier this year. “This flexibility enables developers to stabilize struggling properties using existing portfolio resources, helping ensure the long-term viability of affordable housing developments.″ There was no opposition to AB 2020, according to the last version of the bill analysis. The state’s bill tracking tool shows that no legislator voted against the bill, either in committee hearings or on the Assembly and Senate floors. According to a housing report published by California Housing Partnership, an organization formed to preserve affordable and sustainable homes, California’s taxpayers paid for the construction of 23,000 new affordable housing units in 2025. But the organization said that only amounts to 20% of what the state needs to pay to meet its affordable housing goals. No one from California Housing Partnership responded to The Center Square's request for comment on Tuesday. Wayne Winegarden, an economist at Pasadena-based Pacific Research Institute, told The Center Square on Tuesday that while he thinks AB 2020 is a good bill, he believes a better solution to addressing the state's affordable housing problems involves reducing regulatory delays and costs.

"I think it's a Band-Aid on a bullet wound when you talk about housing affordability issues," Winegarden said. "While this is helpful, it's not getting to the crux of the problem. It's a good bill; he should sign it. It will help some people, but we shouldn't be thinking this is the solution."
