and preserved the artworks. “For almost 50 years, they have been exhibited at the Norton Simon Museum and will continue to be made available to the public for many years,” the statement read. Pawel Sawicki, a spokesperson for the Auschwitz Memorial, stated that the watercolors of Romani victims that Mengele forced Gottliebova Babbitt to paint to document his horrific experiments and racial investigations “must remain at the Memorial” to bear witness to this man’s crimes. He pointed out that these paintings should not be inaccurately labeled as "Nazi-looted art," as Gottliebova Babbitt painted them against her will as a prisoner, and therefore, she was not the owner of the watercolors. While he understands the feelings of the family, Sawicki emphasized that the portraits of Romani and Sinti victims are among the few remaining documents of Mengele's criminal experiments and should be treated as unique documents related to the history of the Auschwitz concentration camp. “We fully respect the rights of those who created some of the documents we have here, and we consider that any loss from the Memorial's collections would represent irreparable harm,” he asserted. “... The loss, even of the smallest piece of documentation, is an irreparable loss and a stain on the memory of the victims of Auschwitz.” ### Advocates Hope Cases Will Be Evaluated on Their Own Merits Joel Greenberg, founder of Art Ashes, a nonprofit organization based in the Philadelphia area that helps Jewish families locate and recover art looted by the Nazis, commented that, in addition to the California law, President Donald Trump signed an update to the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025. This new law permanently removed the statute of limitations, allowing Holocaust survivors and their heirs to indefinitely claim the recovery of these artworks. Greenberg explained that the new federal law granted families the right to reclaim their artworks within six years from when they gain knowledge of who possesses them. “These new laws mean that technical defenses will no longer prevail in court,” he said. “Each case will be judged on its own merits.” He added that the new legislation also ensures that these Jewish families are heard in court and have a fair process to determine ownership of the stolen artworks. “It will ensure that stories about what happened to European Jewry are not lost or forgotten,” he asserted. “The artworks can still be returned to their rightful owners.”

A decades-long battle over artwork stolen during the Holocaust is resurfacing in Los Angeles, where heirs of Jewish victims are seeking the return of works now held by prominent museums in Southern California and at Auschwitz.

Two lawsuits were recently filed following changes to California and federal law that strengthened the ability to pursue US-based claims involving artwork taken from Jewish families during World War II.

One of the cases, filed this week in Los Angeles Superior Court by the Jewish Federation of Greater Los Angeles and its board, renews a dispute with the Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena over “Adam and Eve,” a pair of life-size oil-on-panel paintings created by Lucas Cranach the Elder in 1530.

A separate lawsuit was filed the same day in federal court in Los Angeles by the daughters of Dinah Gottliebova Babbitt, a Holocaust survivor and California-based animator who was imprisoned at Auschwitz.

Babbitt was forced to paint watercolors of fellow prisoners for Josef Mengele, the Nazi physician known as the “Angel of Death.” Her daughters are now seeking the return of those works.

Neither lawsuit specifies the value of the artwork at the center of the disputes.

Representatives for the museums maintain that their institutions have legal title to the artwork and intend to continue displaying the pieces to the public.

The Norton Simon Museum pointed to a 2018 federal court decision that unanimously found the museum held proper title to the Cranach paintings. The US Supreme Court declined to take up the dispute in May 2019, leaving the lower court rulings intact.

According to the museum, the paintings originally belonged to the Russian noble Stroganov family before the Soviet Union put them up for sale at an illicit Berlin auction in 1931, where they were purchased by art dealer Jacques Goudstikker. Following a complicated ownership history, a descendant of the Stroganovs eventually sold the paintings to the museum, which later restored and preserved them.

“For nearly 50 years, they have been on view at the Norton Simon Museum and will continue to be accessible to the public for years to come,” the museum said in a statement.

The cases are part of a broader and often complicated effort to recover art looted by the Nazis. From 1933 to 1945, the Nazi regime seized more than 600,000 works of art across Europe from Jewish families, collectors and museums in what has been described as the largest art theft in history.

More than eight decades later, some of those works remain in major museums around the world. Their disputed ownership has fueled legal and ethical battles between Jewish families seeking the return of property taken during the Holocaust and museums that maintain they legally acquired the works and have a responsibility to preserve and display them.

California lawmakers have also sought to change how those disputes are handled in court.

Assemblyman Jesse Gabriel (D-Woodland Hills) authored Assembly Bill 2867, which Gov. Gavin Newsom signed into law in September 2024. The legislation requires California law to be applied in lawsuits brought by state residents or their heirs seeking the recovery of artwork taken during the Holocaust or other acts of persecution.

Gabriel, who co-chairs the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, introduced the measure following a federal court ruling that allowed the state-owned Thyssen-Bornemisza National Museum in Madrid to retain a multimillion-dollar Impressionist painting by Camille Pissarro.

‘It's our honor to take on this role on behalf of the community and use most of the proceeds to help these elderly survivors’

Two legal actions have been initiated in California by representatives and heirs of Jewish Holocaust victims seeking the recovery of paintings seized by Nazis that currently reside in renowned institutions in Auschwitz and Los Angeles.

These filings mark the first legal challenges mounted following fresh state and federal legislation designed to bolster claims in the U.S. regarding cultural property taken from Jewish families during World War II.

Filed on Monday in Los Angeles Superior Court, one action brought by the Jewish Federation of Greater Los Angeles alongside its board chair Daniel Gryczman targets the Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena, demanding the return of "Adam and Eve," a pair of 1530 life-size panel paintings by Lucas Cranach the Elder.

A second action, submitted the same day in Los Angeles federal court by the daughters of late Holocaust survivor Dinah Gottliebova Babbitt, a California animator held at Auschwitz, demands the surrender of watercolor portraits.

The artist was coerced into creating these images of fellow captives for Josef Mengele, the Nazi doctor known as the "Angel of Death."

Spokespersons representing the institutions state that the museums retain valid legal title to the paintings and plan to maintain public displays. Specific monetary valuations are not stated in the legal complaints.

Tensions over Nazi-confiscated artwork pit the descendants of Jewish families navigating generational trauma against cultural institutions seeking to preserve material evidence from a dark historical period.

The Nazi regime carried out history's largest plunder between 1933 and 1945, stripping Jewish owners, collectors, and public institutions across Europe of more than 600,000 artistic items.

Decades later, numerous creations remain hanging in international institutions, complicating restitution efforts far beyond basic ownership disputes.

Marei von Saher, sole heir to Dutch Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker, assigned her legal rights to the Jewish Federation of Los Angeles, led by president and CEO Rabbi Noah Farkas.

The pair of panel works had been taken from Goudstikker's holdings by Hermann Goring, Adolf Hitler's second-in-command, before passing through several hands and ultimately being purchased in the 1960s by the Pasadena Museum of Modern Art, later renamed the Norton Simon Museum after its major benefactor.

Farkas stated that the federation intends to direct most net financial recoveries toward providing crucial assistance to approximately 2,500 Holocaust survivors residing throughout the Los Angeles region.

"These are incredibly beautiful European masterpieces stolen from a Jewish family to enrich the Nazi party and fund the war and death machine against the people," Farkas noted.

"It's our honor to take on this role on behalf of the community and use most of the proceeds to help these elderly survivors live out the last years of their lives in dignity, comfort and peace – something their family members were denied during the Holocaust."

In a statement, Marei von Saher expressed appreciation to the organization for championing her family's legal battle.

"This effort represents a meaningful step toward justice for Holocaust survivors and victims of Nazi era atrocities," she stated.

California Assemblyman Jesse Gabriel, D-Woodland Hills, drafted Assembly Bill 2867, which Gov. Gavin Newsom signed in September 2024.

The measure mandates the application of state law in cases brought by state residents or heirs attempting to reclaim art taken during the Holocaust or other persecutions.

Gabriel, co-chair of the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, authored the bill following a federal ruling allowing Madrid's state-owned Thyssen-Bornemisza National Museum to retain a valuable impressionist work by Camille Pissarro.

That artwork had been confiscated from the Cassirer family by Nazi authorities in 1939. The lawsuit that catalyzed the statutory revision is scheduled for a federal court hearing in California next month.

Gabriel remarked that public institutions should "do some deep introspection on whether they want to be on the right side of history."

Responding to the suit, the Norton Simon Museum issued a statement highlighting a 2018 federal court ruling that unanimously confirmed the institution's legal ownership of the Cranach works.

The U.S. Supreme Court declined to review lower court decisions in May 2019.

According to the museum, the Cranach panels originally belonged to the Stroganoff family before being offered at an unauthorized 1931 Soviet sale in Berlin, where Goudstikker acquired them.

Following a complex chain of ownership, a Stroganoff descendant sold the works to the institution, which subsequently preserved and restored them.

"For nearly 50 years, they have been on view at the Norton Simon Museum and will continue to be accessible to the public for years to come," the museum stated.

Pawel Sawicki, representing the Auschwitz Memorial, asserted that the watercolors depicting Roma captives—painted under coercion by Gottliebova Babbitt to document Mengele's illicit medical experiments and racial studies— "must remain in the Memorial" as evidence of atrocities.

He argued they should not be categorized as "Nazi-looted art" because the artist created them under duress as an inmate without technical legal ownership.

While acknowledging the family's deep connection, Sawicki emphasized that the portraits of Roma and Sinti victims are rare surviving records of Mengele's horrific experiments and must be safeguarded as historical artifacts specific to Auschwitz.

"While fully respecting the rights of people who created some of the documents here, we are of the opinion that any loss in the collections of the Memorial will constitute irreparable harm," Sawicki said. " … The loss of even the smallest part of the documentation is an irreparable loss and blemish on the memory of the victims of Auschwitz."

Joel Greenberg, founder of Philadelphia-area non-profit Art Ashes, which assists Jewish families in tracking Nazi-stolen property, noted that beyond California's statute, President Donald Trump enacted and refreshed the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025. This legislation permanently eliminated statute-of-limitations deadlines, enabling survivors and heirs to pursue art recovery indefinitely.

Greenberg explained that the federal update allows families up to six years to pursue legal recovery from the point they identify the current possessor of their property.

"These new laws mean that technical defenses will no longer stick in court," he said. "Every case will be heard on its merits."

He added that the revised legal framework guarantees Jewish families procedural fairness and an opportunity to present ownership claims in court.

"It will make sure the stories of what happened to European Jewry is not lost and forgotten," Greenberg remarked. "The art can still be returned to the rightful owner."

“It will make sure the stories of what happened to European Jewry is not lost and forgotten,” he said. “The art can still be returned to the rightful owner.”

LOS ÁNGELES (AP) — Herederos judíos de víctimas del Holocausto y sus representantes presentaron dos demandas en California para hacer valer sus reclamaciones sobre pinturas saqueadas por los nazis que aún cuelgan en las paredes de destacados museos en Los Ángeles y Auschwitz.

Estas demandas son las primeras que se presentan tras la reciente aprobación de leyes por parte de California y el Congreso, que refuerzan las reclamaciones con sede en Estados Unidos sobre obras de arte arrebatadas por la fuerza a familias judías durante la Segunda Guerra Mundial.

Una de las demandas fue presentada el lunes en el Tribunal Superior de Los Ángeles por la Federación Judía del Gran Los Ángeles y su presidente de la junta, Daniel Gryczman, contra el Museo Norton Simon de Pasadena, para la devolución de "Adán y Eva". Se trata de dos magistrales óleos sobre madera, a tamaño natural, creados por Lucas Cranach el Viejo en 1530.

Publicidad

Publicidad

Publicidad

Publicidad

La otra demanda fue presentada en un tribunal federal de Los Ángeles ese mismo día por las hijas de la fallecida Dinah Gottliebova Babbitt, sobreviviente del Holocausto y animadora radicada en California que estuvo detenida en Auschwitz. En ella se exige la devolución de acuarelas de otros prisioneros que la artista fue obligada a pintar para Josef Mengele, un médico nazi que se ganó el apodo de "ángel de la muerte".

Portavoces de ambos museos afirman que esas instituciones poseen legalmente los títulos de las obras y que tienen la intención de seguir exhibiéndolas al público. En las demandas no se especifica el valor monetario de las pinturas.

Obras de arte enfrentan a familias judías contra museos

El tema del arte saqueado por los nazis es un asunto emocional, cargado de implicaciones legales y éticas, que enfrenta a familias judías que han sufrido un trauma intergeneracional contra museos que, en su opinión, intentan preservar un capítulo doloroso, pero importante, de la historia. Entre 1933 y 1945, el régimen nazi orquestó el mayor robo de arte en la historia mundial, apoderándose de más de 600.000 obras de arte en toda Europa pertenecientes a familias judías, coleccionistas y museos. Décadas después, muchas de estas obras maestras se encuentran en destacados museos de todo el mundo, lo que hace que el impulso por recuperarlas sea más complejo que una simple disputa de propiedad.

El rabino Noah Farkas es presidente y director ejecutivo de la Federación Judía de Los Ángeles, la organización a la que Marei von Saher, única heredera del marchante de arte judío neerlandés Jacques Goudstikker, ha cedido sus derechos. Las pinturas fueron confiscadas de la colección de Goudstikker por Hermann Göring, segundo al mando de Adolf Hitler, y pasaron por varias manos antes de ser vendidas en la década de 1960 al Museo de Arte Moderno de Pasadena, que fue rebautizado como Museo Norton Simon en honor a su benefactor.

Publicidad

Publicidad

Publicidad

Publicidad

Farkas dijo que la federación planea utilizar la mayor parte de los ingresos netos del arte recuperado para brindar ayuda a los aproximadamente 2.500 sobrevivientes del Holocausto que viven en el área de Los Ángeles y que la necesitan con urgencia.

"Son obras maestras europeas increíblemente bellas, robadas a una familia judía para enriquecer al partido nazi y financiar la máquina de guerra y de muerte contra la gente", afirmó. "Es un honor para nosotros asumir este papel en nombre de la comunidad y usar la mayor parte de los ingresos para ayudar a estos sobrevivientes ancianos a vivir los últimos años de sus vidas con dignidad, comodidad y paz, algo que a sus familiares les fue negado durante el Holocausto".

Marei von Saher dijo en un comunicado que está agradecida con la organización judía por asumir la causa de su familia.

"Este esfuerzo representa un paso importante hacia la justicia para los sobrevivientes del Holocausto y las víctimas de las atrocidades de la era nazi", señaló.

Nueva legislación da un segundo impulso a las demandas

Jesse Gabriel, asambleísta demócrata por Woodland Hills, California, redactó el Proyecto de Ley de la Asamblea 2867, firmado por el gobernador Gavin Newsom en septiembre de 2024, que exige que la ley estatal se aplique en demandas presentadas por residentes de California o sus herederos para recuperar arte confiscado durante el Holocausto o durante otros actos de persecución. Gabriel, quien copreside el Caucus Judío Legislativo de California, presentó la legislación en respuesta a un fallo de un tribunal federal que permitió que el Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza, de propiedad estatal, en Madrid, conservara una obra maestra impresionista de Camille Pissarro, con un valor de varios millones de dólares.

Publicidad

Publicidad

Publicidad

Publicidad

Esa pintura le fue arrebatada por los nazis a la familia Cassirer en 1939. Se espera que este caso, que impulsó esta nueva ley, sea visto en un tribunal federal en California el próximo mes.

Gabriel sostuvo que es hora de que los museos "hagan una profunda introspección sobre si quieren estar del lado correcto de la historia".

Los museos quieren preservar las pinturas para la posteridad

El Museo Norton Simon difundió un comunicado en el que señaló que un tribunal federal determinó por unanimidad en 2018 que el museo tenía un título válido sobre las pinturas de Cranach. En mayo de 2019, la Corte Suprema de Estados Unidos declinó intervenir en el caso, dejando vigentes los fallos de instancias inferiores.

Indicaron que las pinturas de Cranach, que originalmente pertenecían a la familia Stroganoff, fueron puestas a la venta en 1931 por la Unión Soviética en una subasta ilícita en Berlín, donde fueron adquiridas por Goudstikker. Tras un complicado recorrido, las pinturas fueron vendidas al museo por un descendiente de la familia Stroganoff. Posteriormente, el museo restauró y preservó las piezas.

Publicidad

Publicidad

Publicidad

Publicidad

"Durante casi 50 años, han estado expuestas en el Museo Norton Simon y seguirán siendo accesibles al público durante muchos años", indicó el comunicado.

Pawel Sawicki, portavoz del Memorial de Auschwitz, dijo que las acuarelas de víctimas romaníes que Gottliebova Babbitt fue obligada a pintar por Mengele para documentar sus horrendos experimentos e investigaciones raciales "deben permanecer en el Memorial" para documentar los crímenes del hombre. Señaló que estas pinturas no deben ser caracterizadas erróneamente como "arte saqueado por los nazis" porque Gottliebova Babbitt las pintó contra su voluntad como prisionera y, por lo tanto, no tenía la propiedad de las acuarelas.

Aunque comprende los sentimientos de la familia, Sawicki indicó que los retratos de víctimas romaníes y sinti se encuentran entre los pocos documentos que quedan de los experimentos criminales de Mengele y deben ser tratados como documentos únicos relacionados con la historia del campo de concentración de Auschwitz.

"Respetando plenamente los derechos de las personas que crearon algunos de los documentos que tenemos aquí, opinamos que cualquier pérdida en las colecciones del Memorial constituirá un daño irreparable", afirmó. "... La pérdida incluso de la parte más pequeña de la documentación es una pérdida irreparable y una mancha en la memoria de las víctimas de Auschwitz".

Defensores esperan que los casos ahora se evalúen por sus méritos

Joel Greenberg, fundador de Art Ashes, una organización sin fines de lucro del área de Filadelfia que ayuda a familias judías a rastrear y recuperar arte saqueado por los nazis, comentó que, además de la ley de California, el presidente Donald Trump promulgó una actualización de la Ley de Recuperación de Arte Expropiado del Holocausto de 2025. Esta nueva ley eliminó de manera permanente la fecha de vencimiento para permitir que los sobrevivientes del Holocausto y sus herederos puedan perseguir indefinidamente la recuperación de estas obras de arte.

Publicidad

Publicidad

Publicidad

Publicidad

Greenberg explicó que la nueva ley federal otorgó a las familias el derecho a reclamar su arte hasta por seis años a partir del momento en que se enteran de quién lo posee.

"Estas nuevas leyes significan que las defensas técnicas ya no prosperarán en los tribunales", afirmó. "Cada caso será escuchado por sus méritos".

Agregó que la nueva legislación también garantiza que estas familias judías sean escuchadas en la corte y tengan un proceso justo para determinar la propiedad del arte robado.

"Se asegurará de que las historias de lo que le ocurrió al judaísmo europeo no se pierdan ni se olviden", expresó. "El arte aún puede ser devuelto a su legítimo propietario".

New Bid to Claim Cranach Paintings Held by Norton Simon Museum

By Nina Siegal

Courts have upheld the museum’s title to the paintings once looted by the Nazis, but a lawsuit seeks to press forward with the claim under a new California law.

For nearly two decades, the family of Jacques Goudstikker, an art dealer in Amsterdam whose collection was appropriated by the Nazis, have unsuccessfully sought to reclaim a pair of Renaissance masterpieces, “Adam” and “Eve,” by Lucas Cranach the Elder, from the Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena, Calif.

Multiple court rulings have gone against the heirs whose case reached the U.S. federal appeals court in 2018, but was rejected.

Now the family has taken a new approach by transferring its rights to the Jewish Federation of Los Angeles, a nonprofit organization, and its president, who are pursuing the case under a recent California law designed to provide another avenue for claims that were previously dismissed.

The organization filed suit this week in the Los Angeles Superior Court to recover the paintings.

If the Federation wins, it has pledged to sell the paintings and use the proceeds to provide care, food and services to Holocaust survivors in Los Angeles.

“They are California residents and they can bring this claim to benefit Holocaust survivors,” Charlene von Saher, Goudstikker’s granddaughter, said in an interview. “That’s a mission that’s very important to my mother and I, to my whole family.”

The paintings were among many looted from Goudstikker by the Nazi Reichsmarshall Hermann Goering in 1940 and later recovered by Allied forces who returned them to Dutch officials. But the Dutch tribunal who handled claims after the war sold the two Cranachs to the heir of a family, the Stroganoffs, who pursued a competing claim, arguing that the two paintings had previously been seized by the Soviet authorities after the Russian Revolution.

The Stroganoff heir later sold them to Norton Simon.

The Goudstikkers, and several experts, have challenged the Dutch decision, asserting that, among other things, there was not clear evidence that the Stroganoffs ever held the works at the time of the revolution.

But U.S. courts have ruled against the family, in one instance citing a legal principle, the “act of state” doctrine, that says it is not the place of American courts to interfere in decisions made by a foreign government.

Rabbi Noah Farkas, the president and chief executive of the Jewish Federation of Los Angeles, said recent legislative changes at both the federal and state levels made the new lawsuit possible.

The amended Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act, signed into law in April, stipulates that U.S. defendants in Nazi-era restitution disputes are precluded from using some types of defenses, such as the “act of state” doctrine. In response to the lawsuit, the Norton Simon Museum pointed to the fact that “court after court” has confirmed that the museum foundation has “proper title” to the paintings. In a statement, it rejected the idea that court rulings had been based on any technicalities and argued that the federal court decision that upheld the museum’s good title had come “after years of discovery and testimony from the witnesses” and a “thorough analysis of the evidence.”

“We will continue to make these important artworks accessible to the public, as we have since 1971,” the museum said. Goudstikker bought the Cranach paintings in 1931 at an auction in Berlin of items that had been nationalized by the Soviet government. Though they were listed as having come from the Stroganoff Collection, experts have since challenged that provenance.

Asked this week whether the museum has confirmed that the Stroganoffs once owned the paintings, the museum said there is no doubt that, before Goudstikker’s purchase, the paintings had been looted by the Soviets “either from the Stroganoff family, as Count Stroganoff believed, or from a church in Ukraine.”

Goudstikker’s gallery inventory listed over 1,200 paintings, including the Cranach paintings, when he died in May 1940 while trying to escape the Nazi invasion.

He, his wife, Desirée, and their 1-year-old son, Edward, who went by Edo, escaped Amsterdam on a steamship to Dover, England, but Goudstikker died while crossing the English Channel at night: He fell and broke his neck.

Goering, Hitler’s second in command, was photographed at the Goudstikker Gallery in Amsterdam a few days later, and claimed a large portion of the collection in a manufactured sale.

“Hermann Goering stole these paintings along with about 800 other ones,” said Charlene von Saher said. “It’s pretty clear when you look at the provenance and you see my grandfather’s name and then you see Hermann Goering’s name right after that. That’s a big red flag, one that the Norton Simon Museum has chosen to ignore.”

Desirée Goudstikker and Edo eventually ended up in the United States. After the war, the dealer’s wife, Mrs. Goudstikker, received some compensation from the Dutch state. Edo died in 1996 and his widow, Marei von Saher, has been trying to reclaim his artworks for decades.

Over the years, the von Saher family has won some legal victories, including a landmark restitution case in the Netherlands in 2006, when 202 artworks were returned to them. Some had been on display in major Dutch museums for decades. Jesse Gabriel, the California state assemblyman who authored the California law adopted in 2024, said in an interview that it will make it harder for courts to throw out restitution cases on procedural issues. “The effort behind the law is to make sure that cases are decided on their merits,” Gabriel said. He added, “These are cases that should be based on morality and justice.”

Joel Greenberg, the president and founder of Art Ashes, a nonprofit organization that helps families recover art stolen during the Nazi era, said that if the Federation’s case is successful, it could encourage more Holocaust claimants to come forward.

“It should also encourage museums to give the families what they’re due,” he added. “If they know that the cases will be heard on the merits, they can no longer hide behind technical defenses.”

Charlene von Saher said the family is hopeful.

“They’re exquisite, beautiful paintings, but they are not something I could possibly hang in my house,” she said. “We’ve assigned the claim to the Federation, because we believe in their mission and we want to help people.”

Newsom to decide on bills regulating detention centers

By Sofia Williams; Staff Writer

Sacramento Bee, The · 2026-09-15 · Section: News · Page 1A · 959 words

As the Legislative session came to a close, California legislators sent more than a dozen bills to Gov. Gavin Newsom's desk to regulate federal immigration enforcement and detention and support the state's immigrant communities.

Newsom has until Sept. 30 to approve or veto legislation.

Detention centers The largest portion of immigration-related bills on Newsom's desk regulate detention centers - both the construction of new facilities and the conditions inside.

California has opened two new detention centers in the last year, bringing the state's total count to eight; California City Detention Center opened in August 2025 and the Central Valley Annex facility opened in McFarland, California, this April. The new constructions added nearly 3,000 beds to the state's capacity for those detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Senate Bill 1367 would prohibit a city or county from approving the construction of new detention facilities or the conversion of existing buildings into detention centers. Sen. Sabrina Cervantes, D-Riverside, authored the bill to prevent further expansion of ICE facilities in California, particularly those constructed from sites like warehouses and industrial buildings not meant for human habitation.

Assembly Bills 1633 and 2465 would impose financial penalties on detention centers. AB 1633, authored by Assemblymember Matt Haney, D-San Francisco, would impose a 25% tax on private detention centers. AB 2465, authored by Assemblymember Liz Ortega, D-San Leandro, would prohibit companies that own private detention facilities from collecting tax credits and receiving state grants or loans.

Haney and Ortega rallied alongside advocacy, labor and faith groups Tuesday to urge Newsom to sign the pair of bills. Both would contribute the funds collected from detention centers to a "Due Process for All" fund that supports immigration-related services.

SB 942, or the "Civil Detainees Bill of Rights Act," would establish protections for those in immigration detention. The legislation affirms the rights of those in private detention facilities to access medical and mental health treatment, clean drinking water, food that is safe to consume and livable quarters. It also guarantees the freedom of religion and the ability to send and receive correspondence.

Other bills on Newsom's desk also aim to regulate detention centers, including:

SB 423: Amends the California Public Records Act to require that local agencies disclose records of 911 and other emergency services calls made from immigration detention centers.

SB 941: Prohibits markups of over 35% on products in canteens at private detention facilities.

SB 957: Requires the California attorney general to submit a health and safety oversight plan for private civil detention facilities to the Legislature.

SB 1399: Indefinitely extends the period during which reviews of detention centers can take place at the county level, which was previously set to sunset in 2027.

AB 1801: Prohibits a city, county, or public agency from approving the construction of a private detention facility without notifying the public at least 180 days prior.

Immigration enforcement Bills to regulate federal ICE agents' activity in California have often met opposition in the Legislature, typically from lawmakers who see these efforts as an overreach of state power. However, several statewide measures to regulate ICE currently await Newsom's signature.

AB 1806, authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, D-Encino, would mandate independent state investigations of shootings by ICE agents against unarmed civilians. According to Gabriel, he introduced the bill as a response to two recent shootings at the hands of ICE officers in California: Keith Porter Jr., who was killed Dec. 31 by an off-duty ICE agent, and Carlos Ivan Mendoza Hernandez, who was shot seven times in the face by an ICE agent April 7. AB 1896, known as the Get the Feds Out Act, would disqualify former ICE agents from holding public employment. The legislation was authored by Assemblymember Mark Gonzalez, D-Los Angeles, and backed by Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas, D-Hollister. If Newsom signs the bill, it would be the first law of its kind in the nation. Amid nationwide concerns about ICE officers' use of electroshock gloves in the field, Assemblymember LaShae Sharp-Collins, D-San Diego, authored AB 2760. The bill would ban the use of electroshock gloves in California by both federal and state law enforcement agents. If the bill becomes law, California would become the first state to enact such a ban.

Other bills on Newsom's desk also aim to restrict ICE activity in California, including:

SB 747: Applies existing federal standards to ICE agents in California, allowing claims of constitutional violations at the hands of ICE agents to be prosecuted.

SB 873: Prohibits a person from being subject to civil arrest while traveling to and from or being present at a courthouse for any lawful activity.

SB 938: Ensures immigration agents can't bypass California's basic training requirements if they become state officers.

SB 1004: Bans state and federal law enforcement officers from wearing face masks on duty.

Immigrant services Bills to improve the services available to immigrants and their families are up for Newsom's consideration alongside regulations on ICE officers and detention centers.

SB 1194, authored by Sen. Anna Caballero, D-Merced, would establish the Immigration Legal Fellowship Project to support fellowships for individuals who provide immigration legal services. The program would provide grants or enter into contracts with nonprofits to administer the legal fellows program under the California Department of Social Services.

Under AB 1655, someone held in ICE detention would be classified as "temporarily absent" from their home. This would allow families receiving state benefits, which are determined based on household size, to remain eligible for assistance. Assemblymember Isaac Bryan, D-Jefferson Park, authored the bill after reports that families had lost benefits under the California Work Opportunity and Responsibility to Kids program after a member of their household was deported.

California lawmakers just handed out $1.3 billion to their own districts

Yue Stella Yu

In summary

The California Legislature’s secretive earmark process allows lawmakers and Gov. Gavin Newsom to dole out money for projects with little public scrutiny or notice, raising transparency and equity concerns even among some lawmakers.

$29 million to renovate a gym at a Santa Barbara college in Senate President Pro Tem Monique Limón’s district.

$13 million for a farmers market and food innovation hub in wealthy Marin County, where Gov. Gavin Newsom lives.

$3 million to renovate the San Jose Giants’ minor league baseball stadium in Santa Clara County. 

California lawmakers doled out $1.3 billion in handouts for their legislative districts with almost zero public scrutiny or input during an annual budgeting process that allows legislators and the governor to hand-pick funding recipients in private.

The money, often known as earmarks or “pork-barrel projects,” is commonplace in California and elsewhere, even in years when the state faces huge budget deficits. The practice allows lawmakers to tout their accomplishments and woo voters.

The earmark process is so secretive that few know why some projects make the cut and others don’t, raising equity and transparency concerns, even among lawmakers. Critics argue that it allows elected officials to play favorites. 

“(It) is done all behind closed doors,” said Julie Baker, CEO of California for the Arts. “It is somewhat inequitable … to have a grant making process that everyone’s competing over and then have a process that’s non-transparent.”

Here’s how earmarks work: The leaders in the California Assembly and Senate, both Democrats, allow their colleagues to submit private wish-lists for funds with a suggested spending cap the leaders set. Then billions of dollars for hundreds of projects suddenly appear in a bill heard just days before lawmakers leave for the year, leaving little time for the public to weigh in. Lawmakers don’t put their names on the earmarks, making it hard to identify who requested what.

This year, Limón loosely capped Senate Democrats’ requests at $5 million each, said Sen. Dave Cortese, a San Jose Democrat who secured $6.5 million for his district. Lawmakers do not share their funding requests with each other, he said — at least not before they take credit for them in press releases or ribbon-cutting ceremonies.

“It’s a confidential process between each office and leadership,” he told CalMatters.

But even he bemoaned the opaque nature of it.

“Why couldn’t we do this process a little earlier and get our requests into subcommittees so the public could just see what’s going on?” Cortese said. “There’s nothing to be ashamed of here.”

‘Why did I spend all that time and energy?’

The vast majority of the funding goes to urban counties such as Los Angeles and San Francisco, which are represented by powerful Democrats, and to other pet projects in Democratic leaders’ districts. Areas that are represented by Republicans typically get little to nothing. 

This year, 17 counties, mostly lower population rural counties represented by Republicans, did not appear to receive any earmark funding. 

“The leadership decides the major portions of the budget,” said Sen. Roger Niello, a Roseville Republican and vice chair of the Senate budget committee. “That is frustrating, but it is the system that we have.”

CalMatters compiled the earmarks in the budget measure Assembly Bill 113 and used Digital Democracy’s Find Your Legislators tool to determine which county and legislative district each project falls in.

More than $550 million — 42% of all earmarks identified by CalMatters — went to non-governmental organizations, mostly nonprofits, according to the analysis. It includes at least $93 million for arts projects, museums and murals, as well as funding for immigration services, land conservation and housing and homelessness.

The rest went to city and county governments for infrastructure including parks, community pools, wildfire mitigation and road repairs.

CalMatters reached out to Newsom, Limón, Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas and more than 20 other lawmakers to ask for a list of their funding requests. Few provided them.

Newsom, Rivas and Limón declined to answer questions about specific projects but told CalMatters in general statements that they are proud of the earmarks.

In a statement, Newsom spokesperson Tara Gallegos said the funding in this year’s budget will “make a lasting, meaningful difference in communities across California.”

“From supporting our natural resources, and improving recreation centers to strengthening the arts and expanding food access, these additional investments reflect a continued commitment to building stronger, healthier, and more vibrant communities for all Californians,” the statement read.

Proponents of earmarks say they empower state lawmakers to prioritize projects with urgent needs in their districts instead of funneling the money through lengthy grant applications. The earmarks are also just a sliver of the state’s $352 billion budget, they noted.

“My message to (state agencies) is, ‘You guys take the other 99.9% and leave this fraction of a percent to us,’” Cortese said. “I’ll help target some real need in these districts that you are never going to see in an office in Sacramento.”

But critics bashed state leaders for finding $1.3 billion for earmarks when the state has struggled to backfill major federal cuts to healthcare. State leaders this year relied on windfall revenue from an AI-driven economic boom, some tax increases and suspending payments to schools and state reserves to balance the budget and delay deep healthcare cuts to next year.

“They’ve said, ‘Look … there’s no extra money to spend,’ and then a half billion dollars comes out in the last 48 hours of the session,” said Geoff Green, CEO of CalNonprofits, which represents thousands of nonprofits statewide. “For entities that were working through what we considered normal processes through the entirety of the session, to then see this come out at the last second, it feels like, well, why did I spend all that time and energy?”

Susan Shelley, vice president of communications at the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, accused lawmakers of handing money out to their supporters at the last moment.

“From a taxpayer perspective, we don’t have the money for this,” Shelley said.

Dance troupes, museums and MMA fighters

The biggest allocation this year was $125 million to help buy and transform a defunct Alameda County horse track into a public park — a Newsom priority. Assembly Appropriations Committee Chair Buffy Wicks and Senate Housing Committee Chair Jesse Arreguín, both Oakland Democrats, championed the funding.

Some earmarks benefited groups with wealthy backers. The state gave $25 million to the Innovative Genomics Institute, a UC Berkeley-based genome engineering research facility in Wicks and Arreguín’s districts whose funders include the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, the Li Ka Shing Foundation and the United States Department of Defense. 

Other earmarks include: 

  • $20 million to help build a facility for the Jewish Family and Children’s Services Holocaust Center in San Francisco, which is backed by dozens of foundations and endowment funds. Executive director Anita Friedman said the endowments only fund roughly 2% of its budget.
  • $15 million to renovate the police and firefighters memorials in Sacramento’s Capital Park
  • $1 million for the state’s retirement fund for mixed martial arts fighters, currently funded through ticket and vanity plate sales.

Another $86 million went to arts projects, museums and dance troupes — more than 40% of them in San Francisco. 

That includes $3 million to the ODC Dance Company, whose founder Brenda Way was inducted into the California Hall of Fame by Newsom and first partner Jennifer Siebel Newsom; $2.8 million to the Center for the Art of Translation backed by Bloomberg Philanthropies and the Hawthornden Foundation; and $400,000 to the San Francisco Mime Troupe. 

It’s unclear who advocated for those earmarks. Democratic San Francisco Assemblymember Matt Haney said he did not request any of them. Sen. Scott Wiener and Assemblymember Catherine Stefani, both San Francisco Democrats, did not respond to requests for comment from CalMatters. 

Green, of CalNonprofit, said he worries the money is not reaching those with the most acute needs, but those with the best relationships with lawmakers.

“The capacity of a large, well-staffed institute to access resources is just a completely different universe than a smaller, volunteer, community-based organization in some more rural parts of the state,” he said, adding that the recipients appear to be “folks who have relationships already.”

Relationships matter

Relationships do matter to Cortese. Among the projects he requested funding for, only one — Ashes to Beauty, which received $750,000 — is relatively new to him. He said he’s known the other nonprofits he sought funding for dating to his days as a San Jose city councilmember in the 2000s. 

“If some new group came along and they seemed hopeful … but I didn’t know of them very well, I hadn’t seen their work too much in the community, I’m probably not going to entrust them with $1 million or $800,000,” he said. “It’s not a matter of any kind of favoritism.”

Cortese said his office keeps a long list of requests for funding and considers which groups are “lifting up the greater good of the community.” 

Cortese asked for and received $2.1 million for First-Tee Silicon Valley, which teaches golf and leadership to high-risk kids in marginalized neighborhoods; $2.6 million to environmental nonprofit Our City Forest; and $1 million for Amigos de Guadalupe, an immigration services nonprofit. 

Several earmarks went to nonprofits with ties to the governor. The Redwood High School Foundation, which funds Newsom’s high school alma mater, received $4 million for a “capital project.” Another $250,000 went to Kiss the Ground, a regenerative agriculture nonprofit whose 2020 documentary featured Newsom.

A total of $3.86 million went to the Alliance for Community Empowerment, a Los Angeles nonprofit that serves trauma and poverty survivors. Its founder, Michelle Miranda, sat on a board of community advisers to Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, an Encino Democrat who chairs the budget committee.

Gabriel’s spokesperson Alicia Isaacs-Lee did not address specific projects but said Assembly Democrats fought for “smart, targeted, one-time investments” in healthcare, food banks, legal service providers, fire departments and nonprofits. 

Homeless shelter City of Refuge Sacramento received $1.8 million to open two more homes to serve children, co-founder Rachelle Ditmore told CalMatters. She is a close friend of Sen. Angelique Ashby, a Sacramento Democrat who helped the shelter secure $8 million in 2023. Democratic Assemblymember Maggy Krell, who also represents the area, donated $10,000 from her campaign account to Ditmore’s nonprofit in August 2025. 

But Ditmore told CalMatters that the governor, who signed an executive order on human trafficking at City of Refuge, may have requested the funding this year. 

“This is an authentic place and I’m grateful for history, but also love that this was directed by other eyes who were able to see the value,” Ditmore told CalMatters in an email.

Sen. Lola Smallwood-Cuevas, a Los Angeles Democrat, secured $13.5 million in earmarks this year, including $500,000 for the Los Angeles Black Workers Center, which she co-founded, according to a list provided by her spokesperson Paulette Thornton. 

The center is the only one in the area serving Black workers, and the funding will connect Black residents to quality jobs, Thornton said.

Rural, Republican-led counties get less

Los Angeles County, where nearly a quarter of all Californians live, received at least $300 million in earmarks this year — just under a quarter of the total and more than any other county, data analysis shows. 

Santa Barbara County, Limón’s home county with a population of 450,000, received at least $72.8 million in earmarks, more than any other similarly sized county. Republican-dominated Tulare County, by comparison, received just $200,000 for its 485,000 residents.

The contrast reflects the power of leadership in Sacramento, said Jack Pitney, a political science professor at Claremont McKenna College. 

“Part of the power … is the ability to get benefits for the district, and it’s not surprising that the legislative leaders tend to do pretty well in that respect,” Pitney said.

Last year, a quarter of the earmarks CalMatters identified — more than $100 million — went to the district of former Senate President Pro Tem Mike McGuire, a Santa Rosa Democrat. 

This year, CalMatters identified $83.7 million in earmarks benefiting Limón’s district, including the $29 million gym renovation. Others include:

  • $6 million to acquire and rehabilitate a historical building that housed nonprofit La Casa de la Raza
  • $5 million to restore Pershing Park in Santa Barbara
  • $3.3 million for a community pool in the city of Carpinteria
  • $3 million for a high school community aquatics center.

Rivas’ district received just over $10 million in earmarks, including $2.8 million for a regional soccer complex in Salinas, $2.5 million for a recreational center in King City and $525,000 for arts and culture in Watsonville. His district overlaps with that of Sen. John Laird, a Santa Cruz Democrat who chairs the budget committee. 

Laird’s district received $36.9 million, including: 

  • $10 million for expanding public access to the PG&E-owned North Ranch property
  • $618,000 for highway traffic enforcement on the Bixby Bridge
  • $250,000 to the San Luis Obispo Beaver Brigade, a nonprofit advocating for beavers.

Gabriel’s district saw at least $7 million in earmarks, including $2.5 million to Mid Valley YMCA, $500,000 to Los Angeles youth film nonprofit Kids in the Spotlight and $200,000 to social services group Family Rescue Center.

Niello told CalMatters that GOP senators were only given $1 million each in earmarks to distribute.

“That means that I’m not able to do enough for my district (as) Dave Cortese is for his, and we both have the same size districts. Is that fair? To me, it’s not.”

Bill to prevent homelessness goes to Gov. Newsom's desk

By Madeline Shannon

(The Center Square) – A bill designed to prevent homelessness in California is awaiting Gov. Gavin Newsom's signature after it passed the Legislature late last month.

Assembly Bill 1924, authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, D-Encino, and Assemblymember Sharon Quirk-Silva, DFullerton, requires the California Interagency Council on Homelessness to find strategies to curb the state's growing homelessness problem.

Under the legislation, the strategies have to be submitted in a report due on July 1, 2028.

The root cause of California’s homelessness, according to a legislative analysis of AB 1924, is the rising cost of housing.

Families need to earn roughly $40 an hour to be able to afford a two-bedroom rental, the analysis said.

A housing shortage has made the problem worse, according to the analysis. It noted California needs 2.5 million additional housing units to help eradicate the homelessness problem, including 643,352 very-low income households and 394,910 for lower-income households.

Despite legislation passed over the last several years to allow residential housing on almost any site in the state, housing hasn't improved for many families across California, according to the bill analysis.

"For each homeless individual who is successfully connected with housing, nearly three access homelessness services for the first time,” Gabriel said in the bill analysis. “To make meaningful progress and address California's homelessness epidemic, we can't have more people entering homelessness than exiting it.”

Preventing homelessness in the first place is the most cost-effective way of solving the problem of homelessness, Gabriel wrote in the bill analysis.

“Through stronger guidance and support to those seeking to prevent Californians from becoming unhoused, this legislation will help prevent homelessness before it can occur, better protecting our state's most vulnerable residents and preserving limited state resources,” Gabriel added.

There were no groups or organizations that registered opposition to the bill, according to every version of the bill analysis on the state’s bill tracker website.

Gabriel and Quirk-Silva were not available for an interview on Friday. The Steinberg Institute, a mental health and substance use policy organization that supported the bill, also did not respond to The Center Square. Other organizations in California that address homelessness and Republicans who authored homelessness legislation this year also did not respond.

of the decade," adding that we are quote, "gambling with our lives."

After Coxon posted that message, a more senior Anthropic employee commented that he was correct. A number of AI employees have quit publicly over the past several months and years citing safety concerns. Coxon spoke with CNN's Anderson Cooper earlier.

(BEGIN VIDEOTAPE)

JACOB COXON, FORMER ANTHROPIC AI RESEARCHER: I think it's really important to just look at the rate of progress and say, for example, in areas like coding or math. A couple of years ago, these AIs were just about helping humans a little bit. They could give you suggestions. Now they're close to replacing them.

We still need humans at the moment, but quite plausibly within a year, we'll no longer need humans for doing research in many areas.

(END VIDEOTAPE)

MICHAELSON: Joining me live is Jacob Ward. He is a CNN contributor, a technology journalist and founder of the ripcurrent.com. Jacob, welcome back to The Story Is.

JACOB WARD, CNN CONTRIBUTOR: Hey Elex, it's great to be with you. Thanks so much.

MICHAELSON: I want to put up on the screen your latest post on the ripcurrent.com, and here's what it's titled. "He helped build ChatGPT. Now he says AI could kill us all." That's quite a -- a provocative headline there.

And I want to read a little bit more from what Jacob Coxon posted online that got so much attention. He said, quote, "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. But I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger."

When he says that AI could kill us all, what does that mean? How would that happen?

WARD: Well, this is the question I've been getting all day, and it is -- it is so interesting to think about, right?

Because I mean, we are, I think, already grappling with the idea that this stuff might take all of our jobs and reprogram our brains and reprogram our relationships to one another. But what Coxon and others are talking about here is the capacity of this technology to do things like exploit our infrastructure, you know, set off some sort of environmental disaster, innovate some kind of horrible zoonotic disease we've never thought of or thought to try and build a cure for.

You know, what he's talking about here is the potential that this technology could sort of supersede all other technology. And what's so interesting about this moment we're in right now, Elex, is that all of these different people at all these different companies, their ideas are kind of converging at this one particular moment. I mean, the same week that we've seen Coxon make his move, just on Sunday, we saw the chief scientist of OpenAI write a long blog post, literally, about what he called the alien intellect of AI and how it could pose an enormous problem.

And he's basically sort of arguing, almost begging for authorities to try to institutionalize the internal rules that these companies have for themselves.

So, I think all of these folks are, to some extent or another, recognizing that this thing is very much beyond our control. Not just in the sense where if you ask it a question, it never answers the same way twice, but in that it's inventing new ways to hack your phone or create a new piece of chemistry that they have no way of predicting, and they worry no way of controlling dynamics.

MICHAELSON: So this is stuff created by humans that we continue to make stronger. Clearly, Coxon is sounding the alarm as loud as you can sound an alarm. What is being done to save humanity? Or are we just allowing this to proceed, and we're all, like, walking to a slow death here?

WARD: I mean, this is the thing, right? So Coxon is bringing up a couple of interesting dynamics in the air industry.

One is that as he's described in his -- in his thread on X, and as we've seen researchers as recently as July sign a long letter about, they basically feel like no company can stop itself from continuing this race to the cliff, that the competitive pressure they are under means that they can't reasonably step away.

He says in his Twitter thread that he believes that people at OpenAI, where he worked for three years, haven't internalized the stakes fully. But people at Anthropic, where he says they have, in fact understood it, just don't trust anyone else to make this stuff safely.

And so, the thing he's basically doing here is it reminds me of someone like running out into the street and screaming for help because they can't get anybody to pick up on 911. And that's because there's nobody on the other end of the phone right now. There's really no agency or governmental body that's willing to step in here and make the difference. And that seems to be why Coxon decided to be so loud here.

I mean, you know, this is very much the sort of the attitude that we saw around something like the Manhattan Project, where all of these scientists who otherwise would be utterly morally opposed to the idea of building an atomic weapon, felt they had to before our adversaries did. But the truth is, I mean, in the case of AI, you know, only one person ever walked away from the Manhattan Project for moral reasons. We now -- Coxon is now joining a long list that depending on your definition, extends from either three to maybe 41 people who've lost in the last few years left in the last few years because they're so frightened by this thing. MICHAELSON: You can see Jacob write a lot more about the Manhattan Project and the comparison on his latest Substack post as well. Jacob Ward, thank you so much for being with us. I don't know if I feel better after that, but at least I know that we are getting the word out and -WARD: I've been bumming everyone out all day at least.

MICHAELSON: That's important -- it's an important conversation. Still ahead on The Story Is, California lawmakers approve a bill focused on helping families find healthy foods more easily. What is ultra- processed food? They're going to tell you this could be a national model. It just passed unanimously. The author of it is here live. Next.

(COMMERCIAL BREAK)

MICHAELSON: California lawmakers have just passed a bill aiming to establish an official state seal for non-ultraprocessed foods. Fishel says its purpose is to help people make better-informed and healthier choices about what they eat. The seal would help foods be instantly identifiable, like popular USDA organic label. The bill would also require grocery stores to display non-ultra-processed foods, guaranteeing easier access.

The governor of California, Gavin Newsom, has until the end of the month to either veto or sign this bill into law.

Joining me now is the author of that bill, California Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel.

Welcome to The Story Is, Assemblymember. Thanks so much for being here. So why are you doing this?

JESSE GABRIEL, CALIFORNIA STATE ASSEMBLYMEMBER: Yes, thank you for having me, Elex. It's great to be here. As you and I talked about, this is actually the fourth bill on ultra-processed foods that we have worked on over the past four years. We understand that this is a public health issue. It's something that a lot of parents want to know is that

they can have confidence that the foods that they're feeding their kids don't have harmful additives.

And so, we have worked to phase those additives out of schools, to phase ultra-processed foods out of school. And now we want to take our work to the grocery store. And we've heard from a lot of parents, from a lot of consumers, that they want to eat less ultra-processed foods, but they're not really sure how to identify them and how to identify those foods quickly and easily.

And so, we're going to take the lead, as you mentioned, of the USDA organic model and put a seal right on food so consumers can know quickly and easily which products are healthier and which products are ultra-processed.

MICHAELSON: What is an ultra-processed food?

GABRIEL: So an ultra-processed food, the best way to think about it is this is a food that is the opposite of a whole food. It is industrial, industrially manufactured. The key here, the touchstone, is really a lot of additives. So, if you think about a food that has emulsifiers, artificial colors, artificial flavors, textures, if you pick up a product and turn it over and the label's got 20 ingredients on them, and you need a PhD in chemistry to understand what half of those ingredients are, that's probably an ultra-processed food.

MICHAELSON: So we're in an era where there's not a lot of stuff that's done in a bipartisan way. Not only was this done in a bipartisan way. This was passed unanimously in both the Senate and the Assembly. How did you do that, and why this issue?

GABRIEL: So that was done very intentionally, and that's something that we're really proud of. We said, as we have done this work, that the three legs of our stool are bipartisan, common sense and science based. And so, we have seen that.

We are in a moment where, for all of the disagreements in Washington, for all the dysfunction in Washington, Republicans and Democrats can come together around this very common-sense premise that we should be protecting our kids from harmful food additives, that we shouldn't be exposing them to chemicals that are linked to cancer or reproductive harm or neurobehavioral harm. And so, we've had wonderful conversations with Republican colleagues, said, yes, I get it.

This is -- this is something that we should work on together. And so, as you mentioned, the bill passed the state assembly 72 to 0. We had very progressive Democrats and very conservative Republicans come together to support them.

MICHAELSON: The governor going to sign it?

GABRIEL: I hope so. I hope so. He signed three other bills of ours. He's been a big champion. I think he cares a lot about this issue. So, we're hopeful.

MICHAELSON: We've been talking about this for years, and when I first profiled you doing this, a lot of Republicans mocked you for this, and they thought that this was way over the top.

And then Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. became the Secretary of Health and Human Services and frankly adopted a lot of the stuff you were doing. And now they applaud it, which is how has that been a game changer? And have you worked with the administration at all on this? And do you see this as kind of a national model?

GABRIEL: We do see this as a national model, and we're very proud of the role that California has played in changing the national conversation. I remember that conversation with you, and they were making fun of us and saying we were going to ban Skittles and ketchup and all these things that turned out not to be true. But we have intentionally leaned into the fact that there is bipartisan support for this.

And so, we have been able to change the national conversation. We now have 30, more than 30 states- red states, blue states- that have followed California's lead that have introduced versions of our legislation. We actually had a bill a couple of years ago to phase out four specifically harmful chemicals from food. The Biden FDA then followed our lead to phase out two of those chemicals. So, we're really proud of the work that California has done.

And we think -- we think we're leading the national conversation. We see red states like West Virginia want to follow the California model. That's a very gratifying thing.

MICHAELSON: Has Kennedy done a good job on this? Maybe not everything else, but on this issue.

GABRIEL: So I will say I am appreciative of the fact that we have Democratic and Republican support. I think what I have been disappointed by, and a lot of folks in the Maha movement have been disappointed by, is the lack of action at the federal level. So, there's been a lot of conversation about this. There's been a lot of rhetoric about this.

But when you look at it, they haven't passed a single law. They haven't passed a single regulation. They haven't banned a single chemical. And you also see other folks in the Trump administration, the EPA, going in a different direction. You saw the work that they did with pesticides, which was exactly the opposite of what Secretary Kennedy has talked about.

So, my dad always says actions speak louder than words. We're in California. We're doing the action. And we think that there could be a lot more action in D.C.

MICHAELSON: They just defined ultra-processed food a few weeks ago on the federal level. We'll see what happens next on that. Congratulations on the success of this bill.

GABRIEL: Thank you very much.

Mientras tanto, las atletas jóvenes enfrentan riesgos elevados propios de depresión, ansiedad, luchas con la imagen corporal y trastornos alimentarios.

Los entrenadores a menudo ven a los atletas jóvenes durante muchas horas cada semana y pueden ser los primeros en notar cuando algo está mal. "Este proyecto de ley se trata de transformar la concientización en acciones que salvan vidas", dijo Irwin. AB 1626 Wins Final Passage and Heads to the Governor’s Desk - The San Fernando Valley Sun

SFVS Staff

Last week, the California State Legislature passed AB 1626, key legislation that will put mental health and substance use disorder training in the hands of youth sports coaches. Authored by Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel, Blanca Pacheco and Jacqui Irwin, AB 1626 passed with overwhelming bipartisan support and now heads to Gov. Gavin Newsom’s desk.

For coaches across California, AB 1626 turns good intentions into real preparation. It requires K-12 sports coaches to complete training on recognizing the warning signs of depression, anxiety, eating disorders, substance use disorders and suicidal ideation – and how to connect a struggling student-athlete to resources. It also directs the California Department of Education to build a model training that recreational and club coaches statewide can use to do the same. 

“For many young people, mental health intervention can be the difference between life and death,” said Gabriel. “Coaches are uniquely positioned and are often the first to notice when young people are struggling and in need of help. This bill will empower youth sports coaches with the tools and training they need to help students in crisis.”

“I’m grateful for all the coaches who have helped me build confidence and resilience, on and off the court,” said Stephen Curry, an NBA champion. “Every kid deserves that kind of coach, and we’ve been proud to make investments to ensure coaches in Oakland have the tools to be a great leader. Policies like Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel’s bill help create a strong foundation for coaching practices that can make a lasting impact in an athlete’s life.”

A Crisis Playing Out on California’s Fields and Courts

Studies show that teenagers across the state are struggling with mental health issues at an increasing rate. California’s young men and boys have experienced an alarming rise in suicide rates and feel more disconnected from school, work and relationships. Meanwhile, young female athletes face their own elevated risks of depression, anxiety, body image struggles and eating disorders.

Coaches often see young athletes for numerous hours each week and can be the first to notice when something is wrong. Yet only one in five coaches report feeling highly confident in their ability to support a student dealing with a mental health or substance use disorder, and four in five say they feel less than fully prepared. 

The goal is to ensure the adults who kids already trust are ready to help when it matters most.

Backed by Champions On and Off the Field

AB 1626 is sponsored by the California Alliance of Children and Family Services (CA Alliance), Mental Health America of California, the Play Equity Fund and the California Commission on the Status of Women and Girls. It is backed by State Superintendent of Public Instruction Tony Thurmond, the San Francisco Giants, U.S. Soccer Foundation, San Francisco 49ers, NAMI California, the American Academy of Pediatrics of California, the Association of California School Administrators, and dozens of education, youth and mental health organizations.

“This bill is about turning awareness into life-saving action,” said Irwin. “The community I represent in Ventura County lost a remarkable person when the life of Sarah Shulze was tragically cut short by suicide in 2022. Sarah was a talented multi-event runner, and her loss underscores the urgent need to better equip the adults our students trust to recognize and respond to mental health warning signs.”

“Everyone talks about prevention, but few invest in it. AB 1626 is what prevention looks like in practice,” said Pete Weldy, CEO of CA Alliance. “Youth mental health has reached a crisis point, but early identification can change the trajectory of a young person’s life. When a trusted adult, like a high school coach, is trained to recognize when a young athlete is struggling … that coach can connect that young athlete with care and, in some cases, save their life.” 

What’s Next

After AB 1626 lands on the governor’s desk, he will have until Sept. 30 to decide whether to veto the bill or sign it into law.

California Passes Historic Bill To Label 'Non-Ultraprocessed' Food In Grocery Stores

By Kaetlyn Liddy

Edhat · 2026-09-09 · Section: News · 424 words

California shoppers may soon be able to easily spot foods that are not ultraprocessed if Governor Gavin Newsom signs a new bill.

Assembly Bill 2244, which has already cleared the state Legislature, would create a "Non-Ultraprocessed Certified"

seal for foods and beverages that qualify.

The proposal is the first of its kind in the country and now awaits a decision from Newsom, who must sign or veto it by the end of September, according to National Hog Farmer.

The vote records show that AB 2244 cleared its final legislative votes sans opposition, passing the state Senate by a 32-0 vote and the Assembly 72-0.

The bill was authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, D-Encino, and would require the California Department of Public Health to begin accrediting independent certification agents by June 1, 2029.

Those agents would then determine which products qualify for the seal. Foods that match the state's criteria for ultraprocessed food would not be eligible, the legislation states.

AB 2244 would also require the department to maintain a public webpage listing all currently certified NonUltraprocessed Certified products. Certification agents would report the nutrition details for each product, including ingredients and certification date.

The department would design a standardized seal bearing either "Non-Ultraprocessed Certified Food Standard" or the shorter "Non-UPF Certified," according to the bill. The seal may feature California or whole foods imagery.

According to National Hog Farmer, supporters envision the seal as a cousin to the "USDA Organic" label, which offers an accessible way for shoppers navigating a maze of unfamiliar ingredients and jargon-filled labels.

Because the label would be purely voluntary, manufacturers would not be required to seek certification, according to the Environmental Working Group.

Manufacturers that do seek the label would be required to have their products recertified at least once every three years, plus any time their product is reformulated, according to the bill.

The bill also extends beyond packaging, requiring grocery stores that post more than $10 million in sales on an annual basis to make at least three certified items easy to spot in their stores, assuming they carry more than 25 qualifying products.

Grocery stores could comply with this requirement through the use of signs, separate displays or other means that may aid shoppers in distinguishing the non-ultraprocessed products.

"Parents shouldn't need a Ph.D. in chemistry to understand what they're feeding their kids," Gabriel said, per National Hog Farmer.

The proposal comes in the wake of other California legislation targeting food additives and ultraprocessed products, including a 2025 measure that established a statutory definition of ultraprocessed food, as well as a process for

restricting certain products in public schools.

Campus protest rules bill barely clears the Legislature. What was the debate?

By Tarini Mehta, The Sacramento Bee

Sacramento Bee, The · 2026-09-07 · Section: capitol_alert · 1095 words

A bill pushing for greater transparency around implementation of campus protest rules at California's public universities divided Democratic lawmakers in the final days the legislative session. After spirited debate in both the Senate and Assembly, it made it through with just enough votes in its favor. Now, it heads to Gov. Gavin Newsom's desk for final approval.

Assembly Bill 2551, authored by Assemblymember Sade Elhawary , D- Los Angeles , would require the California State University and request the University of California systems to provide annual data on student code of conduct violations during protests disaggregated by race and gender. The reports would have to include descriptions of the disciplinary action imposed on those students.

The measure also asks that campuses host open forums before the end of 2027 to elicit student feedback on current time, place, and manner policies that restrict when, where and how protests are conducted on campuses.

Elhawary said during a committee hearing TPM policies were "intended to prevent hostile campus environments"

but had arguably increased hostility for students of color.

"Students of color report experiencing violent arrests at peaceful protests, targeted disciplinary actions, and bureaucratic barriers that suppress their right to protest, leading many student organizers to fear severe repercussions and reprisal," Elhawary said. "As a former student activist myself while I was at UCLA , I care deeply about empowering all students and protecting their abilities to organize and advocate. Through data collection and student hearings, this bill helps ensure the equitable and consistent enforcement of time, place and manner policy."

What prompted the bill?

The bill is a direct response to what the author calls unintended consequences of legislation passed in 2024. At that time, following encampments and rallies protesting the ongoing war in Gaza that swept campuses statewide, the legislature required the UC and CSU systems to develop uniform protest policies.

Jewish groups reported antisemitic incidents on campuses. The state passed a law asking the CSU and UC systems to enforce those protest restrictions and "prohibit violent, harassing, intimidating or discriminatory conduct" that creates a hostile environment on campus. The UC and CSU prohibited encampments, restricted masking to conceal identity when violating policies and put in place disciplinary actions to be utilized against those in violation.

Meanwhile, hundreds of student and faculty who participated in pro-Palestinian protests had already been slapped with legal and academic repercussions amid a crackdown on the movement.

In the time since, some students say the implementation of protest policies and the disciplinary actions meted out to violators didn't just create a chilling effect on campus but also disproportionately targeted Muslim, Black and Brown students.

In a 2025 report, the Council on American-Islamic Relations-California - a sponsor of AB 2551 - raised concerns over the newly strengthened campus protest restrictions, especially given what it called "targeted enforcement" of the existing policies. The report said several California universities used law enforcement disproportionately in response to pro-Palestinian protests when compared with other events that violated the same policies. The University of California Student Association , a coalition of student governments across the system, has voiced similar concerns.

However, these allegations of inequitable implementation are so far only anecdotal; there is no data to substantiate them.

That's the gap Elhawary's bill seeks to fill, by mandating that universities provide data on violations of campus protest policies, disciplinary actions taken, and the affected students disaggregated by race and gender.

Despite major amendments, the UC and CSU systems remained opposed to the bill throughout, worrying it could create uncertainty around their current policies and compromise student privacy. At a committee hearing Aug. 30 , a UC spokesperson said disaggregation of the data could enable easy identification of involved students, given the number of total violations is a small number. In a February report, the UC system recorded 71 violations over a oneyear period. The CSU system reported 201 violations in the 2024-2025 academic year. The California Faculty Association , which represents 29,000 professors, lecturers, librarians, counselors, and coaches at the CSU, was a sponsor and strong voice in favor of the bill.

Why were lawmakers divided?

The bill required a simple majority to pass in both the state Senate and Assembly. It passed 23-12 in the Senate and 44-8 in the Assembly with 27 lawmakers who were either absent or abstained.

While the California Legislative Jewish Caucus took no formal position on the bill, six of its members in the Senate and Assembly raised concerns, including that its eventual intent was to repeal the student safety provisions they had fought for in the 2024 legislation that mandated comprehensive campus protest restrictions.

An earlier version of Elhawary's bill did include a provision to sunset that 2024 law by 2029. Following strong opposition from Jewish California, an umbrella advocacy organization for Jewish groups statewide, the bill was watered down to leave the time, place and manner policies intact while pushing for greater transparency and conversation around their implementation.

"It was very concerning to our caucus to see an effort without a conversation to repeal that (2024) bill,"

Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel , D- Encino , said on the Assembly floor. "I worry that the intent of this bill is to begin a process that will ultimately result in the repealing of civil rights protections."

Other critics, like Sen. Josh Becker , D- Menlo Park , chided the bill's "rushed" process and said it wasn't wellthought-out. In June, the author decided to "gut-and-amend" a healthcare bill she had authored and the Assembly had already passed, and replace its contents entirely with a new proposed law to address the students concerns in the current legislative session. That process, critics said, made for inadequate discussion on what is a controversial topic.

Supporters of the bill urged their colleagues to see AB 2551 at face value as a "data bill" that affords the opportunity to evaluate the consequences of past legislation, and not on the basis of its pre-amendment version.

"My daughter sits on a CSU campus. She talked to me about having the feeling of having her voice stifled because of the policies of the university," said Assemblymember Mia Bonta , D- Alameda . "As legislators, we have to create the space to examine the implementation and the impact of the policies that move forward, so that we don't have any student feeling like they are risking being able to continue on with their education because an individual campus may or may not have gotten this right."

The bill now awaits Newsom's signature. The governor has until Sept. 30 to sign or veto bills passed by lawmakers.
