Bay Area lawmakers' bills to combat ICE head to Newsom's desk

By Joyce Chu

San Jose Spotlight · 2026-09-06 · Section: Santa Clara County · 1035 words

Several state bills spurred by Silicon Valley lawmakers to keep federal immigration agents accountable and uphold rights for detainees are headed to the governor's desk.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention facilities have been rife with alleged human rights violations, with reports of inhumane living conditions, sexual abuse, unsanitary food and inadequate medical care. In response, state lawmakers have stepped up to protect immigrant rights with bills that would tax companies operating detention centers, prevent ICE contractors from receiving state grants or loans and allow the federal agency to be sued for monetary damages and First Amendment rights violations.

Gov. Gavin Newsom has until Sept. 30 to approve or veto the bills, which have already been approved by the state Legislature.

Reining in detention centers Assemblymembers Alex Lee and Ash Kalra co-authored Assembly Bill 1633, which would tax private companies operating immigration detention centers. Lee represents North San Jose, Milpitas, Fremont, Newark and Sunol, while Kalra represents East San Jose and South County. The bill is led by San Francisco Assemblymember Matt Haney.

If signed by Newsom, private detention center operators would be taxed 25% starting July 1, 2028. The money would be used to fund immigration services.

"ICE and its corporate profiteers are abducting tens of thousands of innocent people and warehousing them in detention camps," Lee told San José Spotlight.

Two of the largest private prison companies, CoreCivic and The GeoGroup, are the major operators running ICE detention centers. CoreCivic runs two large ICE detentions in California — the nearly 2,000-bed Otay Mesa Detention Center in San Diego County and the 2,560-bed California City Detention Facility in Kern County. The GeoGroup runs five ICE detention facilities in the state— 1,940 bed Adelanto ICE Processing Center in San Bernardino County, the 750-bed Desert View Annex in San Bernardino County (run alongside the Adelanto facility), the 400-bed Mesa Verde ICE Processing Center in Bakersfield, the 700-bed Central Valley Annex in Kern County and the 700-bed Golden State Annex in Kern County.

July 18, 2026 Santa Clara County immigrant network evolved into powerhouse July 13, 2026 Work at South County ICE facility temporarily paused July 11, 2025 Santa Clara County immigrants are self-deporting

The companies' profits have grown as President Donald Trump upped federal immigration enforcement and deportations. In 2025, CoreCivic racked in $2.2 billion in revenue and The GeoGroup made $2.6 billion. CoreCivic sold Otay Mesa Detention Center and the California City Detention Facility to the federal government on July 2, according to a recent filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, as reported by AP, with the federal government paying more than $739 million for Otay Mesa and more than $732 million for City Detention. More than 50 people have died in ICE detention centers during Trump's second administration, the highest level of deaths in at least a decade. Senate Bill 942 — also known as the Civil Detainee Bill of Rights Act — would give immigrants held in detention rights to humane care, safe living conditions and healthy food. It is co-authored by Kalra and state Sen. Dave Cortese.

In addition, Senate Bill 1367, led by state Sen. Sabrina Cervantes from Riverside, would prevent a city or county from approving land use for the building of a detention center or converting a current building to an ICE facility. "I'm glad we were able to pass many pieces of important legislation to hold ICE accountable in California and protect vulnerable communities," Kalra told San José Spotlight. "My committee worked on SB 942, which is the nation's first Detainee Bill of Rights, and will enforce much-needed safety and dignity standards for those held in immigration detention."

Keeping agents in check Multiple bills awaiting Newsom's signature aim to address how ICE agents have largely acted with impunity during raids and arrests.

Assembly Bill 2760, led by Lee and co-authored by Kalra, would ban federal immigration agents, as well as local and state officers, from wearing electric shock gloves — and police departments from purchasing them. Lawmakers passed the last-minute bill in response to the Trump administration's announcement last month to spend up to $20 million on the devices.

Senate Bill 873, co-authored by Kalra, aims to prevent arrests by ICE at courthouses. Senate Bill 747, the No Kings Act, led by state Sen. Scott Wiener of San Francisco, will allow people to sue ICE for constitutional violations. Assembly Bill 1806, spearheaded by Southern California Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, would require the state attorney general to investigate killings of unarmed residents by immigration agents.

Since 2025, federal immigration officers have shot at least 23 people and killed six during immigration enforcement operations, including three U.S. citizens.

While mass enforcement actions like the federal deployment in Los Angeles and Minneapolis, Minnesota haven't occurred in Santa Clara County, the region is one of the most impacted areas for targeted ICE operations, according to the Services, Immigrant Rights and Education Network (SIREN). The organization is part of the Rapid Response Network of Santa Clara County, a group of volunteers that documents ICE activity, sends alerts to residents and provides free emergency legal support for immigrants.

Since the start of 2025 to June 2026, 232 county residents have been detained, according to the network. Fears of ICE have kept San Jose students from attending class and slowed foot traffic at Latino-owned businesses. Some undocumented residents have chosen to self-deport.

Lee also spearheaded Assembly Bill 2465 to ensure ICE contractors such as tech giant Palantir Technologies, which provides the government with data-mining software to track immigrants, do not get government grants or loans. ICE is paying $30 million through 2027 to use Palantir's platform.

In the second quarter of 2026, Palantir made $809 million from government contracts — 90% more than what it brought in a year ago.

The extent to which California would benefit from the bill is unknown, as the state does not track how many tax credits it gives to contractors.

"We have clients and community members who have endured the terrible conditions in these facilities," Huy Tran, executive director of SIREN, told San José Spotlight. "This industry is built on heartbreak and AB 1633 and AB 2465 makes it clear that California will not allow immoral profiteering to go unchecked."

Contact Joyce Chu at joyce@sanjosespotlight.com or @joyce_speaks on X.

Food manufacturers would be able to place the seal on packages, which according to Gabriel, “would provide consumers with a simple, trustworthy way to identify healthier options with a quick glance”.

There is a growing body of evidence to suggest UPFs have a negative impact on health but the evidence is inconclusive as to just how detrimental these food products are.

Bernadette Del Chiaro, the senior vice president for California at the non-profit Environmental Working Group, said in a separate statement: “Consumers deserve labels they can trust. “If enacted, the bill would establish a state-verified seal for foods free from the additives, emulsifiers, food dyes and flavours that have come to define the modern American diet.”

Accredited agencies would be prohibited from passing the seal if food and drinks were not in compliance with the non-UPFs classifications and records would be made available for inspection to ensure compliance.

Here's what the California Legislature passed in 2026

By Madeline Shannon

(The Center Square) – California’s 2025-2026 legislative session wrapped on Tuesday, ending a nearly 21-month-long stretch of passing bills that will impact 39.5 million Californians throughout the state.

Among the most impactful bills were budget legislation, a housing bond and bills that address public safety. Here are some of the biggest bills that passed in 2026.

Assembly Constitutional Amendment 20 The “Save for California’s Future” Act, authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, D-Encino, will increase the amount of money the state puts away in reserves each year.

Effectively the equivalent of California’s savings account, the Budget Stabilization Account will see an increase from 10% to 20% of the state’s general fund revenues during good fiscal years, according to a legislative analysis of the bill. The extra funds deposited in strong budget years would be available during fiscal years when revenues decline.

The bill also puts a constitutional amendment on the Nov. 3 ballot as Proposition 2, which will allow California voters to decide whether to increases the state's "Rainy Day Fund."

“For over a decade, nonpartisan experts have been warning us that we need to grow California's rainy day fund, and we’ve seen that taxpayers pay the price every time a downturn forces sudden cuts to schools, health clinics, public safety and other essential services,” Gabriel told The Center Square in a written response sent on Wednesday. “ACA 20 put Proposition 2 on the ballot so voters will have the chance to fix this problem by requiring the state to save more in good years. It’s a commonsense reform that protects taxpayers from boom-and-bust budgeting."

Senate Bill 417

SB 417, also called The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026, was authored by Senate President Pro Tempore Monique Limón, D-Santa Barbara, and gives California voters the chance to decide whether to let the measure take effect. The bill would allow $11.25 billion of general obligation bonds to pay for housing programs for veterans, youth, students and those experiencing homelessness, according to the bill analysis. Approximately $5.1 billion would be allocated to the state’s Multifamily Housing Program, with at least 10% of units designated for extremely low-income households, while $1.25 billion would be allocated to the CalVet Home Loan Program. Approximately $1.15 billion would be allocated to supportive housing under the umbrella of the Multifamily Housing Program.

“This bill dedicates more than $11 billion to not only increase supply across our state, but also to ensure that Californians from all income levels can keep a roof over their head,” Limón said at a June press conference announcing the bond. “Affordability is not just a one-and-done.”

In addition, $150 million would be used for youth housing, $750 million to affordable housing projects under the California Department of Housing and Community Development’s Portfolio Reinvestment Program, $500 million to the Infill Infrastructure Grant Program, and $450 million to the Serna Program, which fund grants and loans to pay for construction and rehabilitation for agricultural worker housing.

California’s budget bills

California’s budget legislation, coming in at roughly $350 billion, was passed at the end of June and signed immediately by Gov. Gavin Newsom. The budget includes $251.1 billion for the general fund and $1 billion of Proposition 98 to community schools.

Other trailer budget bills increased the cap on the State Route 710 Rehabilitation Account to $15 million, up from the previously-allocated $1.2 million, according to previous reporting by The Center Square.

The Legislature passed the budget during a year that saw the Legislative Analyst’s Office predict a $16.9 billion deficit through 2028. That was despite record revenues brought in by strong stock market activity related to a boom in artificial intelligence technology, The Center Square previously reported.

“I would like taxpayers to know that we took seriously the situation we’re in,” Sen. John Laird, D-Santa Cruz and chair of the Senate Budget and Fiscal Review Committee, told The Center Square on Tuesday. “So we balanced the budget for two years, put $35 billion in reserves, and cut the structural deficit in half, and did our best to triage against the federal cuts to the social safety net.”

Assembly Bill 1577 Introduced by Assemblymember Rebecca Bauer-Kahan, D-San Ramon, AB 1577 requires data centers to report energy usage and information about energy efficiency to the state. The California Energy Commission, the agency tasked with overseeing compliance, would also have to include that data in a report expected to be released in 2029 and publish the data in an anonymized format for the public.

Under this bill, data centers also have to submit energy and efficiency information to local government agencies in the area in which they want to build or operate a data center, according to the bill analysis.

Assemblymember Rebecca Bauer-Kahan, D-San Ramon, talks about Assembly BIll 1577 on the California chamber's floor, Aug. 27, 2026. Bauer-Kahn is author of the bill, which adds requirements for data centers. Photo: Madeline Shannon / The Center Square “This is yet another bill that ensures that data centers here in California work not just for the companies that are building them, but the constituents,” Bauer-Kahan said on the Assembly floor on Aug. 27. “This is a transparency bill on energy. It would ensure that our rig is able to stand up to the needs of these data centers.”

Senate Bill 904

This bill, authored by Sen. Kelly Seyarto, R-Murietta, requires state agencies to assist in expediting rebuilding permits for wildfire survivors by identifying state regulations that would slow down rebuilding and recovery.

The California Department of Housing and Community Development, along with other state agencies, will be required to submit reports to the governor and the Legislature outlining what those regulations are and recommend suspension of those rules, according to a legislative analysis of the bill.

“The reason I did the bill was because we keep trying to reinvent the wheel every time we have a big emergency,” Seyarto told The Center Square on Wednesday. “Part of that wheel was found in the executive orders that were given by the governor after the state of emergency that was declared in the Palisades and Altadena. We’ve had several of those type of fires, and they all need that kind of attention.”

That attention comes from agencies responsible for permitting, studies and other regulatory requirements that impede rebuilding and recovery, Seyarto said.

“What this does is it puts them on a timeline to identify areas that we can take advantage of to be able to get people back into their homes faster and recovery faster, no matter where the fire is,” Seyarto said.

Assembly Bill 1776

The COMPETE Act, authored by Assembly Majority Leader Cecilia Aguiar-Curry, D-Winters, was introduced this year after concerns that large corporations based in California were engaging in anti-competitive behavior, threatening the Golden State’s small businesses.

The legislation would prohibit anyone from conspiring to engage in behavior that could be considered to be monopolistic, as well as monopsonistic - where a single company has control over an entire market as the sole or major purchaser of goods or services.

California Assembly Majoritiy Leader Cecilia Aguilar-Curry, D-Winters, talks about the Compete Act, a new bill to promote competition in markets, during a news conference at the Capitol, Feb. 17, 2026. Photo: Madeline Shannon / The Center Square.

“Markets have changed,” Aguiar-Curry said during a February press conference announcing the legislation. “Industries have consolidated. When competition dries up, our families pay more; our small businesses struggle to compete. Our workers have fewer options and innovation slows down.”

The bill was supported by small business owners, who said in the February press conference that large internet shopping platforms routinely “scraped” the websites of those small businesses, recreating product listings similar to those on sites of small businesses and steering customers towards larger shopping sites, according to previous reporting by The Center Square.

Assembly Bill 2727 Assemblymember Stephanie Nguyen, D-Elk Grove, introduced this bill amid calls for elderly parole reform. The bill increases the eligible age for elderly parole from 50 to 65 and requires those who were convicted of certain sex crimes to serve at least 25 years of their sentence for those crimes. The legislation also requires the state’s Board of Parole Hearings to consider the results of a sexual dangerousness screening, among other things, when determining if someone qualifies for elderly parole after previously being convicted of certain sex crimes.

According to previous reporting by The Center Square, two convicts who were serving sentences for crimes against children were eligible for elderly parole this year. Gregory Lee Vogelsang, 57, was up for elderly parole in May. That parole hearing was met with intense opposition by lawmakers.

Another man, David Allen Funston, 64, pleaded guilty to new child molestation charges brought by the Placer County Sheriff’s Office the day he was set to be released on elderly parole on a different case.

“This bill will put guardrails around these individuals who qualify for elderly parole to ensure the screening is going to say they can be released out in the community and not commit another sexual violent offense,” Nguyen said when presenting the bill for a vote on the Assembly floor in May.

Senate Bill 1090

This bill, introduced by Sen. Sasha Renée Pérez, D-Pasadena, places a three-year moratorium on a previous state law, the Starter Home Revitalization Act, in an effort to help homeowners who lost their homes in the January 2025 Eaton Fire. The 2021 law required cities and counties throughout the state to allow zoning to build more dense single-family housing in an effort to increase construction of homes to address California’s housing shortage. However, after the Eaton Fire damaged or destroyed roughly 6,000 homes, that law was used to buy out homeowners who couldn’t afford to rebuild their homes, Pérez previously said.

“As the rebuilding has begun and we’ve had this huge issue with outside investors and speculators making lowball offers to disaster victims, there’s been real concern about those same developers utilizing these laws to try to increase density,” Pérez told The Center Square on Tuesday. “I want to make sure that the pause is temporary over these next three years, and that we’re giving folks time to rebuild.”

Assembly Bill 2700

Former Assemblymember and current U.S. Rep. James Gallagher, R-Sutter County, introduced AB 2700 to help wildfire victims get restitution money after utility company-caused wildfires. Ultimately, the bill requires the California Energy Commission to compile a report due by Jan. 1, 2028 that assesses the restitution shortfalls for victims of wildfires that started before July 12, 2019. The bill also requires restitution mechanisms to be in place for electricity companies to pay restitution to those victims.

Assemblymember James Gallagher, R-Sutter County, gives his final speech to the California Assembly before moving to Washington, D.C., and starting his tenure in Congress. Photo: Madeline Shannon / The Center Square “It makes sure that our fire victims are fully compensated,” Gallagher said of the bill in May. “There were people who were devastated. We lost community members. We lost homes. People lost everything in these fires.”

Gallagher won a special election in June to the late U.S. Rep. Doug LaMalfa’s seat and left the California Legislature to serve in Congress, according to previous reporting by The Center Square.

Despite controversial security clause, Legislature passes last-minute budget bill

By Sofia Williams, The Sacramento Bee

Sacramento Bee, The · 2026-09-01 · Section: capitol_alert · 607 words

In the final moments of the Legislative session, lawmakers passed a budget bill that drew scrutiny for allocating millions to personal security for current and former state elected officials.

Assembly Bill 113 was the last budget trailer bill to pass through the Legislature during this session, amending the 2026-27 budget to allocate additional funds to issue areas such as healthcare, housing and disaster relief, among others.

The measure would allocate nearly $2.7 billion in climate bond funds to support storm preparation and recovery, wildlife conservation and stewardship of natural resources, according to Assembly Budget Committee chair and bill author Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel , D-Encino, in a presentation during Tuesday's Assembly floor hearing. The measure would also allocate $450 million to greenhouse gas reduction funds for transit and invest in fire mitigation, food banks, healthcare, legal service providers and programs to aid disadvantaged communities. According to Gabriel, these investments are a response to national increases in the cost of living. "We have doubled down," Gabriel said. "We have stepped up to the plate. We have looked to do as much as we can to help our constituents with healthcare and childcare and housing and all of the things that we know people are struggling with. But it is the leadership in the White House and Washington, D.C. , that makes that harder." But Republican lawmakers opposed the bill over one allocation. They said a nearly $20 million increase to California Highway Patrol for transportation security would constitute an undue burden on taxpayers. The funding would come out of the state's Motor Vehicle Account, which is funded by California driver's license registration fees. Assemblymember Jeff Gonzalez , R- Indio , claimed the money would go towards security for former California Attorney General Kamala Harris and Gov. Gavin Newsom - a policy he condemned.

"I know $20 million could go far in any one of my colleagues' districts," Gonzalez said. "This body continues to show that its priorities are out of touch with the realities facing many Californians."

While Newsom has not disclosed whether or how he plans to use the funds, Harris relied on several dozen CHP officers to provide security during her international book tour earlier this year, according to reporting by KCRA 3. However, the bill's proponents say the expanded security funds are necessary, as a number of politicians have experienced threats to their safety amid an increasingly polarized, antagonistic political environment. "I don't want to have to put $20 million into security either," said Assemblymember Chris Rogers , D- Santa Rosa . "But I would hope that some of my colleagues across the aisle would look at their own social media and the way that they have used that to weaponize against us, people on this floor, who have needed more security because they have grown their following at the expense of people's safety."

Members of budget committees in both chambers celebrated the bill, which was the final legislative step to balance the state budget for the upcoming two fiscal years.

"We basically positioned ourselves for next year," said Senate Budget Committee Chair Sen. John Laird , D- Santa Cruz . "We did our best to triage against cuts that were beyond our capacity to deal with, and in certain ones with food and medical care, we bridged it to the next year in the hope that the better budget picture will allow us to

address those cuts. ... This is a good budget. It's the result of a lot of work from people across this chamber and the floor."

The bill passed 29-4 on the Senate floor and 60-10 on the Assembly floor Tuesday morning.

California passes non-UPF food seal, setting potential blueprint for other states

By Elizabeth Crawford

Food Navigator · 2026-09-01 · Section: Regulation · 610 words

California lawmakers unanimously passed AB 2244, creating a government-backed non-UPF food seal that could influence labeling in other states.

California lawmakers have unanimously approved the creation of a first-of-its-kind government-backed certification seal for non-ultraprocessed foods that supporters tout as a way to help consumers "identify healthier options with a quick glance," and which could serve as a blueprint for other states seeking to define, label and regulate UPFs.

Late last week, the state Senate voted 32-0 and the Assembly 72-0 to pass Assembly Bill 2244. If signed by Gov Gavin Newsom by the end of September, the bill would create a standard label with the phrase "Non-Ultraprocessed Certified," which food manufacturers could voluntarily place on products that meet the legislation's standards.

The bill broadly defines UPF as any food or beverage that contains one or more ingredients with a "specific technical effect," including surface-active agents; stabilizers and thickeners, propellants, aerating agents and gases; colors and coloring adjuncts; emulsifiers and emulsifier salts; flavoring agents and adjuvants; flavor enhancers – excluding spices and natural seasonings or flavorings; non-nutritive sweeteners.

It also defines UPFs as containing 10% or more total energy from saturated fat, a milligrams sodium to calorie ratio equal or greater than one to one, and 10% or more total energy from added sugars. Other substances that could trigger the UPF definition include D-sorbitol, erythritol, hydrogenated starch hydrolysates, isomalt, lactitol, monk fruit concentrate, maltitol, stevia glycosides, thaumatin and xylitol.

Manufacturers with products that meet this definition could seek certification from state-accredited third parties, which would need to be renewed at least every three years. The California Department of Public Health has until June 1, 2029, to identify the accreditors.

The bill also would create a Public Health Food and Nutrition Education Fund to support implementation of the label and to educate the public and stakeholders about the requirements, food products and nutrition. The department also could establish "reasonable" fees to register and renew accredited certification agents and food.

A powerful marketing tool A California Certified Non-UPF seal could be a powerful marketing tool for qualifying products given the law would require large grocery chains in California to display products with the seal in prominent high traffic areas in the store.

"This new seal will provide consumers with clear, trustworthy information and make it easier for them to locate healthier foods that are free from harmful additives," said the bill's author, Assembly member Jesse Gabriel, DEncino.

He added the legislation is the most recent step in a journey California began three years ago with the passage of the California Food Safety Act (AB 418 in 2023), followed by the California School Food Safety Act (AB 2316 in 2024)

and most recently The Real Food Healthy Kids Act (AB 1264 in 2025) – all of which Gabriel authored.

These laws are foundational for the current legislation in that they define, for the first time the US, what ultraprocessed foods are, and establish some parameters about where they cannot be sold.

While this legislation, and the previously passed laws on which it is based, only apply in California, the previous bills have spurred copy-cat legislation in states across the country – amplifying the original laws impact and setting the stage for similar replication of AB 2244.

What happens next?

California Gov Gavin Newsom has until September 30 to sign or veto the legislation.

If enacted, CDPH would have to establish the certification framework and accredit third-party certification agents, with the first certified products potentially following once the regulatory infrastructure is in place.

Whether California's seal becomes a recognizable consumer mark or a state-specific experiment could help determine whether the next phase of the US fight over ultra-processed foods plays out in the grocery aisle as well as the statehouse.

California lawmakers pass bills to address antisemitism, deem ‘Jewish’ an ethnicity and protect religious observance

Sharon Udasin

California is poised to become the first state to deem “Jewish” an ethnic and racial identity, after lawmakers gave final approval to the groundbreaking legislation on Monday.

The SB 1387 bill, which would expand the definition of ethnicity “to include Jewish identity” in demographic data collection, will now head to the governor’s desk. If the legislation becomes law, state agency forms that allow for voluntary disclosures of ethnicity or race would also need to offer a “Jewish” option.

Both the State Assembly and Senate granted final approval to the bill in the last few hours of California’s 2026 legislative session, which concluded at the end of the day on Monday. Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, has until Sept. 30 to sign bills into laws or veto them. 

The SB 1387 ethnicity legislation has been a priority among many California Jewish organizations, who argue that Jewish peoplehood should be connected to much more than just religion — and that the law should reflect that understanding. 

This bill, which would take effect in 2030, would affect forms issued by agencies ranging from public schools to unemployment offices to prisons. Data collected would serve to inform research initiatives, identify disparities and guide policy decisions, while banning the disclosure of personal information, per the bill. 

Joining SB 1387 in heading to the governor’s desk are five other bills that are relevant to the state’s 1.2 million Jews and that had the support of the Jewish California coalition.  

On Sunday, the legislature passed AB 1853, a bill that bars threatening false and misleading information from California voter guides. Jewish California, which represents 43 organizations, praised the legislation’s advancement, stressing that 54 Jewish groups voiced their support for the bill within 48 hours of its introduction. 

“Hate speech does not belong in a state-approved document paid by tax dollars,”  David Bocarsly, CEO of Jewish California, said in a statement. 

“AB 1853 boldly declares that our state’s official election documents can’t be used to spread conspiracy theories and bigotry,” added Bocarsly, whose coalition was not only a sponsor of this bill but also of SB 1387.

Also on Sunday, lawmakers approved AB 2664, the Safe Worship Zone Act, which would create a 100-foot zone around the entrances of houses of worship, where no one would be able to come within 8 feet of a congregant without their consent. 

The bill, which received the backing of a wide-ranging interfaith coalition, is modeled after Colorado’s bubble zone law that offers patients protection around reproductive health clinics. 

“The rise of antisemitism is undeniable, and our communities must be protected,” Democratic Assemblymember Rebecca Bauer-Kahan, the bill’s author, said in a statement. 

“AB 2664 gives communities an important tool to push back against harassment and intimidation and protect the sanctity of our houses of worship,” Bauer-Kahan added. 

Meanwhile, on Thursday, the legislature approved AB 395, which would require government agencies, K-12 schools and public universities to avoid scheduling major events or meetings on days “that members of the public would be unable to participate or be present due to the ritual observance of a religious, cultural, or ancestral holiday.”

Among the Jewish observances that would be codified on a list of such holidays are Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and the first and last two days of Passover. 

“For too long and in too many communities, religious minorities and other people of faith have been asked to make difficult choices on the days that matter most to them,” Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, the bill’s author, said in a statement. 

“This legislation would help to prevent that injustice and ensure that Californians of all backgrounds can fully participate, particularly when important decisions are being made,” added Gabriel, who chairs the California Legislative Jewish Caucus.   

Lawmakers on Thursday also approved another Gabriel bill, AB 1836, which seeks to close a gap in the current structure of the California State Nonprofit Security Grant Program. Because the program allocates security funds only for a nonprofit’s physical building, off-site events like menorah lightings on Chanukah were not eligible. 

A fifth bill relevant to the Jewish community, AB 1763, is also heading to Newsom’s desk, after passing in the legislature last Tuesday. This bill would include religious holiday observance as a type of excused absence in schools, without requiring a written request from a parent or guardian. 

A Season of Big Decisions. From the Knesset campaign to American midterms, Jewish communities are weighing what comes next. Help JTA keep delivering the deeper context.

In last days of session, late or absent Assemblymembers called out

By Madeline Shannon

(The Center Square) – Outgoing Assemblymember Stan Ellis, R-Bakersfield, told The Center Square this week that he estimates that California’s taxpayers pay roughly $40,000 an hour for state politicians to conduct the business of governing the Golden State.

That poses a problem when members of the state assembly talk for an hour on resolutions that have little to no impact, and is a waste of taxpayers’ money, he said.

“We came to the floor at 9 o’clock, nobody gets there until 10, everybody’s B.S.’ing, so nothing gets done from nine to 10,” Ellis said of his first months in the Assembly after winning his seat in a February 2025 special election. “Then we do resolutions on Butterfly Day and Rice Day.”

Some resolutions are important, Ellis added, but that spending so much time talking about such resolutions is not a good use of taxpayers’ money.

“I calculated my staff, my salary, I calculated per-diem, I added it all up for all the assemblymembers,” Ellis said. “I came up with a number of $35,000, $40,000 an hour that we are spending of the taxpayers’ money to do resolutions and people showing up for work.”

The one-time assemblyman said that since he doesn’t know how many Assembly services staff members there are and what the amortized cost of rent could be on the capitol, he could be off by as much as 10% to 20%, he added. “There was quite a bit I missed,” Ellis said. “So I estimated some things.”

Ellis also said that members of the Assembly often don’t show up for regularly-scheduled floor sessions on time. Assembly floor sessions are often scheduled for Mondays and Thursdays every week of the legislative session.

“I have suggested if you don’t show up on time, you should not get your per-diem,” Ellis said in a Thursday interview this week.

“Per diems” refers to what legislators are paid every day they are in Sacramento to conduct the business of government, like voting on bills and attending committee meetings.

On Friday, tardy members of the California state assembly were called out on the Assembly floor on one of the last days for politicians to vote on legislation for the year. The deadline to pass legislation this year is Aug. 31, according to the 2026 legislative calendar.

In a floor vote Friday morning on an elections bill authored by Assemblymember Gail Pellerin, D-Santa Cruz, it became apparent that several members of the assembly were not present and had not yet arrived in the assembly chambers for the 9 a.m. floor session.

Members who did not vote on the first bill of the day included Assemblymembers Joaquin Arambula, D-Fresno, Rebecca Bauer-Kahan, D-San Ramon, Steve Bennett, D-Oxnard, Isaac Bryan, D-Los Angeles, Laurie Davies, R-Oceanside, Heath Flora, R-Ripon, Jesse Gabriel, D-Encino, Mike Gipson, D-Gardena, Jeff Gonzalez, R-Indio, Josh Hoover, R-Folsom, Alexandra Macedo, R-Tulare, Tina McKinnor, D-Inglewood, Stephanie Nguyen, D-Elk Grove, Darshana Patel, D-San Diego, Celeste Rodriguez, D-Arleta, Robert Rivas, D-Salinas, Kate Sanchez, R-Rancho Santa Margarita, Avelino Valencia, D-Anaheim and Greg Wallis, R-Rancho Mirage.

It was not immediately clear who was present in the Assembly chambers and abstained from voting on the first bill of the day and who was not there.

“The on-time caucus has been made aware of a rule that if you are more than 30 minutes late, you have to explain yourself to the group,” Assemblymember Heather Hadwick, R-Redding, said on the Assembly floor. “Is that true?”

Hadwick’s question, addressed to Assembly Speaker Pro Tempore Josh Lowenthal, D-Long Beach, who led the Assembly floor session on Friday morning, was asked after a vote on Pellerin’s bill was delayed because several members of the Assembly had not yet arrived for the 9 a.m. floor session.

“We will explain what’s in the rules,” Lowenthal said at the Assembly chamber dais. “Part of the rules we have all voted on and agreed to include Section 110, and I will read those now. If a member is not recorded on the attendance role within 30 minutes after the scheduled start of the session, the member shall stand up before the assembly and explain the reason why the member is late before the member is recorded on the roll call for any vote.”

If a member does not explain the reason for being late, any other member may raise a point of order, Lowenthal continued. “Under this rule, the tardy member’s vote may not be recorded until an explanation is made,” Lowenthal said. “The point of order may be made today.”

As Lowenthal read from the rules, members of the Assembly clapped. Later in the floor session on Friday, Minority Floor Leader Josh Hoover, R-Folsom, asked for fellow Republican Jeff Gonzalez, R-Indio, to explain why he was late to Friday’s floor session. Since Gonzalez had already voted on bills after arriving late, Lowenthal took issue with Hoover’s push for Gonzalez to explain why he was late.

“All members, I would like you to listen to this,” Lowenthal said. “We have already recorded votes today, so by the nature of this point of order, I’m going to say that your point is not well taken. The precedent of what you’re standing up and asking for is an important one.”

Lowenthal also said that many other assemblymembers were frustrated about so many fellow members arriving late, and often voiced that other members don’t consider their time to be as important.

“That’s how people feel. Therefore, that point of order should be made before that member has taken a vote and this chair will honor that,” Lowenthal said. “Please arrive on time, respect your colleagues’ time. And if you aren’t going to be here on time, be ready to explain yourself before the state of California.”

No member of the Assembly explained why they were late during the floor session on Friday morning.

“On days like today, where members have flights to catch, those who don’t live nearby, it’s problematic, because there’s a certain amount of business that needs to get done before the end of session,” Lowenthal told The Center Square after the floor session adjourned on Friday. “Legislators are very busy people, and to say they’re not arriving to the floor on time isn’t an affront on their priorities whatsoever. We get pulled in a million different directions, from our district, from the media, from other things that are happening around the Capitol, including key stakeholder meetings, negotiations on bills, and so forth.”

While his statements on the Assembly floor on Friday were not meant to criticize any one member of the Assembly, Lowenthal said it’s important to prioritize the work the Assembly does as a whole sometimes.

“It’s really an acknowledgment that there are moments in time where the work of the body supersedes other priorities, and this is a healthy reminder we all need to buckle down,” Lowenthal said.

Lowenthal added that the Assembly can’t start floor sessions until a quorum, or a majority of the Assembly, is present. He also added that members of the Assembly have to be acknowledged and seen by Assembly staff, and after roll is taken, they are able to go out into the hallway, the portico or other places around the Assembly chambers. He and two staffers for Rivas and Gabriel confirmed that the speaker of the Assembly is able to vote on bills from the speaker’s office. Gabriel and Gonzalez were not available to answer questions from The Center Square on Friday. Assembly Majority Leader Cecilia Aguiar-Curry, D-Davis, wasn't available to answer questions before the Assembly floor session on Friday.

By Sofia Williams, The Sacramento Bee

Sacramento Bee, The · 2026-08-26 · Section: capitol_alert · 640 words

A bill mandating independent state investigations of shootings by federal immigration enforcement agents landed on Newsom's desk Wednesday after passing an Assembly floor vote.

Assembly Bill 1806 responds to a recent uptick in civilian injuries and deaths at the hands of Immigrations and Customs Enforcement agents, according to bill author Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel , D- Encino . According to reporting by The New York Times, at least 23 people have been shot at by ICE agents since early 2025. The Assembly voted to pass the bill by a 42-13 vote along party lines.

The bill's passage comes on the heels of two ICE-involved shootings in California : Keith Porter Jr ., who was killed Dec. 31 by an off-duty ICE agent, and Carlos Ivan Mendoza Hernandez , who was shot seven times in the face by an ICE agent April 7 .

"This bill is a direct result of the relentless ICE assaults that we saw earlier this year…around the state and around the country," Gabriel said before the final Assembly vote. "As we watched these horrific scenes unfold, where American citizens were shot and killed by federal agents here in the United States of America - something just unthinkable - we believed there had to be transparency and accountability around that."

Prosecutors have yet to decide whether to pursue charges against Brian Palacios , the ICE officer who shot and killed Porter. Mendoza Hernandez , who hit an ICE vehicle while attempting to flee agents, awaits an Oct. 19 hearing on charges of destruction of federal property and assaulting a federal officer.

"When circumstances are highly disputed and questions persist, an independent investigation is not just warranted, it is necessary," Sen. Caroline Menjivar , D- San Fernando Valley , said in a Tuesday presentation on the Senate floor. "In these circumstances, the state has both a moral and legal obligation to protect its residents and uphold the rule of law."

The measure passed the Senate by a 30-9 vote along party lines. Opponents have raised concerns that the bill would authorize an overreach of state power, as it would permit the state prosecutor to conduct investigations into federal ICE agents.

"This is unnecessary," Sen. Tony Strickland , R- Huntington Beach , said on the Senate floor Tuesday. "The federal government already reviews incidents involving officers, and the state can already investigate crimes committed within its jurisdiction."

However, the bill's supporters maintain that increased transparency is necessary to protect against further acts of violence committed by federal law enforcement officers.

"We currently live in a climate where we can't rely on the federal government to conduct their own investigation into shootings," said Shiu-Ming Cheer , the deputy director of immigrant and racial justice at the California Immigrant Policy Center, in an interview with The Sacramento Bee . "We want to make sure there is an investigation and California state officials are able to look at the evidence and decide whether they want to pursue any further steps. This is one way of ensuring that there's some accountability."

The California Immigrant Policy Center is a co-sponsor of the bill alongside the Center for Human Rights and Constitutional Law , the Latino Community Foundation and Service Employees International Union California,

among others.

According to Gabriel, consultations with constitutional experts regarding the bill's language led to a number of amendments that put the legislation on "firm constitutional ground."

"The way the bill is currently written aligns exactly with the way that we respond to officer-involved shootings here in California that result in the death of an unarmed civilian," Gabriel said. "If a peace officer here in the state of California kills an unarmed civilian, then the (attorney general) does an independent investigation. We think that that should happen irrespective of the facts and circumstances."

Aaron Bandler

(Aug. 13, 2026 / JNS)

As the High Holidays loom, the fates of six bills that are “critically important” to California Jews will be decided before the state legislature on Thursday, David Bocarsly, CEO of Jewish California, told JNS.

“In one hearing, we’re going to figure out ‘who shall live and who shall die.’ It’s like a Yom Kippur question,” he told JNS. “There’s a lot of momentum heading into the final floor votes if they pass.”

The central High Holiday “Unetaneh Tokef” prayer states, in part, “Who will live, and who will die? Who in their time, and who in an untimely manner?”

If the bills make it through committee, they will go to a floor vote of the Assembly or Senate over the next couple of weeks, according to Bocarsly.

Unlike other committees, “the appropriations committee is not so transparent,” Bocarsly told JNS. “Decisions are oftentimes made by only a select few lawmakers behind closed doors based on what bills they want to move forward.”

“They can ultimately decide that any bill can’t move forward because of ‘costs’ even if there are other reasons, and we might never know why or why not,” he said.

The Jewish California sponsored all six bills. AB 2664 calls for 100-foot, protest-free buffer zones around entrances and exits to houses of worship, and AB 1836 expands the California Nonprofit Security Grant Program to include offsite events for eligible nonprofits.

AB 1853 bars hateful content in candidate statements in official voter guides, and AB 395 requires public schools and agencies to try to avoid scheduling major events, like graduations and public meetings, on holidays like Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.

AB 1763 excuses absences of religious students in public schools for holidays without requiring written parental requests and principal approvals, and SB 1387 calls upon state agencies to recognize Jews as an ethnicity under state law and in data collection.

Each bill “addresses a different part of the Jewish community’s needs,” some “emergent needs” and others “longstanding issues,” Bocarsly told JNS.

He thinks it will be a “big disappointment” if the bills don’t pass.

“My argument with each of these bills is that they have minimal costs,” he told JNS. “There shouldn’t be a reason why the state says that they can’t afford these bills when they are good policy.”

“While we remain optimistic that these bills will move forward, we will continue to fight to advance our community’s priorities, regardless of the outcome in the Appropriations Committee,” he told JNS.

Tony Strickland: Legislative Democrats' Bizarro World

By Tony Strickland

Orange County Register, The · 2026-08-07 · Section: Commentary · 710 words

"Bizarro World" is a place where everything is backwards, where words mean the opposite of actions, and where common sense is turned upside down. That is how I describe Sacramento and legislative Democrats, who talk about fighting for affordability but do the opposite.

In 2026, Sacramento Democrats and the governor promised that affordability would be a guiding priority. In January, Governor Gavin Newsom presented his state budget as a plan that would supposedly address affordability and support Californians. In March, Assembly Democrats announced their legislative priorities, saying they were "fighting for affordability" while highlighting housing, health care, and responsible government. Senate Democrats also claimed to emphasize affordability in their budget framework, saying they were focused on "the people feeling the greatest financial strain: working families and the middle class." But words alone do not lower the cost of living. Don't listen to the rhetoric. Look at the record.

I hear from constituents who are doing everything right, working hard, paying their bills, and trying to provide for their families. Yet they feel that living in California is becoming harder for them. They pay more for groceries, rent, gas, electricity, insurance, and everyday necessities. Small business owners face rising costs that make it harder to keep their doors open and create jobs. Young Californians wonder whether they will ever be able to afford a home in the communities where they grew up.

Despite repeated promises about addressing affordability, Sacramento Democrats push policies that will make California more expensive for families, students, and small businesses.

This year, they approved $14 billion in massive new taxes that will increase costs for all Californians, including a new software tax that will impact businesses that rely on digital services to operate. If you are a small business owner who depends on software for accounting, payroll, or point-of-sale systems, you can expect higher costs. And a new private healthcare tax means families of four can expect to pay an estimated $425 more per year. This year's budget is a whopping $352 billion, $5 billion more than what was proposed in the May Revision. The AI boom has brought in record-breaking revenues, which means there is no excuse for raising taxes.

A simple first step to address California's affordability crisis would be to pause the state gas tax, which is why I introduced legislation this year to provide relief to drivers. However, Sacramento Democrats and the governor declined to support a one-year suspension of the state gas tax. California drivers pay the highest gas prices in the nation, more than $1.50 per gallon above the national average, costing families hundreds of dollars more each year just to fill up their cars.

Californians are now paying 63.4 cents per gallon in state gas taxes. When Senate Bill 1 was enacted in 2017, the gas tax was 29.7 cents per gallon. In less than a decade, it has more than doubled. This increase is automatic and takes effect every year on July 1.

What is especially frustrating is that I have given my Democratic colleagues multiple opportunities to join me in suspending the gas tax, yet they have repeatedly failed to take meaningful action to provide relief for California drivers.

This proposal was a practical one. Nationally, the governors of Georgia, Indiana, and Utah have temporarily suspended their states' gas taxes to help residents manage rising fuel costs. In Congress, U.S. Senators Mark Kelly and Richard Blumenthal, both Democrats, introduced the Gas Prices Relief Act, which would temporarily suspend

the federal 18.4-cent-per-gallon gas tax through October 1, 2026, to help lower gas prices for drivers. If affordability is truly the priority, this year's budget does not reflect it. Californians want leaders who understand the challenges they face and make decisions that help them get ahead. Affordability should not be a slogan used during budget season or election year and should be the standard by which every policy decision is judged. Instead, Sacramento has become Bizarro World, a place where the party in charge promises affordability while making Californians pay more.

Tony Strickland represents California Senate District 36

California Forever has spent $455,000 since last year lobbying state lawmakers and the governor's office, according to its lobbying report released Friday.

The proposed development appears to have Newsom's blessing. The governor's office called a meeting Thursday to discuss the project with a couple of Solano County supervisors, California Forever representatives and Assemblymember Lori Wilson and Sen. Christopher Cabaldon, who represent the region.

Dee Dee Myers, who heads the governor's office of business and economic development that's been pushing for the development, was also present. In a memo last month, her office called the region a "world-class industrial site" and touted the importance of building a shipyard and an advanced manufacturing hub in the area.

"California is better positioned to attract billions of dollars in investment, tens of thousands of new good-paying jobs and a more resilient supply chain than it has been in decades," the memo said. "And no project represents this opportunity more clearly than the proposed Solano Shipyard and Solano Foundry."

Will Newsom's wildfire plan benefit utilities?

Newsom is also proposing legislation to address growing wildfire risks in California but is not giving specifics. Consumer advocates, wildfire survivors and insurers say he's trying to reduce utilities' liability for causing wildfires, shift wildfire recovery costs to insurance policyholders and make it harder for fire victims to get compensation or legal representation — claims Newsom's office declined to address.

Newsom spokesperson Anthony Martinez said discussions about potential legislation followed a California Earthquake Authority study in April that examined ways to better prepare California for natural disasters. The study was required by a last-minute deal Newsom and state lawmakers struck last year, which required utility companies to pay into the state's wildfire fund while allowing them to shift certain costs onto customers.

Wildfire Survivors First, a utilities-funded coalition despite its name, is lobbying state leaders to adopt several proposals listed in the study, arguing they would reduce wildfire risks and make property insurance more affordable.

Most legislative leaders were tight-lipped about the potential package. Sen. Ben Allen, a Los Angeles Democrat running for state insurance commissioner, said he would "carefully review" any legislation and urged against

proposals to "simply shift around the costs consumers pay." Democratic Sen. Sasha Renée Pérez, who represents Eaton Fire survivors, said she would oppose last-minute deals to cap compensation for fire victims. Business and labor clash over antitrust proposal Lawmakers will determine the fate of a controversial bill that would give Californians the ability to sue large companies in state court for using monopolistic practices to stifle competition.

The bill, known as the COMPETE Act, has infuriated the business community and set the California Chamber of Commerce on a warpath. The powerful industry group has called Assembly Bill 1776 "the largest expansion of antitrust law in world history" and warns its members that the legislation would "leave every business of every size in California vulnerable to massive legal liability."

Business advocates also argue that the bill gives predatory law firms a new way to shake down California businesses by opening the floodgates for what's known as "private right of action" lawsuits. For years, business owners have complained about California laws that allow activists and a cottage industry of lawyers to bombard them with cash demands and lawsuits over disability access, product warning labels, labor complaints and consumer privacy.

The legislation, authored by Assembly Majority Leader Cecilia Aguiar-Curry, a Davis Democrat, has support from labor-friendly progressive lawmakers, but also some who have more moderate records such as Assemblymember Jasmeet Bains and Senator Melissa Hurtado, both Central Valley Democratic lawmakers.

Several of the state's most powerful unions have lined up as co-sponsors, including the California Federation of Labor Unions, SEIU California and the United Food and Commercial Workers.

The bill is scheduled to be heard in the Senate appropriations committee on Aug. 10.

Counties seek reprieve from costly assault claims Los Angeles County is leading a behind-the-scenes effort to limit lawsuits from Californians who allege they were abused as children by public employees while in county or school district custody.

The effort comes in response to a deluge of lawsuits that followed a 2019 law that dramatically expanded the time people have to sue for the alleged abuse. Survivors now have until they turn 40 to file claims, rather than the previous cutoff of age 26 or within five years of becoming aware of trauma caused by the alleged abuse. The resulting litigation and settlements have cost counties and school districts billions of dollars. Last April, the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors approved a $4 billion settlement with 6,800 people who claimed they suffered abuse while in county juvenile detention facilities. Some of those cases dated back more than 65 years.

Lawmakers attempted to broker a compromise, Senate Bill 577, at the end of last session that would satisfy survivors and roll back the scope of the law to provide some financial reprieve to cash-strapped counties and school districts. But that effort, led by Sen. John Laird, a Democrat from Santa Cruz, couldn't gain traction, and Laird eventually shelved the issue.

Now, public employee unions are pushing for a reprieve again, largely to avoid potential pay concessions from their financially burdened public employers. Negotiations will likely take place at the Democratic leadership level between Limón and Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas.

EWG-sponsored California bills to boost consumer safety, choice and transparency

California, the world’s fourth-largest economy, could soon prove – once again – its status as a leader in environmental and public health policy that helps reshape the U.S. marketplace.

When Sacramento lawmakers return from recess next month, they’ll consider four EWG-sponsored bills that address key issues: energy affordability, “forever chemicals” pesticides, toxic chemicals in diapers and ultra-processed foods.

If enacted, these bills would help consumers lead cleaner, healthier lives through transparency, commonsense safety regulations and choice. They face further votes in the legislature in August before being sent to Gov. Gavin Newsom for his signature.

Using solar to lower sky-high electricity bills (Senate Bill 868)
The average California ratepayer faces electricity bills higher than those of most Americans. “Balcony solar” could help.

SB 868 would make it easier for everyone, including renters, apartment and condo dwellers, as well as owners of single-family homes, to plug into the sun using balcony solar systems – small, portable solar panels that can easily be set up on a patio or balcony and taken along when the owner moves.

The systems are inexpensive enough that ratepayers can recoup their investment within a couple of years, putting solar – and savings – within reach of more people. And the costs should decline as the market grows.

But complex rules make accessing balcony solar unnecessarily hard, if not impossible for many.

That’s why EWG is sponsoring this bill, known as the Plug and Play Solar Act, authored by Senator Scott Wiener. If enacted, it would ensure that balcony solar systems meet strict safety standards and remove hurdles for Californians who want to take more ownership over their utility bills.

SB 868 passed in the California Senate in May, and through the Assembly Utilities and Energy Committee in June. No major amendments have been added to this bill and the next step in the process is review by the Assembly Appropriations Committee.

Click here to read SB 868.

Widespread use of PFAS pesticides (Assembly Bill 1603)
This bill would address the use of the toxic “forever chemicals” known as PFAS that are currently being allowed to be used as pesticides in California.

More than 2.5 million pounds of these chemicals are applied to crops each year within the state, contaminating not just produce but soil and water too.

The bill follows EWG research showing state test results finding PFAS pesticides on nine in 10 California-grown samples of peaches, nectarines and plums. It’s critical to address this source of toxic pollution in the state that grows about half the country’s produce.

Our interactive map shows the California fields where PFAS pesticides are applied.

Click here to see the map.

As introduced, AB 1603, by Assemblymember Nick Schultz, would have banned the use, sale and manufacture of PFAS pesticides statewide beginning in 2035. It would have also immediately paused state approvals, phased out by 2030 the PFAS pesticides not allowed in Europe, and required public disclosure of PFAS pesticide uses.

AB 1603 passed the Assembly in May and went on to pass through two Senate policy committees in June, Environmental Quality and Agriculture, where it was heavily amended.

The Senate Appropriations Committee will next review the bill, followed by a full Senate vote.

The bill has been modified to no longer prohibit the sale or use of PFAS pesticides. It requires disclosure only. Still, that’s an important first step in addressing the use of these chemicals.

AB 1603 also maintains a categorical approach – viewing PFAS as a class of chemicals, rather than regulating them one at a time.

Click here to read AB 1603.

Baby diapers made of mystery chemicals (Assembly Bill 1901)
Many categories of personal care products are a virtual black box, their ingredients a mystery.

That’s especially true for baby diapers, since infants and toddlers wear them constantly for at least a couple years. Their developing bodies make them particularly vulnerable to toxic chemical exposure.

AB 1901, by Assemblymember Marc Berman, would require manufacturers of children’s diapers sold, distributed or manufactured in California to fully disclose their ingredients on product packaging and online.

Recent tests have found diapers may contain phthalates, linked to hormone disruption, bleaching agents associated with skin and respiratory irritation, and volatile organic compounds, including hazardous air pollutants like toluene and xylene.

Parents and caregivers deserve to know what chemicals sit for years on their child’s body 24/7.

AB 1901 passed the California State Assembly and the Senate Environmental Quality Committee. In August, the bill heads, with no major changes, to the Senate Appropriations Committee for review.

Click here to read AB 1901.

What is and isn’t ultra-processed food (Assembly Bill 2244)
UPF make up more than two-thirds of children’s diets and more than half of the typical adult diet in the U.S.

AB 2244 addresses the confusion shoppers face in distinguishing ultra-processed from less processed food, with the intent of helping to rein in skyrocketing and harmful UPF consumption.

If enacted, the bill would establish a system for certifying qualifying foods as free from the additives, emulsifiers, food dyes and flavors that often characterize UPF. It would tie that system to California’s first-in-the-nation definition of UPF, which was adopted last year as the result of an earlier bill, also intended to stem the consumption of UPF.

Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel is the lawmaker behind this bill and several other pioneering laws addressing food safety, especially for kids. His work has helped galvanize a national movement to address food chemicals.

AB 2244 passed the Assembly in May, when it was revised to give grocers more flexibility in how they display products sporting the UPF label. The Senate health and judiciary committees have passed the bill, and the Senate appropriations panel will consider it next.

Click here to read AB 2244.

About the Environmental Working Group
The Environmental Working Group is a nonprofit, non-partisan organization that empowers people to live healthier lives in a healthier environment. Through research, advocacy and unique education tools, EWG drives consumer choice and civic action.

Fate of $2B plan to fund Medi-Cal in Dr. Oz's hands - Plan would raise premiums by about $100 a year for the insured

By Grant Stringer gstringer@bayareanewsgroup.com

Walnut Creek Journal · 2026-07-17 · Section: News · Page A9 · 999 words

The fate of the state's $2 billion plan to maintain health insurance for low-income and disabled Californians is now in the hands of Mehmet Oz, the celebrity doctor and Republican administrator of the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.

State Republicans appealed directly to Oz in a July 6 letter, asking him to reject Gov. Gavin Newsom's plan to fund Medi-Cal, the state version of Medicaid, by raising a tax on insurance companies such as Kaiser Permanente and Anthem Blue Cross. Oz's agency has regulatory power over California's plan for the managed care tax. The proposed tax would likely increase the cost of a health insurance premium for a single person by about $100 per year, according to a nonpartisan state analysis. It would replace a portion of federal dollars lost to California as President Donald Trump's administration blocks states from using a budget maneuver to tap more federal dollars for Medicaid. Advocates say more Californians could lose healthcare coverage without the tax hike. A White House representative did not say when federal regulators might issue their decision but took shots at Newsom - a political foil for Trump who is expected to run for president after he leaves the governor's office in January.

"The administration cannot prejudge an application until it's thoroughly reviewed, but Gavin Newsom proudly pushing a plan that could jack up insurance premiums is on par for California Democrats," White House spokesperson Kush Desai wrote in an email.

Christian Beltran, a deputy director of legislation for the California Finance Department, said the proposed tax was crafted to comply with the federal requirements.

"If the federal government denies the proposal," he said, Newsom's administration "will review the rationale for the denial, assess options and determine next steps."

Newsom and state Democrats recently finalized the plan as they searched for ways to comply with elements of Trump's signature "One Big Beautiful Bill" act, which cracked down on tax maneuvers widely used by states to help finance Medicaid. Medi-Cal covers 14 million Californians who are low-income or disabled at no cost or reduced prices. When a patient with Medi-Cal goes to the hospital, the cost of their care is split between the state and federal government.

In the last fiscal year, the federal government spent $120 billion on the program, and California spent $45 billion from the state's general fund. As governor, Newsom has dramatically expanded Medi-Cal to cover more people and more care.

Federal law has long allowed states to tax hospitals and health insurers to inject more funding into their Medicaid programs. For more than a decade, California has taxed health insurance companies and funneled that money to Medi-Cal and the state's general fund. The California Association of Health Plans, which represents health insurance companies, supported the tax because it mainly benefited Medi-Cal.

California also used a budget maneuver to reimburse insurers, while extracting more funding from the federal government. When the state collected taxes on health plans, it would unlock more matching funds from the federal

government. After collecting the additional federal dollars, the state would refund most of the tax to the insurance companies. California made $7.6 billion in net revenue with this arrangement in 2024.

"It's an arcane financing structure that was hidden behind the scenes for a reason," said Rachel Linn Gish, a communications director for the nonprofit Health Access California, which advocates for patients. "It was like, 'Don't look how the sausage is made, we're glad that we're getting the $8 billion for Medi-Cal.' "

Every state but Alaska uses a similar "provider tax," according to the nonpartisan research firm KFF. Republican and Democratic presidents have tried and failed to eliminate such taxes over the decades. The Trump administration ultimately clamped down on the practice last year, describing it as a "loophole."

California Democrats, who anxiously pivoted to focus on "affordability" in the wake of Trump's 2024 re-election, said the president's policy forced them to pursue their planned tax hike on insurers. If approved by federal regulators, the tax would bring in billions of dollars less than the previous practice of taxing and reimbursing insurers while taking in federal funds, and the plan will slightly raise insurance premiums for individual patients. That would come atop other costs that drove a double-digit increase in private premiums at the beginning of 2026. "That is a direct consequence of a federal government that has been relentlessly dismantling safety net programs across the country," Jesse Gabriel, a Democrat who chairs the state's powerful Assembly budget committee, said in June.

The California Association of Health Plans opposed the tax increase, and a spokesperson said lawmakers should have pursued other options. The California Medical Association, which represents doctors, said it would raise costs and make accessing care harder for patients.

"Raising health insurance premiums to help balance the state budget is simply robbing Peter to pay Paul," René Bravo, the association's president, said in a statement. "It will only make it harder for families to keep coverage and get the care they need."

California's current tax will expire at the end of the year, leaving a potential funding gap if federal regulators deny the plan, said Adriana Ramos-Yamamoto, a policy fellow at the left-leaning California Budget and Policy Center. Lawmakers would have to start over, she said, looking for cuts or new revenues to help fund Medi-Cal and the state's priorities.

As Newsom and state Democrats grapple with the Trump administration's historic cuts to Medicaid, food assistance, subsidies for buyers of private health insurance policies and more, they have largely postponed planned cuts to the state's portion of funding for Medi-Cal.

Along with the tax hike, the agreement recently settled upon by Newsom and lawmakers delays the governor's plans to cut or freeze Medi-Cal coverage for immigrants without legal status until next summer. According to Health Access California, those immigrants will keep their dental coverage until July 2027.

Immigrants with legal status, including those granted asylum, will have until then to prepare for fee-for-service Medi-Cal coverage. Under those plans, care is not coordinated for patients - an approach that is less expensive for the state.

Laws that take effect this month

By Jim Glynn Suicide prevention

Madera Tribune · 2026-07-11 · Section: News · Page 5 · 996 words

Usually, legislation passed by the State Senate or Assembly take effect on January 1 of a specified year. However, this year, there are several bills that were passed in the 2023-2024 or 20242025 sessions that became law the first of this month.

Rural hospitals: The governor signed SB 669 (McGuire, 2025) into law on Oct. 11, 2025 and it went into effect on July 1 of this year. It addresses the shortage of maternity-care services in rural sections of the state. According to Sen. McGuire, some communities have become “maternity care deserts,” meaning that they have no maternity services available to the local population.

The new law establishes a 10-year pilot program that provides “standby perinatal services,” beginning with small, rural hospitals in Humbolt and Plumas counties. These hospitals must be more than 60 minutes away from the closest full-service hospitals.

Schools: Three new laws affecting schools went into effect this month, Senate Bill 760, Assembly Bill 727, and Assembly Bill 3216.

All-gender restrooms Senate Bill 760 (Newman, et al., 2023) requires that, as of July 1, schools must have at least one all-gender restroom with clear signage indicating that it is open to all genders. Such restrooms must be open during school hours when students are present and must be fully operational and well stocked, including menstrual products.

This bill is an amendment to the state’s Education Code to “ensure safe, inclusive, and accessible facilities for all students, particularly transgender and gender-nonconforming students.” Theoretically, it strengthens the state’s safety-and-inclusion mandates. And schools are subject to required compliance checks. Existing law, as of July 1, 2025, is intended to help prevent student suicides. According to CalMatters, the new law “requires a public or private school that serves pupils in any of the grades 7 to 12, inclusive, and that issues pupil identification cards, to have printed on the identification cards the number for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.”

Assembly Bill 727 (Gonzalez, et al., 2025) requires public institutions of higher learning, like two-year colleges and state universities, that issue pupil identification cards to print the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline phone number on the cards, including a special text line for a “specified LGBTQ+ suicide hotline.”

Phone-free schools Assembly Bill 3216 (Hoover, et al., 2024) is a bipartisan bill introduced by Assembly members Josh Hoover, David Alvarez, Josh Lowenthal, and Al Muratsuchi. It extends provisions on earlier legislation that is intended to reduce classroom distractions, cut down on cyberbullying, and promote the mental well-being of students.

According to provisions of this bill, school districts, including charter schools, must develop a policy to limit or prohibit students’ use of smartphones while on campus or under school supervision. However, there must be reasonable exemptions for emergencies, safety, and medical needs. CalMatters states that the policy must be reviewed and updated every five years.

Driverless cars Assembly Bill 1777 (Ting, et al., 2024) is a new state law which, according to Alexa Mae Asperin, writing for Fox 11 Los Angeles, “implements new traffic safety regulations specifically targeting driverless robotaxis operating on public roads.” The law, however, has many unknowns, probably because the technology is so new and

is changing so rapidly. Nevertheless, Asperin states, “AB1777 successfully closes a long-standing legal loophole by explicitly giving police the authority to officially cite autonomous vehicle companies for moving violations, mirroring the consequences faced by human drivers.”

At this point, specific financial or criminal punishments for companies that disobey the laws have not been formulated. It will probably be up to the Department of Motor Vehicles to establish protocols.

Police face masks Senate Bill 627, also known as the No Secret Police Act, was sponsored by Senator Scott Wiener, et al. and had support from several organizations, including MALDEF (Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund). The law bans law enforcement officers at both local and state levels from using face coverings. However, clear face shields that do not obscure a person’s identity are excluded.

On Nov. 17, 2025, former U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi filed suit against the Golden State, claiming that the new law would threaten the safety of officers and might cause their families to be harassed. There have been several court battles regarding the new law, both before and after Bondi was fired by President Donald Trump. However, as things stand now, the law is in effect in our state. Convertible pistols Assembly Bill 1127 (Gabriel and Stefani, 2025) went into effect this month. It prohibits the selling, exchanging, giving, transferring, or delivering of semiautomatic machinegun-convertible hand guns. These are pistols with a cruciform trigger bar that can be converted into a machine gun through the installation of a “pistol converter,” that interferes with the trigger mechanism, enabling automatic firing.

The penalties for violating the law are severe. An initial violation will bring a fine of $5,000. A second violation involves a fine and possible suspension or revocation of a dealer’s license. And a third violation will result in a misdemeanor charge and mandated revocation of the sales license. However, the law does not ban the existing possession of converted or convertible hand guns.

According to the All About Lawyer website, the state’s justification for the ban was prompted by the recent increase in such weapons in the hands of the citizenry. It states, “Recoveries of machine gun conversion devices by police, including Glock switches, increased by 784 percent between 2019 and 2023.” Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel said that he hopes this legislation “forces Glock to change its design so switches no longer work.” When interviewed by CBS News, he said that Glock has known about the design vulnerability for a long time. In 2023, 5,816 of these machinegun pistols were seized in California.

Aside from AB 1127, the state is also tightening its policy on the granting of CCW (Concealed Carry Weapon) permits. If this increases public safety, I suppose it’s a good thing, but it is definitely a burden on law-abiding citizens who require personal protection.

· · · Jim Glynn is Professor Emeritus of Sociology. He may be contacted at j glynn@att.net.
