Ballot Propositions: Much to Consider

As we’ve been hearing about this year, taxation for wealthy Californians is a hot topic of debate in the November 3 statewide general election. Overall, there are 14 statewide ballot propositions for voters to consider – with the Proposition 40 tax for billionaires being the most prominent.

There are also two LA County measures on the ballot; and nothing from the City of Long Beach in this election on ballot measures. Deciding on 16 ballot measures – along with who will be the new governor, the next LA County Sheriff, and winners of Congressional and state office races – are giving voters a full plate.

Of the 14 ballot initiatives, five ended up on the ballot through placement by the state legislature (Propositions 1, 2, 4, 5 and 43). Nine were placed there by petition signatures (Propositions 3, 37, 38, 39, 40, 41, 42, 44 and 45).

For LA County’s Measure A, voters will decide on a charter amendment that addresses labor disputes in the county and how they can be resolved. If contract negotiations fall apart, it would force the county and certain unions for public safety employees to go into binding arbitration. Measure E would create protections for the recently created Ethics Commission, which was authorized by L.A. County voters in 2024 through Measure G. It would provide greater independence and structure to the County of Los Angeles Ethics Commission, Office of Ethics Compliance, and Ethics Compliance Officer.

California’s Prop. 40 would levy a one-time 5% tax on the accumulated wealth of taxpayers and trusts with covered assets valued over $1 billion to fund state health care programs, food assistance programs, and public education. It was sponsored by the SEIU-UHW union, which has been leading the campaign in support of the initiative. It has been endorsed by U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders (D-VT), U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-CA), California Democratic Socialists of America, Teamsters California, and UNITE HERE Local 11. It’s been opposed by U.S. Rep. Kevin Kiley (R), Gov. Gavin Newsom (D), Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton, Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra, the California Teachers Association, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California.

Google co-founder Sergey Brin has played a leading role in organizing opposition through two other ballot initiatives. Brin has spent more than $138 million on the campaign against the measure, including getting these two competing initiatives on the ballot – Prop. 41 and Prop. 42.

Prop. 41 requires state laws or ballot initiatives levying a new special tax enacted after January 1, 2026 to require the government entities or departments receiving revenue from the new tax to eliminate their lowest-performing programs and reinvest those savings in higher-performing programs. It would require new tax proposals passed after the start of this year to follow the state’s annual spending limit. The nonpartisan state auditor would review new tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund.

Prop. 42 prohibits the enactment of new taxes after January 1, 2026 on ownership or accumulation of retirement holdings, individually owned assets and other forms of personal savings. It would bar new taxes on personal property such as businesses, investments, retirement accounts, trusts and art collections – which would block what Prop. 40 targets. It would also prohibit retroactive taxes, which would block a key part of Prop. 40: taxing wealth accumulated before the measure takes effect.

In total, opponents have raised more than $205 million to stop Prop. 40, according to campaign finance records accessed by CalMatters.

The Other Ballot Measures

Another potential tax measure for high-income earners in California is Prop. 3, which would make income taxes on higher earners permanent to fund education and healthcare. This tax was first enacted in 2012, and it’s set to expire in 2031. Under the measure, income taxes for top earners range from 10.3% (for individual income over $360,000) to 12.3% (for individual income over $721,000), with graduated rates in between. The California Teachers Association got this measure on the ballot, and it focuses on public education. For the collected taxes, 89% of the funds would go to K-12 public school and 11% would go to community colleges. It typically raises $5 billion to $15 billion a year, which makes up about 3% to 10% of overall K-12 spending.

Prop. 43 relates to taxation that can be adopted through local special taxes, which could include sales taxes, real estate taxes and utility taxes. Opponents say it would protect taxpayers by restoring Proposition 13’s two-thirds vote requirement to pass local special taxes. Courts have allowed special interests to pass earmarked tax increases with fewer votes. Prop. 43 closes this loophole, protecting taxpayers, homeowners and renters, say supporters. Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association is leading the opposition; supporters include California Professional Firefighters, California Federation of Teachers, and Nurse Alliance of SEIU CA.

What happens at upcoming state elections will be affected by Propositions 4, 5 and 39. Prop. 5 is the most discussed of the three, as it’s tied to recall elections of Gov. Gray Davis in 2003, Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021, and the author of Prop. 5, Democrat Josh Newman, a State Senator who was recalled on June 5, 2018.

Prop. 5 would eliminate the successor election when a state officer is recalled, leaving the office vacant until it is filled according to state law. Instead of having the recall election, depending on the office and the timing, a replacement would be appointed or elected in a special election.

If Prop. 5 passes, the governor would call a special election within about four months to replace a recalled state senator or assemblymember. If the governor was recalled within the first two years of their term, the secretary of state would call a special election. During the second two years of that governor’s term, the lieutenant governor would finish that term. The ousted official would be allowed to run for the same office in the special election.

Prop. 4 oversees election administration and campaign financing. It would allow the state and local governments to create programs that provide candidates with public funds under spending limits and eligibility rules. Public funding programs may not use funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety. It’s supported by the California Democratic Party, California Nurses Association, ACLU of California, California Common Cause, and Consumer Watchdog. Opponents include California Republican Party, California Chamber of Commerce, California Taxpayers Association, and Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, and Reform California.

Prop 39 invalidates mail ballots that do not have last four digits of a designated government-issued identification number written on the envelope. It would also prohibit in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote. Supporters include Latino American Political Association, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, and California Women’s Leadership Association. Opponents include ACLU California Action, Common Cause, and League of Women Voters of California.

Bonds, Other Funding Programs

A total of $44.65 billion in bonds could be approved on election day through Prop. 1, 37 and 38. Prop. 1 authorizes $11.25 billion in state general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs, including multifamily rental housing, mortgages for veterans, supportive housing, preservation of existing affordable housing, and downpayment assistance. It would cost the state $500 to $600 million annually for about 25 years to pay off. Supporters are US Vets; CA Federation of Teachers; Self-Help for the Elderly; Habitat for Humanity CA; CA Alliance of Child & Family Services, with no opponents submitted for the ballot.

Prop. 37 authorizes $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of purchase price of a newly constructed home priced below about $1.5 million. Borrowers must be California residents, occupy the home, meet income limits, and pay at least 3% down. Bonds are to be repaid by mortgage payments, and not by the state. Supporters include United Nurses Associations of California, California Conference of Carpenters, and California State Treasurer Fiona Ma. No opponents were submitted.

Prop. 38 authorizes $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research; half of the funds will go to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute, and half to research grants. Estimated fiscal Impact: an increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the research bond, with some or all of that cost offset if the funded research generates revenue. Supporters: Michael J. Fox Foundation, Alzheimer’s Los Angeles, Kidney Cancer Association, American Nurses Assoc/CA. Opponents: Robert M. Kaplan, Ph.D.

Prop. 2 increases the state’s Rainy Day Fund. That funding measure was approved by voters in 2014, to provide funding for education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns. This constitutional amendment would allow the state to deposit up to 20% of its general fund tax revenue in the state’s reserves, up from the current ceiling of 10%. Supporters include CA Professional Firefighters; LA Chamber of Commerce; Gavin Newsom; Xavier Becerra; and Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel. No opponents were submitted.

Prop. 44 imposes penalties on nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers (community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations) that spend less than 90% of revenue on “program services” advancing their charitable purpose, including but not limited to patient services. It’s expected to bring in increased state costs in the low tens of millions of dollars per year, covered by fees. No supporters were submitted. Opponents include American Academy of Pediatrics CA, CA School Nurses Organization, CA Academy of Family Physicians, and CA Medical Association.

The last of the 14 state ballot initiatives doesn’t involve upfront funds allocation, but it does require state and local governments to spend in the high tens of millions and possibly more than $100 million annually in initial costs, partly covered by fees. Prop. 45 amends California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects (including most housing, transportation, water, and health projects) by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. The assessment by Secretary of State’s office is uncertain, with potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects. Supporters include California Children’s Hospital Association, California Water Association, and California Council for Affordable Housing. Opponents include Coalition for Clean Air, CA Environmental Voters, Physicians for Social Responsibility, LA, and National Wildlife Federation.

The last day to register online to vote in the Nov. 3, 2026, general election is Oct. 19. Go to registertovote.ca.gov.

For more information on ballot measures and candidates, you can go to California Secretary of State’s Qualified Statewide Ballot Measures website; you’ll also get a print version in the mail if you’re a registered voter in California. The online version will show any updates to the ballot initiatives since the printing and mailing of the state’s Official Voter Information Guide.

The CalMatters 2026 Voter Guide and Ballotpedia 2026 Ballot Propositions websites offer additional information and perspectives on the November election.

Jon LeSage is a resident of Long Beach and a veteran business media reporter and editor. You can reach him at jtlesage1@yahoo.com.

Kamala Harris’ wasted year

DRIVING THE DAY — Kamala Harris has kept the door open to running for president again in 2028. What she failed to do over the past year, even one-time supporters and allies of the former vice president say, is give voters a reason to reconsider her if she does.

For Harris, according to interviews with nearly 20 Democratic Party donors and strategists in California and across the country, it was a missed opportunity to redefine herself — and ultimately a wasted year.

“She totally blew it,” said Doug Herman, who was a lead mail strategist for Barack Obama‘s 2008 and 2012 campaigns. “She hasn’t gotten into the mix.”

Harris has offered voters almost nothing in the way of specifics about how she would remake a Democratic Party hungry for change after another term of Donald Trump. She hasn’t spoken to how she would expand her own appeal to the voters who rejected her and she remains as reticent of media as ever, continuing to favor appearances before friendly audiences and at times drawing fire for shutting out news organizations altogether. She has entirely sidestepped the ideological civil war consuming the Democrats and has acted more like a party elder at a time when voters and donors are demanding a break with the past.

“I don’t see anything different myself. It seems like more of the same to me,” said Jim Hodges, the former governor of South Carolina, the first state on the Democratic nominating calendar. “Right now Democratic primary voters … are very anxious about a Trump acolyte being in the White House in 2028. And they want to select someone who they think has the best chance to win, but who also meets these requisites: fresh, new. I hear a lot of talk about that — ‘we don’t need recycled candidates.’”

Read more from Melanie and Jeremy on Harris’ lost year.

DEBATE NIGHT — Angelenos have their one and only chance to watch the two candidates for Los Angeles mayor debate on TV tonight — at a key moment in the race.

Incumbent Mayor Karen Bass has been on her heels for most of the summer, plagued by a string of bad headlines and polling showing her rival, Nithya Raman, either tied with the mayor or in the lead.

But the onstage face-off follows a rough week for Raman, who spent most of the week playing defense on public safety. Her interview with an online content creator set off a dayslong back-and-forth about whether she called Bass, Police Chief Jim McDonnell and the LAPD “fascist liars;” her campaign said she was referring to Trump’s immigration agents but quickly disassociated her from the clip. She reiterated her desire to replace McDonnell as chief, but then said she would do so when his term ends in 2030.

And Raman’s record got a tough look from the Los Angeles Times on Monday about how she has shifted her stances on major issues such as police hiring and so-called mansion tax voters approved in 2022.

In short, last week was a referendum on Raman, not Bass’ first term, which is exactly what Bass wants. Expect her to continue hammering Raman on public safety during the debate. Bass plans to keep the pressure on Raman offstage as well. Her campaign will launch a district-by-district tour of the city Wednesday, starting on Raman’s turf.

Raman, meanwhile, will likely seek to bring the focus back on Bass and her handling of the city’s homelessness crisis, budgetary straits and wildfire response — issues that have contributed to the mayor’s consistently high disapproval ratings. And she goes into the debate continuing to chip into Bass’ lock on support from Democratic power players, including recent endorsements from the Sierra Club and SEIU 121RN, a local representing nurses and licensed medical professionals that had backed Bass in 2022 and Raman’s opponent in her 2024 City Council race.

The debate will air from 7 p.m. to 8 p.m on NBC 4, Telemundo 52 and on the their respective websites.

GOOD MORNING. Happy Tuesday. Thanks for waking up with California Playbook.

WHO WON THE DAY? Los Angeles-area lawmakers, whose commutes to Sacramento just got an upgrade. Hollywood Burbank Airport’s new, $1.3 billion terminal opens today and replaces the nearly 100-year old building.

WHERE’S GAVIN? Nothing official announced.

¡HOLA, MADRID! Spain is becoming harder to ignore for anyone following trade, investment, energy, tech, defense and the global economy. Madrid’s political choices increasingly shape debates across Europe, with effects that reach the U.S. and ripple across the globe. Now Madrid Playbook, POLITICO’s first Spanish-language Playbook, is here with the inside line on the people, politics and decisions shaping Spain. Subscribe here

NEWSOMLAND

RAID REBUKE — Gavin Newsom condemned the Department of Homeland Security’s Monday morning raid of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home as “straight out of the authoritarian playbook.”

“Twenty-two days away from the midterm election, another politicized ‘investigation,’’’ Newsom wrote in a post on X. A senior Trump administration official granted anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation told POLITICO that Monday’s search is related to Omar’s immigration paperwork.

STANDING DOWN — Newsom, often one to relish confrontation with the Trump administration, sidestepped a fight over undocumented student workers, POLITICO’s Eric He reports, disappointing immigrant rights activists. The governor’s veto of a bill that would have required the state’s public universities and community colleges to make students in the country illegally eligible for campus employment prolongs a yearslong push for the first-in-the-nation policy that would have benefited roughly 60,000 students.

The governor’s unwillingness to force the issue with Trump stemmed, at least in part, from what he said in his veto message was a concern that the hiring requirement wouldn’t hold up under legal scrutiny since federal law prohibits employers from hiring undocumented workers.

Advocates for the idea that students living in the country illegally should be permitted to work campus jobs have relied heavily on a legal theory a group of UCLA law professors published in 2022 that argued the federal ban doesn’t apply to state agencies.

FOR GOOD MEASURE

FIRST IN PLAYBOOK: PROP 40 PUNCH — The campaign against the wealth tax is launching an ad featuring one of the architects of the measure, French economist Emmanuel Saez, referring to it as an “experiment.” It’s a soundbite the opposition had used before to call into question the soundness of the proposal — it previously launched a website including such a clip — but the six-figure ad buy puts money behind the bet that the quote can be packaged into an effective attack.

On the agenda: Saez, who teaches at UC Berkeley, is set to debate the measure at an event hosted by USC at noon, and later at UCLA at 6 p.m.

Further reading: “Who designed Prop. 40? Meet the academics behind California’s billionaire tax brawl” by the Sacramento Bee’s Ben Paviour

CAMPAIGN YEAR

ON AIR — Steve Hilton is keeping up his “go everywhere” media strategy, appearing tonight on a NewsNation townhall on the midterms co-hosted by Chris Cuomo and Stephen A. Smith. The program, Decision Desk 2026 Have Your Say: A NewsNation Town Hall, airs 5 p.m. to 7 p.m. PT and will also feature former Trump White House chief strategist Steve Bannon, former Chicago Mayor and Obama White House Chief of Staff Rahm Emanuel and Grace Mausser, co-chair of the New York City Democratic Socialists of America.

PARTY DIVIDE — The statewide insurance commissioner’s race has emerged as a flashpoint in the intraparty battle between the Democratic establishment and progressives, POLITICO’s Saqib Rahim writes.

For progressives, the insurance post represents a chance to transform policy in an influential — if little-known — role in the nation’s most populous state. And it offers an alternative route to power for a wing of the Democratic Party that flopped in this year’s gubernatorial race after billionaire Tom Steyer lost in the primary.

Jane Kim, representing the party’s left flank, says the insurance industry needs a “transformative shift,” and has proposed making the state a major provider of insurance against natural disasters for all homeowners. Ben Allen, a veteran Democratic lawmaker, said Kim’s platform was akin to “blowing something up with no plan,” and has proposed an extension of policies set by outgoing Commissioner Ricardo Lara, combined with efforts to reduce fire risk in communities that he says will attract insurers.

LOS ANGELES

FIFA FLOP — Los Angeles hotels experienced lower-than-expected room demand during this summer’s World Cup tournament, according to a new industry report.

The analysis and new survey conducted by the Hospitality Education and Research Organization (HERO), a project of the Hotel Association of Los Angeles (HALA), found that 72% of the hotels surveyed said the World Cup hurt their 2026 financial picture, and nearly three-quarters of hotels held staffing flat or cut it outright.

“Projections for World Cup visitors were based on optimistic assumptions that international spectators would be eager to travel and stay in cities like Los Angeles. When those projections fell flat, hotels and their staff ultimately paid the price,” said Jackie Fillia, HALA President & CEO.

TOP TALKERS

RON’S REGRETS — Democratic megadonor and venture capitalist Ron Conway regrets funding an influential Big Tech political group that has fought strict AI rules, according to former Obama press secretary Jay Carney, who leads communications for Conway’s new AI policy initiative.

“Ron, if he had to do that over again, he wouldn’t make that donation [to Leading the Future],” Carney said in an exclusive interview with POLITICO’s Decoded newsletter, referring to the pro-AI industry super PAC that was also funded by a16z’s Marc Andreessen and OpenAI’s Greg Brockman. Conway donated $500,000 to Think Big, the Democratic arm of LTF, last year.

It’s the first time Conway and Carney have publicly broken with LTF and deals another blow to the ambitious group, which has invested millions in causes like defeating AI safety advocate Alex Bores in a New York Congressional primary. Brockman also recently pulled out of a planned additional $25 million donation to the PAC, amid reported pressure from AI safety advocates within his company.

It also highlights how prominent tech donors are rethinking their allegiances ahead of the midterms amid public scrutiny of the sector, including its ties to bipartisan groups like LTF that have focused on common industry priorities: Billionaire donor Chris Larsen just split from pro-crypto PAC Fairshake following its decision to spend $30 million against Sherrod Brown in the Ohio Senate race. (Conway also notably cut ties with Fairshake over Brown in 2024.)

FIRE SPOTTERS — A network of nearly 1,300 remote, high-tech cameras are filling in blind spots in monitoring California’s most fire-prone areas — and artificial intelligence is helping respond to them, The New York Times reports.

Since 2023, artificial intelligence has instantly scoured Alert California camera footage, spotting wildfires before a 911 call is received in most cases. Officials then use the camera feeds to monitor the fires, coordinating teams at the scene. Real-time views are available to anyone on the Alert California website, and screen grabs and time-lapse footage help fuel fire incident pages and popular apps like Watch Duty.

One fire official says that the network has “changed the world of response.”

AROUND THE STATE

— At least 100 people have been detained in a surge of Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity in the San Joaquin Valley. (CalMatters)

— As overtime spending by the San Francisco Sheriff’s Department has soared, payroll records and overtime logs show the department has devoted millions of overtime dollars to work that fell outside its core responsibilities. (San Francisco Chronicle)

— At least five HIV clinical trials at UC San Diego were paused after the National Institutes of Health issued guidance last week that new enrollments should be put on hold. (San Diego Union-Tribune)

PLAYBOOKERS

Donna Tryfman Makes Her Case for a Bench Above Party Politics

By Alexandra Reed,

8 days ago

Beverly Hills resident Donna Tryfman is making her case for Los Angeles County Superior Court with a record of serious criminal trial work, leadership in the legal profession and support that crosses political lines. Running for Office 131 in the nonpartisan Nov. 3 election, the veteran public defender says the bench should serve everyone who enters a courtroom.

In written remarks supplied for this article, Tryfman rejected the idea of becoming a judge for a political side.

I do not profess to be a judge for a "side." I am everyone's judge.

She enters the runoff after finishing first in the four-candidate June primary. The county's final official returns show Tryfman received 612,858 votes, or 37.31%, ahead of Ross with 546,032 votes, or 33.24%.

Her support includes organizations with different political priorities. Americans for Democratic Action's Southern California chapter lists her among its judicial endorsements, while a Republican Party of Los Angeles County guide for the June primary recommended her for Office 131 through Reform California. The Democratic organization has a dual endorsement in the November contest, supporting both Tryfman and her opponent, David Ross.

Tryfman's campaign endorsement list also includes Democratic Assemblymembers Rick Chavez Zbur and Jesse Gabriel, former state Sen. Robert Hertzberg and former Los Angeles County District Attorney Steve Cooley. Her organizational supporters include labor unions, the Mexican American Bar Association and the Association of Deputy District Attorneys, according to the campaign.

Her coalition also includes a former competitor. In a July 16 campaign announcement, Tryfman identified administrative law judge Troy Slaten, who ran against her in the primary, among her endorsers.

Thrive LA, which describes its voter guide as pragmatic and nonpartisan, also recommends Tryfman. Its explanation emphasizes her capital homicide work, courtroom experience and service as a temporary judge.

That courtroom record is central to her candidacy. Her campaign biography reports more than 100 jury trials involving serious and violent felonies and a current assignment in the Los Angeles County Public Defender's Major Cases Unit, focusing on capital homicide litigation. She joined the office in 1998. In her April 22 West LA Democratic Club candidate questionnaire, she described herself as one of ten attorneys assigned to the unit handling special-circumstance homicides.

On her campaign website, Tryfman connects her courtroom work to the demands of serving on the bench.

That responsibility demands discipline, careful analysis of facts and law, and the ability to make difficult decisions under pressure...

Tryfman also received the 2025 Gideon Award as Felony Attorney of the Year, a distinction she identifies in the information supplied for this article as selected by her peers. The award is also cited in Thrive LA's endorsement.

"My leadership has been consistent," Tryfman said in the written remarks supplied for this article. Her record includes positions within the legal profession and in local public service.

The biography published by Americans for Democratic Action lists her past service as president of the Public Defenders Association and as deputy in charge at Eastlake Juvenile Court from 2016 through 2019. That assignment included supervising attorneys, mentoring younger lawyers and working in a collaborative drug court with prosecutors, judges and treatment providers.

Her legal service also includes work as a judge pro tem in traffic, small claims and unlawful detainer matters. In the April questionnaire, she reported being appointed by the Los Angeles Superior Court in 2018 and having sat approximately 40 times as a judge pro tempore. She also reported a 2025 court appointment to its Mediation Volunteer Panel.

Americans for Democratic Action's biography lists her as vice chair of the Los Angeles County Bar Association's California Conference of Bar Associations delegation and notes service on the association's Criminal Justice Section board.

In Beverly Hills, her public service has included chairing the Rent Stabilization Commission. The city's September 2022 Mayor's Cabinet agenda identifies her as commission chair, documenting a leadership role outside her criminal defense practice.

Her campaign biography also lists chairing the Beverly Hills Unified School District Facilities Committee. Americans for Democratic Action's profile notes her volunteer work as a Teen Court proctor at Dorsey and Hamilton high schools.

Her questionnaire also provides a specific picture of how she would run a courtroom. Tryfman pledged to provide adequate interpreters, explain proceedings in simple language and slow down when necessary to help people understand.

It is of utmost importance to me that everyone feels heard and seen in my courtroom.

Those priorities extend beyond her professional resume. The July campaign announcement pointed to her experience as a widow, single mother and daughter of immigrants as shaping her approach to judicial service.

The Los Angeles County Bar Association's Judicial Elections Evaluation Committee rated Tryfman "Qualified" in its April 27 announcement. Its evaluation considers professional ability, experience, competence, integrity and temperament. Ross received the same rating.

The contest is between two longtime defense attorneys. Ross describes 30 years of service as a public defender and alternate public defender on his campaign website. His campaign also lists support from the Association of Deputy District Attorneys and Cooley, making those endorsements shared rather than exclusive to Tryfman.

Tryfman describes herself in her written remarks as "reasonable, humble, and experienced." Her case to voters rests on extensive trial work, experience presiding in court, professional and civic leadership, and a commitment to treating people fairly regardless of political affiliation.

Disclosure: Russell Stuart of The Beverly Hills Standard, a BHUSD board member, is listed by Tryfman's campaign among her endorsers.

The Knock LA Progressive Voter Guide for the November 2026 General Election - Knock LA

Ground Game LA

Los Angeles, California, and the country at large are in danger. Major budget cuts to social safety nets at the federal level are impacting care in our state and city. Billionaires, tech elites, landlord lobbyists, and more are colluding in the dark to buy candidates that will make our systems continue to work for them rather than for working people. More people fall into homelessness everyday, and are eventually jailed or killed for the crime of having nothing. 

We’ll be honest, the state of everything can be overwhelmingly bleak. And it’s not really helped by the career politicians and “business as normal” candidates who don’t advocate for our communities. We need a lot more than just electoralism, but consider this a starting place. Vote today with our voter guide to find progressive candidates and “harm reduction” options. Tomorrow, find a local organization and give your time and talent to make LA a better place to live. Talk to your neighbors. Hand out water on a hot day. Make a poster, attend a protest. There’s a lot to do!

As always, we hope this voter guide makes your life a little easier in the hustle and bustle of daily tasks and to-dos. It is a labor of love for a better Los Angeles and reflects dozens of conversations with organizers, government staffers, lawyers, and everyday Angelenos. We pour in countless hours of research, writing, fact-checking, and editing to bring you these recommendations. It’s only possible with the powerful team at Knock LA — big props to our volunteers!

If you find this guide useful, we would be so grateful for any donation you can give, especially if you can become a monthly donor. These funds pay our bills and enable us to pay writers and editors for their stories on the BDS movement, LAPD’s surveillance network, and allegations of mistreatment in Project Homekey, among many others.

Knock LA is a journalistic project of Ground Game LA.

November 2026 General Election Races

Click on a section below to jump to those races.

  • City of Los Angeles
  • Los Angeles County
  • Judge of the Superior Court
  • Neighboring LA Cities
  • Ballot Measures
  • California State Legislature
  • US Congress

City of Los Angeles

Mayor: Nithya Raman

When the history books are written, what will they say about Karen Bass? How did someone who came into political life as a radical, traveling to Cuba with the Venceremos Brigade and protesting police brutality, find herself here, writing billion dollar checks to LAPD and smiling with Trump as ICE terrorizes her city? How does someone who co-founds Community Coalition go on to lead police crackdowns on the homeless and end needle exchange programs? How does an anti-apartheid activist live to become a genocide denier?

If we knew how, could we innoculate against it in our leaders and ourselves? All we know is that the world of people Bass fought for, and her willingness to stand up to power, shrank further and further. And that brings us here, to the end of her career — a champion for wealthy NIMBYs and the landlord lobby, trading favors with Airbnb, hoping LAPD’s fearmongering bullshit will let her hold on to a mayorship she doesn’t seem to want of a city that she has long since ceased to understand.

We refused to give her our recommendation in 2022. At first the announcement of her campaign was met with relief by Democrats hoping for an alternative to conservative mall-magnate Rick Caruso. It quickly became apparent, however, that she was completely uninformed about the struggles that had come to define LA politics: the rights of the unhoused, the role of LAPD, development and land use. She campaigned on feeding more and more of our budget into punishment and policing while regurgitating right-wing propaganda about an imaginary crime wave. And she prioritized NIMBYism over desperately needed affordable housing.

As mayor, she found new and unexpected ways to be disappointing. Her signature homelessness program, “Inside Safe,” has spent hundreds of millions of dollars while only a small fraction of its participants ever see permanent housing. Mostly, it serves as an excuse for encampment sweeps. Bass’ entire homelessness program has been focused on reducing visible homelessness rather than actually keeping people housed in the long term. The result has been an enormously expensive and inefficient program that only serves to make Angelenos cynical about the search for solutions.

Under Trump 2.0 Bass has attempted to cast herself as some sort of resistance figure. This is laughable. Days after Trump defeated Kamala Harris in 2024 Bass appointed Jim McDonnell as chief of police — the very same Jim McDonnell whose coziness with ICE led to him becoming the first Los Angeles sheriff to lose reelection in 100 years. This utter lack of concern for immigrant Angelenos is an example of how rudderless her office is.

Meanwhile Bass sat on her hands as LAPD began cracking the heads of anti-ICE and anti-Trump protesters. She took no action to protect her own constituents, who she claimed to support, from shocking violence at the hands of her police. Instead, she fought tooth and nail to give LAPD raises and new positions at the expense of city services — literally, the police defunding the rest of us. 

We haven’t even mentioned her failures surrounding the Palisades Fire, such as choosing to leave town in the face of what was already predicted to be an unprecedented and damaging windstorm. Time and time again she has frozen in the face of emergency — the Palisades fire, the ICE invasion, the Lineage warehouse fire — leaving a void where there should have been leadership. Afterwards there are always platitudes to mouth and scapegoats to find, and a city to pick up the pieces for itself.

Karen Bass has failed as mayor. It is time for her, and Los Angeles, to move on.

We urge you to vote for Councilmember Nithya Raman, whose run offers the possibility of a better Los Angeles. In many ways she was the prototype for all of the left’s electoral victories since 2020, winning a dramatic upset over incumbent David Ryu and putting the torch to the old assumptions of LA politics. She was the first to come into office seeking answers to the housing crisis, and she showed that there was a huge constituency for compassionate solutions to homelessness rather than cops and cages.

Nithya also has helped achieve major victories during her time in office, such as passing and then, with an expanding progressive bloc, strengthening the Tenant Anti-Harassment Ordinance. Her team has also been excellent on treating the unhoused with dignity and working to get people into housing and care rather than relying on violent sweeps, and she has been a consistent advocate for the right to counsel in eviction cases. Without her we certainly wouldn’t have the strongest package of renter protections this city has seen in 40 years. Her team set the model for staffing progressive offices and her housing and homelessness staff have kept her ruthlessly prepared and are lockstep with her in her strategy on building power as a minority progressive voice on council.

As the election has played itself out she seems to have found a voice that many (us!) had been worried she had lost, calling for the expansion of unarmed crisis response and the firing of LAPD Chief McDonnell. She has been quick to call out waste and abuse in the police budget, voting against Bass’ blank checks for LAPD. She is also partnering fruitfully with Controller Kenneth Mejia, promising him the resources and freedom to audit many of the city’s most important projects — authority denied by Mayor Bass. 

Nithya has also clashed with the left in the past, most recently over the implementation of the mansion tax Measure ULA, and understanding those clashes tells us a lot about the frustrations and pitfalls we might see in a Raman administration. During the campaign she has often been compared to Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York, particularly as her social media game has developed. Beyond the DSA endorsements and Indian heritage, however, the two are arriving at the work from very different places. Zohran comes from an organizing background, often citing the taxi drivers’ hunger strike as a pivotal moment in his political consciousness. He understands the inevitability of failing and falling short as he moved to the mayorship, and the role of the movement in keeping the pressure on him to fulfill his promises. That conflict, between the movement and the institution, is part of how he sees his work as developing.

Nithya comes from a policy and academic background, not from organizing. She was brought into politics not just from compassion for the unhoused, but from running the numbers, doing the analysis, and coming to an intellectual understanding of how the city was failing. She’s in many ways a technocrat, looking to subject experts to figure out what needs to be done. In that framework the continued demands of the movement aren’t seen as creating room for her to work. Instead they seem like an annoyance — Why are these people yelling? Don’t they know what the experts say? Don’t they know we’re doing as much as we can? This is a self-destructive approach to conflict, and one which pushes away allies and creates blind spots. Reports and academics, after all, are not the sole sources of knowledge, particularly when it comes to implementation.

What will a Raman administration look like? Will she be able to navigate the crises facing Los Angeles in the next four years: El Niño and climate disaster, another ICE gestapo invasion, the looming chaos of the Olympics, Hollywood consolidating under right-wing oligarchs? Time will tell. But we know our best chance to build a better Los Angeles, here in 2026, is with Raman in the mayor’s office.

Council District 3: Barri Worth Girvan

As we wrote in the Primary Voter Guide, the candidates running in CD 3 offer the same flavor of nothing to residents of the San Fernando Valley — just more cops and policing and a crackdown on homelessness. However, with Celona knocked out of the race, we’ll take a closer look at Barri Worth Girvan and Tim Gaspar.

Tim Gaspar is working hard to position himself as the “public safety candidate,” and with endorsements from just about every police union in LA County, it does seem he’ll win that distinction. His public safety plan is straightforward: more money for more cops and more surveillance technology. He does talk about “stopping crime before it starts,” but don’t be fooled: he’s not talking about affordable housing and higher wages, things that actually stop crime. Nope, he’s talking about programs like the LAPD Cadets — brainwash them young!

Barri Worth Girvan’s public safety platform is vague, but has the same underlying current of more money for cops. She wants to “modernize” the city charter to press for accountability, which sounds promising — but without details, it isn’t something we can put our support behind. 

On homelessness, Girvan has more to say, mostly about cutting red tape and pushing for more accountability for homeless service providers. But, again, she doesn’t talk about how she plans to do that. Gaspar, on the other hand, clearly wants to throw every homeless person in jail with a “zero tolerance” policy on encampments, saying “If help is refused, we’ll use every legal tool to clear the encampment.”

Neither Girvan nor Gaspar are candidates that the Valley truly deserves, but they are, unfortunately, the current available options. We recommend a vote for Girvan, as Gaspar’s absolute adoration of LAPD is something we need much less of in City Council.

Council District 9: Estuardo Mazariegos

Curren Price is lucky to be terming out of office, considering he’s currently on trial for 12 felony counts of corruption. While Price has been councilmember since 2013, CD 9 has been the victim of disinvestment for decades. The district contains the second-largest unhoused population in LA and is home to many Black Angelenos and recent immigrants, and needs a working-class champion to bring resources back into these neighborhoods.

Estuardo Mazariegos is the candidate for the job. An immigrant from Guatemala who grew up in South Central, Estuardo has devoted his life to his community. Over two decades of organizing, he has risen to co-director of Alliance of Californians for Community Empowerment (ACCE), one of the most effective working-class groups in the state and a key part of the coalition behind victories such as the creation of the Tenant Anti-Harassment Ordinance. Mazariegos has spent his career fighting for the often-neglected constituencies of low-income renters to have a voice at City Hall and in Sacramento. 

Mazariegos’ messaging has focused on the wage and rent exploitation by the billionaire class that extracts wealth from CD 9. His decades of both organizing experience and community-led policy advocacy means that his platform is deeply informed by conversations with tenants, workers, and marginalized people in the district. His primary goals are to ensure safe, accessible streets; build affordable housing and protect renters; and create green space and climate improvements in CD 9.

Jose Ugarte, on the other hand, is cut from the same cloth as predecessor Curren Price, whose office he is currently employed by. Ugarte failed to disclose years of income from the lobbying and political consulting firm that he ran at the same time he worked for Price, leading to a $25,000 fine from the Ethics Commission. Ugarte’s limited policy platform includes more homelessness sweeps and 41.18 zones, more bans on sleeping in vehicles, and more LAPD patrols — in short, more criminalization of poverty. He also wants to hire more women and people of color as police officers so the people brutalizing you look like your neighbors.

The choice cannot be clearer: vote for Estuardo Mazariegos.

City Attorney: Marissa Roy

Marissa Roy, deputy attorney general, is the clear and necessary choice. Previously a lawyer with the city attorney and now with the state attorney general, she has extensive litigation experience and the vision to transform the office into a leading force for progressive change. Roy aspires to be a city attorney for the people, using the power of the office to target polluters, slumlords, wage theft, and the Trump administration — which she does not hesitate to call fascist.

City attorney is one of the most important but least understood elected positions in Los Angeles. On the one hand, the office acts as the prosecutor for misdemeanors and has a direct policy impact on the criminalization of poverty and homelessness. On the other, the office is the counsel for the city as both defendant and plaintiff in civil lawsuits. The city attorney also advises City Council on the law and puts proposed ordinances into legal language. It does not take much imagination to see how much potential the office holds… or how badly it could go off the rails. 

The incumbent city attorney, Hydee Feldstein Soto, is one of the most unqualified and incompetent officials in the entire state of California. Her term in office has been marked by abuses of power, humiliating scandals, and ballooning liability payouts that bleed the city budget. This led to her utter defeat in June, knocked out of the general election with less than 20% of the vote. 

Now Roy is in a runoff with District Attorney John McKinney, a latecomer who previously made a failed run for district attorney in 2024 and who was there to absorb the police union’s money when a data breach led to LAPD abandoning the incumbent. McKinney boasts three decades of experience at the DA’s office, which he falsely claims makes him the more qualified candidate. On the contrary, his tough-on-crime posturing — absurd in an office that can only prosecute misdemeanor offenses — reflects a man who had given no thought to what the office entailed before he filed to run. 

In May, he offered the Los Angeles Times this inanity: “McKinney, 58, said he wants more aggressive prosecutions for misdemeanor gun crimes, and believes the city attorney has the power to ‘leverage’ homeless people into mental health or addiction treatment after they’ve been arrested.”

McKinney is, in fact, unqualified for the office — not only has he clearly never considered the specific role of the city attorney, he has not one single day of civil law experience, in an office that is the primary civil litigation firm for the second largest city in America. 

His attempts to patch together a platform read like a game of charades — piecing together “police liability settlement” and “environmental lawsuit” from a consultant’s frantically waving hands. Let’s not fool ourselves. We’ve seen the upshot of an unqualified city attorney — under Feldstein Soto, liability payouts have increased 35% every year, to a crushing $287 million.

What this vitally important office needs is someone who understands the issues and the stakes. Only Marissa Roy has a clear plan to reduce our liabilities but also change the way the office operates. As a former city attorney and someone who has been frankly obsessed with the office for the past six years, Roy understands the power of the office to shape policy, to protect the budget, to advocate for the resident, and to find the windfalls in corporate law enforcement. She has the ability to speak convincingly to any audience without hedging her principles, and knows the value of education and politics that are needed to make progressive policy last.

What we do not need is another “tough prosecutor” who, like Hydee, thinks that glaring angrily at shoplifters can substitute for the management of the legal needs of the entire city of Los Angeles. That sort of leadership has blown a hole in our city budget and left us defenseless against the illegality of the Trump administration.

Marissa Roy is the only candidate in this race who understands the office, who treats it with the seriousness it deserves, and who has a clear vision of how to manage it to the benefit of the city. In many ways, her campaign is one for basic fairness and justice under the law. What if the theft of money from a worker were treated as seriously as the theft of money from a corporation? What if laws around pollution, or predatory lending, or tenant harassment were treated as seriously and pursued as aggressively as sleeping on the street? The choice to treat laws that punish the poor as sacrosanct and laws that restrict the rich as optional is a political one. 

We get to make a different choice. Vote for Marissa Roy.
