LA County

Sheriff: Robert Luna

Sheriff Luna has maintained a subdued status quo over his first term, keeping himself out of the headlines and focusing on rebuilding the many bridges burned by his predecessor, neckless fascist Alex Villanueva. This quiet approach has paid off as a management strategy, but it hasn’t addressed the department’s deep-seated problems; in many ways it seems that the goal of his tenure has been to cut down on scandalous headlines rather than fix underlying issues. Deaths at the county jail, which his department operates, have reached the shocking level of almost one per week, leading to a lawsuit by the state attorney general. No effective steps have been taken against the deputy gangs that thrive in the underbelly of the department. And, during last summer’s protests against the Trump regime’s mass deportation policy, LASD dealt out horrific violence to peaceful demonstrators, gassing and beating without restraint, and Sheriff Luna explicitly lied to the media to justify it.

Lucky for Luna, his opponent in this runoff is neckless fascist Alex Villanueva. The former sheriff’s disgraceful record hardly bears repeating: baselessly investigating political opponents, defying subpoenas, protecting deputy gangs, hiring and promoting abusers, building an unpermitted helipad at his house, and on and on and on. LA’s dollar-store Trump spent the last four years fuming fruitlessly in front of his webcam to an audience of dozens, and has crawled out of his man cave for a campaign that amounts to nothing more than a resentment tour.

From our perspective Luna has failed in many respects, but Villanueva is a man who should never be allowed a scintilla of authority ever again, so we’re going to vote against him. And, let’s be honest, handing Villanueva another thrashing at the ballot box is going to feel fantastic.

Judge of the Superior Court

In Los Angeles, judges are elected to six-year terms in countywide races, which in a county of 10 million people ensures that no candidate can reach more than the tiniest fraction of the electorate. This means that incumbents are impossible to beat unless they’re up to their necks in scandal, and even then a judicial PAC protects even the most loathsome among them. Judicial hopefuls go to war over the open seats — futures are often decided by a game of musical chairs at the County Registrar, leaving a lucky few running unopposed. This is obviously a great system and a credit to democracy.

Finding meaningful information about the candidates also poses an enormous challenge. Your average campaign website has a list of endorsements, some vague language about fairness and the law, and a smiling photo of a person in a suit. That’s why we’re here. Our recommendations are based on dozens of conversations with progressive lawyers and organizers.

Part of the purpose of this guide is to push back against the biases built into what little information is available. The Bar Association, for example, rates candidates on their “qualifications” in a manner that privileges prosecutorial experience over defense or civil work. In the race for Seat 64, for example, they rated Public Defender Haymon as only “qualified” with 26 years of experience, and District Attorney Ghobadi as “well qualified” with 17.

Many other publications also fall for the fiction that “nonpartisan” judicial races are politically neutral. The police unions certainly don’t believe that: they endorse the judges they think will be most friendly to an agenda of criminalization and imprisonment. We also see the intervention of groups like the Crime Survivors PAC, a Trumpist Republican group that prospective judges list proudly on their websites. Even without those extremes, there is a meaningful difference between a judiciary made up of white male ex-DAs and one with a diversity of cultural, class, and professional backgrounds.

Seat 64: DPD Rhonda Haymon

Rhonda Haymon is an experienced trial attorney who boasts more than 25 years as a public defender. In our research we heard both pros and cons: praise for her grit and determination as an advocate, criticism of her ability to work collaboratively. She has the endorsements of Judges Holly Hancock, George Turner, and Ericka Wiley, who won election as part of a movement to expand the diversity of background and experience in the judiciary; she also is endorsed by La Defensa, who helped power slates of progressive judicial candidates in previous cycles. She is highly skeptical of automated “risk assessment” tools, and emphasizes the need to uphold and protect constitutional rights even when they go against the preferences of an individual judge. We recommend her for this seat.

Seat 65: Anna Reitano or Justin Clayton

This is a rarity: a race with no bad choices. 

In the four-way primary we recommended a vote for Reitano, who as part of the original Defenders of Justice slate had the campaign experience to break through and ensure a good candidate in the runoff. The electorate did all of us a favor — no matter what happens, we’ll get a decent result in Seat 65. 

Anna Reitano is an attorney with Los Angeles County Counsel and a former public defender. She emphasizes the breadth of her experience in law as preparing her for an office that might take her to civil trials, family court, or any other branch of the legal arena. During her time as a public defender she emphasized the importance of mental health diversion and treatment.

Justin Clayton is a career public defender and deputy in charge at the Inglewood office. He touts his leadership and management history that will help him control a courtroom, and highlights the need to protect the rights of litigants across language and cultural barriers, vital in a city of over a hundred spoken languages.

Both Reitano and Clayton boast more than a decade of heavy courtroom and trial experience with the public defender’s office. Both have a wide range of endorsements. It’s a shame that two qualified candidates are stuck in competition for a single office.

Seat 87: DPD Anthony Bayne

Anthony Bayne boasts a quarter century of experience at the public defender’s office, including 19 years at the Compton courthouse in roles ranging from defending the most severe felony offenses to the supervision of new misdemeanor attorneys. His broad experience with the courts at every level puts him head and shoulders above his competition for the seat.

Seat 131: DAPD David Ross

For those who don’t know, the county has two public defender offices. The alternate public defender, where Ross has worked for more than 25 years, handles cases where there are multiple defendants or conflicts of interest between them that would disqualify the public defender — the same work, but under a different banner. Before becoming an attorney, he spent a decade as a journalist. He has an excellent resume and a commitment to the people left behind by our system. In interviews he impressed with his thoughtfulness and temperament. He’s both the progressive choice and the most qualified candidate.

Public Defender Donna Tryfman is also in the runoff. She faced allegations of verbal abuse and misconduct during her previous campaign for Beverly Hills School Board, where she ran on a platform of forcing teachers back into the classroom against COVID-19 guidelines. She has also been accused of harassing coworkers who expressed opposition to the genocide in Gaza. We do not believe that she has the character or impartiality to serve on the bench.

Neighboring LA Cities

Burbank

Burbank has a solid progressive bloc of electeds to maintain in 2026, to the benefit of everyone in LA County who can look to these leaders as a blueprint. As a center of the entertainment industry – and home to Warner Brothers, recently bought up by Skydance – Burbank is sure to be a center of political action in the next cycle. Three progressive candidates are running for the three seats available on Burbank City Council.

Mike Van Gorder

We are back again with another recommendation for Mike Van Gorder, who ran in the previous election in a slate with Konstantine Anthony. His platform is refreshingly straightforward on the policies he will be advancing to protect tenants (makes sense since he is a founder of the Glendale Tenants Union and formerly a housing policy analyst for SEIU Local 1000), immigrants, bike and street safety, and small businesses and jobs. Van Gorder’s 2026 campaign has kept his slate of progressive endorsers from his first campaign and added institutional supporters. He has been a strong advocate for entertainment workers and unions – given the major anti-labor changes the film and TV industry has been entertaining, Burbank would do well to bring a good advocate into office and elect Mike Van Gorder.

Nicole Jane Perez

Former Burbank Mayor and councilmember Nicole “Nikki” Perez was Burbank’s first Indigenous and openly LGBTQIA+ councilmember. As a Burbank native with a social work background, her tenure in office has been marked by an impressive array of pro-worker/pro-tenant policies and programs aimed at keeping Burbank affordable, inclusive, and safe. She introduced a ban on Automatic License Plate Readers (including Flock) and has mobilized resources to Burbank residents impacted by ICE. Perez’s continued experienced leadership will be crucial under these federal circumstances.

Nolan Southerland

Nolan Southerland has positioned his campaign to be a promising addition to the Burbank squad. His platform commits to continuing his advocacy as a member of the Burbank Tenants Union and 15 year member of IATSE local 700 through the powers of the seat. Southerland has also garnered the endorsement of City Controller Kenneth Mejia, Burbank elected Kontantine Anthony, and notably the LA Labor Fed, a very rare get for first time candidates. Southerland will be another experienced voice in the pro-entertainment worker bloc on council and his priorities include protecting immigrants, auditing and reviewing military-grade law enforcement equipment, and bus and bike friendly infrastructure.

Santa Monica

Santa Monica City Council (3 Seats): Mayor Caroline Torosis, Danny Ivanov, and Brett Morrow

Santa Monica chooses three new councilmembers for at-large seats this November. There are three solidly pro-tenant options up for election.

Mayor Caroline Torosis has been a champion for renters, establishing Right to Counsel for tenants facing eviction, supporting long-term solution building policies like tenant opportunity-to-purchase which gives tenants a first bite at the apple to buy their building when it goes on the market. She was formerly a Rent Control Board member and has defended Santa Monica’s rent stabilization. 

Santa Monica’s pro-renter slate also includes Chief Communications Officer for the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health Brett Morrow who articulated nuanced housing and development positions which center non-displacement of existing tenants and current Rent Board chair Danny Ivanov who while strong on tenants issues could improve on wealth taxation, immigration, and policing. For their united pro-tenant agenda, and progressive endorsers, they should all have your vote.

Santa Monica Rent Stabilization Board (3 Seats): Sue Himmelrich, Heather Thomason, and Kurt Gonska

Similarly to city council, Santa Monica’s Rent Stabilization Board also has three open seats with a good selection of candidates.

Sue Himmelrich was a volunteer attorney for the Legal Aid Foundation of Los Angeles, major supporter of Measure GS and GSH and is currently Special Counsel at the Western Center on Law & Poverty. Himmelrich also has a strong pro-tenant record in public office for Santa Monica. Her incredible resume fighting for tenants makes her an easy recommendation.

Heather Thomason’s campaign for Rent Stabilization board comes from the experience of being displaced multiple times as a renter. Her story and commitment to renters is well laid out in her Santa Monicans for Renters Right’s questionnaire. She is a WGA member, renter, strong advocate for rent control, and non-displacement. 

Kurt Gonska is running for re-election on the Rent Stabilization Board. Also a strong candidate but not as clear on ULA style Measure GS “taxes prevent development” as we would like. 

Soledad Marcial is also running and it’s worth noting that her website is in English and Spanish. She is from Pico and it is great to see Pico represented through a candidate in this race.

West Hollywood

This November, West Hollywood voters have the opportunity to elect three councilmembers from a pool of candidates. Fortunately, there are three choice candidates: Chelsea Byers, Helen Krieger, and Stephen Post.

You can find everything you need to know about your local voting options can be found on the City Clerk site here.

Chelsea Byers

Chelsea Byers has been an incredible champion for tenants in West Hollywood. As an active partner with organizations like Working Families Party, she has consistently centered renters and affordability in her city. She also pushed to strengthen West Hollywood’s Rent Stabilization Ordinance, which is now among the strongest in California. As extreme heat protections are starting to become a reality here in LA, West Hollywood under Byer’s leadership has already taken steps to protect renters by establishing a maximum indoor temp of 82 degrees for rental units. She has also moved quickly to bolster West Hollywood’s sanctuary city ordinance and vote down Flock contracts. An easy, strong recommendation for Chelsea Byers, so tell your WeHo friends.

Helen Krieger

One of the few candidates who are willing to call out car dependency directly, Helen Krieger’s platform highlights the very real dangers of traffic deaths compared to the falling rates of violent crime. Krieger does invoke active partnership with law enforcement but her approach to Flock cameras shines some light into her perspective on public safety and privacy. She proposes that WeHo might develop its own digital privacy policy but it falls short of being a stalwart opponent to the intrusion of corporate and surveillance architecture in our lives. For a city with historic queer and immigrant communities, we would prefer to see a stronger position on this. 

Walkability and bikeability are major concerns for her as well as development that suits the need for more affordable housing units while tailoring the approach to the neighborhood. Her experience living in New Orleans through Hurricane Katrina and advocating for the development of affordable housing in the aftermath is part of what set Krieger on this path.

Stephen Post

With a strong backing of progressive west side and city wide organizations, Stephen Post has demonstrated that he is paying close attention to the advocates of LA and is serious about effective solutions that put people first. His housing justice approach includes models of social housing, like public housing, and expanding the affordable housing that is so deeply needed in LA. His work with cannabis decriminalization and clear positions on ICE and Flock shows real concern over the needs of targeted and marginalized communities, as opposed to criminalization-for-the-sake-of-public-safety theater. All this in addition to his considerable advocacy lobbying and experience on governmental bodies is a promising sign for people hoping to see a thriving, progressive, West Hollywood.

Ballot Measures

Statewide

State Measure 1: Yes

The approval of Proposition 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in bonds in order to fund affordable housing programs. The majority — $10 billion — would go towards homeownership programs, farmworker housing, affordable student housing, tribal housing, and other initiatives. If voters approve it, the bond sale is expected to finance up to 40,000 multifamily rental units and assist another 40,000 households with buying a home. The remaining $1.25 billion would specifically be allocated to veteran housing.

It is no secret that California’s housing crisis is beyond concerning. Creating financial support for affordable housing, rent-burdened households, and vulnerable populations is a step towards remedying the absolute inhumanity of more than 187,000 people being unhoused in the state of California.

State Measure 2: Yes

If approved, this proposition would amend the California State charter to move 20% of general fund tax revenue into reserves — also known as the Budget Stabilization Account (BSA) — increasing the ceiling from the previous 10%. Approval would also authorize spending tax revenue to pay down the state’s federal unemployment insurance debt, totaling $20 billion, through a change in how “excess” capital gains revenues are calculated. The proposition would change the relationship between deposits into the BSA and the state spending cap, commonly called the Gann Limit. Put in place by voter-approved ballot initiative in 1979, the current spending cap law limits growth in state and local government spending funded by tax revenue and requires that the government will remit funds to taxpayers when the limit is exceeded. Under current law, deposits into state reserves are counted as dollars spent and dollars withdrawn are not counted as spending. The approval of Proposition 2 would codify the inverse: deposits into reserves would not count as spending, while withdrawals would. 

More money in California’s savings account is a good thing. Period. This proposition is opposed by right-wing groups like Reform California, an ultra-conservative PAC that is chaired by conservative activist and sentient frown line Carl DeMaio. So take from that what you will.

State Measure 3: Yes

This ballot measure extends a tax on the top 2% of income earners, first enacted in 2012. The new measure, titled The California Children’s Education and Health Care Protection Act, will make permanent a range of income taxes for high-earning individuals, beginning at 10.3% for people making $360,000 per year and capping at 12.3% for those making $721,000 or more per year. The overwhelming majority of revenue collected from this tax — which totals up to $15 billion annually — funds California’s public schools. The remaining 11% goes to community colleges and any extra is allocated to public healthcare. 

Allowing this tax to expire would cause up to a 10% budget cut for California public schools. One in six public school teachers would face termination as a result. Essential programs, like free lunch initiatives, would be cut, just to fund a handout to the wealthiest Californians. Our recommendation needs no further explanation: vote yes.

State Measure 4: Yes

Prop 4 would end a ban on public financing for campaigns and allow local governments to build programs that provide political candidates with public funds. State law allows charter cities to distribute public funds for campaigns, but not state and county governments. If passed, Prop 4 would require the creation of expenditure limits and other criteria for candidates seeking public funds. Campaigns would be prohibited from using the money for legal defense fees, fines, or repaying personal loans. 

This proposition doesn’t create a public financing plan, but makes it possible for us to fight for the creation of an equitable system. In a world where money still sways elections, public financing has been a powerful tool for working people to participate in politics. If you follow Los Angeles politics — which you probably do, you’re reading Knock LA — you’ve seen matching funds make it possible for progressive challengers to compete with the big money of the Los Angeles Police Protective League (LAPPL) or the landlord lobby. At the same time, many of our favorites in other cities or running for state legislature have been swamped by wealthy interests.

Prop 4 would help us open our elections to candidates who do not have personal fortunes or a network of rich donors. Vote yes.

State Measure 5: Yes

Under current California law, a special election to select a successor occurs at the same time as a successful recall removes someone from office. This bizarre system means that a much smaller plurality of voters can drive a recall and replace a majority-elected official. Prop 5 would require a public office to remain vacant after an official is recalled rather than the position being filled by a simultaneous election. It would also allow said recalled officials to run again for the office they were recalled from if there is a special election, and the measure would authorize the lieutenant governor to step into a gubernatorial vacancy if the governor is recalled. 

Recalls are a tool that conservatives and right-wing activists love to haul out when they’re upset about the policies set by Democratic lawmakers, or even the simple fact of their existence. Unsurprisingly, the California Republican Party came out in opposition to Prop 5, because the current anti-majoritarian recall system is essentially their only chance to capture a statewide race. Anti-progressive, cave-dwelling Reform California is also among this proposition’s opponents. 

This is a basic measure to make our elections more rational and more small-d democratic.

State Measure 37: Yes

Election season is not complete without at least one mysteriously worded ballot measure about homeownership. In that way, Prop 37 provides. 

If passed, Prop 37 would create a second mortgage program for qualified homebuyers on qualified homes, with $25 billion in bonds to fund the program. “Qualified homes” are defined as newly constructed homes, townhomes, row houses, condominiums, and residences in nonresidential buildings — key words: “newly constructed.” Proponents of Prop 37 include, unsurprisingly, realtors and the construction trades. The mortgage under this program would cover up to 17% of the purchase cost, essentially pushing the down payment to 3%. The most likely beneficiary, then, would be a household with stable middle-income work but without the savings for a down payment. 

While this can provide some real benefits for homebuyers without ready capital, it’s not a real solution for the housing crisis. Think of it as an industry subsidy, providing demand-side funding to encourage new construction; realtors like it because it increases home sales, unions like it because it increases construction work.

We’re not opposed to this proposition, but it is hardly a cure for the housing crisis.

State Measure 38: No

This proposition would issue $8.4 billion in bonds to support immunology and Alzheimer’s research. We sure do like medical research, don’t we? 

But there’s a catch. This proposition is designed with a number of specific conditions on who qualifies for this funding. So specific, in fact, that only one institution would qualify: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, which happens to be chaired by the chief funder and proponent of Prop 38. 

This is a total corruption of the ballot process and not how we should be funding medical research. Vote no.

State Measure 39: No

It’s a big, resounding “no” on this one. Prop 39 would require all California voters to show a government-issued ID when voting in person and to provide the last four digits of a government-issued ID when registering to vote by mail. Election officials would also be mandated to maintain “accurate” voter registration lists and to ensure that all voters on said lists are US citizens. As California law stands, voters are already required to show a government-issued ID and social security number when registering to vote, but are not required to do so at polling places. 

This is an anti-democratic move by conservative lawmakers who continue to project about election fraud. It is another way for them to make voting more difficult and to create barriers for young people, people with disabilities, and low-income voters. This measure is supported by the California Republican Party and billionaire-backed Reform California.

Tell them to go to hell and vote no.

State Measure 40: YES!

This measure is a billionaire tax. It would require the approximately 200 billionaires in California — who are defined as taxpayers with assets valued at $1 billion or more — to pay a one-time, 5% tax at the start of 2027. 90% of funds would be earmarked for healthcare, and the remaining 10% allocated to education and food assistance. 

This is absolutely vital. Trump’s administration slashed $100 billion of Medi-Cal’s federal funding. Without Prop 40 revenue, millions of people in California will lose their healthcare. Hospitals will close. Medical workers will be laid off. People will fucking die.

There is another reason this proposition is necessary, and why the worst bootlickers in the state are trying to block it. Prop 40 asks us whether the oligarch class, who have amassed more wealth than any person could spend in a dozen lifetimes, are subjects of our democracy. Everyone subject to this tax will, in spite of it, end the year richer than before. They are not threatened by the hit to their pocketbooks, they are threatened by the possibility that they might be in any way accountable to the people.

The corrupting influence of money in politics can be seen in the ghoulish way some liberal lawmakers and organizations have come out against Prop 40. All we have to say is that those people — Gavin Newsom, Xavier Becerra, Katie Porter, and all the rest — have betrayed you. They have chosen to side with the absolute impunity of the billionaire class over your right to health and life. They would sooner see you and millions of Californians like you sicken and die before calling on the richest people in the history of the world to pay a fraction of their fair share.

Vote yes, and don’t forget.

State Measure 41: NO!

Off the bat, it’s a no. Prop 41 was introduced as a way to nullify and defeat Prop 40. It contains language that could make taxation more complicated, but that’s secondary to its main purpose. 

Along with its companion ballot measure Prop 42, it contains language stating that if this measure receives more votes than Prop 40, then Prop 40 does not go into effect, even if Prop 40 passes. It was put on the ballot to confuse the electorate. No for this one and for the following one, too.

State Measure 42: NO!

This measure would create a ban on new taxes that target personal property, and was, similarly to Prop 41, designed to block the billionaire tax. Like its counterpart, Prop 42 would make Prop 40 null and void if the former receives more votes than the latter. Also like 41, this measure was put on the ballot by the billionaires who think they can put one over on the voters. 

No on both 41 and 42.

State Measure 43: No

Prop 43 is about limiting the ability for new taxes to be proposed and enacted. It would raise the threshold for new, local ballot measures that propose, increase, or extend special taxes initiated by individuals to pass. Currently, the California Constitution requires local tax measures proposed by local governments to be approved by a two-thirds vote and those proposed by citizens to be approved by simple majority. Prop 43, if passed, would push the latter’s threshold for enactment up to a two-thirds vote. Requiring a supermajority would make it almost impossible to pass any tax, destroying the ability of the state to fund itself.

This is more bullshit from the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, one of the most destructive groups in the history of the state. The ultimate goal of this measure is to make it impossible for the state to raise revenue or fulfill the basic functions of a government.

Vote no.

State Measure 44: No

A tough one in terms of parsing the language in its text. If passed, the measure would require federally qualified health centers (FQHCs) to spend at least 90% of their annual revenue on advancing the center’s mission. “Require community health clinics spend 90% of revenue on program services” seems great. However, this would come at a steep cost. This is intended to target executive pay and overhead costs… but what qualifies under this proposition? Does training and recruitment count? What about facility maintenance, or data security, or legal advice to determine Prop 44 compliance? “The Attorney General decides” is not a great way to do business, particularly when noncompliance comes with monetary penalties.

Clinics must meet certain criteria to be classified as an FQHC, including being located in or serving a high-need community and providing services on a sliding scale. So this measure, if passed, would place greater restrictions and penalties on clinics that serve low-income, rural, and non-white communities at a time when the healthcare landscape in California is already precarious. This measure will likely result in clinic closures and the loss of services in vulnerable areas.

State Measure 45: No

The sales pitch on 45 is reform of the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), a 1970 state law that requires public agencies to analyze, disclose, and minimize the significant environmental impacts of proposed discretionary projects before approving them. If passed, the proposition would shorten the review process for development projects deemed “essential,” which includes construction of housing, power infrastructure, and highways, among others.

While CEQA has in some cases been abused to prevent housing and transit projects, the cure can’t be worse than the disease. Prop 45 is a mix of arbitrary timelines and carve-outs that are designed to serve the most destructive developers rather than improve our state’s built infrastructure. The goal of radically shortening the amount of time for public comment and agency review is meant not to improve the review process but to evade it entirely; the time limits that would be imposed on the courts by Prop 45 have been described as “arbitrary and unrealistically short” by the Judicial Council.

Ultimately Prop 45 is a wolf in sheep’s clothing, using the need for housing and transit to fast-track highway construction and AI data centers. 

Over 400 organizations oppose this: including the ACLU, the Sierra Club, the California Firefighters Association, the American Lung Association, and organized labor. That last group is a particularly clear example of the goals of Prop 45, as the building trades will endorse almost anything that increases construction. This proposition, however, is not about actually building out the things we need — it’s a corporate-funded power grab dressed up as reform. 

Vote NO.

Los Angeles County

Measure A: No

This measure amends the LA County Charter to make changes to union bargaining by “public safety” units — most notably the LASD deputies and county firefighters. Public safety units generally have priority in bargaining with the county, and the terms of their agreements have significant impacts on other county workers. 

The primary impact of Measure A would to be to allow any deadlock in union negotiations to be sent to binding arbitration. In a most fundamental sense, this would allow the major public safety units to force contract agreements that ignore the broader financial and policy needs of the county, putting at risk county priorities and the needs of other unions.

We do not need to give the corrupt Sheriff’s Department any more power over the county’s budget. Vote no.

Measure E: Yes

This one is vitally important. By passing this measure, LA County would be locking in the independence of and funding for the County Ethics Commission and Office of Ethics Compliance. $14.3 million per year would be given to the Commission as an independent body. Passing Measure E means more power for ethics investigation and more strength for the Commission to enforce penalties.

Measure E would also remedy one of the more embarrassing moments in county history, the accidental erasure of Measure J in 2024. The popular measure codified a commitment to reducing incarceration, and programs that it funded, like the Office of Diversion and Reentry, which have been incredibly effective at transitioning arrestees to mental health and substance abuse treatment. Restoring Measure J ensures that this funding continues uninterrupted. A clerical error should not have been allowed to overturn the will of millions of Angelenos.

Los Angles City

Measure TE: No

Measure TE is an attempt to create tax exemptions for people whose homes burned in the Palisades Fire should they wish to sell their property. If passed, it would allow these certain residential property owners to be exempt from Measure ULA, which taxes real estate sales that surpass $5.4 million. This exemption would run for five years from the date of the fire, expiring in 2030. 

We want to be clear about something: the loss of a home during a fire is a traumatic and terrible occurrence. The Palisades Fire was a devastating event, and the rebuilding process will be long and difficult. 

We also believe that if passed, Measure TE would set a precedent for wealthy homeowners to opt out of taxes, an option that is not available to people in Altadena who lost their homes in the Eaton Fire. If an individual’s property sells for more than $5.4 million, even as a bare lot, it’s not right to exempt that sale from a tax. $5.4 million is a lot of money for a piece of land without a house on it! To protect the integrity of Measure ULA, we do not support creating carve outs to the mansion tax. The recommendation is no.

Measure LA: Yes

We are fans of this one. If passed, this measure would change the LA City Charter to create capital infrastructure plans and a two-year budget cycle, along with a host of other shifts. Capital infrastructure plans are needed to restore and repair the city’s existing infrastructure. The two-year budget cycle would create more long-term planning, build more financial stability, allow evaluation to occur during off years, and improve oversight. This is a common-sense update that makes the basic functions of the city easier to carry out. We like this. The city needs this.

Measure PL: Yes

This measure is quite technical and of limited scope. If PL passes it would consolidate the Area Planning Commissions and let certain additional decisions be made by the City Planning Department. It would also prevent City Council from killing projects by refusing to put them on agenda, a favorite bribe-inducement strategy of former councilmember and current federal inmate José Huizar. Essentially, the measure streamlines certain planning elements and removes some opportunities for corruption or tomfoolery. 

PL is supported by the Engineers & Architects Association, the union that represents city planners. Vote yes.

Measure EE: Yes

EE is a grab bag of charter reforms. A “yes” vote grants more authority to LAPD’s Inspector General and LAFD’s Independent Assessor, civilian oversight bodies designed to audit the departments and investigate claims of misconduct. It would also raise the penalties for campaign finance violations, something that grassroots progressives could benefit from.

Measure EE also brings down the number of required weekly City Council meetings from three to one. Some feel that would reduce accountability, but we don’t agree; if anything, the current system makes it easier to miss meetings or hide motions in the shuffle.

Another part of EE would raise the threshold for referendums to overturn a City Council action to 15%, similar to voter initiatives. This is not a desirable change but its impact is small enough that it is outweighed by the other parts of the measure.

Measure PRK: Yes!

We love this one. This measure, if passed, would amend the LA City Charter to change the minimum budget allocated to the Department of Recreation and Parks. To put it simply, more money for parks! Los Angeles desperately needs this. Our parks department has struggled to staff and maintain our existing parks, to say nothing of expanding the amount of green space in the city. With our weather we deserve to be a city of world-class parks. Let’s have more playgrounds, more bathrooms, more concerts and programming, and more beautiful spaces to enjoy.

PRK is opposed by the LAPPL, because “How dare you want something nice? What about 300 new cop cars instead?”

Measure PRT: Yes

Not a very consequential measure unless you care a lot about airport commissions. If passed, it would allocate funds for waterfront public access projects and would also require people serving on Airport Commissions to live near the airport (though it doesn’t particularly define “near”). This is a fairly minor change. Don’t lose sleep over it.

Measure FD: Yes

This one is simple. Using a 0.5% sales tax (raising the sales tax from 10.25% to 10.75%), Measure FD would raise funds for the LA Fire Department. No surprises here. As the climate crisis grows and dangerous fire conditions continue to increase, more funding for the fire department is a positive. Los Angeles faces horrific wildfire risks across a huge territory, and we need to grow our fire department staff and facilities and take proactive steps to prevent fires and harden our infrastructure.

Measure FD is primarily opposed by the LA Police Protective League, which is investing millions against it for reasons that seem unclear; as best we can tell it’s a mixture of spite and anti-tax sentiment. They might want to think twice — if the fire department misses out on this revenue, folks might start looking at the LAPD budget sooner rather than later. 

We do need to offer our recommendation with some caveats. First, a sales tax is a regressive tax. Lower income Angelenos will pay more as a percentage of their income than the rich. Second, we simply cannot fund everything forever by carving out fractional cents of sales tax and earmarking it for different departments; this is not a way to manage a budget, and will eventually hit the limit of its usefulness. 

In the long run, we need to talk seriously about the budget, particularly the huge proportion of it eaten up by LAPD and the hundreds of millions in liability claims they face every year. We need to talk about Prop 13 and the hole it has blown in municipal governance in California. And we need to talk about billionaires and concentrations of massive wealth.

In the meantime, we will offer a reserved “yes” on FD.

Measure SC: Yes

This one is quite specific. If passed, it would do what it says on the tin: clarify campaign finance rules for Board of Education elections by making them match the same rules as the Mayor. That’s fine. It could be interesting in the future if voters also pass Prop 4 — maybe matching funds could be extended to the School Board race as well.

Statewide Races

Lieutenant Governor: Fiona Ma

Fiona Ma, California’s treasurer, is an easy choice next to anti-trans, anti-vax, charter-backed Republican Gloria J. Romero. While a comparatively weak position, lieutenant governor is next in line if the governor vacates office or their health is compromised. The role also includes an important role in higher education, and includes a number of regent and trustee board roles.

Michael Tubbs and Oliver Ma were both exciting options for this seat, which the progressive movement is unfortunately still not in a position to crack.

Secretary of State: Shirley N. Weber

The secretary of state oversees state and federal elections, as well as managing the corporate filings for businesses, nonprofits, and lobbyists. Given the attacks on free and fair elections by the Trump administration and the Supreme Court, this normally sleepy office becomes an important line of defense. California’s elections are slow to be certified, and our data on lobbyists and campaign finance is hard to navigate.

Weber is endorsed by a broad coalition of labor organizers, activists, and elected officials. Her goals for the coming term include strengthening cybersecurity and expanding voter registration outreach to high school and college students and the formerly incarcerated. She is also a consistent opponent of GOP-led “voter ID” disenfranchisement schemes.

Controller: Malia Cohen

Similar to the controller for the City of Los Angeles, the controller for the state oversees financial disbursements, audits, and unclaimed property. Given the size and economic power of California, this is no small task. California has a country-scale budget, and transparency is critical for advocacy. Malia Cohen is running for reelection against Herb Morgan, a retired Republican investment firm founder and CIO. No need to overcomplicate this runoff. If you want to keep the office of controller out of Republican hands, vote for Cohen.

Treasurer: Eleni Kounalakis

Eleni Kounalakis, a seasoned democrat and current lieutenant governor of California, is up against Jennifer Hawks, a GOP-backed retired business executive. As lieutenant governor, Kounalakis attempted to disqualify Trump from the 2024 presidential election after a Colorado court case ruled that Trump’s involvement in the January 6 attack constituted engagement in insurrection — a bright spot in a career mostly notable for her ability to leverage her family’s enormous wealth. 

One of the highlights of Hawks’ platform is a proposal to create a spending database including a searchable registry for “repeat recipients” of aid. We do not need more tools in the racist playbook to scapegoat and stigmatize the poor. Hawks is not a worthy candidate and should be nowhere near office.

Attorney General: Rob Bonta

At this historical moment, the most important thing an attorney general can do is use the legal system to throw up roadblocks in the way of the fascist in the White House. By that metric, Bonta has done an excellent job putting his foot on Trump’s neck. His department’s lawsuits have fought the federalization of the national guard, challenged the weakening of environmental standards, and confronted anti-immigrant and anti-trans policies.

We would note, however, his surprising cowardice on the Paramount/Warner Bros merger. The multi-state lawsuit he led was a righteous and legally necessary fight against a merger that not only threatened to do horrific damage to the film industry, but would also hand control of a shocking amount of the news media to allies of Trump and the Saudi government. When Governor Newsom (who has never met an oligarch he didn’t like) intervened on behalf of the merger, Bonta folded.

Michael Gates, his Republican opponent, made a career out of pushing for greater incarceration and opposing affordable housing in Huntington Beach. He had a brief dalliance with the Justice Department, in the dried-out husk of what was once the Civil Rights department, until he was forced out after less than a year for somehow being too toxic and sexist for the Trump administration.

Vote Bonta, but don’t forget.

Insurance Commissioner: Jane Kim

Here’s one you didn’t think you had to think about. The insurance commissioner runs the Department of Insurance, responsible for licensing insurance companies, investigating consumer complaints and insurers, and punishing insurers for regulatory noncompliance. The Department of Insurance impacts home and auto insurance, life insurance, workers’ compensation, and some aspects of health insurance (California, uniquely, splits oversight of health insurance companies between the Department of Managed Health Care, run by the governor, and the independent Department of Insurance).

As insurance rates rise and home insurers abandon the state, working people are being shut out of the economy in a most basic way. Kim wants to create a nonprofit public disaster insurance plan, create transparency around costs and coverage, and use regulatory powers to hold bad actors in the insurance industry accountable. The former San Francisco supervisor carries endorsements from the California Teachers Association, the Working Families Party, and local and national elected officials from Bubba Fish to Bernie Sanders.

Look at this race like Kenneth Mejia’s first run for controller, but with fewer corgis. Insurance commissioner is a technical and regulatory office that most people wouldn’t look twice at, but also offers significant opportunities for a mission-driven public servant to make material improvements in people’s lives.

For insurance commissioner, vote for Jane Kim.

Member State Board of Equalization, 3rd District: Samuel P. Sukaton

What does Board of Equalization even do? Great question; we’ve got answers. The BOE oversees the property tax systems, alcoholic beverage tax, and tax on insurers. It is a five-member body that on paper might seem like a place to park your political career when you’re figuring out your next step. But it might secretly be one of the more underrated tools for budget equity in California.

Our state has been plagued with tax policies that benefit rich homeowners, corporations, and predatory companies. It is not news that right-wing organizations like the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association have been key players in developing and standardizing these regressive, trickle-up taxation schemes to hoard wealth, resources, and power. A sharp administrator with an eye toward making the rich pay their fair share could do a lot for Californians.

That’s why we’re recommending Sam Sukaton, a labor organizer and a representative of the California Working Families Party. He has institutional experience, having worked with the California Public Utilities Commission, Energy Commission, Air Resources Board, and Natural Resources Agency. His campaign commitments include equity for homeowners and small businesses across counties, increased transparency on taxation revenue, and safeguards for the environment. 

Sukaton is part of a wave of candidates, like Controller Kenneth Mejia, who see the potential for progressive policymaking in more obscure and technical roles. Making a better California for everyone requires every tool at our disposal. Sukaton should get your vote.

Assemblymember Mike Gipson is also running for the seat. He has been repeatedly called out by Greenpeace, Courage California, Project Super Bloom, and Knock LA for taking hundreds of thousands of dollars of oil industry money to abstain on or vote against important environmental bills — at the same time as he was representing one of the most pollution-impacted districts. He doesn’t deserve a second act at the BOE.

Superintendent of Public Instruction: Richard Barrera

The superintendent is the elected executive of the state Department of Education… for now. It’s possible that the position may change significantly in the future, including no longer being elected, but that would be after this round of elections. 

The wide-open field attracted a number of strong candidates, and Richard Barrera was one of the better options. The president of the San Diego Unified School District School Board and himself a product of public schools, Barrera has earned major support from teachers and labor. His platform emphasizes the need for strong investment in teacher development and retention, nurses and counselors in schools, and protection of LGBTQ+ students. With his extensive experience and relationships with the unions that educate our kids, he’s well-qualified to take the lead as superintendent.

This contrasts dramatically with his opponent, Republican Sonja Shaw, a bigoted maniac without any background in education. Shaw’s candidacy is driven by her hatred of LGBTQ+ youth and her opposition to COVID-19 vaccines and masks. Her platform is short on education policy and long on conspiracy, and could be quite simply summed up as “more dead kids.” It is vital that California reject this hatemonger and the sick ideology that she represents.

State Senate

State Senate District 20: Caroline Menjivar

Caroline Menjivar has been a strong progressive advocate for this Burbank and San Fernando Valley district during her first term, and has earned a second. Her work in the Senate has included legislation designed to increase oversight and accountability to address prison sexual abuse, including by reducing the use of strip searches, defending LGBT rights, and promoting tenancy protections for small businesses. 

Republican Tony Rodriguez offers a warmed-over mash of pro-cop and anti-regulation platitudes that leave one with the impression that he’s not sure what office he’s running for. Vote Menjivar.

State Senate District 22: No Recommendation

Democrat Susan Rubio has a sad track record of supporting corporate interests, including failing to support restrictions on private equity takeovers of health facilities (AB 3129), a state tax on the sale of user data by large corporations (SB 1327), increased regulation of driverless cars (SB 915), and local control over oil and gas operations (AB 3233). She also failed to support a key criminal justice reform of the school-to-prison pipeline that would have ended a requirement that school principals must notify police of students caught possessing small amounts of narcotics (AB 2441). 

Mike Netter is a Republican activist and conservative media personality and a strong supporter of President Trump.

Neither of these candidates deserve your vote.

State Senate District 24: John Erickson

West Hollywood City Councilman John Erickson is a long-time advocate for progressive priorities including renter protections, universal childcare, Medicare for All, and safe streets for pedestrians and bicyclists. John is endorsed by numerous labor unions representing working people, as well many progressive politicians. 

Erickson faces Brian Goldsmith in this Dem-on-Dem runoff. Goldsmith is a tech entrepreneur and Democratic consultant who proudly boasts endorsements from HIllary Clinton, Traci Park, Rick Caruso, and the LAPD union, as well as right wing incumbents District Attorney Hochman and City Attorney Feldstein Soto. He has little to offer California beyond the status quo.

State Senate District 26: Sara Rascón

A brawl of a primary has left two candidates standing, both vying for the progressive mantle. Of the two, Sarah Rascón should get your vote.

Glassell Park resident Sara Rascón was born and raised in El Sereno and brings a local’s eye to the needs of the district. Her career has been defined by public service (working in the Mayor’s office, the East LA Planning Commission, and the Mountains Recreation & Conservation Authority), giving her experience with how the many interlocking wheels of local government actually move. At the same time, she has a clear understanding of herself as part of the larger movement and has been on the ground with the Rapid Response Networks that sprang up to defend the city from ICE. 

Rascón’s policy goals are clear and principled. She calls for the repeal of Costa-Hawkins, for single payer healthcare, and for the expansion of unarmed crisis response. She also has a particular knowledge of and interest in reforms in the practices of the Department of Children and Family Services, having gone through family court herself as a child. Her endorsers include Controller Kenneth Mejia, outgoing Senator Maria Elena Durazo, and organizations like the Working Families Party, La Defensa, and Planned Parenthood.

Her opponent, Sara Hernandez, poses an unusual situation. Her highly professional campaign, which has raised a great deal of money and courted a great many endorsers, presents her as a progressive. Her stances around reproductive health, transportation, childcare, and gender affirming care are largely the sort of things we’d like to see in our legislators. Under other circumstances – like against a GOP candidate, or a less accomplished opponent – that might be enough. 

However, Hernandez has given us many reasons to be skeptical of her candidacy. Her campaign has been supported by more than $2.5 million in outside spending, and a look under the hood finds not just the usual landlords and business interests, but an explicitly anti-union PAC started by crypto billionaires, an anti-regulation PAC funded by Meta and Google, and another whose funders include Phillip Morris tobacco of all things.

In an interview with the Larchmont Chronicle she unequivocally stated her support for 41.18, the anti-homeless banishment law. For a so-called progressive to support 41.18, particularly after it was found to be an absolute failure, is shocking, and can only reflect deep ignorance or bias against the unhoused. 

Hernandez also takes pains to disguise her role at City Hall, where she worked from 2014-2016 as downtown director and special counsel for former-Councilmember and current federal inmate Jose Huizar, all while he was deep in the cash-for-development bribery scheme that eventually sent him to prison. After leaving his office she worked at biglaw firm DLA Piper on “land use” – getting developments through the PLUM committee and approval process.

As we peel back the layers here, it becomes clear that there is only one actual progressive choice in this race. Vote for Rascón.

State Senate District 28: Lola Smallwood-Cuevas

Lola Smallwood-Cuevas is one of LA’s most progressive assemblymembers, having passed legislation to increase worker protections, pushed to end oil drilling at the Inglewood Oil Field in her district, and supported anti-displacement policies in South LA. She also co-authored a criminal justice bill that would have ended the requirement that schools report student behavioral or drug possession issues to law enforcement (AB 2441). She has passed legislation to expand postpartum mental health care and, along with Assemblymember Sade Elhawary, to help inmate firefighters transition to unionized trades jobs. Her record is strong.

Republican Joe Lisuzzo parrots outdated tough-on-crime nonsense and has no concern for the needs of working class people. Lola deserves your vote.

State Senate District 30: No Recommendation

In two terms representing this southeast Los Angeles County district, Democrat Bob Archuleta has repeatedly favored corporate interests over his own constituents. He has failed to support new laws protecting renters, including limits on the deductions a landlord can take out of a security deposit. He has failed to support proposed laws to increase transparency of corporate entities and to restrict private equity from taking over healthcare facilities. He also has a mixed record on criminal justice reform and the environment.

Unfortunately, the assemblymember’s lone opponent, Republican Araceli Martinez, is a right-wing agitator who has appeared at local colleges with a “Deport All Illegals” sign as part of a controversial political stunt.

In a district that consistently votes for the Democratic Party by 20% margins, we can’t put our name behind Bob.

State Assembly

State Assembly District 34: Randall Putz

Republican Tom Lackey is term-limited out in this sprawling High Desert district. Democrat Randall Putz is an active leader in the Big Bear Lake community, having served  as city councilmember, mayor, and school board member (among other positions) over the past 15 years. His platform includes ensuring big corporations pay their fair share, fighting to hold law enforcement accountable, procuring more state support for affordable housing, and enacting tenant protections.

Republican Charles Hughes is a former prison guard who has locked up endorsements from police associations and Republican politicians. 

Putz is the clear choice in this race.

State Assembly District 39: No Recommendation

Democrat assemblymember Juan Carrillo, who immigrated from Mexico at age 15, remains a disappointment in this Latine-majority district that includes parts of Palmdale, Lancaster, and Victorville. During his time as a member of the Palmdale City Council, Carrillo voted to prevent stronger oversight over offshore drilling platforms while voting to allow private equity takeovers of hospitals and the subcontracting of public jobs.

Carrillo faces Republican Paul Marsh in a rematch of 2022 and 2024, both of which Carillo won with 57% of the vote. Neither candidate deserves a recommendation in this uncompetitive race.

State Assembly District 40: Pilar Schiavo

Assemblymember Pilar Schiavo has represented this swing district in Santa Clarita and Northwest San Fernando Valley since 2022. Schiavo, a former union organizer for the California Nurses Association, has supported tenant protections, worker rights, and affordable housing, but has been an inconsistent ally on criminal justice reforms. 

Her challenger, former police officer Rickey Hayes, is running on a purely reactionary platform of increasing criminal sentences and bringing back “conservative values,” whatever those might be. Vote Schiavo.

State Assembly District 41: John Harabedian

Assemblymember John Harabedian compiled a strong voting record in his first term in the assembly, supporting progressive initiatives on affordable housing, criminal justice reform, and consumer protection. 

His Republican opponent, Adam Vena, is an anti-trans agitator who has faced domestic abuse allegations. 

Not a complicated decision. Vote Harabedian.

State Assembly District 42: No Recommendation

A lot of yikes in this open seat race. Only one Democrat qualified for the ballot after another well-funded Democrat filed their paperwork incorrectly and was booted from the race. That leaves voters to choose between Democrat Deborah Klein Lopez and Republican Ted Nordblum in this very blue Ventura County district that also includes Malibu, Pacific Palisades, and Brentwood. Both of them are running on crime fearmongering (despite remarkable decreases in the crime rate) and shoveling more and more of our state’s resources into the bottomless pit of police funding.

State Assembly District 43: Celeste Rodriguez

Assemblymember Celeste Rodriguez exceeded our expectations in her first term in office, amassing a good voting record on progressive priorities, including criminal justice reform, worker protections, and affordable housing. Her accomplishments include bills to protect the children of immigrant families as well as the authoring of AB 969 to expand assistance for victims of domestic violence. 

Her opponent, Ricardo Benitez, is a MAGA Republican and repeat candidate, who has been humiliatingly thrashed in four or five previous races. Celeste took over 70% in the primary, so we think she’ll cruise to victory. But there’s no reason not to run up the score — vote for Celeste Rodriguez.

State Assembly District 44: Nick Shultz

In his first term, Nick Shultz authored and passed several criminal justice reforms, sponsored critical environmental protections bills, and had a strong voting record in support of progressive priorities. He also rejected all corporate campaign donations from the real estate, oil and gas, healthcare, and tech industries. At the same time, as chair of the public safety committee, he has allowed some highly regressive bills to advance past his desk. He deserves another term — but keep up the pressure to make sure he stays on the right path.

State Assembly District 46: No Recommendation

Jesse Gabriel continues to accept large amounts of corporate campaign donations from the real estate, oil and gas, and healthcare industries, as well from police associations. We have given him lukewarm recommendations in the past, but at this point we are fully sick of this corporate influence. California remains one of 29 states that permit corporations to donate directly to candidates, and this will never change with Democrats like Gabriel in the Assembly. Skip this race.

State Assembly District 48: No Recommendation

Blanca Rubio remains one of the worst Democrats in the Assembly, with a track record for raking in egregious amounts of corporate donations and failing to support progressive legislation. In 2025, she voted against increased oversight over offshore oil drilling and did not support a bill to prohibit ICE agents from wearing masks, failing to do the bare minimum. Unfortunately, a progressive voice did not step up to challenge Rubio. Republican Dan Tran, a real estate business owner, can not be recommended either.

State Assembly District 49: Mike Fong

Mike Fong continues to be a reliable supporter of progressive legislation in this district stretching from Monterey Park to Arcadia. In 2025, he voted for bills increasing environmental protections for offshore oil drilling, limiting the terms and conditions of youth probation, and prohibiting investor-owned utilities from using ratepayer funds to pay for lobbying and political ads. 

His opponent, Long Liu, is a right-wing anti-LGBT conspiracy theorist who wants to criminalize homelessness. He shouldn’t be anywhere near the government.

Vote Fong.

State Assembly District 51: Colin Hernandez

Voters in this district, which stretches from Santa Monica to East Hollywood, have an exciting opportunity to send a progressive fighter to Sacramento. Colin Hernandez, a native Angeleno, is running on a platform of childcare for all, universal healthcare, improving public transit, and LGBTQ+ rights. He also advocates for a wealth tax on billionaires and raising taxes on the largest corporations. 

Current Assemblymember Rick Chavez Zbur has been in establishment Democratic politics for decades, having fundraised for Governor Bill Clinton. He is in an enviable political situation: with massive financial support, well-worn political connections, and a bright blue district, there are few people in the state who could drive as much legislative progress as Zbur — at least in theory. The reality has been very different. With all this political capital, he focused on chairing a select committee on retail theft and has done the bare minimum with regard to progressive priorities.

With thousands in campaign donations going to Zbur from real estate and landlord lobbying associations, charter schools, gas companies, Amazon, and Airbnb, perhaps his inaction is a feature and not a bug. 

Colin Hernandez is the clear choice here.

State Assembly District 52: Jessica Caloza

Jessica Caloza won a competitive race for this seat in 2024 and has compiled a solid voting record during her first term in the assembly. Her priorities include strengthening our sanctuary state protections and reducing the sharing of sensitive immigration information with the federal government. She also sees homelessness as an issue to be tackled with services, not handcuffs.

Her opponent is a Republican pianist who favors cooperation with ICE agents. Caloza is the easy choice in this race.

State Assembly District 53: No Recommendation

In her first term in office, Michelle Rodriguez sank to our low expectations. She voted against stronger oversight for offshore drilling, against allowing judges to offer diversion programs rather than rely on punishment, and against a bill requiring courts to advise defendants of the possible immigration consequences of a guilty plea. Unfortunately her opponent in the general is a replacement-level Republican.

State Assembly District 54: No Recommendation

In his first term, Mark Gonzalez passed a bill to make it easier for cities to seize and destroy recreational vehicles that thousands of unhoused residents rely on as their only home. He also voted to shield oil companies who expand oil drilling in Kern County from environmental review and litigation (SB 237) and failed to support a bill that would have banned all unnecessary uses of forever chemicals (SB 682). He also is pushing for further criminalization and institutionalization of the homeless. In his previous role as chair of the LA County Democratic Party, Gonzalez consistently schemed against reformers and progressives; his place in Los Angeles politics has been singularly toxic and destructive.

Literally no other candidates qualified for the ballot in this race, somehow, so we’re stuck. There’s no point in degrading your ballot with a vote for him.

State Assembly District 55: Isaac Bryan

Assemblymember Isaac Bryan continues to be an effective progressive advocate in Sacramento. Bryan achieved a monumental environmental justice victory in 2024: closure of the Inglewood Oil Field by 2030. This oil field in South LA has been linked with higher rates of asthma, heart conditions, and premature and low birthweight babies in the community for decades. Bryan has also been a consistent voice for criminal legal reform and prisoner rights. His advocacy ended the shameful practice of the state paying incarcerated firefighters only $1 per hour despite fighting the same wildfires and facing the same dangers as other firefighters; Bryan’s bill raised their wage to $7.25 per hour. His record is that of a legislator who followed through on his campaign promises, and who pushes forward the goals of the movement that elected him.

Vote Bryan.

State Assembly District 56: No Recommendation

Democrat Lisa Calderon remains a disappointment in this Dem-leaning district stretching from Pico Rivera to Diamond Bar. With a record of collecting large oil and gas contributions, Calderon surprised no one in 2025 with her failure to support bills to lower residents’ gas and electric bills by prohibiting utilities from spending ratepayer money on lobbying and political ads. Perhaps more surprising, she did not support a bill prohibiting ICE from wearing face masks. Her Republican opponent is a right-wing Christian nationalist. Neither deserves your vote.

State Assembly District 57: Sade Elhawary

Sade Elhawary, an LA native who was the first of her family to attend college, compiled a stellar voting record in her first term in the assembly. She also advocated for bills to allow judges to offer criminal diversion programs instead of punishment and to protect employees from invasive surveillance technology. She has racked up endorsements from progressive and labor groups, and criminal law reformers consider her a champion in Sacramento. Vote Sade.

State Assembly District 61: Tina McKinnor

Assemblymember Tina McKinnor is a prominent progressive voice in the state legislature, championing bills on renter protection, reentry programs, and reparations. In 2025, McKinnor finally ended a bizarre California quirk by passing a law to require landlords to provide and maintain a working stove and refrigerator. This success built upon her 2023 bill to limit security deposits to one month’s rent.

McKinnor also authored a novel bill in 2025 to allow colleges to give admissions preference to descendants of slavery, which passed both the assembly and state senate before being vetoed by Governor Newsom without explanation. Give McKinnor your support.

State Assembly District 62: José Solache

While not a progressive, José Solache’s voting record in his first term was better than expected. Essentially he’s someone that we can work with. We remain concerned about the corporate campaign donations he accepts, but he is a far better option than his anti-immigrant Republican opponent.

State Assembly District 64: No Recommendation

Blanca Pacheco is a fake. She is deceiving the residents of Downey and Norwalk by masquerading as a Democrat while voting like a Republican. In 2025, she had the most conservative voting record of any Democrat in the assembly; Courage Score considers her the worst in the eleven years that they have tracked the legislature. She has voted against or failed to support criminal justice reforms, environmental protections, workers’ rights, social housing, the regulation of forever chemicals, and on and on and on.

We expect her to cruise to victory; in this solidly blue district, she faces a Republican challenger who she’s beaten twice before by margins of more than 20%. If you live in this district and are interested in organizing to oust Pacheco in 2028, please reach out to Knock LA.

State Assembly District 65: No Recommendation

Democrat Mike Gipson poorly represented this district for more than a decade, and voters in Watts, Compton, Carson, Wilmington, and San Pedro had an opportunity to choose a new kind of representative.

Unfortunately, the corporate money that kept Gipson afloat was able to box out progressive Fatima Iqbal-Zubair, leaving a race between Ayanna Davis and Republican Lydia Gutiérrez.

Gipson’s preferred successor, Ayanna Davis, is a former principal who has received large campaign donations from the oil companies that long bought out Gipson, as well as support from Airbnb and many police unions. Her endorsements page is an interesting performance, with liberal and progressive organizations featured prominently at the top and right-wing endorsements buried further down. When pressed on some of the major issues of the day, she has made familiar dodges — she refuses to either endorse or oppose the billionaire tax, and offers what appears to be a pre-distributed spiel about AI data centers needing to use clean energy and create jobs.

Gutierrez is terrible on most issues and incoherent on others, though we would note that she strongly opposes AI data center construction. Take note — it would be disastrous for Democrats to cede that issue to the right wing.

As it is, Davis appears a lock to win, and the district will face another decade of corporate misrepresentation. No recommendation.

State Assembly District 66: Sara Deen

Pakistani American Sara Deen is a dentist and president of the Palos Verdes School Board. She initially separated herself from the pack in this open race with her endorsements from nurses’ and teachers’ unions, and her opposition to the genocide in Gaza. On the School Board she had to battle Moms For Liberty to stand up for LGBT students’ rights. She also opposes the use of Flock cameras and similar abusive surveillance, which her opponent welcomed.

Paul Seo is a former prosecutor for Los Angeles County and current mayor of Palos Verdes; he is endorsed by every major police association, trumpets his prosecutorial credentials, and has made increasing police headcount a major part of his platform. Advocates of criminal justice reform agree that he would be a disaster.

State Assembly District 67: No Recommendation

Union leader Ada Briceño, our preferred candidate in the primary, was narrowly pushed out of the top two by Cerritos mayor Mark Pulido. Pulido, like Sara Hernandez, was the beneficiary of a brutal flood of outside spending by crypto billionaires, Google, Meta, Airbnb, and Uber. More than $5 million propped him up, and a couple million more were spent directly attacking Briceño. In the end, demonstrating both the strength and limits of this strategy, Pulido’s lead was less than 2,000 votes but it was enough to box her out.

Now Pulido is in a runoff against Paulo Morales, a Republican cop. Let’s be clear: the Republican Party is a fascist organization, and anything that empowers it pushes the country further toward disaster. That said, how is it possible that Pulido couldn’t manage stronger answers than Morales on dealing with ICE or gender-affirming care, of all things? The bar is on the floor.

Ever since Citizens United opened the floodgates, massive wealth has warped politics across the country. This spending needs to be understood as corruption, and we have to ask what those millions of dollars are buying. The state legislature will inevitably be called upon to regulate the industries and specific companies funding his run. Do we trust Pulido to take a stand against the data centers his donors will build? When Uber asks to continue misclassifying drivers as independent contractors, will he speak against them? Airbnb wants free rein to rent out our city for the Olympics — will he let them? Do you trust him to put the needs of the people before the needs of the companies who handed him power? 

We don’t. We can’t make a recommendation in this race.

State Assembly District 69: No Recommendation

Incumbent Josh Lowenthal has compiled another decent voting record with his second term in office. While he supported good bills — like one that would have prevented price gouging under emergency declarations and the No Secret Police Act (preventing law enforcement from wearing masks while operating in California) — a big red flag is that he has authored AB 1953, a bill that would require eligible dwellings to be made available for short-term rentals during declared disasters and tourism events.

After seeing the major price-gouging from Airbnb and other short-term rental businesses after the Eaton and Palisades fires in early 2025, it is reasonable to believe that this bill would open the door for continued abuses by the short-term rental market. Short-term rentals have been a contributor to LA’s housing crisis, driving up annual rents and removing units from the rental market.

Lowenthal is endorsed by Democrats for Israel. And he refers to homeless encampments as “blight” and drivers of crime.

However, Lowenthal’s only opponent, Carolyn J. Essex, doesn’t have a defined policy platform available on her site or any social media. A flyer posted to her LinkedIn does mention her support of affordable housing with wraparound health services, but there isn’t anything else to base a recommendation on.

So, we have no recommendation for this office.

US Congress

More than a few congressional races in the June primary came out differently than we would have liked. In a number of cases, worthwhile candidates failed to make the top two, leaving cartoonish right-wing opponents as the only alternatives to terrible incumbents. The Republican Party has been fully compromised by fascism and in most of these cases we — and you — would probably pull the lever for the Democrat, a perfectly reasonable response. But you didn’t come to Knock LA just to get a list of Democrats, you came here to dig into the details. There are a number of candidates we’re happily backing, but there are others who simply do not deserve a recommendation even if you find yourself voting for them as a matter of harm reduction.

House of Representatives

District 23: Tessa Lynn Hodge

This Republican stronghold in San Bernardino County is represented by MAGA jackass Jay Obernolte, a man with nothing to recommend him. Most recently he’s become a shill for AI, promoting its use in schools and the military.

His challenger, High Desert native Hodge, is a social worker who calls for ushering in single-payer healthcare, creating a path to citizenship for undocumented residents, and expanding education and economic opportunities in rural areas. She also is forthright in calling for an end to the Gaza genocide and stopping military aid to Israel.

It will be an uphill battle for Hodge: Obernolte took 57% of the vote in the primary. On the other hand, his primary share was 63% in 2024. Perhaps his grip on the district is not as strong as it once was; perhaps the electoral wave will surprise us.

District 26: No Recommendation

Rep. Julia Brownley is retiring after representing this Ventura County–based district for 14 years. She has endorsed conservative Democrat Jacqui Irwin as her replacement.
