El estado aprueba $2.5 millones para mejoras en el Centro Comunitario de Goleta y la Biblioteca del Valle de Goleta

Indy Staff

Los comunicados de prensa se publican en Independent.com as como un servicio comunitario gratuito.

GOLETA, CA, octubre 9, 2026 – La Ciudad de Goleta se complace en anunciar que ha obtenido $2.5 millones en fondos estatales para apoyar mejoras en dos importantes instalaciones comunitarias: $2 millones para mejorar las instalaciones de cuidado infantil y educación preescolar del Centro Comunitario de Goleta (GCC, por sus siglas en inglés) y $500,000 para renovar la Biblioteca del Valle de Goleta.

Los fondos están incluidos en el Proyecto de Ley AB 113, la Ley de Presupuesto de 2026, cuyo autor es el asambleísta estatal Jesse Gabriel y que fue promulgada por el gobernador el 18 de septiembre de 2026. Estos fondos se obtuvieron con el apoyo de la presidenta pro tempore del Senado, Monique Limón, el asambleísta estatal Gregg Hart y el gobernador Gavin Newsom. Ayudarán a mejorar estas instalaciones, que brindan servicios a los residentes de Goleta y a integrantes de la comunidad de todas las edades.

La presidenta pro tempore del Senado, Monique Limón, declaró: “El Centro Comunitario de Goleta y la Biblioteca del Valle de Goleta son espacios esenciales en los que los integrantes de la comunidad confían para recibir servicios como cuidado infantil y actividades después de clases. Me enorgullece haber conseguido fondos para ayudar a modernizar nuestra biblioteca y nuestro centro comunitario, que cada año atienden a cientos de niños de Goleta. Al hacer que la Biblioteca del Valle de Goleta sea más accesible, modernizar los espacios interiores con tecnología y reemplazar las aulas obsoletas del centro comunitario, estamos invirtiendo en el futuro de nuestros niños”.

“Estamos agradecidos con la presidenta pro tempore del Senado, Monique Limón y el asambleísta Gregg Hart por reconocer la importancia de estas instalaciones y apoyar estos proyectos”, declaró la alcaldesa de Goleta, Paula Perotte. “El Centro Comunitario y la Biblioteca significan mucho para nuestra comunidad, y estos fondos ayudarán a garantizar que sigan siendo lugares acogedores y accesibles para los residentes de Goleta y los integrantes de la comunidad durante muchos años”.

$2 millones para las instalaciones de cuidado infantil del Centro Comunitario de Goleta

El Centro Comunitario de Goleta, ubicado en 5679 Hollister Avenue, es un punto de encuentro para programas y servicios comunitarios. En sus instalaciones tienen su sede diversas organizaciones y se realizan actividades que benefician a residentes de todas las edades y procedencias.Dos organizaciones que llevan muchos años ocupando espacios en el GCC, Rainbow School y CommUnify, ofrecen educación para la primera infancia y programas Head Start a familias de la localidad. Actualmente, sus programas funcionan en edificios portátiles que han llegado al final de su vida útil y necesitan ser reemplazados.

Los $2 millones en fondos estatales ayudarán a financiar la demolición y el reemplazo de los dos edificios portátiles, lo que permitirá contar con instalaciones mejoradas para los programas de educación para la primera infancia y Head Start en la comunidad de Goleta.

$500,000 para mejoras en la Biblioteca del Valle de Goleta

La Biblioteca del Valle de Goleta, ubicada en 500 N. Fairview Avenue, ha brindado servicios a la comunidad durante más de 50 años, desde su apertura en 1972. Actualmente, el edificio está recibiendo sus primeras mejoras importantes en varias décadas como parte del Proyecto de Mejoras de Accesibilidad conforme a la Ley para Estadounidenses con Discapacidades (ADA, por sus siglas en inglés), Seguridad y Edificio de la Biblioteca del Valle de Goleta.

Los $500,000 en fondos estatales contribuirán a financiar renovaciones para que el edificio cumpla con las normas vigentes de los códigos de construcción y mejore su accesibilidad, seguridad y sostenibilidad. Estas mejoras forman parte de los esfuerzos más amplios de la Ciudad para preservar y modernizar la biblioteca en beneficio de las generaciones actuales y futuras. Las mejoras de infraestructura de la Biblioteca del Valle de Goleta también se complementan con la campaña de recaudación de fondos para infraestructura Writing the Next Chapter (Escribiendo el próximo capítulo), respaldada por la comunidad y lanzada en 2026 para financiar la renovación del mobiliario interior y otras mejoras.

La Ciudad de Goleta expresa su agradecimiento a la presidenta pro tempore del Senado, Monique Limón, al asambleísta estatal Gregg Hart y al gobernador Gavin Newsom por su liderazgo y apoyo para conseguir estos fondos.

Para obtener más información sobre el Centro Comunitario de Goleta, visite Ciudad de Goleta — Centro Comunitario de Goleta. Para obtener información sobre el proyecto de la Biblioteca del Valle de Goleta, visite Biblioteca del Valle de Goleta.

Image

"Today’s legislation builds on prior work to address UPFs and other foods and ingredients linked to serious health harms, including cancer, cardiovascular disease, Type 2 diabetes, metabolic disorders, reproductive harm, and other chronic conditions. Last year, the Governor signed the Healthy Foods, Healthy Kids Act (AB 1264, Gabriel), making California the first state to officially define UPFs and setting a timeline for phasing them out of schools. The certification program and label created through today’s legislation reflect the same commonsense, market-based approach that made the USDA Organic label a success: give manufacturers a voluntary standard, and let consumers do the rest."

Certificate is by way of two paths, organizations, Non-UPF Verified and WiseCode, of which Non-UPF vehemently opposed the bill based upon a compromised certification process allowed in the bill. The contention by Megan of Non-UPF Verified is

  • Does the non-UPF certification examine the processing methods used for ingredients and finished products
  • Does it instead focus on the lists of ingredients on labels
  • A certification by "Non-UPF Verified" asks
    • How were the ingredients and finished product actually made
    • What is the ingredient integrity and formulation, and processing limits and methods

IG statement by non-UltraProcessed Verified "We’re reviewing California’s legislation closely. Reckoning with Scott Wiener’s Record on Palestine

Nadia Rahman

24 min readOct 8, 2026

Examining the San Francisco congressional candidate’s abysmal track record on Palestinian rights.

We are about to start a new era in San Francisco. This is the first time in nearly 40 years that San Francisco’s congressional seat has been open and truly competitive. And after four decades of being held by a pro-Israel Democrat, it’s time for change.

The congressional race in San Francisco matters a lot on a number of issues, and this is the only elected seat in the city that has decisive impacts abroad — including in Palestine.

Today, three full years into the U.S.-backed genocide Israel is committing against the Palestinians and the total decimation of Gaza, we need to have a reckoning on U.S. responsibility, and how that translates back into the San Francisco congressional race.

Over the course of the 2026 congressional campaign, Senator Scott Wiener and his team have attempted to launder his record on Palestine by pivoting his narrative to sound acceptable while simultaneously accusing anyone questioning his track record of unfair treatment because he is Jewish.

This manipulation is enough to get most people to back down. I suspect this is why no local media has examined Senator Wiener’s actual track record on Palestine with any kind of critical lens and actual substance.

There has been news reporting on some of Senator Wiener’s big pivots, including after the viral “yes/no” genocide question at the first forum of the primary campaign in January 2026, but no deeper examination of his two-decade long career as an elected official.

Senator Wiener has a very public track record as one of the most pro-Israel legislators in California, and in the context of how public perception about Palestine has transformed in the United States over the last few years, the lack of exploration of this issue by mainstream media initially frustrated me. It felt like a dereliction of duty.

Absent action from the press on this front, local advocates who have borne witness and been impacted by this issue must do the work of presenting the facts of Senator Wiener’s full record on Palestine.

This essay is an examination of Senator Wiener’s track record on the issue by me, an advocate for Palestinian rights who has already been targeted and smeared on this issue by the people running the operation to elect Senator Wiener to congress. It expands on the “no endorsement” write-up on Senator Wiener I included in my 2024 endorsement guide.

In summary, the harm Senator Wiener has done on the issue of Palestine and to Palestinian rights over the course of his political career far outweighs his last-minute shift in policies that sound good at surface level, but are designed to maintain a status quo in which the U.S. maintains its complicity, and Israel has no incentive to change course or face consequences for its crimes against the Palestinian people or its aggression in the region and its larger goals for geographic expansion.

What is examined in this essay:

  • Censoring criticism of Israel in public education
  • Working to oppose the San Francisco ceasefire resolution
  • Suppressing the university campus encampment movement in California
  • Crushing dissent by targeting Palestine advocates and organizations
  • Ostracizing anti-Zionist Jews and organizations
  • Campaigning against the Palestinian right of return in the California Democratic Party
  • Amplifying propaganda and problematic rhetoric online
  • Committing to remain staunchly pro-Israel
  • Meeting with Israeli President Isaac Herzog four months into the genocide
  • Why Senator Wiener’s current policy positions on Palestine are insufficient
  • How Senator Wiener Has Campaigned in the Congressional Race
  • The Stakes of the San Francisco Congressional Race

Censoring Public Education: Ethnic Studies & AB 715

On the Ethnic Studies front, Senator Wiener has actively worked to undermine teaching about Palestine and Israel and Arab American history, and has repeatedly conflated the political ideology of Zionism with the religion of Judaism.

Sharing the actual history of Palestinian murder and displacement, and the experience of people impacted by Israel’s apartheid government and military occupation of Palestinian territories, has been mischaracterized as promoting anti-Jewish bias and antisemitism in schools.

The result has been an inordinate amount of pressure gutting the Ethnic Studies curriculum which has had a real impact across the state, including the Pajaro Valley Unified School District, and the San Francisco Unified School District which faced attacks in both 2025 and 2026 in the form of organized efforts to get rid of the ethnic studies requirement altogether, targeting its leadership, and creating a chilling environment for all teachers who are attempting to address one of the most pressing issues of our time — Israeli’s genocide in Gaza — in the classroom.

Although Senator Wiener has refrained from publicly commenting on the most recent Ethnic Studies fights in San Francisco, he has made his feelings and preferences clear to district officials, including to the office of the Superintendent and elected school board members. Those preferences included pausing the curriculum altogether, removing the mandate for it, and reducing the year-long requirement to a semester during the summer 2025 fight. His pressure on the Ethnic Studies fight locally was only put on pause once he started to actively campaign for congress and doing so became a liability for him.

The reality of the political situation is that California’s Israel Lobby has shifted to attacking the Ethnic Studies program at the local level, school district by school district because they have failed at derailing the program at the state level.

The most recent attempt to undermine the Ethnic Studies program via state legislation, AB 1468, failed in May 2025. Senator Wiener was a co-author on the bill.

AB 1468 was drafted by the Legislative Jewish Caucus, which Senator Wiener was co-chair of at the time, without input from the legislature’s other diversity caucuses. It amassed significant opposition, including from the California Teachers Association, and it failed to garner support of the diversity caucuses — namely the Black, Latino, and AAPI caucuses which represent the four foundational groups in the core Ethnic Studies curriculum.

The failure of AB 1468 led to the introduction of AB 715, the pro-Israel public education censorship bill marketed by the Legislative Jewish Caucus as a bill to address antisemitism in K-12 public education. Senator Wiener was a principal co-author of AB 715 and actively engineered its passage through the legislature.

A diverse statewide coalition of more than 120 organizations representing labor, civil rights organizations, and a diverse array of identity groups — including California ACLU Action, the California Teachers Association, and the California Federation of Teachers — formed to oppose AB 715 over concerns that the bill attempted censor education about Israel’s genocide in Palestine and Palestinian representation and narratives — effectively weaponizing accusations of antisemitism to chill speech within the classroom.

Despite overwhelming grassroots opposition, the legislature passed a watered down version of AB 715 (a previous version of the bill prohibited calling Israel a “settler-colonial state” among other extreme Zionist amendments), it was signed into law by Governor Gavin Newsom, and went into effect on January 1, 2026.

The law is the first of its kind in the nation and sets a dangerous precedent designed to be replicated state-by-state to censor criticism of Israel and education about Palestine.

Opposing the San Francisco Ceasefire Resolution

Senator Wiener actively opposed and attempted to whip support against the San Francisco ceasefire resolution in late 2023/early 2024. As one of the organizers supporting AROC’s organizing efforts for the resolution who was in contact with multiple Supervisors about it at the time, I saw firsthand the pressure Senator Wiener and his operatives exerted in an attempt to get the Supervisors to vote ‘no’ on the resolution.

Senator Wiener’s public opposition to the San Francisco ceasefire resolution is well documented in news reports (SF Chronicle, SF Standard). He went as far as speaking at a vigil organized by JCRC Bay Area in opposition to the ceasefire across from San Francisco City Hall the day the resolution was introduced.

Senator Wiener claims to have called for a ceasefire in November 2023 and this is a talking point he is currently campaigning on, despite readily available evidence to the contrary.

This example illustrates how Senator Wiener’s policy positions on Palestine sound good but are actually misleading: he claims to have been calling for a ceasefire since November 2023, but when the opportunity to adopt a resolution at the city and county level in San Francisco presented itself, Senator Wiener not only opposed it, but also leveraged his influence to attempt to ensure it failed.

Suppressing the Campus Encampment Movement in California

The Palestine solidarity campus encampment movement began in California at Stanford University on October 20, 2023. The movement expanded to campuses around the world in the days, weeks, and months that followed.

However, in the United States, the anti-war movement — which in past iterations played significant roles in shifting public opinion on the Vietnam war and apartheid South Africa — was demonized by elected officials, subjected to state-sanctioned violence, doxxed by external organizations, and threatened with suspension and expulsion by cowardly administrations, and ultimately targeted for visa cancellations and deportations by the Trump administration.

In California, the legislature’s Jewish Caucus which was co-chaired by Senator Wiener at the time, made weaponizing antisemitism to stifle campus protest a policy priority for the 2024 legislative session:

This weaponization materialized as SB 1287 — a law designed to stifle the pro-Palestine campus protest in response to the encampment movement in the name of Jewish safety. The bill was opposed by California ACLU Action and a coalition of civil rights organizations on the basis that it undermined the first amendment and would chill free speech on college campuses in California, specifically related to Israel’s genocide in Gaza. Senator Wiener’s role with SB 1287 was to shape the legislation, champion it, and serve as a co-sponsor for it.

The bill passed the legislature and was signed into law by Governor Gavin Newsom in September 2024. As a direct result of this law, the president of the UC system which oversees 10 campuses issued a complete ban on encampments, effectively dealing a death blow to the movement in California:

The resulting Time, Place, and Manner (TPM) policies adopted by California universities as a result of SB 1287 have resulted in student horror stories impacting campus activism and disproportionately impacting Black and Brown students. To address these issues, Assemblymember Sade Elhawary authored AB 2551 in the most recent legislative session which passed the legislature but was vetoed by Governor Gavin Newsom last month.

The second glaring issue of bias in respect to Senator Wiener and the campus encampment movement in California occurred in the aftermath of a violent and destructive Zionist mob attack at the UCLA pro-Palestine encampment in late April 2024.

In response, Senator Wiener authored the letter below on behalf of the Jewish Caucus. While the violence was condemned, the caucus and Senator Wiener failed to identify who perpetrated the violence — Zionists against the pro-Palestine protestors — before pivoting to concerns of Jewish safety and condemnation of the university’s administration.

The letter demonstrates a clear failure in being forthright and honest about the situation, the parties at fault, and holding those at fault for the destruction and violence that occurred at the encampment that night — the Zionists — accountable.

California's new non-UPF label law draws skepticism, ire from industry

Scott Miller

California recently became the first state to establish a certification program for non-ultraprocessed food labeling, but inconsistencies between AB 2244 and existing legislation left food manufacturers questioning which definition of UPFs to use.

At a Glance

• California created the first state certification for non-ultraprocessed foods under AB 2244.
• The new law's UPF definition may conflict with the state’s 2025 Real Food, Healthy Kids Act (AB 1264).
• The voluntary program may have been modeled after USDA organic label.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom may be preparing for a food fight.

On Sept. 28, his office released an announcement about the signing of several important pieces of legislation, some of which will attempt to regulate the food industry. The biggest news was the creation of a labeling program — and the accompanying state certification process — for products that are not considered ultraprocessed foods (UPFs).

Donnelly McDowell, a partner at Kelley Drye specializing in consumer protection, highlighted a hint from the press release: The process might be modeled after USDA organic certification.

“Certification bodies would look at ingredient formulations for products and confirm that they don't meet California's definition for ultraprocessed foods,” McDowell explained. “Where it gets really complicated is thinking about the broader federal and state regulation of ultraprocessed foods because there's no consensus yet on the definition.”

Now, as a federal definition looms, Newsom passed the first state law to create a certification process for non-UPF labeling. The law itself, however, contains some concerning inconsistencies for members of the food industry.

Zero consensus on UPFs

Several programs already exist that offer a non-UPF certification, but consensus on a unified national definition for UPFs remains difficult to find.

California’s new law, AB 2244, was reportedly designed around the definition for “ultraprocessed foods of concern” established in 2025’s “Real Food, Healthy Kids Act,” or AB 1264. The most specific version of this definition can be found in Section 104662 of the California Health and Safety Code.

It starts by clarifying that a UPF means any food or beverage containing 1) one of the substances described within the definition, which includes stabilizers, thickeners and other functional ingredients defined deeper within the legislation; 2) high amounts of saturated fat, sodium or added sugar, or 3) a nonnutritive sweetener or other substance described elsewhere in the law.

Nate Rose, VP of communications and public affairs at the California Grocers Association (CGA), called this a “three-pronged” approach.

In AB 1264, “There’s a three-pronged test to decide if the food is ultraprocessed, and then there are a number of qualifiers that were worked out to try to cover foods that could land in this middle zone,” Rose said. “Healthy foods, right, like Greek yogurt, could contain pectin as a thickener, for example.

“For most of the legislative session, we were working with the author of AB 2244 [assemblymember Jesse Gabriel] under the assumption that they were going to use those exact definitions. But when AB 2244 was amended, those qualifiers were not brought over, just the three-prong test. Now, a number of foods commonly held to be healthy are on an island where they're not considered ultraprocessed foods under AB 1264 — but under AB 2244, they would not qualify for a non-ultraprocessed food label.”

How AB 2244 defines UPFs

The bill downplays its own association with the Real Food, Healthy Kids Act, referencing it as “existing law” that defines UPFs “for certain school-related purposes.” Then it declares that existing law also requires the State Department of Public Health to define, on or before June 1, 2028, “ultraprocessed foods of concern” … the same language used in the Real Food, Healthy Kids Act to reference its own detailed definition.

AB 2244 kicks the can down the road on various promises, setting milestones all the way out to 2040. With this announcement coming right before a contentious national midterm election, California’s last-minute swerve on setting a real consequence behind noncompliance with a strict statewide definition could indicate a political play.

Regardless of which UPF definition this law may use (or promise to define later), AB 2244 leaves critical questions unanswered about what constitutes a UPF — which unfortunately also leaves food developers well beyond the Golden State in the lurch.

Newsom signs California law creating state 'Non-Ultraprocessed Certified' food seal - Washington Report

On October 8, 2026, in Nutrition, by Tom Super

WHAT HAPPENED: Governor Gavin Newsom last week signed AB 2244 into law, creating a state “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified” label for foods that meet California’s standard for non-ultraprocessed foods (UPFs). The bill passed both chambers of the Legislature unanimously last month. It was authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino) and co-sponsored by the Environmental Working Group.

HOW IT WOULD WORK: The seal is voluntary for manufacturers and modeled on the USDA Organic label. The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) will oversee the program, and food manufacturers will apply to accredited certification agents to use the seal.

WHAT QUALIFIES: Products containing chemical additives, synthetic dyes, flavor enhancers or nonnutritive sweeteners do not qualify for the seal. Products classified as “ultraprocessed food of concern” or “restricted school food” are also ineligible. Large grocery chains with more than $10 million in annual sales that carry at least 25 certified product types must make those items stand out through signage or physical separation.

WHY IT MATTERS: AB 2244 is the first state-backed certification program of its kind, and it takes effect while federal regulators are still working on their own definition. HHS and USDA recently sent the federal government’s first proposed UPF definition to the Office of Management and Budget for review but have not released specific ingredient thresholds or processing standards. Meaning individual states are creating UPF certification programs while the federal government is still defining the term. Food manufacturers selling nationwide may have to meet different requirements state by state.

NCC TAKE: NCC opposes any government effort to define or classify foods as “ultraprocessed,” at the state or federal level. As outlined in NCC’s October 2025 comments to FDA and USDA, processing-based classification is scientifically flawed and misleading to consumers. It groups nutritionally dissimilar foods based on how they are made rather than what they contain, ignores nutrient density and protein quality, and is applied inconsistently. A state-backed seal that signals some foods as “healthier” based on processing risks stigmatizes affordable, nutrient-dense foods that millions of families, schools and nutrition assistance programs rely on.

WHAT’S NEXT: CDPH must accredit certification agents by June 1, 2029, before any products can carry the seal. At the federal level, the HHS-USDA proposed UPF definition remains under OMB review. NCC will continue to engage as both the federal definition and state-level efforts move forward.

California steps out front in targeting ultraprocessed food

10/07/26 6:03 AM By Tim Hearden No Comments
  • California created a first‑in‑the‑nation voluntary “non‑ultraprocessed” food seal, launching in 2029, even as federal agencies work toward a unified UPF definition.
  • Experts warn this could lead to state-by-state inconsistencies for manufacturers, while supporters say it gives consumers clearer guidance similar to the USDA Organic label.
  • The law bars products with chemical additives, synthetic dyes, flavor enhancers or nonnutritive sweeteners.

As the federal government is still trying to determine what it is, California has taken another step in targeting ultraprocessed foods, establishing a first-in-the-nation, state-backed voluntary certification and seal for foods that qualify as non-ultraprocessed.

Under AB 2244, authored by Asm. Jesse Gabriel, D-Encino, the state Department of Public Health will accredit certifiers by June 1, 2029, and the seals will begin appearing on eligible grocery store packaging.

Large grocery chains making more than $10 million in annual sales and that stock at least 25 certified non-UPF product types must prominently display or group these items using special signage or physical separation.

The bill was cosponsored by the Environmental Working Group, whose senior vice president for California, Bernadette Del Chiaro, said it will set “a higher bar for what we consider healthy food and helping consumers make wise choices.

“Consumers deserve labels they can trust,” she said in a statement. “And families deserve a simple way to tell which foods are closer to what comes from a kitchen rather than a factory.”

But food industry experts say the prospect of states taking actions on ultraprocessed foods before a unified definition is formed could cause complications.

Anna Rosales, vice president of science and technology at the Institute of Food Technologists, responded in a blog post that the new law “raises a more complicated question: What are the implications of individual states creating certification programs around UPFs while the federal government is still working to define the term?”

She says the timing “highlights the importance of establishing a consistent, science-based framework as UPF policy continues to evolve.”

Federal definitions proposed

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and USDA just submitted the federal government’s first official proposed definition of UPFs to the Office of Management and Budget for final review. However, the agencies didn’t disclose specific ingredient thresholds or processing standards.

Interested in more coverage and insights? Receive a free month of Agri-Pulse West. 

The agencies propose a rule to end the practice where food companies make “Generally Recognized as Safe” (GRAS) determinations for food additives without notifying the Food and Drug Administration. The agencies are taking public comments through Dec. 5 and must review and respond to them before issuing a final rule.

For California to move forward with its own definitions isn’t unprecedented, noted Selina Wang, a professor of cooperative extension at the University of California, Davis.

“I think there were things that were added to Prop 65 that were not on the FDA’s list,” Wang told Agri-Pulse, referring to the state’s voter-approved law that requires businesses to warn people before exposing them to chemicals known to cause cancer, birth defects or reproductive harm.

However, if states begin imposing their own definitions of UPFs, it could create a checkerboard of different rules that manufacturers must navigate, she argued.

“I think what California is trying to do is make it easier for consumers to be aware, especially of how children are exposed to a lot of these ultraprocessed foods and marketing,” Wang said. “I can see that. … But manufacturers are selling these products around the country, so I guess they will have to figure out state by state how they must disclose ingredients. They may have to meet different requirements to sell products into California.”

Under AB 2244, products containing chemical additives, synthetic dyes, flavor enhancers or nonnutritive sweeteners do not qualify for the seal. The bill builds on prior legislation by Gabriel, AB 1264 in 2025, which defined ultraprocessed foods and set strict school nutrition phase-outs.

Food classifications

Some 15 countries define UPFs by using the Nova food classification system created in 2009 by a team of researchers in Brazil, which groups foods into four categories:

  • Unprocessed or minimally processed.
  • Processed culinary ingredients.
  • Processed foods.
  • Ultraprocessed foods.

 That last category, ultraprocessed foods, consists of industrial formulations made mostly or entirely from substances extracted from foods or synthesized in a laboratory.

However, California defines food categories based on a hybrid model, which requires both specific industrial ingredients and high saturated fat, added sugar or sodium counts.

“I think the research has shown that ultraprocessed foods are not good for human health,” said Wang, director of the UC Davis Olive Center. “I think to the extent possible, people are more aware of potential negative health outcomes from these foods, which is not a bad thing. At the same time, there are still a lot of things we don’t know, including very clear and practical definitions. There’s still a lot of work that needs to be done.”

For instance, whole wheat bread or yogurt from the store may be processed, but they’re better nutritionally than many other ultraprocessed food options, Wang said.

“There’s a spectrum of good and bad,” she said. “I think there’s a lot of nuance there and we have not figured out how to communicate clearly yet. This is kind of getting ahead of that.”

The UPF bill was among a package of 10 health-related bills signed by the governor, including legislation to create a program to find locally based vendors to provide healthy foods to California public schools.

Like the USDA Organic seal

“While Washington D.C. is paralyzed by inaction, Republicans and Democrats in California are joining forces to empower consumers to avoid harmful ultra-processed foods,” Gabriel, the bill’s author, said in a statement.

“Like the USDA Organic label, this new seal will provide consumers with clear, trustworthy information and make it easier for them to locate healthier foods that are free from harmful additives. Parents shouldn’t need a Ph.D. in chemistry to understand what they’re feeding their kids. California began this movement three years ago by banning the most dangerous food additives, and with Governor Newsom’s continued leadership we are taking another big step forward today.”

by Marion Nestle

Oct 7 2026

California passes Non-Ultraprocessed Food Label!

I first heard this big news from FoodNavigator:

California signs voluntary non-UPF label into law: Gov. Gavin Newsom’s signing of AB 2244 into law creates the first state-backed, voluntary label for non-UPF qualifying products, amid a pending federal UPF definition. Read more.California is the first state with a government-backed label for qualifying foods that are not considered ultra-processed, following Gov. Gavin Newsom’s signing of Assembly Bill 2244, legislation introduced by Assembly member Jesse Gabriel, D-Encino.

The new law establishes a voluntary “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified” label intended to help consumers more easily identify foods that meet California’s non-UPF standard. The label is the latest step in California’s broader effort to address ultra-processed foods, with implications to set a blueprint for the rest of the country. According to the governor’s office, the label will provide front-of-package information for shoppers while also improving visibility of qualifying products on shelves.

While the federal government is dithering about what it sees as a vexing problem—defining ultra-processed foods—California has just passed its own non-UPF standard. Its definition:

Existing law defines, for certain school-related purposes, “ultraprocessed food” as any food or beverage that contains a specified substance and either high amounts of saturated fat, sodium, or added sugar or a nonnutritive sweetener or other substance, as specified.

The school food definition specifies amounts per serving of trans fats, salt, sugar, and calories, and artificial colors. This definition adds artificial sweeteners.

Why is the federal government having so much trouble with this? Well, the makers of ultra-processed foods don’t want it defined unless the definition focuses on nutrients.

The Institute of Food Technologist, for example, wants “policymakers to focus on the nutritional quality of foods rather than processing level alone and cautioned against relying on existing UPF classification systems as the basis for public policy (view IFT comments).”

Many commonly used UPF classification systems focus primarily on processing intensity rather than nutritional value. As a result, foods such as whole-grain bread, yogurt, fortified cereals, infant formula, allergy-friendly foods, and medical nutrition products can be categorized as ultra-processed despite providing important nutritional benefits. That distinction matters. Policies based largely on processing criteria could unintentionally penalize foods that help consumers meet nutrient needs and support broader public health objectives.

Medical foods could easily be exempted from the definition. So could those considered “healthy” by the FDA.

The arguments aren’t really about the science; they are about protecting sales of ultra-processed foods.

By this time, it’s pretty obvious that eating real food and reducing intake of ultra-processed foods is likely to promote health.

California’s new Non-UPF label is a good first step,

I can’t wait to see what it looks like.

Food Fight Continues: California’s Non-Ultraprocessed Foods Certification | JD Supra

Last week, California Governor Newsom signed legislation creating a first-in-the-nation label for non-ultraprocessed foods. AB 2244 (Gabriel) establishes a “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified” food standard. The program is voluntary and market-based: manufacturers opt in, and consumers decide.

The bill builds on last year’s Real Food, Healthy Kids Act (AB 1264), which made California the first state to officially define “ultraprocessed foods” (UPFs) and set a timeline for phasing some of them out of school meals. It also follows the state’s 2023 ban on certain food additives in the California Food Safety Act (AB 418), which outlaws four chemical additives in foods and beverages starting in 2027.

How Certification Works

Only CDPH-accredited certification agents may certify a product, and the bill defines a "food product" as a finished food or beverage with its own UPC.

An agent may not certify a product that:

  • meets AB 1264's "additive criteria" for UPF (Health & Safety Code § 104661(a)(2)), which cover certain colors, emulsifiers, stabilizers and thickeners, flavoring agents and flavor enhancers, nonnutritive sweeteners, surface-active agents, and propellants and gases;
  • is an “ultraprocessed food of concern” (as determined by future regulations); or
  • is a “restricted school food” (as determined by future regulations).

The last two categories depend on forthcoming regulations, so the certification criteria are not presently fully known.

Certification is not permanent. Products must be recertified at least every three years, and a reformulated product must be recertified before it carries the seal.

Agents must register with CDPH, complete CDPH training, renew annually, and report each certified product's name, ingredients, nutrition facts, manufacturer and brand, GTIN and UPC, and certification date. Registration information is public, and CDPH will post a list of all certified products online.

The Non-Ultraprocessed Foods Seal

CDPH will design one standardized seal, which may use the phrase "Non-Ultraprocessed Certified Food Standard" or "Non-UPF Certified" along with California and whole-food imagery. Only products certified by an accredited agent may bear it.

Manufacturers have placement flexibility: the seal can go on the principal display panel, the information panel, or elsewhere on the package, as long as it does not obscure required information such as the nutrition facts panel or statement of identity.

CDPH may charge fees for agent registration, renewal and product certification, capped at its reasonable costs of administration and enforcement. Those fees fund a new Public Health Food and Nutrition Education Fund.

The Grocery Store Display Mandate

Once CDPH creates the seal, grocery stores with more than $10 million in gross annual store sales that offer more than 25 certified items must make at least three certified items “clearly identifiable.” That means displaying them so a reasonable consumer can readily distinguish them, through physical separation, signage or other visual cues.

The mandate excludes gas-station food marts and convenience stores selling a limited line of groceries.

Enforcement: Private Parties Can Sue Over Seal Misuse

The most notable feature for potential claims is the law allows a consumer, business entity or nonprofit, alongside CDPH and public prosecutors, to seek an injunction against anyone who engages, has engaged or proposes to engage in misuse of the seal. The remedy stated is injunctive; the article does not specify civil penalties. It is possible that consumer claims may reference violation of this law with other consumer protection laws to raise a claim for damages.

Four acts are unlawful:

  • Certifying products without registering as an accredited agent.
  • Willfully making false statements, or knowingly omitting required facts, in agent registration.
  • Willfully making false statements, or knowingly omitting required facts, to an accredited agent.
  • Using the seal on a product that does not meet the article's requirements.

Grocery display violations, by contrast, may be enjoined only by the Attorney General, county counsel, city attorneys or city prosecutors.

Although the law does not expressly authorize attorneys’ fees, successful private plaintiffs may seek them under California’s private attorney general statute, Code of Civil Procedure § 1021.5, if they satisfy its requirements—creating potential fee exposure in addition to injunctive relief.

Next Steps

The next key date is June 1, 2028, the deadline for CDPH to adopt regulations to define “ultraprocessed foods of concern” and “restricted school foods” under AB 1264. CDPH must accredit certification agents by June 1, 2029, so certified products are unlikely to reach shelves before then. CDPH may also adopt implementing regulations for AB 2244, and stakeholders should watch that rulemaking closely. Manufacturers should screen products against the AB 1264 criteria now and build certification into planned reformulation workflows. Large grocers should plan shelf, signage and training policies that support the law’s mandates.

County elections offices have mailed ballots for the November 3, 2026 general election to all of California's record 23.2 million registered voters, the Secretary of State confirmed on October 6, and every one of them carries 14 statewide propositions. Five were placed on the ballot by the Legislature and nine by petition. Together they would authorize $19.65 billion in general obligation bonds, make a 2012 income-tax increase permanent, impose a one-time tax on billionaires and, through two companion measures, possibly cancel that tax, change how recalls work, require voter ID, and rewrite California's environmental review law for most housing and infrastructure.

This guide takes the measures in ballot order. For each, the mechanics and fiscal estimates are the Legislative Analyst's Office's, as printed in the Secretary of State's Voter Information Guide; supporters and opponents are the ones listed there; the money is from the Fair Political Practices Commission's top-contributor list, last updated October 5; and the polling is the Public Policy Institute of California's September survey of 1,103 likely voters (fielded September 4–10, margin of error ±3.8 points), with later polls noted where they exist. Registration closes October 19; same-day registration runs October 20 through Election Day; polls are open 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. on November 3, and mailed ballots count if postmarked by that day and received by November 10.

California propositions 2026: The 14 measures at a glance

The table gives each measure's type, the LAO's one-line fiscal summary and the PPIC September result. Money is in the chart that follows.

42Bars new personal-property and retroactive taxesPetitionRevenues may not rise as much54–43

44Clinics must spend 90% of revenue on servicesPetitionLow tens of millions, fee-funded34–61
45Expedited CEQA track for nine project typesPetitionHigh tens of millions to $100M+ a year initially49–46

One funder shapes the chart.

Building a Better California, whose top donors the FPPC identifies as Google co-founder Sergey Brin and venture capitalist L. John Doerr III, has given $88.5 million to the main No on 40 committee, $58.35 million to Yes on 41 and $97.8 million to Yes on 42, a combined $244.65 million aimed at the billionaire tax by our count (up $23 million in the four days between the FPPC's October 1 and October 5 updates), plus $10 million to Yes on 45, $6 million to Yes on 37 and $1 million to Yes on 1.

Proposition 1: An $11.25 billion housing bond with no organized opposition

Prop 1 (SB 417, Chapter 16 of 2026) authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. Ten billion goes to state housing programs: $7.2 billion for affordable multifamily rental housing (including $150 million for youth housing), $1.1 billion for homeownership assistance, $500 million for infrastructure, $450 million for farmworker housing, $350 million split between UC and CSU student housing, $200 million for tribal housing and $200 million for local pilot programs. The remaining $1.25 billion funds veterans' home loans and is repaid by the veterans themselves; the LAO notes those payments "have always covered the amount owed on the bonds."

The LAO puts the General Fund cost at "$500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years," about a quarter of one percent of the budget, and says the funds would subsidize "up to 40,000 multifamily rental units." Supporters listed are US Vets, the California Federation of Teachers, Self-Help for the Elderly, Habitat for Humanity California and the California Alliance of Child and Family Services. No argument against was submitted. Supporting committees report $7.9 million from top contributors, including $1 million each from Airbnb, two carpenters' councils and Building a Better California, and $500,000 from Anthropic; no opposing committee has raised $1 million. PPIC: 55% yes, 43% no.

Proposition 2: Doubling the rainy-day fund cap to 20%

Prop 2 (ACA 20, Chapter 130 of 2026) changes the Budget Stabilization Account rules voters set in 2014. Today the state must deposit 0.75% of General Fund taxes each year until the fund reaches 10% of General Fund taxes, after which the money goes to infrastructure. Prop 2 raises that ceiling to 20%, adds larger deposits "in years when revenues from taxes on investment gains are very high," and extends the state's required extra debt payments from 2030 to 2040 while widening what they can cover, including payments owed to schools and repayment of federal loans. Deposits would no longer count toward the state appropriations limit until withdrawn. The state currently holds about $20 billion in general-purpose reserves.

The LAO's fiscal line is simply "State budget reserves would be higher." Supporters listed are the California Professional Firefighters, the Los Angeles Area Chamber of Commerce, Governor Newsom, Xavier Becerra and Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel. The guide's index page lists no opponents, but an argument against is printed, signed by Assembly Budget Vice Chair David Tangipa, Senator Steven Choi and Reform California's Carl DeMaio. No committee on either side has raised $1 million. PPIC: 60% yes, 39% no.

Proposition 3: Making the 2012 high-income tax rates permanent

Prop 3 is a citizen initiative, not a legislative measure. It makes permanent the higher income-tax brackets voters approved in Proposition 30 (2012) and extended in Proposition 55 (2016), which are set to run through 2030. Those rates are 10.3% on single-filer income from $371,000 to $446,000, 11.3% from $446,000 to $743,000 and 12.3% above $743,000 (double those thresholds for joint filers); without Prop 3, income above $371,000 would revert to 9.3% after 2030. The LAO says the top 2% of taxpayers pay these rates and "pay about half of all state income taxes."

The LAO estimates Prop 3 "would bring in between $5 billion and $15 billion each year" after 2030, with "roughly 40 percent" going to schools and community colleges and the rest to other state programs and reserves. The Attorney General's summary describes the education portion as split 89% to K–12 and 11% to community colleges; the two figures describe different things, the share of the total and the split within education, and both are in the guide. Supporters listed are the California Teachers Association, the California School Nurses Organization, the California State PTA and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California; opponents are the California Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce. The yes side reports $49.3 million from top contributors, $33.3 million of it from CTA and $7.5 million from the National Education Association; no opposing committee has reached $1 million. PPIC: 58% yes, 40% no. UC Berkeley's IGS poll of September 15–20 found 54% yes, 34% no. CNN reported during the September 30 debate that Xavier Becerra "previously said he would support" Prop 3.

Proposition 4: Lifting the ban on public campaign financing

Prop 4 (SB 42, Chapter 245 of 2025) repeals the state law that bars governments from using public funds for candidates' campaigns, a ban that already does not apply to charter cities such as Los Angeles, San Francisco, Long Beach, Oakland and Berkeley. The LAO is explicit that "Proposition 4 does not create a public campaign finance system"; it lets the state and local governments create one, subject to limits: no money earmarked for education, transportation or public safety, no public funds for legal defense or fines or repaying personal loans, and candidates must "show broad-based support in their district and agree to spending limits." The Fair Political Practices Commission would issue guidance but is not required to administer local programs. It also triples the maximum fine for campaign contributions by foreign entities.

State cost: "a few hundred thousand dollars each year" for FPPC guidance; the cost of any future program "could be significant for governments that choose to create them." Supporters listed are the League of Women Voters of California, the California Nurses Association, Mental Health Advocacy, Social Security Works and Consumer Watchdog; opponents are the California Taxpayers Association, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and United Latinos Action. Former FPPC chair Dan Schnur signs the argument against, and the San Francisco Chronicle's editorial board came out against it on October 6. No committee on either side has raised $1 million. PPIC: 42% yes, 53% no; IGS: 35% yes, 35% no, 30% undecided.

Proposition 5: Taking the replacement question off recall ballots

Prop 5 (SCA 1, Chapter 204 of 2024) removes the second question, who should replace a recalled official, from recall elections. If a governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor serves either until the next statewide election or, if the recall comes late in the term, for the rest of it; vacancies in other offices are filled the way they are now, by special election for legislators and by gubernatorial appointment for other state offices. A recalled official could run in the resulting special election. The LAO notes the title's "statewide officers" understates the scope: the analysis applies the change to legislative recalls too.

The LAO's background: 11 state recalls have qualified since 1913 and six succeeded; the 2003 governor's recall drew 135 replacement candidates and 2021's drew 46. Fiscal effect is "unknown," with possible savings or costs "of millions of dollars" per recall. The index page lists no supporters or opponents, but arguments are printed: the League of Women Voters, California Common Cause and Dan Schnur in favor; Senate Minority Leader Brian Jones and Assemblymember Joe Patterson against. The yes campaign's contact is former senator Josh Newman, himself recalled in 2018. No committee has raised $1 million. PPIC: 35% yes, 59% no, the weakest position of any measure on the ballot.

Proposition 37: A $25 billion state loan program for middle-income homebuyers

Prop 37, the "California Middle-Class Home Ownership and Family Home Construction Act," authorizes the California Housing Finance Agency to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds and lend buyers up to 17% of a home's price as a fixed-rate second loan, with the buyer putting down at least 3%. Borrowers must have lived in California for a year, occupy the home, and earn no more than twice the area median income; the home must be newly built or the first sale of a converted nonresidential property, priced below roughly $1 million to $1.5 million depending on county. Developers may opt into a "qualified builder option" that trades higher labor standards for more flexible construction-defect rules.

Because borrowers' payments repay the bonds, the LAO finds "no direct state or local costs," while flagging that investor appetite and whether the program actually increases construction are unknown. Proponent is former Senate leader Robert Hertzberg. Supporters listed are the United Nurses Associations of California, the California Conference of Carpenters and Treasurer Fiona Ma; no argument against was submitted. Supporting committees report $29.55 million from top contributors, led by the California Association of Realtors ($14.85 million through its Homeownership for Families committee, plus $7 million directly) and Building a Better California ($6 million). PPIC: 61% yes, 35% no, the strongest position on the ballot.

Proposition 38: An $8.4 billion bond for immunology research

Prop 38, the "California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative," authorizes $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, at least $4.2 billion of it on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's. Half goes to a single research institute, selected by the Department of Public Health and affiliated with a UC campus; half goes to competitive grants awarded by a council of seven UC campuses and 10 to 15 other California institutions. Any treatment developed with the money must be sold in California at a 20% discount, and 10% of resulting revenue goes to the state until the bond is repaid.

The LAO's cost: "$500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years," with the state possibly recovering "part or all of this cost in subsequent decades if the funded research leads to discoveries that generate revenue." The guide's bond overview notes that Props 1 and 38 together would cost "about $1 billion each year." Proponent is billionaire spinal-surgery inventor Gary K. Michelson, whose entities account for $31.2 million of the yes side's $48.2 million. Supporters listed are the Michael J. Fox Foundation, Alzheimer's Los Angeles, the Kidney Cancer Association and the American Nurses Association of California; the sole listed opponent is Stanford's Robert M. Kaplan, who signed the argument against, and the San Francisco Chronicle editorialized against it on October 3. PPIC: 55% yes, 42% no.

Proposition 39: Voter ID, mail-ballot ID numbers and citizenship checks

Prop 39 amends the Constitution to require voters to present government-issued identification to vote in person, to designate a government ID number in their registration in order to vote by mail, and to write the last four digits of that number on the mail-ballot envelope, with a mismatch invalidating the ballot.

It directs elections officials to make "best efforts" to verify registered voters' citizenship using government data, report each county's verified share annually, create a free state voter ID card, and have the State Auditor review compliance every odd year. The LAO notes it "requires the Legislature to pass additional laws to implement the measure," including which IDs qualify. In November 2024, about 13 million of California's 16 million voters voted by mail.

Cost: "tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars" a year, depending on those future decisions. Proponents are Carl DeMaio, Tony Strickland and Donald DiConstanzo. Supporters listed are the Transparency Foundation, the Latino American Political Association, the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association and the California Women's Leadership Association; opponents are ACLU California Action, Common Cause and the League of Women Voters of California, with Senator Alex Padilla signing a rebuttal. The yes side reports $22 million from top contributors, $17 million of it from Illinois shipping-supply billionaire Richard Uihlein; the no side's three committees report $21.0 million, led by the California Democratic Party ($5.45 million across two committees), the Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria ($2 million) and Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings ($1 million). PPIC: 43% yes, 55% no; IGS: 39–52; an NBCUniversal/Telemundo poll of September 21–24 reported by NBC found 49–42 in favor, and a survey sponsored by the Independent Voter Project, an advocacy group, fielded September 23–October 2 found 43–40 in favor with 17% undecided.

At the September 30 debate, Becerra said the measure "would make it harder for Californians to vote"; Hilton, who supports it, said "there's a majority in this state who agree that it's reasonable to show ID when you vote."

Proposition 40: The one-time 5% billionaire tax

Prop 40, the 2026 Billionaire Tax Act, imposes a one-time tax of 5% on the net worth of anyone who was a California resident on January 1, 2026 and is worth $1 billion or more, measured as of December 31, 2026, payable with 2026 income taxes or in five annual installments with a 7.5% deferral charge.

Real estate and most retirement accounts are excluded; businesses, securities, art, collectibles and intellectual property worldwide count. Ninety percent of the money goes to health care and 10% to education and food assistance, and the revenue is exempt from the Prop 98 school guarantee, reserve rules and the state spending limit. The LAO expects "tens of billions of dollars spread over several years" and a possible ongoing loss of "less than $1 billion per year" in income tax as some billionaires leave. Our full explainer is here.

The guide's analysis carries a warning that applies to the next two measures: "If Proposition 41 or 42 on this same ballot receive more 'yes' votes than Proposition 40, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters." Proponent is SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, whose entities supply $31.8 million of the yes committee's $32.3 million. The main opposition committee reports $88.7 million, $88.5 million of it from Building a Better California, and a second, Golden State Promise, $10.45 million from Ripple Labs and Chris Larsen. Supporters listed are Senator Bernie Sanders and SEIU-UHW; opponents listed are the California Primary Care Association, the California School Boards Association and the California Taxpayers Association, and the argument against states that Governor Newsom and both candidates for governor oppose it, which both confirmed at the September 30 debate. PPIC: 52% yes, 46% no; IGS: 45–42 with 13% undecided, down from 48–41 in August; NBC-reported: 48–38; the Independent Voter Project's advocacy-sponsored survey: 38–42 against after respondents heard the LAO's fiscal estimate.

Proposition 41: Audits for special taxes, and a bar on taxes exempt from the spending limit

Prop 41 does two things. It requires the State Auditor to review programs funded by any new voter-initiated special tax before the initiative reaches the ballot, with the summary printed in the Voter Information Guide, and to audit programs funded by new special taxes every four years, paid from the tax. And it provides that "no state tax that is enacted or takes effect on or after January 1, 2026, shall be exempted or excluded from the Government Spending Limitation," the appropriations limit voters adopted in 1979. Prop 40 exempts its revenue from that limit, which is why the guide flags the conflict; Prop 41's text does not mention Prop 40 but applies to measures "on the ballot at the same election."

Fiscal effect: "unknown," with audit costs "in the range of the low millions of dollars per year" and higher guide printing costs. Supporters listed are the California Society of CPAs, the CalAsian Chamber of Commerce and the California Taxpayers Association; the sole listed opponent is SEIU-UHW. The yes committee reports $58.4 million, $58.35 million of it from Building a Better California; the only opposition is the Yes on 40 committee. PPIC: 51% yes, 44% no; IGS: 37–33 with 30% undecided.

Proposition 42: A constitutional ban on new personal-property and retroactive taxes

Prop 42, the "Retirement and Personal Savings Protection Act," bars any new state tax "on the ownership or control of retirement holdings, individually owned assets, and other forms of personal savings," a term its text defines to include financial assets, investment accounts, business interests, digital assets and intellectual property, and bars retroactive taxes, including any "imposed on a taxpayer based upon their residency status on a date prior to the effective date of the tax." Both provisions apply to taxes enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026, including measures on the same ballot. The LAO's background notes that today "there is no tax for simply owning" financial assets; the measure would keep it that way.

Fiscal effect: a "possibility that tax revenues will be lower in the future." Supporters listed are the California Professional Firefighters, the State Building and Construction Trades Council and AMVETS; the sole listed opponent is SEIU-UHW. The yes committee reports $97.8 million, all but $22,537 of it from Building a Better California, the largest single-committee total on the ballot. PPIC: 54% yes, 43% no; IGS: 43–34. On PPIC's numbers Prop 42 outpolls Prop 40, which is the scenario in which the courts would decide whether the billionaire tax takes effect.

Proposition 43: A two-thirds vote for voter-initiated local special taxes

Prop 43 (ACA 22, Resolution Chapter 132 of 2026) is the Legislature's answer to court decisions that let local special taxes placed on the ballot by citizen petition pass with a simple majority, while taxes placed by local governments need two-thirds. From January 1, 2027, voter-initiated special taxes would need two-thirds as well. It passed the Senate 35–1 and the Assembly 68–2.

Fiscal effect: "possibility that local government tax revenues will not go up as much in the future." Supporters listed are the California Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce, with Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association as the campaign contact; opponents are the California Professional Firefighters, the California Federation of Teachers and SEIU's Nurse Alliance. The yes side reports $14 million, $9.85 million of it from the California Business Roundtable Issues PAC (top donors Peter Thiel and Kim DeGeorge); the no side $5.4 million, led by SEIU. PPIC: 43% yes, 51% no; IGS: 31–40 with 29% undecided.

Proposition 44: Requiring nonprofit clinics to spend 90% of revenue on services

Prop 44, the "Clinic Funding Accountability and Transparency Act," requires private nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers to spend at least 90% of annual revenue on "program services," with the Attorney General defining the term. Clinics that fall short pay the shortfall to the state as a penalty, refundable if they comply within five years; the state keeps unrefunded penalties for clinic workforce programs. The LAO counts "about 2,000 safety net clinics" in California and says they "currently report spending an average of about 80 percent of their revenue on providing health care services."

Enforcement would cost "the low tens of millions of dollars per year," charged back to clinics as fees; the LAO adds that "some clinics that could not meet the minimum spending requirement might close instead."

Proponents are Shawna Brown and Sean Fleming; the yes campaign's contact is SEIU-UHW, and its committee's $16.9 million comes entirely from an SEIU-UHW political issues committee. The index page lists no organizational supporters. Opponents listed are the American Academy of Pediatrics California, the California School Nurses Organization, the California Academy of Family Physicians and the California Medical Association; the clinics' own committee reports $16.8 million, led by AltaMed ($5.5 million). PPIC: 34% yes, 61% no.

Proposition 45: An optional fast track through CEQA for nine project types

Prop 45, the "Building an Affordable California Act," creates an optional set of procedures under the California Environmental Quality Act for projects it defines as essential: housing, water systems (excluding Delta conveyance), clean energy (excluding nuclear), health facilities, fire and police stations, wildfire risk reduction, broadband, education facilities and transportation (excluding high-speed rail). For those projects it sets binding time limits, including a 365-business-day limit to finish an environmental impact report, lets the applicant propose a single alternative instead of requiring the agency to develop several, freezes the applicable standards at the date of application, limits tribal consultation to federally recognized tribes, caps public comment periods, and bars courts from halting an entire project over a CEQA violation; they could stop only the deficient part while the agency fixes it. Applicants choose between the new track and existing law.

Initial state and local costs would be "in the high tens of millions of dollars annually, potentially exceeding $100 million annually," partly offset by fees; the long-term effect is "uncertain, but potentially more significant," in either direction. Proponent is attorney Kurt Oneto, who also filed Props 41 and 42. Supporters listed are the California Children's Hospital Association, the California Water Association and the California Council for Affordable Housing; opponents are the Coalition for Clean Air, California Environmental Voters, Physicians for Social Responsibility Los Angeles and the National Wildlife Federation. The yes side reports $30.4 million, led by Building a Better California ($10 million), the California Building Industry Association and its committee ($7.9 million combined, with KB Home and Lennar as top donors), CalChamber and Edison International ($2 million each); the no side $22.2 million, led by Clean and Healthy California ($7.1 million), Wendy Schmidt ($5 million) and the building trades and laborers' unions. PPIC: 49% yes, 46% no, the closest race on the ballot.

California propositions 2026 and the dates that decide them:

Ballots are in the mail. The next reads on these measures come from PPIC's October survey, expected late in the month, and from the FPPC's weekly contributor updates, where the billionaire-tax contest has already absorbed more than a third of all reported money. Three mechanics are worth carrying to the ballot box: Props 40, 41 and 42 are scored against each other, and the measure with the most yes votes prevails where they conflict; Props 1 and 38 together commit about $1 billion a year of General Fund money for two decades; and Props 4, 5, 39 and 45 each depend on later action, by the Legislature or by local governments, before they change anything on the ground. The Secretary of State certifies the results on December 11.

This guide reflects the Voter Information Guide as published, the FPPC contributor list as of October 5, 2026, and polling fielded through October 2, 2026. The FPPC list updates weekly during the campaign.

Proposition 2 could end California's feast-or-famine money problem

Paul Thornton

Extreme revenue swings are a feature of California’s state budget, not a bug. In 2022, the state had a staggering surplus of $97.5 billion; by the next year, it was in the hole for $32 billion. 

This is not a new trend. California’s highly progressive income tax system relies heavily on revenue from the rich, exposing it to the stock market’s boom-and-bust cycles and forcing lawmakers to slash programs during financial hardship. This volatility was the reason voters in 2014 agreed to strengthen the much smaller rainy day fund started 10 years prior, requiring the state to put aside money during flush years to help with periodic financial famines. 

But its maximum size – 10% of the state’s general fund tax revenue – hasn’t been enough to completely stabilize state budgets, and now voters are being asked to expand it by passing Proposition 2 on the Nov. 3 ballot. Proposition 2 would increase  the savings cap to 20% and, importantly, exempt deposits from counting toward the so-called Gann Limit, the 1979 constitutional spending ceiling that holds the budget in line with economic and population growth. It would also allow larger deposits in especially good budget years, hastening the reserve fund fill-up.  

The measure comes after the state’s nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office last year recommended lifting the rainy-day fund cap to 20% immediately and to 50% over the next three decades as a way to avoid significant cuts to core services or tax increases in the future. 

In a state with exceptional wealth alongside rampant poverty, this kind of prudent budgeting make sense to me. Those benefiting from new or augmented programs – such as universal transitional kindergarten, established in 2021 – shouldn’t have to face sudden, devastating cuts when the stock market tanks and revenues retreat. 

As the LAO noted, California ranks in the top five states for revenue volatility but lags behind the national average for the portion of its budget kept in reserve. Currently, the state automatically sets aside 1.5% of said revenue annually – though deposits can be suspended or reduced in budget emergencies – to pay down certain debts and top up the fund until it’s considered full. Proposition 2 would keep the 1.5% automatic set-aside but allow for more money to flow into the fund in years when capital-gains tax revenue is high.  

Proposition 2 is opposed by some of the legislative Republicans who voted against the bill that put it on the ballot. They argue that the budget has grown wildly out of line with the population and the economy (they’re right about that – it’s up more than 60% since 2019) and that lawmakers should control spending, not stash away more money in a “slush fund.”

They also object to the spending-limit sidestep and say rainy-fund deposits should count as spending because, as Assemblymember David Tangipa (R-Fresno) told me, “the government is not supposed to hoard money.” Revenue beyond what is needed for current spending should be returned to voters, as the Gann limit requires.  

“It's very misleading to me to tell people that this is a savings measure when it's not,” said Tangipa, who signed the ballot argument against Proposition 2 and believes expanding the rainy day fund gives Democrats an excuse to avoid making needed cuts.  “It is actually to help the Legislature spend more money.”

But Proposition 2 isn’t being sold as a budget panacea. In its report supporting a rainy-day fund increase, the LAO estimated Proposition 2 would cover half of projected deficits in the future – and about three-quarters with additional expansions to the rainy-day fund.

That would still mean cutting funding for existing programs in some years, but not anything close to the lacerating reductions in the 2000s after the dot-com bubble burst and during the global economic downturn, before the state had a useful reserve. Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), who sponsored the bill putting Proposition 2 on the ballot, said former legislators who served during the Great Recession told him they had to consider cuts far more catastrophic than the current Legislature has had to deal with thanks to healthier reserves. 

The rainy-day fund has put California in a better position to weather deficits. But as the LAO warned last year, the state is headed for deep cuts or more tax increases if it isn’t allowed to save much more. If Proposition 2 gives me the chance to help California avoid the worst of that, I’m happy to take it. 

What do you think? Golden State is a public forum. Send your responses for possible publication to forum@golden-state.org.
