California Labels "Real" Food. Will Grocers Make Shoppers Feel Something?

California Just Put a Seal on “Real” Food. Now Comes the Hard Part.

For the first time, a state government wants to show, right on the package, that a food isn’t ultra-processed.

When I first wrote about California’s move to become the first state in the nation to legally define ultra-processed food back in April, I said that “in my view, it is the most coherent food policy framework any U.S. government body has produced.” On September 28, Gov. Newsom signed AB 2244 into law which creates a standardized “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified” seal that manufacturers can put on qualifying products. It passed the Legislature 104 to 0, which tells you something about where the politics of this issue are right now. Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, who wrote the bill, likes to say parents shouldn’t need a PhD in chemistry to understand what they’re feeding their kids.

It is important to note that this program is voluntary. A company that wants the seal pays an accredited certification agent who registered with the California Department of Public Health to review the product. The agent can’t certify anything that contains the additives listed in the state’s definition of ultra-processed food (think emulsifiers, stabilizers and thickeners, colors, flavor enhancers and non-nutritive sweeteners), or anything classified as an “ultraprocessed food of concern” or a “restricted school food.”

Grocers, those with more than $10 million in annual sales, will have to make certified products clearly identifiable on the shelf, this rule kicks in once a store carries more than 25 certified items and has to highlight at least three through signage, placement or separate displays. With the average supermarket selling about $37 million a year, that $10 million threshold covers nearly every full-size grocery store in the state. That turns a labeling law into a merchandising mandate, and that’s the part shoppers will actually notice.

Don’t expect to see the seal next week. The Department of Public Health still has to build the whole framework and accredit certifiers, and the first certified products are years away as the deadline is June 1, 2029 with certification renewed every three years.

The fine print

Claudia Lewis, co-chair of Venable’s FDA group, spotted something in her client alert that every brand manager should read carefully. The seal’s eligibility test borrows only the additive criteria from the Real Food, Healthy Kids Act, the 2025 law that gave California the nation’s first statutory definition of ultra-processed food. It doesn’t use that law’s complete definition. So a product that California itself wouldn’t call ultra-processed could still fail to earn the seal. Lewis warns companies not to “assume that a product is eligible for certification” just because they cleared the state’s broader definition.

Here’s the problem with that fine print: the state now has two tests for the same idea, and they don’t line up perfectly. If the lawyers need a client alert to sort it out, I’m not sure how a mom with two kids in the cart at 6 p.m. is supposed to.

What I like

This is a positive label. Most of what we’ve done in food policy for decades has been warning labels and “free-from” claims that tell you what’s missing. This seal points shoppers toward something, and that is a friendlier message at the shelf.

Today our aisles are filled with private “clean” and “real food” marks, each with its own rules. I’ve watched shoppers many times stand in an aisle in front of a kid’s cereal box trying to figure out which claim or badge means. A single state standard with enforcement behind it (misuse of the seal can be taken to court) is a real improvement over the CPG honor system.

And it will push reformulation the same way we have seen brands add protein and fiber to meet the needs of the GLP-1 shopper. As retailers have to spotlight certified products, the folks in R&D kitchens are already figuring out how to clean up their ingredient lists

What I don’t like

Food processing and nutrition are different issues. The California UPF seal is built around additives, so a full-sugar granola bar could earn it while a stevia-sweetened yogurt can’t. The additive list in California’s definition includes stevia and monk fruit, which means plenty of the reduced-sugar products that nutritionists have been urging brands to create won’t qualify. A full-sugar product made with a short ingredient list could.

Cost is another issue. Certification isn’t free, and it must be renewed. The state hasn’t said what it will cost, and that’s a question small brands will want answered before they apply for the seal. The big CPG companies can easily absorb that cost, but the small, regional brands that often make exactly the kind of simple food this law celebrates may find the paperwork and fees harder to justify.

The industry isn’t on board either. The Consumer Brands Association, the Calorie Control Council, the California Manufacturers & Technology Association and the Food Ingredient Safety Coalition all opposed the bill, and their objections deserve a hearing. According to the Senate Judiciary Committee’s analysis, their biggest complaint is that the seal borrows definitions written for school meals and applies them to the entire grocery store. They offered an example: California’s definition of ultra-processed food exempts alcoholic beverages. That means a spirit or a flavored malt beverage could qualify for the “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified” seal, while a low-fat yogurt sweetened with stevia, or a bagged salad whose dressing uses a common emulsifier, might not.

They also argued the timing is backward. Key terms like “ultraprocessed food of concern” and “restricted school food” still have to be defined by the Department of Public Health through a rulemaking that hadn’t started when the committee reviewed the bill. When the committee reviewed the bill, certifiers were supposed to be approved on the same date those definitions were due, leaving no time to settle the rules before products were tested against them. There’s also a legal concern; anyone can sue over misuse of the seal, and there’s already a private “Non-UPF” label on the market that looks similar, which opponents say invites lawsuits born out of consumer confusion. The opponents of the bill warned that if Washington writes its own definition of ultra-processed food, California’s could fall out of step, forcing brands to reformulate and re-certify all over again.

Will other states follow?

I have no doubt they will. Gabriel’s earlier additive bills have inspired similar legislation in more than 30 states, and a law that passes without a single “no” vote is catnip for legislators everywhere. I am watching Texas, New York and Pennsylvania, all of which have been active on food additives.

I’ve been covering the grocery business long enough to remember what organic looked like before 2002: a patchwork of state and private certifiers, each with its own definition, and shoppers who had no idea whether “organic” in one state meant the same thing in another. It took the National Organic Program to clean that up. We saw it again with GMO labeling, when Vermont’s law forced Washington to write a national disclosure standard because the industry couldn’t live with (or afford) 50 different packages.

Now imagine a Texas seal that allows stevia and a California seal that doesn’t. A national brand could need a California package and a Texas package, each with its own certification. Many will simply skip certification altogether, which defeats the purpose. My concern is that others will lobby hard for a federal standard, and depending on who writes it, that could end up weaker than what California just passed.

Will it confuse shoppers?

In the short term, yes. Consumers already believe “natural” means something it doesn’t. A “Non-Ultraprocessed” seal will be read by most people as “healthy,” and that isn’t what it certifies. Add a second state with different rules, plus the private seals that are popping up on packages, and we’ll have more labels competing for the shoppers’ attention.

My Bottom Line

I support what California is trying to do. Shoppers want help, and a clear, enforceable seal beats dozens of self-made marketing badges. But the state needs to line up its own definitions before this rolls out, and the industry, retailers and regulators should be talking now about a national standard that doesn’t water things down. If we get 20 states writing 20 versions of this seal, the people it was meant to help will end up more confused than they are today.

The Bell, the Aisle of Shame and Why Most Grocers Still Don’t Get It

Somewhere in a Trader Joe’s right now, a crew member in a flowered shirt is ringing a bell, and shoppers are smiling.

That bell came up more than once when I joined a panel at Groceryshop called “Store Innovations that Match Consumer Expectations.” Stuart Samuel of Retail Futures at IGD moderated, and I shared the stage with Rick LaBerge of Haribo America and Katie Blackburn of WHSmith North America. A candy company, a travel retailer and a grocery guy might sound like an odd mix. It turned out to be one of the more useful conversations I’ve had on a stage this year, because we kept landing in the same place. Shoppers want to feel something when they walk into a store, and too many retailers have forgotten how to give them that.

Candy, nostalgia and a factory in Wisconsin

Rick talked about how Haribo connects with people through nostalgia. Almost everyone has a gummy bear memory. What struck me was how they’re pairing that with a steady stream of new ideas: a Harry Potter licensing partnership, seasonal products, and the pick-and-mix counters in their U.S. stores. Rick described it as a live test kitchen, where they can try new flavors and textures and see what people actually reach for.

Their Wisconsin manufacturing plant makes a lot of that possible. Producing here lets them localize products and move quickly on trends, so they can keep the core items rolling in huge volumes while still experimenting with small runs. Plenty of grocers could take a lesson from that. Rick emphasized that their assortment pays the bills, and what’s new gets people to come back.

A billion travelers and one airport store

Katie made a point I hadn’t thought much about. A traveler sprinting to a gate needs water and a charger in 45 seconds. Someone with a delayed flight wants a treat and take their time looking around the store. WHSmith is designing for both. She described their programmatic retail media network, which reaches the roughly one billion travelers who move through U.S. airports each year, and their LaGuardia store as an example of balancing the essentials with something new.

The part of her story I found most interesting was the unglamorous work underneath it. WHSmith has been investing in new distribution centers and ranging tools so products are actually on the shelf and staff aren’t spending their shifts chasing inventory. The goal is to free those people up to talk with customers. I’ve walked more stores than I can count where the associates are too busy stocking to look up.

Then I got on my soapbox

I told the Groceryshop attendees that retail needs passion and emotion, and most traditional grocers have none.

Look at who’s winning. Trader Joe’s has its bell and a crew that seems to actually enjoy being there. Aldi fans have turned the center aisle of rotating specials into the “aisle of shame,” and they talk about it online like it’s a treasure hunt. Wegmans curates its stores so carefully that people plan road trips around them. Then there’s Erewhon, which sells some of the most expensive groceries in the country and has customers who treat a visit like an event. Nobody would call Erewhon a bargain, and people keep coming back again and again for a single Japanese strawberry priced at $20 or a celeb’s smoothie recipe for $21.

Compare that with the average supermarket, where the experience is fluorescent lights, a long checkout line and a loyalty app that mostly sends you coupons for things you’ve never bought. The moment something more convenient comes along, they’re gone.

I also talked about restaurant-style concepts inside grocery stores, which I believe is one of the biggest opportunities in this business. Hy-Vee’s Market Grills and Pullman Market show that when grocers do it right, food service becomes a reason to visit, food service becomes a reason to visit on its own. (It’s also why I’m launching Retail Plate with my co-founder and longtime friend Korry Stagnito later this month, but more on that another time.)

Amazon, Buc-ee’s and Lululemon

We spent some time on Amazon’s physical store strategy, including the Whole Foods Daily Shop format and the way the company is using benefits tied to Prime as a tool to hold on to shoppers and workers. Amazon keeps testing and adjusting, and I think grocers make a mistake when they write off each experiment as a failure. Amazon learns from every one of them.

The panel also shared a lot of admiration for Buc-ee’s. It’s a gas station, and people drive out of their way to go there. The restrooms are spotless. The smoked brisket sandwich is famous, but seriously for my taste buds the Beaver Nuggets are even better! The store is designed around the customer rather than for the convenience of the operator. Lululemon came up too, for turning its stores into community spaces with run clubs, events and classes. People go to a Lululemon store even when they don’t need leggings.

Not one of these is a traditional grocer, yet each has made its stores into a destination, and that should be the standard grocery is measured against.

My Bottom Line

Walking off that stage, I kept thinking about how often our industry treats emotion as a marketing problem. You can’t buy that with an ad campaign. It comes from staff who have time to engage and a few surprises every visit and a sense that someone actually cares about the experience. Haribo and WHSmith are building the operational foundation that makes that possible. Most grocers are still trying to win on price and promotions, and that’s not enough. If your store closed tomorrow, would your shoppers miss it or just drive to the next one?

A behind-the-scenes note: I use AI tools to help with research, tagging, proofreading, and fact-checking on The Lempert Report. The take is always mine - 40 years in this industry doesn’t come from a prompt.

CaliToday News – Thống đốc California Gavin Newsom vào ngày 29 tháng 9 đã ký ban hành gần hai mươi dự luật nhằm bảo vệ người nhập cư và kiềm chế hoạt động của Cơ quan Thực thi Di trú và Hải quan Hoa Kỳ (ICE), trong đó có các dự luật do các nhà lập pháp vùng Thung lũng Silicon dẫn đầu.

Các luật mới bao gồm quy định cấm lực lượng thực thi pháp luật sử dụng găng tay phóng điện và đánh thuế vào các đơn vị vận hành trung tâm giam giữ tư nhân. Dân biểu Alex Lee (đại diện khu vực North San Jose, Milpitas, Fremont, Newark và Sunol) cùng Dân biểu Ash Kalra (đại diện East San Jose và South County) đã đồng tác giả Dự luật Hạ viện AB 1633. Dự luật này áp mức thuế 25% lên các nhà vận hành trại giam tư nhân bắt đầu từ ngày 1 tháng 7 năm 2028, với nguồn tiền thu được sẽ dùng để tài trợ cho các dịch vụ hỗ trợ người nhập cư.

Ông Alex Lee cho biết trung bình có hơn 6,000 người bị giam giữ tại các cơ sở tư nhân ở California – những nơi bị cáo buộc có nhiều vi phạm nhân quyền, điều kiện sống vô nhân đạo, lạm dụng tình dục, thực phẩm mất vệ sinh và chăm sóc y tế yếu kém. Trong nhiệm kỳ thứ hai của chính quyền Tổng thống Donald Trump, hơn 50 người đã tử vong tại các trung tâm giam giữ của ICE, mức tử vong cao nhất trong ít nhất một thập kỷ qua.

Hai tập đoàn nhà tù tư nhân lớn nhất đang điều hành các trại giam của ICE tại California là CoreCivic và The GeoGroup. CoreCivic quản lý hai cơ sở gồm Trại giam Otay Mesa gần 2,000 giường ở San Diego County và Cơ sở giam giữ California City 2,560 giường ở Kern County. The GeoGroup quản lý 5 cơ sở gồm: Adelanto ICE Processing Center (1,940 giường), Desert View Annex (750 giường) ở San Bernardino County, Mesa Verde ICE Processing Center (400 giường) ở Bakersfield, Central Valley Annex (700 giường) và Golden State Annex (700 giường) cùng ở Kern County.

Một đạo luật quan trọng khác là Dự luật Thượng viện SB 942 (hay Đạo luật về Quyền của người bị giam giữ dân sự – Civil Detainee Bill of Rights Act), do ông Kalra và Thượng nghị sĩ tiểu bang Dave Cortese đồng tác giả, nhằm bảo đảm quyền được chăm sóc nhân đạo, điều kiện sống an toàn và thực phẩm lành mạnh cho người bị tạm giữ.

Ngoài ra, hàng loạt dự luật khác cũng nhắm vào việc các nhân viên di trú hành động thiếu trách nhiệm giải trình khi truy quét và bắt giữ. Kể từ năm 2025, các nhân viên di trú liên bang đã bắn ít nhất 23 người và làm chết 6 người trong các chiến dịch thực thi, bao gồm 3 công dân Hoa Kỳ. Tại Santa Clara County, mạng lưới Rapid Response Network cho biết từ đầu năm 2025 đến tháng 6 năm 2026, đã có 232 cư dân bị nhân viên di trú liên bang bắt giữ.

Các dự luật liên quan khác gồm:

  • Dự luật Thượng viện SB 747 (No Kings Act) do Thượng nghị sĩ Scott Wiener dẫn đầu, cho phép người dân kiện ICE vì các vi phạm hiến pháp.
  • Dự luật Hạ viện AB 1806 do Dân biểu Jesse Gabriel dẫn đầu, yêu cầu Tổng Chưởng lý tiểu bang điều tra các vụ nhân viên di trú nổ súng gây thiệt mạng cho cư dân không có vũ khí.
  • Dự luật Thượng viện SB 873 do ông Kalra đồng tác giả, nhằm ngăn chặn ICE tiến hành bắt giữ tại các tòa án.

Riêng Dự luật Hạ viện AB 2465 do Dân biểu Alex Lee đề xuất nhằm ngăn các nhà thầu của ICE nhận trợ cấp hoặc các khoản vay từ chính quyền đã bị Thống đốc phủ quyết.

California’s ‘orphaned’ ballot measures

By WILL MCCARTHY, JEREMY B. WHITE and NICOLE NORMAN

LEFT BEHIND: Over the last two and a half years, California lawmakers spent countless hours drafting, debating and voting on a group of government reform ballot measures to put before voters. The same energy has not been put toward campaigns to pass them.

Proposition 5, which would change how successors are chosen in recalls, was set for the ballot way back in August 2024. Proposition 4, which would allow for the public financing of campaigns, landed in October 2025. Proposition 2, which would double the amount the state can deposit into its reserves, was rushed to the November ballot earlier this spring.

All aim to reform a somewhat wonky aspect of how government operates, and none of them are easily explainable to voters in a single sentence. And yet each of them have a limited, or non-existent public presence and campaign.

“You get these orphaned initiatives,” said Thad Kousser, a professor of political science at the University of San Diego. “So voters are left with very few bits of information on what’s going to be the most crowded ballot in a decade.”

The recall measure’s travails underscore how quickly a political window can close. In the aftermath of the failed attempt to recall Gov. Gavin Newsom, triumphant Democrats said they were determined to change a system that would allow a challenger — like MAGA tribune Larry Elder — to become governor with fewer votes than the number cast against a recall. Secretary of State Shirley Weber vowed action, and election committees revved up.

But the momentum soon ebbed. Policymakers couldn’t agree on the changes. Polls showed voters were tepid on changing a process that many see as an important check on elected officials. By the time former State Sen. Josh Newman finally got his measure through, the Newsom recall — and the sense of urgency it engendered — were distant memories.

A spokesperson for the Prop 5 campaign did not reply to requests for comment, although Newman said in a recent interview that he was “not optimistic” about the recall reform measure’s chances.

Historically, the vast majority of measures placed on the ballot by the legislature have won — a full 69% between 1910 and 2025. In the past, that outcome has been largely a function of how many votes it takes for lawmakers to put measures before voters, a two-thirds majority of both houses traditionally meaning that the issue was highly popular.

But polling for the three government reform measures is scattershot. A September Public Policy Institute of California poll had Prop 4 and Prop 5 with only 42% and 35% support, respectively, while Prop 2 had the support of 60% of voters (a later Berkeley IGS poll put Prop 4’s support at 35% for, 35% against, and 30% undecided).

Prop 5 does not appear to have any financial backing or a campaign committee organized to pass the measure. The committee for Prop 4 has a single, $235,000 contribution from Movement Voter PAC, a progressive organizing group. Prop 2’s committee received a $150,000 contribution from Google last week.

Assemblymember Alex Lee, one of the coauthors of the legislation that placed Prop 4 on the ballot, said the measure was in a “good place” and that undecided voters are “ready to be persuaded.” The Prop 4 campaign has begun holding public events and is planning a bus tour at some point this fall.

“I knew the other marquee efforts would absorb the media attention,” Lee said. “Really it’s just about the voter education campaign.”

Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, author of Prop 2, said you likely won’t see large ad spends or public appearances to drum up support for expanding the state’s budget reserves. Given the solid polling and what he called the “common sense wisdom” of the measure, he’s confident in its passage.

Meant to shield the state’s budget from the volatility of the stock market, the measure has the support of a wide range of groups, from the California Chamber of Commerce to SEIU. Even so, Gabriel said he expected a “lean campaign” that will “rely a lot on member-to-member communication.”

Each of the government reform measures share at least one key advantage: None face organized opposition.

“Its not like we have to raise X millions of dollars,” Lee said.

Welcome to Ballot Measure Weekly, a special Monday edition of Playbook PM focused on California’s lively realm of ballot measure campaigns. Questions? Concerns? Tips? Drop ballot measures reporter Will McCarthy a line at wmccarthy@politico.com.

A highly subjective ranking of the ballot measures — past and future, certain and possible — getting our attention this week.

1. Prop 37: The campaign for a measure to provide loans to help middle-income families purchase homes contributed $300,000 to the California Democratic Party last week, apparently viewing the measure in good financial standing.

2. Prop 38: The No on Prop 38 campaign is operating with a single six-figure check as it tries to run a campaign against billionaire Gary Michelson’s immunology bond ballot measure. The $3,000 contribution comes from Robert Kaplan, the director of research at the Stanford School of Medicine Clinical Excellence Research Center. Michelson has contributed over $10 million to the initiative, which has come under criticism in recent weeks.

3. Prop 45: A group of Republican county organizations came out against Prop 45 last week, even as the Yes campaign faced scrutiny for donations to Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio’s Reform California organization. The Yes campaign, meanwhile, released a report showing what it says would be the “significant economic benefits” of Prop 45, including adding 20,000 homes a year.

4. Fund scientific research (2028): Newsom climbed the Golden Gate Bridge with State Sen. Scott Wiener and a camera crew to sign a $7.5 billion research bond that aims to combat federal funding cuts. The measure will be on the ballot in 2028. “I’m proud to sign a bond to invest in the future of the state of California,” Newsom said in a video from the bridge.

5. Prop 40: Heavily outspent and facing enormous establishment resistance, the wealth tax campaign is hoping America’s most prominent progressive can carry it to victory. Sen. Bernie Sanders is rallying for Prop 40 in Los Angeles today after swinging through San Francisco on Saturday, where he described the campaign as a Democrat-defining battle over “the most important ballot initiative in the country.”

6. Prop 39: DeMaio is continuing on his “Barbecue, Beer, & Ballots” tour through California, attending his tenth barbecue of the last week in Ramona today as the campaign looks to help pass Prop 39. As Will wrote for POLITICO Magazine last week, DeMaio’s grassroots army has become a major factor in his rise in state politics.

7. Measure ER (Los Angeles County): A one-half cent sales tax narrowly approved by Los Angeles County voters in June took effect on Oct. 1. But it could be a while before the $1 billion it is expected to generate each year for health care can actually be spent. A lawsuit, brought by the Libertarian Party of LA County, will have to play out in LA County Superior Court before the proceeds can be used.

FIRST IN PLAYBOOK — Californians for Voting Rights, one of the committees organized to defeat Prop 39, is launching a pair of advertisements in the Bay Area hammering on the “consequences voters will face” should the measure pass. In the first spot, the No campaign characterizes Prop 39 as a “MAGA power grab” led by President Donald Trump. The second warns people of longer lines in order to vote. The seven-figure buy is the committee’s first time on air.

HE’S BACK: Former Gov. Jerry Brown will tonight join journalist Miriam Pawel, the author of nonfiction works about the Brown family and Cesar Chavez, for a conversation launching her latest book: “California Dreams: The Making and Remaking of the University of California.” The discussion will “explore the history of the University of California, its relationship with California’s political and social life, and the continuing importance of public higher education,” and the event will run from 6 p.m. to 8 p.m. at the California State Library. The retired Brown’s appearance is his latest since he visited the state Capitol during end-of-session proceedings and penned a call for global nuclear disarmament. Register here.

THE BOOGEYMAN: Democrats’ top Senate super PAC is flooding the airwaves with ads hitting Republicans on Jeffrey Epstein, the late financier and convicted sex offender. They have data to back it up, POLITICO’s Andrew Howard reports.

Internal polling of over 4,500 voters from Senate Majority PAC, conducted by the Democratic firm Blue Rose Research late last week and shared with POLITICO, found that a 44% plurality of voters — including the same percentage of swing voters — think the Epstein issue is “serious” and that Republicans should be held responsible.

And while nothing trumps affordability as the issue du jour on the campaign trail this fall, state-level research from SMP found that the Epstein ads can shift races three to six points in Democrats’ direction.

Food Labels Tout Non-Ultraprocessed Food in Bid to Fix US Diets

Skye Witley

Packaged food labels boasting products that aren’t ultraprocessed are popping up in grocery aisles across the country, with California shoppers soon to see a state-sponsored version hitting shelves.

A new state law enacted last week joins an emerging crop of third-party certifications aiming to help consumers identify minimally processed foods.

Their rising popularity dovetails with growing concerns over the health impacts of ultraprocessed products containing industrial ingredients, which accounted for more than half the calories Americans consumed between August 2021 and August 2023, according to a 2025 report from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

In response, the White House, federal courts, Congress, and states are all seeing heightened activity around ultraprocessed products made by food and beverage giants.

“The reason why front of package labels matter is because consumers only spend a few seconds making decisions about what to purchase, and so they rely on shortcuts to be able to make those decisions, particularly around nutrition information, because nutrition information is very complex,” said Lindsey Smith Taillie, a nutrition epidemiologist and co-director of the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill’s Global Food Research Program.

California’s state-backed seal follows the launch of three privately offered certification programs enabling manufacturers to market their products as non-ultraprocessed, the first of which began operating in December 2024.

Proponents argue the labels will help consumers distinguish healthier options while incentivizing manufacturers to invest in less processed products. California Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D), who sponsored the bill behind the state’s new seal, likened it to the USDA Organic label, which helped standardize a market worth $70 billion in 2025.

“You’re giving consumers more information,” Gabriel said in an interview. “But I think you could also imagine a lot of scenarios where companies will want the benefits of being able to advertise and put the seal on their product — and so they may be inclined to reformulate.”

Some public health experts, however, are concerned the rapid deployment of these labels, which all use different criteria, risks confusing consumers.

“Labels are a roadmap for industry and for consumers, and if you have the wrong map, you’re going to lead consumers in a wrong direction,” said Dariush Mozaffarian, a public health scientist and director of the Food is Medicine Institute at Tufts University.

Industry Pressure

These proliferating options for marketing food as non-ultraprocessed are designed to appeal to an industry under pressure.

There’s no federal standard informing what is or is not ultraprocessed, but the White House is currently reviewing a definition advanced by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., which he’s said may eventually inform federal labeling standards.

California and Arizona are the only states with statutory definitions, though other states have attempted to establish legal definitions.

Several leading food manufacturers are also defending against lawsuits alleging ultraprocessed foods contributed to plaintiffs’ development of diseases such as type 2 diabetes.

Food companies have cited the scrutiny in filings to the US Securities and Exchange Commission this year, and in August, CEOs urged the White House to delay defining ultraprocessed foods for fear it could intensify the litigation.

Those pressures could “increase our compliance costs or adversely affect consumer demand for certain of our products,” The Campbell’s Company said in its annual 10-K form filed Sept. 24 to the SEC.

The Power of Labels

Because California’s seal may not hit grocery shelves for several years, private certifiers argue their labels can fill the gap and help consumers vote with their dollars.

“We collectively have the power to change the way our food is grown and made without relying on government action,” said Megan Westgate, the CEO of Non-UPF Verified, one of the three private certifiers deploying these labels.

Westgate, whose organization urged Newsom’s office to veto the state-backed seal, said her label is already being deployed on hundreds of products.

California’s new law, meanwhile, gives the Department of Public Health until June 2029 to finalize its seal.

A government-backed seal can help eliminate consumer skepticism about the varying standards and profit motives of private labels, said Alyssa Moran, a University of Pennsylvania professor who advised Gabriel’s office on the label.

Two of the privately-endorsed non-ultraprocessed labels are offered by nonprofits that levy verification fees for their seal’s use, as does the third label offered by technology company WISECode.

Public Health Implications

Critics say the patchwork of labels with varying thresholds risks confusing consumers and is too incremental to substantially change consumer’s diets in a way that will improve their health.

“The reason why governments like to introduce them is because it lets them — I don’t know a nicer way to say this — basically claim to have taken action while avoiding the complex legal or regulatory process that would be required to do the mandatory warning labels,” said Smith Taillie.

Warning labels can incite legal challenges. A federal judge recently blocked a Texas law mandating warnings on products containing certain ingredients on free speech grounds, after which Louisiana delayed its implementation of a similar law by a year. A New Mexico warning label targeting products made with PFAS was also blocked by a federal judge in September.

There’s alos concern that companies could intentionally place non-ultraprocessed labels on products with poor nutrient profiles as a way to make them appear healthier.

“You are going to end up with a version of all-natural Cheetos that are still made through the same processes of Cheetos, but they’re not using any of those additives,” Smith Tallie said.

California’s approach isn’t perfect, Moran said. But it provides a testing ground to assess how well the labeling scheme influences consumers and industry.

“Now we’ll have the data to be able to kind of build on California’s experience and improve our food policies for the future,” she said.

Newsom enfrenta al ICE con una nueva ley que protege a las familias migrantes de California

El gobernador firmó la AB 1655; modifica las reglas de CalWORKs para que a los hogares no se les reduzca automáticamente la asistencia

  • 5 de octubre de 2026
  • 14:27
  • 5 minutos de lectura'

LA NACION

California sumó una nueva medida frente a las políticas federales de inmigración. La ley AB 1655 modifica las reglas de CalWORKs para evitar que una detención migratoria reduzca la ayuda económica destinada a un hogar, con el objetivo de evitar que las familias pierdan parte de la ayuda cuando uno de sus integrantes queda bajo custodia.

California cambia las reglas de CalWORKs ante las detenciones de ICE

El gobernador Gavin Newsom firmó el 29 de septiembre la AB 1655, impulsada por el asambleísta Isaac Bryan, que modifica las normas del programa California Work Opportunity and Responsibility to Kids, conocido como CalWORKs.

La legislación establece que un niño u otro integrante de la unidad familiar que sea detenido en una instalación federal de detención migratoria podrá ser considerado temporalmente ausente del hogar durante todo el período de detención.

CalWORKs proporciona ayuda económica y otros servicios a familias de bajos ingresos mediante una combinación de fondos federales, estatales y de los condados.

Hasta ahora, las reglas contemplaban situaciones de ausencia temporal, entre ellas la hospitalización de un niño, pero la nueva legislación incorpora expresamente la detención migratoria federal dentro de esas excepciones.

Lo más importante de la AB 1655 es:

  • Un niño o cualquier otro integrante de la unidad de asistencia que permanezca detenido en una instalación federal de detención migratoria será considerado temporalmente ausente del hogar durante el tiempo que dure la detención.
  • La familia podrá ser elegible para recibir la asistencia y los servicios de CalWORKs, siempre que cumpla las condiciones establecidas por la ley.
  • Los demás integrantes de la unidad familiar deberán reunir los requisitos de elegibilidad correspondientes.
  • Si la persona detenida se encuentra fuera de California, deberá tener la intención de regresar al estado una vez que sea liberada.
  • La persona detenida deberá ser legalmente elegible para recibir los beneficios de CalWORKs por todos los demás criterios, independientemente de su situación de detención.
  • Una declaración escrita y jurada presentada por el solicitante o beneficiario podrá ser suficiente para acreditar que un integrante de la unidad familiar se encuentra detenido en una instalación de inmigración.
  • El Departamento de Servicios Sociales del estado podrá comenzar a implementar estas disposiciones mediante cartas dirigidas a todos los condados u otras instrucciones escritas mientras se adoptan las reglamentaciones correspondientes.

De esta manera, la detención de un integrante de la familia no implicará automáticamente que su parte de la asistencia económica desaparezca durante el período en que permanece bajo custodia federal.

California fija cuándo comenzará a aplicarse la nueva protección

La AB 1655 no entra en funcionamiento inmediatamente. Las nuevas disposiciones comenzarán a aplicarse el 1° de julio de 2027 o en la fecha en que el Departamento de Servicios Sociales informe que el sistema estatal puede implementar las automatizaciones necesarias, lo que ocurra más tarde.

La referencia al sistema automatizado es importante porque la aplicación de la nueva regla requiere modificar la manera en que se determina la asistencia de CalWORKs. Por eso, la legislación vincula su entrada en vigor con la capacidad técnica del sistema estatal para procesar la nueva situación de los integrantes detenidos.

Mientras se adoptan las reglamentaciones definitivas, el Departamento de Servicios Sociales podrá administrar e implementar la norma mediante instrucciones escritas dirigidas a los condados. Esas tendrán la misma fuerza y efecto que las reglamentaciones hasta que se aprueben las normas correspondientes.

Las leyes que firmó Gavin Newsom junto con AB 1655

El paquete anunciado por el gobernador incluyó las siguientes leyes:

  • AB 1627, de la asambleísta Anamarie Ávila Farías: empleo público y descalificaciones.
  • AB 1633, del asambleísta Matt Haney: tributación de instalaciones privadas de detención.
  • AB 1650, de la asambleísta Jessica Caloza: vehículos alquilados utilizados por las fuerzas de seguridad.
  • AB 1655, del asambleísta Isaac Bryan: CalWORKs, ausencia temporal y detención migratoria.
  • AB 1801, del asambleísta Alex Lee: aprobación de instalaciones de detención por parte de agencias públicas.
  • AB 1806, del asambleísta Jesse Gabriel: Departamento de Justicia.
  • AB 1807, del asambleísta Jesse Gabriel: uso de propiedades estatales para tareas de control migratorio.
  • AB 1994, del asambleísta David Alvarez: Defending Immigrant Victims Act.
  • AB 2318, de la asambleísta Sade Elhawary: fuerzas de seguridad y asistencia médica.
  • AB 2495, del asambleísta Ash Kalra: prácticas ilegales relacionadas con la inmigración.
  • AB 2760, de la asambleísta Dra. LaShae Sharp-Collins: dispositivos portátiles de electrochoque utilizados por las fuerzas de seguridad.
  • SB 420, del senador Steve Padilla: impuesto sobre la propiedad y exención para instalaciones de detención.
  • SB 423, de la senadora Lena Gonzalez: Ley de Registros Públicos de California y centros privados de detención.
  • SB 747, del senador Scott Wiener: derechos civiles y privación de derechos, privilegios e inmunidades constitucionales federales.
  • SB 873, de la senadora Eloise Gómez Reyes: protección frente a arrestos civiles en los tribunales.
  • SB 937, de la senadora Lena Gonzalez: granadas aturdidoras y cargas explosivas para irrupciones.
  • SB 942, de la senadora Anna Caballero: personas detenidas bajo custodia civil.
  • SB 957, de la senadora Sasha Renée Pérez: instalaciones de detención civil.
  • SB 1004, del senador Scott Wiener: uso de máscaras por parte de las fuerzas de seguridad.
  • SB 1367, de la senadora Sabrina Cervantes: planificación y zonificación de instalaciones de detención.
  • SB 1399, de la senadora María Elena Durazo: revisiones de instalaciones cerradas de detención migratoria civil.

Election 2026 · November 3, 2026 General Election

Los Angeles ballot guide: November 3, 2026

Voters in the City of Los Angeles have 54 races and 26 measures on the November 3, 2026 ballot, counted across all districts: the City of Los Angeles (4 races, 8 measures), school and college districts (5 races, 2 measures), Los Angeles County (6 races, 2 measures), the State of California (28 races, 14 measures) and federal offices (11 races). Which of them appear on a ballot depends on the voter's address.

Show only my ballot

Key dates for November 3

  • The County starts mailing vote-by-mail ballots
  • Last day to register to vote. After that you can still register conditionally and cast a provisional ballot.
  • Election Day. Ballots turned in by hand are due by 8 p.m.

Returning your ballot

LA County accepts ballots three ways. The County and the Secretary of State set the rules and deadlines:

  • Drop box: official drop box locations and hours.
  • Vote center: vote center locations and hours.
  • Mail: LA County's vote-by-mail instructions and the Secretary of State's deadlines.

You can track your ballot after you return it.

Results: official counts come from LA County and the Secretary of State. Counts are unofficial until each certifies them.

City of Los Angeles

Races

  • Mayor

    Karen Ruth Bass (incumbent), Nithya Raman

  • City Attorney

    John McKinney, Marissa Roy

  • Member of the City Council, Council District 3

    Timothy K. Gaspar, Barri Worth Girvan

  • Member of the City Council, Council District 9

    Estuardo Mazariegos, Jose Ugarte

Measures

  • Proposition TE: Transfer tax exemption for Palisades Fire victims

    Proposition TE would exempt some Palisades Fire victims from the City's Measure ULA tax on high-value property sales. The exemption covers homes damaged or destroyed in the fire that are sold by the person who owned them on the day the fire started, between January 7, 2025 and January 6, 2030.

  • Charter Amendment LA: Budget, infrastructure and contracting changes

    Charter Amendment LA would move the City from a one-year to a two-year budget, require a long-term plan for infrastructure, and let the City Council change or eliminate the Board of Public Works. It would also drop the Charter's ban on the City mortgaging its property or running businesses, and change some contracting rules.

  • Charter Amendment PL: Planning appeals and approvals

    Charter Amendment PL would replace the City's seven Area Planning Commissions with one Neighborhood Appeals Commission and change how and when the City Council reviews planning decisions. It would also let the Council change the Charter's limit on building size by ordinance.

  • Charter Amendment EE: Ethics, elections and governance

    Charter Amendment EE would raise penalties for campaign finance violations, bar Ethics Commissioners from running for City or LAUSD office for five years after they leave, and make it harder to qualify a referendum. It would also give the Police Inspector General and the Fire Department's Independent Assessor more independence from their commissions, and let the City Council meet weekly instead of three days a week.

  • Charter Amendment PRK: Minimum budget for Recreation and Parks

    Charter Amendment PRK would double the minimum share of City money that must go to the Department of Recreation and Parks, phased in over ten years. It does not create a new tax, so the money would come from other parts of the City budget.

  • Charter Amendment PRT: Airports, Harbor, and Water and Power

    Charter Amendment PRT would change rules for the City's three self-funded departments: the airports, the Port and the Department of Water and Power. It lengthens the leases the airports and DWP can sign, requires more airport commissioners from near LAX and Van Nuys, writes the Port's spending on waterfront public access into the Charter, and makes Port lease applicants disclose effects on jobs.

  • Charter Amendment SC: Campaign finance rules for school board races

    Charter Amendment SC would delete the separate, detailed campaign finance rules for LAUSD Board of Education races from the City Charter and apply the rules for mayoral candidates instead, with some exceptions. It would let the City Council make later changes to these rules by ordinance. Only LAUSD voters decide it.

  • Initiative Ordinance FD: Half-cent sales tax for the Fire Department

    Initiative Ordinance FD would add a half-cent sales tax in the City of Los Angeles, raising the rate from 10.25% to 10.75%, to pay for the Los Angeles Fire Department. The City estimates it would raise about $345 million a year, and it would last until voters end it.

  • Proposition 1: $11.25 billion state housing bond

    Proposition 1 would let the state borrow $11.25 billion by selling bonds for housing. About $10 billion would go to state housing programs, mostly for building and renovating affordable rental housing, plus homebuyer help, farmworker, tribal and student housing, and housing infrastructure. The other $1.25 billion would fund home loans for veterans.

  • Proposition 2: Larger state rainy day fund

    Proposition 2 would change the State Constitution so the state keeps saving in its main rainy day fund until the fund equals 20% of General Fund taxes, up from 10% today, and saves more in years when revenue from investment gains is very high. It would also extend required extra debt payments from 2030 to 2040 and stop counting rainy day fund deposits toward the state spending limit until the money is taken out.

  • Proposition 3: Make high-income tax rates permanent

    Proposition 3 would make permanent the higher state income tax rates on high earners that voters first approved in 2012 (Proposition 30) and extended in 2016 (Proposition 55). Those rates are now set to expire in 2031. They apply to income over about $371,000 for single filers and $742,000 for joint filers (2025 levels, adjusted for inflation).

  • Proposition 4: Allow public funding of election campaigns

    Proposition 4 would lift the state ban on using public money to pay for candidates' campaigns, so state and local governments could create public campaign financing programs if they chose. It does not create any program itself. It sets broad rules: money meant for education, transportation or public safety can't be used, candidates must show broad support and accept spending limits, and public funds can't pay legal fees, fines or repay a candidate's own loans.

  • Proposition 5: Change how recalled state officials are replaced

    Proposition 5 would remove the second question from state recall elections, the one asking who should replace the official if recalled. If a Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would become Governor, either for the rest of the term or until voters elect a new Governor, depending on timing. Other recalled offices would be filled the way vacancies are filled now: a special election for legislators and appointment by the Governor for most other offices.

  • Proposition 37: State loans for middle-income buyers of new homes

    Proposition 37 would let the California Housing Finance Agency sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund a new down payment loan program. Loans could cover up to 17% of the price of a newly built home, and buyers would put down at least 3%. Buyers must live in the home, be state residents and earn no more than twice their area's typical income. Homeowners' loan payments, not the state, would repay the bonds.

  • Proposition 38: $8.4 billion bond for immunology research

    Proposition 38 would let the state borrow $8.4 billion by selling bonds for research on immunology and immunotherapy, with at least $4.2 billion for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's disease. About half would go to one research institute tied to a University of California campus, chosen by the Department of Public Health, and half to research grants. Treatments developed with the money would generally have to be sold in California at a 20% discount.

  • Proposition 39: Voter ID for in-person and mail voting

    Proposition 39 would require voters to show government-issued ID to vote in person. To vote by mail, voters would have to pick a government ID number for their registration and write its last four digits on each ballot envelope, and ballots would not count if the number does not match. It would also require elections officials to try to verify voters' citizenship and report on it each year, and the state to offer a free voter ID card.

  • Proposition 40: One-time 5% tax on billionaires

    Proposition 40 would impose a one-time state tax of 5% of net worth on billionaires who lived in California on January 1, 2026. The tax would be due in 2027, with an option to pay over five years at a higher cost. Real estate and most pensions and retirement accounts would be left out. Ninety percent of the money would go to health care and the rest to education and food aid.

  • Proposition 41: Audits for new state special taxes; spending limit rule

    Proposition 41 would bar new state taxes whose revenue is excluded from the state spending limit, and would cancel such taxes enacted after January 1, 2026. It would also require the State Auditor to review programs that a voter-proposed statewide special tax would fund, before the measure reaches the ballot, and to audit programs funded by new or increased state special taxes every four years. If it gets more yes votes than Proposition 40, the billionaire tax, Proposition 40 could be stopped even if a majority approves it.

  • Proposition 42: Ban new state taxes on personal property

    Proposition 42 would bar any new state tax on owning financial assets or other personal property, meaning everything people own other than real estate. It would also limit new state taxes that apply retroactively to things that happened before the tax took effect. It applies to taxes enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026, and would cancel conflicting taxes enacted after that date. If it gets more yes votes than Proposition 40, the billionaire tax, Proposition 40 could be stopped even if a majority approves it.

  • Proposition 43: Two-thirds vote for voter-proposed local special taxes

    Proposition 43 would require a two-thirds vote to approve local special taxes that voters put on the ballot by petition, starting January 1, 2027. Special taxes are taxes dedicated to a specific purpose. Special taxes placed on the ballot by a city council or other local board already need two-thirds, but court decisions let voter-proposed special taxes pass with a simple majority. It would also bar local governments and voters from adopting new taxes based on property value, with exceptions already in the Constitution.

  • Proposition 44: Spending rule for community health clinics

    Proposition 44 would require private nonprofit safety net clinics, known as Federally Qualified Health Centers, to spend at least 90% of their revenue each year on health care services. Clinics that fall short would pay the state a penalty equal to the shortfall. They could get it back by complying within five years; otherwise the money would go to clinic workforce programs.

  • Proposition 45: Faster environmental review for some projects

    Proposition 45 would change the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) for projects it defines as "essential," including most housing, transportation, water and health projects. Project applicants could choose tighter deadlines for environmental review, permits and lawsuits, a narrower review of alternatives, and court challenges that could stop only the part of a project that failed review rather than the whole project.

California targets ultra-processed foods with sweeping new health legislation

Governor Gavin Newsom has signed a sweeping package of preventive health measures in California, introducing a certification label for non-ultra-processed foods, tighter restrictions on vaping products, new children’s meal nutrition standards and an expanded Farm to School programme.

Source: Governor Gavin Newsom

California has introduced a package of new health measures targeting ultra-processed foods, sugary drinks, vaping and over-the-counter weight-loss products as part of the state’s efforts to prevent illness and promote healthier lifestyles.

Governor Gavin Newsom signed the legislation, which includes measures designed to make healthier food easier to identify, improve nutrition standards for children and restrict access to potentially harmful products.

The measures form part of California’s broader approach to preventive healthcare, with the state seeking to reduce exposure to substances and products associated with long-term health risks.

We should be about healthcare, not sick-care, recognising that preventing illnesses is far preferable to finding – and affording – treatments. It’s why California is focused on making whole, healthy foods as accessible as possible, why we’re making healthier choices easier. California has never been afraid to challenge the status quo and we’ll keep innovating, trying new things and clearing the way for the rest of the country to follow.”

Governor Gavin Newsom.

New food labelling measures

One of the measures creates a certification and label for non-ultraprocessed foods. The scheme is intended to give consumers clearer information about food products and make healthier options easier to identify in shops.

”Parents shouldn’t need a PhD in chemistry to understand what they’re feeding their kids,” said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino). ”California began this movement three years ago by banning the most dangerous food additives, and with Governor Newsom’s continued leadership we are taking another big step forward today.”

California previously became the first US state to formally define ultra-processed foods and establish a timetable for phasing them out of school meals.

The legislation also introduces several measures aimed at protecting children’s health. Chain restaurants will be required to offer at least one children’s meal meeting minimum nutrition standards, while menus must identify drinks containing more than the recommended daily intake of sugar.

The state will also prohibit the sale of over-the-counter diet pills and dietary supplements marketed for weight loss or muscle building to people under 18.

Manufacturers will additionally have to disclose ingredients intentionally added to children’s nappies.

Boosting Farm to School

The legislation also strengthens California’s Farm to School programme by creating a scheme to identify local suppliers able to provide healthy food to public schools.

First Partner Jennifer Siebel Newsom has championed the programme alongside the Governor, with California also providing two free school meals each day to children.

Since its launch, the Farm to School programme has connected more than half of California’s public school students with locally sourced school meals while supporting farmers and local economies. The state’s universal school meals programme has also served almost 3.5 billion free meals since 2021.

The latest legislation expands California’s focus on prevention by combining food labelling, school nutrition, restrictions on potentially harmful products and measures aimed at reducing tobacco and vaping-related risks.

Pérez: West Altadena left in the dark — Feldstein Soto nails Lyft for $272.5M — Hochman lands Braun’s Law — Gabriel, Curry coach the coaches

October 5, 2026

Reading Time: 4 mins read

Pérez says fire report confirms west Altadena warning failure

State Sen. Sasha Renée Pérez (D-Pasadena, Alhambra, Altadena, Glendale, Arcadia, Monrovia) said a new state-commissioned report confirms that warnings about the Eaton Fire’s spread into west Altadena never reached fire commanders, leaving the historically Black and brown neighborhood without evacuation orders for hours. That neighborhood suffered 18 of the fire’s 19 deaths.

The 724-page report by UL Research Institutes’ Fire Safety Research Institute, commissioned by Gov. Gavin Newsom, found that critical warnings from paramedics in west Altadena never reached incident commanders during the Eaton Fire. The report’s 175 findings and 266 recommendations also concluded that the destruction from the Eaton and Palisades fires came from many interconnected systems failing under extreme conditions, not a single point of failure.

“In the case of the Eaton Fire, we know that vital communication in the immediate hours after the fire’s ignition were not relayed to fire commanders. As a result, evacuation notices were not issued until hours later in west Altadena. This working-class neighborhood with its historically Black and brown residents suffered 18 of the fire’s 19 deaths,” said Pérez.

The findings come as a question is already in court. In January, Southern California Edison filed cross-complaints accusing LA County agencies, including the county Fire Department and Office of Emergency Management, of failing to send timely evacuation warnings. According to the utility, West Altadena residents did not receive warnings until 3:25 a.m. The county declined to comment on the filings at the time, and is itself suing Edison over the fire.

West Altadena families have also gone to court. The family of Stacey Darden, who died in the fire, filed a wrongful death suit against Edison and Genasys, the company that supplied the county’s emergency alert software. The suit alleges Genasys’ preset alert zones left most of west Altadena out of the initial warnings.

Feldstein Soto, state win $272.5 million Lyft driver settlement

Los Angeles City Attorney Hydee Feldstein Soto joined California Attorney General Rob Bonta and the city attorneys of San Francisco and San Diego on Oct. 1 in announcing a $272.5 million settlement with Lyft over allegations the company misclassified its drivers as independent contractors from 2016 to 2020.

Bonta called it the largest misclassification settlement in California history. At least $237,075,000, or 87%, is reserved for drivers, with payments based on hours and miles driven between April 5, 2016, and Dec. 15, 2020. The settlement still needs court approval. Lyft does not admit wrongdoing, and in a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, it said it can spread payments over four years.

“Los Angeles and our statewide partners will not allow businesses to exploit their workers and evade their obligations under the law. When companies misclassify their workers, they deny them critical protections and shift the burden onto taxpayers,” said Feldstein Soto.

The coalition sued in 2020, alleging that Lyft denied drivers minimum wage, overtime and reimbursement for work expenses. The suit followed the California Supreme Court’s 2018 Dynamex decision, which adopted the “ABC test” for classifying workers, later written into law under AB 5.

The settlement covers the period before voters passed Proposition 22, the 2020 ballot measure backed by Lyft and Uber that classified rideshare drivers as independent contractors.

A third-party administrator will set up a website, email address and call center for drivers who believe they are eligible. The coalition said it will release details soon.

Hochman-backed bills, including Braun’s Law, get signed

Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman saw Gov. Gavin Newsom sign five bills sponsored by his office, including Braun’s Law, named for a Loyola High School student killed in Manhattan Beach by a suspected repeat drunk driver.

SB 907, by State Sen. Bob Archuleta (D-Pico Rivera, Norwalk, Whittier, Cerritos, Downey, La Mirada), requires that drivers whose DUI charges are pleaded down to a lesser charge still receive a formal warning that they could face second-degree murder charges if they drive impaired again and kill someone. The law is named for Braun Levi, 18, who was killed in May 2025. It also increases penalties for hit-and-runs causing death or injury by drivers with a DUI-related conviction in the past 10 years.

“District attorneys are only as strong as the laws we enforce. The new laws sponsored by my office will make a tangible difference in public safety, deterring crime and protecting victims across the state,” said Hochman.

AB 2310, by Assemblymember Juan Carrillo (D-Palmdale, Lancaster, Littlerock, Lake Los Angeles) and Assemblymember Jacqui Irwin (D-Agoura Hills, Calabasas, Malibu, Westlake Village, Topanga), toughens penalties for illegally dumping toxic materials, including wildfire and construction debris. It also makes transporting toxic waste for illegal dumping a crime, and lets courts order property owners to clean up dumped material.

SB 1211, by State Sen. Lena Gonzalez (D-Long Beach), gives prosecutors access to the case files they need to investigate wrongful-conviction claims. The other two new laws let prosecutors bring multi-county labor trafficking and wage theft cases where victims live or work, and let animal control keep animals seized in cruelty cases if owners don’t pay for their care within 14 days.

Gabriel’s mental health training bill signed, with Curry assist

Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino, Woodland Hills, Tarzana, Reseda, Canoga Park, Van Nuys) won Gov. Gavin Newsom’s signature on AB 1626, which requires K-12 sports coaches to be trained to recognize mental health and substance use warning signs in student athletes.

The training covers depression, anxiety, eating disorders, substance use disorders and suicidal thoughts, and how to connect a struggling student to help. The law also directs the California Department of Education to build a model training for recreational and club coaches.

Assemblywomen Blanca Pacheco (D-Downey, Norwalk, La Mirada) and Jacqui Irwin co-authored the bill, which passed with bipartisan support. Only one in five coaches say they feel highly confident supporting a student with a mental health or substance use problem, according to Gabriel’s office.

“Coaches are trusted mentors who are often among the first to recognize when a young person is struggling or in crisis. AB 1626 will give youth sports coaches the tools and training they need to recognize warning signs, respond appropriately, and connect young athletes with support,” said Gabriel.

Pacheco said the law works alongside her own AB 1665. Irwin pointed to Sarah Shulze, a Ventura County runner who died by suicide in 2022, as a reason to better equip the adults students trust.

Golden State Warriors star Stephen Curry backed the bill through his Eat. Learn. Play. foundation.

“Every kid deserves that kind of coach, and we’ve been proud to make investments to ensure coaches in Oakland have the tools to be a great leader,” said Curry.

Back to the Future: How 2026’s Wild Harvest Is Changing Everything

How 2026’s Wild Harvest Is Reshaping Wine

The 2026 vintage is garnering headlines for all of the wrong reasons. After a spring of grape-destroying hail and frost caused losses of up to 90% in regions of the US and France, harvest kicked off weeks ahead of the “normal” schedule in France, California, Spain and Italy, with very little to show.

The French Ministry of Agriculture is forecasting the lowest production levels in 70 years, and California growers are expecting, in some cases, 50% less than usual.

Amid record-low wine consumption levels, a micro yield is causing less concern than it would have 10 or 20 years ago, but vintners are concerned that climate change is becoming, instead of just a perennial problem, an existential crisis.

Julien Brustis, winemaker and CEO at Château Tour des Termes in Saint-Estèphe, explains that while he, like many of his colleagues, looks to the past for inspiration, current and future conditions require a shift in mindset and approach.

“We look at what made Bordeaux great in the past, but we’re not trying to recreate the past,” Brustis explains. “We use today’s knowledge to think about what will make Bordeaux great in 2055. And the rule behind it is quite simple: no compromise between great wine and a better future.”

Here’s how winemakers are planning for future harvests today.

Why Winemakers Value Old Vines—and How a New Seal Help You Find Them

“Old vines” may sound straightforward, but it’s one of the wine world’s more ambiguous terms. Does it mean vines that are 20 years old? Thirty? Fifty? And when those words appear on a bottle, how can shoppers know exactly what they mean?

A new seal from the Old Vine Registry aims to provide an answer. Launching October 1, the OVR Seal will identify wines made with grapes from registered vineyards that meet specific age requirements.

“One of the problems with the generic term ‘old vines’ is that wine producers can put those two words on their labels without any real regulatory oversight and without providing any additional information to the consumer,” explains wine journalist Alder Yarrow, the architect and manager of the Old Vine Registry.

“The Old Vine Registry defines an old vineyard as one that was planted at least 35 years ago at minimum,” Yarrow continues. The OVR Seal divides qualifying vineyards into five age categories: 35+, 50+, 75+, 100+, and 150+ years, provided that at least 85% of the grapes come from officially registered vineyards.

The seal provides far more detail than a simple “vieilles vignes” designation, Yarrow adds. Consumers can also scan a QR code or search the registry to learn more about the vineyard.

Dom Pérignon’s New Champagne Drop Features Damien Hirst Work

Dom Pérignon and Damien Hirst are giving Champagne a decidedly artistic upgrade with a lavish duo of bottles featuring new work from the acclaimed British artist.

The famed and at-times-controversial artist lends his considerable skill set to two new label designs, an extension of his Kaleidoscope series. The partnership proved a natural fit, bridging the gap between the careful curation of a wine vintage and the thoughtful artwork of Hirst, the Champagne brand said.

“The edition brings together art, creation and winemaking at the meeting point between craftsmanship and imagination, tradition, and reinvention,” Dom Pérignon said in a statement announced the luxe launch. The release marks another crossover between the worlds of art, design and champagne, the maison said, having worked with the likes of rock legend Iggy Pop and actress Zoë Kravitz on a limited-edition 2025 series.

20,000 Bottles of Rare Wine Worth Millions Unclaimed After Sherry-Lehmann Implosion

Some 20,000 bottles of rare wine worth millions of dollars remain unclaimed more than three years after the implosion of New York City wine store Sherry-Lehmann, The Post has learned.

Cratefuls of rare vintages are sitting in the basement floor of a tower at Blue Hill Plaza, a nondescript office development in Rockland County, after the FBI raided the space as part of an ongoing fraud investigation, according to a lawyer representing the landlord.

The landlord, Hong Kong-based Glorious Sun, took charge of the $16 million collection after Sherry-Lehmann’s storage business defaulted on its rent at Blue Hill Plaza. Now, it is scrambling to return the wines to their original owners in order to rent the space to a paying tenant, the attorney said.

Glorious Sun even placed an ad in Wine Specator this summer.

“Attention” the ad states in bright red all caps lettering. “We may have your wine. If you stored wine with Sherry-Lehmann (or Wine Caves) please contact Blue Hill Plaza.”

THE TRANSPARENCY BEAT

What To Know About California’s New Ultra-Processed Foods Label

California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a bill that would allow food companies to put a non-ultra-processed food (UPF) label on their products.

The law creates the first seal in the U.S. that would appear on products as long as they meet standards for not being ultra-processed, according to California lawmaker Jesse Gabriel, who sponsored the bill.

Modeled after the “USDA Organic” label -- which appears on products that meet federal standards set by the U.S. Department of Agriculture -- California’s process would be overseen by the California Department of Public Health.

Food manufacturers would apply to accredited certification agents to use a “California Certified” seal on their packaging. Products would have to be recertified every three years.

The law also requires grocery stores in California with gross sales of more than $10 million to prominently display products with the seal in a “designated high-traffic area.”

The state’s definition of UPFs includes food and beverages that contain a “specified substance” -- such as colors or stabilizers -- and either high amounts of saturated fat, sodium or added sugar or a nonnutritive sweetener.

A Landmark Bill Will Track and Disclose PFAs & Pesticide Use in California

Gov. Gavin Newsom today signed groundbreaking legislation that takes a first step in addressing the widespread use of toxic PFAS “forever chemicals” pesticides on California produce.

The new law, AB 1603, authored by Assemblymember Nick Schultz (D-Burbank), requires the state to monitor and disclose PFAS pesticide use. State agencies do not track the concerning use of toxic PFAS on crops – but that will change now that the Environmental Working Group has raised concerns.

EWG found that more than 2.5 million pounds of PFAS pesticides are applied to Golden State crops each year, contaminating produce – in addition to soil and water – sold in the state and throughout the U.S.

EWG’s research also found PFAS pesticides on nine in 10 California-grown samples of non-organic peaches, nectarines and plums tested by the state, as well as in local waterways and sediment.

The new law establishes a class-based definition of PFAS pesticides, consistent with other California laws and regulations already addressing these chemicals. That definition matters: It ensures tracking and disclosure requirements can’t be sidestepped with chemical-by-chemical loopholes.

The definition would also lay the groundwork for action that avoids “regrettable substitutions” – PFAS replacements that can also have health concerns.

Though thousands of PFAS are used today, comprehensive toxicity data is available about very few. But what is known is alarming: The health harms linked to the most well-studied PFAS, including cancer, suppression of the immune system and reproductive and developmental harm, show up at doses far lower than regulators once considered safe.

Big Food Is Paying Influencers To Combat MAHA

Some of the biggest food and agriculture corporations in the US are funding a campaign that pays social media influencers to combat elements of Robert F Kennedy Jr’s Make America Healthy Again platform, according to an investigation by the Guardian and Documented, an investigative watchdog and journalism project.

The ascension of RFK Jr to secretary of health and human services has boosted his putative campaign to end chronic illness in the US, which he believes is primarily caused by processed foods and dyes, exposure to certain chemicals, and poor farming practices, along with an overuse of what he falsely claims are dangerous vaccines.

A KFF poll from May 2026 reveals that some Maha themes resonate with a broad segment of US adults. About four in 10 say they support the Maha movement, while a majority of the public say there is not enough regulation of pesticides used in agriculture (64%) or of chemical food additives (75%).

But several large corporations are fighting back. An effort by the Center for Food Integrity, an industry-funded non-profit, tracks public sentiment around key issues central to Maha and suggests ways that agricultural interests can counter those narratives by appealing to emotion or scientific reasoning.

They call it Gaha: Growing a Healthier America. Documents show the coordinated effort is tracking Maha closely and researching ways to respond to the movement’s claims without alienating its supporters. They are focused on several key areas: seed oils, pesticides, high-fructose corn syrup, regenerative agriculture, organic farming, raw milk/dairy and “big ag”, internal documents obtained by the Guardian and Documented show.

The campaign involves deploying social media influencers with significant reach online in an effort to rebuild trust in the industries that the Maha movement has made their target. The Gaha influencer campaign officially launched late last year. In February, CFI compiled a report listing dozens of sponsored posts on platforms such as online blogs, Facebook, TikTok and Instagram about key Gaha subjects. So far, at least six influencers have signed on to the Gaha campaign, reaching a total audience of more than 2.6 million viewers.

THE JET SET

How the Travel Agent Became Chic (Again)

Remember travel agents in the ’90s? You’d pull up to a brick-and-mortar storefront, rifle through some Disney World pamphlets, and they’d circle a bunch of options in yellow highlighter. Then the internet arrived with platforms like Google Flights and Expedia, and we all became our own agents, hunched over our laptops with 14 tabs open and the creeping sense that we’d forgotten something.

But now, the travel agent has returned, rebranded as the “travel advisor,” or sometimes as a “trip designer.” They’re found across Instagram, posting a never-ending stream of curated travel content, often with a caption insinuating that all of this could be yours. And just like that—the travel agent became chic again.

The nuance here is that luxury travel advisors are fewer agents than overall trip designers, fixers, negotiators, and, on occasion, miracle workers.

At Embark Beyond, a luxury travel and destination events company, advisor Avi Hagby learned that her client was assigned a “remote stand” on a commercial flight, which means taking a bus from the gate to the plane, which is not, Avi felt, how one begins a holiday. Hagby had three hours to fix it—and a few calls later, including one to an airport authority Avi counts as a friend, the plane, with 118 passengers aboard, was miraculously moved to a proper jet bridge.

And in the world of travel advisors, stories like that are far from uncommon. Another Embark Beyond client once hosted an anniversary party on a chartered 210-foot yacht, but didn’t want their 150 guests to have to remove their heels as yacht customs demand—so every deck was carpeted for a cool $80,000. A honeymooning bride had Dyson hair dryers waiting for her at six stops across Sri Lanka, Laos, and Kenya. When another bride chipped her tooth while boarding a jet to Paris, a cosmetic dentist was booked before her first lunch. When a sheikh was traveling the Seychelles and a storm had swept the sand from their favorite beach, an advisor helped barge in sand from neighboring islands to make it right.

Want the Best Fall Foliage Drive in America? Go Here

Don’t let summer have all the road trip fun. It’s time to put on your driving gloves for fall, and according to travel experts, there’s only one road in the U.S. you need to travel this season: New Hampshire’s Kancamagus Highway.

“I often compare the emotional experience of driving the Kancamagus Highway in autumn to driving California’s Pacific Coast Highway,” Mina Shafiee, founder of Inspo Travel, shared with Travel + Leisure. “The landscapes couldn’t be more different, but both drives make the journey itself the experience.” On the Kancamagus, she added, “You’re not simply looking at fall foliage from a scenic overlook—you feel immersed in the season. There’s the crisp air, the changing canopy surrounding the road, mountain views appearing between the trees, and those moments when you want to pull over simply because the landscape has changed again.”

The Kancamagus, for the uninitiated, is technically a portion of NH Route 112, which runs east to west, connecting Lincoln to Conway. The 34.5-mile drive is a recognized National Scenic Byway, providing drivers with plenty of places to stop to learn about New England history and, naturally, to take in jaw-dropping views of the region’s famed foliage. And really, you won’t want to speed down this road one bit.

“I would build a fall weekend around it,” Shafiee said of taking the slow lane. “Pair the drive with a stay in the White Mountains—Omni Mount Washington Resort for the quintessential grand New England experience, or a smaller inn for something more intimate—and give yourself time to stop, walk, eat locally, and actually experience the season. The beauty of the Kancamagus is that the drive isn’t transportation between experiences; the drive is one of the experiences.”
