Newsom Signs Bill Creating 1st Non-UPF Food Label; Grocers Face New Rules

Lorrie Griffith

California Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed legislation creating a first-in-the-nation certification and front-of-package label for non-ultraprocessed foods, part of a package of health bills that also carries new requirements for supplement sales, tobacco retailing and chain restaurant menus.

The non-UPF measure – AB 2244 by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino) – establishes a voluntary Non-Ultraprocessed Certified standard modeled on the USDA Organic label, giving manufacturers a certification to pursue and consumers front-of-package information, along with what the governor’s office described as improved access to healthier options through strategic in-store placement. The bill cleared the Legislature and was sent to Newsom’s desk at the beginning of September.

“Like the USDA Organic label, this new seal will provide consumers with clear, trustworthy information and make it easier for them to locate healthier foods that are free from harmful additives,” Gabriel said. “Parents shouldn’t need a Ph.D. in chemistry to understand what they’re feeding their kids. California began this movement three years ago by banning the most dangerous food additives, and with Governor Newsom’s continued leadership we are taking another big step forward today.”

The legislation builds on last year’s Healthy Foods, Healthy Kids Act, also by Gabriel, which made California the first state to officially define ultraprocessed foods and set a timeline for phasing them out of schools.

The California Grocers Association expressed its disappointment at label’s passage. Spokesperson Nate Rose told The Shelby Report,  “CGA worked tirelessly throughout the legislative session to find common ground with Asm. Gabriel on AB 2244. Our amendments removed the mandate for dedicated shelf space of non-ultra processed food and the private right of action and instead included good-faith compliance protections and a sunset of the retail display requirement.

“Ultimately, CGA was disappointed by last minute amendments to how non-ultra processed foods are defined. We believe AB 2244 will not provide the clarity shoppers need to make healthier buying decisions and is likely to only lead to more confusion as to what an ultra processed food is and isn’t,” Rose added.

What else the package includes for retailers

Several other bills in the package touch grocery and convenience store operations:

  • AB 2030 bans the sale of over-the-counter diet pills and dietary supplements marketed for weight loss or muscle building to anyone under 18, affecting retailers with wellness and supplement sections (see more below).
  • AB 762 and AB 2667 ban single-use, battery-embedded vapes and restrict advertising of vape products designed to resemble items marketed to minors, while tobacco retailers must display lung cancer screening awareness signage.
  • SB 869 requires menus to flag drinks containing more than the recommended daily intake of added sugar, and SB 977 requires chain restaurants to offer at least one children’s meal meeting a minimum nutrition standard, provisions that could reach grocery foodservice operations depending on implementing rules.
  • AB 1731 creates a program to source healthy foods from locally based vendors for California public schools, extending the state’s Farm to School efforts.

Supplement industry pushes back

The Council for Responsible Nutrition, the trade association for the dietary supplement and functional food industry, expressed deep disappointment with the signing of AB 2030, warning the law’s approach could create barriers to lawful products, confuse consumers and leave retailers uncertain about which supplements fall within its restrictions.

The law prohibits sales of supplements “labeled, marketed or otherwise represented for weight loss or muscle-building” and over-the-counter diet pills to consumers under 18 without a prescription, establishes age-verification requirements for retail and remote sales and authorizes civil penalties of up to $500 per violation. CRN said courts may consider statements that even “imply” those effects, claims about metabolism or strength, and how products are grouped in stores or online, a framework the association warned could sweep in fiber and protein supplements, general wellness products and even multivitamins.

“Protecting young people from eating disorders is an important objective that we share,” said Steve Mister, president and CEO of CRN. “But that objective deserves policies grounded in evidence, not broad restrictions that cast suspicion on lawful products without establishing that those restrictions will address the problem.”

The governor’s office, in signing the bill, cited findings that nearly 1 in 10 adolescents have used nonprescribed weight loss or muscle-building products, which it said are too often mislabeled or tainted with harmful substances such as steroids. CRN had urged lawmakers to instead base restrictions on a public health assessment of specific products by the California Department of Public Health, and noted the California law closely tracks a 2023 New York law it has petitioned the U.S. Supreme Court to review on First Amendment grounds.

The governor’s office framed the package as advancing prevention-focused healthcare, citing the state’s universal school meals program, which has served nearly 3.5 billion free meals since 2021, and its Farm to School program. Newsom said California is “focused on making whole, healthy foods as accessible as possible” and “making healthier choices easier.”

California endurece las reglas sobre la detención privada y los operativos migratorios federales

Selene Rivera

Los Ángeles
 — California endurece las reglas para las empresas privadas de detención migratoria y pone nuevos límites a ciertas operaciones federales. El cambio llega tras la firma de tres nuevas leyes por parte del gobernador Gavin Newsom.

Las medidas, AB 1633, AB 1806 y AB 1807, abordan tres áreas distintas: los ingresos de las compañías privadas de detención, las investigaciones de tiroteos mortales que involucren a agentes federales de inmigración y el uso de propiedades estatales durante operativos migratorios.

Las leyes forman parte de un paquete más amplio de medidas relacionadas con la inmigración que Newsom firmó a finales de septiembre.

**Un nuevo impuesto para las empresas de detención**

La AB 1633, presentada por el asambleísta Matt Haney, establece un impuesto del 25% sobre los ingresos brutos de las corporaciones con fines de lucro que operen centros privados de detención migratoria.

Los recursos recaudados serán destinados al nuevo Fondo Due Process for All, creado para financiar servicios relacionados con inmigración.

La medida coloca a California en una posición poco común frente a la industria privada de detención migratoria. Un análisis fiscal legislativo estimó que el impuesto podría generar alrededor de 177 millones de dólares.

La iniciativa busca que una parte de los ingresos provenientes de estas instalaciones se destine a servicios para personas y familias que enfrentan procesos migratorios.

**Investigación independiente tras tiroteos mortales**

La AB 1806, del asambleísta Jesse Gabriel, establece un nuevo mecanismo de supervisión cuando un agente federal de inmigración mata a tiros a un civil desarmado en California.

La ley ordena al fiscal general del estado realizar una investigación independiente de estos casos. Si se determina que existen fundamentos para presentar cargos, el fiscal general deberá iniciar un proceso penal. Además, los resultados de la investigación deberán hacerse públicos.

La medida busca establecer una revisión estatal independiente en incidentes que involucran a agentes federales, ampliando la participación de las autoridades de California en este tipo de casos.

Los autores de la ley también citaron varios casos recientes para explicar la necesidad de una investigación independiente, entre ellos los de Renee Good y Alex Pretti en Minneapolis y el de Keith Porter Jr., quien murió tras recibir disparos de un agente de inmigración fuera de servicio en Northridge.

“Estas nuevas leyes fortalecerán el estado de derecho y protegerán a las personas que llaman hogar a nuestro estado”, dijo el asambleísta Gabriel.

**Propiedades estatales, fuera de los operativos migratorios**

La tercera medida, AB 1807, también presentada por Gabriel, establece restricciones sobre el uso de propiedades pertenecientes al estado.

La ley prohíbe utilizar terrenos e instalaciones estatales, incluidos estacionamientos y garajes, para preparar, procesar o detener personas durante operaciones de control migratorio, exige que las agencias estatales identifiquen propiedades vulnerables, coloquen señalización, establezcan límites de acceso y desarrollen procedimientos para impedir actividades federales de inmigración no autorizadas en terrenos estatales.

La legislación también establece procedimientos para documentar intentos o usos de propiedades estatales relacionados con estos operativos y contempla determinadas excepciones.

Las dos medidas, AB1806 y AB1807, contaron con el respaldo de una coalición de más de 100 organizaciones de derechos de los inmigrantes, sindicatos, grupos de asistencia legal, organizaciones de derechos civiles y comunidades religiosas.

**Una nueva etapa en el enfrentamiento migratorio**

Las tres leyes representan distintos frentes de la estrategia de California frente a las operaciones federales de inmigración: una medida fiscal dirigida a empresas privadas de detención, una nueva vía de investigación estatal y restricciones al uso de recursos y propiedades estatales.

El California Immigrant Policy Center, una de las organizaciones que respaldó las medidas, celebró la decisión de Newsom y destacó el papel de familias, trabajadores, líderes religiosos, sindicatos y organizaciones comunitarias que participaron en la campaña a favor de las leyes.

“Este año, California dejó claro que nadie está por encima de la ley y tomó medidas directas contra las ganancias de las corporaciones que separan a las familias”, dijo Masih Fouladi, director ejecutivo del California Immigrant Policy Center.

“Con la AB 1633, California se convirtió en el primer estado del país en imponer un impuesto a las corporaciones privadas de detención migratoria, y esos fondos se destinarán a garantizar el debido proceso para las familias inmigrantes”, dijo Fouladi.

El activista añadió que con la AB 1806, las familias que pierdan a un ser querido a manos de un agente federal de inmigración tendrán derecho a una investigación independiente y a obtener respuestas claras.

“Y con la AB 1807, nuestros edificios y terrenos estatales, espacios que nos pertenecen a todos, ya no podrán utilizarse para preparar operativos contra nuestros vecinos”, sostuvo.

Las medidas llegan en medio de un enfrentamiento más amplio entre California y el gobierno federal sobre las políticas de inmigración y la manera en que se llevan a cabo las operaciones federales dentro del estado.

Con estas nuevas leyes, California suma herramientas estatales para supervisar distintos aspectos relacionados con la detención privada y las operaciones federales de inmigración, mientras continúa el debate nacional sobre el alcance de la autoridad federal y el papel de los estados.

Shiu-Ming Cheer, subdirectora del California Immigrant Policy Center, sostuvo que ninguna persona debería morir a manos de un funcionario del gobierno ni mientras se encuentra bajo custodia gubernamental.

“La promulgación de la AB 1806 y la AB 1807 envía un mensaje claro: California garantizará que los recursos estatales se utilicen para proteger la seguridad y los derechos de todos los californianos, no para facilitar peligrosos operativos migratorios, detenciones y deportaciones”, dijo.

California Creates a 'Non-Ultraprocessed Certified' Food Seal

AB 2244, signed Sept. 28, sets up a voluntary state seal for foods that pass California's ultra-processed test. Who certifies, what's excluded, and when it starts.

By Chris Carrillo · Reviewed by Armin Rad, Co-Founder & CTO, Aurascan · October 2, 2026

On September 28, 2026, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 2244 into law, creating the nation's first official voluntary "Non-Ultraprocessed Certified" food standard. Administered by the California Department of Public Health (CDPH), the measure sets up state-accredited certification agents, bars products containing specified additives from carrying the seal, and requires large grocery supermarkets stocking certified items to make them easy for consumers to find.

Key takeaways:

  • Governor Gavin Newsom signed AB 2244 on September 28, 2026, establishing the nation's first official voluntary 'Non-Ultraprocessed Certified' seal.
  • The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) must accredit certification agents by June 1, 2029, and will maintain a public registry of compliant products.
  • Items containing specified additives, ultraprocessed foods of concern, or restricted school foods are legally barred from carrying the seal.
  • Certified foods must be recertified at least every three years, and a reformulated product must be recertified before it can carry the seal.
  • Large grocery retailers with annual sales over $10 million stocking more than 25 certified products must make at least 3 of them easy for shoppers to spot.

What happened

On September 28, 2026, California enacted AB 2244, authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel. The bill was approved by Governor Gavin Newsom and filed with the Secretary of State on September 28, 2026, officially recorded as Chapter 721, Statutes of 2026. According to Gabriel's office, the signing took place at a ceremony at UCLA Mattel Children's Hospital.

The measure advanced through the California Legislature with unanimous bipartisan support, passing with a 32-0 vote in the Senate and a 72-0 vote in the Assembly. AB 2244 was signed alongside a broader package of ten health measures that day, including Senate Bill 869 regarding menu added-sugar warnings and Senate Bill 977 concerning children's meals.

Public health and medical organizations actively supported the legislation, including the Environmental Working Group, the California Medical Association, the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American Diabetes Association, and the American Heart Association. Gabriel's office says the seal is modeled after the "USDA Organic" label.

What changed

AB 2244 establishes a formal, state-defined mechanism to verify that a food product is not ultraprocessed. Under the statute, CDPH must accredit certification agents no later than June 1, 2029. These accredited agents will evaluate food products and issue certifications allowing brands to display the official seal.

The statute sets strict eligibility standards. A certification agent cannot certify any product that meets the additive criteria for ultraprocessed food under California Health and Safety Code Section 104661(a)(2). That test is about additives alone: a product does not also need high saturated fat, sodium or added sugar to be barred from the seal. Additionally, products classified by CDPH as an "ultraprocessed food of concern" or a "restricted school food" under Section 104662 are entirely disqualified from receiving certification.

To ensure ongoing product integrity, certifications do not last indefinitely. Any certified food product must undergo mandatory recertification at least once every three years. Furthermore, if a manufacturer reformulates an ingredient blend, that product must be recertified before it can lawfully continue carrying the seal.

CDPH is directed to create a standardized seal that may include phrasing like "Non-Ultraprocessed Certified Food Standard" or "Non-UPF Certified" and feature whole-food or California imagery. Brands may place this seal on the principal display panel or information panel, provided it does not obscure other required information, such as the statement of identity or the Nutrition Facts panel.

Accountability mechanisms include a public tracking database. Accredited certifiers must report to CDPH each certified item's product name, full ingredient list, Nutrition Facts panel details, manufacturer, brand, Global Trade Item Number (GTIN) and UPC, and the date certified. CDPH will host and maintain a publicly accessible webpage cataloging all active certified products.

Misusing the seal is explicitly unlawful under California law. The statute grants enforcement powers to enjoin unauthorized use to the CDPH, the California Attorney General, county counsel, and city attorneys. In addition, private rights of action allow consumers, businesses and nonprofit organizations to seek injunctive relief against improper seal usage.

CDPH is authorized to assess registration fees on certifying agents and certification fees on participating products. All collected fees will be deposited into a newly established state treasury fund: the Public Health Food and Nutrition Education Fund.

Who is affected

Food manufacturers seeking to differentiate their products in the retail market are central to this law. Participation is voluntary. A brand that wants the seal has to go through an accredited certification agent, recertify at least every three years, and recertify again after any reformulation. For shoppers, the same skills in How to Read a Food Label: The Ingredient List, Line by Line still apply until certified products appear.

Grocery retailers get a display duty once CDPH creates the standardized seal. Supermarkets and grocery stores with annual gross sales exceeding $10 million that stock more than 25 certified items must make at least 3 certified items "clearly identifiable" to consumers. The law lists physical separation, signage or other visual cues as ways to do it. Gas-station marts and convenience stores are exempt from this requirement, and a store is deemed compliant if it shows a good-faith effort and reasonable policies, procedures or employee training. This grocer display mandate includes a sunset provision repealing the requirement on January 1, 2040.

Certification agents are the third group. Each must register with CDPH, complete department training, renew every year, and report every product it certifies; CDPH may audit their procedures and records.

What it means for shoppers

For consumers navigating crowded grocery store aisles, AB 2244 introduces a verifiable, state-regulated benchmark. Rather than relying on self-declared marketing terms like "natural" or "wholesome," shoppers will have a seal tied to specific ingredient exclusions written into state law.

The law targets additive classes such as emulsifiers, stabilizers and thickeners, colors other than the natural colors listed in 21 CFR Part 73, flavoring agents and nonnutritive sweeteners. For what those additives look like on a label, see Emulsifiers on Ingredient Lists Explained: Lecithin to Polysorbate 80 and Food Gums on 6 Scanned Labels: From Five Thickeners to Zero.

Shoppers will also have an objective verification tool beyond packaging claims. Because CDPH will host an open registry tracking certified UPCs and ingredients, consumers will be able to confirm whether an item on the shelf holds an active certification.

The background

AB 2244 builds directly upon groundwork laid by previous California legislation, specifically AB 1264 enacted in 2025 and effective January 1, 2026. That earlier statute added Section 104661 to the California Health and Safety Code, establishing the statutory baseline definition for ultraprocessed food that the new certification program utilizes.

Under Section 104661, a food is ultraprocessed if it contains a substance from FDA's Substances Added to Food inventory with one of the listed technical effects, plus either high saturated fat, sodium or added sugar, or a nonnutritive sweetener or one of the listed sweeteners such as sucralose, erythritol, steviol glycosides, monk fruit (Luo Han) concentrate, sorbitol or xylitol. These technical additive effects include:

  • Surface-active agents, emulsifiers, and emulsifier salts
  • Stabilizers and thickeners
  • Propellants, aerating agents, and gases
  • Colors and coloring adjuncts
  • Flavoring agents, adjuvants, and flavor enhancers (excluding standard spices and natural seasonings under 21 CFR 182.10)
  • Nonnutritive sweeteners

Section 104661 specifically notes that salt, traditional culinary spices, and natural color additives exempt from certification under 21 CFR Part 73 do not trigger an ultraprocessed designation on their own. Raw agricultural commodities and minimally processed whole foods are also expressly excluded from the definition.

Existing law further requires CDPH to adopt formal administrative regulations defining "ultraprocessed foods of concern" and "restricted school foods" on or before June 1, 2028. AB 2244 links its certification prohibitions directly to those upcoming standards.

What to watch next

Several regulatory milestones will dictate how quickly certified products reach consumer shopping baskets:

  • June 1, 2028: CDPH is required to adopt regulations defining "ultraprocessed foods of concern" and "restricted school foods" under existing Health and Safety Code provisions.
  • June 1, 2029: Statutory deadline for CDPH to accredit certification agents.
  • Ongoing: Design and release of the standardized seal graphic by CDPH, alongside fee schedule determinations.

Significant details remain undisclosed by state officials. The bill materials name no brand or manufacturer that plans to seek the seal. CDPH has not yet unveiled the visual design of the seal, nor has it published the fee schedule for certifier registration or product filing. The entities that will apply to serve as accredited certifiers remain unknown.

Critically, state statutes do not establish a fixed date by which certified items must be on store shelves, and there are no official projections estimating how many packaged products will ultimately qualify. At the federal level, the FDA and USDA have asked for public input to help develop a uniform definition of ultra-processed foods. The California seal is a state program, and nothing in the bill gives a federal agency a role in it. There is also no data yet on whether the seal will change what people buy or their health.

Common questions

  • What is California AB 2244?
  • California AB 2244 is a state law signed on September 28, 2026, creating a voluntary 'Non-Ultraprocessed Certified' seal for packaged foods, administered by the California Department of Public Health.
  • Is the Non-Ultraprocessed Certified seal mandatory for all food brands?
  • No. The certification standard established under AB 2244 is completely voluntary. Food manufacturers can choose whether to apply for certification through state-accredited agents.
  • When will consumers see the non-ultraprocessed seal on grocery shelves?
  • State law requires the California Department of Public Health to accredit certifying agents no later than June 1, 2029. A specific date for when certified products will first appear on retail shelves was not disclosed.
  • Which ingredients disqualify a food product from certification?
  • A product cannot be certified if it meets the additive criteria in Health and Safety Code 104661(a)(2): a substance from FDA's Substances Added to Food database with a listed technical effect, such as emulsifiers, stabilizers and thickeners, colors, flavoring agents or nonnutritive sweeteners. Salt, spices and natural colors listed in 21 CFR Part 73 do not count by themselves. Products classified as ultraprocessed foods of concern or restricted school foods are also barred.
  • What rules apply to grocery stores under AB 2244?
  • Grocery stores with gross annual sales exceeding $10 million that stock more than 25 certified products must make at least 3 certified items clearly identifiable using signage, physical separation, or visual cues. Convenience stores are exempt.
  • How often must certified products be recertified?
  • Certified food products must undergo mandatory recertification at least once every three years, and any product reformulation requires recertification before continuing to display the seal.

Sources

  • AB 2244 Bill Text - Food: Non-Ultraprocessed Certified food standard (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
  • California Health and Safety Code Section 104661 (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov)
  • Substances Added to Food (formerly EAFUS) (fda.gov)
  • Ultra-Processed Foods (fda.gov)

California becomes first state to list ‘Jewish’ as an ethnicity

Niva Ashkenazi

Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a bill Sept. 30 that makes California the first state to officially treat Jewish identity as an ethnicity. The bill, known as SB 1387, adds “Jewish” to a list of about 50 racial and ethnic identities recognized by the state for data collection. 

David Bocarsly, CEO of Jewish California, a statewide coalition of 46 Jewish groups that backed the bill, framed its passage as a major turning point. 

“This is a historic step for the Jewish community,” Bocarsly said in a statement. “Under the shadow of Nazi race theory, American Jewish leaders asked the government to count us only as a religion. That was an understandable attempt at self-preservation, and it didn’t work. Our community was mischaracterized and misunderstood, and we were excluded from interethnic coalitions and the data that shapes policy.”

State Sen. Henry Stern (D-Sherman Oaks), a member of the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, authored SB 1387, which will update state forms such as unemployment claims or hate-crime reports.

Supporters say the law will produce better data for tracking and combating antisemitism and for identifying disparities in health and education. They also say it will more accurately reflect secular Jews who see their identity as ancestral or cultural rather than religious.

Newsom signed the bill over the objections of some in the Jewish community, led by progressive groups including Jewish Voice for Peace and Bend the Arc, which said a single Jewish ethnicity box flattens the community’s diversity, singles out one religion for ethnic status and creates a government record of who is Jewish.

The bill passed in the Assembly’s final floor vote on Sep. 1, with 74 votes in favor and five abstentions. It passed the state Senate on Aug. 31 with 39 votes and one abstention. No one voted against it in either chamber.

SB 1387 was one of six bills sponsored by Jewish California in this legislative session. Newsom signed all six. The new laws strengthen security at houses of worship, limit hate speech in the state’s voter guides and expand religious accommodations at public forums and schools. 

On Sept. 29, Newsom signed Assemblymember Rebecca Bauer-Kahan’s (D-Orinda) Safe Worship Zone Act, or AB 2664, which bars anyone from approaching a congregant within 8 feet without consent inside a 100-foot zone around house-of-worship entrances. 

AB 1853, authored by Assemblymembers Gail Pellerin (D-Santa Cruz) and Marc Berman (D-Menlo Park), lets election officials reject threatening, false or misleading candidate statements in voter guides. Legislators introduced the bill after an antisemitic screed by a gubernatorial candidate was published in the state’s voter guide for the June 2 primary election.

AB 1836 expands the State Nonprofit Security Grant Program to cover off-site events like Pride marches and menorah lightings. AB 395 asks state agencies and public colleges to avoid scheduling major events on religious and cultural holidays, adding Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and Passover to state law for the first time. Both bills were authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), who chairs the California Legislative Jewish Caucus. 

Jewish California also sponsored a bill from a non-caucus member. AB 1763, by Assemblymember Alex Lee (D-San Jose), guarantees K-12 students excused absences for religious holidays without prior approval.

All six laws take effect Jan. 1.

The Jewish ethnicity law gives state agencies two years to update their forms and data systems. The timeline mirrors AB 91, the 2025 law that added Middle Eastern and North African categories, including Israeli, to state forms on the same 2029 schedule.

Newsom also vetoed one bill that Jewish California initially opposed: AB 2551, which first sought to repeal SB 1287, a law that established “time, place and manner” restrictions for college protests. AB 2551 would have required the California State University system to report annually on student code-of-conduct violations tied to campus protests. 

Jewish California changed its position on the bill to neutral after working with the bill’s author, Assemblymember Sade Elhawary (D-South Los Angeles), to remove the language repealing SB 1287. 

“Given the numerous ways that the campus community can already provide perspective to policy leaders,” Newsom wrote in a Sept. 27 veto message, “it is unnecessary to require an additional forum outside these established processes.”

Newsom just put new limits on ICE. Here’s what’s changing in LA

Martín Macías, Jr.

A tax on immigration detention center operators. Bans on shock-gloves used by immigration agents and the use of state property for detentions or staging during ICE operations.

Those regulations are at the center of California bills signed into law Tuesday by Gov. Gavin Newsom that aim to put restraints on federal immigration enforcement activity. 

California lawmakers don’t have authority to shape federal immigration policy. But state Democrats authored a set of bills this year aiming to hold ICE accountable. Facing a Wednesday deadline, Newsom signed 21 bills that advanced to his desk, though some legislation was weakened as it made its way through the Senate and Assembly.
The governor also vetoed a handful of ICE-related bills, including legislation that would’ve prevented local and state law enforcement from picking up second jobs with ICE.

“We will continue protecting our people, upholding the rule of law, and making clear that if the federal government operates in California we will hold them accountable,” Newsom said in a public statement on Tuesday. 

Angelica Salas, executive director of the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, or CHIRLA, said in an email to LA Public Press the newly signed laws signal to California’s immigrants that they are valued.

“At a time when cruel federal immigration policies are creating fear, separation, and suffering, California is choosing a different path—one rooted in dignity, humanity, and belonging,” Salas said.

Newsom signed the legislative package after Department of Homeland Security agents arrested about 100,000 immigrants in July and August combined, compared to roughly 31,000 arrests in April and 32,000 in May. The federal agency is also working to hire 5,000 new agents.

Asked to comment on the legislative package signed by Newsom, a DHS spokesperson said in an email to LA Public Press that California has a constitutional obligation to enforce immigration law. 

“While California sanctuary politicians continue to release pedophiles, rapists, gang members, and murderers onto their streets, our brave law enforcement will continue to risk their lives to arrest these heinous criminals and make California safe again,” the spokesperson said. DHS didn’t respond to a request to name their spokesperson.

People with no criminal record make up the overwhelming majority of immigrants targeted by ICE nationwide, according to federal data. 

Below are some of the key immigration-related bills that Newsom signed and vetoed. A list of all the signed bills is available here.

Approved: AB 1627

This bill prevents DHS agents with histories of misconduct from joining law enforcement agencies in the Golden State.

In a public statement Tuesday, AB 1627 author Assemblymember Anamarie Ávila Farías, a Democrat representing the city of Martinez in California’s East Bay, thanked Newsom for his signature.

“Our kids deserve role models in uniform, not individuals tied to fear and intimidation,” Ávila Farías said. “Federal agents who have disregarded constitutional rights are not to be entrusted with peace enforcement roles in our state.”

AB 1627 is set to take effect Jan. 1, 2027.

Approved: AB 1633

This bill establishes a 25% tax on the gross income for operators of the 8 private detention centers in California. As it made its way through the Senate, implementation of the bill was delayed from 2027 to 2028. 

The tax, which was decreased from 50% to 25% by state Senators, is expected to generate $177 million annually and fund legal services for immigrants. 

A DHS spokesperson said in an email that the tax won’t deter the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign.

“No tax will stop ICE from deporting criminal illegal aliens to make California safe again,” the spokesperson said. “We need California to cooperate with our officers and stop releasing criminals from their jails into California’s neighborhoods.”

AB 1633 is set to take effect July 1, 2028.

Approved: AB 1650

The Slam the Brakes on ICE Act will require federal agents renting vehicles in the state to publicly display the name and logo for their agency on the front door panels of the vehicles.

While the bill’s author, LA Democratic Assemblymember Jessica Caloza, told LA Public Press the legislation will make it easier to spot rental vehicles used during DHS operations, immigrant defense groups said the bill contains loopholes for agents.

Exempt from the law are officers engaged in “surveillance, active undercover operations or investigative activities,” along with vehicles used for the “transport of a person who is already in lawful custodial status.”

The law also wouldn’t apply if an officer “reasonably determines” that displaying the agency name and logo would compromise their safety or the security of the person being transported.

In a public statement Tuesday, Caloza thanked Newsom for his signature and said her legislation requires “commonsense transparency.”

“No family should have to live in fear every time an unmarked vehicle drives through their neighborhood, wondering who is inside or why they are there,” Caloza said. “Public safety requires transparency, accountability, and respect for human dignity.”

AB 1650 is set to take effect Jan. 1, 2027.

Approved: SB 1367

Newsom also signed Riverside Democratic Sen. Sabrina Cervantes’ bill prohibiting the expansion of ICE detention centers.

Senate Bill 1367 bars local governments from issuing new land-use permits for construction of  detention facilities operated on behalf of a government agency. The law also blocks any permitting changes that would allow DHS to convert an existing building, such as a warehouse, into a detention center.

DHS spent more than $3 billion in the last year purchasing warehouses to convert into immigration detention centers and signed a $10 billion contract last month to build new detention facilities, none of which are currently slated to be built in California.

ICE detention centers in California are plagued by overcrowding and unsanitary conditions, according to state inspectors. Immigrants detained at the facilities have also reported a lack of proper medical care, violence by guards, and dirty food.

At least 58 people have died in ICE custody so far in President Donald Trump’s second presidency.

Cervantes said in a public statement Tuesday that SB 1367 blocks DHS from using property in California to build facilities where “human rights violations” occur.

“California will not stand by and allow the establishment of more detention facilities to serve as sites for government-sanctioned acts of inhumanity,” Cervantes said. “These facilities are operated by private entities to purposefully evade legal standards and avoid public accountability.” 

The legislation is sponsored by Southern California-based Inland Coalition for Immigrant Justice, or IC4IJ.

Hector Pereyra, political manager for IC4IJ said in a public statement that SB 1367 prevents the expansion of facilities that put profit ahead of the wellbeing of immigrants.

“SB 1367 is a victory for communities across California and makes clear that our communities are not marketplaces for mass incarceration,” Pereyra said.

SB 1367 is set to take effect Jan. 1, 2027.

Approved: AB 1806

This bill requires the Attorney General to conduct an independent investigation into fatal shootings of unarmed civilians by a immigration enforcement officer. 

Encino Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, who authored the bill, said in a public statement in August that he wrote the legislation following federal prosecutors’ unwillingness to investigate DHS agents who fatally shot Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis.

In LA, Keith Porter was fatally shot by an off-duty ICE agent on New Year’s Eve. The LA County District Attorney hasn’t announced whether he’ll criminally charge the agent.

Of the 11 people shot by ICE agents nationwide this year, only one was shot in California. In April, Carlos Ivan Mendoza Hernandez was shot and wounded by immigration agents during an arrest in Patterson in the Central Valley.

AB 1806 is set to take effect Jan. 1, 2027.

Approved: AB 1807

This bill bars state-owned structures, parks or other property from being used for ICE staging, processing or detention.

Asm. Gabriel, who authored the bill, said in a public statement both AB 1806 and 1807 will “strengthen the rule of law” in California.

“California must continue to push back against the Trump Administration to protect our immigrant communities and our constitutional rights,” Gabriel said.

AB 1807 takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.

Approved: SB 873

This bill, authored by San Bernardino Democratic Sen. Eloise Gómez Reyes, requires immigration agents to present identification and a valid judicial warrant before making arrests within 1,000 feet of a California courthouse.

In LA and across the country, DHS agents have continuously arrested immigrants at courthouses, including during check-ins with immigration officials and during court hearings. In June, a federal judge banned DHS from arresting people inside immigration courts.

Reyes said in a public statement her legislation aims to ensure ICE operations don’t prevent people from participating in the judicial process.

“Justice cannot work when people are afraid to walk through courthouse doors,” Reyes said. “No victim, witness, or family member should have to choose between seeking justice and risking civil arrest.”

Tina Rosales-Torres, policy advocate for Western Center on Law & Poverty, said in a statement that ICE arrests at courthouses are a threat to democracy. 

“When immigrants are afraid to enter our courthouses because they fear being arrested by ICE, it undermines more than their individual ability to seek justice, it threatens the principles that protect all of us,” Rosales-Torres said. 

SB 873 takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.

Approved: AB 2760

This bill bars local and federal law enforcement from using “wearable electroshock” devices in California and prohibits the use of state funds to purchase them.

ICE is spending $16.7 million to purchase 6,000 pairs of electroshock gloves for its agents over the next five months.

The law also requires the California Justice Department to study the devices’ safety and reporting findings to lawmakers by 2029. State legislators could extend or revise the law based on those findings before the law sunsets on Jan. 1, 2030.

Kevin Johnson, a professor emeritus at the University of California, Davis School of Law told the Associated Press on Tuesday that courts will likely rule that California can’t bar federal agents from wearing the gloves because the U.S. Constitution generally privileges federal law over any conflicting state law.

Spokespeople for the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department and Los Angeles Police Department told LA Public Press the agencies don’t own or utilize any electroshock gloves.

AB 2760 takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.

Vetoed: AB 1537

The No Side Jobs for ICE Act, authored by LA Democratic Assemblymember Isaac Bryan, would have prohibited members of local enforcement from having a second job detaining, arresting or deporting people while enforcing federal immigration law.

The bill would’ve required officers to report secondary job offers from DHS or other agencies to their employers and failure to comply with the law could’ve resulted in an officer being decertified, according to the bill’s text.

The bill was opposed by the Peace Officers Research Association of California.

In March, the LA City Council approved an ordinance barring city workers from working second jobs with DHS or any entity involved in immigration enforcement.

Following Newsom’s veto, he issued a statement Wednesday calling the bill’s prohibition on second jobs for law enforcement officers “a step too far.” 

The statement said officers in California already operate under personal conduct standards and could have their peace officer status revoked for violating them.

In a text message to LA Public Press, Bryan said he was disappointed with the veto.

“We have to do everything we can to protect our communities from ICE terror, including cutting off their recruitment efforts to local law enforcement,” Bryan said.

In a statement emailed Wednesday to LA Public Press, the ICE Out of California coalition said the veto leaves the public in the dark about secondary work local law enforcement is engaged in.

“At the end of the day, we are forced to ask: what are they hiding,” the statement said. “How many sheriffs and police are secretly moonlighting for ICE and abducting our neighbors?”

Vetoed: AB 2465

The bill would’ve banned businesses from receiving tax credits or state-approved loans and grants if they own, operate, manage or are invested in private immigration detention centers.

The first-of-its-kind bill, authored by San Leandro Democratic Assemblymember Liz Ortega, would’ve also applied to businesses who contract with agencies engaged in immigration enforcement.

“I was three years old when my parents brought me here. I’m not spending one dime of California money on helping ICE lock up kids like me,” Ortega said in a public statement in August.

Health care providers contracting with private immigration detention centers would’ve been exempt from the bill.

In his veto message Wednesday, Newsom said that while he agreed with the goal of the legislation, he was concerned it could harm legitimate state economic development programs or hurt businesses providing goods to a range of agencies.

Vetoed: SB 1105

The Protect California Rights Act would’ve prevented law enforcement agencies in the state from joining interagency task forces with the federal government unless agreements are in writing and expressly state that agencies won’t engage in racial or identity profiling. 

In his veto message Wednesday, Newsom said state law already prohibits racial profiling and that the bill could harm existing and future interagency agreements that facilitate critical information sharing and public safety initiatives, such as preparing for the 2028 Olympics in LA.

Newsom signs California's first non-ultraprocessed food seal law

By Angeleno Daily staff · October 1, 2026 · 2 min read

Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a bill making California the first state to put a "Non-Ultraprocessed Certified" seal on grocery packaging.

Newsom signed Assembly Bill 2244 on Monday, Sept. 28, at UCLA Mattel Children's Hospital, as first reported by the Los Angeles Times. The bill passed both chambers unanimously: 72-0 in the Assembly and 32-0 in the Senate.

The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) will design the seal, modeled after the USDA Organic label. The department must accredit agents to certify products by June 1, 2028. Grocery stores will then be required to prominently display certified items, and a public state website will list every product that earns the seal.

"Parents shouldn't need a Ph.D. in chemistry to understand what they're feeding their kids," Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, the Encino Democrat who authored the bill, said at the Sept. 28 signing ceremony.

Ultraprocessed foods are generally defined as products containing preservatives, flavorings or other additives not found in a home kitchen. Existing California law already defines them for school meals as foods high in saturated fat, sodium, added sugar or non-nutritive sweeteners. The new seal extends that concept to retail shelves statewide.

A USC Keck School of Medicine study published in November 2025 tracked 85 young adults over four years and found a 10% increase in ultraprocessed food consumption was associated with a 64% higher risk of prediabetes. Researchers noted the study was observational. Experts at UC Davis have cautioned that most research in this area relies on self-reported dietary data.

Not everyone is sold on a state-level approach. Anna Rosales, vice president of science and policy at the Institute of Food Technologists, warned that "[m]anufacturers, retailers, schools, and consumers could eventually face different interpretations of what qualifies as an ultra-processed food." The IFT noted that whole-grain bread, yogurt, fortified cereals and infant formula can all be classified as ultraprocessed under common systems despite providing nutritional benefits.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration and the Department of Agriculture are working on a uniform federal definition, which the FDA has called a priority for 2026.

For LA shoppers, the practical change is still about 20 months away. The CDPH rulemaking process and the June 2028 certification deadline will determine which products carry the new seal and how stores arrange them on shelves.

California Creates First State-Level Non-Ultraprocessed Food Label Amid Federal Definition Gap

State certification program launches ahead of federal standards, raising compliance questions for food manufacturers

California has enacted the nation’s first state-level certification program for non-ultraprocessed foods, establishing a voluntary front-of-package seal intended to help shoppers identify products free from industrial additives. Gov. Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 2244 into law on Monday, directing the California Department of Public Health to design a label modeled after the USDA Organic seal and to accredit certifying agents by June 1, 2028.

The legislation moves forward despite the absence of a federal definition for ultraprocessed foods (UPFs). The U.S. Food and Drug Administration and the Department of Agriculture are currently collaborating to establish uniform national standards, but no timeline for completion exists. California’s preemptive action creates an immediate regulatory framework that could serve as a de facto national standard or trigger a patchwork of conflicting state requirements.

Under the new law, grocery retailers must prominently display products bearing the “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified” seal. The state health department will also maintain a public online registry of certified items. While the specific criteria for the consumer-facing label are still being developed, existing California statute defines ultraprocessed foods for school meals as items containing high levels of saturated fat, sodium, added sugar, or non-nutritive sweeteners, including both artificial options like aspartame and plant-based alternatives such as stevia.

Industry experts warn that state-level certification ahead of federal guidance introduces significant compliance complexity. Anna Rosales, vice president of science and policy at the Institute of Food Technologists, noted that manufacturers, retailers, and institutions may soon face divergent interpretations of what qualifies as ultra-processed across different jurisdictions. If other states adopt their own definitions before Washington acts, food companies could be forced to navigate multiple, potentially contradictory labeling regimes for the same products.

The scientific foundation for regulating UPFs relies primarily on the Nova classification system, developed in the early 2000s by nutritional epidemiologist Carlos Monteiro at the University of São Paulo. Nova categorizes foods by processing degree rather than nutrient content alone, flagging products containing preservatives, flavor enhancers, and other industrial substances not typically used in home cooking. U.S. researchers widely use Nova because no domestic equivalent exists, though UC Davis experts have cautioned that most evidence linking UPFs to adverse health outcomes remains observational.

Recent clinical research has begun to strengthen that evidentiary base. A study published last year by USC’s Keck School of Medicine found associations between increased UPF consumption and higher prediabetes risk using blood sample analysis, moving beyond self-reported dietary data. Nevertheless, the distinction between minimally processed and ultraprocessed foods remains difficult for consumers to parse without standardized labeling, a gap AB 2244 aims to address.

Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), the bill’s author, framed the measure as a bipartisan effort to protect families while federal agencies remain stalled. The law does not ban any products or mandate reformulation; it creates a market signal through verified labeling. Certification will be voluntary, meaning participation depends on whether manufacturers believe the seal carries sufficient consumer recognition to justify the cost of third-party verification.

The California Department of Public Health must now draft technical specifications for the certification process, select accredited agents, and finalize the visual design of the seal well before the 2028 accreditation deadline. Stakeholder input from food scientists, nutritionists, and industry representatives is expected to shape how strictly the state interprets “non-ultraprocessed” for retail products versus the existing school meal definition.
