Talkin’ MAHA and the Midterms - Food and Environment Reporting Network

As the fight for Congress grows more tense, the difference between victory for Red or Blue may hinge on the MAHA movement. Are its members satisfied with what the GOP and Donald Trump have done for them? Do they feel betrayed by everything that hasn’t gone their way? RFK Jr. may still be their charismatic leader, but he’s not on the ballot. Theodore Ross sits down with three great FERN reporters — Jill Filipovic, Jane Black, and Teresa Cotsirilos — to get their take on where the movement is headed and which party benefits now that food politics is driving the debate. This interview is part of FERN’s special series, “MAHA and the Midterms,” in partnership with Mother Jones and Politico.

TRANSCRIPT

Teresa Cotsirilos: You’re listening to REAP/SOW: dispatches from the front lines of food, farming, and the environment. I’m your host, Teresa Cotsirilos.

Vani Hari: Let’s be very clear, you cannot claim to care about health while protecting poison.

Teresa: That’s Vani Hari, though you probably know her as Food Babe. She’s an activist, influencer, and leader in the Make America Healthy Again movement. Last April, she helped lead a pretty enraged protest in front of the Supreme Court.

Protesters: People versus Poison.

Vani Hari: You’re not loud enough.

Protesters: People versus Poison.

Vani Hari: Let them hear you inside.

Protesters: People versus Poison.

Teresa: The Court was reviewing a case against Bayer, the corporation that manufactures the weed killer glyphosate. A few months later, the justices ruled in favor of the company and effectively blocked states’ ability to sue Bayer over this pesticide, even though many experts believe it causes cancer.

In 2024, the MAHA movement helped Trump take back the White House, but after suffering political defeats on glyphosate and other issues, some MAHA leaders are getting fed up. They might jump ship on their MAGA allies. In this midterm season, that makes them a force to be reckoned with.

We just published a whole series on this with our partners over at Mother Jones. Our Editor-in-Chief, Theodore Ross, recently sat down with me and the other two awesome reporters on this series, Jill Filipovic and Jane Black, to talk about what this MAHA-MAGA crackup could look like, how it could influence certain midterm races, and how all this political drama actually impacts food policy.

I’ll let Ted take it from here.

Theodore Ross: Welcome. I just want to say hi to everyone. I’m going to do a little introduction. Then we’re going to get into the substance of the issue at hand. Let me start with Teresa Cotsirilos, who is a staff writer and producer at FERN. Welcome, Teresa.

Teresa: Thank you.

Theodore: Next up is Jane Black. Jane is the co-founder of Consumed, a Substack newsletter that explains the forces shaping our food system. I will point out that is also what FERN does, but that’s okay. There’s plenty of room in the space.

Then finally, we have Jill Filipovic. I will give her a proper introduction, but I am first going to read her Instagram bio, which I find very amusing. It is, “Full-time eater, most-of-the-time writer, recovering lawyer, occasional yoga teacher. Hashtag cats.” I like that. Hi, Jill.

Jill Filipovic: Thank you. Hi.

Theodore: Let me get the rest of your bio in. You’re also working on a book about how American patriarchy shapes women’s rights worldwide. You write a newsletter as well called Throughline.com. Welcome all three of you. I’m very happy to have you here. All right. I’m going to jump right in, and I’m going to start with Jill.

Jill, the MAHA movement, politically, is in my imagination really associated with women, the MAHA moms, but you’re arguing in your piece that they’ve been pushed aside in terms of genuine political power. How did that happen?

Jill: Yes, it’s a very strange dynamic in the Trump administration that MAHA is so associated with women, and for good reason. Women really powered the movement. They’re its foot soldiers. They’re its social media advocates. They’re often the public face of the movement. Within the Trump administration, the people that have been elevated to positions of power, RFK Jr., many members of his HHS, the former leader of the FDA have almost universally been men.

Those men, in their positions of power, are not really prioritizing the issues that the MAHA moms most care about. They’re bizarrely taking on a lot of the issues that actually the health-adjacent men of the manosphere really focus on.

Theodore: The protein. The protein dudes.

Jill: Things like protein, testosterone, sperm count. The issues that the MAHA women have really been pushing for many years now, things like glyphosate, things like ultra-processed foods, things like getting healthier foods onto children’s plates and on grocery store shelves have been either pushed to the side or even directly opposed by this administration.

Theodore: That’s a pretty good distillation, both of your article and the situation. I want to ask you a follow-up. Teresa and Jane, feel free to jump in on this one too. Do you think that this political shift, this shift within MAHA with the women being pushed to the side and the men being left in control of the policy and the politics, do you think that was inevitable? Did that have to happen?

Jill: No, it absolutely was not inevitable. I do think it is reflective of a broader problem within conservative movements, where the Republican Party is hugely disproportionately male in terms of not just its voters, but certainly in terms of its makeup. There are many, many more Republican men in Congress than there are Republican women. That’s true on the Democratic side as well, but the proportions are not nearly as extreme.

I will say, the MAHA women, they’re mad about this. They feel like they’re being taken for granted by the Republican Party. They’re really putting, I don’t want to say threat, but they’re putting it out there that they are loyal to their movement and to their ideology, and not necessarily to Trump and Trumpism.

Theodore: Yes, go ahead Jane. Yes, sorry. Go ahead.

Jane Black: I was just going to say, I think that that has made a big impact. I think the fact that many of these women, Vani Hari, Kelly Ryerson, who goes by Glyphosate Girl, they were Democrats before they were Republicans. It’s very clear that they hitched their wagon to this because they saw somebody who was willing to do something. When it seems like they’re not willing to do something, they’ve been very clear that they will take their vote elsewhere.

We will see whether they’re able to move voters that are very loyal to Donald Trump and came to MAHA through Trump rather than the other way around, but I think they have clocked a couple of wins in stopping certain things from happening by making that threat very clear.

Theodore: Yes, I think that’s a good point.

Jill: Also, the bigger question is whether Democrats harness their power, right?

Theodore: Yes.

Jane: Yes.

Jill: A lot of these women are looking for somewhere to go. Most of the MAHA women I talk to, they continue to be pretty loyal to RFK Jr. They have not turned on him. They really do see him as a rightful figurehead.

Theodore: Let’s talk about RFK Jr. for a second, though, in this context. We talk about whether or not it was always going to go this way with women being betrayed and the men getting the spoils. Jill, you said, no, you don’t think that’s inevitable, but I think that the gymnastics that you see some of the MAHA moms having to go through not to criticize RFK Jr. after he has essentially, well, I don’t know if sold them out is the right term, but certainly hasn’t delivered exactly what he promised. I don’t know how they get back into it, meaning the women, unless they criticize RFK Jr., and I don’t see how they criticize RFK Jr.

Jill: Yes, there is not a lot of criticism of RFK Jr. within this movement. My sense of what one of them would say if they were here right now is that he is doing his best under really difficult circumstances. Again, that’s their words, not mine.

Theodore: I understand.

Jill: I think their perception is that his heart is in the right place. He is still an advocate for their movement within the White House. That there are all these different factions within the White House that are competing, and that he doesn’t always win, but that on balance, he is a net good for their movement rather than a net negative.

I also think they see Trump as someone who is persuadable, someone who is unpredictable and because of that unpredictability, may go their way more than a Democratic president, for example, who might signal that they are kind of in the pocket or at least sympathetic to big food, big pharma, and big polluter.

Theodore: That’s probably the right political calculation to make, that you never know where Trump is going to go, so you might as well stay on his good side. All right. I’m going to switch gears a little bit. Teresa, I want to talk to you about your article and your interest in Zach Lahn.

You wrote a profile of Lahn, who is pronounced interestingly. It’s spelled L-A-H-N, but pronounced “Lane.”

Teresa: Lahn likes private plane.

Theodore: I know. It really was a revelation for me when I figured that out. He’s running for governor in Iowa, and he was the first candidate endorsed by the MAHA pack. He’s a darling of the movement, really. He even defeated a Trump-endorsed candidate in the primaries. What you write about, and I’d like you to talk a little bit about, is the political transformation that he’s undergone, which suggests that he’s not as committed to MAHA issues as he might seem. Let’s talk about that.

Who was Zach Lahn before he became who he now is?

Teresa: Squash also has extremely strong opinions about this, and that’s why he’s entered the chat. He’ll probably be here intermittently throughout this conversation.

Theodore: That’s okay.

Teresa: [laughs] The question was, who is he?

Theodore: Well, tell me who he was, right?

Teresa: Who he was.

Theodore: Who was Zach Lahn?

Teresa: Zach Lahn is fascinating. Zach Lahn started his career in kind of right-wing, libertarian, Tea Party-esque, conservative politics, and then got his big break in his 20s when he was hired to be the director of the Montana branch of Americans for Prosperity. While he worked for Americans for Prosperity, this was in the 2010s, the organization was obviously waging a war of attrition against Obamacare. Zach Lahn, specifically, was implicated in some extremely underhanded political maneuverings to punish and push out Republican representatives in Montana who were hesitant to fully support Americans for Prosperity’s agenda.

Theodore: Let me just cut in for a second here, Teresa. For people who don’t know Americans for Prosperity, it’s an advocacy group that is largely funded and was founded by the Koch family network. The Koch brothers, one of them is now dead. They are a very libertarian Republican group, very well-funded. Interestingly enough, and I’m thinking you’re going to probably get to it, they made a lot of their money in the business world on chemicals for agriculture. That’s going to be a big part of this transformation.

Teresa: The TLDR here is that he spent a lot of his career very closely affiliated with a family that made a lot of its money in the exact same industrial agricultural practices that MAHA is now against, and that have, arguably, I think it’s been argued persuasively, poisoned much of the state of Iowa, which is where Zach Lahn is from.

Theodore: Poisoned the water in Iowa.

Teresa: Poisoned the water. Arguably, also, the people and the land. We can get into that. It might be across the board at this point, very sadly and disturbingly. He’s affiliated himself very closely with them. Also, the Kochs are famous. These are people who are known for political machinations behind the scenes to push things in certain directions, and that is where Zach Lahn came up. They’re also known for advocating for policies that are diametrically opposed to many of the policies that MAHA advocates want, and that Zach Lahn is currently advocating for.

One of the things that I wrestled with in my piece that was really interesting to think about was, did Zach Lahn have some sort of ideological awakening where he changed, or is he hitching his wagon to the most convenient spot and is, in fact, still a libertarian connected to the Kochs who will not actually do any of the things that his MAHA supporters want him to do?

Theodore: I guess we’ll see, if he wins.

Teresa: Zach Lahn did not agree to an interview with me and has not taken power yet. I have my suspicions, but we don’t really know.

Theodore: All right. I’m going to turn to you, Jane, and we’ll talk a little bit about your story. Jesse Gabriel, he’s a lesser-known figure. He’s a Democrat. He’s from California. He’s been pushing for a lot of issues that the MAHA folks might like. From the other side of the aisle, for people out there who don’t really know who Gabriel is, tell us a little bit about him in the context of food issues.

Jane: Well, that’s exactly why I wanted to profile Jesse Gabriel, because nobody has heard of him. I really believe that he is, at this point, America’s de facto food safety chief. He has passed bill after bill in the state of California that remove dyes and chemical additives from foods.

One of the things that RFK has said he wanted to do since day one was define what ultra-processed foods are. State of California, with a bill written by Jesse Gabriel, has already done that. They have directed the state to identify ultra-processed foods of concern and remove them from children’s school lunches. These are exactly the things that the MAHA movement says it wants to do, being done by a centrist, pragmatic, incrementalist Democrat. It’s absolutely amazing.

One of the other things I find really interesting about him is that he’s everything Republicans would hate. He went to Berkeley. He studied constitutional law at Harvard. He defended the Dreamers. He was on the team that defended the Dreamers at the Supreme Court. Yet, he is absolutely laser-focused on bipartisanship and making this issue, which he thinks is very important, something that everybody can buy into. When he started doing this, he could have rammed something through the California state legislature. Democrats do that all the time. He actually made changes to bills to bring Republicans in because that’s the way he thinks things should get done.

What I find so fascinating about him is that he’s very clearly not MAHA. He does not identify as MAHA. He does everything in every way that people say does not work in the Trump era, and he somehow made it work. I just think those are the people that we should be putting the spotlight on because I feel like people in America, on the right and the left, say they’re sick of polarization, and yet who gets all the headlines?

Theodore: And yet, yes. Polarization does sell, I think, along with other things, but yes, that’s a very good point. I want to try to understand Lahn and Gabriel in the context of each other. Teresa, you nicely point out in your piece, how some of Lahn’s positions wouldn’t be shocking if they came from Elizabeth Warren. It suggests a thing about MAHA that’s really important. These Democratic coded issues on food have at least for now jumped to the right, but no one knows if that’s permanent.

This is for all three of you. Jill, you can feel free to weigh on this too. How do you see that playing out on the midterms? Will it stay where it is right now?

Teresa: There’s one thing I want to add to that quickly, just because you brought up the Elizabeth Warren stuff, which is, I think that the implications for Democrats about the power of certain types of messaging in the midterms is actually even bigger than that. Because Zach Lahn has not just co-opted food safety messaging and messaging around organics, regenerative farming, the lack of certain things around pesticides that have become a big part of MAHA.

Theodore: Antitrust too.

Teresa: That’s where I’m going with this. His antitrust rhetoric is not just MAHA-esque. His antitrust rhetoric could very easily be a speech that Bernie would make in Iowa. In the Mother Jones video version of this story, there is a compare and contrast between what Zach Lahn is saying and then a speech that Bernie made in Iowa, and it is extremely similar.

In terms of messaging that could appeal in a bipartisan manner, Zach Lahn is betting that it extends beyond the classic MAHA messaging and extends to the AOC, Warren, Sanders branch of the party. I just wanted to put a finer point on that. I think it’s fascinating.

Theodore: No, I think that’s a really, really good point. I think it was Jill who was saying this, that these are swingy voters. These are voters that went from one direction to the other. Where do you think they’re going to stick, Jane? Looking at Jesse Gabriel, he’s not exactly the idea of a Democrat co-opting MAHA issues. He was doing this before MAHA. He’s been doing this for a while. Is anybody going to follow his lead?

Jane: Yes, and I’ve written about this before. I think the Democrats are just dropping the ball on this. It is just gobsmacking to me.

Teresa: It’s what they specialize in.

Jane: Yes, it was their issue. They totally let the Republicans run away from it. Poll after poll shows that this is a bipartisan issue. This is not a Republican issue. This is not a Democratic issue. It’s popular with Democrats, it’s popular with Republicans, and it’s particularly popular with independents, which is who both sides need. You would be silly, that’s the nicest word I can come up with, not to jump on the ball. I have talked to people who have said, “Oh, yes, we know, but we’re really focused on affordability.” I just think it is a big mess.

There are not enough people who really know and care about food to understand how essential this is. There’s a recent poll that showed that 84% of Americans say that it’s the government’s responsibility to keep food safe from harmful ingredients and pesticides, and fewer than half of Americans think that the government is doing a good job. What more do you need?

Theodore: That’s a very weird outcome. It makes sense in the current political context, but the fact is that, yes, the lettuce problems we’re having this summer to the side, the US does a pretty good job of keeping our food safe. However, people currently don’t think of it that way. Am I wrong? Do you disagree with that, Jane?

Jane: I think that part of it has been built up. The definition of what food safety means has expanded. It’s not just cyclospora. People now think that it is a food safety issue that there is blue dye in Cool Ranch Doritos. You could ask why there’s blue dye in Cool Ranch Doritos. That’s a legitimate question, but now people think that they’re unsafe because of it. I think that’s part of it.

One of the things I just want to put a finer point on with those numbers, it says people want the government to take action. I can’t think of very many things that the lion’s share of Americans are like, “You know what? The government is really the best person to do this.” That’s what they’re saying here. That’s what is just mind-boggling to me that more people have not seen what Jesse Gabriel has done, and there aren’t more Zach Lahns out there, basically.

Theodore: I know, Jill, you wanted to say this, but I want to just point out before, Jill, you say something. Gobsmacked is not a term you hear in spoken speech that often. I credit you for that. That’s a great term. I think we should all be using gobsmacked. Jill, what were you going to say?

Jill: I think Jane is exactly right that it is totally shocking that Democrats haven’t jumped on this. Look, yes, we had Michelle Obama and Let’s Move, and her vegetable garden, and healthy school lunches that Republicans threw absolute fits about. I feel like maybe Democrats are still lightly traumatized by that and think that that’s still the moment we’re in. Obviously, they’re wrong.

The women that are powering the MAHA movement are the same women that have powered Democratic movements. Not literally the same women, but large numbers of mothers, women who are really connected with their communities, women who care about a handful of specific issues. Those women, we see different iterations of them in the history of Democratic politics.

They are the Black women who run Souls to the Polls drives and are part of the reason why Black women are the backbone of the Democratic Party. They are the suburban wine moms who the leftist podcasters love to make fun of, but who are also people who really do fuel this party. This, to me, just strikes me as such a missed opportunity for Democrats to talk about the issues that the MAHA moms care about, to harness their energy, to harness their rage, to harness their anxiety, which is where I think a lot of this comes from.

I have a small child, and it is really mind-boggling what goes into food that is advertised to children and aimed at children. I joke that I am like MAHA-lite, even though I vaccinate my kid, and obviously I’m not, I don’t know, mainlining beef tallow. When it comes to the food stuff, and frankly, when it comes to the issues that MAHA voters themselves tell pollsters they care about the most, ultra-processed foods, I guess they say less about pollution, but they talk a lot about pesticides, they talk a lot about food safety, broadly defined, as Jane said. Those are really the top issues that they care about, healthy food and school lunches. They’re pretty normie stuff.

They’re the same stuff that you would hear any parent on a playground in Berkeley or Brooklyn talking about.

I think Democrats can shave off the anti-vax stuff. That gets a lot of billing and for good reason. It’s scary. It’s dangerous. It’s wrong. It should get a lot of press. The beef tallow stuff, whatever, gets a lot of press because it’s weird and that’s interesting. Actually, the issues that most of these voters prioritize are the same issues that a lot of liberals care about.

I do think that we don’t have to take every single MAHA crazy in order to get a critical mass of the MAHA movement to support Democratic politicians. I think, as it stands, they’re really focusing on the really divisive and not super helpful stuff like the vaccines, and missing the opportunity to capture voters who are otherwise politically unengaged, but don’t want their kids eating blue dye, whatever, in their Cool Ranch Doritos or eating Cool Ranch Doritos at all.

Theodore: I just want to say I really like Cool Ranch Doritos, but if RFK Jr. wants to take them away from me, I will do that. That will be my sacrifice to the health of the United States is that I will forego Cool Ranch Doritos. I just also want to point out that I agree with everything you both are saying about this.

I will give a little credit to, at least from a rhetorical perspective, and maybe if the Democrats take back the House and/or Senate, they’ll change things here too. Cory Booker and Chellie Pingree. There is some movement. There are some Democrats who are acting or at least talking about these issues in a way that seems to make sense.

Jane: Yes, but those are the same two people who have been talking about it my whole life, and Rosa DeLauro, when Jim McGovern has the Hunger. They each have their own thing, but that’s it. If you look at, again, Jesse Gabriel, he has passed more influential legislation on food than any of those people. It’s in California, so it matters.

Theodore: Yes, that’s a good point. All right. I’m going to shift gears a little bit to a broader question. We do a lot of coverage at FERN. The MAHA movement, we talk about it, we think about it. We’re so invested in the things that are happening with it within the flow of events that we don’t always pull back and ask ourselves, do we think, do all three of you think that the emergence of the MAHA movement is a good thing for American politics?

We can decide if that’s a net good thing minus the clearly bad vaccine thing. I’m talking about the food thing. I’m not trying to balance the scales here, but is it a good thing? Teresa, why don’t you go first?

Teresa: I think that one of the issues with the MAHA movement is that these two branches, including the anti-vax branch, these are inextricable from each other and a package deal in many issues and in many cases, and therein lies the issue. I think that framing of the question is challenging.

Theodore: No, it’s a really fair point to make, Teresa. I just want to point out that a lot of the MAHA figures that we’ve been able to talk to directly, it’s a Republican movement. They won’t always talk to anyone who’s not Republican. FERN is independent and nonpartisan, but that doesn’t mean they’ll talk to us. They want to split the vaccine issue away from the food issue. They seem to have no problem with the cognitive dissonance of saying, “Well, look, I don’t care about vaccines. I can vaccinate my kids. Whatever RFK Jr., who is my messianic leader, is up to, that’s none of my business.” Yes, I think that’s a really good point.

Teresa: I do have problems with that. Putting the framing of the question aside and looking at the things they’re advocating for in the food system specifically, I think that it is really important that this is coming up. I think that all my cards on the table, my framing on this, and my perspective on this has been very heavily framed by Jane, so I think we should bounce to her after you talk to me. I’m very grateful that we’re talking about these issues openly. I think that it’s about time. I’m relieved that it’s bipartisan.

The food branch of the movement has successfully brought up things that we should have started talking about in a bipartisan mainstream way a long time ago. The pesticide stuff in particular. Prior to MAHA, I at least always saw it personally, as someone who covers it, as a difficult thing to cover and talk about because the damage that pesticides do to a person is very incremental, which is one of the ways that many pesticide companies and manufacturers get away with spraying them.

You get cancer 35 years later. Many people exposed to glyphosate. There are far worse ones on the market. Paraquat is one that comes up a lot as well. A lot of people exposed to these pesticides have been in the industry. They’ve been exposed to 10 other things. It’s like some really nice cushioning for that corporation if they want to get out of being sued. As a journalist, I’ve always found it difficult to cover because it’s hard to prove that it was actually that pesticide.

This has always been a rather challenging issue because of its incremental damage, in many cases, and the fact that they have been able to package compelling messaging on this in a way that people really care about, I think, is very powerful. I think that branch of it is really beneficial, and I don’t think you can actually untangle the two, which I think therein lies the problem.

I’m curious, Jill and Jane, if you agree.

Theodore: Who wants to go next?

Jane: I’ll go next because it’s interesting. I’ve not taught you well, Teresa, because I disagree that you can’t untangle them. I think that the media seems unable to untangle them. When you look at what is popular, it is the food stuff. The vaccine stuff is absolutely unpopular. The fact that people in the MAHA movement have decided to give RFK Jr. more space and forgiveness or whatever it is, that’s a political calculation that they’re making.

If you look at what’s popular and what the American people want, it is the food change, not the vaccine change. That’s what I focus on. When I focus on that, I think he just nailed the framing. He just nailed it in a way that Michael Pollan and Michelle Obama could not. I covered her breaking ground on the garden and all of this stuff. It resonated with me. I wanted to go to the farmers’ market. I wanted to cook. I wanted to do all of these things.

Then when you went between the coasts, you saw that there were people who, the way that they heard it was, go do this. Oh, guess what? You can’t do that. There is no farmers’ market. You can’t afford the farmers’ market. You don’t have time to cook. Nobody wants to be told that the right thing to do is something that they simply cannot do.

What he’s done is just changed the framing, which is, it’s big corporations taking advantage of you. You should be mad as hell and not going to take it anymore. Is this country ready for that message? A populist message? It is the exact same message that worked 100 years ago when they created the FDA. There is an exact parallel between the messaging and the creation of regulation. Of course, the problem now is that we’ve got the message and a complete refusal to regulate.

I think that the messaging is great. I just want somebody to deliver on the regulation that needs to happen.

Theodore: Yes, don’t we all? Yes, go ahead.

Teresa: I’m just so happy that you brought up the class messaging around how the

Democrats have framed this historically and then how MAHA has hit on it, because this is something that has been driving me crazy and that I’m deeply fascinated by. It’s something that in my story, watching Zach Lahn, a very experienced political operative, frame this, and watching what he has done with gender, race, and class and how he has transformed himself, has been really fascinating and such a clapback to what the Democrats have done historically and how they’ve talked about issues. How do you manage to alienate so many people from an issue that actually everyone cares about? [laughs] They managed it, occasionally.

Anyway, to Jill. Sorry to jump in.

Theodore: What are you thinking, Jill?

Jill: I would say the biggest thing that has changed from the Obama era until now in American politics is algorithmic social media. Which did not exist the way that it exists now when Obama was president, and when Michelle Obama was building out her vegetable garden. When we talk about the interwovenness of the anti-vaccine movement and MAHA writ large and the food aspect of MAHA, I think they’ve become interwoven. They didn’t start out that way.

I think one thing that happened is that a lot of women who were concerned about their health, a lot of the MAHA women I talk to talk about experiencing chronic inflammation or some sort of ill health that traditional medicine is not able to solve for them. They get put on drugs, and they go the pharma traditional medicine route and they find it really unsatisfying. Then they change the way that they eat, they change the way that they approach the consumer choices that they’re making, and then they see real differences.

I think a lot of these women come into this movement through food because they want to feed their children healthy food. Just from personal experience. When I had a kid, the way that I approached a grocery store shelf, I’ve always been a pretty healthy eater. I’m not microwaving my black plastic. When I was thinking about what I’m putting into the body of this tiny brand-new person in the world, it ramped up my anxiety because I was so worried about what I was feeding him. B, it made me a lot more careful and a lot more cautious about what I was exposing him and then also, by extension, myself too.

I think a lot of women, a lot of mothers, and a lot of parents have that experience. When you have algorithmic social media, and you feel like this kind of lite-crazy person for caring so much about how you’re feeding yourself and your family, and you can’t necessarily talk to other members of your community about it, you go on social media, and you wind up down these rabbit holes.

When the only people that take you seriously are other people on the internet, and where those internet passages lead are eventually, not just the beef tallow people who, God bless, do your thing, but the raw milk people and eventually the anti-vaccine people, you feel like you found a community that finally takes you seriously, that finally understands.

I’m trying to think of the best way to articulate this, but I have felt like a crazy person sometimes being like, how is everyone around me feeding their kids stuff with 96 unpronounceable chemicals on the label? I realize it makes me sound like a MAHA mom, and everything’s a chemical, but it’s not all terrible, whatever. I have started to feel, yes, it’s very destabilizing. Feeling like you’re the only person around that cares about something that feels major.

Theodore: Well, it doesn’t make you a MAHA mom necessarily. It may or may not make you a MAHA mom.

Jill: It may or may not.

Theodore: What it suggests is that you’re looking for some agency, and people are finding agency in this political messaging and in this political movement, even if they don’t agree on all of the stuff. Even if it’s not the right messenger, say, for you, Jill, and I feel the same way about food. I think all of those things make a lot of sense if it wasn’t wrapped up in, for me, RFK Jr.

Jane: See, the agency is exactly the point because that was what went wrong with Michael Pollan and Michelle Obama, who I admire very much. It was, you were telling them to do something that you couldn’t do, and so you were telling them that you’re a failure, and you were saying, “I’m creating this alternative food system, I’m voting with my dollar, and you are failing.”

The point you make, Jill, about social media is you’re much more easily able to connect with someone who will validate you. Then while they’re validating you, they’re also like, “Oh, and also you need this stack of peptides and you can buy them from me.”

Theodore: CDC is filled with fraud.

Jane: Right, and so you end up there. It is that populist rage that someone is doing this to you is what makes it work. That’s what makes it work.

Teresa: Yes.

Theodore: All right. I think that’s a good point to stop it at. Populist rage is a good place for us to end this discussion. First, I’m going to thank you all. You had an amazing contribution to this conversation. I also want to point out to anybody who’s watching this video or maybe listening to it as a podcast that these articles that they are based on are well worth your time. It is a series in partnership with Mother Jones. We also have a piece with Politico as well, MAHA & the Midterms. I heartily encourage you to go check it out at our website or wherever you can find it.

I just want to say thanks again.

Jane: Thank you, Ted.

Jill: Thank you.

Teresa: REAP/SOW is a production of the Food and Environment Reporting Network. Our executive producers are Theodore Ross, Tom Laskawy, and Brent Cunningham. Our sound engineer is Cody Nelson. Our audience lead is Dom Altomari, and our assistant engagement producer is Milla Douer. Our content creator intern is Carlin McCarthy. I’m your host, Teresa Cotsirilos.

FERN News is our home on YouTube. Special thanks to Mother Jones for their incredible collaboration on this series. Find out more about FERN and donate to support our independent nonprofit reporting at www.thefern.org.

California creates a non-ultraprocessed food seal for the state

Douglas Brown

The Non-GMO Project, which runs Non-UPF Verified, opposed the voluntary seal, which won't go into effect until at least 2029. Get the details of the new legislation.

At a Glance: California officials must accredit non-UPF certifiers by June 1, 2029. The new standard borrows California's 2025 school UPF definition. With the new law, state and local prosecutors can sue brands that misuse the certification.

Critics of ultra-processed food enjoyed a big boost Monday, when California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a bill creating a voluntary, state-backed Non-Ultra-processed Certified seal that could require some large grocers to spotlight certified products. The law could help natural and organic brands stand out on conventional grocery shelves, and the seal enters a marketplace that already supports at least two private non-UPF certifications.

Now, the work heads to the California Department of Public Health, which is tasked with creating the seal and rolling it out. Manufacturers seeking the seal will apply to third-party certifiers, a model that mirrors how brands gain USDA Organic certification.

“Like the USDA Organic label, this new seal will provide consumers with clear, trustworthy information and make it easier for them to locate healthier foods that are free from harmful additives,” Assembly member Jesse Gabriel, D-Encino, the bill's author, says in an Environmental Working Group news release. “Parents shouldn't need a Ph.D. in chemistry to understand what they're feeding their kids.” The group co-sponsored the bill.

The bill passed both chambers unanimously, 32-0 in the Senate and 72-0 in the Assembly.

Experts raise concerns about new law

California’s standard, which won’t reach store shelves until the middle of 2029 at the earliest, will enter a marketplace with at least two non-UPF certification regimes: Non-UPF Verified and WiseCode. Megan Westgate, CEO and founder of the Non-GMO Project, which runs Non-UPF Verified, praised California for helping to move forward the national conversation about ultra-processed foods. But Non-UPF Verified opposed the legislation and asked Newsom to veto the bill. Non-UPF Verified’s problem with California’s standard hinged on certification integrity, Westgate says.

“Any rigorous non-UPF certification must examine the processing methods used for ingredients and finished products,” rather than just focusing on the lists of ingredients on labels, Westgate says. “Non-UPF Verified asks, ‘How were the ingredients and finished product actually made?’ Any products bearing our verification mark must meet rigorous requirements for ingredient integrity and formulation, and processing limits and methods.”

The new standard draws from an earlier law that defined ultra-processed food and set a timeline for phasing the worst of it out of schools. That definition classifies a food as ultra-processed if it contains an additive with certain technical effects, such as an emulsifier, stabilizer, color or flavoring agent, and is also high in saturated fat, sodium or added sugar or contains a nonnutritive sweetener. The same definition now also determines which grocery products can qualify for the seal. Products that fall within the state’s definition of ultra-processed cannot emblazon packaging with the seal. The department must finish writing its rules on which foods are disqualified by June 1, 2028, and accredit third-party certifiers by June 1, 2029.

Once it’s up and running, the department, the attorney general and local prosecutors can go to court to stop brands from misusing the seal. That enforcement matters. Many natural and organic products industry stakeholders will point toward the legal teeth as one reason for USDA Organic’s success.

Anna Rosales, vice president of science and policy at the Institute of Food Technologists, wrote in a blog post Monday that even as California crafts ultra-processed food policy, the FDA and USDA together are working on a uniform federal definition. If other states follow California’s lead on ultra-processed foods before a federal definition is finalized, she writes, manufacturers, retailers and schools could face conflicting rules about what counts as ultra-processed. She also argues that nutritional quality, rather than processing alone, should serve as the foundation of any standards. The Institute’s position contrasts with Non-UPF Verified’s emphasis on the importance of assessing processing. California’s definition falls somewhere between the two, identifying a list of additives along with thresholds for saturated fat, sodium and added sugar.

While the law doesn’t require brands to apply for the seal, it does compel grocery stores with more han $10 million in annual sales that carry more than 25 state-certified products to highlight at least three of them. Grocers can use dedicated displays, signage or other shelf cues to showcase certified products.

Alyssa Moran, deputy director of the Center for Food and Nutrition Policy at the University of Pennsylvania, says in the Environmental Working Group news release that “because companies are not required to disclose an ingredient’s purpose, it can be really difficult even for experts, even for people like me who have a doctoral degree in nutrition, to look at a food package and determine whether a food is ultra-processed or not.

“If we want to meaningfully curb disease, we need a suite of complementary policies that limit the availability of ultra-processed foods while promoting non-ultra-processed alternatives.”

NewsletterMorning Rounds

CDC measles death count still lags Pennsylvania’s

Pressure to regulate kratom, new California laws on food processing, and more health news

By Theresa Gaffney

Sept. 30, 2026

Addiction Reporter

Theresa Gaffney

[email protected]

Theresa covers substance use and addiction and co-writes the Morning Rounds newsletter. You can reach Theresa on Signal at theresagaff.97.

Good morning. In Monday’s newsletter, Amanda wrote about a study on rising mortality rates for treatable surgical conditions like appendicitis. If you were looking for the right link for that, here it is. Scroll down past the first five abstracts for the research in question.

A grassroots movement goes corporate

Has the Make America Healthy Again movement changed? If yesterday’s MAHA Summit is any indication, STAT’s Isabella Cueto and Daniel Payne write, then the answer is yes.

The movement first coalesced around mistrust of the health system and corporate influence. But yesterday, government officials and private sector leaders mingled in a chandeliered Waldorf Astoria ballroom while reporters were largely excluded. Most panels featured firms from the sponsor page. Some longtime MAHA supporters were appalled.

“There are a lot of people very upset about it,” said Jeffrey Tucker, president and founder of the MAHA-aligned Brownstone Institute. “It’s just this weird attempt to capture the reins of the MAHA label for something that doesn’t seem to have much to do with MAHA.” Read more on how the day played out and what it signals for the future.

CDC measles death count still lags Pennsylvania’s

The CDC has updated its website to show two measles deaths in the U.S. this year. That means the agency is still out of step with Pennsylvania, where officials count four measles-related deaths in a historic outbreak. As The Washington Post reported yesterday, it’s unclear which of those four the CDC added to its count.

A recent First Opinion essay explains the key difference between “dying from” a disease and “dying with” one, including a helpful explanation of how death certificates work. “If we wanted to be literal about it, the cause of death for nearly everyone would be cardiac arrest, since in the end our hearts stop,” the authors wrote. I recommend reading the essay in full.

In the meantime, Americans are confused about health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s stance on the measles vaccine. Kennedy has made misleading claims about shots, including recently at a conference for Children’s Health Defense, an anti-vaccine nonprofit he helped start. According to the latest survey from UPenn’s Annenberg Public Policy Center, 31% of adults believe that Kennedy recommends children be vaccinated against measles. Another 29% believe he doesn’t recommend it, and 40% are unsure.

Lawmakers want Trump to rethink import rules

A growing number of congressional lawmakers are urging the Trump administration to rethink a federal rule going into effect next month over concerns it will prevent Americans from obtaining prescription medicines from licensed international pharmacies.

The pending rule requires medicines mailed from abroad to go through a customs process that includes a licensed customs broker and a financial guarantee in the form of an entry bond. These steps could ultimately add costs the medication recipients will have to pay. STAT’s Ed Silverman wrote about the concerns. Read more.

What’s the right way to regulate kratom?

Pressure for regulatory action on kratom is mounting after two students at the University of Mississippi died this month, with kratom products found on the scene in both cases. (Authorities have not said that kratom contributed to either death.) The DEA recently proposed temporarily designating a kratom derivative, 7-OH, as Schedule I when above a certain threshold of potency. That would put it in the category of drugs that carry the most risk without any medical benefit. The move, which hasn’t been finalized yet, would get certain products off gas station shelves, though milder kratom leaf products would continue to fly under regulatory radar.

I spoke with addiction and policy experts about whether or not this is the right approach. Some people felt strongly that kratom should be banned, while others pushed for a regulated marketplace. And not everyone has the opinion you’d think they would — I spoke to a harm reduction advocate, for example, who supported the DEA’s proposed rule. Read more to find out why.

So what about those mice with half-human brains??

Did stories like “Flowers for Algernon” or the cartoon “Pinky and the Brain” come to mind when you read earlier this month about the “cerebral organoids” (brains) that scientists are growing inside mice? As STAT columnist Paul Knoepfler writes in his latest essay, science is starting to catch up with fiction, and it’s opening up an ethical minefield.

“The biggest question about this kind of research from both a biology and ethics perspective is: What does having all those human brain cells in the cortex do to mice?” Knoefpler writes. Some of the results were expected, but others only created more questions. Read more to process what it all means.

New California laws on food processing, hepatitis C

Gavin Newsom spent Sunday practicing his autograph — the California governor signed more than 200 bills into law over the weekend. This may be of interest to STAT readers:

  • One new law makes it illegal for commercial health insurers to require prior authorization for antiviral drugs that treat hepatitis C. “First in the nation!” Infectious disease doctor Jeffrey Klausner posted online. “Let’s build a movement across the US to liberate hepatitis C treatments from the grips of commercial insurers and get people cured.” For more than a decade, people diagnosed with hep C have struggled to access the highly effective medications. But as STAT’s Nicholas Florko reported in 2022, a major part of the problem is prisons’ blatant refusal to test and treat people with the condition.

After resting his hand a bit, Newsom signed some more bills on Monday, including this:

  • California will now officially offer a front-of-package seal that manufacturers can place on their products to show that they are not ultra-processed. STAT’s Sarah Todd first wrote about the bill when it was proposed in March. She also profiled state legislator Jesse Gabriel, who introduced the bill alongside a whole suite of proposals aimed at reducing the health harms of ultra-processed foods. “Jesse Gabriel has passed more food policy in three years than most legislators enact in their entire careers,” Scott Faber from the nonprofit Environmental Working Group told Sarah.

What we’re reading

California creates new label to help shoppers spot less-processed foods

  • California has created a new “non-ultra-processed certified” label for qualifying food products.

  • The state will oversee the certification process and maintain a public list of certified products.

  • Large grocery stores that meet certain requirements will have to make certified products easier to spot.

Figuring out how processed a food is can be surprisingly difficult. Even when shoppers carefully read an ingredient list, it may not always be obvious how a product was made or why certain ingredients were added.

That’s the issue California’s new law is designed to address. Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed Assembly Bill 2244, creating a standardized “non-ultra-processed certified” label for foods that meet the state’s requirements.

The law is intended to give shoppers a simpler way to identify products that are not classified as ultra-processed under California law. The Environmental Working Group (EWG), which co-sponsored the legislation, says the label could make it easier for consumers to compare products while grocery shopping.

“Like the USDA Organic label, this new seal will provide consumers with clear, trustworthy information and make it easier for them to locate healthier foods that are free from harmful additives,” Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino) said in a news release. “Parents shouldn't need a Ph.D. in chemistry to understand what they’re feeding their kids.

“California began this movement three years ago by banning the most dangerous food additives, and with Governor Newsom’s continued leadership we are taking another big step forward today.”

How the new food label will work

Under the law, foods classified as ultra-processed under California’s standards won’t be allowed to carry the new certification. Products also won’t qualify if they contain certain substances or additives used to manipulate a food’s taste or quality, including dyes, flavor enhancers, non-sugar sweeteners, and processing aids.

The California Department of Public Health will oversee the certification program. Third-party certifiers will evaluate products, and those certifiers will have to be approved by the state. Products will need to be recertified at least every three years.

The law also includes several transparency measures. Certification agents must register with the state, California can audit certification records, and the state will maintain a public online list of certified products. Misusing the label will also be illegal and subject to enforcement.

What this means for shoppers

The new label won't appear overnight. California must first establish the certification system, with the state directed to accredit third-party certifiers by June 1, 2029.

Once the program is operating, some large grocery stores will also have to make certified products easier to find. The requirement applies to stores that sell more than 25 individual non-ultra-processed-certified product types and generate more than $10 million in annual sales.

For consumers, the biggest change will be having another piece of information to consider while shopping. Rather than trying to determine whether a product meets California’s definition of ultra-processed by studying the ingredient list alone, shoppers will eventually be able to look for the state-backed certification.

Until then, consumers can continue checking ingredient lists and use resources such as EWG’s Food Scores database, which identifies less-processed products and flags ultra-processed foods and drinks.

Kristen DalliManaging Editor

Губернатор Калифорнии Гэвин Ньюсом подписал закон о создании добровольной программы сертификации и маркировки продуктов питания, не подвергавшихся сверхпереработке.

Законопроект № 2244, автором которого является член Ассамблеи Джесси Габриэль, учреждает, по словам сторонников, первую в своем роде программу сертификации в США. Законодательство создает знак «Сертифицировано как не подвергавшееся сверхглубокой обработке» для пищевых продуктов, отвечающих определенным стандартам, касающимся обработки и ингредиентов.

В рамках этой программы производители смогут подавать заявки на сертификацию через аккредитованных агентов по сертификации под надзором Департамента общественного здравоохранения Калифорнии.

Данная схема разработана по образцу программы USDA Organic и призвана предоставить потребителям индикатор на лицевой стороне упаковки, указывающий на соответствие продуктов определению «не подвергавшиеся сверхпереработке», принятому в Калифорнии.

Законодательство также обязывает продуктовые магазины упростить поиск сертифицированных товаров для потребителей за счет размещения соответствующей информации внутри магазина.

Габриэль заявил, что новый знак качества предоставит потребителям «четкую и достоверную информацию» о продуктах питания, которые они покупают.

В 2025 году Ньюсом подписал закон «Здоровое питание, здоровые дети», который установил законодательное определение ультрапереработанных продуктов питания и определил процедуру поэтапного исключения определенных продуктов из школ Калифорнии.

Введение системы сертификации происходит на фоне продолжающихся дискуссий правительств, организаций здравоохранения и пищевой промышленности о роли ультрапереработанных продуктов питания в рационе.

생활경제

캘리포니아 주상원 제24선거구 브라이언 골드스미스 후보

댓글 2026-09-30 (수) 04:12:04

▶ 안전, 교육, 소상공인 지원을 최우선으로 AAPI 지역사회에 대한 결의 재확인

캘리포니아 로스앤젤레스 – 로스앤젤레스 토박이이자 캘리포니아 주상원 제24선거구에 출마한 브라이언 골드스미스 후보가 오늘 가디나에서 열린 지역사회 오찬 행사에서 아시아계 미국인 및 태평양 제도민 (AAPI) 주민에 대한 결의를 재확인했다.

골드스미스 후보는 이날 오찬 자리에서 캘리포니아 주상원 제24선거구에 17만9,000명 이상의 AAPI 주민이 거주하고 있음을 언급하며, 지역사회와 열린 대화를 유지하는 것이 중요하다고 강조했다. 그는 당선 후에도 AAPI 지역사회 구성원들과 정기적으로 소통하며, 지역구 전역의 주민들에게 영향을 미치는 현안에 대해 직접 의견을 청취하겠다고 거듭 밝혔다.

이러한 다짐은 골드스미스 후보가 그동안 해당 지역구의 AAPI 주민들과 나눠온 대화에 기반을 둔 것이다. 그는 올해 초 토랜스와 웨스트 로스앤젤레스에서 지역사회 모임을 두 차례 열고 AAPI 주민들과 한 자리에서 만나 지역구에 영향을 미치는 현안을 논의한 바 있다. 당시 주민들은 보도 보수 지연, 공공 안전, 생활비 부담 등을 비롯한 다양한 문제를 제기했다. 골드스미스 후보는 이러한 대화를 통해 AAPI 지역사회와 지속적인 대화를 유지하고 주민들이 그들의 우려 사항을 직접 전달할 수 있는 기회를 보장하는 것이 얼마나 중요한지 다시금 확인했다고 말했다.

브라이언 골드스미스 후보는 “캘리포니아 주상원 제24선거구는 깊은 역사를 지닌 활기찬 AAPI 지역사회의 터전입니다. 이 지역들은 우리 지역 유산의 핵심이며, 우리는 그 유산이 보존되고 기념될 수 있도록 해야 합니다”라고 말했다. 이어 “이와 동시에, AAPI 지역사회를 겨냥한 증오 범죄와 폭력이 급증하면서 많은 주민, 특히 노인과 가족들이 불안감을 느끼고 있습니다. 어떠한 형태의 증오라도 결코 용납될 수 없습니다. 당선된다면, 모든 주민이 자신의 동네에서 안전함을 느낄 수 있도록 힘쓰고, 새크라멘토에서 AAPI 지역사회의 우선과제를 해결하기 위해 열린 소통 창구를 유지할 것을 약속드립니다”라고 덧붙였다.

브라이언의 주상원의원으로서 중점을 두는 분야는 다음과 같다.
•일자리 및 저렴한 서민 주택 확대, 소상공인 지원, 에너지 비용 절감, 의료 서비스 접근성 보호
•공공 정책을 통한 범죄 및 노숙자 문제 해결, 그리고 비영리 단체와의 협력으로 실질적 성과 도출
•변화하는 경제에 대비한 아동 교육, 청소년 정신 건강 문제 해결, 기후 변화에 대응한 기반 시설 구축, 정부 운영 효율성 제고
•이민자 가정을 보호하는 동시에 인종 차별, 반유대주의, 아시아계 혐오 범죄를 지속적으로 규탄하며 맞서 대응하기

캘리포니아 주상원 제24선거구는 랜초 팔로스 버디스 (Rancho Palos Verdes), 토랜스 (Torrance), 말리부 (Malibu), 산타모니타 (Santa Monica), 베벌리힐스 (Beverly Hills)를 포함하여 로스앤젤레스 카운티의 사우스 베이 (South Bay), 웨스트사이드 (Westside) 및 서부 지역사회를 아우른다. 브라이언은 2026년 12월 마지막 임기를 마치고 물러나는 현직 벤 앨런 (Ben Allen) 주상원의원의 뒤를 잇는 것을 목표로 한다.

골드스미스 후보는 수상 경력을 지닌 언론인이자 기업가로, 다수의 민주당 소속 연방하원의원의 당선을 돕는 등 여러 후보와 비영리 단체 및 기업에 자문을 제공해왔다. 그는 10년 넘게 야후 뉴스 (Yahoo News), 디 애틀랜틱 (The Atlantic), CBS 뉴스 (CBS News), CNN에서 정치 칼럼니스트이자 해설자로 활동했으며, ‘케이티 쿠릭 미디어 (Katie Couric Media)’에서는 수석 정치 프로듀서로도 일했다. 하버드 칼리지와 스탠퍼드 법학대학원을 졸업한 골드스미스 후보는 기술과 경제적 접근성 확대에 초점을 맞춘 캘리포니아의 스타트업 두 곳을 설립하기도 했다.

골드스미스 후보는 이 지역과 뿌리 깊은 인연을 맺고 있다. 그의 조부모는 1950년대에 베벌리힐스에 정착했고 부모님이 그 뒤를 이었으며, 현재 그 또한 교육자인 아내 클레어 (Claire) 및 어린 두 자녀와 함께 이곳에서 가정을 꾸리고 살아가고 있다.

선출직 공직에 이번에 첫 도전하는 골드스미스 후보는 다음과 같은 폭 넓은 분야의 저명한 선출직 공직자, 단체 및 지역사회 지도자들의 지지를 얻었다: 힐러리 로담 클린턴 (Hillary Rodham Clinton) 전 연방국무장관 겸 연방상원의원, 낸시 펠로시 (Nancy Pelosi) 전 연방하원의장, 바바라 박서 (Barbara Boxer) 전 연방상원의원 및 전 연방하원의원 (명예위원장), 개비 기퍼즈 (Gabby Giffords) 전 연방하원의원, 헨리 스턴 (Henry Stern) 가주상원의원 (제27지구) 기후변화 정책 입법 합동 위원회 부의장 및 비상 관리 입법 합동 위원회 위원장, 조시 베커 (Josh Becker) 가주상원의원 (제13지구) 천연자원 및 수자원 위원회 위원장 겸 경제개발 및 혁신 특별위원회 위원장, 제시 가브리엘 (Josh Becker) 가주하원의원 (제46지구) 예산위원회 의장 및 캘리포니아 유대인 입법 코커스 공동의장, 릭 차베스 즈버 (Rick Chavez Zbur) 가주하원의원 (제51지구) 민주당 코커스 의장, 피트 부티지지 (Pete Buttigieg) 전 연방교통부 장관 겸 전 사우스 벤드 시장, 안토니오 비야라이고사 (Antonio Villaraigosa) 전 LA 시장 및 가주하원의장, 밥 허츠버그 (Bob Hertzberg) 전 가주상원 원내대표 및 전 주하원의장, 프란 파블리 (Fran Pavley) 전 가주상하원의원 및 전 주하원의원 및 전 아고라 힐스 시장.

골드스미스 후보는 또한 총기 안전 정책 옹호 비영리 단체인 ‘에브리타운 총기 안전 행동 기금 (Everytown for Gun Safety)’, LA 지역 노조 연맹 IATSE지부, LA 경찰보호연맹 (LAPPL·Los Angeles Police Protective League), LA 학교 경찰 관리자 협회 (PASPMA· Los Angeles School Police Management Association), LA 학교 경찰협회 (LASPA·Los Angeles School Police Association), 캘리포니아 고속도로 순찰대원 협회 (CAHP·California Association of Highway Patrolmen), 팀스터스 합동 협의회 42지부 (Teamsters Joint Council 42), ILWU 지역지부 13 (Local 13)·63 (Local 63)·94(Local 94), 캘리포니아 주의회 유대인 코커스 (California Legislative Jewish Caucus), 로스앤젤레스 이스라엘 지지 민주당원 (Democrats for Israel Los Angeles), 아시아계 기업인협회 (Asian Business Association), 블루 웨이브 민주당 클럽 (Blue Wave Democratic Club)을 비롯해 LA와 캘리포니아, 그리고 전국 각지에서 150명(개) 이상의 지도자 및 단체로 구성된 광범위한 연합체의 지지를 얻었다. 골드스미스 후보의 선거 캠페인은 벤 앨런 (Ben Allen) 현역 주상원의원의 후임을 선출하는 이번 2026년 선거에서 지지세를 확대하며 강력한 추진력을 얻고 있다.

공식 지지 명단 전체는 아래 링크에서 확인할 수 있다: https://www.briangoldsmith.com/endorsements.

브라이언 골드스미스 후보 소개:
브라이언 골드스미스 후보는 수상 경력을 보유한 저널리스트이자 기업가이며, 민주당 컨설턴트로 활동해 왔다. 그는 자신의 기업을 통해 여러 후보자들과 비영리 단체들 및 기업들에 자문을 제공해왔다. 브라이언은 ‘스크라이버(Scriber)’라는 문자 기반 구독 서비스를 설립했고, 훗날 영국의 ‘시드러 (Seedrs)’에 인수된 지분형 크라우드펀딩 기업인 ‘정션 (Junction)’을 공동 설립했다.
정치 칼럼니스트이자 평론가로 정기적으로 활동하는 브라이언 후보는 ‘케이티 쿠릭 미디어 (Katie Couric Media)’, ‘야후 뉴스 (Yahoo News)’, ‘애틀랜틱 (The Atlantic)’, ‘CBS 뉴스’, ‘CNN’ 등에서 10년 이상 언론인으로 근무했다. CBS 재직 당시, 브라이언 후보는 팀과 함께 한2008년 대선 캠페인 보도 및 자신이 제작한 사라 페일린과 큐릭 (Couric)과의 인터뷰로 알프레드 I. 듀폰상을 수상했다. 사회 생활 초기, 브라이언 후보는 딕 게파트 (Dick Gephardt) 연방하원 민주당 원내대표의 보좌관 및 USC 남가주 대학 공공외교 센터의 프로젝트 매니저로도 근무했다.

브라이언 후보는 미국 전기 자동차 일자리 연합 (American EV Jobs Alliance) 이사회의 창립 이사였으며 현재 태평양 국제 정책 협의회 (Pacific Council on International Policy)와 카시 센터 (Karsh Center) 이사회 이사로도 활동하고 있다. 그리고 그와 그의 가족은 ‘베이비2베이비 (Baby2Baby)’와 ‘아워 빅 키친 LA (Our Big Kitchen LA)’에서 활발하게 활동하는 자원봉사하고 있다. 그는 하버드 대학과 스탠포드 법학대학원을 졸업했으며, 클린턴 전 대통령과 부시 전 대통령이 공동 설립한 ‘대통령 지도력 장학 프로그램 (Presidential Leadership Scholars)’의 첫 장학생이었다.

로스앤젤레스 토박이 출신인 브라이언 후보는 교육자인 아내 클레어 (Claire) 및 두 자녀인 엘리자 (Eliza)와 테디 (Teddy)와 함께 주상원 제24선거구에 거주하고 있다.

Newsom Signs Law to Create First-of-A-Kind Non-UPF Certified Label in California Anay Mridul . Anay Mridul.

5 Mins Read

California Governor Gavin Newsom has signed a bipartisan bill that creates a non-UPF certification label for food products in the state, a first for the country.

California’s war on ultra-processed foods (UPFs) has reached new heights, with the US state becoming the first to create a voluntary label for non-UPFs.

Governor Gavin Newsom has signed into law AB 2244, a bill supported across party lines that enables food manufacturers to use a front-of-pack ‘Non-Ultraprocessed Certified’ seal on products that meet certain criteria.

“We should be about healthcare, not sick-care, recognising that preventing illnesses is far preferable to finding – and affording – treatments,” Newsom said. “It’s why California is focused on making whole, healthy foods as accessible as possible, why we’re making healthier choices easier.”

UPFs have become a hot-button issue in food policy in the US, with the federal government promising to take action against the category but finding it hard to develop a standardised definition for these products.

The nation’s largest state, however, has come up with its own definition, and has been ahead of the curve on anti-UPF policymaking – last year, Newsom signed a bill that would phase out the most concerning of these products from schools.

“California has never been afraid to challenge the status quo, and we’ll keep innovating, trying new things, and clearing the way for the rest of the country to follow,” the governor said.

Taking inspiration from the USDA Organic label The reason policymaking around UPFs isn’t straightforward is due to the lack of a clear definition. The category first appeared in the Nova classification in 2009, whose description of foods with industrial formulations and techniques and cosmetic additives bundled everything from Coke and Doritos to whole-grain bread or fortified soy milk under one umbrella.

It’s why many health experts have criticised the Nova definition of UPFs as too broad and misleading. It risks alienating foods that are actually good for you, and while studies have linked UPFs to a host of health ailments (including early death), leading health voices have warned against conflating processing with nutrition.

To address this gap, California’s 2025 legislation defined UPFs as products that contain certain stabilisers, thickeners, emulsifiers, flavouring and colouring agents, non-nutritive sweeteners, and high amounts of saturated fat, sodium or added sugar.

This will apply to products that companies want to use the new Non-Ultraprocessed Certified (previously called California Certified) label on. It’s modelled on the USDA Organic seal, for which companies voluntarily pay to have their products certified by an independent agent.

The non-UPF is said to reflect the same “common-sense, market-based approach” that made the USDA Organic label a success. The new law creates a system overseen by the California Department of Public Health, where food manufacturers can apply to accredited certification agents to use California’s new health-focused seal on products that are not ultraprocessed.

“Like the USDA Organic label, this new seal will provide consumers with clear, trustworthy information and make it easier for them to locate healthier foods that are free from harmful additives,” said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, who authored AB 2244.

The bill would also require supermarkets with over $10M in annual sales and more than 25 non-UPF-certified products instore to prominently display at least three items bearing the Non-Ultraprocessed Certified label at visible points like checkout and store entrances. Moreover, the state will maintain a publicly available list of these products, audit certification records, and enforce standards for the seal.

California’s non-UPF label contrasts with federal policy efforts The anti-UPF law allows companies to apply for the seal starting June 2028, and if they receive the certification, they’ll need to renew it every three years.

The bill was first introduced in February, and received bipartisan support on its path to Newsom’s desk, with a 72-0 vote in the Assembly and a 32-0 vote in the Senate.

It follows the passage of the Healthy Foods, Healthy Kids Act that kickstarted the effort to ban UPfs from schools, a bill also introduced by Gabriel, alongside the California Food Safety Act in 2023 and the California School Food Safety Act in 2024, which his office says “helped change the national conversation about food additives and ultra-processed foods, shaped federal policy, and inspired similar legislation across more than 30 other states”.

Several other states have imposed restrictions on UPFs, including Arizona, Texas, Louisiana, and West Virginia. A host of non-UPF certifications have cropped up over the last couple of years from the likes of the Non-UPF Program, the Non-GMO Project, and Wisecode.

These come as UPFs now top Americans’ list of health concerns, with 72% of them trying to avoid these products in their diets, and 79% feeling they’re a “significant threat” to public health. That said, the share of people who take processing levels into account before deciding whether to buy a food has reduced slightly, from 80% in 2025 to 73% this year.

At the federal level, the Trump administration blamed “highly processed foods” for diet-related diseases in the new (and highly criticised) dietary guidelines. And Congress is considering a bill that would ban UPFs from being marketed to children and require them to carry front-of-pack warning labels.

Health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, a prominent critic of these products, has said the FDA “will act” on a petition calling for the revocation of the GRAS status of certain UPFs. However, FDA officials have ruled out an outright ban, while continuing to delay the agency’s release of a definition of these foods.

“While Washington DC is paralysed by inaction, Republicans and Democrats in California are joining forces to empower consumers to avoid harmful UPFs,” Gabriel said. “California began this movement three years ago by banning the most dangerous food additives, and with Governor Newsom’s continued leadership, we are taking another big step forward today.”

Gov. Newsom signs bill to ban use of shock gloves and other legislation aimed at immigration enforcement

Daniel Macht

Gov. Newsom signs a package of anti-ICE bills

KCRA / KQCA US

Gov. Newsom signs bill to ban use of shock gloves and other legislation aimed at immigration enforcement

SACRAMENTO, Calif. —

California Gov. Gavin Newsom on Tuesday signed multiple bills that his office said would expand oversight of federal immigration enforcement in California.

The bills cover law enforcement practices, detention centers that operate in the state and are aimed at strengthening legal protections for immigrants.

Among the provisions in the package of legislation:

  • A ban on shock gloves by law enforcement.
  • Restrictions on the use of flash-bang grenades and explosive breaching charges during immigration enforcement.
  • A ban on ICE officers who have committed serious misconduct from becoming peace officers or public employees in California.
  • A new 25% tax on private detention centers where the revenue will go toward immigration-related services.
  • Expanded health oversight requirements for civil detention facilities.
  • Expanded public access to records related to private detention facilities, and a mandate that the attorney general develop and report a proposed oversight plan for private civil detention facilities.
  • More public input on potential facilities through more planning and zoning requirements.
  • A restriction on the use of state-owned facilities for immigration-enforcement staging.
  • Clear identification via a temporary decal on rental vehicles used by law enforcement for immigration operations, with some exceptions.
  • Individuals given the ability to sue federal government officials who have violated their constitutional rights.
  • Protections for people traveling to or from courthouses from civil arrest.
  • Strengthened protections for immigrant victims.
  • Keeping eligibility for CalWORKS assistance when a child or household member is detained by federal immigration authorities, in certain cases.
  • Protections for immigrant victims seeking assistance under California law.

“Trump has put his political interests above the health, safety and livelihood of American families,” Newsom said in a statement. “California is taking action to strengthen transparency, accountability, and oversight around immigration enforcement in our state. This is about stepping up where the federal government has failed our communities.”

Election 2026 · State of California

California Assembly District 46

Jesse Gabriel (incumbent) and Tracey Schroeder are the candidates for California Assembly District 46 on the November 3, 2026 ballot.

The State Assembly is one of the two houses of the California Legislature, which holds the state's lawmaking power. The Assembly has 80 members. Its members write and vote on state laws and, with the Senate, pass the state budget, which the Constitution requires by June 15 each year.

Summary by CityHallPass, not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: LA County's official election information.

Who votes Voters in the 46th Assembly District
Term and pay Two-year term. A person may serve no more than 12 years in the Legislature, in the Senate, the Assembly or both (California Constitution, article IV, section 2). Salary: $134,694 a year, effective December 1, 2025.
How it works Top two from the June 2 primary, regardless of party. Most votes wins.
Party labels Party preference printed on the ballot

What it means for the City of LA

About 97% of the district's land lies inside the City of Los Angeles, across the west and central San Fernando Valley. State laws bind the City, and the state budget funds programs the City runs. Example: state law requires the City to plan housing for all income levels and update that plan on a set schedule (Government Code sections 65580 and 65588).

Primary results, June 2, 2026

Jesse Gabriel 68,506 66.2%

The candidates

Jesse Gabriel Incumbent

Gabriel is a graduate of UC Berkeley and Harvard Law School and worked as a constitutional rights attorney before entering public service (Assembly biography). He was first elected to the Assembly in 2018 (Daily News). Speaker Robert Rivas named him chair of the Budget Committee in November 2023 (LA Times), and he is also co-chair of the Legislative Jewish Caucus (Assembly biography). He lives in the San Fernando Valley (Assembly biography), and his office's press releases identify him as D-Encino (press release).

Tracey Schroeder

Schroeder told LA School Report in 2022 that she had spent 24 years teaching in the Los Angeles Unified School District, and she ran for the LAUSD Board of Education in District 4 that year (LA School Report). Her campaign site says she is a UCLA graduate with a master's degree from Phillips Graduate Institute and a third-generation Valley resident (campaign site). In a 2024 questionnaire, under other political positions held, she listed only union roles: National Education Association Representative Assembly and the United Teachers Los Angeles House of Representatives (Daily News). She ran against Gabriel in November 2024 (Daily News).

The job

Powers. The California Constitution gives the state’s lawmaking power to the Legislature, which is the Senate plus the 80-member Assembly (art. IV, sec. 1). A bill needs a majority of each house to pass (art. IV, sec. 8). The Legislature can override a Governor’s veto with two-thirds of each house (art. IV, sec. 10). Tax increases need two-thirds of each house (art. XIII A, sec. 3). The Legislature can also put constitutional amendments on the ballot by a two-thirds vote of each house (art. XVIII, sec. 1). The Legislature placed five of the 14 statewide measures on this ballot: Props 1, 2, 4, 5 and 43 (Secretary of State voter guide).

Budget. The Legislature must pass the budget bill by midnight on June 15, and a majority vote is enough (art. IV, sec. 12). CalMatters reported that the 2026-27 budget deal totaled $352 billion, added taxes, including a sales tax on everyday computer software, and gave counties $900 million for homelessness (CalMatters). Gabriel chairs the Assembly Budget Committee; his office says that in that role he works with legislative leaders and the Governor to write the state budget (Assembly biography).

The district.

  • About 502,000 people live in the 46th District, and the Census Bureau’s 2020-2024 survey estimates the population as 40% Latino, 39% white, 12% Asian and 4% Black, with a median household income of $91,381 (Census Reporter).
  • LAist describes it as straddling Los Angeles and Ventura counties along the 101 Freeway, from Van Nuys to Bell Canyon, with voter registration 48.4% Democratic, 20.8% Republican and 23.7% no party preference (LAist).
  • Almost all of it is in the City of LA. Of the district’s 1,425 LA County voting precincts, 1,414 are in the City (County Registrar precinct map). By land area, about 97% is in the City (City council district map).
  • City neighborhoods, by share of the district’s land (Neighborhood Council areas): Woodland Hills-Warner Center (21%), Encino (18%), West Hills (13%), Tarzana (11%), Reseda (8%), Lake Balboa (8%), Van Nuys (7%), Winnetka (6%) and Canoga Park (5%) (City Neighborhood Councils).
  • City Council districts, by share of land: CD 3 (Bob Blumenfield, 47%), CD 4 (Nithya Raman, 17%), CD 6 (Imelda Padilla, 17%), CD 12 (John Lee, 13%) and a sliver of CD 2 (Adrin Nazarian, 1%) (City council district map).
  • Land shares come from overlaying the County’s Assembly district map on the City’s Neighborhood Council and Council district maps. They measure area, not people.

Records

Jesse Gabriel

Office and roles. Gabriel has been in the Assembly since 2018 (Daily News). His office lists these assignments: chair of the Budget Committee, member of Governmental Organization, vice chair of the Joint Legislative Budget Committee, and alternate on all six budget subcommittees (committee page).

Bills, 2025-26 session. Counting only bills whose final version lists him as a lead author, the Legislature’s bill data shows Gabriel on 81 Assembly bills and one constitutional amendment in the regular session, 16 of them shared with other lead authors. Many are budget bills he introduced as Budget chair; dozens of others he introduced were later taken over by the Budget Committee and are not counted. As of the data’s Oct 1, 2026 update, after the Governor’s Sept 30 deadline to act on bills (art. IV, sec. 10), 26 of the 81 bills had become law, none was vetoed and 55 did not pass (bill data). Eight of the 26 were signed on Sept 29 and 30 (Governor’s office, Sept 29; Sept 29; Sept 30). In the 2025 special session he also carried budget bills with Sen. Scott Wiener; one, AB 4, became law (bill data). Laws include:

  • AB 1127 (Chapter 572, 2025), which bars dealers from selling pistols that can be easily converted to automatic fire (KQED).

  • AB 1806 and AB 1807. The Governor signed both on Sept 29, 2026 (Governor’s office). AB 1806 requires the Attorney General to investigate fatal shootings of unarmed civilians by immigration officers. AB 1807 bars federal immigration agents from using state property for immigration enforcement (Gabriel’s office).
  • Signed Sept 29, 2026: AB 1924 (a statewide homelessness prevention strategy) and AB 2020 (housing program financing) (Governor’s office).

Bills, 2023-24 session. He was a lead author on the final version of 68 measures: 58 bills, of which 25 became law and 5 were vetoed, and 10 resolutions, 9 of them adopted (Legislature’s bill data). California launches first US voluntary label for non-ultraprocessed foods

Palate Shift

California has created the first voluntary 'Non-Ultraprocessed Certified' label in the United States. Governor Gavin Newsom signed the bipartisan bill AB 2244 into law, establishing a government-overseen seal for food products that meet specific criteria for minimal processing.

The label is modeled after the USDA Organic seal. Companies can voluntarily pay to have their products certified by an independent agent accredited by the California Department of Public Health. The certification must be renewed every three years, and the seal will be placed on the front of product packaging. It will be available for use starting in June 2028.

The law defines ultraprocessed foods as products containing certain stabilisers, thickeners, emulsifiers, flavouring and colouring agents, non-nutritive sweeteners, and high amounts of saturated fat, sodium, or added sugar. This definition is based on California’s 2025 legislation. Governor Gavin Newsom said: "We should be about healthcare, not sick-care, recognising that preventing illnesses is far preferable to finding, and affording, treatments."

Label tied to broader push for healthier food environments

This new label is part of a series of California laws targeting ultraprocessed foods. The bill was first introduced in February and passed unanimously in both legislative chambers. It passed the Assembly with a 72-0 vote and the Senate with a 32-0 vote.

Supermarkets with over $10 million in annual sales and more than 25 non-UPF-certified products must display at least three certified items at visible locations like checkout aisles and store entrances. The state will maintain a publicly available list of certified products, audit certification records, and enforce standards for the seal.

This effort builds on prior legislation. The Healthy Foods, Healthy Kids Act, also introduced by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, aimed to ban UPFs from schools. The California Food Safety Act passed in 2023, and the California School Food Safety Act passed in 2024. Gabriel’s office stated these prior bills helped change the national conversation about food additives and UPFs, shaped federal policy, and inspired similar legislation in over 30 other states. Other states that have imposed restrictions on UPFs include Arizona, Texas, Louisiana, and West Virginia.

Public concern rises as federal action lags

While most Americans seek to avoid ultraprocessed foods and view them as a health threat, federal efforts to define or regulate them remain stalled. 72% of Americans are trying to avoid UPFs in their diets, and 79% feel they are a 'significant threat' to public health. The share of Americans who consider processing levels before buying food decreased from 80% in 2025 to 73% in the current year.

In this regulatory vacuum, non-UPF certifications have emerged from groups like the Non-UPF Program, the Non-GMO Project, and Wisecode. The Trump administration blamed 'highly processed foods' for diet-related diseases in the new dietary guidelines. Congress is considering a bill to ban UPFs from being marketed to children and require front-of-pack warning labels.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Said the FDA 'will act' on a petition to revoke GRAS status for certain UPFs. However, FDA officials have ruled out an outright ban on UPFs and continue to delay the release of a federal definition, leaving states like California to lead. The seal will be available for use starting June 2028, with certification required to be renewed every three years.
