New California law creates non-ultra-processed food seal

By Coral Beach

Published: September 29, 2026, 12:04 am

California Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed a bill into law that will make it possible for food companies to label their products with a “non-ultra-processed certified” seal.

The bill was introduced by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, D-Encino, and received bipartisan support in the Assembly and Senate.

“While Washington D.C. is paralyzed by inaction, Republicans and Democrats in California are joining forces to empower consumers to avoid harmful ultra-processed foods,” said Gabriel.

“Like the USDA Organic label, this new seal will provide consumers with clear, trustworthy information and make it easier for them to locate healthier foods that are free from harmful additives. Parents shouldn't need a Ph.D. in chemistry to understand what they’re feeding their kids.

“California began this movement three years ago by banning the most dangerous food additives, and with Gov. Newsom’s continued leadership we are taking another big step forward today.”

The new law builds on a 2025 law, also authored by Gabriel, which created the first U.S. legal definition of UPF and banned it from public schools.

The California Department of Public Health will oversee certification of products that meet the state’s non-UPF standard, approving and accrediting third-party certifiers to conduct product certifications. The products must be recertified at least every three years. The law directs the department to accredit these third-party certifiers no later than June 1, 2029.

Only products that meet these requirements will be allowed to display the seal. A food will not qualify for the label if it contains substances or additives, including dyes, flavor enhancers, non-sugar sweeteners or processing aids, used to manipulate the taste or quality of foods.

Several consumer groups applauded the new law, including the Environmental Working Group.

“Today California raised the bar for what we consider healthy food,” said Bernadette Del Chiaro, EWG senior vice president for California. “Consumers deserve labels they can trust, and with Gov. Newsom’s signature, families now have a simple way to tell which foods are closer to what comes from a kitchen rather than a factory.”

The law includes the following oversight and transparency measures:

  • Certification agents must register with the state
  • The state can audit certification records at any time
  • The state must maintain a public, online list of certified products
  • Misuse of the label will be illegal and subject to enforcement

In addition to creating the label, the law requires large food retailers to display certified products so consumers can easily identify them, for instance, through special signage or physical separation within the store. This requirement applies to grocery stores that sell more than 25 individual non-UPF-certified products and brings in more than $10 million in annual sales.

Research has shown that UPF make up more than two-thirds of children’s diets and more than half of adult diets.

Scientific research has linked diets high in UPF to serious health harms, including cancer, heart disease, Type 2 diabetes, metabolic disorders and mental health issues.

Coral Beach

Managing Editor Coral Beach is a print journalist with more than 35 years experience as a reporter and editor for daily newspapers, trade publications and freelance clients including the Kansas City Star and Independence Examiner.

California Creates a First-in-the-Nation Label for Non-Ultraprocessed Foods - California Gazette

Governor Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 2244 on September 28, 2026. The law creates the first government-backed “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified” food label in the United States. Manufacturers can choose to certify qualifying products, and large California grocery stores will be required to display certified items prominently.

Key Takeaways

  • AB 2244, by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), sets up a voluntary state certification program with a standardized seal reading “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified Food Standard” or “Non-UPF Certified.”
  • The California Department of Public Health will oversee accredited third-party agents that verify whether products meet the standard.
  • Grocery stores with more than $10 million in annual sales that carry more than 25 certified product types must display those products in easy-to-identify locations, such as through special signage or separate placement.
  • Certified products must be recertified at least every three years, and misuse of the label is subject to enforcement.
  • The bill passed the Legislature unanimously and was signed as part of a ten-bill package that also requires added-sugar warnings on chain restaurant menus and nutrition standards for children’s meals.

How The Non-UPF Certified Label Works

AB 2244 does not ban any food or require any manufacturer to change a product. It creates a voluntary standard: food makers whose products meet California’s definition of non-ultraprocessed can apply for certification and put the seal on their packaging. The Governor’s office compared the approach to the USDA Organic label, which gives manufacturers a voluntary benchmark and leaves the decision to shoppers.

Certification runs through accredited third-party agents, not state inspectors, with the California Department of Public Health overseeing the system. Under the bill text, an agent cannot certify a product that is classified under state law as an ultraprocessed food, an ultraprocessed food of concern, or a restricted school food. Products that rely on additives such as dyes, flavor enhancers, non-sugar sweeteners, and certain processing aids will not qualify.

The seal is not permanent. Each certified product must be recertified at least every three years, and misuse of the label is subject to enforcement. The law also creates the Public Health Food and Nutrition Education Fund to pay for implementation and to educate shoppers and industry about the new standard.

What The Law Means For California Grocers

For grocery retailers, the key provision is about store layout. Stores with more than $10 million in annual sales that stock more than 25 certified product types must make those items easy to find, for example through dedicated signage or separate placement in the store. Where products sit on a shelf strongly affects what shoppers buy. The law adds certification to the factors that decide where products go.

The thresholds limit the requirement to larger operations. Small neighborhood markets and independent grocers under the sales threshold are not covered, while regional and statewide chains will need to plan for certified sections or signage once certified products reach their shelves in volume.

A New Market Signal For Food Manufacturers

For food manufacturers, especially California’s many natural and minimally processed food brands, the label offers a state-backed way to set products apart on crowded shelves. Combined with the required in-store visibility at large grocers, certification could become a practical marketing tool for brands whose products already meet the standard.

For companies with ultraprocessed products, nothing is required. Those products stay legal and on shelves. However, reformulating a product to earn the seal becomes a possible business decision in the country’s most populous state, which has long influenced national food and consumer product standards.

What Shoppers Will See

For California shoppers, the change is about clarity. Ingredient lists can be long and hard to read, and “ultraprocessed” has had no consistent meaning on packaging. Assemblymember Gabriel summed up the aim this way: “Parents shouldn’t need a Ph.D. in chemistry to understand what they’re feeding their kids.”

The label won’t appear on shelves right away. The Department of Public Health must first accredit certification agents, and manufacturers must then apply and qualify. The seal is expected to appear gradually, not all at once.

A Broader Package Built On Earlier Food Laws

AB 2244 builds on the Healthy Foods, Healthy Kids Act, AB 1264, which Newsom signed in October 2025. That law made California the first state to officially define ultraprocessed foods and set a timeline for phasing them out of school meals. The new label applies that school-focused definition to the grocery aisle.

The same signing package includes several related measures:

  • SB 869 requires chain restaurant menus to flag drinks that contain more than the recommended daily intake of added sugar.
  • SB 977 requires chain restaurants to offer at least one children’s meal that meets a minimum nutrition standard.
  • AB 1731 creates a program through the Office of Farm to Fork to connect local vendors with California public institutions.

Newsom framed the package around prevention, saying the state “should be about healthcare, not sick-care.”

Other States May Follow California’s Model

California has often set standards that spread beyond its borders, and food policy has followed that pattern. Its earlier restrictions on certain food additives drew national attention and similar proposals in other states. Because AB 2244 is voluntary and market-based, not a ban, it may be easier for other states to adopt. Food industry observers have already described it as a possible blueprint.

How widely the label spreads will depend on what happens once certification begins: how many manufacturers apply, how quickly large grocers set up displays, and whether shoppers come to recognize the seal.

FAQs

What Is The California Non-Ultraprocessed Certified Label?

It is a voluntary, state-backed seal created by AB 2244 for food products that meet California’s non-ultraprocessed standard. The seal reads “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified Food Standard” or “Non-UPF Certified.”

Is The Non-UPF Label Mandatory For Food Companies?

No. Manufacturers decide whether to seek certification. Products that don’t carry the label remain legal to sell in California.

Who Certifies Foods As Non-Ultraprocessed In California?

Accredited third-party certification agents verify products, with oversight from the California Department of Public Health. Certified products must be recertified at least every three years.

Which Grocery Stores Must Display Certified Products?

Stores with more than $10 million in annual sales that carry more than 25 certified product types must display those products in easy-to-identify locations, such as through signage or separate placement.

When Will Shoppers See The Non-UPF Label In Stores?

The label will appear gradually. The Department of Public Health must first accredit certification agents, and manufacturers must then apply for and receive certification.

Gavin Newsom Just Signed a First-in-the-Nation Law for Non-Ultra-Processed Foods

The new measure could change how Californians shop for packaged foods — and what they see when they walk down the grocery aisle.

By Stacey Leasca Stacey Leasca

Stacey Leasca is an award-winning journalist with nearly two decades of newsroom experience. She is also the co-founder of Be a Travel Writer, an online course for the next generation of travel journalists.

Food & Wine's Editorial Guidelines

Updated on September 29, 2026

Add Us On
  • California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 2244 into law on Sept. 28, 2026, creating a voluntary “non-ultra-processed certified” seal for foods that California law does not classify as ultra-processed.
  • The bill reflects growing concern about ultra-processed foods, which account for about 60% of the American diet and are associated with increased risks of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and other chronic conditions.
  • The legislation also requires grocery stores to prominently display certified products, supporting broader efforts to improve food transparency and public health.

Update, Sept. 28, 2026: On Sept. 28, California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed A.B. 2244 into law, creating what his office called a first-in-the-nation state label for non-ultra-processed foods. The bill passed with bipartisan support. This final version also replaces the “California Certified” name with a seal bearing the phrase “non-ultra-processed certified.”

“We should be about healthcare, not sick-care, recognizing that preventing illnesses is far preferable to finding — and affording — treatments,” Newsom said in a statement. “It’s why California is focused on making whole, healthy foods as accessible as possible, why we’re making healthier choices easier. California has never been afraid to challenge the status quo, and we’ll keep innovating, trying new things, and clearing the way for the rest of the country to follow.”

The Environmental Working Group (EWG), an organization that co-sponsored the bill, provided more details about its mechanics, including that the California Department of Public Health will oversee product certification and accredit third-party certifiers by June 1, 2029.

EWG also noted that the new law requires “large food retailers to display certified products so consumers can easily identify them,” through measures such as special signage or “physical separation within the store.” (This requirement, it added, applies only to grocery stores that sell more than 25 individual non-UPF-certified products and generate more than $10 million in annual sales, meaning smaller shops would not be required to do the same.)

“Because companies are not required to disclose an ingredient’s purpose, it can be really difficult even for experts, even for people like me who have a doctoral degree in nutrition, to look at a food package and determine whether a food is ultra-processed or not,” Alyssa Moran, the deputy director of the Center for Food and Nutrition Policy at the University of Pennsylvania, shared with EWG. “If we want to meaningfully curb disease, we need a suite of complementary policies that limit the availability of ultra-processed foods while promoting non-ultra-processed alternatives. I firmly believe this is the only way we’ll make progress.”

See Food & Wine’s original reporting on this bill below.

On March 25, Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino) announced he was introducing Assembly Bill (AB) 2244, which he explained in a statement is intended to “empower Californians to make better-informed and healthier choices by increasing transparency around ultra-processed foods.”

If the bill passes, it will establish the first “California Certified” seal, which can be displayed on products that meet standards for minimal processing. As Gabriel explained, it’s akin to the “USDA Organic” label, which helps consumers quickly identify organic foods on shelves. It would also require grocery stores across the state to prominently showcase products bearing the seal.

“Parents shouldn’t need a Ph.D. in chemistry to understand what they’re feeding their kids,” Gabriel said. “Like the USDA Organic label, this new seal will empower consumers with clear, trustworthy information and make it easier for them to locate healthier foods that are free from harmful additives. While Washington, D.C. is paralyzed by inaction, California is stepping up to protect our kids and confront the health risks associated with ultra-processed foods.”

A similar label is already making its way to stores across the U.S. In October, the Non-UPF Program, a nonprofit dedicated to reducing ultra-processed foods in American diets, announced it was overseeing the first U.S. certification for non-ultra-processed foods. As Food & Wine previously reported, food producers wanting to use the label must also meet a strict set of criteria based on the NOVA framework, which classifies foods into four groups according to their level of processing: groups 1-3 for unprocessed or minimally processed foods, and group 4 for ultra-processed foods.

Both the Non-UPF Program and the new bill in California are in response to the growing body of research showing the potentially harmful effects of ultra-processed foods, which now account for 60% of total energy intake in the American diet. That includes increasing a person’s risk for heart disease, diabetes, and a host of chronic conditions.

“Ultra-processed foods clearly increase chronic disease risk. Many of these foods are engineered to be optimally rewarding and easy to over-consume,” Alyssa J. Moran, the deputy director at the Center for Food and Nutrition Policy, shared in Gabriel’s statement. “And food companies are constantly adding new ingredients to the food supply without disclosing their purposes, making it almost impossible for most people to know whether a packaged food is ultra-processed or not. Clear, science-based labels make it easier for consumers to identify healthier items. They also serve as the foundation for other policies, like requirements for retail marketing.”

This also isn’t the first bill like it to be introduced and ultimately passed in California. The state also famously enacted the “Skittles Ban“ in 2023, which banned four food additives: Red dye No. 3, potassium bromate, brominated vegetable oil, and Propylparaben, all of which must be removed from products sold in the state by 2027. Gabriel also authored the Real Food, Healthy Kids Act, signed into state law last year, which prohibits ultra-processed foods from public school meals by 2035.

What counts as “minimally processed”?

Minimally processed foods are altered for safety or convenience—but still look a lot like their original form. Think canned beans, frozen vegetables, plain yogurt, eggs, milk, or olive oil.

Ultra-processed foods, on the other hand, tend to include additives you wouldn’t use at home—like artificial flavors or emulsifiers—and are designed to be ready-to-eat (think soda, chips, instant noodles).
A simple rule: the shorter and more recognizable the ingredient list, the better.

This latest bill, like the others, is garnering plenty of praise, including from Melanie Benesh, the vice president of government affairs for the Environmental Working Group, who shared in a statement, “The astronomical growth of ultra-processed foods has created one of the most pressing public health challenges America faces today. Americans overwhelmingly believe that UPFs are linked to long-term health risks and want to reduce their consumption, but many don’t know where to start.”

“By creating a simple, voluntary ‘California certified’ label for non-UPF foods, AB 2244 will help consumers navigate confusing grocery aisles. It will help people quickly and easily identify non-UPF foods and give companies that want to help consumers a powerful incentive to offer more non-UPF options,” Benesh added.

This bill has a ways to go before becoming law. So far, it’s been referred to the committee on health. You can track the bill’s progress and changes at egiscan.com.

The move comes despite the lack of a nationwide definition for what makes a food “ultraprocessed.” Some experts argue that a patchwork of state-by-state labeling, like California’s, could confuse the food industry as a whole.

Experts say ultraprocessed foods are those that have one or more ingredients that wouldn’t be found in a kitchen. Existing state law defines ultraprocessed foods, for school-provided meals, as any food or beverage that contains high amounts of saturated fat, sodium, added sugar or non-nutritive sweetener — the latter can be artificial (aspartame) or plant-based (Stevia) but are low in calories.

What the new law does

Under Assembly Bill 2244, the California Department of Public Health will be tasked with creating a standard non-ultraprocessed-food label that will be modeled after the widely recognized “USDA Organic” label, according to a news release from Newsom’s office.

“The seal will provide consumers with a simple, trustworthy way to identify healthier options with a quick glance,” the release states.

The state public health department will be required to accredit agents to certify food products as non-ultraprocessed no later than June 1, 2028.

Non-ultraprocessed foods that bear the new label will be listed on a public website maintained by the state public health department.

The bill also will require grocery stores in California to prominently display products bearing the “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified” seal.

A move to ‘empower consumers’

The term “ultraprocessed foods” was coined by nutritional epidemiologist Carlos Monteiro and his team at the University of São Paulo in the early 2000s.

They developed the Nova system, which classifies the degree to which a food product is processed, from minimal to ultraprocessed.

As the Mayo Clinic notes, “processing” can include washing, chopping, drying, packaging and a number of other things. Foods “cross into ultra-processed territory when they contain preservatives, flavorings and other food additives, or substances … to enhance flavor and increase shelf life.”

Researchers throughout the United States widely regard the Nova system when studying the correlation between the prolonged consumption of ultraprocessed foods and resulting health implications because the U.S. doesn’t have a definition of its own.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration is currently working with the Department of Agriculture to develop a uniform definition of ultraprocessed foods.

“While Washington D.C. is paralyzed by inaction, Republicans and Democrats in California are joining forces to empower consumers to avoid harmful ultra-processed foods,” said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), author of Assembly Bill 2244. “Parents shouldn’t need a Ph.D. in chemistry to understand what they’re feeding their kids.”

Reasons for caution

Last year, researchers with USC’s Keck School of Medicine published a study that found that an increase in ultraprocessed food intake was associated with a higher risk of prediabetes, or early-stage high blood sugar that can lead to diabetes — part of their study process included taking blood samples.

However, experts at UC Davis have previously noted that the vast majority of research on ultraprocessed foods has been observational, meaning people are asked to report what they eat and scientists take that information and use statistical analysis to explore associations with various health outcomes.

Many consumers struggle to distinguish between minimally processed and highly processed products due to confusing labels and marketing practices.

Anna Rosales, of the Institute of Food Technologists, said California’s new food label may sound straightforward, but for food scientists, regulators, manufacturers and others across the food system, the new law raises a more complicated question.

“What are the implications of individual states creating certification programs around UPFs while the federal government is still working to define the term?” wrote Rosales, vice president of science and policy for the nonprofit, in a news release.

As California ushers in its certification label, she said, other states could adopt similar certification programs or develop their own definitions of ultraprocessed foods while a uniform federal definition is still in the works.

“[M]anufacturers, retailers, schools, and consumers could eventually face different interpretations of what qualifies as an ultra-processed food,” Rosales said.

California Creates First Statewide ‘Non-Ultraprocessed’ Food Label as UPF Debate Intensifies

Tuesday September 29, 2026 – California is taking another major step into the national debate over ultra-processed foods, becoming the first U.S. state to establish an official certification and labeling program for foods that qualify as non-ultraprocessed.

Governor Gavin Newsom signed AB 2244, authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, on September 28, 2026. The legislation creates a state-backed “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified” food standard designed to make qualifying products easier for consumers to identify. The move follows California’s 2025 legislation establishing a legal framework for defining ultra-processed foods and restricting certain products in public schools.

The new law represents an important development for food manufacturers and retailers because California’s large consumer market has historically given its regulations influence beyond the state’s borders.

How California’s Non-Ultraprocessed Food Label Will Work

Participation in California’s certification program is voluntary. Food manufacturers whose products satisfy the state standard will be able to use the certification to identify those products as non-ultraprocessed.

According to Food Dive, large grocery stores that sell at least 25 products carrying the certification will also be required to display qualifying products prominently, giving the program an in-store merchandising component rather than limiting it to package labeling.

California officials describe the program as a consumer-information initiative. The Newsom administration says the label will provide front-of-package information while helping shoppers locate qualifying products through improved placement inside stores. State officials have compared the voluntary approach to certification systems such as USDA Organic: manufacturers can choose whether to participate, while consumers decide how much importance to attach to the certification.

The initiative is notable because it approaches the UPF debate from the opposite direction of a warning label. Instead of marking foods as “ultraprocessed,” California is creating an affirmative certification for products meeting its non-UPF standard.

What Does California Consider an Ultra-Processed Food?

The question is more complicated than it might initially appear.

There is currently no universally accepted definition of an ultra-processed food in the United States. Different classification systems can categorize the same product differently, depending on whether they emphasize industrial processing methods, ingredients and additives, nutritional composition, or a combination of factors.

California moved ahead of federal regulators in 2025 with the Real Food, Healthy Kids Act, AB 1264. The law established a state framework that looks at industrial additives and ingredients as well as nutritional characteristics such as saturated fat, sodium and added sugar. California law also excludes several categories, including raw agricultural commodities and certain minimally processed foods.

That distinction matters because “processed” and “unhealthy” are not necessarily synonymous.

Food processing includes everything from freezing and pasteurization to fermentation and fortification. Processing can improve food safety, extend shelf life and make nutritious foods more accessible. Critics of broad UPF classification systems therefore caution that products such as yogurt, tofu and whole-grain bread can sometimes fall into ultra-processed categories even though they may contribute useful nutrients to a balanced diet.

California’s model consequently places significant emphasis on both ingredients and nutritional composition rather than treating industrial processing alone as the determining factor.

Why Ultra-Processed Foods Have Become a Major Policy Issue

The California legislation arrives amid growing attention to ultra-processed foods from scientists, policymakers and consumers.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration says researchers have found associations between high consumption of foods commonly categorized as ultra-processed and outcomes including obesity, cardiovascular disease and certain cancers. At the same time, federal regulators acknowledge that significant scientific questions remain about exactly how and why UPFs may affect health.

The issue is especially significant because ultra-processed foods make up a substantial portion of the American diet. The FDA estimates that about 70% of the U.S. food supply consists of foods commonly considered ultra-processed and says children obtain more than 60% of their calories from such products.

Association, however, does not mean that every product classified as ultra-processed carries the same nutritional or health implications. That is one reason the definition itself has become central to the regulatory debate.

FDA and USDA Are Working on a Federal UPF Definition

California is moving faster than Washington on the issue.

In July 2025, the FDA and U.S. Department of Agriculture launched an effort to develop a uniform federal definition of ultra-processed foods. Regulators requested input on whether a definition should consider additives, processing techniques, nutritional composition, energy density, palatability and other characteristics.

Federal officials have said a common definition could provide consistency for scientific research and future food and nutrition policies. The FDA has also partnered with the National Institutes of Health on nutrition regulatory science research intended to improve understanding of the relationship between ultra-processed foods and health.

The absence of a completed national standard has created an opening for states such as California to develop their own approaches.

Food Industry Raises Concerns About Multiple Standards

That state-by-state movement is also generating concern within the food industry and scientific community.

The Institute of Food Technologists has warned that manufacturers could eventually encounter different definitions of “ultra-processed” depending on the jurisdiction. According to Food Dive, the organization argues that a consistent, science-based framework would help prevent conflicting requirements and consumer confusion.

The stakes extend beyond package labels. How governments ultimately define ultra-processed foods could affect school meals, government nutrition programs, product reformulation, dietary recommendations and front-of-package labeling.

Private certification programs are also emerging. Food Dive notes that programs including the Non-GMO Project’s Non-UPF Verified Standard and the nonprofit Non-UPF Program already offer their own approaches to identifying foods considered non-ultraprocessed.

As a result, consumers could encounter several different “non-UPF” claims based on standards that are not identical.

California Is Already Targeting UPFs in Schools

The certification program is part of a broader California food-policy strategy.

Under the Real Food, Healthy Kids Act, signed in October 2025, the California Department of Public Health is developing regulations for “Ultraprocessed Foods of Concern” and “Restricted School Foods.” The law establishes a long-term process for reducing certain foods in California public schools.

State budget documents say schools are expected to begin phasing out designated foods by July 1, 2029, with their sale prohibited beginning July 1, 2035, subject to the definitions and regulations developed under the law.

Those definitions are still being developed. In September 2026, California officials opened a public-input process asking stakeholders what the Department of Public Health should consider when defining the relevant categories.

What California’s UPF Label Could Mean for Food Manufacturers

For food companies, California’s certification could create both marketing opportunities and operational challenges.

Brands whose products qualify may use the non-UPF certification to differentiate themselves as consumer demand for simpler ingredients and greater food transparency grows. Manufacturers whose products fall outside the standard may have additional incentives to reconsider ingredients, sodium, added sugars, saturated fat or certain additives.

The larger question is whether California’s policy becomes a model for other states.

If additional jurisdictions adopt similar programs using different definitions, national food manufacturers could face a fragmented regulatory environment. Conversely, California’s approach could contribute to pressure for a single federal standard.

Either outcome makes the definition of “ultra-processed food” increasingly important to the U.S. food industry.

California has now moved the debate from academic research and dietary guidance into grocery-store labeling and merchandising. Whether its “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified” seal becomes a widely recognized consumer signal will depend on manufacturer participation, implementation of the state standard, consumer response and the direction ultimately taken by federal regulators.

What is already clear is that ultra-processed foods have moved rapidly from a nutrition-science debate into a significant food policy, labeling and product-development issue for the U.S. packaged food industry.

MAHA's AI bet

With help from Amanda Chu and Daniel Lippman

Driving the Day

MAHA SETS ITS SIGHTS ON AI — Leaders of the Make America Healthy Again movement are embracing artificial intelligence to help their mission to address chronic disease, even as public unease about AI grows nationwide, Amanda reports.

On Monday, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. touted AI’s potential to analyze vast quantities of health data and lower health care costs at a summit hosted by the MAHA Institute, one of his movement’s nonprofit arms.

“If we don’t solve the problem of chronic disease, we’re not going to lower health care costs, and we need [super intelligence] to do that, and we need to consolidate all of these data sets and make them readable,” he told a crowd of MAHA supporters and executives. Last week, President Donald Trump ordered his agencies to refer to artificial intelligence as “super intelligence.” Kennedy added that he recently met with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

Details: The half-day event centered on how the government can streamline access to health data and best leverage its large databases to improve public health. Speakers included Mark Gorton, president of the MAHA Institute; Nicole Kleinstreuer, a deputy director at the National Institutes of Health; and Dan Brillman and Amy Gleason, deputy administrators at the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.

“Solving the health data problem is important for a number of multitrillion-dollar companies, and the MAHA Institute can channel corporate reform energy towards targeted policy plans and help them coordinate data modernization strategies,” Gorton said in his opening remarks.

Gleason spearheaded CMS’ Kill the Clipboard initiative, which allows patients to access their health records via QR codes and use AI to understand their health information. “AI can help solve a lot of this, but it does need the data to be able to do that. It needs innovation. It needs people to move faster,” Gleason said.

Some attendees voiced concerns about data privacy and corporate overreach. “When it comes to sharing our personal information. … I think we have to be very cautious,” said one attendee, adding that there are “too many unknowns.”

What’s next: The event precedes the flagship MAHA Summit taking place today, which has secured corporate donors spanning the American economy from OpenAI and Anthropic to Walmart.

Several panels at today’s event will focus on AI, including “AI and Healthcare” and “Building the AI Health Stack.”

WELCOME TO TUESDAY PULSE. Will you be attending the MAHA Summit this morning? Let us know. Send your tips, scoops and feedback to khooper@politico.com and sgardner@politico.com, and follow along @kelhoops and @sophie\_gardnerJ.

AROUND THE AGENCIES

BY THE NUMBERS — The labor union that represents employees at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Atlanta headquarters has launched a new website with detailed information on how much the agency’s workforce has decreased since the start of the second Trump administration.

The American Federation of Government Employees Local 2883’s website relies on data from the Office of Personnel Management, the Department of Health and Human Services’ employee directory and “union data” to offer the clearest picture yet of how the Trump administration has reshaped the CDC’s workforce.

According to the findings, the agency lost 30 percent of its workforce from March 2025 to May 2026 — about 3,539 people — though some remain on administrative leave as a result of the Trump administration’s reduction-in-force efforts. The analysis didn’t include contractors or members of the U.S. Public Health Service, uniformed public health professionals who often serve at the CDC.

“Dr. Schwartz and CDC’s new leadership are evaluating the agency’s structure and operations to ensure CDC can effectively advance the priorities of President Trump and Secretary Kennedy and fulfill its core public health mission,” an HHS spokesperson told POLITICO.

Details: The largest share of employees who left the agency — 857 — voluntarily retired, while 216 more opted for early retirement and 837 quit.

Another 800-plus were affected by the Trump administration’s RIFs, with 572 fired and 271 placed on administrative leave. Smaller shares left because of expired terms or other forms of termination or separation.

The CDC’s Office of Health Equity and Office of Equal Employment Opportunity lost all their employees, according to the website, and the Office of Human Resources lost nearly all its workers. HHS said last year that it was working to “centralize” human resources.

The National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities lost about half its staff, as did the National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion and the Office of Communications. At the time, HHS said some of the areas cut at the CDC would be moved to a new agency, called the Administration for a Healthy America, but that agency hasn’t been created, likely because Congress hasn’t funded it.

In the States

NEWSOM’S MAHA BID — California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat who’s increasingly been courting voters aligned with Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again coalition, is touting a new MAHA-aligned accomplishment, POLITICO’s Nicole Norman reports.

In 2029, his state will likely become the first to label non-ultra-processed products in grocery stores — a year after he signed legislation defining “ultra-processed” foods and phasing those foods out of school lunches.

“California has never been afraid to challenge the status quo, and we’ll keep innovating, trying new things, and clearing the way for the rest of the country to follow,” Newsom said in a statement.

Details: The latest legislation — AB 2244 from Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, a Southern California Democrat — would allow outside companies registered with the state to certify products as non-ultra-processed, making them eligible to carry the state-sponsored seal. Grocery stores with gross sales of more than $10 million a year would also be required to prominently display three certified items if they carry 25 or more products bearing the seal.

Why it matters: The MAHA voter base that helped carry Trump to victory in 2024 is unimpressed with potential Republican presidential candidates and searching for its next champion. But it’s unclear whether Newsom’s action on healthy food would help him court those voters if he runs, as the governor also took firm stances on vaccines and masking during the Covid-19 pandemic.

Lobby Watch

FORMER HHS OFFICIAL’S NEW GIG — Miller Strategies is bringing on Braden Murphy, who was most recently deputy assistant secretary for legislation at the Department of Health and Human Services, as the GOP lobby shop continues to deepen its ties to Trump, our colleagues at POLITICO Influence report.

Murphy advised Kennedy on congressional affairs involving divisions like the Food and Drug Administration, the National Institutes of Health and the CDC. He also helped shepherd several HHS appointees through the Senate confirmation process. Before joining the administration, he worked for House Budget Chair Jodey Arrington (R-Texas) and former Speaker Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.).

Miller Strategies also announced it is bringing on Noah Pollak, who was a senior adviser in Education Secretary Linda McMahon’s office and the Treasury Department’s Terrorism and Financial Intelligence office.

Jeff Miller, founder and CEO of Miller Strategies, said Pollak and Murphy “helped deliver many of President Trump’s legislative priorities over the past two years.”

Names in the News

Shannon Hunt-Scott, co-founder and president of the Scott Foundation, will be named C4 board chair of Reproductive Freedom for All today, replacing Kimberly Peeler-Allen.

California pondrá en marcha un sello voluntario para identificar alimentos no ultraprocesados y los supermercados con ventas brutas superiores a USD 10 millones deberán hacer visibles los productos certificados.

La ley, firmada por el gobernador Gavin Newsom, permitirá a los fabricantes solicitar una autorización estatal para incorporar el distintivo en sus envases.

El programa estará a cargo del Departamento de Salud Pública de California. Los productores deberán presentar sus artículos ante agentes acreditados, que evaluarán si cumplen la definición estatal de alimento no ultraprocesado.

La certificación no obliga a reformular productos ni exige a las empresas sumarse al esquema, según ABC News.

La autorización tendrá una vigencia de tres años

La certificación será optativa para los fabricantes. Sin embargo, ningún producto podrá exhibir el sello sin la evaluación y el aval previo de un agente acreditado por el estado.

Una vez concedida, la autorización tendrá una duración de tres años. Al terminar ese período, cada alimento deberá pasar por una renovación para conservar la identificación, informó ABC News.

La ley AB 2244 fue impulsada por el asambleísta demócrata Jesse Gabriel, representante de Encino.

De acuerdo con el comunicado del Gobierno de California, la norma establece un estándar para determinar qué productos podrán presentarse como no ultraprocesados.

El objetivo es trasladar a la parte frontal del paquete una información que los compradores suelen buscar en las listas de ingredientes, los datos nutricionales y los aditivos.

El estado tomó como referencia el sello orgánico del Departamento de Agricultura de Estados Unidos (USDA), aunque ambas certificaciones evalúan condiciones diferentes.

California combinará la presencia de aditivos con el perfil nutricional

Para el estado, un alimento o bebida ultraprocesado contiene una “sustancia especificada”, como colorantes o estabilizantes, y registra a la vez niveles altos de grasas saturadas, sodio o azúcar añadida.

Esta categoría también incluye productos con edulcorantes no nutritivos, según explicó ABC News.

Por lo tanto, para acceder al distintivo un artículo deberá ajustarse al estándar definido por California. No será suficiente con que el fabricante lo promocione como natural, saludable u orgánico.

KTLA indicó que la etiqueta se llamará “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified”, mientras que ABC News informó que los envases aprobados llevarán la inscripción “California Certified”.

El comunicado oficial solo aludió a un sello para alimentos certificados como no ultraprocesados, sin precisar el nombre definitivo que aparecerá en los paquetes.

Esa diferencia deja pendiente la presentación final del distintivo. Los materiales divulgados hasta el momento tampoco detallan el procedimiento que deberán seguir los agentes certificadores para comprobar cada requisito.

Los supermercados deberán exhibir los productos en sectores de alta circulación

La norma alcanza también a los comercios. Los supermercados de California que superen el nivel de facturación establecido tendrán que destacar los artículos certificados en zonas de alta circulación de clientes, según ABC News.

La exigencia busca evitar que la certificación pase inadvertida cuando los alimentos lleguen a las góndolas. KTLA señaló que la legislación no determina si las tiendas deberán emplear carteles, señalización en los estantes u otro sistema de identificación.

“Como la etiqueta orgánica del USDA, este nuevo sello ofrecerá a los consumidores información clara y confiable”, afirmó Gabriel en declaraciones a KTLA.

Siguiendo esta línea, el legislador sostuvo que la medida apunta a facilitar las decisiones de compra de las familias.

“Los padres no deberían necesitar un doctorado en química” para saber qué comen sus hijos, añadió el asambleísta ante el medio local.

Newsom vinculó la medida con la prevención de enfermedades

El Gobierno de California incluyó el nuevo programa en un paquete de leyes referidas a la alimentación, la salud infantil, los vapeadores y los suplementos.

La administración estatal sostiene que esas iniciativas pretenden reforzar la prevención y facilitar el acceso a opciones nutricionales.

“El sistema de salud debería concentrarse en prevenir enfermedades y no solo en tratarlas”, señaló Newsom en el comunicado oficial.

El gobernador relacionó el sello con el acceso a alimentos frescos y con decisiones de compra más simples para las familias.

En declaraciones recogidas por ABC News, Newsom sostuvo además que California debe dar prioridad a la atención sanitaria frente al tratamiento de enfermedades y hacer más accesibles los alimentos integrales y saludables.

La legislación se inscribe en un debate sanitario más amplio. ABC News citó un estudio de 2022 de los Centros para el Control y la Prevención de Enfermedades de Estados Unidos (CDC) y la Universidad de São Paulo, que vinculó una mayor proporción de calorías procedentes de alimentos ultraprocesados con un aumento de las enfermedades cardiovasculares.

Organizaciones y críticos reclaman reglas claras para el nuevo distintivo

La Environmental Working Group (EWG) respaldó la promulgación de la norma. Su vicepresidenta sénior para California, Bernadette Del Chiaro, dijo a ABC News que la medida ofrece a las familias una referencia para diferenciar alimentos más cercanos a los preparados en una cocina de aquellos elaborados industrialmente.

“Los consumidores merecen etiquetas en las que puedan confiar”, afirmó Del Chiaro al medio estadounidense. La organización consideró que el sistema mejora la identificación de los alimentos.

También surgieron advertencias sobre los límites de estas herramientas. KTLA recogió cuestionamientos de críticos que apuntan a que los distintos programas de certificación pueden utilizar definiciones, estándares y mecanismos de verificación diferentes.

El alcance práctico del sello dependerá de la claridad y consistencia de los criterios estatales, así como de los detalles de su implementación.

La certificación tendrá que traducir esos requisitos en una señal comprensible para quienes compran los productos.

Newsom signs first-in-the-nation bills targeting federal immigration enforcement in California

New laws target ICE detention facilities, the use of state resources in operations, and set up likely legal battles over state versus federal authority

By Jenny Huh
Published 6:05 PM PDT September 29, 2026

SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Governor Gavin Newsom signed a package of bills Tuesday morning addressing federal immigration enforcement in California, setting up another potential clash between the state and the Trump administration over who has authority where.

For California Democratic lawmakers, these efforts began in January, at the start of the legislative session, with several of the bills set to take effect soon.

“California is proud of the fact that we offer sanctuary,” Democratic Assemblymember Alex Lee, co-author of several of the signed bills, said.

By law -- Senate Bill 54 -- California state and local law enforcement agencies cannot assist with federal immigration enforcement efforts.

One of the new laws temporarily bans “shock gloves,” which can deliver an electric shock when they come into contact with skin.

Concerns over the electroshock technology grew after reports that ICE may begin using the gloves. Law enforcement officials, including Sacramento County Sheriff Jim Cooper, strongly opposed California’s ban, arguing the gloves could be an effective de-escalation tool.

“It is insane that Democrat politicians are taking this tool our of the tool kit of law enforcement,” Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio said. “Well then why don't you study it first, and then if there's a problem, you can ban it.”

But Assemblymember Lee countered that the devices should not be considered a de-escalation tool once an officer has made physical contact with someone.

“Once you lay hands on someone, you’re not really de-escalating anymore; you’re subduing, you’re dominating someone,” Lee said.

The ban starts in January and will remain in place until 2030. It also requires a state study of safety and community impacts. The law does not apply to conventional tasers, stun guns, or similar technologies utilized by law enforcement.

Another law takes effect July 2028 and would impose a 25% annual tax on the gross income of private, for-profit detention facilities that contract with ICE. There are eight such facilities in California, operated by two companies -- The GEO Group and CoreCivic. 

“There are massive corporations here in our state that are profiting off of family separation, human suffering,” bill author Democratic Assemblymember Matt Haney said. “We might not be able to control everything about federal immigration policy, but we do have the ability to regulate those who are doing business in our state.”

Haney said facilities that do not want to pay the tax could leave California.

The revenue would be used for immigration services, including legal assistance for detainees.

The bill was amended from its original form, which proposed a 50% annual tax on the gross receipts of these facilities. Implementation was also delayed until 2028. Gross income starting in 2027 will be taxed. 

“To make sure that our state resources are used to protect our residents and not to harm them. These are taxpayer dollars. They should be benefiting them,” Democratic Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel said.

Under two bills by Gabriel, starting in January, federal agents would be barred from using state resources, including state-owned property such as parking lots, for enforcement staging, processing, detention, or operations.

The measures would also create independent state investigations into fatal shootings involving federal immigration agents.

“We want to make sure that we’re not part of [immigration operations], that we’re not assisting it,” Gabriel said.

Legal challenges may follow over the question of state versus federal authority.

The White House responded to the new laws, writing, “Gavin Newsom has no authority over federal law enforcement. The Trump administration will not abide by his unconstitutional legislation. Our law enforcement officers will continue arresting and removing criminal illegal aliens from American communities while radical Democrats in California refuse to cooperate and instead choose to release criminal illegal aliens from their jails into communities to terrorize innocent Americans.”

And the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, responded, “Enforcing federal immigration laws is a clear federal responsibility under Article I, Article II, and the Supremacy Clause. No tax will stop ICE from deporting criminal illegal aliens to make California safe again. We need California to cooperate with our officers and stop RELEASING criminals from their jails into California’s neighborhoods. 7 of the 10 safest cities in America cooperate with ICE."

Every decision is made with careful consideration and appropriately reviewed to ensure that any technology ICE utilizes is consistent with all applicable law enforcement policies and standards. Our officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics and regularly receive ongoing use of force training. The latest ICE use of force policy is available here. While California sanctuary politicians continue to release pedophiles, rapists, gang members, and murderers onto their streets, our brave law enforcement will continue to risk their lives to arrest these heinous criminals and make California safe again.”

Other immigration bills signed by Newsom in this more-than-20-bill-package include a ban on local, state, and federal law enforcement using extreme masking.

The bill by Democratic state Senator Scott Wiener went through several amendments and legal challenges before reaching the governor's desk.

Supporters of the bill say the intention of Senate Bill 1004 is to limit the use of ski masks or any unnecessary obscuring of law enforcement officials' faces. Supporters say identification is a crucial part of holding agencies accountable.

The bill does offer exemptions for safety reasons, for instance, like with motorcycle helmets and SWAT gear.

Another Wiener bill, called the "No Kings Act," was also signed by Newsom.

This would allow people to sue federal immigration agents for alleged constitutional violations. Supporters say under current law, individuals may sue state and local law enforcement officers for constitutional violations but that federal officers are largely shielded from similar lawsuits.

Another bill would require clear identification on rental vehicles if these cars are being used by law enforcement for detention or arrest purposes in the state. Another protects people from civil arrest while they are accessing California courthouses for lawful purposes.

Pushing back on Trump agenda, Newsom signs bill targeting immigration enforcement

The new laws impose new restrictions on law enforcement and protections for immigrants.

Alan Riquelmy / September 29, 2026

SACRAMENTO, Calif. (CN) — California Governor Gavin Newsom on Tuesday continued his legislative onslaught against the Trump administration, signing several bills targeting federal immigration actions.

One high-profile bill that’s now law, Senate Bill 1004, prohibits all law enforcement officers in the state against wearing masks, with some exceptions. Another — Senate Bill 747, called the No Kings Act — enables state residents to sue federal officials for constitutional violations.

State Senator Scott Wiener, a San Francisco Democrat and vocal opponent of President Donald Trump, wrote both bills.

“When federal agents act lawlessly, they should be held accountable the same as any other lawbreaker,” Wiener said in a statement. “But for too long, a loophole in the law has shielded them from accountability.”

Wiener’s bills are two out of several signed by Newsom. Others impose restrictions on shock gloves and flash-bang grenades, and levy a 25% tax on private detention facilities.

“Trump has put his political interests above the health, safety and livelihood of American families,” Newsom said in a statement, adding: “California is taking action to strengthen transparency, accountability, and oversight around immigration enforcement in our state. We will continue protecting our people, upholding the rule of law, and making clear that if the federal government operates in California, we will hold them accountable.”

Federal immigration action across the nation, including California, helped spark legislation to rein in the Trump administration. Trump and Newsom have exchanged verbal barbs for months.

Newsom’s office said the bills create stronger standards for law enforcement and protect civil rights, as well as families and communities across California.

Senate Bill 937 — written by state Senator Lena Gonzalez, a Long Beach Democrat — adds flash-bang grenades to a list of items prohibited for use to disperse protests, with exceptions. Assembly Bill 1627 — by Assemblymember Anamarie Ávila Farías, a Martinez Democrat — prohibits Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who committed serious misconduct from serving as California police officers or public employees.

Assembly Bill 1807 — by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, an Encino Democrat — prohibits state-owned property from being used for immigration enforcement. Additionally, California must identify property immigration authorities likely could use, placing signs, and potentially barriers, stopping that use.

The 25% tax on income from companies running immigration detention facilities stems from Assembly Bill 1633 by Assemblymember Matt Haney, a San Francisco Democrat. The revenue gained will fund immigration-related services.

“For years, private corporations have made hundreds of millions of dollars locking people up for ICE while California families and communities are left to deal with the consequences,” Haney said in a statement. “Now, California is the first state in the country to say: If you are going to make money off mass detention and family separation in our state, you are going to pay for the harm you cause.”

The new laws also provide protections to immigrants.

Senate Bil 873 — by state Senator Eloise Gómez Reyes, a Colton Democrat — prohibits the civil arrest of someone traveling to or from a courthouse or while at a courthouse. The bill signing falls on the heels of a June decision by a federal judge that blocked a new policy allowing for civil arrests at courthouses.

“Justice cannot work when people are afraid to walk through courthouse doors,” Reyes said in a statement. “No victim, witness, or family member should have to choose between seeking justice and risking civil arrest.”

Other protections added by the bill signings include Assembly Bill 1994 — by Assemblymember David Alvarez, a San Diego Democrat — called the Defending Immigrant Victims Act.

The new law requires law enforcement, along with any agency prosecuting a criminal act, to provide an immigrant victim rights and resources card to crime victims. The cards will contain information about how to remain eligible for certain visas and instructions for consulting an immigration attorney.

California Governor Gavin Newsom has signed legislation creating a voluntary certification and labelling programme for non-ultra-processed foods, alongside new requirements covering sugar warnings on restaurant menus and children’s meals.

Assembly Bill 2244, authored by Assembly Member Jesse Gabriel, establishes what supporters describe as the first certification programme of its kind in the US. The bill was announced earlier this year, with Newsom's signing making it official this week.

The legislation creates a ‘Non-Ultra-processed Certified’ seal for food products that meet specified standards relating to processing and ingredients – generally, foods considered 'non-UPF' will be those that are free from synthetic additives, such as artificial colours and flavours.

Under the programme, manufacturers will be able to apply for certification through accredited certification agents, with oversight from the California Department of Public Health.

The scheme is modelled on the USDA Organic programme and is intended to provide consumers with a front-of-pack indicator for products that meet California’s definition of non-ultra-processed foods.

The legislation also requires grocery stores to make certified products easier for consumers to locate through in-store placement.

Gabriel said the new seal would provide consumers with “clear trustworthy information” about the foods they buy. He added: “Parents shouldn’t need a PHD in chemistry to understand what they’re feeding their kids.”

In 2025, Newsom signed the Healthy Foods, Healthy Kids Act, which established a statutory definition of ultra-processed foods and set out a process for phasing certain products out of California Schools.

California has also introduced restrictions on a number of food additives through legislation including the California Food Safety Act of 2023 and the California School Food Safety Act of 2024.

Alongside AB2244, Newsom signed legislation requiring chain restaurants to offer at least one children’s meal that meets minimum nutritional standards.

Senate Bill 869 will require restaurant menus to identify drinks containing more than the recommended daily intake of added sugar. The measures form part of a wider package of legislation focused on nutrition, food access and public health.

Other bills signed by Newsom include legislation establishing a programme to identify locally based suppliers able to provide healthy food to California public schools. The state has also banned the sale of over-the-counter diet pills and dietary supplements marketed for weight loss or muscle building to people under 18.

Newsom said the measures were intended to shift the focus of healthcare towards prevention.

He added: “We should be about health care, not sick care, recognising that preventing illnesses is far preferable to finding and affording treatments.”

The introduction of the certification scheme comes as governments, health organisations and the food industry continue to debate the role of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) in diets.

The City Council is the lawmaking body of the City of Los Angeles. It has 15 members, and each one is elected by the voters of one district. The Council passes City laws, called ordinances, which the Mayor can approve or veto. It also approves or changes the budget the Mayor proposes each year.

The candidates

Timothy K. Gaspar

Gaspar, 44 (LA Times), grew up in Canoga Park and went to El Camino Real High School, Pierce College and Cal State Northridge (campaign bio; LAist). He founded Gaspar Insurance in 2008 and sold it in 2021, the LA Times reported (LA Times). He has served on the boards of Discovery Cube Los Angeles, the Metropolitan YMCA, Viewpoint School and the Woodland Hills/Warner Center Chamber of Commerce, and lives in Woodland Hills (campaign bio). He lists no prior political office (Daily News questionnaire).

Barri Worth Girvan

Worth Girvan, 43 (LA Times), was born and raised in the West Valley, graduated from UC San Diego, has a master's degree from USC and lives in Woodland Hills (campaign bio). She worked for Assemblymember Lloyd Levine, was West Valley area director for Mayor Antonio Villaraigosa and district director for state Senate Majority Leader Bob Hertzberg, and directed government affairs for the Jewish Federation of Greater Los Angeles (LAist). She is director of community affairs for County Supervisor Lindsey Horvath (LA Times). She has not held public office; she is an elected member of the LA County Democratic Party (Daily News questionnaire).

The job

What a Councilmember does. The 15-member City Council passes City laws, adopts the budget the Mayor proposes, and approves or rejects the Mayor’s picks to run most departments and sit on commissions, LAist explains (LAist). Ordinances go to the Mayor, who can approve or veto them, and the Council can override a veto by a two-thirds vote (City Charter Sec. 250, as reproduced in Council File 26-0489). Under current Charter text the Council can change the Mayor’s budget by June 1, and a Mayor’s veto of those changes takes a two-thirds vote to override (Charter Secs. 313 and 315, as printed in the November 2026 Voter Information Pamphlet). The FY 2026-27 City budget is $14.85 billion (Mayor’s office).

Each member also runs a district office that works with more than 40 City departments on local services and plays “a vital role in shaping development” in the district (LAist). The anti-camping law, LAMC 41.18, lets Council members designate areas near schools, libraries, senior centers and other sensitive places as no-camping zones (LA Times). Each member represents about 260,000 people (LAist).

The district. Council District 3 covers the southwest San Fernando Valley: Woodland Hills, Tarzana, Canoga Park, Winnetka and Reseda (LAist; Daily News). South of Ventura Boulevard are hillside ranch homes. Flatter areas to the north mix single-family homes with apartments and commercial strips (LAist). Bob Blumenfield has held the seat since 2013 and is termed out (Daily News). LAist says the district’s voters “historically have sent centrist (for Los Angeles) Democrats and Republicans” to the Council.

Local issues in the news.

  • Rams Village and Warner Center. The Rams’ owner is building a 52-acre complex in Woodland Hills with the team headquarters, more than 3,000 homes, venues, a hotel and shops (LA Times, Aug 18, 2026). The LA Times put its cost at more than $10 billion (LA Times, April 2025). A separate $2 billion plan, Viva L.A., would add four senior-housing towers of 34 to 42 stories with 3,192 units under the Mayor’s Executive Directive 1 (LA Times, Aug 18, 2026). LAist notes that nearby former rocket-engine land in Canoga Park is still awaiting environmental cleanup.
  • Woodland Hills Country Club. A developer, Arrimus Capital, proposed 398 homes on the golf course under a state fast-track law, AB 2011. In August 2026 the Council voted 11-1 to start a zoning change and then approved it unanimously, and City Planning found the site is mountain lion habitat (Daily News, Aug 21; Daily News, Aug 26; LA Times, Aug 22). Abundant Housing LA and other housing groups opposed Blumenfield’s move (Daily News, Aug 26).
  • Fire risk. Parts of the district are in “very high” fire hazard severity zones near the Santa Monica Mountains (Daily News, Aug 21).
  • Other issues. LA Public Press lists housing and homelessness, public safety, transportation and closing gaps in the LA River bike path as issues the next member will face (LA Public Press).

Records

Neither candidate has held City office, so neither has a Council voting record.

Timothy K. Gaspar

Business. Gaspar founded Gaspar Insurance in 2008. His campaign says it grew to more than 60 employees and 11,000 clients (campaign site). He sold it in 2021 and now campaigns full time, his spokesperson told the LA Times (LA Times).

Civic roles. His campaign lists leadership roles with Discovery Cube Los Angeles, the Metropolitan YMCA of Los Angeles, Viewpoint School, the Woodland Hills/Warner Center Chamber of Commerce and the CSUN Nazarian School of Business (campaign site). LA Public Press also lists the Viewpoint School board of trustees (LA Public Press).

In a June 2025 campaign essay he opposed two proposed UNITE HERE Local 11 initiatives: a $30 citywide minimum wage and voter approval for large new hotels (campaign essay, June 26, 2025). Barri Worth Girvan

Public-sector career. She interned for Rep. Brad Sherman, worked in Assemblymember Lloyd Levine’s field office, was West Valley area director for Mayor Antonio Villaraigosa and district director for Senate Majority Leader Bob Hertzberg, and directed government affairs for the Jewish Federation of Greater Los Angeles (LAist). She is director of community affairs for Supervisor Lindsey Horvath (LA Times), where LAist says she worked on fire recovery and constituent services (LAist).

Ethics and lawsuits. No public enforcement actions found in FPPC, City Ethics Commission or FEC records (FPPC case search; City Ethics enforcement orders; FEC legal search). She is not a State Bar licensee (State Bar search). Searched Sept. 30, 2026.
