Election 2026 · State of California

Proposition 2: Larger state rainy day fund

Proposition 2 would change the State Constitution so the state keeps saving in its main rainy day fund until the fund equals 20% of General Fund taxes, up from 10% today, and saves more in years when revenue from investment gains is very high. It would also extend required extra debt payments from 2030 to 2040 and stop counting rainy day fund deposits toward the state spending limit until the money is taken out.

Summary by CityHallPass, not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 2.

At a glance

Proposition 2
Rainy day fund cap 10% of General Fund taxes today; 20% if Prop 2 passes
Rainy day fund balance $15.1 billion projected at the end of 2026-27 (Assembly Budget Committee)
Vote needed Simple majority
Legislature's vote Assembly 59-8, Senate 29-2 (June 25, 2026)
Money raised For: $125,484.25 since July 1, 2026, by one committee controlled by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel. Against: no committee
Outside spending Against: $37,500 by Reform California (shared with other props). For: under $2,000
Latest public poll PPIC, Sept. 4-10: 60% yes, 39% no (likely voters)

What does a yes vote on Proposition 2 mean?

Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would change. As a result, state budget reserves would be higher. The state also would be required to make extra debt payments for longer.

What does a no vote on Proposition 2 mean?

Rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts would not change.

What would Proposition 2 cost?

The Legislative Analyst says state budget reserves would be higher, which would make it somewhat easier to balance the budget when revenue falls. The state might also make more debt payments than it would otherwise. The analysis gives no dollar figure.

What it means for the City of LA

Proposition 2 changes only state accounts. It does not change the City of Los Angeles's own reserve rules or spending limit, and the Legislative Analyst does not estimate any local effect. Its effect on the City would come through the state budget, which pays for programs the City relies on, such as state homelessness grants. A larger state reserve is meant to make state cuts less likely in a downturn, but the measure does not guarantee any program's funding.

The details

Official title Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Type Legislative constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by the Legislature (ACA 20, Resolution Chapter 130, Statutes of 2026)
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide. Under the State Constitution (Article XVIII, Section 4), an amendment takes effect if "approved by a majority of votes cast thereon."

The question on your ballot

Increases California's Rainy Day Fund, approved by voters in 2014, to provide funding for education, health care, public safety, and other essential services during economic downturns. Fiscal Impact: State budget reserves would be higher. Supporters: CA Professional Firefighters; LA Chamber of Commerce; Gavin Newsom; Xavier Becerra; Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel Opponents: None submitted

This is not the Proposition 2 on the November 5, 2024 ballot, the bond for public school and college facilities, which passed with 58.7% of the vote (Secretary of State, November 2024 Statement of Vote).

What would change

Today If Proposition 2 passes
Rainy day fund cap Deposits stop once the fund reaches 10% of General Fund taxes; money that would have gone in must go to infrastructure (LAO analysis) Deposits continue until the fund reaches 20% (LAO analysis)
Yearly set-aside 1.5% of General Fund tax revenue, half to the rainy day fund and half to debt payments, plus extra when capital gains revenue tops 8% of General Fund taxes (Budget Center) The 1.5% stays. Capital gains revenue between 8% and 10% of General Fund taxes still counts as extra; above 10%, 1.5 times the amount counts (Budget Center; text, Sec. 20)
Extra debt payments Required through 2030, and only for state pension and retiree health debts (LAO analysis) Required through 2040. Can also go to money owed to schools and community colleges, loans from other state funds, and federal unemployment insurance loans (LAO analysis)
State spending limit (Gann limit) Money put into the rainy day fund counts toward the limit when deposited (LAO analysis) Starting in 2027-28, deposits do not count; withdrawals count when taken out. The same applies to the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account, up to 10% of General Fund taxes a year (text, Sec. 20(i)-(j))
Declaring a budget emergency The Governor must issue a proclamation before deposits can be cut or money withdrawn (Budget Center) The Governor’s May budget revision counts as the proclamation if it proposes cutting deposits or withdrawing money and emergency conditions exist (text, Sec. 22(c))
School funding guarantee (Prop. 98) Unchanged Unchanged. The text says nothing in it “is intended to change the calculation or funding of the minimum guarantee” (text, First (b)(8))

What stays the same: the state can still cut deposits or withdraw money in a budget emergency, with the same definition of emergency. No more than half the fund can be withdrawn in the first year of an emergency. Required debt payments still cannot be suspended (Budget Center).

What it means for the City of Los Angeles

  • No direct change for the City. Proposition 2 amends only Sections 20 and 22 of Article XVI of the State Constitution, which govern state reserves (ACA 20 status). The Legislative Analyst’s analysis covers only the state budget (LAO analysis).
  • The City’s own reserves follow City policy. The City’s Reserve Fund must equal 5% of General Fund revenue, and the City’s goal is 10% across its Reserve Fund, Budget Stabilization Fund and unappropriated balance (City 2026-27 Proposed Budget, General Fund Reserves Policy). Proposition 2 does not change these.
  • Indirect effect through the state budget. The City budgets state money for some programs, such as the state’s Homeless Housing, Assistance and Prevention (HHAP) grants (City 2026-27 Proposed Budget). The Analyst says higher reserves “would make balancing the budget somewhat easier when revenues decline” (LAO analysis). The measure does not set aside money for any local program. The Budget Center says money set aside in boom years would not be available then for needs such as “support for local governments to address homelessness” (Budget Center).
  • The Los Angeles Area Chamber of Commerce is one of the signers of the argument in favor (arguments). We found no City Council position on Proposition 2 as of Sept. 30, 2026.

How it got on the ballot

ACA 20 needed a two-thirds vote of each house (ACA 20 status). It was filed with the Secretary of State without a Governor’s signature (ACA 20 history).

  • June 22, 2026: ACA 20 was introduced. Its lead authors are Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel and Valencia and Senators Hurtado and John Laird. The Assembly voted 51-16 to suspend two of its rules the same day (ACA 20 history; ACA 20 status).
  • June 25, 2026: The Assembly tabled amendments offered by Assemblymember David Tangipa, 55-18, then adopted ACA 20, 59-8. The Senate withdrew it from committee and adopted it the same day, 29-2. It was filed as Resolution Chapter 130 (ACA 20 votes; ACA 20 history). The Assembly no votes were DeMaio, Dixon, Ellis, Hadwick, Macedo, Patterson, Sanchez and Tangipa. The Senate no votes were Choi and Grove (ACA 20 votes).
  • The Governor’s office listed the amendment as part of the 2026-27 budget agreement announced June 26 (Governor’s office). The Assembly Budget Committee’s floor report says the rainy day fund changes were “completed in conjunction with legislative approval of ACA 20” (Assembly floor report, p. 6).

Why the vote threshold is a simple majority. The State Constitution says a proposed amendment “shall be submitted to the electors and, if approved by a majority of votes cast thereon, takes effect” (Cal. Const. art. XVIII, sec. 4).

Related past measures.

  • Proposition 58 (2004) created the rainy day fund, the Budget Stabilization Account (Budget Center).
  • Proposition 2 (November 2014) set the current deposit, debt payment and 10% cap rules (LAO analysis). It passed with 69.1% statewide and 69.8% in Los Angeles County (Statement of Vote, 2014).
  • Proposition 4 (1979) created the state spending limit, known as the Gann limit (Budget Center).

What each side says

In the state voter guide. Arguments are the authors’ opinions and are not checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments).

Argument in favor, signed by Darrell Roberts of California Professional Firefighters, Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel and Maria S. Salinas of the Los Angeles Area Chamber of Commerce (argument in favor):

  • The state budget swung “from a $100 billion surplus to a $50 billion deficit in just a few years.”
  • It doubles the reserve requirement “so California has a real cushion.”
  • It makes the state bank more of a revenue spike “instead of committing it to new ongoing spending.”
  • The Legislative Analyst “has recommended that the state should be saving significantly more than current rules require.”

Their rebuttal, signed by Linda Darling-Hammond of the State Board of Education, Carmela Coyle of the California Hospital Association and Francisco J. Silva of the California Primary Care Association, calls the taxpayer rebate “a 50-year-old accounting gimmick that rewards spending instead of saving” (rebuttal).

Argument against, signed by Assemblymember David Tangipa, Sen. Steven Choi and Carl DeMaio of Reform California (argument against):

  • It lets politicians “gut the voter-imposed spending limit” and creates a “SLUSH FUND.”
  • It “cancels your tax rebate,” which the Constitution requires when revenue exceeds the spending limit.
  • The state budget “has grown by 76% since 2018.”
  • “Within 24 hours” of putting it on the ballot, the same politicians “voted to suspend more than $5 billion in required deposits.”

Outside the guide.

  • The Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association recommends a no vote. Its guide says the measure’s reserve changes make sense “from the perspective of addressing revenue volatility” but calls it “little more than a Band-Aid on a severed limb” because it does not undo earlier changes to the Gann limit (HJTA 2026 voting guide).
  • Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón said the budget deal addresses “our short and long-term financial future by building up our rainy day fund” (Governor’s office).

Checking the main factual claims against official records.

Claim Who makes it What the records show
The Legislative Analyst recommended saving more Yes campaign In February 2026 the Analyst recommended raising the cap to 50% by 2055, starting with 20% “immediately after the next statewide election.” It estimated current rules would cover about 30% of future funding shortfalls (LAO handout, Feb. 18, 2026, p. 7).
Prop 2 cancels taxpayer rebates No campaign If revenue exceeds the limit two years in a row, the excess is split between taxpayers and schools (Budget Center). Prop 2 takes rainy day fund deposits, and holding account deposits up to 10% of General Fund taxes, out of the limit until withdrawn (text). That lowers counted spending in deposit years, which makes an excess less likely then. The Analyst does not estimate the effect on rebates (LAO analysis).
Lawmakers suspended more than $5 billion in deposits within 24 hours No campaign The Assembly floor report says 2025-26 “true up” deposits to the rainy day fund “remain suspended” under the 2026-27 budget (Assembly floor report, p. 10). The report does not give the amount. The same package raises reserves to an estimated $28.8 billion, including $15.1 billion in the rainy day fund (same page).
Prop 2 makes the budget more volatile No campaign The Analyst says more reserves “would make balancing the budget somewhat easier when revenues decline” (LAO analysis).
Education funding is protected Yes campaign The text says it does not change the Prop. 98 guarantee (text). The rebuttal to the argument in favor says Prop 2 dedicates no new dollars to schools, health care or public safety (rebuttal). Both are consistent with the text.

We did not check the “$100 billion surplus to $50 billion deficit” or “76% since 2018” figures against official budget records.

Who supports and opposes it

Supporters

  • On the ballot label: California Professional Firefighters, Los Angeles Area Chamber of Commerce, Gov. Gavin Newsom, Xavier Becerra and Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (ballot label).
  • The campaign’s coalition list adds Speaker Robert Rivas, Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón, SEIU California, the California Hospital Association, California Primary Care Association, Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, State Board of Education President Linda Darling-Hammond, 21st Century Alliance and California Environmental Voters (Yes on Prop 2).
  • California Democratic Party (CDP positions, Aug. 2, 2026).
  • League of Women Voters of California (LWVC recommendations).
  • California State PTA, which voted to support on Aug. 8, 2026 (CAPTA).

Opponents

  • Reform California and its chairman, Assemblymember Carl DeMaio; Assemblymember David Tangipa; Sen. Steven Choi. The argument against also names the Transparency Foundation (argument against).
  • Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (HJTA 2026 voting guide).
  • The legislators who voted no, listed above (ACA 20 votes).

Editorial boards and others. The Daily News editorial board recommends no: “Vote no on Prop. 2 and elect more prudent state lawmakers” (Daily News, Oct. 7, 2026). The Mercury News and East Bay Times editorial boards list a yes vote in their endorsements roundup (Mercury News, Oct. 13, 2026). We found no LA Times editorial board position as of Sept. 30, 2026, and no published position from the California Republican Party. The California Budget & Policy Center analyzed the measure without taking a position (Budget Center).

Money for and against

For Proposition 2 Against Proposition 2
Committees One: Yes on Proposition 2, a Ballot Measure Committee Controlled by Jesse Gabriel (ID 1485332) None registered
Raised, July 1 to Sept. 19, 2026 $65,038.90 $0
Raised, Sept. 20 to 28 (late reports) $60,445.35 $0
Spent, July 1 to Sept. 19 $135,419.66, of which $121,263.50 was unpaid bills $0
Cash on hand, Sept. 19 $109,432.74 $0
Independent spending $1,853.98 $37,500 (shared with other props)

Source: the committee’s campaign statements (July 1-Sept. 19; 2025) and late contribution reports through Sept. 28, from the Cal-Access raw data export of Sept. 30, analyzed by CityHallPass. The Secretary of State’s contribution totals page still listed no committees, as of its Aug. 2 update, when checked on Sept. 30.

The committee was called “United for Justice, A Ballot Measure Committee Controlled by Jesse Gabriel” until June 30, 2026, and took its Proposition 2 name with the July-September statement. Before July it raised $67,075.09, mostly a $48,950 transfer from another Gabriel committee, Californians for Justice, in December 2025 (Cal-Access raw data export; 2025 statement).

Who is giving

Method: every itemized contribution to committee 1485332 from Jan. 1, 2025 through the late reports of Sept. 28, 2026, from the Cal-Access raw data export, analyzed by CityHallPass.

Donor Amount Share of $192,559.34

21st Century Alliance (Sept. 21, 2026) $50,000 26.0%
Californians for Justice, a Ballot Measure Committee Controlled by Jesse Gabriel (Dec. 2025 and Jan. 2026) $49,000 25.4%
Centene and its affiliate Health Net (in-kind, fundraiser, Jan. 2026) $18,075.09 9.4%
California Democratic Party (in-kind literature, staff and voter data, Sept. 2026) $15,484.25 8.0%
One individual (Sept. 11, 2026) $10,000 5.2%

Source: Cal-Access raw data export and the committee’s July-Sept. statement, analyzed by CityHallPass.

All six donors have California addresses. Since the committee took its Proposition 2 name, the money has come from a labor union committee (SEIU), a business-backed group (21st Century Alliance), the Democratic Party and one individual. The committee did not reach the $1 million level that triggers an FPPC top-10 list (FPPC top-10 list).

How the money was spent. Of $135,419.66 in spending reported for July 1 to Sept. 19, $121,263.50 was bills not yet paid and $9,117.26 was paid out, including $7,500 to LAFC StadiumCo for fundraising events (July-Sept. statement). The statement data we used do not name the vendors owed the unpaid bills.

Outside spending

Independent expenditures reported through Sept. 28, 2026 (Cal-Access raw data export):

  • Against: Reform California with Carl DeMaio (ID 1268914) reported $37,500 for slate mailers, door hangers and campaign management on July 1 and Aug. 27. The same payments are listed against several other propositions, so the Proposition 2 share cannot be separated.
  • For: the California Democratic Party reported $1,493.45 for walk pieces and door hangers, and United Domestic Workers of America Issues PAC reported $360.53, also shared with other props.

Independent analysis

  • Legislative Analyst. Besides the official analysis (LAO analysis), the Analyst says revenue declines over a bad recession “can equal 50 percent or more of annual General Fund revenues.” In a February presentation to the Senate Budget Committee, its simulations found current rules would cover about 30% of funding shortfalls over 50 years; raising the cap to 50% by 2055 with stronger deposit rules would cover about 75% (LAO handout, pp. 6-7). The handout does not model Proposition 2 as written.
  • Budget Center. The California Budget & Policy Center says that if Prop 2’s capital gains rules had applied from 2010-11 to 2023-24, the state would have set aside more in six of those 14 years, less than 1% to 2% of General Fund revenue each time. It says the change could take hundreds of millions of dollars, or more than $1 billion, off the table in some years. It also says a higher cap means less “spillover” money for infrastructure, and that using debt payments on federal unemployment insurance loans would shift a cost from businesses to the state (Budget Center).
  • Current reserves. The 2026-27 budget projects $28.8 billion in reserves: $15.1 billion in the rainy day fund, $9.2 billion in the school reserve and $4.5 billion in the operating reserve, plus $6.4 billion in the temporary holding account (Assembly floor report, p. 10).

Interaction with other measures on this ballot

  • The Legislative Analyst’s analysis names no conflict between Proposition 2 and other measures on this ballot (LAO analysis).
  • Proposition 41 also deals with the state spending limit, in a different way: it would stop new state taxes from being excluded from the limit (LAO analysis of Prop 41). Proposition 2 concerns reserve deposits, not taxes. See our Proposition 41 page.
  • Proposition 3 would keep higher income tax rates on high earners after 2031 (Prop 3 analysis). Rainy day fund deposits are set as shares of General Fund revenue, so more revenue means larger required deposits under either current rules or Proposition 2 (LAO analysis). See our Proposition 3 page.

If it passes

  • When it takes effect. A constitutional amendment takes effect on the fifth day after the Secretary of State files the statement of the vote (Cal. Const. art. XVIII, sec. 4). The spending limit changes apply starting in the 2027-28 fiscal year (text, Sec. 20(i)).
  • Budget emergencies. The Governor could use the May budget revision as the emergency proclamation (text, Sec. 22(c)).
  • Debt payments. The Assembly Budget Committee says the new debt payment rules would give the state another way to pay an estimated $3.9 billion owed to schools and community colleges for 2025-26 (Assembly floor report, p. 6).
  • Legal challenges. We found no reported legal challenge as of Sept. 30, 2026.

Key moments

We found no debate focused on Proposition 2 in news coverage as of Sept. 30, 2026.

  • LAO reserve recommendations (Feb. 18, 2026). The Analyst recommended raising the rainy day fund cap to 50% by 2055 (LAO handout).
  • Budget deal and three-day passage (June 22-25, 2026). ACA 20 was introduced June 22 and adopted by both houses June 25, alongside the 2026-27 budget (ACA 20 history; Governor’s office).
  • Committee renamed (July 2026). Gabriel’s ballot committee took the Yes on Proposition 2 name (July-Sept. statement).

Polls

Pollster Field dates Sample Margin of error Yes No Undecided
PPIC Statewide Survey Sept. 4-10, 2026 1,103 likely voters (online, English and Spanish, Ipsos KnowledgePanel) ±3.8 points 60% 39% 1%

Source: PPIC, September 2026, pp. 6-7, 22 and 29. Respondents read the ballot title and label. Support was 82% among Democrats, 22% among Republicans and 60% among independents. One percent of likely voters named Proposition 2 as the measure they were most interested in. We found no other public poll on Proposition 2.

Election 2026 · State of California

California Assembly District 40

Rickey Tracy Hayes II and Pilar Schiavo (incumbent) are the candidates for California Assembly District 40 on the November 3, 2026 ballot.

The State Assembly is one of the two houses of the California Legislature, which holds the state's lawmaking power. The Assembly has 80 members. Its members write and vote on state laws and, with the Senate, pass the state budget, which the Constitution requires by June 15 each year.

Summary by CityHallPass, not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: LA County's official election information.

Who votes Voters in the 40th Assembly District
Term and pay Two-year term. A person may serve no more than 12 years in the Legislature, in the Senate, the Assembly or both (California Constitution, article IV, section 2). Salary: $134,694 a year, effective December 1, 2025.
How it works Top two from the June 2 primary, regardless of party. Most votes wins.
Party labels Party preference printed on the ballot

What it means for the City of LA

State laws bind the City, and the state budget funds programs the City runs. Example: state law requires the City to plan housing for all income levels and update that plan on a set schedule (Government Code sections 65580 and 65588). About 227,700 of the district's 517,000 residents live in the City of Los Angeles, in Chatsworth, Porter Ranch, Granada Hills, Northridge and part of North Hills.

At a glance

Rickey Tracy Hayes II Pilar Schiavo
June 2 primary (4 candidates) 22.3%, second 55.6%, first

Pilar Schiavo (DEM) 74,496 55.6%
Rickey Tracy Hayes II (REP) 29,879 22.3%
Elizabeth Wong Ahlers (REP) 18,694 14.0%

The candidates

Rickey Tracy Hayes II

Hayes describes himself as a Marine Corps veteran, a former custody officer and police officer, and an IBEW Local 47 journeyman lineman who became an energy infrastructure executive (campaign site). He gave his job as director of North America field operations and listed no prior elected office in a 2026 questionnaire (SCNG questionnaire). His campaign says he has lived in the Santa Clarita Valley for more than a decade and has roots in Compton and Long Beach (campaign site).

Pilar Schiavo Incumbent

Schiavo was elected to the Assembly in November 2022 and re-elected in 2024 (Assembly bio). The Daily News's election-night count in 2024 had her at 50.7% to 49.3% for Republican Patrick Gipson (Daily News). Before that she was a nurse advocate and small business owner who worked in the labor movement for more than 20 years (Assembly bio). She chairs the Assembly Committee on Military and Veterans Affairs and lives in Chatsworth (Assembly bio). The Assembly is her first elected office (SCNG questionnaire).

The job

The district. The 40th Assembly District covers the Santa Clarita Valley, Castaic, Val Verde and the northwest San Fernando Valley (Assembly bio).

  • City of LA. The Assembly’s district page counts 227,698 City of LA residents in the district, 44% of its 517,084 people (2020 Census) (district map page). The rest live in Santa Clarita (229,156), Stevenson Ranch, Castaic, Val Verde and other unincorporated areas (district map page). The City neighborhoods are Chatsworth, Porter Ranch, Granada Hills, Northridge and the western part of North Hills, based on an overlay of the County’s district map on the City’s Neighborhood Council map (County district layer; City Neighborhood Councils).
  • People. The Census Bureau’s 2020-2024 survey estimates 515,952 residents, about 39% white (not Latino), 34% Latino, 16% Asian and 5% Black, with a median household income of $121,328 (Census Reporter).
  • Voters. On May 18, 2026 the district had 345,107 registered voters: 40.3% Democratic, 30.2% Republican and 22.4% no party preference (Secretary of State). In the June primary 133,924 votes were cast in this race (Statement of Vote).
  • Local issue. The Chiquita Canyon Landfill near Castaic and Val Verde has had an underground “elevated temperature” event that led to several bills from this seat (AB 28; AB 985).

What an Assemblymember does.

  • Laws. The Assembly and Senate write and pass state laws. A bill becomes law when both houses pass it and the Governor signs it (Constitution, art. IV, sec. 10).
  • Budget. The Legislature must pass the budget by midnight on June 15, and a simple majority of each house is enough (art. IV, sec. 12). CalMatters reported the 2026-27 budget deal at $352 billion (CalMatters).
  • Taxes. Any state tax increase needs two thirds of each house (art. XIII A, sec. 3).
  • What it means for the City. The same budget deal gave counties $900 million for homelessness, CalMatters reported (CalMatters). State law also sets the City’s housing planning duties (Gov. Code 65588).

Records

Rickey Tracy Hayes II

Career. Hayes’s campaign describes him as a Marine Corps veteran, a former custody officer and police officer, an IBEW Local 47 journeyman lineman and an energy infrastructure executive (campaign site). He lists his current job as director of North America field operations and calls himself “an infrastructure executive” (SCNG questionnaire). His site does not name the police agencies or his employers (campaign site).

Public office. He listed no other political positions held (SCNG questionnaire).

Party. The California Republican Party’s 2026 endorsement list skips Assembly District 40 (CAGOP). The Yuba County Republican Party gave his campaign $9,500 (Cal-Access).

Ethics and court records. No complaints or enforcement actions were found in FPPC, City Ethics Commission or FEC records (FEC searched Oct. 1, 2026), and no license in his name at the State Bar. No court judgment against him was found in CourtListener records (searched Sept. 30, 2026).

Pilar Schiavo

Office. Schiavo was elected to this seat in November 2022. Her Assembly site says the Speaker named her Assistant Majority Whip when she took office, and that she now chairs the Committee on Military and Veterans Affairs (Assembly bio). In 2026 she said she sits on the Assembly’s health budget subcommittee and the Select Committee on Retail Theft (SCNG questionnaire).

Bills. Counts are from the Legislature’s bill data as of Oct 1, 2026, after the Governor’s Sept 30 deadline to act on bills. A bill counts if she is a lead author of its final version, alone or jointly; constitutional amendments and resolutions are left out. That adds three bills she co-led: AB 1217 (2023, with Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel and Sabrina Cervantes), AB 2262 (2024, with Assemblymembers Eloise Gómez Reyes and Stephanie Nguyen) and SB 296 (2026, with Sens. Bob Archuleta and Suzette Martinez Valladares). It leaves out AB 1359. She led it at first, but it became law with Assemblymember Diane Papan as lead author.

Sept 30 was the Governor’s deadline to sign or veto bills passed this session (Constitution, art. IV, sec. 10).

Laws she wrote include:

  • AB 28 (2026): rules for landfills with high underground temperatures, after the Chiquita Canyon event.
  • AB 2390 (2026): streamlined approval of housing that meets objective standards. Signed Sept 29, 2026 (Governor’s office).
  • AB 2219 (2026): the Faster Services for Veterans Act, which she says will connect veterans to VA and state services more quickly. Signed Sept 28, 2026 (Governor’s office).
  • AB 985 (2025): property tax reassessment for homes near the Chiquita Canyon Landfill.

The Governor vetoed AB 539 (insurer prior authorizations) on Sept 20, 2026 (bill data). The Governor signed AB 2219 (veterans) on Sept 28 (Governor’s office) and AB 2390 (streamlined housing approvals) on Sept 29 (Governor’s office). Vetoed bills from 2023-24 include AB 2670 (an abortion services awareness campaign), AB 608 (Medi-Cal perinatal services), AB 1423 (PFAS in artificial turf) and AB 2637 (health facility financing). State budget deficit Balance it “entirely” with spending cuts, no new taxes. Audit programs and cut those that miss their goals. Election 2026 · Los Angeles County

LA County Superior Court Judge, Office 131

David Ross and Donna Tryfman are the candidates for LA County Superior Court Judge, Office 131 on the November 3, 2026 ballot.

Superior court judges run the trial courts in California, where a judge, and sometimes a jury, hears testimony and other evidence and decides cases by applying the law to the facts. Each county has one superior court that handles all types of cases. Office No. 131 is one seat on the Los Angeles County Superior Court.

Summary by CityHallPass, not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: LA County's official election information.

Who votes Every Los Angeles County voter
Term and pay Six-year term. A superior court judge must have been a lawyer admitted to practice in California, or a judge of a California court of record, for at least 10 years before election or appointment. The LA Times reports the salary is more than $244,000 a year.
How it works Open seat, no incumbent. Two candidates. Most votes wins.
Party labels Nonpartisan

What it means for the City of LA

Superior court judges are elected by voters across the whole county, so every City of Los Angeles voter gets this contest. The Los Angeles County Superior Court is the trial court for the entire county, including the City.

Ross was born and raised in Los Angeles, graduated from Beverly Hills High School and UC Davis, and earned his law degree at the University of West Los Angeles (CityWatch; State Bar). Before law he was a legislative aide to an Indiana congressman and a TV reporter and documentary producer (LA Times). He was a Riverside County deputy public defender for five years and has been a Los Angeles County deputy alternate public defender since 2000, in the Torrance office since 2018 (LA Times). He has not held public office.

Donna Tryfman

Tryfman is the daughter of Holocaust survivors (Daily News). She graduated from Brandeis University in 1989 and the University of La Verne College of Law in 1994, and worked at the Law Offices of Mark J. Werksman (campaign bio; State Bar). She has been a Los Angeles County deputy public defender since 1998 and now works in the Major Crimes Unit on special-circumstances homicide cases (LA Times). She served on the Beverly Hills Rent Stabilization Commission from 2019 to 2024, chairing it in 2022 (MetNews), and ran unsuccessfully for the Beverly Hills school board in 2020 (Daily News).

The job

What a judge does. Superior courts have trial jurisdiction over all criminal and civil cases in the county. Judges serve six-year terms and are elected on a nonpartisan ballot. When a seat opens between elections, the Governor fills it by appointment (Judicial Council fact sheet). LAist lists the kinds of cases the LA court hears: child custody and divorce, landlord and tenant disputes, contract fights, theft and murder trials, probate and small claims. Judges have discretion over things like sentence length and damage awards (LAist).

Size. Hoodline, citing the court, calls it the nation’s largest trial court system and reports 36 courthouses in 12 judicial districts, more than 580 judicial officers and about 5,000 full-time employees serving 9.5 million residents (Hoodline). LAist counts more than 400 judges (LAist). Superior courts also have commissioners and referees, according to the Judicial Council fact sheet. The court says it receives about 1.3 million filings a year (ABC7).

Budget. The court’s funding comes through the state budget. In September 2026 the court said it is underfunded by $233.7 million, that the current state budget covers 76.77% of its calculated need (the lowest level since 2021), and that it would offer $35,000 to employees who agree to leave. It warned of longer lines and slower processing (ABC7).

Pay. The LA Times reports a superior court judge’s salary is more than $244,000 a year (LA Times).

Rules for candidates. The Code of Judicial Ethics bars judicial candidates from making statements “that commit the candidate … with respect to cases, controversies, or issues that are likely to come before the courts” (Canon 5B(1)(a), Code of Judicial Ethics). As a result, candidates talk about how they would do the job rather than where they stand on issues.

Discipline. The Commission on Judicial Performance handles complaints against judges. In 2025 it received complaints about 1,116 judges and justices, opened 99 preliminary investigations and took 15 public actions, the Metropolitan News-Enterprise reported from its annual report (MetNews).

Bar ratings. The Los Angeles County Bar Association’s Judicial Elections Evaluation Committee rates candidates Exceptionally Well Qualified, Well Qualified, Qualified or Not Qualified. It issued its 2026 ratings on April 22, 2026, for the primary (LACBA report). LAist notes the LACBA is a private, volunteer membership group separate from the State Bar (LAist). No separate general-election report was found.

This seat. Office No. 131 is an open seat. Judge Joseph Brandolino, who held it, announced he would retire effective March 31, 2026, the Metropolitan News-Enterprise reported (MetNews, Jan 30, 2026).

Records

David Ross

Legal career. Ross was admitted to the State Bar on Dec. 12, 1994 (bar number 174591). His profile lists the University of West Los Angeles law school and the Alternate Public Defender’s office in Torrance, and shows no public discipline (State Bar profile).

  • He was a Riverside County deputy public defender for five years. In 2000 he joined the Los Angeles County Alternate Public Defender’s office, working in branches including Long Beach and Compton, and has been in Torrance since 2018 (LA Times).
  • His campaign says he has represented more than 10,000 indigent defendants, tried 113 jury trials and handled more than 2,000 preliminary hearings (Beverly Hills Standard, citing the campaign). The LA Times reports “more than 110 jury trials” from his website (LA Times).
  • His title is Grade IV deputy alternate public defender (Beverly Hills Standard). The campaign also says he taught as an adjunct professor at Western State University College of Law from 2002 to 2006 and served as a judge pro tem in small claims and limited civil cases (Beverly Hills Standard).

Before law. He was a legislative aide to Rep. Floyd J. Fithian of Indiana, produced segments of the PBS series “Congress: We The People,” and worked as a TV reporter in Tennessee and Kansas (CityWatch; Daily News questionnaire).

Ballot designation. His designation on the ballot is “Deputy Alternate Public Defender, County of Los Angeles” (final candidate list).

Prior campaigns. None found. He was the first candidate to file for this seat, in January 2026 (MetNews, Jan 30, 2026).

Ethics and court records. His State Bar history shows only his 1994 admission, with no discipline or administrative actions (State Bar profile). No public enforcement actions were found in FPPC or FEC records that refer to him (FPPC case search; FEC legal search). He has sat as a judge pro tem; the Commission on Judicial Performance’s list of public decisions by judge’s name includes no David Ross (CJP). Searched Sept. 30, 2026.

Donna Tryfman

Legal career. Tryfman was admitted to the State Bar on June 12, 1995 (bar number 176744). Her profile lists the University of La Verne College of Law, criminal law as her practice area, and Hebrew and Spanish as languages, and shows no public discipline (State Bar profile).

  • She has been a Los Angeles County deputy public defender since 1998. From 2016 to 2019 she was deputy in charge at Eastlake Juvenile Court, supervising 25 lawyers. She has worked in collaborative drug court. She is now in the Major Crimes Unit, handling only special-circumstances homicides (LA Times). She says she has tried more than 100 jury trials (Daily News questionnaire).
  • The Metropolitan News-Enterprise reports her office performance evaluations give her an overall rating of “competent,” with comments that she “asks for the most serious cases and never backs down from a challenge” (MetNews editorial, Apr 1, 2026).
  • She was president of the statewide Public Defenders Association from 2015 to 2020 (MetNews editorial). Her campaign bio says she received the Gideon Award as felony attorney of the year in 2025 (LA Times).
  • She has served as a judge pro tem in traffic and small claims cases and on the court’s Mediation Volunteer Panel (Daily News editorial). She is vice chair of the LACBA delegation to the California Conference of Bar Associations and has chaired its Criminal Justice Section (MetNews editorial).

Public roles. She served on the Beverly Hills Rent Stabilization Commission from 2019 to 2024 and chaired it in 2022 (MetNews editorial).

Prior campaign. She ran for the Beverly Hills Unified School District board in 2020 and lost (Daily News editorial).

Ethics and court records. Her State Bar history shows only her 1995 admission, with no discipline or administrative actions (State Bar profile). No public enforcement actions were found in FPPC or FEC records, including for her 2020 school board campaign (FPPC case search; FEC legal search). She is not a judge, so the Commission on Judicial Performance has no record on her. Searched Sept. 30, 2026.

Where they stand

Under the Code of Judicial Ethics, judicial candidates may not commit themselves on issues likely to come before the court (Code of Judicial Ethics, Canon 5B). The rows below come from the questions the LA Times and the Southern California News Group asked every candidate (Ross questionnaire; Tryfman questionnaire), plus a CityWatch interview with Ross.

Issue David Ross Donna Tryfman
Court delays and access Would start by “setting expectations of the parties before me” (CityWatch). No specific proposal. Would explore “expanding digital access to the courts in underserved communities” (LA Times, May 1, 2026). Has written in favor of the court’s volunteer mediation program (campaign blog). No specific proposal.
Juries Opposes a voluntary jury system and opposes jury service over Zoom (CityWatch). No stated position.
Use of discretion (sentencing, diversion) Would consider treatment-based supervision or community programs where legally eligible, and custody where alternatives fail (CityWatch). No specific proposal. Prefers “a rehabilitative, holistic approach” with “sufficient mitigating factors,” while “some cases … require custody time” (SCNG questionnaire). Would explain sentencing decisions and be consistent (SCNG questionnaire). No specific proposal.
Conflicts and misconduct Would recuse “promptly” on a clear conflict, and disclose on the record when a campaign supporter appears (SCNG questionnaire; CityWatch). Claims against anyone “must be taken very seriously,” with full constitutional rights for the accused (SCNG questionnaire). No specific proposal.
Role of a judge “There is no place in our court system … for judicial activism” (SCNG questionnaire). Named Justices Kagan, Sotomayor and Jackson as “current judicial heroes” in the Daily News survey (Daily News editorial). “The legislature puts forth policy. Courts resolve disputes” (SCNG questionnaire).

Endorsements

David Ross

From his campaign site, checked Sept 30, 2026. Titles are listed “for identification purposes only.”

  • Judges: about 90 current and retired judicial officers, including Supervising Judge Yvette Verastegui of the Criminal Division, Judges Pat Connolly, Lynn Olson, Richard Goul and Ericka Wiley, and Judge Eric C.   • Former and current officials: former District Attorney Steve Cooley; former state Controller Betty Yee; former Attorney General Bill Lockyer; Assemblymembers Nick Schultz and Pilar Schiavo; former City Councilmembers Paul Koretz and Joel Wachs; Glendale Mayor Ardy Kassakhian; West Hollywood Mayor John Heilman; Rancho Palos Verdes Mayor Paul Seo; South Pasadena Mayor Sheila Rossi; Long Beach City Prosecutor Doug Haubert; Burbank Councilmember Konstantine Anthony (campaign list).
  • Unions and prosecutors’ group: IUOE Local 12; IBEW Local 47; Ironworkers Locals 416 and 433; UNITE HERE Local 11; IATSE 33; APWU Local 64; ILWU Locals 13, 20, 27, 56, 63, 65 and 94 and the ILWU Southern California District Council; Los Angeles Association of Deputy District Attorneys (campaign list).
  • Organizations: La Defensa, LA Forward, Knock LA, Working Families Party, Women’s March Action, CA NOW, Americans for Democratic Action, and more than 20 Democratic clubs, including East Area Progressive Democrats, Stonewall Young Democrats and Black Los Angeles Young Democrats (campaign list).
  • Newspapers: the Los Angeles Sentinel is listed (campaign list). The Southern California News Group chose Tryfman and said it did not back Ross “due to his touting of support from the far-left groups,” naming La Defensa; it called the two “both solid candidates” (Daily News, May 19, 2026).

Donna Tryfman

From her campaign site, checked Sept 30, 2026. Titles are listed “for identification purposes only.”

  • Judges: Court of Appeal Justice Anne H. Egerton and about 45 current and retired Superior Court judges and commissioners, including Judges David Berger, Wendy Segall, Lauren Weis Birnstein and David Walgren. Troy Slaten, who finished fourth in the primary, is also listed (campaign list).
  • Elected officials: Assemblymembers Rick Chavez Zbur and Jesse Gabriel; former state Sen. Robert Hertzberg; former District Attorney Steve Cooley; Beverly Hills Councilmember John Mirisch; Beverly Hills school board President Judith Manouchehri and other board members (campaign list).
  • Public Defender’s office: Public Defender Ricardo D. García, Chief Deputy Justine Esack and other office leaders; several head deputy and deputy district attorneys (campaign list).
  • Unions and prosecutors’ group: SEIU Local 721, UNITE HERE Local 11, Western States Regional Council of Carpenters, IBEW Local 11, Local 250, and the Association of Deputy District Attorneys (campaign list).
  • Organizations: Mexican American Bar Association, National Women’s Political Caucus, Thrive LA, Crime Survivors PAC, Citizens for Accountable Leadership (her committee paid it $4,000 for slate mailers, Cal-Access filings), Stonewall Democratic Club, Democratic Party of the San Fernando Valley and about 15 other Democratic clubs (campaign list).
  • Newspapers: Southern California News Group, which publishes the Daily News and 10 other papers (editorial, May 19, 2026), repeated in its general-election judicial list on Oct 9, 2026 (Daily News); Metropolitan News-Enterprise (editorial, Apr 1, 2026); Colorado Boulevard and LA Progressive are listed on her page.

Both lists: Steve Cooley, UNITE HERE Local 11 and a prosecutors’ association (listed as the “Los Angeles Association of Deputy District Attorneys” by Ross and “Association of Deputy District Attorneys” by Tryfman) appear on both pages. So do two judges, Abby Baron and Osman Abbasi (Ross list; Tryfman list; both checked Sept 30, 2026). No LA Times endorsement was found for this race.

Polls

No public polls of this race were found.

Money

Election 2026 · State of California

California State Senate District 24

John M. Erickson and Brian Goldsmith are the candidates for California State Senate District 24 on the November 3, 2026 ballot.

The State Senate is one of the two houses of the California Legislature, which holds the state's lawmaking power. The Senate has 40 members elected to four-year terms, with half of the seats up every two years; even-numbered districts are on the 2026 ballot. Senators write and vote on state laws and, with the Assembly, pass the state budget, which the Constitution requires by June 15 each year.

Summary by CityHallPass, not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: LA County's official election information.

Who votes Voters in the 24th State Senate District
Term and pay Four-year term. A person may serve no more than 12 years in the Legislature, in the Senate, the Assembly or both (California Constitution, article IV, section 2). Salary: $134,694 a year, effective December 1, 2025.
How it works Top two from the June 2 primary, regardless of party. Most votes wins. This is an open seat: Sen. Ben Allen is termed out.
Party labels Party preference printed on the ballot

What it means for the City of LA

State laws bind the City, and the state budget funds programs the City runs. Example: state law requires the City to plan housing for all income levels and update that plan on a set schedule (Government Code sections 65580 and 65588). The district includes Westside and Hollywood-area City neighborhoods, from Bel Air and Pacific Palisades to Venice and Westchester.

At a glance

The candidates

John M. Erickson

Erickson grew up in Ripon, Wisconsin, and holds a bachelor's degree from the University of Wisconsin Oshkosh and a doctorate from Claremont Graduate University, WeHo Times reported (WeHo Times). He was a council deputy and city staffer in West Hollywood, a legislative representative for LAX and a vice president at Planned Parenthood Los Angeles. He is now chief of staff at Alliance for a Better Community (same article). He was elected to the West Hollywood City Council in 2020, served as mayor in 2024 and was re-elected that year (Beverly Press). Gov. Jerry Brown appointed him to the California Commission on the Status of Women and Girls in 2017 (WeHo Times).

Brian Goldsmith

Goldsmith grew up in Brentwood and lives in Beverly Hills (Beverly Press; SCNG questionnaire). He went to Harvard and holds a law degree from Stanford, and he worked on Hillary Clinton's 2000 Senate campaign (Daily News; Beverly Press). He produced news for Katie Couric at CBS and Yahoo and worked on Pete Buttigieg's 2020 presidential campaign (Beverly Press). CalMatters describes him as a former senior adviser to Democratic Majority for Israel (CalMatters). He runs Kona Media & Message, a Democratic media consulting firm, and has never held elected office (SCNG).

The job

The district. The 24th Senate District runs along the coast from the Santa Monica Mountains to the Palos Verdes Peninsula.

  • Cities. Agoura Hills, Beverly Hills, Calabasas, El Segundo, Gardena, Hermosa Beach, Hidden Hills, Lomita, Malibu, Manhattan Beach, Palos Verdes Estates, Rancho Palos Verdes, Redondo Beach, Rolling Hills, Rolling Hills Estates, Santa Monica, Torrance, West Hollywood and Westlake Village. It also takes in the unincorporated Santa Monica Mountains and Marina del Rey (Senate District 24 page).
  • City of LA. The same page lists these Los Angeles neighborhoods: Bel Air, Beverly Grove, Brentwood, Fairfax, Holmby Hills, Hollywood, Hollywood Hills, Little Holmby, Mid City West, Pacific Palisades, Playa del Rey, Sunset Hills, Venice, Westwood and Westwood Village. An overlay of the County’s district map on City Neighborhood Council boundaries also shows parts of Westchester/Playa and West LA-Sawtelle (County district layer).
  • People. The Census Bureau’s 2020-2024 survey estimates 1,003,720 residents. About 55% are white (not Latino), 17% Asian, 16% Latino and 4% Black (Census Reporter).
  • Fires. CalMatters describes the district as “home to hundreds of thousands of people displaced by the Los Angeles wildfires in 2025” (CalMatters).
  • Voters. On May 18, 2026 the district had 702,277 registered voters: 49.3% Democratic, 20.8% Republican and 23.1% no party preference (Secretary of State). In the June primary 304,378 votes were cast in this race (Statement of Vote).

What a senator does.

  • Laws. The Senate and Assembly write and pass state laws. A bill becomes law when both houses pass it and the Governor signs it (Constitution, art. IV).
  • Budget. The Legislature must pass the budget by midnight on June 15, and a simple majority of each house is enough (art. IV, sec. 12). CalMatters reported the 2026-27 budget deal at $352 billion (CalMatters).
  • Taxes. Any state tax increase needs two thirds of each house (art. XIII A, sec. 3).
  • Appointments. Only the Senate votes to confirm many of the Governor’s appointees. Its Rules Committee holds those hearings (Senate Rules Committee).
  • What it means for the City. The same budget deal gave counties $900 million for homelessness, CalMatters reported (CalMatters). State law also sets the City’s housing planning duties (Gov. Code 65588).

Records

John M. Erickson

Office. Erickson has been on the West Hollywood City Council since 2020. He was mayor in 2024 and was re-elected that year (Beverly Press). He has been vice president of the California Contract Cities Association. He has served with the National League of Cities, the Clean Power Alliance and the Santa Monica Bay Restoration Commission (WeHo Times).

Council record, as reported. West Hollywood’s council records could not be opened, so these items come from news reports:

  • WeHo Times reported that on the council he supported expanded tenant protections, helped launch the WeHo Cares homelessness program, and backed an anti-gun violence ordinance and a drone program (WeHo Times).
  • He told the Santa Monica Daily Press that he co-authored what he called “the highest minimum wage in the county.” He also cited West Hollywood’s cap on yearly rent increases at 3% (SMDP).
  • He told the Beverly Press that he wrote a rule letting seniors and disabled tenants move from a second-floor to a first-floor unit and keep their rent-controlled rent. He also said the city had a $31 million budget surplus while he served (Beverly Press).

Travel. On April 1, 2024 the West Hollywood council approved sending Erickson, then mayor, to the Paris Olympics Pride House handoff. Councilmember Lauren Meister cast the only no vote (Beverly Press).

Other work. He was vice president of Planned Parenthood Los Angeles. He has served on the national board of the National Organization for Women, and WeHo Times reported that he “previously led the ACLU of Southern California” (WeHo Times). The Daily News editorial board described that role as president (Daily News).

Ethics and court records. The FPPC lists no enforcement case or penalty against him. No City Ethics Commission orders, FEC enforcement cases (searched Oct. 1, 2026), State Bar license or court case naming him as a party (CourtListener) were found (searched Sept. 30, 2026).

Brian Goldsmith

Career.

  • Goldsmith is a Democratic media consultant and principal of Kona Media & Message (SCNG).
  • The Daily News reported that he founded two technology startups (Daily News).
  • He was a news producer for Katie Couric at CBS and Yahoo, including the 2008 interview with Sarah Palin, and joined Pete Buttigieg’s 2020 presidential campaign (Beverly Press).
  • The Daily News editorial board wrote that he has advised campaigns going back to Hillary Clinton’s 2000 Senate race (Daily News).
  • CalMatters describes him as a former senior adviser to Democratic Majority for Israel (CalMatters).

Campaign work on Prop 36. He wrote that he “made ads in support of” Proposition 36, the 2024 measure that raised penalties for some theft and drug crimes. He also supported Nathan Hochman for District Attorney (SCNG).

Public office. None. He lists no prior office (SCNG).

Ethics and court records. No enforcement actions found in FPPC, City Ethics Commission or FEC records (FEC searched Oct. 1, 2026), and no license in his name at the State Bar. No court case naming him as a party was found in CourtListener federal and appellate records (searched Sept. 30, 2026).

Where they stand

Most of these issues come from the Daily News editorial board’s interviews with both candidates (Daily News, Sept 26, 2026). The rest come from the Southern California News Group questionnaire, which Goldsmith answered (SCNG, May 5, 2026), and from profiles of both candidates in the Beverly Press and Santa Monica Daily Press. No Erickson questionnaire was found.

Issue John M. Erickson Brian Goldsmith
Housing “Practical zoning changes,” especially near transit (Daily News). Record: cites West Hollywood’s 3% cap on yearly rent increases (SMDP). He criticized Goldsmith for not backing rent control (Daily News). Measure success by “housing units produced.” More modular housing, review of building codes, public land for workforce housing, and down payment help for first-time buyers (Daily News; SCNG).
High-speed rail Finish the Central Valley segment and connect it to Metrolink and Caltrain. No new tax for the project (Daily News). No more money “unless I see a realistic plan for concluding this project on time and on budget” (Daily News).
Taxes Supports Prop 40, the one-time wealth tax (Daily News). Says “the wealthy top 1%” should pay more (Beverly Press). Opposes Prop 40. No changes to Prop 13 now. Open to “longer term reforms” for non-residential property if homeowners and apartment owners are protected (Daily News). Wants a rainy day fund “at least twice its current size” (SCNG).
Public safety pensions Wants to pass again AB 1383, which the Governor vetoed. The bill would let cities raise police and firefighter pensions (Daily News). No stated position.
Crime and treatment No specific proposal found. Fully fund Prop 36. Widen who qualifies for CARE Court. Find a way to provide involuntary treatment for people on the streets with mental illness or addiction (Beverly Press; SCNG).
Schools Explore “sustainable revenue solutions” for schools (SMDP). No specific proposal. End social promotion: “Students need to meet basic standards.” Put more resources into students who are behind in reading and math (Daily News; Beverly Press).
Film and TV jobs Stop studio mergers, including through lawsuits. More arts investment. He says tax credits in other states “are starting to fail” (Beverly Press). Expand the state film tax credit, lift its caps, and cover above-the-line costs such as actors and directors. Lobby for a federal credit (Beverly Press; SMDP).
Fire recovery and insurance “Government to step up and support implementation at the local level.” No specific proposal (SMDP). No specific proposal. He called the fires “a failure at every level of government” (Beverly Press).
Youth and social media No stated position. Supports banning social media for children under 16 (SCNG).

Endorsements

John M. Erickson

Election 2026 · State of California

California Assembly District 55

Ashley M. Brown and Isaac G. Bryan (incumbent) are the candidates for California Assembly District 55 on the November 3, 2026 ballot.

The State Assembly is one of the two houses of the California Legislature, which holds the state's lawmaking power. The Assembly has 80 members. Its members write and vote on state laws and, with the Senate, pass the state budget, which the Constitution requires by June 15 each year.

Summary by CityHallPass, not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: LA County's official election information.

Who votes Voters in the 55th Assembly District
Term and pay Two-year term. A person may serve no more than 12 years in the Legislature, in the Senate, the Assembly or both (California Constitution, article IV, section 2). Salary: $134,694 a year, effective December 1, 2025.
How it works Top two from the June 2 primary, regardless of party. Most votes wins.
Party labels Party preference printed on the ballot

What it means for the City of LA

About 84% of the district's voting precincts and 75% of its land are in the City of Los Angeles, from Mar Vista, Del Rey and Palms to Mid City, West Adams and the Crenshaw area. It also includes Culver City, View Park-Windsor Hills and Ladera Heights. State laws bind the City, and the state budget funds programs the City runs. Example: state law requires the City to plan housing for all income levels and update that plan on a set schedule (Government Code sections 65580 and 65588).

The candidates

Ashley M. Brown

Brown lists her job as a psychiatric social worker for the Los Angeles Unified School District (Orange County Register questionnaire). In that questionnaire she says she works in schools and mental health systems, names mental health and maternal health as her focus, and lists no other political positions held (Orange County Register questionnaire). Her education and earlier career were not found in public sources.

Isaac G. Bryan Incumbent

Bryan was the founding director of the UCLA Black Policy Project and director of public policy for UCLA's Ralph J. Bunche Center, and worked for the City of Los Angeles, where he wrote the City's first report on the needs of formerly incarcerated residents (Assembly biography). Born to a teenage mother, he was raised in a large foster and adoptive family (The Voice of Black Los Angeles). He was first elected to the Assembly in 2021 (Daily News), served as Majority Leader until November 2023 (LA Times), and now chairs the Natural Resources Committee (Assembly biography).

The job

Powers. The California Constitution gives the state’s lawmaking power to the Legislature, which is the Senate plus the 80-member Assembly (art. IV, sec. 1). A bill needs a majority of each house to pass (art. IV, sec. 8). The Legislature can override a Governor’s veto with two-thirds of each house (art. IV, sec. 10). Tax increases need two-thirds of each house (art. XIII A, sec. 3). The Legislature can put constitutional amendments on the ballot by a two-thirds vote of each house (art. XVIII, sec. 1). Five of the 14 statewide measures on this ballot (Props 1, 2, 4, 5 and 43) were placed there by the Legislature (Secretary of State voter guide).

Budget. The Legislature must pass the budget bill by midnight on June 15, and a majority vote is enough (art. IV, sec. 12). CalMatters reported that the 2026-27 budget deal totaled $352 billion. It added taxes, including a sales tax on some computer software, and gave counties $900 million for homelessness (CalMatters).

The district.

  • About 467,000 people live in the 55th District. The Census Bureau’s 2020-2024 survey estimates the population as 34% Latino, 29% white, 20% Black and 10% Asian, with a median household income of $93,558 (Census Reporter).
  • The Daily News lists Crenshaw, Culver City, Ladera Heights, Mar Vista, Del Rey, Palms, Pico-Robertson, Beverly Grove and Mid-Wilshire (Daily News). LAist gives voter registration as 63.1% Democratic, 20.8% no party preference and 9.7% Republican (LAist).
  • Of the district’s 1,702 LA County voting precincts, 1,425 are in the City of LA, 167 in Culver City, and 110 in unincorporated View Park and Ladera Heights (County Registrar precinct map).
  • City neighborhoods, by share of the district’s land (Neighborhood Council map): Mar Vista (10%), Empowerment Congress West (8%), South Robertson (8%), Del Rey (7%), United Neighborhoods (6%), West Adams (5%), Mid City West (5%), Mid City (5%), P.I.C.O. (5%), Park Mesa Heights (4%), Empowerment Congress North (4%), Empowerment Congress Central (3%) and Palms (2%).
  • City Council districts, by share of land (Council district map): CD 10 (Heather Hutt, 30%), CD 11 (Traci Park, 17%), CD 5 (Katy Yaroslavsky, 17%) and CD 8 (Marqueece Harris-Dawson, 12%).
  • Land shares come from laying the County’s Assembly district map over the City’s Neighborhood Council and Council district maps. They measure area, not people.

Records

Isaac G. Bryan

Office and roles. Bryan chairs the Natural Resources Committee and the Select Committee on the Status of Boys and Men of Color. He sits on Governmental Organization, Judiciary, Privacy and Consumer Protection, and the Joint Legislative Committee on Climate Change Policies, and is vice chair of the Legislative Black Caucus (Assembly biography). He was Majority Leader under Speaker Robert Rivas until November 2023, when Rivas replaced him with Cecilia Aguiar-Curry and made him chair of Natural Resources (LA Times).

Bills, 2025-26 session. The Legislature’s bill data lists Bryan as a lead author of the final version of 41 bills, alone or jointly; resolutions are left out. He co-led six of them with another lead author: AB 562 (Solache), AB 1645 (Mark González), AB 1900 (Kalra), AB 2157 (Connolly), AB 2204 (Gabriel) and SB 352 (Sen. Eloise Gómez Reyes). The count leaves out AB 40 and AB 1138: he was lead author of earlier versions, but the final versions list Assemblymembers Mia Bonta and Rick Chavez Zbur. As of the Oct 1, 2026 data file, after the Governor’s Sept 30 deadline to act on bills (art. IV, sec. 10), 28 had become law, 4 were vetoed and 9 did not pass (bill data; Governor’s Sept 30 update).

  • Laws include AB 246 (the Social Security Tenant Protection Act of 2025), AB 247 (wages for incarcerated fire crew members), AB 1388 (law enforcement settlement agreements), AB 1455 (emergency rules for ember-resistant zones), AB 1768, which lets Los Angeles and Contra Costa counties seek local sales taxes above the state cap, and AB 2157 (extending the Displaced Oil and Gas Worker Pilot Program; led by Assemblymember Damon Connolly, with Bryan as joint lead author).
  • Vetoed: AB 7, which would have allowed college admissions preference for descendants of people enslaved in the United States. On Sept 27 the Governor also vetoed AB 1099, on intake for developmental services, and AB 1647, on transferring juveniles to adult criminal court (Governor’s Sept 27 update).
  • Signed Sept 27 to 29: AB 1661, on low-production oil wells and health payments near the Baldwin Hills (LA Focus), and AB 1457, on environmental justice in general plans, both signed Sept 27 (Governor’s office); and AB 1349, which targets “ghost tickets” sold by resellers, signed Sept 27. Newsom asked Bryan to revisit its exemptions for some sellers (LA Times). Also signed Sept 27: AB 1573 on housing element target populations, AB 2162 on county housing funds for nonminor dependents and young adults, and AB 1646 on visits at juvenile facilities, with Asm. Mark González as joint lead author (Governor’s Sept 27 update). AB 1655, on CalWORKs aid during a parent’s immigration detention, was signed Sept 29 (Governor’s office).
  • Vetoed Sept 30, 2026: AB 1537, barring California peace officers from side jobs in immigration enforcement (see Key moments) (veto message).
  • Signed Sept 30, 2026: AB 2599, requiring corporate disclosure of ties to slavery (LA Sentinel; Alliance for Reparations, Reconciliation, and Truth, via IBW21); AB 1883 on workplace surveillance tools, with a signing message (Governor’s office); and two he co-led, AB 1645 (the HUGS Act on prison visits, led by Asm. Mark González) and AB 2204 (organized sports in prisons, led by Asm. Jesse Gabriel) (Governor’s Sept 30 update).

Bills, 2023-24 session. He was a lead author of the final version of 51 bills, alone or jointly; resolutions are left out. Of those, 26 became law, 6 were vetoed and 19 did not pass (bill data). His laws include AB 2716 on low-production oil wells in the Baldwin Hills and AB 1986 on banned books in state prisons. He was a joint lead author of AB 1, collective bargaining for legislative staff (led by Asm. Tina McKinnor); AB 3089, a formal state apology for slavery (led by Asm. Reggie Jones-Sawyer); and AB 2602 on contracts for digital replicas of performers (led by Asm. Ash Kalra).
