s01965:
原创 纳粹抢走的传世名画现身美国，犹太后代起诉博物馆还回来，被拒

2026-09-20 16:04 来源: 云景史记

发布于：河南省

大规模暴行幸存者后代起诉加州博物馆，要求归还纳粹掠夺艺术品。“我们很荣幸代表社区承担这一角色，并将大部分收益用于帮助这些年迈的幸存者。”

犹太人大规模遇害事件的代表及后代近日在加州提起两起诉讼，要求追回目前由奥斯威辛纪念馆和洛杉矶地区知名文化机构收藏的、曾遭纳粹掠夺的画作。这起法律行动，是在美国近期出台州级和联邦立法，加强二战期间犹太家庭被掠文化财产追索权之后发生的。

其中一起诉讼于周一在洛杉矶高级法院提起。大洛杉矶犹太人联合会及其董事会主席丹尼尔·格里茨曼起诉位于帕萨迪纳的诺顿·西蒙博物馆，要求归还老卢卡斯·克拉纳赫于1530年创作的两幅真人大小的木板油画《亚当与夏娃》。

另一起诉讼同日提交至洛杉矶联邦法院。已故大规模迫害幸存者、曾被囚于奥斯威辛的加州动画师迪娜·戈特利博娃·巴比特的女儿们，要求交还一批水彩肖像画。

巴比特是在纳粹医生约瑟夫·门格勒的胁迫下创作这些画作的。门格勒因其残酷的人体实验而被称为“死亡天使”，这些肖像描绘的是与她一同被囚禁的人。诺顿·西蒙博物馆声称对相关画作拥有合法所有权，并计划继续公开展出。奥斯威辛纪念馆则认为，相关水彩画应继续留在纪念馆内。诉状未透露这些作品的具体估值。

围绕纳粹掠夺艺术品的争议，将承受代际创伤的犹太家庭后代与试图保存这一黑暗历史时期物证的文化机构置于对立面。在1933年至1945年之间，纳粹政权实施了历史上规模最大的掠夺行动，从欧洲各地的犹太业主、收藏家和公共机构手中夺走了超过60万件艺术品。

数十年后，许多作品仍陈列在世界各地的机构中，使得归还工作远不只是一般意义上的所有权争端。荷兰犹太艺术品商雅克·古德斯蒂克的唯一继承人玛蕾·冯·萨赫尔，已将其法律权利转让给大洛杉矶犹太人联合会。该联合会由主席兼首席执行官诺亚·法卡斯领导。

这两幅木板画曾被阿道夫·希特勒的副手赫尔曼·戈林从古德斯蒂克的藏品中夺走，随后几经转手，最终于20世纪60年代由帕萨迪纳现代艺术博物馆购得。该馆后来以主要资助人之名更名为诺顿·西蒙博物馆。

法卡斯表示，联合会计划将追回款项中的大部分净收益，用于帮助居住在洛杉矶地区约2500名大屠杀幸存者。法卡斯说：“这些是极其精美的欧洲艺术杰作。它们从一个犹太家庭手中被盗，用来充实纳粹党，并资助针对人民的战争和死亡机器。”

他说：“我们很荣幸代表社区承担这一角色，并将大部分收益用于帮助这些年迈的幸存者，让他们在生命最后几年享有尊严、安适与平静——而这些正是他们的家人在那场浩劫期间被剥夺的。”玛蕾·冯·萨赫尔在一份声明中感谢该组织支持其家族的法律诉讼。她表示：“这项努力是为大屠杀幸存者及纳粹时代暴行受害者寻求正义的重要一步。”

加州民主党州众议员杰西·加布里埃尔起草了第2867号议会法案，加州州长加文·纽森于2024年9月签署该法案。该法案规定，在加州居民或其继承人试图追回大规模迫害期间被掠夺艺术品的案件中，应适用加州法律。

加布里埃尔担任加州立法机构犹太人党团联合主席。他起草该法案的背景是，一项联邦裁决允许西班牙马德里国有的提森-博内米萨国家博物馆保留法国印象派画家卡米耶·毕沙罗的一件珍贵作品。该作品1939年被纳粹当局从卡西雷尔家族手中没收。促成此次立法修订的相关诉讼，计划于下月在加州联邦法院开庭审理。

加布里埃尔表示，公共机构应当“认真反思，自己是否愿意站在历史正确的一边”。诺顿·西蒙博物馆回应称，2018年一项联邦法院裁决一致确认，该馆对克拉纳赫画作享有合法所有权。美国联邦最高法院于2019年5月拒绝审查下级法院的裁决。

博物馆称，这两幅克拉纳赫作品最初属于斯特罗加诺夫家族，1931年在柏林一次未经授权的苏联出售中，古德斯蒂克购得这些画作。经过复杂的流转后，斯特罗加诺夫家族的一名后代将作品出售给该馆，博物馆随后对其进行了保存和修复。博物馆表示：“近50年来，这些作品一直在诺顿·西蒙博物馆展出，未来数年仍将继续向公众开放。”

奥斯威辛纪念馆代表帕维尔·萨维茨基表示，巴比特在胁迫下创作的罗姆人囚犯水彩肖像，记录了门格勒非法进行的医学实验和种族研究，“必须留在纪念馆内”，作为暴行的证据。

萨维茨基表示，这些作品不应被归类为“纳粹掠夺艺术品”，因为创作者当时作为囚犯是在胁迫下作画，并不具备严格法律意义上的所有权。萨维茨基承认，这家人与作品有着深厚联系。但他强调，这些罗姆人和辛提人受害者的肖像，是记载门格勒恐怖实验的罕见留存资料，必须作为奥斯威辛特有的历史文物得到保护。

萨维茨基说：“我们完全尊重创作此处部分文件者的权利，但我们认为，纪念馆馆藏的任何损失都将造成无法弥补的伤害。即使失去哪怕最小一部分记录，都是无法弥补的损失，也会损害对奥斯威辛受害者的纪念。”

费城地区非营利组织“艺术灰烬”创始人乔尔·格林伯格表示，除加州法律外，美国总统唐纳德·特朗普还签署并更新了2025年《大规模暴行被掠夺艺术品追索法》。 这项立法永久取消了诉讼时效限制，使幸存者及其继承人能够无限期追索艺术品。

格林伯格解释说，联邦法律修订后，家庭从确认其财产现持有人之日起，有6年时间寻求法律追偿。他说：“这些新法律意味着技术性抗辩将不再能在法庭上成立。每一个案件都将依其事实和案情获得审理。”他补充说，修订后的法律框架确保犹太家庭获得程序上的公平，并有机会在法庭上陈述其所有权主张。

格林伯格说：“这将确保欧洲犹太人曾经遭遇的一切不会被遗忘。这些艺术品仍有可能归还给合法所有人。” 这些艺术品仍有可能归还给合法所有人。

Familiares de personas judías que sobrevivieron al Holocausto han presentado en días recientes dos demandas en California con las que argumentan que son los dueños legítimos de varias piezas de arte que fueron saqueadas o robadas por los nazis y ahora están en museos.

Las demandas responden a una ley aprobada en California en 2024 y a una ley federal estadounidense votada en 2025.

La ley estatal facilita presentar estos reclamos a descendientes de sobrevivientes. Mientras que la ley federal eliminó el plazo, originalmente previsto para diciembre de este año, en el que se permitía a personas que sobrevivieron el Holocausto y después se asentaron en Estados Unidos, o a sus allegados, hacer tales reclamos civiles por propiedad que les quitaron entre 1933 y 1945. Ahora el plazo, en vez de ser una fecha fija, es de seis años después de enterarse de en dónde está la pieza que vinculan a sus familiares.

Las demandas fueron presentadas por separado, aunque ambas en cortes de Los Ángeles. Una es en contra del museo Norton Simon, en Pasadena, y la otra es contra el Museo de Auschwitz-Birkenau. Por su parte, ambos museos argumentan que las obras merecen seguir en exhibición al público.

Retratos en acuarela

La disputa con el museo de Auschwitz-Birkenau Memorial, erigido en remembranza donde era el campo de concentración y exterminio, es por una serie de retratos hechos con acuarela por Dinah Gottliebova Babbitt de compañeros en cautiverio.

Sus hijas están demandando porque dicen que su madre siempre quiso recuperar las pinturas, que fue forzada a hacer por el nazi Joseph Mengele (apodado El ángel de la muerte por sus experimentos sádicos con los prisioneros de Auschwitz).

Las pintó, según las hijas de Gottliebova Babbit, “con la condición de que ella y su madre fueran eximidas de las cámaras de gas”, pero que “Mengele le quitó los retratos” después, y ella “nunca los vendió, asignó, transfirió ni cedió de manera voluntaria”.

“La pertenencia que reclama el museo es por transacciones y actos posguerra mediante personas que no tenían derecho legal a las acuarelas”, denuncia la demanda, según consigna The New York Times.

El museo de Auschwitz Memorial dice que técnicamente las acuarelas no consisten de arte que haya sido saqueado por los nazis, porque Gottlieva Babitt los pintó ya siendo prisionera por lo que la pertenencia está más en tela de duda. “Comprendemos que hay un vínculo emocional de la familia a estas obras que Dina Gottliebova hizo por órdenes de Josef Mengele en circunstancias en que su vida se vio afectada”, dijo Paweł Sawicki, portavoz del museo.

Agregó que “los retratos de víctimas gitanas rom son de los pocos restos de documentos hechos por Mengele como parte de sus experimentos criminales”, y en tanto “deben permanecer” en el museo porque son “documentos relacionados a la historia de Auschwitz que pintan un recuerdo de sus víctimas”.

Un pedazo de ‘restitución’

La otra demanda apunta al museo Norton Simon, donde yace la obra Adán y Eva de Lucas Carnach el Viejo, artista renacentista conocido por escenas bíblicas y retratos de figuras como Martín Lutero.

El díptico fue una de varias piezas que el segunda mano de Hitler, Hermann Göring, le quitó al mercader de arte neerlandés Jacques Goudstikker.

La colección de Goudstikker después fue recuperada por las fuerzas aliadas, que le dieron las obras al Gobierno posguerra de Países Bajos. El díptico de Adán y Eva luego fue vendido al museo Norton Simon en 1971.

La demanda argumenta que otras partes de la colección de Goudstikker ya han sido recuperadas por la heredera del hombre, Marei von Saher, y que le correspondería obtener también el díptico, que la mujer ha estado pidiendo al Norton Simon por años.

En 2018, Von Saher había demandado de manera directa para conseguir Adán y Eva, aunque un tribunal falló a favor del museo Norton Simon. En esta ocasión la demanda al respecto fue presentada por la Jewish Federation of Los Angeles, a la que Von Saher le cedió el derecho de obtener el díptico con la condición de que después sea vendido y los fondos utilizados para “cuidar a sobrevivientes del Holocausto en el área de LA que viven en la pobreza”.

Volver a obtener la obra sería “un pedazo del rompecabezas para la restitución del legado de mi abuelo y de su colección”, dijo Charlène von Saher, hija de Marei, al diario Los Angeles Times.

La Fundación de Arte Norton Simon dijo en un comunicado que el museo tiene los títulos de propiedad apropiados sobre la obra, y que un tribunal federal lo había establecido así en 2018. La fundación agregó que Adán y Eva “han estado en exhibición por más de 50 años en el museo y seguirán siendo accesibles ahí al público por muchos años”.

Un historial complejo

Las recientes leyes de California y del Congreso estadounidense sobre reclamos de arte posiblemente robada responden a un caso similar.

Ese caso se centró en una obra maestra del impresionista Camille Pissarro que muestra una escena cotidiana en París y fue pintada en 1897.

En 2022, un tribunal federal en Estados Unidos determinó que el Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza, en Madrid, tendría el título de propiedad sobre la obra, que originalmente colgaba en el hogar de la familia Cassirer en 1939.

Los nazis le dijeron a Lilly Cassirer Neubauer que la única manera en que iba a poder salir de Alemania era si les cedía la pintura, y a cambio le permitirían obtener visas para ella y su esposo. Un tasador de arte presentó documentos según los cuales los Cassirer presuntamente habían conseguido 360 dólares a cambio de la pintura. Hoy en día, se estima que el cuadro Rue Saint-Honoré por la tarde con efecto de lluvia vale unos 20 millones de dólares.

El nieto de Lilly Cassirer, Claude, vive en Los Ángeles. Con la nueva ley de California ha revivido el caso, y la Corte Suprema de Estados Unidos ordenó a tribunales federales que volvieran a revisar su previo fallo. La audiencia al respecto está prevista para octubre.

La ley en California fue impulsada por el asambleísta Jesse Gabriel, que dijo a The Associated Press que es momento de que museos alrededor del mundo “hagan actos de introspección sobre si quieren estar en el lado correcto de la historia”.

The central question in a new lawsuit against Pasadena's Norton Simon Museum is whether Marei von Saher can revive her claim to two Renaissance panels after earlier federal litigation failed. The Jewish Federation of Los Angeles filed the case on September 14 in L.A. Superior Court, seeking recovery of Lucas Cranach the Elder's Adam and Eve, a roughly 500-year-old diptych that Nazi forces seized from Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker's Amsterdam gallery in 1940.

The federation acted with von Saher's authorization and says it will use most of the net proceeds to support impoverished Holocaust survivors living in the Los Angeles area, according to LAist. Goudstikker died in an accident while fleeing the German invasion of the Netherlands in May 1940, and Nazi air force commander Hermann Göring personally seized more than 800 works from his gallery, including the Cranach panels, which Göring later displayed at his Carinhall estate near Berlin, according to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency.

The Norton Simon Museum has not disputed that the artwork was originally looted by the Nazis, the LAist report notes. Instead, the museum's foundation maintains it holds proper title to the diptych, pointing to the painting's chain of ownership after the war.

A Twisting Chain of Title After the War

The Dutch government sold the Adam and Eve panels in 1966 for 60,000 guilders to Prince George Stroganoff-Scherbatoff, an exiled Russian aristocrat who claimed the Bolshevik government had illegally confiscated the works from his family during the 1917 Russian Revolution, according to The Art Newspaper. Industrialist Norton Simon then bought the 6-foot-tall panels from Stroganoff-Scherbatoff in 1971 for $800,000, placing them on public display at the Pasadena museum that now carries his name, per the same account.

Von Saher first sued the Norton Simon Museum in federal court back in 2007. That case ended in 2016 when U.S. District Judge John F. Walter ruled the museum held proper title because Goudstikker's estate had missed post-war Dutch filing deadlines, a decision the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed in 2018, according to Courthouse News. The Ninth Circuit went further that same year, ruling that a court could not declare the sale illegal simply because a foreign government had carried it out, and the U.S. Supreme Court later declined to hear the case, leaving that ruling standing, per LAist.

The broader Goudstikker collection has already seen a measure of justice. In 2006, the Dutch government returned 202 other artworks from the collection to von Saher under a national restitution policy reform, which led to a landmark Christie's New York auction where the recovered Old Master works sold for more than $100 million, the Art Newspaper reported.

A New California Law Reopens the Door

The new filing relies on a 2024 California law that allows petitions to recover cultural property taken or otherwise lost through political persecution, per LAist. Governor Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 2867 in September 2024, directing that California substantive law apply in state claims involving property stolen through political persecution and creating a route for certain previously dismissed Nazi-looted-art cases to be brought again, according to the Office of Governor Gavin Newsom.

What AB 2867 Changes — and What It Does Not

AB 2867 does not reopen every previously dismissed property case. According to the bill text, a cause of action dismissed on specified grounds may be brought again within two years of the law's effective date or the entry of final judgment and termination of all appeals, whichever is later. The timing rule supplies a procedural opportunity to refile; the new case still presents the underlying title dispute for adjudication.

The Cranach case also differs from other restitution disputes in both the artwork and the legal history. The Los Angeles Times reported that von Saher secured the return of more than 200 other Goudstikker paintings from the Netherlands in 2006, distinguishing that restitution from the still-contested diptych. Separately, Claude Cassirer sued the Thyssen-Bornemisza Collection and Spain in 2005 over Camille Pissarro's painting held in Madrid, a claim involving a different family, work and foreign collection, according to the same newspaper.

Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel introduced the bill specifically in response to a January 2024 Ninth Circuit ruling that allowed a Spanish museum to keep Camille Pissarro's Rue Saint-Honoré in the Afternoon, Effect of Rain, a painting the Jewish Cassirer family had surrendered under Nazi duress in 1939, according to the Los Angeles Times. Under California substantive law, a thief cannot convey valid legal title to stolen property no matter how much time has passed, a standard that stands in contrast to European legal doctrines allowing possessory title transfers or administrative cutoffs, according to Courthouse News.

The lawsuit names the Norton Simon Museum and two related foundations as defendants, per LAist. Rabbi Noah Farkas said the suit seeks to reverse an injustice caused by the Nazi theft of a Jewish family's property, while Joel Greenberg said the museum does not have good title and that retaining the art is immoral and unethical, LAist reported.

Part of a Wider Wave of Claims

The Pasadena case was filed the same week as another major California lawsuit, brought by the daughters of Auschwitz survivor Dina Gottliebova Babbitt against the Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum over watercolors she was forced to paint for Nazi doctor Josef Mengele, according to the Los Angeles Times. Both filings arrive as California's statutory window for reviving dismissed claims edges closer to closing.

Court filings and art-market valuations place Cranach's diptych at roughly $24 million, with the artist's work having sold for millions of dollars at auction, according to the Jewish Journal. The case echoes another well-known restitution fight, in which Maria Altmann recovered a Gustav Klimt work the Nazis had looted from her family in Austria, per LAist.

The dispute also lands amid other ongoing restitution battles Hoodline has followed, including a 16th-century painting tied to Göring loot sitting unresolved at a Boston museum. For now, the Norton Simon Art Foundation says it has proper title to Adam and Eve, setting up another lengthy legal test of whether California's new statute can succeed where a decade of federal litigation could not.

Toxics off the table rally: We won't let Big Food do to our democracy what it has done to our diet

Ken gives opening remarks at rally against industry-backed bill

Ken Cook

Sep 17, 2026

On September 15, EWG hosted the “Toxics off the table!” rally in Washington, D.C., to call on lawmakers to oppose the FRESH Act- an industry-backed bill that would make it easier for companies to add new chemicals to our food with less government oversight and erase hundreds of state food safety laws that protect families from toxic ingredients.

Sign our petition here: https://act.ewg.org/7vTW0NMIQkyucQ6wVRE8qg2

Below are Ken’s opening remarks at the rally:

Hello everyone. Thank you for coming.

I’m Ken Cook with Environmental Working Group. Welcome to the Toxics off the table Rally.

So many amazing food movement leaders here today—here from Congress, state legislatures, nonprofits, the academy, the private sector.

Those of you who know me know I am not one to court controversy. But I want to start by acknowledging the food movement leader who by all rights should be here today. A leader who has done more than anyone in Washington to set us on course to fight chronic disease and obesity by insisting that food is medicine, especially for our kids. A leader who has championed the idea that it is a central duty of government to ensure that our kids get fresh food. Clean food. Real food.

That leader could not be here in person today, but we know you are here in spirit…Michelle Obama.

We are here today united in the cause of stopping something very wrong from happening up on that Hill behind us. We are going to stop Big Food’s FRESH Act from ever becoming the law of the land. And today, an amazing cross section of food movement leaders will tell you in shocking detail exactly why it is essential that we stand our ground.

But first, let me put a positive spin on this rally. Because we wouldn’t be here to stop something wrong if we hadn’t been doing somethings right with our food system to make America healthy. This was well before anyone said we needed to make America healthy again.

If dozens of state legislatures of every color—red, blue and purple--are following the lead California established in 2023—banning or labeling sketchy food ingredients and additives, taking on Big Food’s biggest profit center—the scourge of ultra-processed food, we must be doing something right.

State government has long been seen as the laboratory of democracy. Lately it’s been the kitchen.

It all started with a dad who happened to be a member of the California Assembly, who insisted that his kids, and all kids, deserved clean healthy food. That dad stands here to fight alongside us today.

California Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel.

Think about it. We have California governor Gavin Newsom and Texas Governor Greg Abbot signing laws to clean up the food in their states.

Jesse, we must be doing something right.

If Democratic governor Katie Hobbs in Arizona and Republican Governor Patrick Morrisey of West Virginia are signing food reform bills, we must be doing something right.

Food reform bills are moving in state after state—we map them all on the EWG web site and it’s hard to keep up. There’s an important food reform bill sitting on New York Governor Kathy Hochul’s desk right now.

Are we going to do a lot more? You’re damn right we are. We are not tired of winning. Not tired here in America—not tired around the world. Because this is a global movement.

That’s right. The food companies that that compromised and degraded our diets for profit want to do the very same thing to our democracy—for profit.

There’s no hiding your anti-democratic ambitions behind your front group, Americans for Ingredient Transparency. We’re calling food companies and their brands by name. www.ewg.org/bigfood

Newsom’s deference and an AI proxy war

DRIVING THE DAY — Gavin Newsom is giving Kamala Harris the right of first refusal in the 2028 presidential race, telling CNN’s Jake Tapper that he would not run if Harris launched another bid for the White House. As Melanie writes, they were Newsom’s most definitive comments yet about a potential collision of ambitions with his fellow Californian.

Newsom cast his thinking in politically strategic, not sentimental, terms, suggesting it would benefit every other primary candidate if they did compete. “First of all, electorally, it’s a gift from God for everybody else. They can enjoy the hell out of it. Mutually assured destruction. It services no greater good,” Newsom said.

RACE AGAINST ROBOTS — The race to succeed Nancy Pelosi is suddenly turning into a proxy fight over the Democratic Party’s approach to regulating AI amid escalating warnings about the dire risks of advanced models.

Scott Wiener, a prominent state senator and the front-runner in the race, has been one of the most prolific authors of AI safety regulations in the country. But Pelosi’s preferred successor, Supervisor Connie Chan, is now scrambling to outflank him on the issue, arguing his proposals do not go far enough and repeatedly hitting Wiener for Anthropic’s $500,000 contribution to an outside PAC supporting him.

“Scott Wiener has been saying that he’s been writing AI legislation. But we know who’s writing it with him, and it’s people like AI companies, Anthropic,” Chan told Playbook. “The effective guardrail is actually preventing the industry to develop any further, and so that they (cannot) create damage that we cannot recover from.”

Chan hasn’t gone as far as endorsing a national pause on advanced AI models or a ban on superintelligence, as some progressives like Sen. Bernie Sanders propose. But she wants to require that labor unions — who she’s closely aligned with — be involved in AI deployment decisions, and she’s called for an “immediate moratorium” on all data center projects across the country.

Wiener has taken a more measured approach, calling on AI companies to slow development until safety guardrails are enacted. He and his supporters say Chan’s positions are vague and unrealistic, arguing that Congress can make AI safer without killing innovation in a sector that has fueled San Francisco and Silicon Valley’s economic recovery.

“That is not actual constructive policy, that is political grandstanding,” Wiener told Playbook, referring to Chan’s more hardline approach. “She has all sorts of hot takes now. Some of us have actually been working on this issue for years.”

Wiener’s policy platform also calls for a host of accountability measures — including the creation of a new federal AI regulatory agency, minimum safety standards for advanced models, whistleblower protections and “steep fines” for companies that don’t comply — though he doesn’t call for an outright pause on AI development or bans on data centers. Instead, Wiener wants to require data center developers to show their projects won’t harm water supplies or raise electricity bills.

The contrast between Wiener and Chan comes as polling suggests that voters across the country are increasingly skeptical of AI and data center development — and amid high-profile calls from AI leaders to slow down. The race in San Francisco, home to much of the AI sector, will test how much anti-AI sentiment resonates with an electorate on the front line of the technology’s development.

“Wiener’s positions resonate with voters here because they’re more up to speed and they’re more knowledgeable about the benefits, as well as the dangers,” said Sam Singer, a veteran San Francisco consultant who works for a PAC that supports Wiener.

Tensions over AI have been heightened as Pelosi campaigns hard for Chan and hosts multiple Washington fundraisers on her behalf. Pelosi was a vocal opponent of SB 1047, Wiener’s 2024 proposal that aimed to set a first-in-the-nation standard for AI safety regulations, including a “kill switch” requirement for large models that could behave dangerously.

Pelosi, at the time, sided with prominent venture capitalists, including Ron Conway and Marc Andreessen, in opposing the bill. Newsom vetoed it, and Wiener’s allies argued Pelosi’s opposition was an effort to undercut him amid rumblings that he was preparing to run for her seat.

“While Washington sat on its hands, Scott began fighting the AI corporations to adopt strong safety regulations,” Joe Arellano, a spokesperson for Wiener, told Playbook.

Last year, Wiener succeeded in passing SB 53, a scaled back AI-safety law that requires major companies to reveal their safety protocols. But Wiener has recently invoked SB 1047 to criticize Pelosi, arguing that the U.S. would be more prepared for escalating concerns about AI dangers had the bill become law.

Wiener’s criticism came after Pelosi and a host of her allies in Congress, including Rep. Zoe Lofgren, released a letter chiding him for launching an AI-powered chatbot to mimic Chan. (Pelosi called the chatbot offensive, and Wiener eventually took it down).

Chan has in recent days dismissed Wiener’s criticism of her chief supporter, saying, “I’m not Nancy Pelosi.” Chan questions SB 1047’s significance, arguing that her proposals would go further by not allowing dangerous AI models to be developed in the first place. She also argues that SB 1047 wouldn’t have included some potentially dangerous models because its regulations would only have applied to larger models.

“Our approach to AI, clearly, is very people-centered,” Chan said. “We’re going to bring unions to the table. It means that we want human oversights.”

WHO WON THE DAY? Kamala Harris. For whatever else people are reading into Newsom’s remarks, he appeared to be handing her the keys.

WHERE’S GAVIN? Signing more bills.

EDUCATION — FUNDING FIGHT — The California Teachers Association is taking Newsom to court over a maneuver in this year’s budget deal that withholds $3.9 billion in funding for public schools that the state is using temporarily as a loan to other parts of the budget. The powerful labor union, which is no stranger to publicly feuding with the governor over the budget, plans to announce a lawsuit today over the deferral that they have argued “ignores the state constitution.”

A broad coalition of education groups, including teachers unions and administrative groups, campaigned to oppose Newsom’s deferral plan that lawmakers ultimately approved. The funding, the school groups argue, is critical to help several school districts pay off large contracts they signed this year with teachers amid a wave of labor tension and strike threats across the state. Department of Finance officials have defended the deferral as necessary to “mitigate against potential future reductions in revenues” as the state stares down years of projected budget deficits. — Eric He

HEALTH — FIRST IN PLAYBOOK: JUNK FOOD JUNKET — Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel will appear in Washington today alongside congressional Democrats to drum up opposition to a piece of draft legislation he says would be “a slap in the face to the MAHA movement.”

A food industry-backed draft by Florida Republican Rep. Kat Cammack known as the FRESH and Affordable Foods Act would preempt state food regulations and overhaul how ingredients are reviewed in the U.S.

“The industry understands that it’s losing. It’s losing in blue states like California. It’s losing in red states,” he said. “So now they’re going to go to Congress and try to preempt all that.”

The MAHA-backed push to regulate ultraprocessed foods has been met with fierce opposition in D.C. from industry groups like the Consumer Brands Association, who also pushed back against several of Gabriel’s UPF-focused efforts. The group that represents household names like Doritos and Kraft Mac & Cheese has thrown its weight behind Cammack’s proposal and is part of a group spending big in the midterms to back candidates that support their ideas.

While HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. hasn’t weighed in on Cammack’s proposal, it would undo regulations he has largely encouraged states to pursue.

“If Republican leadership lets that proposal get traction, it tells you everything you need to know about where they really stand,” Gabriel said. — Nicole Norman

CALIFORNIA CURRENTS — WAIVER WALKTHROUGH — The Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to dismantle California’s unique authority to write its own emissions standards represent a fight that is as critical as it is wonky. With that in mind, California Currents has a guide to the battle that will likely determine whether the state can meet its ambitious climate goals.

TOP TALKERS — SLOW YOUR ROLL — Harris joined calls to slow down the pace of artificial intelligence development, warning Monday that the technology could “escape human control” without stronger safeguards. “The frontier of artificial intelligence is advancing at an alarming speed,” the former vice president said in a statement on X, arguing that slowing the development of the most advanced AI systems doesn’t mean giving up on the potential “life-saving benefits in fields like medicine.”

SKID ROW TROUBLES — The largest provider of housing for formerly homeless residents in Los Angeles’ Skid Row area has warned city officials it is running out of money and will collapse unless it receives more public funding or other assistance, its leader told Liam Dillon. The prospect of SRO Housing’s failure puts thousands of the city’s most vulnerable tenants at risk and creates a significant new problem for Mayor Karen Bass.

Gym Memberships, Farmers Market Ties and MMA Fighters Helped Secure Millions in Newsom’s Final Budget

By: HSJC Newsroom

Date:

September 15, 2026

California lawmakers wrapped up this year’s state budget with the usual flurry of last-minute deals — but tucked inside the massive spending package was something far less visible to the public: roughly $1.3 billion in earmarks steered to pet projects in individual legislators’ districts, decided largely behind closed doors.

The list of beneficiaries ranges widely. Senate President Pro Tem Monique Limón, a Santa Barbara Democrat, secured $29 million to renovate a college gym in her district. Marin County, where Gov. Gavin Newsom lives, landed $13 million for a farmers market and food innovation center. And in Santa Clara County, $3 million will go toward fixing up the ballpark used by the San Jose Giants minor league team.

These kinds of targeted allocations — often called earmarks or “pork-barrel” spending — aren’t new to California politics, and they show up even in years when the state is grappling with massive deficits. They let individual lawmakers claim credit for bringing home money to their communities. But the process by which the money gets divvied up remains largely hidden from public view, drawing criticism even from some legislators who benefit from it.

“It is done all behind closed doors,” said Julie Baker, CEO of California for the Arts. “It is somewhat inequitable … to have a grant-making process that everyone’s competing over and then have a process that’s non-transparent.”

The mechanics are straightforward, if opaque. Assembly and Senate leadership — both controlled by Democrats — set rough spending limits and invite members to privately submit wish lists. Then, just days before the Legislature adjourns for the year, the requests materialize as line items in a budget bill, leaving almost no time for public review. Lawmakers’ names typically aren’t attached to specific requests, making it difficult to trace who asked for what.

This year, Limón set an informal cap of roughly $5 million per senator, according to Sen. Dave Cortese, a San Jose Democrat who ultimately secured $6.5 million in earmarks for his district. Cortese said lawmakers generally don’t share their requests with one another ahead of time — at least not until they’re ready to announce the funding publicly.

“It’s a confidential process between each office and leadership,” Cortese told CalMatters.

Even so, he acknowledged the process could use more sunlight. “Why couldn’t we do this process a little earlier and get our requests into subcommittees so the public could just see what’s going on?” he said. “There’s nothing to be ashamed of here.”

Money flows to the powerful

The bulk of this year’s earmark funding flowed to urban, Democratic-controlled areas — particularly Los Angeles and San Francisco — along with districts represented by legislative leadership. Republican-held districts, by contrast, generally received little or nothing. At least 17 counties, most of them rural and represented by GOP lawmakers, appear to have gotten no earmark funding at all this year.

“The leadership decides the major portions of the budget,” said Sen. Roger Niello, a Roseville Republican and vice chair of the Senate Budget Committee. “That is frustrating, but it is the system that we have.”

A CalMatters review of Assembly Bill 113, the budget measure containing the earmarks, found that more than $550 million — about 42% of the total identified — went to nonprofits and other non-governmental organizations. That includes at least $93 million for arts programs, museums and murals, along with funding for immigration services, land conservation, and housing and homelessness programs. The remainder went largely to city and county governments for infrastructure work such as parks, pools, wildfire prevention and road repairs.

CalMatters requested detailed funding lists from Newsom, Limón, Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas and more than 20 other lawmakers. Most declined to provide them. Newsom, Rivas and Limón would not discuss individual projects but each issued general statements defending the practice.

A spokesperson for Newsom, Tara Gallegos, said the spending will “make a lasting, meaningful difference in communities across California,” touting investments in natural resources, recreation, the arts and food access.

Supporters argue the earmarks let lawmakers respond quickly to local needs without forcing communities through lengthy state grant applications — and that the total amount is a tiny fraction of California’s $352 billion budget.

“My message to (state agencies) is, ‘You guys take the other 99.9% and leave this fraction of a percent to us,’” Cortese said. “I’ll help target some real need in these districts that you are never going to see in an office in Sacramento.”

Not everyone is convinced. Critics point out that lawmakers found room for $1.3 billion in local pet projects even as the state struggles to offset deep federal cuts to healthcare. This year’s budget leaned on an unexpected windfall tied to the AI industry boom, some tax hikes, and delayed payments to schools and reserve funds to avoid immediate healthcare cuts — pushing tougher decisions into next year.

“They’ve said, ‘Look … there’s no extra money to spend,’ and then a half billion dollars comes out in the last 48 hours of the session,” said Geoff Green, CEO of CalNonprofits, which represents thousands of California nonprofit organizations. “For entities that were working through what we considered normal processes through the entirety of the session, to then see this come out at the last second, it feels like, well, why did I spend all that time and energy?”

Susan Shelley, vice president of communications for the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, was blunter still, suggesting lawmakers were rewarding allies at taxpayer expense. “From a taxpayer perspective, we don’t have the money for this,” she said.

From MMA fighters to museums

The single largest allocation this year — $125 million — will help convert the shuttered Golden Gate Fields horse racing track in Alameda County into a public park, a priority championed by Newsom along with Assembly Appropriations Chair Buffy Wicks and Senate Housing Chair Jesse Arreguín, both Oakland Democrats.

Some funding went to organizations with deep-pocketed existing backers. UC Berkeley’s Innovative Genomics Institute, located in Wicks and Arreguín’s districts, received $25 million despite counting the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, the Li Ka Shing Foundation and the U.S. Department of Defense among its funders.

Other notable earmarks include $20 million toward a new facility for San Francisco’s Jewish Family and Children’s Services Holocaust Center, which is backed by dozens of foundations (though its executive director says endowments cover only about 2% of its budget); $15 million to renovate police and firefighter memorials at Sacramento’s Capitol Park; and $1 million to help fund the state’s newly created retirement program for mixed martial arts fighters, which is otherwise supported through ticket sales and specialty license plates.

Roughly $86 million went toward arts organizations, museums and performance groups — with more than 40% of that landing in San Francisco alone. Recipients included $3 million for the ODC Dance Company, whose founder was inducted into the California Hall of Fame by Newsom and his former wife, Jennifer Siebel Newsom; $2.8 million for the Center for the Art of Translation, which counts Bloomberg Philanthropies among its supporters; and $400,000 for the San Francisco Mime Troupe. San Francisco-area lawmakers contacted by CalMatters either denied requesting the funds or did not respond to inquiries about who did.

Green, of CalNonprofits, worries the system favors organizations with the best political connections rather than the greatest need. “The capacity of a large, well-staffed institute to access resources is just a completely different universe than a smaller, volunteer, community-based organization in some more rural parts of the state,” he said.

Familiar names, familiar funding

For Cortese, relationships play an explicit role in his decision-making. Of the groups he sponsored for funding this year, only one nonprofit, Ashes to Beauty, was new to him; the rest are organizations he’s worked with since his time on the San Jose City Council in the 2000s.

“If some new group came along and they seemed hopeful … but I didn’t know of them very well, I hadn’t seen their work too much in the community, I’m probably not going to entrust them with $1 million or $800,000,” he said. “It’s not a matter of any kind of favoritism.”

Cortese’s earmarks this year included $2.1 million for First Tee Silicon Valley, which teaches golf and leadership skills to at-risk youth; $2.6 million for the environmental nonprofit Our City Forest; and $1 million for the immigration services group Amigos de Guadalupe.

Several earmarks this year benefited organizations with personal ties to Newsom. The Redwood High School Foundation, tied to the governor’s alma mater, received $4 million for a capital project. Kiss the Ground, a regenerative agriculture nonprofit whose 2020 documentary featured Newsom, received $250,000.

In Los Angeles, the Alliance for Community Empowerment received nearly $3.9 million. Its founder previously served on a community advisory board for Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, an Encino Democrat who chairs the Assembly Budget Committee. Gabriel’s office did not address specific projects but said Assembly Democrats prioritized “smart, targeted, one-time investments” in healthcare, food banks, legal aid and local fire agencies.

In Sacramento, the homeless shelter City of Refuge received $1.8 million to open two new homes for children. Its co-founder is a close friend of Sen. Angelique Ashby, a Sacramento Democrat who has previously helped the organization secure state funding. A neighboring assemblymember also donated to the nonprofit from her campaign account last year. The shelter’s leader said she believes the governor’s office, which has previously visited the facility as part of anti-trafficking initiatives, may have also advocated for this year’s funding.

Sen. Lola Smallwood-Cuevas, a Los Angeles Democrat, secured $13.5 million in earmarks, including $500,000 for the Los Angeles Black Workers Center, which she co-founded before joining the Legislature. Her office said the organization is the only one of its kind serving Black workers in the region.

Geography still shapes the outcome

Los Angeles County — home to roughly a quarter of all Californians — received at least $300 million in earmarks this year, more than any other county and nearly a quarter of the statewide total. Santa Barbara County, Limón’s home turf, took in at least $72.8 million despite having a population of only about 450,000. Tulare County, with a similarly sized population but represented largely by Republicans, received just $200,000.

“Part of the power … is the ability to get benefits for the district, and it’s not surprising that the legislative leaders tend to do pretty well in that respect,” said Jack Pitney, a political science professor at Claremont McKenna College.

Limón’s district alone accounted for $83.7 million in earmarks, including the $29 million gym renovation, $6 million to rehabilitate a historic building tied to the nonprofit La Casa de la Raza, $5 million for Pershing Park improvements, $3.3 million for a community pool in Carpinteria and $3 million for a high school aquatics center.

Rivas’ Central Coast district received about $10 million, including funding for a Salinas soccer complex, a King City recreation center and arts programming in Watsonville. Sen. John Laird, a Santa Cruz Democrat who chairs the Senate Budget Committee and represents an overlapping area, secured $36.9 million for his district, including $10 million to expand public access to PG&E-owned land, funding for highway safety enforcement near Bixby Bridge, and $250,000 for a nonprofit dedicated to beaver conservation.

Gabriel’s district received at least $7 million, including money for a local YMCA, a youth filmmaking nonprofit and a family services organization.

Republican lawmakers, meanwhile, say they’re working with far less. Niello said GOP senators were limited to roughly $1 million apiece to distribute this year.

“That means that I’m not able to do enough for my district (as) Dave Cortese is for his, and we both have the same size districts,” Niello said. “Is that fair? To me, it’s not.”

Key Findings

The California election has entered its final stretch, with the governor’s race at the top of the ticket and 52 House races that will help determine the party in control of the 120th Congress. The November 3 ballot also includes 14 state propositions—five legislative measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—the most since the November 2016 election. The 2025–26 legislative session ended in late August with a flurry of bills sent to Governor Newsom to sign or veto in September. The recent trends in job growth, consumer prices, and interest rates send mixed signals about the US and California economy.

These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey on topics including the November races, legislative ballot measures, and citizens’ initiatives, as well as state and national issues that was conducted September 4–September 10, 2026:

  • Xavier Becerra (D) continues to lead Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a similarly wide margin (62% to 36%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty-five percent say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote. Fifty-eight percent say that voting is more important this year than in past midterms. After reading the ballot titles and labels, majorities would vote yes on Proposition 1 (55%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (60%; Rainy Day Fund). Three other legislative ballot measures fall short of a majority.
  • Fifty-two percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would also vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (61%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (55%; Immunology Bond), Proposition 41 (51%; Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), and Proposition 42 (54%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Partisans vary in their support for these citizens’ initiatives. Three other citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Overwhelming majorities agree that there are too many propositions on the state ballot.
  • Majorities of adults and likely voters think that the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Fifty-one percent of adults and likely voters say that they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance, while 45 percent of adults and 48 percent of likely voters approve of the state legislature. Majorities of adults and likely voters report that recent price increases have caused financial hardships for their household. Seventy percent of Californians think that the state is divided into economic groups, the haves and have-nots. Majorities of adults and likely voters say that they can trust the state government in Sacramento to do what is right “only some of the time.”
  • Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-three percent of adults and 27 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance, while 17 percent of adults and 16 percent of likely voters approve of the US Congress. Seven in ten Californians are dissatisfied with the availability of affordable health care and believe that the US government is responsible for ensuring that all Americans have access to health care. Fewer than half say the major parties have a lot or some good ideas. Overwhelming majorities say they can trust the federal government to do what is right “only some of the time.”

November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures

The top two vote-getters in the California June primary for statewide elected offices and for federal and state legislative seats are on the November ballot. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom, who is termed out of office. There are 52 House races in California that will help determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will also decide on 14 state propositions this fall—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax measures and multibillion-dollar state bonds.

Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. In our July survey, Becerra led Hilton by 25 points (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 93 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 92 percent of Republicans favor Hilton, while independents lean toward the Democratic candidate (57% Becerra, 38% Hilton). Majorities favor Becerra over Hilton across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and in the state’s major regions except for the Central Valley (46% Becerra, 52% Hilton).

Affordability and the cost of living have been the top issue on Californians’ minds in our recent polling. Sixty-five percent of likely voters say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote (30% somewhat, 5% not too important). In our February survey, the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability were very important to 61 percent of likely voters and to majorities across parties, regions, and demographic groups. Today, majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions hold this view. Notably, partisans are largely in agreement: 69 percent of Democrats, 65 percent of Republicans, and 59 percent of independents say that the gubernatorial candidates’ affordability positions are very important. Becerra supporters (66%) express this opinion as often as Hilton supporters (65%). Seven in ten or more of those who live in the Inland Empire (79%) or Los Angeles (70%), those who have incomes of $40,000 to $99,999 (74%), those who have children 18 or younger in their household (74%), Latinos (71%), renters (70%), and women (70%) say the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote.

Many Californians are watching news about the gubernatorial candidates. About six in ten likely voters say they are following news about candidates for the governor’s election either very (18%) or fairly (40%) closely. By comparison, in our May survey before the June primary, about seven in ten likely voters were very (23%) or fairly closely (48%) following the news about candidates in the governor’s election, including majorities across partisan groups (68% Democrats, 76% Republicans, 65% independents) and demographic groups and regions. Similar shares were closely following the news about candidates in the gubernatorial election in September 2018 (21% very, 41% fairly), while fewer were in September 2022 (17% very, 33% fairly), and overwhelming majorities were in September 2021 (40% very, 41% fairly) prior to the special election on the recall of Governor Newsom. Today, partisans vary in following the news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely (57% Democrats, 68% Republicans, 50% independents), as do Becerra and Hilton supporters (53% to 69%).

House Races. When asked about their House district race, most likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a wide margin (62% to 36%). Likely voter preferences were similar in July (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (64% Democrat, 35% Republican) and February (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, likely voters’ preferences for the Democratic candidate and the Republican candidate are similar in the governor’s race and the House race. More than nine in ten Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while independents say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (59% to 36%). Majorities say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district races across demographic groups and major state regions with the exception of the Central Valley (47%).

Many Californians believe that their vote matters in the 2026 midterm election. When asked about the importance of voting this year compared to past midterm elections, 58 percent of likely voters say it is more important, 39 percent say it is about as important as in past years, and only 2 percent say voting is less important to them. Californians are more likely to say that voting in the midterm is more important to them this year than they were in September 2022 (43%) and in September 2018 (52%). Today, Democratic likely voters (69%) are much more likely than Republicans (50%) and independents (45%) to say that voting in this midterm is more important this year. Majorities across the state’s regions say that voting in this midterm election is more important this year. Those who say they would vote for Democratic candidates (64%) are more likely than those supporting Republican candidates (49%) in their local House races to say that voting is more important to them this year than in past midterms.

Legislative Ballot Measures. We also gauged support for five state propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.

  • Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Fifty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute that authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 43 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (75% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 56% independents) and between homeowners and renters (49% to 72%). Half or more across the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
  • Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the state’s rainy day fund, approved by voters in 2014 to provide funding for economic downturns; 39 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (82% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 60% independents). Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 2 across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and the state’s major regions.
  • Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns). Forty-two percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute that repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 53 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (55% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 41% independents). Half or more would vote no across the state’s major regions.
  • Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Thirty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment; 59 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 5 falls short of a majority across partisan groups (40% Democrats, 34% Republicans, 28% independents) and across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
  • Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services). Forty-three percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 51 percent would vote no. Support varies across partisan groups (33% Democrats, 61% Republicans, 43% independents) and state regions (60% Central Valley; 50% Orange/San Diego; 43% Los Angeles; 35% Inland Empire; 32% San Francisco Bay Area).

When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 9 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (5% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 1% Proposition 4; 1% Proposition 5; 1% Proposition 43). In contrast, 56 percent are most interested in one of the three citizens’ initiatives: Proposition 39 (23%; Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification), Proposition 3 (17%; Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes), and Proposition 40 (16%; Imposes One-Time Tax). Partisans vary sharply in having the most interest in Proposition 39 (7% Democrats, 52% Republicans, 23% independents), Proposition 3 (26% Democrats, 3% Republicans, 14% independents), and Proposition 40 (20% Democrats, 7% Republicans, 19% independents).

Citizens’ Initiatives on the November Ballot

In addition to the five legislative measures, the November ballot includes nine citizens’ initiatives. Most likely voters agree with the statement that there are too many propositions on the state ballot (37% strongly agree, 40% somewhat). Most across demographic, partisan, and regional groups agree at least somewhat. Three in ten or more across partisan, demographic, and regional groups strongly agree with this view, with the exception of 18- to 34-year-olds (16% strongly).

Majorities of likely voters say they would vote yes (58%, 40% no) on Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes), which would make existing voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 permanent. Support for Proposition 3 varies across partisan groups. Proposition 3 garners majority support among most demographic and regional groups, but opinions are more divided among likely voters who are white (48% support), age 55 and older (46%), and reside in the Central Valley (48%).

Six in ten likely voters (61%) would vote yes on Proposition 37 (Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Home-Buyers); about one in three would vote no (35%). If passed, it would authorize $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible California residents fixed-rate mortgages of newly constructed homes below $1.5 million. Solid majorities of Democrats (76%) and independents (62%) would vote yes, compared to fewer Republicans (35%). Majorities across demographic and regional groups would vote yes.

Majorities of likely voters (55%, 42% no) support Proposition 38 (Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research. Half or more across demographic and regional groups support Proposition 38, with exceptions among likely voters who are white (46%) and those in the Central Valley (44%).

Four in ten likely voters (43%, 55% no) say they would vote yes on Proposition 39 (Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification), which would invalidate mail ballots that do not have the last four digits of a government-issued identification number written on the envelope and prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Over eight in ten Republicans (85%) are in support, compared to far fewer independents (43%) and Democrats (19%). Support falls short at half or below among most demographic and regional groups, with exceptions among those age 55 and older and residents in the Central Valley and Inland Empire (57% each).

After reading the ballot title and label, 52 percent of California likely voters say they would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax), which would impose a 5 percent tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion; 46 percent would vote no. About seven in ten Democrats (72%) would vote yes on this citizens’ initiative, compared to nearly half of independents (46%) and just two in ten Republicans (21%). The share of likely voters in support varies across demographic and regional groups, and support for Proposition 40 declines sharply as age increases.

A slim majority of likely voters would vote yes (51%, 44% no) on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1 this year that exempt their revenues from the voter-approved state spending limit and requires audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Three in four Republicans and half of independents (51%) support this proposition, compared to about four in ten Democrats (38%). Support varies across demographic and regional groups.

When it comes to Proposition 42 (Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes), which would prohibit new state taxes imposed on the ownership of personal property other than real estate, a majority of likely voters would vote yes (54%, 43% no). Partisan views vary, with three in four Republicans (74%) and six in ten independents (61%) saying they would vote yes, compared to four in ten Democrats (39%). Half or more across most demographic and regional groups are in support, but this share falls short of half among likely voters in the San Francisco Bay Area (45%), those earning under $40,000 (43%), renters (41%), and those age 18 to 34 (36%).

Just one in three likely voters in the state say they would vote yes (34%, 61% no) on Proposition 44 (Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services), which would impose penalties on nonprofit community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations that spend less than 90 percent of revenue on program services. Roughly one in three across partisan groups would vote yes, and about four in ten or fewer across demographic and regional groups are in support.

When it comes to Proposition 45 (Modifies Environmental Review)— which would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals— likely voters are divided (49% yes, 46% no). Roughly half or fewer among partisans would vote yes if the election were held today. Views vary across demographic and regional groups, with likely voters who are Latino (55%) and those earning $40,000 to $99,999 (56%) among the most likely to express support.

State of the State

Majorities of California adults (54%) and likely voters (52%) say the state is headed in the wrong direction. This belief is held by nearly all Republicans (94%) and a majority of independents (55%), compared to one in three Democrats (32%). Residents in the Central Valley (62%), the Inland Empire (62%), and Orange/San Diego (56%) are more pessimistic about the direction of the state than those in Los Angeles (48%) and the San Francisco Bay Area (46%).

Californians are much more pessimistic about economic conditions over the next year, with seven in ten adults (71%) and likely voters (73%) as well six in ten or more across parties (61% Democrats, 90% Republicans, 72% independents) expecting bad economic times for the state. About seven in ten Californians have been pessimistic about the economy since June 2025, and majorities have held this view since November 2021. Today, economic pessimism is widespread, with two in three or more across regions and demographic groups expecting bad economic times in the next year.

When asked if California is divided into two economic groups, the haves and have-nots, seven in ten adults (70%) and likely voters (69%) say the state is divided this way. When asked which economic group they are in, 55 percent of adults and 63 percent of likely voters say they are part of the haves.

About six in ten Californians and half of likely voters say recent price increases have caused financial hardship for them and their household. Findings were similar in May and over half of Californians have said price increases have caused hardship each time we’ve asked this question dating back to March 2022. Today, majorities of Democrats (55%), independents (55%), and Republicans (51%) say recent price increases have caused hardship, as do majorities across regions. Hardship declines sharply across income groups, and there are notable differences across racial/ethnic groups, with Latinos (68%) and African Americans (64%) more likely than Asian Americans (46%) and whites (52%) to say recent price increases have caused hardship.

In addition to rising prices, many Californians say the cost of housing places a financial strain on their family, with 24 percent saying a lot of strain and 20 percent saying a little strain. Views were nearly identical last December (25% a lot, 20% a little). The share saying housing costs place financial strain on their family decreases sharply with rising income (67% less than $40,000, 57% $40,000 to $99,999, 32% $100,000 or more). Majorities of African Americans (54%) and Latinos (52%) say housing costs place a strain on their finances, compared to fewer than four in ten Asian Americans (37%) and whites (36%).

Half of adults and likely voters continue to approve of the way Gavin Newsom is handling his job as governor. Approval is shaped by partisan views with most Democrats approving, while independents are divided, and nearly all Republicans disapprove. Residents in Los Angeles and the San Francisco Bay Area are more approving than those elsewhere. Majorities of African Americans, Latinos, and Asian Americans approve, while fewer whites do so.

Views of the California State Legislature are somewhat similar. Forty-five percent of adults and 48 percent of likely voters approve of the job the state legislature is doing. Partisans disagree on legislative approval with two in three Democrats approving, while nine in ten Republicans and half of independents disapprove. Across regions and demographic groups, approval is highest among San Francisco Bay Area residents (55%), college graduates (53%), Asian Americans (52%), and Latinos (51%).

When asked about trust in government, four in ten Californians say they can trust the state government in Sacramento to do what is right just about always (4%) or most of the time (36%), while six in ten say state government can be trusted only some of the time (59%). Views are nearly identical when asked about trust in local government (4% just about always, 37% most of the time, 58% only some of the time).

State of the Nation

Just two months before the consequential 2026 midterm elections, about eight in ten Californians (79% adults, 77% likely voters) think things in the nation are generally going in the wrong direction. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (80%) share this view, while about half of Republicans (52%) think the nation is going in the right direction. Overwhelming majorities across regions and demographic groups say the country is headed in the wrong direction. Californians overall are more likely to hold this pessimistic view than adults nationwide (69%), according to an August Reuters/Ipsos poll. Overwhelming majorities of Californians also expect bad economic times for the country over the next year (76% adults, 75% likely voters).

Meanwhile, about a quarter approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president (23% adults, 27% likely voters). Even fewer approve of the way Congress is handling its job (17% adults, 16% likely voters). This is a record low approval rating of Donald Trump across both his terms. Overwhelming majorities of Democrats (94%) and independents (78%) disapprove of Donald Trump; two in three Republicans (66%) approve—a significant decline from 84 percent in February 2025. Two in three or more Californians across demographic groups and regions disapprove of the president and Congress.

When asked about their level of trust in the federal government in Washington, eight in ten California adults (80%) and likely voters (83%) say they can trust it to do what is right only some of the time. In comparison, far fewer trust the federal government just about always (2% adults, 2% likely voters) or most of the time (16% adults, 13% likely voters). The overall share saying they trust the federal government only some of the time was similar last June (79%). Today, two in three or more across partisan groups, regions, and demographic groups say they trust the federal government to do what is right only some of the time.

Seven in ten Californians say they are very (41% adults, 46% likely voters) or somewhat (29% adults, 26% likely voters) dissatisfied with the availability of affordable health care in the country. Overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents are dissatisfied, including more than half of Democrats (55%) who say they are very dissatisfied. A majority of Republicans say they are satisfied (10% very, 46% somewhat). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups say they are dissatisfied.

Seven in ten adults and two in three likely voters also believe that the federal government is responsible for ensuring that all Americans have access to health care, while about three in ten believe health care access is an individual’s own responsibility. Nine in ten Democrats and seven in ten independents say ensuring access to health care is the federal government’s responsibility, while seven in ten Republicans say it is an individual’s responsibility to secure their own access to health care. Residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles are more likely than residents elsewhere in the state to say the federal government has this responsibility. Seven in ten or more African Americans (85%), Latinos (75%), and Asian Americans (71%) say ensuring access to health care is the federal government’s responsibility, compared to a smaller majority of white adults (57%). The share who views this as the federal government’s responsibility declines with rising age and income.

Four in ten Californians say the Democratic Party has a lot (11%) or some (29%) good ideas, while an additional three in ten (28%) say it has a few good ideas. About a quarter (23%) say it has almost no good ideas, and one in ten are unsure (9%). About two in three Democrats say their party has a lot or some good ideas, while two in three Republicans (66%) say the Democratic Party has almost no good ideas. African Americans and Latinos are more likely than Asian Americans and whites to say the Democratic Party has at least some good ideas.

About a quarter of California adults say the Republican Party has a lot (9%) or some (17%) good ideas, while an additional two in ten (22%) say it has a few good ideas. More than four in ten say it has almost no good ideas (44%), and one in ten are unsure (10%). Seven in ten Republicans say their party has at least some good ideas. Seven in ten Democrats and four in ten independents say the Republican Party has almost no good ideas. Across regions, residents in the Central Valley are the most likely to say the Republican Party has at least some good ideas. A majority of San Francisco Bay Area (53%) residents and nearly half of Los Angeles (48%) residents say it has almost no good ideas.

When asked about politicians who identify as democratic socialists, about three in ten Californians say they have a lot (12%) or some (19%) good ideas, while two in ten say they have a few good ideas (20%) and three in ten (31%) say they have almost no good ideas. However, nearly two in ten (17%) are unsure. Notably, a majority of Democrats say these politicians have at least some good ideas, compared to three in ten independent and 5 percent of Republicans. Seven in ten Republicans say these politicians have almost no good ideas.

San Francisco Bay Area residents are the most likely to say democratic socialist politicians have at least some good ideas while Inland Empire residents are the least likely to say so. Young adults age 18 to 34 (38%) are more likely than adults 55 and over (28%) to think these politicians have good ideas. College graduates (38%) are more likely than residents who have no college experience (25%) to say this (33% some college). According to a July Reuters/Ipsos poll, Californians’ views of the ideas of the Democratic Party and Democratic socialist politicians are similar to the views of Americans overall, while Californians’ views of the Republican Party’s ideas are much more negative.

Methodology

The PPIC Statewide Survey has been conducted since April 1998 to provide a voice for the public, inform policymakers, encourage discussion, and raise awareness of critical issues facing California. The coauthors of this report include survey director Mark Baldassare, who holds the Miller Chair in Public Policy; associate survey director and research fellow Dean Bonner, survey analyst Lauren Mora; and survey analyst Deja Thomas, who was the project manager for this survey. The Californians and Their Government survey on state, local, and national issues is supported with funding from the Arjay R. and Frances F. Miller Foundation. The PPIC Statewide Survey invites input, comments, and suggestions from policy and public opinion experts and from its own advisory committee members, but survey methods, questions, and content are determined solely by PPIC’s survey team. We thank Paul Lewis and Eric McGhee for helpful reviews of an earlier report draft.

Findings in this report are based on a survey of 1,745 California adult residents. The median time to complete the survey was 14.2 minutes. The survey was conducted from September 4–10, 2026.

The survey was conducted by Ipsos, using its online KnowledgePanel, in English and Spanish according to respondents’ preferences. KnowledgePanel members are recruited through probability-based sampling and include both those with internet access and those without. KnowledgePanel provides internet access for those who do not have it and, if needed, a device to access the internet when they join the panel. KnowledgePanel members are primarily recruited using address-based sampling (ABS) methodology, which improves population coverage, particularly for hard-to-reach populations such as young adults and minority groups. ABS-recruited Latinos are supplemented with a dual-frame random digit dialing (RDD) sampling methodology that targets telephone exchanges associated with areas with a higher concentration of Latinos to provide the capability to conduct representative online surveys with Latinos, including those who speak only Spanish. KnowledgePanel’s recruitment was originally based on a national RDD frame and switched to the primarily ABS-based methodology in 2009. KnowledgePanel includes households with landlines and cell phones, including those with cell phones only and those without phones. ABS allows probability-based sampling of addresses from the US Postal Service’s Delivery Sequence File (DSF). The DSF-based sampling frame used for address selection is enhanced with a series of refinements—such as the appendage of various ancillary data to each address from commercial and government data sources—to facilitate complex stratification plans. Taking advantage of such refinements, quarterly samples are selected using a stratified sampling methodology that aims to retain the representativeness of the panel. KnowledgePanel recruits new panel members throughout the year to offset panel attrition.

To qualify for the survey, a panel member must be age 18 or older and reside in California. A general population sample of Californians was selected using Ipsos’s PPS (probability proportional to size) sampling procedure to select study-specific samples. Briefly, to select such samples, the panel is first weighted to population benchmarks and those panel weights are used as the measure of size for a PPS sample selection that yields a fully representative sample. A total of 1,811 respondents completed the survey out of 3,046 panelists who were sampled, for a response rate of 59 percent. To ensure the highest data quality, we flagged respondents who sped through the survey, which we defined as completing the survey in one-fourth of the overall median time (less than 4 minutes). We also flagged respondents if their self-reported age or gender did not match the data stored in their profile. A total of 66 cases were removed after this review process, resulting in 1,745 total qualified and valid cases.

Accent on Languages, Inc., translated new survey questions into Spanish, with assistance from Renatta DeFever.

We use the US Census Bureau’s 2024 American Community Survey’s (ACS) Public Use Microdata Series for California (with regional coding information from the University of Minnesota’s Integrated Public Use Microdata Series for California) to compare certain demographic characteristics of the survey sample—region, age, gender, race/ethnicity, education, and income—with the characteristics of California’s adult population. The survey sample was closely comparable to the ACS figures. We also used voter registration data from the California Secretary of State to compare the party registration of registered voters in our sample to party registration statewide. The sample of Californians is first weighted using an initial sampling or base weight that corrects for any differences in the probability of selecting various segments of the KnowledgePanel sample. This base weight is further adjusted using an iterative proportional fitting (raking) procedure that aligns sample demographics to population benchmarks from the 2024 ACS data as well as party registration benchmarks from the California Secretary of State’s voter registration file.

The sampling error, taking design effects from weighting into consideration, is ±3.0 percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the total unweighted sample of 1,745 adults. This means that 95 times out of 100, the results will be within 3.0 percentage points of what they would be if all adults in California were interviewed. The sampling error for unweighted subgroups is larger: for the 1,475 registered voters, the sampling error is ±3.3 percent; for the 1,103 likely voters, it is ±3.8 percent. Sampling error is only one type of error to which surveys are subject. Results may also be affected by factors such as question wording, question order, and survey timing.

We present results for five geographic regions, accounting for approximately 90 percent of the state population. “Central Valley” includes Butte, Colusa, El Dorado, Fresno, Glenn, Kern, Kings, Madera, Merced, Placer, Sacramento, San Joaquin, Shasta, Stanislaus, Sutter, Tehama, Tulare, Yolo, and Yuba Counties. “San Francisco Bay Area” includes Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, Napa, San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, Solano, and Sonoma Counties. “Los Angeles” refers to Los Angeles County, “Inland Empire” refers to Riverside and San Bernardino Counties, and “Orange/San Diego” refers to Orange and San Diego Counties. Residents of other geographic areas are included in the results reported for all adults, registered voters, and likely voters, but sample sizes for these less-populous areas are not large enough to report separately.

We present results for non-Hispanic whites, who account for 35 percent of the state’s adult population, and also for Latinos, who account for 38 percent of the state’s adult population and constitute one of the fastest-growing voter groups. We also present results for non-Hispanic Asian Americans, who make up about 17 percent of the state’s adult population, and non-Hispanic African Americans, who comprise about 5 percent. Results for other racial/ethnic groups—such as Native Americans—are included in the results reported for all adults, registered voters, and likely voters, but sample sizes are not large enough for separate analysis. Results for African American and Asian American likely voters are combined with those of other racial/ethnic groups because sample sizes for African American and Asian American likely voters are too small for separate analysis. We compare the opinions of those who report they are registered Democrats, registered Republicans, and decline-to-state or independent voters; the results for those who say they are registered to vote in other parties are not large enough for separate analysis. We also analyze the responses of likely voters—so designated per their responses to survey questions about voter registration, previous election participation, intentions to vote this year, attention to election news, and current interest in politics.
