Authors

Mark Baldassare is the Statewide Survey Director at the Public Policy Institute of California, where he holds the Arjay and Frances Fearing Miller Chair in Public Policy. He is a leading expert on public opinion and survey methodology and has directed the PPIC Statewide Survey since 1998. He is an authority on elections, voter behavior, and political and fiscal reform, and the author of ten books and numerous publications. Previously, he served as PPIC’s president and CEO, director of research, and senior fellow. Before joining PPIC, he was a professor of urban and regional planning in the School of Social Ecology at the University of California, Irvine, where he held the Johnson Chair in Civic Governance. He has conducted surveys for the Los Angeles Times, the San Francisco Chronicle, and the California Business Roundtable. He holds a PhD in sociology from the University of California, Berkeley.

Dean Bonner is associate survey director and research fellow at PPIC, where he coauthors the PPIC Statewide Survey—a large-scale public opinion project designed to develop an in-depth profile of the social, economic, and political attitudes at work in California elections and policymaking. He has expertise in public opinion and survey research, political attitudes and participation, and voting behavior. Before joining PPIC, he taught political science at Tulane University and was a research associate at the University of New Orleans Survey Research Center. He holds a PhD and MA in political science from the University of New Orleans.

Lauren Mora is a survey analyst at the Public Policy Institute of California, where she works with the statewide survey team. Prior to joining PPIC, she was a research assistant with the race and ethnicity team at the Pew Research Center, where she played a key role in quantitative and qualitative studies on Latino and Asian Americans. She holds a BA in geography/environmental studies from the University of California, Los Angeles.

Deja Thomas is a survey analyst at the Public Policy Institute of California, where she works with the statewide survey team. Prior to joining PPIC, she was a research assistant with the social and demographic trends team at the Pew Research Center. In that role, she contributed to a variety of national quantitative and qualitative survey studies. She holds a BA in psychology from the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa.

California's Non-Ultraprocessed Seal: Newsom Decides by Sept 30

California passed AB 2244 to create a voluntary 'Non-Ultraprocessed Certified' seal. What would qualify, what would not, and what happens after Newsom's Sept 30 deadline.

By Chris Carrillo · Reviewed by Armin Rad, Co-Founder & CTO, Aurascan · October 3, 2026

Update, October 2, 2026: Governor Gavin Newsom signed AB 2244 on September 28, 2026 (Chapter 721, Statutes of 2026). For what the new law does, read California Creates a 'Non-Ultraprocessed Certified' Food Seal.

SACRAMENTO, Calif. (September 13, 2026) -- In late August 2026, the California Legislature passed Assembly Bill 2244 to establish a voluntary, state-verified Non-Ultraprocessed Certified seal. Governor Gavin Newsom has until September 30, 2026, to sign or veto the measure, which directs state health regulators to accredit third-party certifiers by June 1, 2029.

Key takeaways:

  • California Assembly Bill 2244 passed the state legislature in late August 2026, and Governor Gavin Newsom has until September 30, 2026, to take action.
  • If enacted, the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) must accredit third-party certifiers by June 1, 2029, under a mandatory three-year recertification cycle.
  • Disqualifying ingredients include synthetic color additives, non-sugar sweeteners, artificial flavor enhancers, and industrial processing aids.
  • Large grocery retail stores operating in California that stock certified foods would be required to provide clear in-store promotional shelf tagging.

What happened in the California legislature?

In late August 2026, the California State Legislature approved Assembly Bill 2244 (AB 2244), introduced by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino). Following final legislative passage, the enrolled bill was formally transmitted to the governor's office. According to the official California AB 2244 Bill Text and Status record. Under California constitutional rules, Governor Gavin Newsom has until September 30, 2026, to either sign the measure into law, allow it to become law without a signature, or exercise a gubernatorial veto.

AB 2244 establishes a formal, voluntary certification framework across California's commercial grocery sector. Rather than introducing mandatory warning labels or negative stop-sign disclosures on retail packages, the legislation creates an affirmative, state-backed regulatory standard: the Non-Ultraprocessed Certified seal. This seal is intended to allow shoppers to quickly identify packaged food items that are manufactured without specific classes of cosmetic food additives, high-intensity artificial flavors, or intensive industrial modification.

The measure reflects a notable shift in state-level public health and food regulation policy, as reported by Food Safety Magazine. While prior statutory initiatives primarily targeted individual chemical compounds or specific synthetic additives, AB 2244 establishes an overarching standard addressing systemic industrial formulation practices across packaged food categories.

What changed under the new standard?

Under AB 2244, the California Department of Public Health (CDPH) is instructed to develop comprehensive technical criteria and accredit qualified, independent third-party certifying entities no later than June 1, 2029. Food brands choosing to feature the Non-Ultraprocessed Certified seal on consumer packaging will be required to submit ingredient documentation, undergo independent verification through accredited certifiers, and complete a formal recertification process at least once every three years.

The certification criteria established in the bill set explicit boundaries prohibiting specific industrial ingredients and processing techniques. A packaged food product is disqualified from receiving the certification seal if it contains any of the following:

  • Synthetic food dyes and certified color additives.
  • Non-sugar sweeteners, such as aspartame, acesulfame potassium, sucralose, or saccharin.
  • Industrial flavor enhancers, such as monosodium glutamate or disodium inosinate.
  • Certain processing aids specified in the bill.

Beyond front-of-package labeling rules, AB 2244 sets specific retail merchandising mandates. Commercial grocery store operators in California that carry certified products will be required to feature distinct visual cues, such as shelf markers or promotional point-of-sale displays, ensuring visibility for certified items in grocery aisles.

Who is affected across retail and supply chains?

AB 2244 directly impacts packaged food manufacturers, retail grocery operators, state public health agencies, and consumers across California. Food companies selling packaged products in the state will have the option to evaluate their existing recipes against CDPH standards if they wish to apply for the voluntary seal. Recent analyses from Agri-Pulse Communications indicate that food processors are already reviewing ingredient specifications to assess compliance feasibility.

Packaged goods formulated with traditional kitchen ingredients can qualify under the standard, whereas products containing heavily modified chemical substitutes will not. For example, a traditional five-ingredient vanilla ice cream formulated solely with cream, milk, cane sugar, egg yolks, and vanilla extract would meet the criteria for the seal. In contrast, an ice cream formulation containing synthetic colorants, non-nutritive artificial sweeteners, polydextrose, and industrial emulsifiers would be barred from receiving certification.

Major supermarket chains operating physical retail locations within California will also need to update their internal planograms, shelf-tagging systems, and point-of-sale marketing displays to accommodate the mandatory in-store highlighting requirements for certified items.

What it means for shoppers in grocery aisles?

For consumers evaluating packaged food options in grocery aisles, the Non-Ultraprocessed Certified seal provides a voluntary front-of-pack indicator verified by accredited third parties under state oversight. This framework differs from mandatory negative warning systems, offering an affirmative label for products formulated without prohibited industrial additives.

Shoppers seeking to avoid specific synthetic ingredients will be able to identify qualifying products directly on the front panel without needing to read complex ingredient lists. For example, processed products formulated with synthetic dyes, such as those tracked on the FDA Dye Tracker Now Says End of 2027: Who's Done dashboard or on menus evaluated in EWG Checked 12 Fast-Food Menus: Dyes on All but Two, would not be eligible for the certification seal.

Similarly, products containing non-sugar sweeteners, such as those reviewed in EFSA Clears the Aspartame-Acesulfame Salt (E 962) and Sucralose Re-Evaluated: What EFSA's 2026 Safety Review Found, or specialized industrial baking additives discussed in FDA Reassesses ADA Dough Conditioner: What It Means for Bread, will be excluded from obtaining the seal.

At the same time, the presence of a non-ultraprocessed seal does not mean a food product is inherently low in total calories, saturated fat, or sodium, nor does it guarantee specific individual health outcomes. Items such as butter, unrefined sugars, and aged cheeses represent minimally processed culinary ingredients under standard classification systems, but individual nutritional requirements vary. Furthermore, current scientific evidence cannot establish uniform metabolic or clinical outcomes across all individuals simply based on the presence or absence of processed food classifications.

The background behind ultra-processed food policy?

California's legislative initiative comes amid ongoing scientific discussion regarding dietary patterns and ultra-processed foods (UPFs). Public health researchers frequently utilize the NOVA classification system, developed by researchers at the University of São Paulo, which categorizes food items into four distinct groups based on the nature, extent, and purpose of industrial processing, ranging from unprocessed or minimally processed foods (Group 1) to ultra-processed formulations (Group 4).

Observational studies have reported statistical associations between high dietary consumption of ultra-processed foods and increased risks of chronic conditions, including type 2 diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular disease, although these studies cannot prove cause and effect. As noted in a release by the Environmental Working Group, public health advocates view clear labeling standards as an essential mechanism to support consumer choice. To establish clear statutory definitions, California previously enacted AB 1264, which established a formal state definition of ultra-processed foods.

Related regulatory assessments are occurring at both state and federal levels. State-level policy variations are tracked across the country in Which Food Additives Are Banned in Which US State (2026 Tracker), while actions on historic colorants are detailed in FDA Revokes Orange B: The Sausage-Casing Dye Nobody Used. On August 10, 2026, federal public health agencies submitted preliminary definition proposals for administrative review, as detailed in our analysis of the US to Define 'Ultra-Processed Food': What the Proposal Means.

What to watch next before the deadline?

The immediate regulatory milestone is September 30, 2026, which is the statutory deadline for Governor Gavin Newsom to sign or veto AB 2244. If the bill is enacted into law, the formal implementation timeline will follow several procedural steps:

  • September 30, 2026: Final deadline for gubernatorial approval or veto action.
  • 2027 to 2028: CDPH public rulemaking proceedings, technical formulation standards development, and public comment periods.
  • June 1, 2029: Statutory deadline for CDPH to accredit third-party certifying entities and begin accepting manufacturer applications.
  • Post-2029: Initial distribution of certified packaging in retail stores and implementation of mandatory retail shelf-highlighting requirements in California supermarkets.

Common questions

  • What is California Assembly Bill 2244?
  • California AB 2244 is a state bill passed in late August 2026 that directs the California Department of Public Health to establish a voluntary, state-verified 'Non-Ultraprocessed Certified' seal for qualifying food products.
  • When does Governor Newsom have to make a decision on AB 2244?
  • Governor Gavin Newsom has until September 30, 2026, to sign the bill into law, let it pass without signature, or veto it.
  • Which ingredients disqualify a food from the Non-Ultraprocessed Certified seal?
  • Foods containing synthetic food dyes, non-sugar sweeteners, artificial flavor enhancers, and certain industrial processing aids or texturizers are disqualified from receiving the seal.
  • When would the Non-Ultraprocessed Certified seal appear on store shelves?
  • If the bill is enacted, state regulators must accredit certifying entities by June 1, 2029, with certified products and store shelf tagging appearing following the completion of that process.
  • Is participation in the California Non-Ultraprocessed certification program mandatory?
  • No. Participation is voluntary for food manufacturers, but qualifying grocery store chains that stock certified products must highlight them with clear in-store shelf tags.
  • How often must food products be recertified under AB 2244?
  • Food manufacturers that participate in the program must undergo recertification through accredited third-party certifiers at least once every three years.

  • California AB 2244 Bill Text and Status (legiscan.com)

California Bill to Create Non-Ultraprocessed Certification Passes State Legislature

The state-backed program would create a certification and seal for products that don't fall under statutory definitions of UPFs.

September 10, 2026

By: Mike Montemarano

A California State Assembly bill, AB2244, which would establish a state-backed Non-Ultra-processed Certification for food products, has passed through the legislature and now sits on Gov. Gavin Newsom’s desk.

The bill establishes a voluntary certification process that would allow food manufacturers to have their products evaluated by independent certifiers to determine if those products are non-ultra-processed, at which point the product would be permitted to bear a “Non-Ultra-processed Certified” seal.

Existing California law, for school-related purposes, defines ultra-processed foods (UPFs) as foods or beverages that contain “a specified substance and either high amounts of saturated fat, sodium, or added sugar or a non-nutritive sweetener or other substance, as specified.” Additionally, the state’s Department of Health is currently tasked with defining ultra-processed foods of concern for general purposes, and that definition would also apply to the certification.

The current bill would require the California Department of Health, by June 1, 2029, to accredit certification agents for the new certification. Certified products would be given permission to bear a standardized seal.

The bill was modeled after the USDA Organic program and is intended to help consumers with a simple, trustworthy way to identify non-ultra-processed foods at a quick glance, Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, the bill’s author, said.

“This new seal will provide consumers with clear, trustworthy information and make it easier for them to locate healthier foods that are free from harmful additives,” Gabriel stated. “Parents shouldn’t need a PhD in chemistry to understand what they’re feeding their kids. California began this movement three years ago by banning the most dangerous food additives, and this week’s vote is the next big step toward protecting our kids from harmful ultra-processed foods.”

AB 2244 passed with the support of a bipartisan coalition and was endorsed by the Environmental Working Group, the California Medical Association, the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American Diabetes Association, the American Heart Association, the Crohn’s and Colitis Foundation, and the United Nurses Associations of California.

“Once again, California is leading the way by helping consumers identify and avoid UPFs,” said Melanie Benesh, vice president of government affairs at the Environmental Working Group. “Last year, California enacted the nation’s first definition of UPFs. This week, California has taken the next step by helping consumers distinguish between processed foods, which are part of a healthy diet, and ultra-processed foods, which are engineered to be overeaten. Our food should nourish us, not make us sick. EWG is so grateful that Assemblymember Gabriel is continuing to put our health first.”

“As a dietitian and nutrition researcher, it is clear to me that most people want to choose healthy foods for their kids,” said Alyssa J. Moran, deputy director of the Center for Food and Nutrition Policy at the University of Pennsylvania. “But nutrition information is not easy to interpret, and junk foods tend to dominate grocery store shelves. By clearly labeling foods non-ultra-processed and making them easy to find in stores, this bill sets people up for success.”

“We have a long road ahead to a food supply free from harmful chemicals and a healthier America,” said Todd Wagner, entrepreneur and co-founder of FoodFight USA. “In the meantime, we must give consumers the tools and knowledge to make healthier food choices. By creating a ‘Non-Ultra-processed Certified’ seal to help identify healthier, non-UPF options, Assemblymember Gabriel continues to advance California’s leadership in the fight to reduce consumption of the hyperpalatable, addictive ultra-processed foods driving our nation’s chronic disease crisis.”

What’s really in what we eat? California approves the first label for non-ultra-processed foods

Francesca Biagioli

Posted on 10/09/2026

A new label would help U.S. shoppers spot non-ultra-processed foods. Passed unanimously, it now awaits the governor's signature.

Figuring out what’s actually in your food isn’t always straightforward. One glance at the label and you’re staring down a wall of ingredients, unfamiliar names, and numbers that tell you almost nothing about how processed the product really is.

California is trying to fix exactly that. The state legislature has passed AB 2244, a bill that, if signed by Governor Gavin Newsom, would create an official certification program for non-ultra-processed foods.

The goal is a clearly recognizable seal on the packaging, the “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified” mark, letting shoppers spot at a glance which products meet certain criteria.

What makes the approach interesting is that it flags a positive trait directly, rather than just warning shoppers about what to cut back on.

The bill was introduced by a Democratic member of the California State Assembly, and it sailed through with a strikingly lopsided vote: 32-0 in the Senate and 72-0 in the Assembly.

Now it’s on Governor Newsom’s desk. He’ll have to decide whether to sign it into law or veto it.

How the new label would actually work

If the law takes effect, a company won’t be able to simply decide on its own to slap “non ultra-processed” on a package.

The label can only be used after certification by a body accredited by the California Department of Public Health (CDPH).

The law requires the CDPH to accredit these certifying bodies by June 1, 2029. From there, it’s up to them to check products and determine whether they qualify for certification under the law.

The standardized seal can read “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified Food Standard” or the shorthand “Non-UPF Certified”, placed on the front of the package, the information panel, or elsewhere, as long as it doesn’t cover mandatory info like the nutrition facts table.

Which foods qualify

The program isn’t limited to a specific product category: it covers foods and beverages sold at retail, meaning the stuff we normally find on supermarket shelves and in grocery stores. Only products meeting California’s criteria for non-ultra-processed status will get the mark.

Certification isn’t permanent, either: every product has to be recertified at least every three years. Change the recipe, and a new check is needed before the label can keep being used.

One of the more interesting pieces of the bill is transparency. Certifying bodies will have to report product information to the Department of Public Health, including product name, ingredients, nutritional values, manufacturer and brand, identification codes, and certification date.

The department will also need to set up a public webpage listing every food currently certified as “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified.”

Certifying bodies must register with the department and renew their accreditation every year, and the CDPH can review their procedures and paperwork or run audits whenever it wants.

The law also sets penalties for misuse of the label. Slapping the logo on a product that doesn’t meet the requirements, or certifying foods without being an accredited body, would be illegal.

Supermarkets will have to make it visible, too

This isn’t just about packaging. The law also spells out specific obligations for larger grocery chains. Once the standardized label exists, stores with annual revenue above $10 million that carry more than 25 certified products will need to make at least 3 of them clearly identifiable.

They can do this by physically separating the products, using signage, or other visual cues that let shoppers tell them apart from everything else on the shelf.

California already had a definition of ultra-processed

The bill doesn’t come out of nowhere. It builds on a legislative path California had already started on ultra-processed foods. In 2025, Governor Newsom signed AB 1264, the Real Food, Healthy Kids Act, which introduced a statutory definition of ultra-processed foods tied to school nutrition rules and kicked off a process to limit certain products in California schools.

AB 2244 would be the logical next step: not just defining what counts as ultra-processed, but building a visual tool that lets shoppers spot what doesn’t.

Behind the initiative is the growing scientific interest in a possible link between heavy consumption of ultra-processed foods and a range of health problems.

In the statement announcing the bill’s passage, Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel’s office cites research linking high consumption of these foods to cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, certain cancers, metabolic disorders, and other chronic conditions.

That doesn’t mean every processed food is something to avoid. California’s own framing draws a line between “processed” and “ultra-processed.”

It’s precisely this fuzzy boundary that the bill’s backers point to as a reason for an easily recognizable certification system.

If Newsom gives the green light, California could become the first US state with an official certification program for non-ultra-processed foods, a label meant to make that information obvious the moment you’re standing in the aisle.

The article draws upon studies published and recommendations from international institutions and/or experts. We do not make claims in the medical-scientific field and report the facts as they are. Sources are indicated at the end of each article.

California Lawmakers Pass Bill to Create Landmark ‘Non-Ultra-Processed’ Food Label

By Environmental Working Group

September 10, 2026 | 4 min to read

Submit release Save for later Share

Photo credit: AdobeStock

SACRAMENTO – The California Legislature has taken a major step toward protecting public health by passing a first-of-its-kind bill to create a certified “non-ultra-processed” food label intended to make it easier for consumers to choose less-processed foods in the grocery store.

Assembly Bill 2244, authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino ), would develop a state certification program for products that are not ultra-processed, or UPF. If enacted, it would create a new standardized and government-backed seal for non-UPF foods.

It would also require some of the largest grocery stores to highlight these products in store so they’re easier for shoppers to identify.

The Environmental Working Group is cosponsoring the bill, which now heads to Gov. Gavin Newsom’s desk for his signature.

“Parents shouldn’t need a Ph.D. in chemistry to understand what they’re feeding their kids,” said Gabriel.

“AB 2244 will empower consumers with clear, trustworthy information and make it easier for them to locate healthier foods that are free from harmful additives. This new seal doesn’t limit consumer choice, it just makes informed choice possible,” he added.

Under AB 2244, the state would create a standardized label bearing the phrase “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified.” Products would not be permitted to carry the new label if they are classified as UPF under state law.

Some types of food, such as substances or additives used to manipulate taste and quality, would not qualify for the new label. These food chemicals, such as dyes, flavor enhancers, non-sugar sweeteners and processing aids, are used to make food hyperpalatable and irresistible.

AB 2244 builds on a precedent-setting earlier law by Gabriel. AB 1264 set the first U.S. legal definition of UPF and banned the worst UPF from K-12 public schools.

If Newson signs AB 2244, the California Department of Public Health would oversee approved agents’ independent certification of products that meet the state’s non-UPF standard and qualify to use the label.

AB 2244 would direct the department to accredit these third-party agents no later than June 1, 2029. It would also require product recertification at least every three years.

“This is about setting a higher bar for what we consider healthy food and helping consumers make wise choices,” said Bernadette Del Chiaro, EWG senior vice president for California.

“Consumers deserve labels they can trust. And families deserve a simple way to tell which foods are closer to what comes from a kitchen rather than a factory.”

“If enacted, the bill would establish a state-verified seal for foods free from the additives, emulsifiers, food dyes and flavors that have come to define the modern American diet,” she added.

The bill includes these strong oversight and transparency measures:

  • Certification agents must register with the state and disclose all certified products
  • The state can audit certification records at any time
  • The state would maintain a public, online list of certified products
  • Misuse of the label would be illegal and subject to enforcement

These provisions are designed to ensure the label’s credibility.

In addition to creating the label, the bill would require large food retailers to display certified products carrying the label in a way that’s easy for consumers to identify, such as through special signage or physical separation within the store.

This requirement would apply to any grocery store that sells more than 25 individual non-UPF-certified product types and brings in more than $10 million in annual sales.

UPF are industrially manufactured, chemically modified products often made with harmful additives to enhance taste, texture, appearance and shelf life.

In the U.S., these foods make up more than two-thirds of children’s diets and more than half the typical adult diet.

Experts say ultra-processed food and drinks, particularly soda, are engineered to trick people into consuming more than they want.

California’s legislature unanimously passed a bill establishing the nation’s first “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified” seal for food manufacturers lable products that meet associated standards.

Assembly Bill 2244, modeled after the “USDA Organic” label, aims to help consumers quickly identify healthier food options and would require grocery stores in California to display products bearing the label.

The bill is authored by Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), who last year also penned a bill signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom that established the nation’s first statutory definition of ultra-processed foods and a process to ban products from California schools.

The bill, which passed 104-0 combining the state assembly and state senate votes, was delivered to Newsom’s desk Tuesday. He has until Sept. 30 to veto or sign it into law.

What it is: The legislature is asking voters to approve a constitutional amendment to change rules for building state budget reserves and paying down extra state debts. California is close to becoming the first state with an official label for food that isn’t ultra-processed.

Lawmakers in Sacramento have passed a bill creating a “non-ultraprocessed certified” seal that food makers can put on qualifying products. The same measure would require large grocery stores to give those cleaner options a more prominent placement on their shelves. Governor Gavin Newsom is yet to sign off on it.

If it takes effect, the seal will be voluntary, and a product qualifies for the label as long as it stays outside the definition that California already put on the books last year, when it became the first state to define and phase out ultra-processed foods and restrict their use in public school meals.

Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, who wrote the bill, modeled it on the USDA Organic seal, arguing it would give shoppers a shortcut through the ingredient list.

“Like the USDA Organic label, this new seal will provide consumers with clear, trustworthy information and make it easier for them to locate healthier foods that are free from harmful additives,” Gabriel said in a statement. “Parents shouldn’t need a Ph.D. in chemistry to understand what they’re feeding their kids,” the Assemblymember added.

The seal would enter a market already crowded with private labels. Several groups have already rolled out their own versions, including the Non-GMO Project and a nonprofit called the Non-UPF Program. Each uses its own standard, and consumer welfare advocates worry that having several competing labels will confuse shoppers rather than guide them.

The nonprofit nutrition watchdog, Center for Science in the Public Interest (CSPI), has raised the same concern, warning that some of the labels lack strong nutrition criteria and could end up on products too high in sugar or sodium to qualify for the FDA’s “Healthy” label.

“If your primary goal is instead to seek out minimally processed foods or eat more healthfully overall, there are better approaches than looking for foods with non-UPF labels,” the group said.

Sources: Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, CDC, Johns Hopkins, CSPI, Food Dive

Sarah Zimmerman

Dive Brief

The landmark measure establishes a voluntary certification system and requires large grocery stores to prominently display cleaner label food options.

Published Sept. 8, 2026

Dive Brief:

  • California lawmakers approved a “non-ultraprocessed certified” seal for food manufacturers under a landmark state measure. It also requires grocers to more prominently display cleaner label options for consumers.
  • The bill, which still needs the governor’s approval, establishes a certification process for a voluntary label that can be used on products that do not fall under the state’s definition of ultraprocessed foods established last year.
  • The legislation comes as more third-party certifiers debut non-ultraprocessed labels for food companies, often with conflicting definitions on what makes a product clean label.

Dive Insight:

Modeled after the “USDA Organic” seal, California’s non-ultraprocessed label is meant to provide consumers with a “trustworthy way to identify healthier options,” according to bill sponsor Assemblyman Jesse Gabriel.

“Like the USDA Organic label, this new seal will provide consumers with clear, trustworthy information and make it easier for them to locate healthier foods that are free from harmful additives,” Gabriel said in a statement. “Parents shouldn’t need a Ph.D. in chemistry to understand what they’re feeding their kids.”

Last year, California became the first state in the nation to define and ban ultraprocessed foods. It came as more consumers and the Make America Healthy Again movement scrutinize ingredients and more clearly link processed foods to negative impacts on public health. California defines foods as ultraprocessed if they contain an additive such as flavoring or emulsifiers, or are high in saturated fat, added sugar or sodium.

While California does not lay out specifications for what makes a food non-ultraprocessed in its new certification, the measure says that foods cannot bear the seal if they meet the state’s definition of ultraprocessed.

The California label would add to a growing list of non-ultraprocessed seals available for food manufacturers to position their products as healthier. Other options include the Non-UPF Verified Standard from the Non-GMO Project and the Non-UPF Certified seal from the nonprofit Non-UPF Program.

As more labels hit the market, some consumer welfare groups have warned these seals could confuse shoppers as they rely on different definitions and verification methods. The Center for Science in the Public Interest said labels have inconsistent approaches and in some cases, lack strong nutrition criteria, which could incentivize companies to use the non-UPF certification even when they have too much sugar or sodium to qualify for the “FDA Healthy” label.

“If your primary goal is instead to seek out minimally processed foods or eat more healthfully overall, there are better approaches than looking for foods with non-UPF labels,” CSPI said.

California legislature approves first-in-nation ‘Non-Ultra-Processed’ Food Label Program

MMR

SACRAMENTO, Calif. — California lawmakers recently approved landmark legislation that would create the nation’s first state-certified label identifying foods that are not ultra-processed, giving consumers a new tool to make healthier food choices.

Assembly Bill 2244, authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), would establish a state certification program for products that meet California’s standards for non-ultra-processed foods. The measure, co-sponsored by the Environmental Working Group (EWG), now awaits Gov. Gavin Newsom’s signature.

If signed into law, products meeting the criteria could display a government-backed “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified” seal, while larger grocery retailers would be required to make certified products easier for shoppers to identify through signage or product placement.

“Parents shouldn’t need a Ph.D. in chemistry to understand what they’re feeding their kids,” Gabriel said in a statement. “AB 2244 will provide consumers with clear, trustworthy information and make it easier to find healthier foods that are free from harmful additives.”

The bill builds on Gabriel’s earlier legislation, AB 1264, which established California’s legal definition of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) and restricted certain products from K-12 public schools.

Under AB 2244, foods containing ingredients commonly associated with ultra-processing, including certain dyes, flavor enhancers, artificial sweeteners and processing aids, would not qualify for certification. The California Department of Public Health would oversee the program and accredit third-party certifying organizations by June 2029. Certified products would be required to undergo recertification at least every three years.

Supporters say the measure would increase transparency and accountability through state oversight, public disclosure of certified products and enforcement against misuse of the label.

The retailer requirement would apply to grocery stores generating more than $10 million in annual sales that carry at least 25 certified non-UPF products.

Advocates cite growing concerns about the health effects of ultra-processed foods, which account for more than half of the average American diet and more than two-thirds of children's diets. Research has linked high consumption of UPFs to obesity, Type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, certain cancers and other chronic health conditions.

“Consumers deserve labels they can trust,” said Bernadette Del Chiaro, EWG’s senior vice president for California. “This bill creates a simple way for families to identify foods that are closer to what comes from a kitchen rather than a factory.”

Nutrition experts say front-of-package labeling can help consumers make healthier choices at a time when identifying ultra-processed foods remains difficult.

Alyssa Moran, deputy director of the Center for Food and Nutrition Policy at the University of Pennsylvania, said even nutrition experts can struggle to determine whether a food is ultra-processed based solely on ingredient lists.

“Clear, science-backed labels on the front of food packages can be highly influential in helping people make better choices,” Moran said.

The California legislature has passed legislation to increase transparency around ultraprocessed foods. Authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D - Encino), Assembly Bill 2244 establishes a first-in-the-nation “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified” seal for food manufacturers to place on products that meet clear standards for not being ultra-processed. Modeled after the “USDA Organic” label, the "seal would provide consumers with a simple, trustworthy way to identify healthier options with a quick glance," Gabriel said. The bill also would require grocery stores in California to display products bearing the label.

“While Washington D.C. is paralyzed by inaction, Republicans and Democrats in California are joining forces to empower consumers to avoid harmful ultra-processed foods,” said Gabriel. “Like the USDA Organic label, this new seal will provide consumers with clear, trustworthy information and make it easier for them to locate healthier foods that are free from harmful additives. Parents shouldn't need a Ph.D. in chemistry to understand what they’re feeding their kids. California began this movement three years ago by banning the most dangerous food additives, and this week’s vote is the next big step toward protecting our kids from harmful ultra-processed foods.”

Supporters of AB 2244 include the Environmental Working Group, the California Medical Association, the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American Diabetes Association, the American Heart Association, the Crohn’s & Colitis Foundation and the United Nurses Associations of California. The bill passed the State Senate on a vote of 32-0 and the State Assembly 72-0.

Last year, Gabriel authored and Governor Gavin Newsom signed into law The Real Food, Healthy Kids Act (AB 1264), legislation which established the nation’s first statutory definition of ultra-processed foods and set up a process to ban products from California schools. Assemblymember Gabriel also passed into law two other bills with bipartisan support: the California Food Safety Act (AB 418, 2023) and the California School Food Safety Act (AB 2316, 2024), which he says have "helped change the national conversation about food additives and ultra-processed foods, shaped federal policy, and inspired similar legislation across more than 30 other states."

Калифорния одобряет добровольный знак для продуктов без глубокой переработки

Законодатели Калифорнии одобрили меру, которая создаст добровольный сертифицированный знак для производителей продуктов, не прошедших глубокую переработку, а также обязательства для продавцов размещать более заметно варианты с более чистым составом. Законопроект, ожидающий одобрения губернатора, устанавливает процесс сертификации для продуктов, которые не соответствуют определению продуктов глубокой переработки, принятому в штате в прошлом году.

По данным источника, законодательство разработано по образцу знака USDA Organic и направлено на то, чтобы дать потребителям надежный способ выявлять более здоровые варианты, как заявил член Ассамблеи Джесси Габриэль, автор законопроекта. Габриэль отметил, что знак предоставит четкую информацию и поможет родителям избежать необходимости иметь диплом химика, чтобы понимать маркировку продуктов.

В прошлом году Калифорния стала первым штатом, который дал определение продуктам глубокой переработки и запретил их, что произошло на фоне растущего внимания потребителей и движения «Сделаем Америку снова здоровой». Штат определяет продукты глубокой переработки как те, которые содержат добавки, такие как ароматизаторы или эмульгаторы, или высокий уровень насыщенных жиров, добавленного сахара или натрия. Новая сертификация не уточняет, что делает продукт не прошедшим глубокую переработку, но запрещает использование знака на продуктах, соответствующих определению глубокой переработки.

Калифорнийский знак присоединяется к растущему списку знаков для продуктов без глубокой переработки, включая стандарт Non-UPF Verified от проекта Non-GMO и знак Non-UPF Certified от некоммерческой программы Non-UPF. Однако организации по защите прав потребителей предупредили, что эти знаки могут запутывать покупателей из-за различий в определениях и методах проверки.Центр науки в интересах общества отметил, что знаки имеют непоследовательные подходы и иногда не имеют строгих критериев питательной ценности, что может привести к тому, что компании будут использовать сертификацию non-UPF даже для продуктов с избыточным содержанием сахара или натрия. Организация предположила, что потребителям, ищущим минимально обработанные или более здоровые продукты, возможно, лучше подойдут другие подходы, чем полагаться на знаки non-UPF.

California just won $2.1B from Meta. Here’s how the state could spend it

By Tyler Katzenberger
Return to Homepage

SACRAMENTO, California — California just won a tentative $2.1 billion payout from tech giant Meta's settlement in a child safety lawsuit — the largest share any U.S. state or territory is receiving from a pot of up to $18 billion.

Now the challenge is figuring out how to spend it.

Meta reached the settlement with dozens of state attorneys general amid a high-profile trial in California, alleging the social media company intentionally hooked kids on its platforms while misleading users about their potential harms. Part of the funds are contingent upon other tech companies meeting certain kids' safety commitments that Meta also agreed to.

Conversations with 16 California state lawmakers who are positioned to have a say in how the money is spent, plus the candidates vying to become governor, revealed nearly a dozen competing ideas for how to cash in.

Some politicians want to put the money into enforcing social media laws. Some think that the settlement cash should backfill behavioral health services or suicide prevention programs as Republican-backed federal health care cuts take a hit on California's budget. Others hope to fund research exploring social media's impacts on children, finance community nonprofits that mentor young kids or offer schools grants to implement student smartphone bans.

But with only so much money to go around — and strings attached to more than a third of it — state leaders likely won't be able to fund all of their ideas.

"Many of those proposals cost money," said Jesse Gabriel, a powerful Democratic lawmaker who chairs the Assembly Budget Committee. "We're going to need to think very thoughtfully and carefully consider how we can best deploy those resources to support young people."

As the candidate heavily favored to win the governor's race in November, Democrat Xavier Becerra, will likely have the most control over how the money is spent. He's keeping his options open.

Becerra spokesperson Jonathan Underland told POLITICO the settlement "is pretty clear that these dollars are for keeping kids safe online." He didn't offer specifics beyond that, instead saying that the former U.S. health secretary "will work with the Legislature, local governments and experts to make sure the next generation reaps the benefits."

Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton had a far different vision for the settlement, which he called "a complete waste of time and money."

"We have the highest taxes in the country and the highest cost of living," Hilton said. "If there's money available, then it should be used to reduce the burden on working people and small businesses."

Becerra's view seems in line with how other blue-state leaders are approaching the settlement.

In New Jersey, Gov. Mikie Sherrill's office told POLITICO that they're still discussing how to spend the Garden State's maximum payout of $752 million, though they indicated the Democrat is seeking "the biggest possible impact for our kids and their mental health."

And in New York, officials expect an up to $1.15 billion payout from the settlement will start arriving at the end of the year — weeks before Gov. Kathy Hochul is expected to propose their budget.

The Democratic governor, who is seeking a second full term this year, has been supportive of efforts to limit the impact of social media on minors, backing measures like prohibiting algorithmic feeds for young peoples' accounts. Hochul's team has also identified broad areas for use like after school and mental health services.

Brooklyn Democratic state Sen. Andrew Gounardes, a leading proponent for regulating social media platforms in the Legislature, wants the cash to go toward youth mental health services, like expanding beds in care facilities.

"I would love to see investments in things like playgrounds and parks and broken basketball and tennis courts," Gounardes told POLITICO. "One of the reasons why we've made this case that children have been trapped in their phones is that they're not experiencing life in the real world."

Seeking 'karmic' uses for cash

California's share of the settlement, like other states', comes with restrictions. Roughly $660 million is contingent on social media competitors Snap, TikTok and YouTube agreeing to Meta's settlement terms, meaning a third of the state's total award might never materialize. Another $200 million of the total payout sits beyond lawmakers' reach because, under a provision unique to California, it's earmarked for enforcing consumer protection and privacy laws, including $100 million to be spent at "the sole discretion" of Attorney General Rob Bonta.

For the remaining cash, settlement terms dictate states should prioritize initiatives "related to the prevention or remediation of mental health or other harms to young Californians associated with social media use." But that's a broad mandate, leaving lawmakers plenty of room to deliberate how they spend the money.

Five assemblymembers who proposed a ban this year on "addictive" social media features for teens under 16 — Democrats Josh Lowenthal, Buffy Wicks and Rebecca Bauer-Kahan, plus Republicans Joe Patterson and Josh Hoover — said the money should be used to police Facebook, Instagram and other companies' compliance with kids' safety rules.

Their proposal, contained in AB 1709, would establish an "eSafety Commission" tasked with helping the attorney general enforce restrictions on personalized feeds, infinite scrolling and other engagement-maximizing features. Gov. Gavin Newsom appears likely to sign the bill this month, but it doesn't earmark money for the proposed seven-member body.

Wicks said that funding enforcement efforts would tackle a perennial challenge: ensuring tech giants are actually following California's social media regulations. Independent reports have found compliance is spotty, partly because the attorney general's office is consistently overworked but often the only prosecutor empowered to prosecute violations.

"The attorney general does such a great job, and he needs more resources," Wicks added.

Moreover, Patterson said, funding enforcement is "more important now" because child safety features mandated in the settlement only apply to Meta. "You've got to get everybody on a level playing field. I don't think it's fair that it only applies to Meta," he added.

But California's two health committee chairs, Assemblymember Mia Bonta and state Sen. Akilah Weber Pierson, feel a pressing need is mental health services. Both pointed out that federal budget cuts approved last year under H.R. 1 disproportionately impacted health care, and they saw the settlement as a prime opportunity to backfill programs focused on youth well-being.

Bonta said that hiring new school behavioral health specialists to treat youth mental health issues tied to chronic social media use, like anxiety, depression and eating disorders, would be a "very karmic use" of the settlement funds.

A handful of her Democratic colleagues agreed mental health resources should be prioritized, but they looked to other programs.

Assembly Budget Committee member Pilar Schiavo suggested funding the state's 988 suicide crisis hotline or funneling cash to Medi-Cal programs targeted at low-income families.

Assemblymember Avelino Valencia, who chairs a select committee on boys' and men's mental health, felt that funding youth mentorship programs like Big Brothers, Big Sisters would help give kids more reasons to log off social media and focus on real-world connections.

"There's a lack of structure for young people — young men in particular — hence why they're gravitating toward pornography online, gaming online, [and] toward gambling, because it's that immediate gratification," Valencia said. "We're never going to be able to beat that, but at least providing an option to help mitigate the impact is something I'm passionate about."

Nick Reisman, Dustin Racioppi, Rachel Bluth and Marisa Guerra Echeverria contributed to this report.

A version of this story first appeared in California Decoded, POLITICO's morning newsletter for Pros about how the Golden State is shaping tech policy within its borders and beyond. Like this content? POLITICO Pro subscribers receive it daily. Learn more at www.politicopro.com.

IN THE RED — Eric Jones, the Our Revolution-backed Democrat challenging longtime Rep. Mike Thompson in the Napa Valley, is now trying to beat him by courting the right.

In recent weeks, Jones has touted endorsements from all six Republican opponents and one independent that he and Thompson faced in the June primary. He launched a group titled Californians Against the Democratic Establishment to boost his outreach to GOP and independent voters. And he’s been spotted at at least two Republican fundraisers (Jones said he attended the events, but did not donate).

It’s a stark contrast (though not the only recent exception) to many other Democrats who’ve waged anti-incumbent, generational challenges across the country this cycle by running as ultra-progressive Democrats or democratic socialists.

Jones, a 35-year-old venture capitalist who appealed to progressives in the primary — and finished nearly 20 percentage points behind Thompson — told Playbook that voters at both ends of the political spectrum are frustrated by the cost of living and the status quo in Washington. Thompson, 75, has represented the district for nearly 30 years and is backed by much of the Democratic establishment.

“Even though our values may be different, we all recognize the problem, which is corruption in establishment politics,” Jones said. “The flavor of anti-establishment will be different all across the country. But the agreement is that this Democratic Party is not for us.”

There is logic to Jones’ strategy. Thompson, who had strong support among Democratic primary voters, received 41 percent of the district’s vote in June — compared with 22 percent for Jones and nearly 21 percent for Republican Ray Riehle (who’s leading Jones’ outreach to Republicans). It’s those latter voters who may be up for grabs.

To that end, Jones, who has poured more than $5.3 million into the race, has Republicans advising him now, too. His campaign advisers include heavyweight Democratic consultants like Mark Longabaugh, Julian Mulvey, Steve Spinner and Robb Korinke, but also veteran Republican strategist Rob Stutzman and Crystal Martin, a GOP consultant from the Central Valley.

Jones, who supports expanding Medicare and banning corporate PAC money in elections, said he’s made inroads with Republican voters by talking about issues like term limits and banning members of Congress from trading stocks as he campaigns in rural parts of the district. Swaths of Yuba and Sutter counties in the Central Valley and Sierra Foothills were recently drawn into the district when voters approved California’s new, Democratic-drawn congressional map.

But … he has to sell it. And Thompson’s campaign has pounced on Jones’ overtures to Republican voters, portraying him as a political chameleon.

“We don’t know what Eric Jones believes because he changes his mind every time he enters a new room,” said Thomas Dowling, Thompson’s campaign manager. “He’s lied about the stocks he owned, he’s lied about his career as a San Francisco venture capitalist, and he’s lied about when he moved to the district.”

(Jones says he has been a resident of Napa since 2021, though he previously told Playbook that he forgot to update his old San Francisco voter registration until January 2025. Jones also said at a March event that he doesn’t own stocks. His campaign said the $500,000 to $1 million of “ownership in stock” listed on his candidate financial disclosure is a dividend-paying stake in a private company, not a publicly-traded stock.)

WHERE’S GAVIN? In South Carolina, and then North Carolina, on the third day of his campaign swing through the South. He told Don Lemon it is “absolutely not” a kickoff to 2028.

D.C. SCRUTINY — House Republicans are investigating “potential waste, fraud and abuse” of federal homelessness dollars in Los Angeles, and they want to hear from Karen Bass. The Los Angeles mayor was asked to testify before the DOGE subpanel of the House oversight committee on Sept. 15, according to a letter from GOP Rep. Tim Burchett.

The invitation was first reported by LAist, which has published multiple stories about apparent misuse of funds by the LA Homeless Services Authority.

A spokesperson for Bass did not say whether Bass planned to accept the invitation and told Playbook the mayor’s office “recently received the letter and is currently preparing a response.” Bass told a Fox 11 reporter she is “talking to my lawyers” about it.

Bass has frequently touted the relationships she formed across the aisle during her time in Congress, but the tone of Burchett’s letter indicates she may face a grilling before the committee. He writes that her administration’s approach to homelessness has led to “deteriorating public health, increased lawlessness and a bleak environment for small businesses.”

Rep. Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on House oversight, laced into Republicans for their “partisan effort.”

“This is clearly another attempt by Donald Trump and House Republicans to launch a witch hunt against Mayor Karen Bass and Los Angeles,” the former Long Beach mayor said in a statement.

NEWSOMLAND

EARLY REVIEWS — The South Carolina Republican Party was urging followers — apparently with little success — to attend Newsom events as he worked the Lowcountry, The Post and Courier reported.

“Come out, bring a sign, and help us remind Gavin that while we’re always happy to welcome visitors, we’re not interested in bringing California politics to South Carolina,” read one email.

Bigger government. Failed liberal policies. California can keep it. Don’t California My South Carolina.”

Now the challenge: figuring out how to spend it, Tyler Katzenberger reports for POLITICO Pro Technology: California Decoded.

Lawmakers who spoke with Decoded pitched nearly a dozen competing ideas for spending the payout. Some wanted to invest the money back into enforcing social media laws. Jaff, a retired Canadian Armed Forces officer who writes on security and geopolitics, has sparked controversy and argued that months of U.S. airstrikes had not ended Iran’s institutional capacity to fight and that a ground campaign, if pursued, would require far more troops than the active U.S. Army currently fields.

Jaff proposed, among other options, a federally run program that would discharge student-loan, credit-card, and other consumer debts after 24 or 36 months of service and extend GI Bill benefits, saying young Americans carrying high non-mortgage debt were the cohort the Pentagon would need. The wider conflict that began with joint U.S. and Israeli strikes earlier in 2026 has included periods of intense bombing, a June memorandum of understanding that later lapsed, renewed missile and drone exchanges, disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, and disputed civilian casualties, including a Sept. 1 wedding-site strike in southern Iran that U.S. officials said they were investigating. As of early September 2026, fighting had again eased into intermittent strikes and political statements rather than a declared full ground invasion, with U.S. officials describing major combat as having ended after about six weeks while Iran continued limited retaliation and oil and shipping markets remained volatile.

Benjamin Azariah Southworth, a 40-year-old Los Angeles podcaster and former host of the Christian youth program “The Remix” and the podcast “Yass, Jesus!,” was arrested Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026, at his home in the city’s Westlake neighborhood after a federal grand jury indicted him on charges of threatening the president, cyberstalking and making harassing interstate telephone calls.

Prosecutors allege that between January and May 2026 he posted videos on Instagram and other platforms calling for President Donald Trump’s assassination, including a March 31 clip in which he said “Kill Donald Trump,” and later depicted a knife attack in the Oval Office; they also accuse him of publishing the home address and phone numbers of Trump’s personal attorney and contacting the attorney’s family. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said his office “will not tolerate threats of political violence in the United States” and would prosecute anyone who crosses that line “to the fullest extent of the law,” while Attorney General Todd Blanche said the Justice Department would respond with the full force of the law as threats against the president escalate. Southworth pleaded not guilty at his initial appearance the same day. Trump has faced multiple documented attempts and plots in recent years, including the July 13, 2024, rally shooting in Butler, Pennsylvania, in which Thomas Matthew Crooks wounded Trump in the ear and killed a spectator; the September 2024 incident at Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach, Florida, in which Ryan Wesley Routh was later convicted and sentenced to life; and an April 25, 2026, armed breach at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner in which a gunman fired at officers before being subdued.

Additional reported incidents include a February 2026 armed intrusion at Mar-a-Lago while Trump was in Washington and intelligence warnings of foreign plots, which together have led to heightened Secret Service operations, criminal convictions, and ongoing federal investigations rather than a change in the president’s public schedule.

CALIFORNIA TAXPAYERS MAY SOON FOOT THE BILL FOR GOVERNOR/TOP DEMS SECURITY DETAILS 🚔

California lawmakers on Sept. 1, 2026, the last day of the legislative session, passed Assembly Bill 113, a budget trailer measure authored by Assembly Budget Committee Chair Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), that adds $20 million from the Motor Vehicle Account—funded by vehicle registration and driver’s license fees—to the California Highway Patrol for security services for current and former state constitutional officers, legislators, judges and their immediate families. A companion measure, Senate Bill 194, would expand existing CHP authority, which already allows protection of current or former constitutional officers when a threat assessment finds it necessary, to cover immediate family members and to keep an assigned level of protection in place for at least six months before reassessment.

Gov. Gavin Newsom’s term ends in January 2027; has not said whether he would request the detail, and security would still depend on a CHP threat analysis rather than being automatic. Existing state law already permits the CHP commissioner to provide physical security for former governors and other constitutional officers, and former Vice President Kamala Harris, a former California attorney general, has used CHP protection after federal coverage ended; the new package is therefore an expansion of funding and family coverage rather than an entirely new category of protection. Republican legislators argued the Motor Vehicle Account earmark was an inappropriate use of driver fees and that campaign accounts could cover personal security, while supporters said rising threats against public officials justified the increase.

Both bills await the governor’s signature, and is most likely to be passed into law.

Bill on non-UPF certification passes in California

SACRAMENTO, CALIF. — The California legislature has passed Assembly Bill 2244 that would establish a non-ultra-processed certified seal that food manufacturers could place on their products that meet standards for not being ultra-processed.

“While Washington, DC, is paralyzed by inaction, Republicans and Democrats in California are joining forces to empower consumers to avoid harmful ultra-processed foods,” said Jesse Gabriel, the assembly member who authored the bill. “Like the USDA Organic label, this new seal will provide consumers with clear, trustworthy information and make it easier for them to locate healthier foods that are free from harmful additives. Parents shouldn’t need a PhD in chemistry to understand what they’re feeding their kids.”

The bill passed by a vote of 32-0 in the state Senate and by a vote of 72-0 in the state Assembly. California Governor Gavin Newsom has until Sept.30 to decide whether to veto the bill or sign it into law.

No federal law defines ultra-processed food, but the US Department of Health and the US Department of Agriculture have submitted for final review a proposed definition.

The bill in California would establish a process overseen by the California Department of Health where food manufacturers could apply to accredited certification agents to use the non-ultra-processed certified label on their packaging.

A state law in California regarding certain school-related purposes defines ultra-processed food as any food or beverage that contains a specific substance and either high amounts of saturated fat, sodium, or added sugar or a non-nutritive sweetener or other substance. The law requires the California Department of Health to define ultra-processed foods of concern and restricted school foods by June 1, 2028.

California passes bill creating 'Non-Ultra-Processed' Food certification label - Washington Report

On September 3, 2026, in Labeling, by Tom Super

WHAT HAPPENED: The California Legislature this week passed Assembly Bill 2244 (AB 2244), which would establish a first-of-its-kind state certification seal for food products that meet standards for not being “ultra-processed.” The bill, authored by Assembly Member Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), passed unanimously, with a 32-0 vote in the Senate and a 72-0 vote in the Assembly, before the Legislature closed its regular session for the year.

WHAT IT WOULD DO: Modeled after the USDA Organic label, AB 2244 would create a voluntary certification program allowing qualifying manufacturers to display a “Non-Ultra processed Certified” seal on packaging. The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) would oversee the program, appointing accredited certification agents no later than June 1, 2029 to review manufacturer applications and monitor compliance.

The bill would also require large grocery retailers — those selling more than 25 individual non-UPF-certified product types and generating more than $10 million in annual sales — to make certified products clearly identifiable in-store, through signage, physical separation, or other visual cues. A Public Health Food and Nutrition Education Fund would be established, funded by certification agent registration fees, to support implementation and consumer education.

HOW UPFs ARE DEFINED: The bill broadly defines UPF as any food or beverage containing one or more ingredients with a “specific technical effect,” including surface-active agents, stabilizers and thickeners, propellants, colors, and emulsifiers, among others. Products containing dyes, flavor enhancers, non-sugar sweeteners, and certain other additives would not qualify for the seal.

WHY IT MATTERS: AB 2244 would be the first state-level, government-backed certification program of its kind for non-ultra-processed foods. While the bill applies only in California, the state’s prior UPF-related legislation has prompted similar bills in other states, raising the prospect that AB 2244 could serve as a model nationally.

NCC’s TAKE: While AB 2244 is a state matter rather than a federal one, NCC has strong concerns with any effort to define or classify foods as “ultra-processed” or not, including at the state level. As outlined in NCC’s October 2025 comments to FDA and USDA, NCC believes process-based classification systems — including the NOVA framework that underlies much of the current UPF discourse — are scientifically flawed and misleading. Such systems ignore nutrient density and protein quality, apply inconsistently even among trained nutrition professionals, and lump nutritionally disparate foods together based solely on how they are made rather than what they contain. A breaded chicken tender, which delivers high-quality, complete protein along with iron, zinc and B-vitamins, is treated the same as candy or soda simply because both meet a “processed” threshold. NCC continues to urge policymakers to center any food policy on nutritional composition, not processing method, and cautions that classification schemes like AB 2244’s could stigmatize affordable, nutrient-dense foods that millions of families, schools and food assistance programs rely on.

WHAT’S NEXT: The bill heads to Governor Gavin Newsom, who has until September 30 to sign or veto it; he is expected to sign.

Are you ready for non-ultraprocessed food labels? California is

09/02/26 6:08 AM By Sara Wyant No Comments

As some Trump administration officials and MAHA influencers continue to discourage consumption of ultraprocessed foods, California lawmakers think they have a way to make your food choices easier in a new bill that will allow agents to certify and companies to label foods that are deemed as non-ultraprocessed.

The California Legislature overwhelmingly passed AB 2244 with a 32-0 vote in the Senate and a 72-0 vote in the Assembly before closing their regular legislative session for the year on Monday. Gov. Gavin Newsom has until Sept. 30 to sign or veto it, but he’s expected to sign.

Authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, D-Encino, the measure would establish a first-in-the-nation “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified” seal that food manufacturers could voluntarily place on products that meet standards for not being ultra-processed.

Gabriel said the seal would simplify shopping for consumers to find "healthier" food. "The bill also would require grocery stores in California to display products bearing the 'Non-Ultraprocessed Certified' seal, thereby making it easier for busy families to find healthier foods quickly and conveniently,” Gabriel noted in a release.

“Like the USDA organic label, this new seal will provide consumers with clear, trustworthy information and make it easier for them to locate healthier foods that are free from harmful additives," Gabriel added. "Parents shouldn't need a Ph.D. in chemistry to understand what they’re feeding their kids. California began this movement three years ago by banning the most dangerous food additives, and this week’s vote is the next big step toward protecting our kids from harmful ultra-processed foods.”

The measure builds on previous efforts to cut back on ultraprocessed foods.

The Real Food, Healthy Kids Act was signed into law by Newsom in October 2025 and mandates a gradual phaseout of UPFs in California’s public schools. It also requires the State Department of Public Health to adopt regulations by June 1, 2028, formally defining UPFs.

Under AB 2244, accredited certification agents would apply this forthcoming definition in determining product eligibility for the “California Certified” seal.

A similar effort is underway with the Non-UPF Program, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit that offers a certification label on foods, identifying them as non-ultra-processed. The organization uses a set of criteria based on the NOVA framework, which classifies foods into four groups according to their level of processing: Groups 1-3 for unprocessed or minimally processed foods, and group 4 for ultra-processed foods.

However, in California and across the country, farmers and food manufacturers will be closely watching to see how the details emerge. Some sources tell us that lawsuits are expected, but there are still several unknowns on implementation.

The bill requires the State Department of Public Health, no later than June 1, 2029, to accredit certification agents that can certify products as ″Non-Ultraprocessed Certified.″ Here are other key components:

  • It prohibits an accredited certification agent from certifying a food product as ″Non-Ultraprocessed Certified″ if it is classified as an ultraprocessed food (UPF), ultraprocessed food of concern (UPF of concern), or a restricted school food.
  • It requires DPH to create a specified standardized ″Non-Ultraprocessed Certified″ seal.
  • Authorizes a food product to bear the seal only if the product has been certified by an accredited certification agent.
  • Authorizes DPH, among other parties, including public attorneys and private entities, as specified, to enjoin a person who engages, has engages, or proposes to engage in the misuse of the seal.
  • This bill would create the Public Health Food and Nutrition Education Fund for the purposes of supporting the implementation of the Non-Ultraprocessed Certified label requirements and educating the public and stakeholders about the label requirements, food products, and nutrition. The Fund would establish fees for registration and renewal of accredited certification agents and certification of food.
  • Requires a grocery store with gross annual store sales of more than $10 million to make clearly identifiable, as defined, at least three or more ″Non-Ultraprocessed Certified″ items if the grocery store offers for sale more than 25 certified items.
  • Requires a grocery store to be deemed in compliance with this bill if it demonstrates that it has made a good faith effort to comply, as specified.
  • Repeals the provisions of this bill on Jan. 1, 2040.

Sara Wyant

JTA — La Californie s’apprête à devenir le premier État à reconnaître l’identité « juive » comme une identité ethnique et raciale, les législateurs ayant donné lundi leur accord définitif à cette loi novatrice.

Le projet de loi SB 1387, qui élargirait la définition de l’ethnicité « pour y inclure l’identité juive » dans la collecte de données démographiques, sera désormais soumis au gouverneur. Si ce texte est promulgué, les formulaires des agences de l’État permettant de déclarer volontairement son appartenance ethnique ou raciale devront également proposer l’option « juif ».

L’Assemblée de l’État et le Sénat ont tous deux donné leur accord définitif au projet de loi dans les dernières heures de la session législative californienne de 2026, qui s’est achevée lundi en fin de journée. Le gouverneur démocrate Gavin Newsom a jusqu’au 30 septembre pour signer les projets de loi ou y opposer son veto.

Le projet de loi SB 1387 sur l’appartenance ethnique a constitué une priorité pour de nombreuses organisations juives californiennes, qui font valoir que l’identité juive ne se limite pas à la seule religion — et que la loi devrait refléter cette conception.

Ce projet de loi, qui entrerait en vigueur en 2030, concernerait les formulaires émis par divers organismes, allant des écoles publiques aux agences pour l’emploi en passant par les établissements pénitentiaires. Les données collectées serviraient à alimenter des initiatives de recherche, à identifier les disparités et à orienter les décisions politiques, tout en interdisant la divulgation d’informations personnelles, conformément au texte.

Outre le projet de loi SB 1387, cinq autres projets de loi concernant les 1,2 million de Juifs de l’État, et qui ont bénéficié du soutien de la Jewish California Coalition (JCC), sont en passe d’être soumis au gouverneur.

Dimanche, l’Assemblée législative a adopté le projet de loi AB 1853, qui interdit la présence d’informations menaçantes, fausses ou trompeuses dans les guides électoraux californiens. La JCC, qui représente 43 associations, s’est félicitée de l’avancement de ce texte, soulignant que 54 groupes juifs avaient exprimé leur soutien au projet de loi dans les 48 heures suivant son dépôt.

« Les discours de haine n’ont pas leur place dans un document approuvé par l’État et financé par l’argent des contribuables », a déclaré David Bocarsly, PDG de Jewish California Coalition, dans un communiqué.

« Le projet de loi AB 1853 affirme avec force que les documents électoraux officiels de notre État ne peuvent pas être utilisés pour diffuser des théories du complot et des idées sectaires », a ajouté Bocarsly, dont la coalition était non seulement l’un des promoteurs de ce projet de loi, mais aussi de celui portant le numéro SB 1387.

Dimanche également, les législateurs ont approuvé le projet de loi AB 2664, intitulé « Safe Worship Zone Act » (loi sur les zones de sécurité autour des lieux de culte), qui créerait une zone de 30 mètres autour des entrées des lieux de culte, dans laquelle personne ne pourrait s’approcher à moins de 2,4 mètres d’un fidèle sans son consentement.

Ce projet de loi, qui a reçu le soutien d’une vaste coalition interconfessionnelle, s’inspire de la loi du Colorado sur les « zones de protection » (bubble zone law), qui assure la sécurité des patients aux abords des centres de santé reproductive.

« La montée de l’antisémitisme est indéniable et nos communautés doivent être protégées », a déclaré la députée démocrate Rebecca Bauer-Kahan, auteure du projet de loi, dans un communiqué.

« Le projet de loi AB 2664 offre aux collectivités un outil important pour lutter contre le harcèlement et l’intimidation et pour protéger le caractère sacré de nos lieux de culte », a ajouté Bauer-Kahan.

Par ailleurs, jeudi, l’Assemblée législative a approuvé la loi AB 395, qui imposerait aux organismes publics, aux établissements scolaires de la maternelle à la terminale et aux universités publiques d’éviter de programmer des événements ou des réunions majeurs les jours « où le public ne serait pas en mesure d’y participer ou d’y assister en raison de la célébration rituelle d’une fête religieuse, culturelle ou ancestrale ».

Parmi les fêtes juives qui seraient inscrites sur la liste de ces jours fériés figurent Rosh HaShana, Yom Kippour ainsi que le premier et les deux derniers jours de Pessah.

« Depuis trop longtemps et dans trop de communautés, les minorités religieuses et les autres croyants ont été contraints de faire des choix difficiles les jours qui comptent le plus pour eux », a déclaré Jesse Gabriel, député démocrate et auteur du projet de loi, dans un communiqué.

« Cette législation contribuerait à mettre fin à cette injustice et à garantir que les Californiens de toutes origines puissent participer pleinement, en particulier lorsque des décisions importantes sont prises », a ajouté Gabriel, qui préside le California Legislative Jewish Caucus.

Jeudi, les législateurs ont également approuvé un autre projet de loi de Gabriel, l’AB 1836, qui vise à combler une lacune dans la structure actuelle du programme californien de subventions à la sécurité des associations à but non lucratif (California State Nonprofit Security Grant Program). Ce programme allouant des fonds de sécurité uniquement aux locaux physiques d’une association à but non lucratif, les événements organisés hors site, tels que les allumages de la menorah à Hanoukka, n’étaient pas éligibles.

Un cinquième projet de loi concernant la communauté juive, l’AB 1763, est également en passe d’être soumis au gouverneur Newsom après son adoption par l’Assemblée mardi dernier. Ce projet de loi permettrait de considérer la célébration des fêtes religieuses comme un motif d’absence justifiée à l’école, sans qu’une demande écrite d’un parent ou d’un tuteur soit requise.
