Calif. Bill Creating 'Non-Ultraprocessed' Food Label Sent To Governor

Shelby Report Staff

The California Legislature has passed a bill that would create a state-certified “non-ultra-processed” food label and require large grocery stores to highlight certified products in-store. The measure has been passed along to Gov. Gavin Newsom for his signature. He has until Sept. 30 to sign.

Assembly Bill 2244, authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, D-Encino, would establish a state certification program for products that are not classified as ultra-processed under state law, creating a standardized seal reading “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified.” Products containing additives such as dyes, flavor enhancers, non-sugar sweeteners and certain processing aids would not qualify.

Of particular note for retailers, the bill would require grocery stores that sell more than 25 individual non-UPF-certified product types and generate more than $10 million in annual sales to display certified products in a way that is easy for consumers to identify, such as through special signage or physical separation within the store.

“Parents shouldn’t need a Ph.D. in chemistry to understand what they’re feeding their kids,” Gabriel said. “AB 2244 will empower consumers with clear, trustworthy information and make it easier for them to locate healthier foods that are free from harmful additives. This new seal doesn’t limit consumer choice, it just makes informed choice possible.”

How certification would work

If signed, the California Department of Public Health would oversee independent certification of qualifying products by approved third-party agents, which the department would be directed to accredit no later than June 1, 2029. Products would require recertification at least every three years.

The bill includes oversight provisions:

  • Certification agents must register with the state and disclose all certified products;
  • The state can audit certification records at any time and would maintain a public online list of certified products; and
  • Misuse of the label would be subject to enforcement.

AB 2244 builds on Gabriel’s AB 1264, signed last October, which established the first U.S. legal definition of ultra-processed foods and set a phased removal of “UPFs of concern” from California K-12 public schools by 2032.

The Environmental Working Group cosponsored the bill. “This is about setting a higher bar for what we consider healthy food and helping consumers make wise choices,” said Bernadette Del Chiaro, SVP for California for EWG. Supporters point to research associating diets high in ultra-processed foods with health conditions including cardiovascular disease and Type 2 diabetes.

Industry pushback on UPF definitions

The bill advances as the FDA and USDA work toward a federally recognized uniform definition of ultra-processed foods, an effort the packaged food industry has sharply criticized. In an Aug. 10 statement on the federal definition, Rhonda Bentz, EVP of public affairs for the Consumer Brands Association, said any definition capturing a broad swath of the food supply “lacks a sound scientific foundation” and warned it would create consumer confusion and increase grocery costs.

“America’s packaged food supply is safe and has been a staple in American households for decades,” Bentz said, adding that “any so-called definition that captures nearly 80 percent of the nation’s food supply while picking winners and losers is fundamentally flawed, not based on sound science and politically motivated.”

California’s separate push raises the prospect of differing state and federal standards for manufacturers and retailers navigating labeling requirements.

California bill to classify Jews as an ethnic group heads to Newsom

Asaf Elia-Shalev

California is on track to become the first state to classify “Jewish” as an ethnic identity for the purpose of collecting demographic data, after lawmakers gave final approval to SB 1387 in the closing hours of the 2026 legislative session on Aug. 31.

The votes on the bill weren’t close. Lawmakers in both houses overwhelmingly supported the legislation, which would require state agencies to list “Jewish” as an option on government forms that give Californians the choice of selecting their ancestry or ethnicity.

The bill now heads to the desk of Gov. Gavin Newsom, who has until Sept. 30 to sign it into law or veto it. If he does nothing, the bill becomes law without his signature.

With an estimated 1.2 million Jews, California is home to the second-largest Jewish population of any state, trailing only New York. 

Existing law recognizes Jewish only as a religious identity, which supporters of the bill call a misclassification. They say the bill is needed to ensure Jewish Californians are accurately counted in state data, helping track everything from antisemitic hate crimes to disparities in public health and education.

“Good data makes good policy, and this bill means hate crime reports, health surveys, and education data will finally reflect who we actually are,” David Bocarsly, CEO of Jewish California, an advocacy coalition of more than 40 groups, said in a statement. 

The bill drew support from many Bay Area Jewish organizations including the Jewish Federation Bay Area, Jewish Family and Children’s Services, Jewish Silicon Valley and the Bay Area Center to Counter Antisemitism.

Not everyone in the Jewish community backs the bill. Opponents, including two California chapters of Jewish Voice for Peace, Berkeley’s Beyt Tikkun Synagogue and the Workers Circle of Northern California, argue the measure is unnecessary and potentially risky, pointing to the historic use of lists of Jews to target them.

If the bill becomes law, the new Jewish category won’t take effect until Jan. 1, 2029, giving agencies such as public schools, the state employment service and prisons time to update their forms and data systems. Agencies can seek an exemption only if compliance would cost them federal funding. The timeline mirrors a 2025 law, AB 91, which added similar categories for Middle Eastern and North African ancestries, including Israel, and is on the same 2029 schedule.

Five other bills backed by Jewish California also made it to the governor’s desk, marking an overwhelming success rate for the coalition this session.

Lawmakers approved the Safe Worship Zone Act, AB 2664, which creates a 100-foot buffer around house-of-worship entrances in which no one may approach a congregant within 8 feet without consent. Modeled on a Colorado law protecting reproductive-health clinic patients, the bill drew backing from a wide interfaith coalition and came as a reaction to protests outside Los Angeles synagogues in 2024 that left congregants feeling harassed and intimidated. It defeated critics concerned that it would restrict free-speech and protest rights near religious sites that also host political events.

“The rise of antisemitism is undeniable, and our communities must be protected,” Assemblymember Rebecca Bauer-Kahan, the bill’s author and East Bay representative, said in a statement. “AB 2664 gives communities an important tool to push back against harassment and intimidation and protect the sanctity of our houses of worship.”

Lawmakers also passed AB 1853, which bars threatening, false and misleading information from California voter guides. It was introduced after a candidate statement containing antisemitic conspiracy theories and white nationalist rhetoric was mailed to 23 million households ahead of the June primary. 

Also approved was AB 1836, expanding the state’s Nonprofit Security Grant Program to cover off-site events like Pride parades and outdoor religious gatherings such as menorah lightings.

Lawmakers passed AB 395, requiring state agencies and public colleges to make a “good faith, reasonable effort” to avoid scheduling major events on religious and cultural holidays. It marks the first time that Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and Passover have been written into California statute. 

“For too long and in too many communities, religious minorities and other people of faith have been asked to make difficult choices on the days that matter most to them,” Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, the bill’s author, said in a statement. Gabriel, who represents San Fernando Valley, chairs the California Legislative Jewish Caucus.

Lawmakers also approved AB 1763, guaranteeing K-12 students an excused absence for religious holidays, removing a requirement that parents get prior written approval.

SACRAMENTO — The last budget bill of California’s two-year legislative session cleared the Assembly on Tuesday, 60 to 11, sending Governor Gavin Newsom a measure that releases roughly $2.7 billion in climate bond money, $450 million in transit grants, and $5 million for the state’s wolf program. Democrats presented the bill as a shield against federal policy. Republicans argued that a state collecting more revenue than ever is spending it on the wrong things, and they gave most of the debate to a single $20 million line item.

The measure is what the Capitol calls a budget bill junior. Rather than replace the Budget Act of 2026, which Newsom signed on June 29, Assembly Bill 113 amends it to finish appropriations lawmakers deliberately left open in June, most of them the climate spending the two houses could not settle before the summer recess. Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, a Democrat from Encino who chairs the Assembly Budget Committee, presented it on the floor. Because the bill carries an urgency clause, it needed a two-thirds vote, or 54 of the Assembly’s 80 members, and it takes effect the moment the Governor signs it. The clause also allowed the vote to happen at all, since the state Constitution bars most bills from passing on or after September 1 in an even-numbered year.

Two accounts of the same budget

Gabriel opened by measuring the budget against Washington rather than against the Assembly’s Republicans. He told members the Legislature had balanced the state’s books for two years rather than one, shielded health care and safety-net programs from the reductions in H.R. 1, and placed a constitutional amendment strengthening the Rainy Day Fund on the November ballot. “The budget is the ultimate group project,” he said, thanking the committee for 65 hearings.

Assemblymember David Tangipa of Fresno, the budget committee’s vice chair, answered on the size of the budget rather than its contents. “The state of California has never had more money available to it,” he said, arguing that a record year undercuts the majority’s account of hard choices. He said the plan assumes the stock market will keep performing indefinitely, warned that a correction would arrive sooner rather than later, and said the Legislative Analyst’s Office has told lawmakers the budget has grown too convoluted to track. “Math doesn’t play partisan games,” he said.

Republicans built the rest of their opposition around $20 million for the California Highway Patrol. As KCRA first reported the night before the vote, the money would pay for officers to serve as personal security for current and former state elected officials and their families depending on the results of a threat assessment, and it would come out of the Motor Vehicle Account that drivers pay into through registration fees. Assemblymember Jeff Gonzalez, a Republican whose 36th Assembly District covers the southeastern corner of the state, described the appropriation as protection for the families of Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris, and said his own district cannot get officers for its highways. “We desperately need more CHP resources to patrol Highway 74, Highway 371, and our entire mountain communities,” he said.

The Governor’s office defended the spending as routine. “Protecting current and former officials facing credible threats as a result of their public service has long been a bipartisan notion, and these security decisions are based solely on threat assessments by law enforcement,” spokesman Brandon Richards told KCRA. Senate Republicans objected to the funding source rather than the purpose. Senator Roger Niello, the Republican vice chair of the Senate Budget Committee, said the Motor Vehicle Account is forecast to run out of money within two to three years, and noted that California already allows campaign funds to be spent on security. “It is in my opinion inappropriate, and it might even be unconstitutional,” Niello said.

The security money produced the sharpest exchange on the floor. Assemblymember Chris Rogers, a Democrat from Santa Rosa, said he did not want to spend it either, then told Republicans to consider their own social media posts and the threats members’ families have described. Assemblymember Joe Patterson, a Republican from Rocklin, called the suggestion that Republicans were endangering colleagues “complete and utter bull crap,” and pointed to the assassination attempts on President Donald Trump.

Assemblymember Sharon Quirk-Silva, a Democrat from Fullerton who chaired the budget subcommittee on state administration, urged opponents into the process rather than out of it. “Get involved in the budget, go to hearings,” she said. She said her constituents are counting pennies over rent, groceries, and whether a child can sign up for soccer, and that responsibility for affordability is shared. “We all have work to do together, my friends,” she said.

Closing, Gabriel returned to federal policy. He cited the health care reductions in H.R. 1, tariffs he called taxes on goods Americans need, and what he described as Washington politicizing disaster aid in the state that sends the most tax money to the federal government. He asked for an aye vote “because this budget invests in all of our communities.”

Five million dollars for wolf conflicts

Assembly Bill 113 raises the Department of Fish and Wildlife’s General Fund support from $180,595,000 to $185,595,000 and assigns the entire increase to wolves: “$2,500,000 shall be available for wolf-livestock compensation and $2,500,000 shall be available for other related activities including, but not limited to, rapid-response and wolf management needs.”

The money arrives after the state’s compensation program spent more than two years with almost nothing to pay out. The Legislature created the Wolf-Livestock Compensation Pilot Program with $3 million in the 2021 Budget Act, and the Department of Fish and Wildlife exhausted the fund in March 2024. A later $600,000 appropriation was small enough that the department narrowed the program to direct livestock losses, dropping applications for nonlethal deterrents and for the “pay for presence” payments meant to offset the cost of ranching inside wolf territory.

In January, the California Farm Bureau, the California Cattlemen’s Association, and the Rural County Representatives of California asked lawmakers for $30 million for the wolf program in the 2026-27 budget, including $25 million for compensation and deterrence and roughly $1 million for additional department staff. The budget Newsom signed in June contained none of it. Tuesday’s $5 million is the first substantial state money the program has received since the pilot fund ran dry.

State Senator Megan Dahle, a Republican from Bieber whose First Senate District covers 14 counties across the northeastern corner of the state, announced the appropriation Tuesday afternoon. Dahle said what ranchers most need is for wolves to be removed from state and federal endangered species protections and for permits allowing them to act when wolves attack livestock. “For now, that means we need a consistently funded compensation program and other support for ranchers,” she said. Her office said the second $2.5 million could pay for investigations of suspected attacks, collaring wolves, and tracking wolf activity in areas the animals have newly reached, none of which the bill itself specifies.

A companion measure is already on the Governor’s desk. Senate Bill 1135, by Senator Catherine Blakespear, a Democrat from Encinitas, renames the pilot the California Wolf-Livestock Coexistence and Compensation Program and writes it into the Fish and Game Code alongside a broader wildlife coexistence program. The Assembly passed it 58 to 17 on August 19, the Senate concurred 31 to 9 on August 26, and it was presented to the Governor on August 31. The bill appropriates nothing on its own; each program it creates operates only upon appropriation by the Legislature.

The bill’s larger natural resources spending comes almost entirely from Proposition 4, the climate bond voters approved in 2024. It sends $60 million to the Department of Conservation for the Regional Forest and Fire Capacity Program, which distributes block grants by region for wildfire planning and project development. CAL FIRE receives a series of local assistance appropriations from the same bond, among them $61.4 million for fire prevention and $19.6 million in grants covering fuel reduction, defensible space, and reforestation.

<h1 class="entry-title mb-4">California Homelessness Prevention Bill Heads to Newsom as Advocates Urge Signature</h1> </header>
<article class="post-268568 post type-post status-publish format-standard has-post-thumbnail hentry category-breaking-news category-homeless-state-of-california category-state-of-california tag-ab-1924 tag-all-home tag-california-housing tag-destination-home tag-homelessness-prevention tag-inner-city-law-center author-dmg" id="post-268568">

<div class="post-meta"><span class="post-meta__author">By <a href="https://davisvanguard.org/author/dmg/">David M. Greenwald</a></span><span class="post-meta__date">September 1, 2026</span></div>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">SACRAMENTO, Calif. — California lawmakers have sent legislation establishing the state’s first comprehensive homelessness prevention strategy to Gov. Gavin Newsom, shifting the focus from responding to people after they lose their housing toward preventing homelessness before it occurs.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Assembly Bill 1924, authored by Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel, D-Encino, and Sharon Quirk-Silva, D-Fullerton, cleared the Senate on a 40-0 vote and the Assembly 77-1. The measure now awaits action from Newsom, who has until Sept. 30 to sign or veto it.</p><div class="mmt-a9c22174-2d36-40ea-b2b4-d05c75d4e743 mmt-primary" id="mmt-a9c22174-2d36-40ea-b2b4-d05c75d4e743_1" style="display: block;"><div id="mmt-a9c22174-2d36-40ea-b2b4-d05c75d4e743_1_zone" style="visibility: visible !important;"><div class="videoMainContainer" id="mmt-a9c22174-2d36-40ea-b2b4-d05c75d4e743_1_1_ad" style="pointer-events: auto;"><div data-stn-player="rkmiwj3w"><stn-player data-stn-player="rkmiwj3w" style="display: block; <p class="wp-block-paragraph">Inner City Law Center, a co-sponsor of AB 1924, is joining Destination: Home and All Home in urging Newsom to sign the legislation, arguing that California cannot meaningfully reduce homelessness without addressing the flow of people losing their housing each year.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The legislation marks the latest development in an effort previously covered by the Vanguard as lawmakers sought to move California’s homelessness policy upstream, emphasizing prevention alongside the billions of dollars the state has invested in shelters, services and permanent housing.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">California has nearly 190,000 people experiencing homelessness, according to supporters of AB 1924. For every person who exits homelessness, nearly three people experience homelessness for the first time, a ratio that rises to four newly homeless people for every person exiting homelessness in Los Angeles County.</p>

This legislation will implement a proven strategy and require real accountability so we can finally start to move the needle on this terrible crisis.”</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">AB 1924 would direct the California Interagency Council on Homelessness to develop a statewide homelessness prevention strategy with measurable goals and accountability measures.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Relevant state agencies would also be required to develop their own homelessness prevention action plans, while the state would identify and distribute evidence-based model practices that local governments and service providers could adopt.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The approach is intended to create a statewide framework around prevention programs that already operate in Santa Clara and Sonoma counties and elsewhere in California.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Some existing programs use homelessness prevention units to identify people considered at high risk of losing their housing and intervene before they enter homelessness. Supporters argue that California currently lacks a statewide framework for connecting those programs, evaluating their effectiveness and expanding successful approaches.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">“California cannot solve homelessness by waiting until someone has already lost their home. We must do more to keep people housed in the first place, especially when timely support can prevent a family from losing everything,” Quirk-Silva said.</p>

width: 728px; height: 280px; overflow: hidden;"><div id="google_ads_iframe_/20842576,22780797127/CUC01M/CUC01M-DDI.A_1__container__" style="border: 0pt; margin: auto; text-align: center;"></div></div></div></div></div><p class="wp-block-paragraph">“AB 1924 gives California a stronger framework to identify what works, coordinate prevention efforts, and measure whether we are reaching the people who need help before they enter homelessness,” she continued. “Thank you, Assemblymember Gabriel, for ensuring California is smarter with our resources and giving families a better chance to remain safely and securely housed.”</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The legislation reflects an increasingly prominent argument among homelessness advocates: California’s response cannot rely exclusively on providing services and housing after people become homeless if new households continue falling into homelessness faster than others can exit.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Mike Feuer, senior policy adviser at Inner City Law Center, said prevention offers both a humanitarian and fiscal alternative to waiting until people have already lost their homes.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">“Preventing homelessness is much more humane and vastly less expensive than waiting to react to it. Yet for all California’s investments on homelessness, the state has done little to prevent it in the first place,” Feuer said.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">“This bill makes prevention a strategic priority, moving California toward the cutting edge of nationwide efforts to solve our homelessness crisis.”</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">All Home Interim CEO Brett Andrews pointed to existing prevention efforts in both Northern and Southern California as evidence that a broader strategy could work.</p>
<div class="mmt-biacdsid-f2ic-jitb-kmil-ictoamttthtc mmt-primary mmt-flight mmt-repeatable mmt-r-other" id="mmt-biacdsid-f2ic-jitb-kmil-ictoamttthtc_3" style="display: block;"><div id="mmt-biacdsid-f2ic-jitb-kmil-ictoamttthtc_3_zone" style="display: flex; width: 320px; height: 50px; overflow: hidden;"><div id="google_ads_iframe_/20842576,22780797127/CUC01M/CUC01M-DDI.A_2__container__" style="border: 0pt; margin: auto; text-align: center;"></div></div></div></div></div><p class="wp-block-paragraph">“We’ve seen prevention programs in the Bay Area and Los Angeles start turning the tide on people becoming homeless,” Andrews said. “This bill would direct California to develop a statewide strategy to implement these critical programs for the first time.”</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">“Independent researchers have proven how effective homelessness prevention can be at keeping people housed even months after they received assistance, and we hope the state will build off this experience to bring these programs statewide,” Andrews added.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">Destination: Home CEO Jennifer Loving similarly argued that preventing people from losing housing should become a central component of California’s response to homelessness.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">“The best way to end homelessness is to stop it before it starts. Prevention is not only the most compassionate approach, it is also cost-effective, proven to work, and gives families a chance to stay safely housed before a crisis becomes a catastrophe,” Loving said.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">“California has an opportunity right now to make prevention a priority through AB 1924 and take a meaningful first step toward helping thousands of families stay in their homes.”</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">The legislation would not replace California’s existing investments in shelters, supportive housing and other programs serving people who are already homeless. Instead, it seeks to establish prevention as a coordinated component of the state’s broader homelessness strategy.</p>

height: 250px;"></div></div></div></div></div><p class="wp-block-paragraph">That distinction is significant because the state has spent heavily on responding to homelessness after people lose their housing while continuing to face a substantial inflow of newly homeless residents.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">AB 1924 would attempt to address that gap by requiring statewide goals, agency action plans, accountability measures and evidence-based practices intended to help local governments intervene earlier.</p>
<p class="wp-block-paragraph">With overwhelming bipartisan support in both chambers of the Legislature, the decision now rests with Newsom. The governor has until Sept. 30 to determine whether the statewide prevention strategy becomes law.</p>

Another ‘Housing First’ Bill Passed by Legislature: No Fixed Timelines for Reductions, No Automatic Consequences if Goals are Missed – California Globe

Friday, the California Legislature passed Assembly Bill 1924 by Assemblyman Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), and Assemblywoman Sharon Quirk-Silva (D-Fullerton), legislation they say is “poised to address a critical part of California’s homelessness epidemic by preventing displacement before it occurs.”

It’s another bill banging on the “Housing First” drum. It specifically says right on the bill, “An act relating to housing.” It sounds like yet another funding vehicle to nonprofits and NGAs, to “house” the homeless – but before they are homeless?

However, far too much of homeless housing throughout the state sits empty, while dubious nonprofits linked to the housing projects are facing federal fraud charges. So why would lawmakers keep allocating money for failed and fraudulent housing plans?

The original bill language proposed establishing a new Secretary of Housing and Homelessness, but Governor Gavin Newsom already did that in last year’s budget, as successors to parts of the former Business, Consumer Services, and Housing Agency. Governor Newsom appointed and swore in Tomiquia Moss as the first Secretary around June 30, 2026.

The bill directs the state to build California’s first comprehensive homelessness prevention strategy, complete with measurable goals, accountability benchmarks, and model best practices that cities and counties can use as guidance, the authors claim.

What AB 1924 does is requires the California Interagency Council on Homelessness to develop and publicly issue a statewide homelessness prevention strategy by July 1, 2028, and incorporate it into the council’s Action Plan to Prevent and End Homelessness.

If anyone at the state could actually have developed a “statewide homelessness prevention strategy,” we wouldn’t need AB 1924, or any other ongoing homeless spending bill – given that the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office reported that since 2019, California government has spent $37 billion on housing-and-homelessness-related programs… and we still have more than 190,000 homeless living on the streets. 

Also, according to the actual bill, AB 1924 does not set specific targets. 

The authors state “Nearly 190,000 Californians are experiencing homelessness, and for every person who exits it, nearly three more fall into homelessness for the first time — a ratio that climbs to 4-to-1 in regions like Los Angeles County.”

Laughably, “AB 1924 directs the state to spend that money more efficiently, by keeping people from falling in the first place.”

So now lawmakers and their appointees are going to double down on homelessness spending by attempting to “prevent” it, after failing to decrease the homeless population in nearly eight years under Gov. Gavin Newsom.

The strategy under AB 1924 must include:

  • A baseline estimate of first-time homelessness and progress assessments.
  • Inventories of definitions, current actions, gaps, and state resources for prevention.
  • Agency-specific homelessness prevention action plans (developed with council staff, limited to each agency’s existing authority and resources).
  • Recommendations for coordination, high-impact activities, and legislative/executive actions.
  • Statewide goals, metrics, and evidence-based model practices (targeting those at risk via factors like prior homelessness, income at or below 30% of area median income, rent burden; interventions such as emergency rental assistance, eviction defense, case management; data use; and coordination).

The bill explicitly limits new work: agencies do not have to collect new primary data, build predictive models, stand up new reporting systems, or expand programs. They must use reasonably available information.

There are no statutory numerical targets, no fixed timelines for reductions, and no automatic consequences if goals are missed. Everything is constrained to existing authority and resources, so the metrics may describe coordination more than new capacity, leaving a lot of wiggle room for no results, but lots of taxpayer funding spent. 

“Achievable progress” language gives the council flexibility but also room to set soft goals.

Third-party evaluations of selected programs are only recommended, not required.

In short, AB 1924 creates a framework for prevention metrics rather than the metrics themselves. 

The bill now awaits the Governor’s signature or veto. 

AB 1924 passed the State Senate by a 40-0 vote, and the State Assembly by a vote of 77-1. Only Assemblyman Carl DeMaio voted against AB 1924. Were the others thinking that this bill may actually solve homelessness, or was voting on it just the path of least resistance?

The Legislature fights back

By BLAKE JONES, RACHEL BLUTH, MELANIE MASON and DUSTIN GARDINER

CAUGHT IN A JAM — Gavin Newsom usually gets what he wants from the California Legislature, which made his concessions in an eleventh-hour wildfire liability push all the more striking.

A final deal reached over the weekend dropped the governor’s most contentious proposals, including eliminating insurance companies’ ability to recoup losses from a wildfire recovery fund, limiting payouts for emotional distress and preventing local governments from recovering the full cost of replacing damaged infrastructure.

The rare stumble — coming in the final months of Newsom’s tenure — marked an uncommon show of defiance by a Legislature that hasn’t overridden a veto in decades and has acquiesced when the governor made late pushes for a suite of environmental laws in 2022 and an infrastructure package the following year.

Lawmakers, staffers and other negotiators who spoke to Playbook attributed the governor’s loss to a slew of factors, including the tight timeline on which he demanded major changes to a politically fraught policy with billions of dollars at stake.

“My hope is that the incoming governor is going to be in lockstep conversations with us, so we can get to solutions before the last day of session,” state Sen. Lola Smallwood-Cuevas said. (A spokesperson for Xavier Becerra, the front-runner to succeed Newsom, did not respond to a request for comment on the deal.)

Members often attribute their willingness to acquiesce to the governor to the leverage he holds by having power over whether their bills are signed or vetoed — which is still the case this year. But soon, he’ll lose that authority, which is making at least one Democratic lawmaker openly consider a precedent-breaking veto override.

“I would hope our leadership would look at that, because he’s not going to be here next year. There will be nothing sensitive if we override vetoes and he’s not here,” said state Sen. Caroline Menjivar.

To some members, Newsom had simply asked for too much. The governor met resistance in the Senate, in particular, where the energy committee chair is state Sen. Ben Allen, a Democrat from a wildfire-stricken Los Angeles region currently in a tight election for statewide insurance commissioner. He said Newsom went a “step too far” in proposing to eliminate the ability of insurance companies to recoup some of their losses from power companies, a move that insurers and consumer advocates said could raise premiums and lower coverage in fire-prone areas.

The governor’s plan set off an all-out lobbying fight after he unveiled it earlier this month. Outside groups poured millions of dollars into swaying legislators, and a broad coalition of insurers, local governments and consumer advocates came out against it.

“The primary challenge was the volume of the opposition from the institutional stakeholders — including insurance companies, hedge funds, and trial lawyers — who have made billions off the current system,” said Newsom adviser Ann Patterson.

In a year where political campaigns have increasingly railed against utilities, taking any action that could be seen as a win for utilities was a political nonstarter for some.

“What he was doing was incredibly unpopular,” said a senior Senate staffer granted anonymity to describe private negotiations. “When he runs for president in two years, I’ll be happy. I’ll be happy they can’t use this against him.”

from Noah Baustin, Jeremy B. White, Marisa Guerra Echeverria and Camille von Kaenel on how — and why — Newsom’s late-session drive fell short.

California prepara una etiqueta para alimentos no ultraprocesados

Velsid

Para responder a la falta de un criterio federal unificado, California ha impulsado una etiqueta para alimentos no ultraprocesados, basada en un sello oficial auditado y con presencia obligatoria en grandes supermercados, buscando así ofrecer a los consumidores una guía clara y directa que les ayude en sus compras diarias. …

California prepara una etiqueta para alimentos no ultraprocesados que pretende facilitar a los consumidores la identificación de productos que no encajan en la categoría de alimentos ultraprocesados. El proyecto AB 2244, impulsado por el asambleísta Jesse Gabriel, propone crear un sello oficial denominado «Non-Ultraprocessed Certified» y establecer un sistema de certificación independiente supervisado por las autoridades sanitarias del Estado.

El proyecto ha avanzado con rapidez en la legislatura californiana, aunque todavía debe completar su tramitación antes de llegar al gobernador Gavin Newsom. La iniciativa resulta especialmente interesante por una razón que puede pasar desapercibida, el hecho de que Estados Unidos no cuenta todavía con una definición federal única y generalmente aceptada de qué es exactamente un alimento ultraprocesado.

De hecho, la propia FDA (Administración de Alimentos y Medicamentos) y el Departamento de Agricultura de Estados Unidos (USDA) reconocieron esta situación en el 2025, cuando pusieron en marcha un proceso conjunto para intentar desarrollar una definición uniforme de los denominados UPF (ultra-processed foods) para todo el país. Surge una pregunta de forma casi inevitable: si Washington todavía está intentando decidir qué debe entenderse jurídicamente como alimento ultraprocesado, ¿cómo puede California crear mientras tanto una etiqueta oficial para identificar los alimentos que no lo son?

El pasado mes de octubre, Gavin Newsom firmó la AB 1264, una ley pionera que introdujo en California una definición legal de alimento ultraprocesado, estableciendo también medidas para retirar progresivamente de los comedores escolares los productos considerados especialmente preocupantes. Por tanto, ya no es correcto afirmar que en todo Estados Unidos no existe ninguna definición legal de alimento ultraprocesado; lo que no existe es una definición federal uniforme. California dispone de una definición legal propia para determinados fines, mientras que el Gobierno federal todavía trabaja en la suya.

Funcionamiento del sistema de certificación «Non-Ultraprocessed Certified»

El proyecto no pretende esperar a que Washington termine su proceso. Si finalmente se convierte en ley, California creará el sello «Non-Ultraprocessed Certified» que solamente podrán utilizar los productos certificados por agentes acreditados del Departamento de Salud Pública de California. Estos agentes tendrán que estar registrados, facilitar información sobre los productos certificados y someterse a posibles auditorías. Además, el Estado mantendrá una lista pública de los alimentos que cuenten con la certificación.

El sistema también contempla que la certificación no sea permanente, los productos alimenticios deberán ser recertificados cada tres años y, si se reformulan, tendrán que volver a obtener la certificación antes de poder continuar utilizando el sello acreditativo. El objetivo es evitar que un producto pueda conservar indefinidamente una etiqueta aunque su composición haya cambiado.

Pero la propuesta va incluso más allá del envase: los grandes supermercados que superen los 10 millones de dólares de ventas anuales y comercialicen más de 25 productos certificados deberán hacer claramente identificables al menos tres de ellos mediante separación física, carteles u otros elementos visuales. La idea es que la información no quede escondida en la letra pequeña del etiquetado, sino que pueda utilizarse directamente en el momento de comprar.

El reto de la identificación para el consumidor

Aquí aparece uno de los elementos más interesantes de este proyecto: el problema de los alimentos ultraprocesados no es únicamente determinar qué productos entran en la categoría, sino también conseguir que el consumidor pueda reconocerlos de una forma sencilla. La información nutricional y la lista de ingredientes ya existen, pero interpretar determinados ingredientes, aditivos y funciones tecnológicas puede resultar complicado incluso para los profesionales de la nutrición.

Por eso, una etiqueta frontal o un sello de certificación puede tener un efecto diferente al de la información tradicional que aparece en el envase. En vez de obligar al consumidor a interpretar una lista de ingredientes, el sistema pretende ofrecer una respuesta mucho más sencilla: indicar que un determinado producto ha sido sometido a un procedimiento de certificación y cumple el estándar californiano para ser considerado no ultraprocesado.

Estándar californiano vs. Clasificación NOVA

Pero precisamente aquí aparece otra cuestión de fondo: ¿de qué estándar estamos hablando? En este punto es donde conviene separar dos conceptos que pueden confundirse fácilmente: la legislación californiana y la clasificación NOVA.

NOVA es probablemente el sistema de clasificación de alimentos ultraprocesados más conocido a nivel internacional. Fue desarrollado por investigadores brasileños y divide los alimentos en cuatro grandes grupos según su grado de procesamiento, situando a los ultraprocesados en el denominado grupo 4. Desde hace años esta clasificación se utiliza ampliamente en la investigación nutricional, sirviendo como referencia para estudiar la relación entre el consumo de alimentos ultraprocesados y los distintos problemas de salud.

Sin embargo, la ley AB 2244 no convierte a NOVA en una ley de California. El texto legislativo vincula la certificación «Non-Ultraprocessed Certified» a los criterios establecidos por la propia legislación californiana y, en particular, a las definiciones y criterios contenidos en las disposiciones que regulan los alimentos ultraprocesados. Esta situación tiene una consecuencia importante: si NOVA cambia, la etiqueta californiana no cambiará automáticamente.

La revisión de NOVA y el debate sobre la estabilidad jurídica

Decimos esto porque precisamente NOVA se encuentra en un momento de revisión. La clasificación que se utiliza actualmente nació en 2009 y ha recibido críticas por considerar fundamentalmente el grado y la naturaleza del procesamiento. Sus defensores aseguran que esta característica resulta esencial para comprender el papel de los ultraprocesados en la alimentación moderna, pero otros investigadores han señalado que el sistema puede ser demasiado rígido y que no siempre tiene suficientemente en cuenta el valor nutricional, la composición o la llamada matriz alimentaria del producto.

Por este motivo se ha puesto en marcha un proyecto para estudiar una posible actualización de NOVA. Entre los elementos que se pretende valorar están precisamente el contenido nutricional y la matriz alimentaria, con el propósito de conseguir una clasificación más matizada. El proyecto está dirigido por la profesora Susanne Bügel, de la Universidad de Copenhague, y está previsto que se desarrolle a lo largo de este año. La posible reforma abre un debate especialmente relevante para cualquier política pública basada en la clasificación de los ultraprocesados: si determinados productos cambian de categoría en una futura versión de NOVA, ¿deberían cambiar también las leyes y las etiquetas que se hayan construido utilizando esa clasificación?

En el caso de California al menos por ahora, la respuesta es no de forma automática. El proyecto de ley AB 2244 se apoya en una definición jurídica propia, no en la obligación de seguir cualquier futura versión de NOVA. Si NOVA fuera modificada, California tendría que decidir posteriormente si mantiene sus criterios, si los adapta o si modifica su legislación. La ventaja de esta fórmula es que proporciona estabilidad jurídica, ya que una clasificación científica externa no puede modificar por sí sola qué productos pueden llevar un sello oficial del Estado.

Pero esto también plantea un problema, si la ciencia nutricional evoluciona y una nueva clasificación internacional llega a conclusiones diferentes sobre determinados alimentos, puede aparecer una distancia entre la definición científica más reciente y el criterio utilizado por la legislación californiana.

El contexto regulatorio en Estados Unidos

Mientras California ya ha establecido una definición legal para determinados usos y avanza hacia un sistema de certificación de productos no ultraprocesados, el Gobierno federal está intentando construir una definición que pueda aplicarse de forma uniforme en todo el país. La FDA y el USDA solicitaron en 2025 información sobre prácticamente todos los elementos que podrían utilizarse para definir un UPF: ingredientes, aditivos, procesos físicos, biológicos y químicos, composición nutricional, densidad energética e incluso características como la palatabilidad. También preguntaron expresamente si el término «ultraprocesado» es el más adecuado para describir esta categoría de alimentos.

Esto demuestra que la cuestión está bastante lejos de ser puramente semántica. Definir un alimento como ultraprocesado puede tener consecuencias regulatorias, comerciales y de etiquetado. Una definición demasiado amplia podría incluir productos que no tienen las mismas características nutricionales o sanitarias, mientras que una demasiado restrictiva podría dejar fuera productos alimenticios que precisamente pretenden ser objeto de las nuevas políticas de salud pública.

Además, los distintos estados están buscando soluciones diferentes. De hecho, la propia documentación federal del 2025 recogía propuestas estatales que utilizaban criterios basados en determinados ingredientes, procesos de fabricación o combinaciones de ingredientes. La ausencia de una definición federal común ha permitido, por tanto, que aparezcan diferentes aproximaciones jurídicas dentro del mismo país.

Un cambio de paradigma: la señal positiva al consumidor

California intenta ahora dar un paso adicional, no solamente prohibir o restringir determinados productos en las escuelas, sino también crear una señal positiva para los consumidores. En vez de limitarse a decir qué alimentos son problemáticos, el Estado pretende identificar aquellos que cumplen un estándar para poder ser considerados «no ultraprocesados». Se trata de un cambio de perspectiva significativo: la regulación tradicional suele centrarse en advertencias, prohibiciones o restricciones, mientras que la ley AB 2244 plantea utilizar la certificación como herramienta de mercado, dando visibilidad a determinados productos y facilitando que los consumidores puedan localizarlos en los supermercados.

Queda una última cuestión que será decisiva: ¿qué productos acabarán obteniendo realmente el sello? El texto aprobado por la Legislatura establece el mecanismo de certificación, la supervisión pública, las auditorías y las obligaciones de transparencia, pero serán las normas y los procedimientos de aplicación los que tendrán que convertir los criterios legales en decisiones concretas sobre los productos alimenticios.

Por tanto, la historia de la etiqueta californiana todavía no ha acabado: primero deberá culminar la tramitación legislativa de la ley AB 2244 y, posteriormente, tendrá que construirse todo el sistema administrativo que permita certificar los productos. En este sentido hay que destacar que el Departamento de Salud Pública deberá acreditar a los agentes certificadores como máximo el 1 de junio de 2029.

La paradoja californiana y el dilema global

Pero también está pendiente una cuestión mucho más amplia y de importancia: ¿qué definición acabará adoptando Estados Unidos para los alimentos ultraprocesados? California ha decidido no esperar a que exista esa respuesta federal, ha construido su propia definición legal y pretende utilizarla ahora para crear una etiqueta que ayude a los consumidores a identificar alimentos que cumplen el estándar de «no ultraprocesados». Pero la posible reforma de NOVA y el futuro estándar federal muestran que el concepto todavía está en evolución, algo que se debería señalar en este artículo de EWG (Environmental Working Group).

Precisamente esa es la paradoja: California quiere poner una etiqueta a los alimentos que no son ultraprocesados antes de que Estados Unidos haya conseguido ponerse de acuerdo sobre una definición federal única de qué es un alimento ultraprocesado. Lejos de ser un detalle técnico, esta cuestión puede determinar qué productos podrán llevar el futuro sello, cómo deberán reformularse algunos alimentos y hasta qué punto las políticas de alimentación de los distintos estados terminarán convergiendo o seguirán caminos diferentes.

El caso de California pone sobre la mesa una cuestión que va mucho más allá de Estados Unidos. En Europa tampoco existe una definición legal armonizada de «alimento ultraprocesado» y el término «natural» tampoco cuenta con una definición jurídica general que permita al consumidor saber exactamente qué significa cuando aparece asociado a un alimento. Al final, nos encontramos ante una contradicción: cada vez se utilizan más conceptos como «ultraprocesado», «natural» o «menos procesado» para orientar las decisiones de compra, pero no siempre existe un marco legal común que determine con precisión qué productos pueden utilizar esas denominaciones. Y cuando las palabras que deberían ayudar al consumidor a entender un alimento carecen de un significado claro y compartido, la información puede acabar siendo más confusa que transparente.

Mar Gavilán y Javier Muniesa

En 2005, fundamos el primer blog gastronómico colaborativo en España, que rápidamente se convirtió en un referente en el ámbito gastronómico. Para nosotros, ha sido un sueño hecho realidad combinar nuestras pasiones por la gastronomía, la creatividad y la divulgación. Ahora nuestro objetivo es inspirar, informar, deleitar y conectar con todos los entusiastas de la cocina.

Bass orders independent review after LAPD releases video of two deaths

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass announced Friday, after the LAPD released video footage from two separate incidents resulting in death, that she will issue an Executive Directive ordering an independent evaluation of officer-involved deaths and severe injuries, with particular focus on cases involving people experiencing mental health crises.

The first incident began July 13 in Chatsworth, when police responded to a report that 58-year-old Jose Carlos Hoyos-Munoz had stabbed two family members, leading to a standoff before he was taken into custody. He was later transferred to a Los Angeles jail, where LAPD officials said he became combative and uncooperative with detention officers during booking. Video released Friday showed officers using physical force, including strikes, while he was restrained and handcuffed. He was later found unconscious and not breathing in his cell and was pronounced dead at the scene, more than two weeks before LAPD made the footage public.

The second incident occurred July 29 in central Los Angeles, after a 911 caller reported 33-year-old Alejandro Garcia was walking through traffic near the 10 Freeway swinging a baseball bat and smashing car windows. Officers located Garcia, and the encounter ended when officers opened fire as he advanced toward them with the bat. He died after being taken to a hospital.

“These two videos were incredibly difficult to watch. People who experience behavioral or mental health crises often do not receive the proper care they desperately need. Without it, they can deteriorate into behavior that can result in severe injury or death,” said Bass.

“Decades of disinvestment in community-based mental and behavioral health services have left too many Angelenos without access to timely and appropriate care, increasing the likelihood that people in crisis will come into contact with law enforcement. LAPD officers do not enter the force to become first responders to mental health crises and are not equipped with the proper training to do so,” said Bass.

“Therefore, I will be issuing an Executive Directive calling for an independent evaluation of officer-involved deaths and severe injuries, with particular attention to injuries and deaths that might involve individuals experiencing a mental health crisis. This independent review will aim to identify systemic gaps, strengthen policies and training, and enhance public and officer safety. It will also examine what type of mental health support officers should receive following a critical incident,” the Mayor added.

“We must also expand civilian crisis response and co-response models that can support individuals in crisis who have not exhibited violent behavior, reducing the need for armed officers. Public safety cannot be achieved through law enforcement alone,” said Bass.

Gabriel’s bill protects Pride parades, community festivals from hate

Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino, Canoga Park, Winnetka, Calabasas, Reseda, Northridge, Tarzana, Woodland Hills, West Hills, Hidden Hills, Bell Canyon, Lake Balboa, Van Nuys, Warner Center) announced this week that his legislation (AB 1836) expanding the state’s Nonprofit Security Grant Program to cover offsite events like Pride parades and cultural festivals, passed both houses of the Legislature with unanimous bipartisan support.

Gabriel authored the bill with Assemblymember Chris Ward (D-San Diego), chair of the California Legislative LGBTQ Caucus. Since 2015, the grant program has helped hundreds of houses of worship, community centers and reproductive health clinics secure physical locations, but that funding has stopped at the front door, according to Gabriel’s office.

AB 1836 would let organizations use the grants for security at offsite gatherings as well, where the release cites recent deadly attacks at a Hanukkah celebration in Sydney and a Pride parade in Berlin as examples of the risk. The bill is sponsored by Jewish California and Equality California and backed by more than 100 organizations representing LGBTQ+, Jewish, Muslim, Hindu, Christian, Latino and Asian American communities.

“California is stepping up to protect our communities, so that Californians of all faiths and backgrounds can gather together and celebrate without fear. This bill sends a powerful message that California will continue to stand with the LGBTQ+ community and all others targeted by hate. We will never let hate win,” said Gabriel, who chairs the California Legislative Jewish Caucus.

Gabriel authored the original 2019 legislation creating California’s Nonprofit Security Grant Program, the first state-funded program of its kind in the nation, following the deadly shooting at a synagogue in Poway. The state has committed more than $380 million to the program since, and Gabriel helped secure $80 million in ongoing annual funding in this year’s state budget. In the most recent funding cycle, more than 1,600 organizations applied, making it the most popular grant program administered by the Governor’s Office of Emergency Services.

The bill now heads to Gov. Gavin Newsom’s desk, where he has until Sept. 30 to sign or veto it.

Zbur’s hotel worker bill heads to the Governor’s desk

Assemblymember Rick Chavez Zbur (D-Hollywood, West Hollywood, Beverly Hills, Santa Monica, West Los Angeles, Westwood Village) announced Sunday that his legislation (AB 2181) protecting hospitality jobs by preventing speculative development scenarios from inflating hotel and motel ground lease costs passed the state Senate and received final concurrence in the Assembly.

Many California hotels operate under long-term ground leases with rent resets tied to appraised land value, and those valuations have increasingly factored in hypothetical residential redevelopment scenarios based on density bonuses that were never actually pursued or approved, according to Zbur’s office.

“California’s density bonus laws are an important tool for encouraging more affordable housing, but they should not be used to inflate land values based on hypothetical projects that have never been pursued or approved. When speculative development scenarios drive up ground rents for operating hotels, the consequences are very real for the workers whose livelihoods depend on those businesses. AB 2181 establishes reasonable guardrails to protect hospitality jobs while preserving our important housing tools and future opportunities for redevelopment,” said Zbur.

Maria Espinoza, a housekeeper at the Sandbourne Santa Monica, said the bill matters directly to workers like her.

“Every day, I clean rooms, turn over beds, and make sure guests have a good experience. It’s hard work, and it’s work that keeps our hotels running. But too often, the people who do this work, the housekeepers, the servers, the front desk staff, don’t have a real voice in the decisions that affect our jobs and our workplaces. That’s why AB 2181 matters,” said Espinoza.

The bill now heads to Gov. Gavin Newsom for consideration.

Valladares says Senate Democrats blocked her DSA resolution

State Sen. Suzette Martinez Valladares (R-Lancaster, Palmdale, Santa Clarita, portions of the Antelope Valley) said Friday that Senate Democratic leadership refused to allow debate or a vote on her resolution condemning the Democratic Socialists of America’s (DSA) platform, a measure she authored with six Republican colleagues.

Valladares characterized the DSA platform in her release as incompatible with American values, citing the group’s positions on private property, policing and government control of economic sectors, and drew a comparison to historical governments built on Marxist and socialist foundations.

Valladares tied the resolution to broader affordability concerns in California, including high gas prices and a state unemployment debt she put at $20 billion.

“If these ideas come from real desperation over the cost of living and fear about a fading American Dream, we owe Californians an honest conversation about why this agenda is a recipe for disaster, not a slogan. We have to lower costs and expand opportunities for working families. This agenda is not compatible with American values or the values of the families I represent. It should not be controversial for my colleagues to say so,” said Valladares.

“If the DSA agenda is so defensible, debate it. If affordability and public safety are priorities, prove it. Stop silencing the people’s representatives and start delivering results for the people you serve,” added Valladares.

California Passes Bill to Create Certification Seal for Non-Ultra-Processed Foods

By Food Safety Magazine Editorial Team

August 31, 2026

The California Legislature has passed Assembly Bill 2244 (AB 2244), which would establish a first-of-its-kind state certification seal for food products that meet standards for not being ultra-processed.

Authored by California Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-46), AB 2244 has unanimously passed both the State Senate and Assembly. The legislation now heads to Governor Gavin Newsom, who has until September 30, 2026 to sign or veto the bill.

AB 2244 would create a voluntary certification program through which qualifying manufacturers could display a “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified” seal on food packaging. Modeled after the “USDA Organic” label, the certification is intended to help consumers identify products that meet California’s standards for not being ultra-processed.

The California Department of Public Health (CDPH) would oversee the certification program, under which food manufacturers could apply to accredited certification agents for authorization to use the seal. Grocery stores in California also would be required to display certified products, making them more visible to consumers.

Assemblymember Gabriel’s office previously said the certification program was intended to provide a voluntary incentive for food manufacturers to reformulate products to meet the state’s standards for non-UPFs.

California Builds on Efforts to Regulate Ultra-Processed Foods

If signed by Governor Newsom, AB 2244 would advance California’s ongoing efforts to establish policies around UPFs at a time when the definition and regulation of the category remain subjects of debate among scientists, regulators, public health experts, and industry.

AB 2244 follows California’s Real Food, Healthy Kids Act (AB 1264), which Governor Newsom signed into law in 2025. The law established the country’s first statutory framework for defining ultra-processed foods (UPFs) and created a process for identifying and phasing out certain UPFs from California schools.

The Real Food, Healthy Kids Act categorizes UPFs as those high in saturated fat, added sugar, or sodium, or which contain non-sugar sweeteners or certain additives like colorants, flavorings, sweeteners, emulsifiers, and thickening agents.

It is possible that California’s definition for UPFs may be superseded by a federal statutory definition for the category, which, as of August 2026, has been drafted and is pending White House review.

Update, September 29, 2026: The bill has been signed into law by Governor Gavin Newsom.

The Food Safety Magazine editorial team comprises Bailee Henderson, Director of Content Strategy and news editor ✉, and Adrienne Blume, M.A., Director of Editorial and Industry Engagement.

California lawmakers pass bill to create non-ultra-processed food label

By Los Angeles Issue on 31 August 2026

California lawmakers have passed legislation aimed at establishing a first-of-its-kind certification for non-ultra-processed foods to help consumers identify healthier options in grocery stores.

Assembly Bill 2244, authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, would create a standardized “Non-Ultraprocessed Certified” label for products that meet specific state standards. The bill, which is co-sponsored by the Environmental Working Group, has been sent to Governor Gavin Newsom for his signature.

The proposed law would prohibit products from carrying the label if they contain certain additives used to manipulate taste or quality, including dyes, flavor enhancers, non-sugar sweeteners, and various processing aids. Assemblymember Gabriel indicated that the measure is intended to empower consumers with trustworthy information and make it easier to locate foods free from harmful additives without requiring advanced scientific knowledge to interpret packaging.

In addition to the new labeling, the bill requires big grocery retailers to make certified products more visible to shoppers. Any store with more than $10 million in annual sales that carries at least 25 different types of certified non-ultra-processed products must use methods such as special signage or physical separation within the store to highlight them.

If enacted, the California Department of Public Health will manage the program by accrediting third-party agents to perform independent certifications. The department is directed to complete this accreditation process by June 1, 2029, and products would be required to undergo recertification at least once every three years. To maintain credibility, the bill includes oversight measures such as mandatory registration for certification agents, state auditing authority, and the maintenance of a public online list of all certified products.

The legislation follows a previous law by Gabriel that defined ultra-processed foods and banned them from K-12 public schools. The new bill addresses concerns over the prevalence of industrially manufactured, chemically modified foods in the American diet. Research shows these products make up more than 66% of children’s diets and more than 50% of typical adult diets in the United States.

Medical experts have associated high consumption of ultra-processed foods with an increase in obesity, heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and various mental health issues. Supporters of the bill note that while federal oversight of food additives has been slow to evolve, state-level action can provide the transparency necessary for families to choose foods closer to traditional kitchen preparation rather than industrial manufacturing.

A number of bills related to LGBTQ health issues and youth passed out of the California Legislature this session and are headed to the desk of Governor Gavin Newsom. He has until September 30 to either sign them into law or veto the legislation.

Senate Bill 1023 authored by gay state Senator John Laird (D-Santa Cruz) aims to ensure nonprofit service providers that furnish an injectable form of the HIV prevention medication PrEP via their own pharmacies can recoup their costs for doing so. As the Bay Area Reporter has previously reported, some insurance policies restrict injectable PrEP coverage to their medical benefit for policyholders, which can cause problems for agencies like the San Francisco AIDS Foundation in being reimbursed.

Laird’s bill, which passed out of the Legislature August 25, is among the Legislative LGBTQ Caucus’ priority bills this session. Co-sponsors of it include gay outgoing Insurance Commissioner Ricardo Lara and the Department of Insurance, statewide LGBTQ advocacy organization Equality California, and nonprofit healthcare providers AIDS Project LA Health and the Los Angeles LGBT Center.

“PrEP works, and people should be able to access it regardless of where they receive care,” stated Laird. “SB 1023 removes a barrier that has made it harder for community clinics and smaller providers to offer this important HIV prevention medication. I’m pleased to see it pass the Legislature and look forward to the governor’s consideration.”

SB 1114 from gay Senator Christopher Cabaldon (D-Yolo) aims to strengthen privacy protections for sexual orientation, gender identity, and intersex data by limiting when state agencies can share the SOGI information. If signed into law by Newsom, sent the bill August 26, then LGBTQ data couldn’t be disclosed outside of California state government, except under limited circumstances.

Assembly Bill 1930 authored by gay Assemblymember Rick Chavez Zbur (D-Hollywood) aims to strengthen state privacy protections for confidential medical information. Sent to Newsom August 27, AB 1930 comes amid politically motivated investigations being initiated by the Trump administration and Republican officials in other states who are targeting providers of abortion and gender-affirming care in California and other states.

“California cannot allow hostile jurisdictions to use our institutions to target patients and providers for health care that is lawful in our state,” stated Zbur. “AB 1930 gives our attorney general an important opportunity to step in when private information about reproductive or gender-affirming healthcare is being sought. I’m proud this bill has passed the Legislature, and I urge Governor Newsom to sign it into law.”

If it is enacted, business entities in the Golden State would have to notify the California attorney general before responding to a subpoena or inquiry regarding healthcare they provide that is legally protected under state law. The attorney general would also be allowed to intervene in any civil action brought by a state business entity that faces a legal inquiry or summons related to the care they provide.

“California is a safe haven for reproductive rights and gender-affirming care. In the face of ongoing attacks by the Trump administration, I'm proud to sponsor legislation that strengthens our role as a safe haven,” stated California Attorney General Rob Bonta. “These medical decisions are deeply personal and should be made by patients with their providers, free from interference by politicians. California will not be intimidated into abandoning our values.”

AB 2164 authored by Assemblymember Rebecca Bauer-Kahan (D-Orinda) would prohibit California’s governor from recognizing a request for extradition of a person related to their providing a legally protected healthcare activity in the Golden State such as gender-affirming care except under certain circumstances. It passed out of the Legislature August 25.

Also sent to Newsom that day was AB 1876 authored by Assemblymember Dawn Addis (D-Morro Bay) aimed at protecting intersex youth and adults. It would clarify that intersex traits, as well as gender identity and other characteristics, are included under state law prohibiting sex discrimination by health plans and insurers.

Youth bills sent to governor

One of the bills related to LGBTQ youth passed out of the Legislature this year is Zbur’s AB 1967 that would ensure young adults ages 18 to 21 are not blocked from extended foster care when they are no longer receiving support and are at risk of homelessness. Adopted August 27 by legislators, it would require county social workers to immediately review petitions filed by LGBTQ or straight youth seeking to enter the state’s foster care system due to being abused or neglected at home and determine whether to open a juvenile dependency case within 21 days.

SB 998 by Senators Lena Gonzalez (D-Long Beach) and Akilah Weber Pierson (D-San Diego), passed out of the Legislature August 26, would require the state’s Office of Civil Rights to appoint an LGBTQ+ discrimination prevention coordinator to develop educational materials for school teachers, staff, governing board and body members, administrators, and other local educational agency personnel so they can identify and proactively prevent LGBTQ+ discrimination at their school sites.

Lesbian state Senator Caroline Menjivar (D-San Fernando Valley) saw her SB 608 aimed at ensuring students in grades seven to 12 can get condoms from school-based health centers be sent to Newsom August 26. Former versions of her legislation were vetoed by the governor due to their costs to implement, so it remains to be seen if it will finally become law this year.

Another bill, AB 1578 authored by gay Assemblymember Corey A. Jackson, Ph.D., (D-Moreno Valley), would require elected school board members and other public office holders across California to complete at least one hour of antihate speech training and education within six months of taking office and subsequently every four years thereafter. Sent to Newsom August 30, the bill’s requirements would kick in on January 1, 2028.

Other bills await final enactment

Sent to Newsom August 27 was AB 1836 co-authored by gay Assemblymember Chris Ward (D-San Diego) and Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino) that would allow nonprofit hosts of community events such as Pride celebrations and other LGBTQ public gatherings to seek funding upward of $500,000 for security measures via the state’s Nonprofit Security Grant Program. It currently covers nonprofit facilities but not off-site events put on by such entities.

“California is stepping up to protect our communities, so that Californians of all faiths and backgrounds can gather together and celebrate without fear,” stated Gabriel, who chairs the Legislature’s Jewish caucus. “This bill sends a powerful message that California will continue to stand with the LGBTQ+ community and all others targeted by hate. We will never let hate win.”

Sent to the inactive file August 30 was AB 1540 by gay Assemblymember Mark González (D-Los Angeles) that aims to have dedicated counselors for LGBTQ callers to California’s 988 suicide prevention hotline via state officials requesting the federal Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration allow it to have a “Press 3” option. The Trump administration eliminated the option at the national level last summer but is supposed to revive it by the end of the year after out congressmembers and their allies secured funding for the LGBTQ-dedicated counselors. González instead added his bill language and funding to implement it to a pair of budget bills that are now before Newsom.

Remarking on what has transpired over the last year, nonbinary Trevor Project CEO Jaymes Black noted, “LGBTQ+ youth suicide is a public health emergency that requires an urgent response. We need to integrate suicide prevention efforts for this high-risk group into our country’s public health infrastructure. It is no hyperbole to say that, right now, young people’s lives are on the line.”

As the B.A.R. reported online August 25, bills dealing with access to state services by transgender veterans ousted from the military by the Trump administration and when survivors of conversion therapy can file legal claims against practitioners of the discredited therapy practice made it out of the Legislature this month. So did bills allowing employees to take bereavement leave after the death of a chosen family member and requiring college satellite campuses to have staff dedicated to work with LGBTQ students.

The B.A.R. tracked 21 bills dealing with LGBTQ concerns this year. Four were shelved by legislators, while Newsom in July enacted one establishing for educators a permanent training program on how to address suicidal ideation among middle and high school students.

A fifth this month was gutted and amended a second time by bisexual Senator Sasha Renée Pérez (D-Pasadena), who changed the focus of her SB 957 from social media companies needing to notify users when they have received an administrative subpoena to now be aimed at protecting the health and safety of people housed in private civil immigration detention facilities.
