Methodology

This report is based on a review of publicly available campaign finance, lobbying, charitable giving, governance, and ethics disclosures from California state agencies and other public sources. Unless otherwise noted, campaign finance data reflect disclosures available as of August 2, 2026.

Campaign Finance Analysis Campaign finance data were compiled using Power Search Software, maintained by MapLight in partnership with the California Secretary of State, utilizing the Advanced Search database. The database was used to identify campaign contributions made by Sempra, Southern California Edison, and Pacific Gas & Electric, including contributions made through affiliated political committees where applicable.

Legislative leadership was identified using official leadership rosters published by the California Senate and California Assembly. Those officials were cross-referenced with campaign finance disclosures to identify utility contributions. The analysis includes Governor Gavin Newsom, legislative leaders, and the chairs and vice chairs of committees with significant authority over the legislative process, including the Senate and Assembly Rules Committees, Senate and Assembly Appropriations Committees, the Senate Energy, Utilities & Communications Committee, and the Assembly Utilities & Energy Committee.

Because the Assembly maintains a substantially larger leadership structure than the Senate, the analysis was limited to the Assembly’s principal leadership positions: Speaker, Speaker pro Tempore, Majority Leader, Majority Whip, Republican Leader, and Democratic Caucus Chair. Assistant leadership positions were excluded. Legislative caucuses and caucus-controlled political committees were identified through targeted database searches using terms including “caucus,” “leadership,” “legislative,” “Latino,” “African American,” “Black,” “LGBT,” “Jewish,” and “Asian Pacific Islander,” as well as searches for the names of known legislative caucuses.

Campaign contributions to individual elected officials reflect each official’s California state career totals, including contributions received while running for or serving in the California Legislature or statewide office. For Governor Gavin Newsom, this includes contributions to campaigns for Lieutenant Governor and Governor. Contributions to political parties, political committees, ballot measure committees, legislative caucuses, and other organizations reflect contributions reported between January 1, 2019, and August 2, 2026, corresponding with Governor Newsom’s tenure in office. Power Search Software was also used to identify campaign finance activity related to Governor Newsom’s 2021 recall election and statewide ballot measures he publicly supported or opposed during his administration.

Lobbying Disclosure Analysis Lobbying expenditures were compiled from California Secretary of State CAL-ACCESS lobbying disclosure filings for Sempra, Southern California Edison, and Pacific Gas & Electric. The analysis includes reported lobbying expenditures from 2019 through the Sixth Quarter of the 2025–2026 legislative session, including both general lobbying expenditures and California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) lobbying expenditures. Behested Payments Behested payment data were compiled from the California Fair Political Practices Commission (FPPC) Form 803 database. Form 803 requires elected state officers and members of the California Public Utilities Commission to disclose payments made at their behest for legislative, governmental, or charitable purposes when payments from a single source total $5,000 or more during a calendar year. All Form 803 filings available through August 2, 2026, were reviewed for this analysis.

Utility Charitable Giving Utility charitable giving was analyzed using Form 77-M reports filed with the California Public Utilities Commission for 2023, 2024, and 2025. PG&E and Sempra report charitable contributions in dedicated charitable giving schedules, which were used directly for this analysis. Southern California Edison reports dues, donations, subscriptions, and contributions in a combined schedule. Each Edison entry was individually reviewed using the accompanying expense codes, and only expenditures classified as charitable contributions were included. Payments categorized as dues, subscriptions, office expenses, or other non-charitable expenditures were excluded from the charitable giving totals.

Wildfire Victims First Analysis The analysis of Wildfire Victims First was based on publicly available information, including the organization’s website, public statements, Meta’s Ad Library, the organization’s Facebook page, and campaign finance disclosures available through Power Search Software and CAL-ACCESS. Because Wildfire Victims First is not registered as a California political committee, major donor, or lobbying employer, comprehensive financial disclosure is not publicly available.

Organizations identified as coalition members, financial supporters, or affiliated entities were cross-referenced against campaign finance records and utility charitable giving reported in Form 77-M filings to identify financial relationships with California for-profit utilities.

Governance Analysis The governance analysis examined nonprofit organizations, trade associations, coalitions, civic organizations, and other institutions identified through utility charitable giving disclosures. Businesses, government agencies, and individual elected officials were excluded from this portion of the analysis.

Each organization was reviewed to identify documented relationships with California for-profit utilities and classified according to the highest level of demonstrated utility involvement.

California Banned Glock Sales on July 1. On August 4, SAF, NRA and FPC Filed to Stop It - USA Carry

Luke McCoy

Key Takeaways

  • A coalition of gun owners and organizations filed a motion to block California’s ban on Glock pistols, set for a hearing on September 4, 2026.
  • The case, Jaymes v. Bonta, challenges California’s AB 1127 law, which prohibits the sale of certain semiautomatic pistols defined as machinegun-convertible.
  • The plaintiffs argue that the ban infringes on Second Amendment rights, given that Glock pistols qualify as ‘arms’ under the law.
  • California’s handgun roster has already faced scrutiny, with plaintiffs asserting that the state fails to justify its new restrictions on firearms sales.
  • The sales ban took effect July 1, 2026, and the ongoing legal battle impacts retail availability for handgun buyers in California.

SAN DIEGO, CA — A coalition of gun owners, retailers and Second Amendment organizations asked a federal judge on August 4, 2026, to block California’s ban on the commercial sale of Glock and Glock-style pistols, and the judge has set a hearing for September 4.

The motion for a preliminary injunction was filed in the United States District Court for the Southern District of California under case number 20-cv-2190-DMS-DEB, with Lana Rae Renna as the first-named plaintiff. The defendants are California Attorney General Robert Bonta and Allison Mendoza, director of the California Department of Justice Bureau of Firearms. The Honorable Dana M. Sabraw is set to hear argument at 1:30 p.m. on September 4, 2026. A preliminary injunction is simply a court order pausing a law while the case is litigated, so plaintiffs are not asking the judge to strike the statute yet. They are asking him to stop it from operating in the meantime.

The plaintiff group is deep. Individual Californians including Danielle Jaymes, Laura Schwartz, Michael Schwartz, Robert Macomber, Clint Freeman, John Klier, John Phillips, Cheryl Prince and Darin Prince are joined by retailers PWGG, L.P., North County Shooting Center, Inc., and Gunfighter Tactical, LLC, along with the Firearms Policy Coalition, San Diego County Gun Owners PAC, the Citizens Committee for the Right to Keep and Bear Arms, the Second Amendment Foundation, and the National Rifle Association.

The law at issue is AB 1127, authored by Assemblymember Gabriel and signed by Governor Gavin Newsom on October 10, 2025, as Chapter 572. Read the enrolled text and the mechanics are narrower than the shorthand suggests, and broader in effect. On and after July 1, 2026, a licensed firearms dealer may not sell, offer for sale, exchange, give, transfer or deliver any semiautomatic “machinegun-convertible pistol,” which the bill defines as any semiautomatic pistol with a cruciform trigger bar that can be readily converted by hand or with common household tools into a machinegun by the installation or attachment of a pistol converter. A “pistol converter” is defined as a device that replaces the backplate at the rear of the slide, interferes with the trigger mechanism, and thereby lets the pistol fire more than one shot with a single function of the trigger.

Note what the statute does not require. It does not require that a converter be present. The trigger for the sales ban is the geometry of the pistol itself, and the cruciform trigger bar is a defining feature of the Glock design and of pistols built on that platform. AB 1127 separately expands California’s definition of “machinegun” to include a machinegun-convertible pistol that is actually equipped with a converter, which folds it into the existing prohibition on manufacturing, selling, possessing or transporting a machinegun, a violation punishable as a felony. So the conduct everyone agrees is criminal was already criminal. What the new law adds is a ban on the retail sale of the unmodified pistol.

Dealer penalties escalate. A first violation draws a fine, a second draws a fine that may result in suspension or revocation of the dealer’s license and removal from state centralized lists, and a third is a misdemeanor that must result in revocation and removal.

The Second Amendment Foundation announced the challenge on October 13, 2025, three days after the signing, as Jaymes v. Bonta, and said it was joined by the NRA, FPC, a licensed retailer and two individual plaintiffs. SAF Director of Legal Operations Bill Sack tied the new law directly to California’s handgun roster. “Prior to AB 1127, Gen 3 Glock, and similar handguns built on the Glock platform, were available for commercial sale because they were grandfathered onto California’s handgun roster,” Sack said. “California is already subject to an injunction because the California Handgun Roster unconstitutionally bans handguns in common use for lawful purposes. Rather than heed the demands of the Second Amendment and their own courts, California lawmakers have responded by doubling down and expanding their handgun ban. We’ll see them in court.”

“Just as we’ve done in numerous other cases in the state, we will vigorously defend this unconstitutional infringement on the Second Amendment rights of Californians,” said SAF founder and Executive Vice President Alan M. Gottlieb.

The August motion was filed under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(d), the rule that lets a party bring in claims about events that happened after the original complaint was filed. In plain terms, the roster case was already on the docket, the state passed a new restriction while that case was pending, and the plaintiffs are litigating the new restriction inside the existing case rather than starting over.

The argument itself follows the familiar two-step. Plaintiffs contend Penal Code section 27595 implicates the Second Amendment because Glock pistols are “arms” covered by the plain text, and that once the text is implicated the burden shifts to California to show its ban fits the nation’s historical tradition of firearms regulation, which plaintiffs say the state cannot do. That is the framework the Supreme Court set out in Bruen. Plaintiffs also argue the remaining preliminary injunction factors favor them and ask the court to waive bond or require only nominal security, which is the money a party normally has to post to cover the other side’s losses if the injunction turns out to have been wrongly granted.

The sales ban took effect July 1, 2026. The motion to halt it was filed August 4. That means Californians walking into a gun store today are already living under the restriction the court will take up on September 4, and every week that passes is a week a common, widely owned handgun platform cannot be bought at retail in the state. That is not an abstraction for the shooter deciding on a first defensive pistol. It is a shrinking counter. Californians already work under one of the tightest firearms regimes in the country, and my California concealed carry guide covers the permit side of that picture.

Now that California legislators are back from their summer recess, a host of LGBTQ bills await their fates in the Legislature. A deadline looms next week for bills with fiscal costs to survive votes in the appropriations committees, while the two legislative chambers have until August 31 to send legislation to Governor Gavin Newsom to sign into law.

One bill establishing a permanent online youth suicide prevention training program was enacted last month by Newsom, a Democrat in his final year as governor, with a second bill addressing suicide ideation among LGBTQ young people still pending before lawmakers. (See related story.) They are among 21 bills dealing with LGBTQ concerns that the Bay Area Reporter has been tracking this year.

Similar to past legislative sessions, this year’s LGBTQ bills package in Sacramento is again skewing toward addressing the needs of queer and transgender young people. Senate Bill 934 authored by gay Senator Scott Wiener (D-San Francisco) would allow people who were subjected to the debunked practice of conversion therapy in which they try to change their sexual orientation or gender identity to have more time to bring a civil suit against the practitioner.

It has taken on more relevance following the U.S. Supreme Court this year ruling 8-1 to strike Colorado’s ban of the practice based on free speech grounds. It also ordered lower federal courts to review if similar bans like the one adopted by California are also unconstitutional. The Golden State in 2012 was the first to ban the use of conversion therapy in minors for the purpose of changing their sexual orientation, with two dozen states following suit.

No matter what the court decides, Wiener’s bill would clarify that plaintiffs could cite scientific principles and consensus around proper medical care to demonstrate conversion therapy’s harm in bringing forward a malpractice claim. It would also extend the deadline for doing so, with someone under 18 years old at the time of being subjected to the therapy allowed to file a claim before age 40.

For people older than 18 when they underwent conversion therapy, they’d be able to file a claim within 10 years of their last session. A person would also be able to bring a claim within five years of their discovering an injury or illness due to the efforts to change their being LGBTQ.

“We can’t allow this awful Supreme Court decision to jeopardize the life of even a single child,” stated Wiener as his bill moved through the review process this spring. “Conversion therapy is psychological torture, and every major medical association has declared it to be quackery. At a time when many powerful people are trying to erase the LGBTQ community, I’m grateful to my colleagues in the Legislature for having our backs.”

SB 1328 introduced by lesbian Senator Sabrina Cervantes (D-Riverside) would require California’s colleges and universities to designate a confidential employee at satellite campuses, branch campuses, and outreach centers to support the needs of LGBTQ+ students, faculty, and staff. It follows on a bill passed in 2024 that required such a person on the main campuses of higher education institutions.

SB 998 by Senators Lena Gonzalez (D-Long Beach) and Akilah Weber Pierson (D-San Diego) would among its provisions require the state’s Office of Civil Rights to appoint an LGBTQ+ discrimination prevention coordinator to develop educational materials for school teachers, staff, governing board and body members, administrators, and other local educational agency personnel so they can identify and proactively prevent LGBTQ+ discrimination at their school sites.

Intersex youth and adults would be provided protection under Assembly Bill 1876 authored by Assemblymember Dawn Addis (D-Morro Bay). It would clarify that intersex traits, as well as gender identity and other characteristics, are included under state law prohibiting sex discrimination by health plans and insurers.

All of the bills are before the appropriations committee in either the state Assembly or Senate. Several bills have been sent to the committees’ suspense files over the last month, raising doubts about their being voted out on August 13, as often such bills are blocked from moving forward even if they previously had gained support.

One is AB 1578 authored by gay Assemblymember Corey A. Jackson, Ph.D., (D-Moreno Valley) that would require elected school board members and other public office holders across California to complete at least one hour of anti-hate speech training and education within six months of taking office and subsequently every four years thereafter. The requirement would begin on January 1, 2028, if his bill becomes law.

SB 1149 authored by Senator María Elena Durazo (D-Los Angeles) aims to allow workers to take bereavement leave for chosen and extended family members, similar to previous legislation Durazo saw become law that extended paid family leave provisions to workers in need of caring for chosen or extended family members, not merely their immediate family. It was sent to the Assembly’s suspense file in July.

Also sent the chamber’s suspense file was SB 1023 by gay state Senator John Laird (D-Santa Cruz) aimed at addressing hiccups with insurance policies covering the cost of an injectable form of the HIV prevention medication PrEP. Some health plans restrict injectable PrEP coverage to their medical benefit for policyholders, which causes problems for nonprofit service providers that provide it via their own pharmacies in recouping their costs for doing so.

Joining the suspense file Monday were two bills authored by gay Assemblymember Rick Chavez Zbur (D–Hollywood). Under AB 1967 county social workers would need to immediately review petitions filed by LGBTQ or straight youth seeking to enter the state’s foster care system due to being abused or neglected at home and determine whether to open a juvenile dependency case within 21 days. It also would ensure young adults ages 18 to 21 are not blocked from extended foster care when they are no longer receiving support and are at risk of homelessness.

“For many youth in foster care, extended foster care can be the difference between stability and homelessness,” stated Zbur upon the bill being sent to the Senate. “These young people are often navigating homelessness, unsafe living situations, unemployment, mental health challenges, and disruptions to education or healthcare all at once. California has a responsibility to make sure that youth in foster care can access the support systems designed to help them transition safely into adulthood.”

Zbur’s AB 1930 aims to strengthen state privacy protections for confidential medical information. It comes amid politically motivated investigations being initiated by the Trump administration and Republican officials in other states who are targeting providers of abortion and gender-affirming care in California and other states.

AB 1930 would require business entities in California to notify the California attorney general before responding to a subpoena or inquiry regarding health care they provide that is legally protected in the Golden State. The attorney general would also be allowed to intervene in any civil action brought by a state business entity that faces a legal inquiry or summons related to the care they provide.

“Patients seeking reproductive or gender-affirming health care deserve privacy, dignity, and the freedom to make personal medical decisions without fear of political intimidation,” stated Zbur upon the bill’s passage out of the Assembly earlier this year. “As extremist politicians across the country attempt to criminalize legally protected health care, California must continue standing firmly on the side of patients, families, providers, and the rule of law. AB 1930 strengthens our ability to protect people seeking lawful medical care in our state from politically motivated attacks and invasions of privacy.”

Placed on suspense this week was AB 1775 by gay Assemblymember Chris Ward (D-San Diego) that would allow access to state programs by transgender veterans being forced out of the military under an executive order issued by President Donald Trump last year. It would make sure such service members discharged under the policy would still qualify for housing assistance and professional licensing support afforded to them by the state, as well as be able to utilize discharge upgrade services as they transition back to civilian life.

Also sent to the suspense file this week was AB 1836 co-authored by Ward and Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino). It would allow nonprofits that host community events such as Pride celebrations and other LGBTQ community events to seek funding upward of $500,000 for security measures via the state’s Nonprofit Security Grant Program. It currently covers nonprofit facilities but not off-site events put on by such entities.

Other health bills under consideration

Several other pieces of legislation related to health issues await votes by the appropriations committees. Lesbian state Senator Caroline Menjivar (D-San Fernando Valley) is trying to pass a condom access in schools bill after seeing former versions of her legislation be vetoed by Newsom. Her SB 608 would ensure students in grades 7-12 can get the prophylactics from school-based health centers. It also would prohibit a retail establishment from furnishing nonprescription contraception to a person solely on the basis of age.

SB 1114 from gay Senator Christopher Cabaldon (D-Yolo) would strengthen privacy protections for sexual orientation, gender identity, and intersex data by limiting when state agencies can share the SOGI information. It would ensure the LGBTQ data cannot be disclosed outside of California state government, except under limited circumstances.

AB 2164 authored by Assemblymember Rebecca Bauer-Kahan (D-Orinda) would prohibit California’s governor from recognizing a request for extradition of a person related to their providing a legally protected health care activity in the Golden State such as gender-affirming care except under certain circumstances.

Bills change focus, stall

Two bisexual legislators gut and amended their bills from their initial focus. Senator Sasha Renée Pérez (D-Pasadena) changed her SB 957 from mandating safety policies be in place for California users of online dating apps to now require social media companies to notify users when they have received an administrative subpoena.

Set to be heard Wednesday by the Assembly’s appropriations committee, SB 957 has been dubbed the Stopping Harmful Information Exploitation and Lawless Data Sharing (SHIELD) Act. It would place restrictions on how such companies respond to subpoenas and allow the state’s attorney general to intervene in such matters.

“People should be able to use social media to stay informed and keep one another safe without worrying that their activity could result in retaliation from the federal government,” noted Pérez. “No one in this state should be intimidated into silence out of fear that their personal information will be secretly shared with federal authorities.”

In noting its support for the bill, the California Legislative LGBTQ Caucus pointed out that “recent reporting and research have highlighted how social media platforms collect and infer deeply sensitive information about users, including data related to gender identity, sexual orientation, and personal beliefs. In the wrong hands, this information can be used to target, harass, or even endanger LGBTQ+ individuals.”

Assemblymember Sade Elhawary (D-South Los Angeles) altered the focus of her AB 2551 from being about LGBTQ health data to instead be about protests on college campuses and was placed on the suspense file Monday. Meanwhile, her AB 2014 dealing with gender-based bias in court proceedings was held in committee in May, as was Jackson’s AB 2119 aimed at addressing gender bias in sexual assault and domestic violence investigations.

Gay Assemblymember José Luis Solache Jr. (D-Lynwood) had hoped to move forward his AB 908 aimed at monitoring compliance among school districts with a state law requiring the adoption of instructional materials inclusive of LGBTQ history. It stalled last summer and didn’t move forward this year.

Prop 2: Supersizing California's Slush Fund

California Current

Proposition 2 Doubles California’s Already Bloated Slush Fund

Like all good political deception, the case for Proposition 2, formally known as the Budget Stabilization Account Cap Increase and Gann Limit Changes Amendment, includes a note of truth. California’s tax revenues do swing wildly.

That truth has been twisted by supporters of Prop 2 into a call for the doubling of the amount put aside for “emergencies” or other “unexpected” occurrences. “It’s just a sensible ‘rainy day’ measure,” they say. But if one looks into the proposal, they’ll find that description holds no water.

The real score?

Proposition 2’s passage would create a supersized slush fund out of which billions of unaccountable spending will pour. Its passage will amend the state’s constitution and allow legislators to spend an additional $20 to $25 billion however, whenever, and on whomever they see fit.

Proposition 2 would raise the cap on California’s Budget Stabilization Account from 10 per cent to 20 per cent of General Fund revenues. In boom years, this would create an extra $20 billion to $25 billion of taxpayer funds which sits outside the usual spending constraints. Prop 2’s architecture is that of a huge discretionary reserve under the control of the same people who have spent the past decade treating every surplus as permanent and every shortfall as a reason for additional taxation.

“It’s a Fiscal Emergency!” Really?

The coalition of big spenders advancing Proposition 2 includes Governor Gavin Newsom, Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas, Senate President pro Tem Monique Limón and Assembly member Jesse Gabriel. None are fiscal conservatives who have recently discovered the virtues of restraint. They are counting on a simple marketing strategy to float this idea in November and hope that most voters won’t read the deadly boring small print. Or have forgotten how Sacramento works.

If this constitutional amendment passes, don’t be surprised to find an increase in California’s “Rainy Days.” The process for accessing these funds is easy: the governor simply cries out “emergency” and a simple majority of votes in the legislature releases the money into the general fund.

In the 2024/25 fiscal year, $5 Billion poured out. In the 2025/2026 fiscal year, another $7.1 Billion was drained. A “fiscal emergency” were the governor’s magic words to unlock billions.

Anyone recall the emergency?

California already has mechanisms intended to capture surplus revenue. Proposition 98’s education guarantee and the Gann Limit already impose a degree of discipline on budget spending. Proposition 2 provides the wiggle room to sidestep this established framework by placing enormous sums outside those mandated spending limits. The practical effect of Prop 2 would be less voter influence over a much larger pot of money, rather than tighter control.

Under Prop 2, every time a “rainy day” occurs, California taxpayers will get soaked.

Recurring “Inconveniences”

The scale of the additional slush fund capacity is worthy of perspective. During COVID, the Employment Development Department is estimated to have lost around $20 billion to unemployment fraud. Problems in Medi-Cal provider fraud, In-Home Supportive Services, and homelessness programs, have produced documented losses with estimates of ongoing leakage that run into the billions each year. The state has, on more than one occasion, found itself unable to track outcomes for tens of billions spent on homelessness. Rather than address these billion-dollar leaks with any great urgency, Sacramento politicians are hoping to divert more taxpayer funds under their own control and less public scrutiny.

If the genuine goal were budget stability, one might expect at least some attention to the tax structure that produces the swings or addressing the administrative failures that allow so much of the money to escape once collected.

Large-scale fraud should not be treated as a recurring inconvenience, Yet no structural repair of the budget process appears anywhere in the current Prop 2 proposal.

What Prop 2 does feature is a larger claim on future capital-gains receipts and unencumbered freedom in their subsequent (mis)use.

Way back in 1972 Albert Hammond channeled California’s rainy days as a way to contrast deceptive marketing with the hidden, grim reality beneath it:

“It never rains in California,

But girl, don’t they warn ya?

It pours. Man, it pours.“

Proposition 2 doesn’t fix the plumbing or repair California’s leaky financial roof. It simply pours billions of unaccountable dollars into the hands of the same spend-happy politicians who’ve squandered it before.

Vote NO on Proposition 2.

California voters to decide on Proposition 2 to expand rainy day fund | California Politics 360

Kurtis Ming

California voters to decide on Proposition 2 to expand rainy day fund | California Politics 360

California voters will decide this fall whether to approve Proposition 2, a measure that would double the cap on the state’s rainy day fund from 10% to 20% of annual tax revenue.

California’s rainy day fund, approved by voters more than two decades ago, has helped the state navigate financial challenges, including the pandemic and budget shortfalls, while protecting funding for schools, public safety, and other critical services.

“We’ve been able to stock money aside in the rainy day fund. And in years when we’ve needed it, we’ve been able to draw down from it. Part of the challenge, though, is that the rainy day fund is limited to 10% of the general fund,” said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, a Democrat from Encino.

Under current state law, California lawmakers and the governor are limited in how much money they can keep in the state’s main savings account. Gabriel said, “10% is just not enough, given the, the, the volatility that we’ve experienced.”

The state’s finances have experienced significant swings in recent years. According to the Department of Finance, California had an estimated $101 billion surplus in 2022-23, but just two years later, the state was facing a projected $47 billion deficit for 2024-25.

The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office has analyzed the state’s finances through thousands of scenarios over the next 50 years and predicts continued volatility, saying cuts to core services or tax increases would often be necessary.

“We don’t want to be in a position when the economy turns to have to start to think about, are we scaling back fire protection? Are we scaling back funding for education? Are we cutting funding for health care? We want to make sure that that funding for essential services is there,” Gabriel said.

Proposition 2 would double the cap on the rainy day fund to 20% of annual tax revenue. For example, if California collects $250 billion in annual taxes, the reserve account could hold up to $50 billion, compared to the current cap of $25 billion. In surplus years, state leaders would be required to save more and pay down debt before spending on new programs or services.

“And before we start spending money on new programs and services or other ideas that elected officials have, let’s keep putting money in our savings account until we get that 20% number,” Gabriel said.

Critics of Proposition 2 argue that the measure enables overspending and encourages wasteful financial practices.

“California doesn’t have a revenue problem, it has a wasteful spending problem,” said Republican State Senator Tony Strickland of Huntington Beach.

Strickland said he supports the concept of a rainy day fund but believes surplus tax revenue should be used to pay off debts, get refunded to Californians and provide tax cuts.

“I think the people should benefit from some of that surplus, are the hardworking families, and lower their burden, because right now we have an affordability crisis in California,” Strickland said.

He compared Proposition 2 to using one credit card to pay off another. “So all this does is allow the addiction to spending to continue with the legislature. And who ends up paying the bill in the long term, it ends up being those hardworking California families,” Strickland said.

The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office has recommended eventually raising the rainy day fund cap to 50%, but Proposition 2 proposes increasing it from 10% to 20%.

If approved, the measure would allow state lawmakers and the governor to use reserve funds to pay off debts, including the $20 billion loan owed to the federal government from the pandemic. However, the measure does not require them to pay off the debt.

Public Defender Donna Tryfman: Strives to be Prompt, Prepared and Polite in Her Race for LA County Judge!

CAMPAIGN 26 - The campaign between Donna Tryfman and David Ross has turned into a barn burner of sorts with Tryfman edging out a first-place finish in the June 2nd Primary, capturing 37.21% of the vote or 612,858. Ross was a close second also advancing with 33% or 546,032 votes.

Carlos Dammeir, who finished third, has endorsed Ross, while fourth-place finisher Troy Slaten is backing Tryfman, in a contest that tallied over 1.7 million voters.

Tryfman, who previously ran for a seat on the Beverly Hills school board in 2020, currently serves as a volunteer, temporary Judge pro tempore, assigned to traffic and small claims cases.

The candidate is 59 years old, and a graduate of the University of La Verne School of Law. Originally from Queens, New York, Tryfman is a widow of seven years and has one daughter.

Tryfman, whose parents are Holocaust survivors, describes herself as a critical thinker, who views public advocacy and service as her life's passions.

A lover of musicals and concerts, the candidate enjoys the rigors of the campaign trail and speaking with the electorate.

"I love pounding the pavement," noted the candidate.

Whether greeting voters at Griffith Park or meeting with members of the numerous democratic clubs and organizations she has addressed, Tryfman has secured the endorsement of the Stonewall & San Fernando Democrats as well as California Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (CA-46).

Assigned to the Major Cases Unit of the LA Public Defender's Office, Tryfman serves with honor and integrity, and sees herself in this public trust as "fair to a fault."

Below is our extensive interview on her overall approach to becoming "everyone's judge" here in Los Angeles County:

Your legal career has been spent primarily as a public defender representing criminal defendants. How would you assure victims, prosecutors, law enforcement, and the broader public that you would approach every case from a neutral judicial perspective rather than an advocacy role?

My career has certainly included serving as a public defender, but it has also encompassed decades of substantive courtroom experience handling a wide range of complex criminal matters. Throughout that time, my professional responsibility has been to uphold the Constitution and ensure that legal proceedings are fair.

My experience has also taught me to set aside personal opinions, listen carefully and respectfully, and dignify the process by taking it seriously. A judge's responsibility is not to advocate for either side, but to serve as a neutral decision-maker who faithfully applies the law to the facts. I understand that distinction, and my career has prepared me well for it. Every day as an attorney, I have analyzed evidence, assessed the strengths and weaknesses of cases, negotiated resolutions when appropriate, litigated motions, conducted trials, and worked professionally with prosecutors, law enforcement officers, victims, witnesses, and the court.

Those experiences have reinforced the importance of objectivity, careful legal analysis, and treating everyone with respect. My experience has also given me a unique perspective on the criminal justice system. I have represented individuals from all walks of life, while working alongside dedicated prosecutors, law enforcement professionals, and victim advocates who share the common goal of promoting justice and public safety.

The oath of a judge requires complete impartiality. If entrusted with that responsibility, I will approach every case with an open mind, decide each matter solely on the evidence presented and the applicable law, and ensure that every person who enters my courtroom is heard fairly and treated with dignity. My commitment will not be to any party or perspective—it will be to the rule of law, the integrity of the judicial process, and equal justice for all.

Los Angeles courts continue to struggle with case backlogs and delays. What specific steps would you take as a judge to improve efficiency while still protecting due process rights for all parties?

My years of handling demanding criminal calendars have taught me that efficiency is not achieved by rushing cases. It is achieved through preparation, consistency, thoughtful case management, and respect for everyone's time.

When a courtroom is well organized and expectations are clear, cases move more efficiently, litigants have greater confidence in the process, and due process is fully protected. My goal would be to ensure that every case is resolved as promptly as the law allows, without ever sacrificing fairness, impartiality, or the integrity of the judicial process. Specifically, my custom and habits as an attorney directly translate to the bench.

First, I would be prompt. Being on time is respectful to all the litigants and staff. Second, I'd be prepared. There is no replacement for actually doing the work. I would ensure I know all the cases I am handling and prepare them to be called---reading motions, doing research, scheduling further status conferences.

Finally, I'd be polite. In a hectic courtroom setting, the judge must project and model the behavior expected from everyone in the courtroom and that begins with proper courtroom decorum. When a courtroom is well organized and expectations are clear, cases move more efficiently, litigants have greater confidence in the process, and due process is fully protected.

Having handled homicide and other serious felony cases, what lessons have you learned about sentencing, rehabilitation, and public safety, and how would those experiences influence your decisions from the bench?

Over the course of my career, I have handled homicide cases and many of the most serious felony matters in our criminal justice system. Those cases have taught me that there are no easy answers in criminal law. Every file represents real people, not just numbers—victims and their families whose lives have been forever changed, defendants whose liberty is at stake, and communities that rightly expect both justice and public safety.

One of the most important lessons I have learned is that sentencing is among the most significant responsibilities a judge undertakes because liberty is involved often after another human being has been impacted by that person's actions. It requires more than simply knowing the applicable law. It requires careful listening, thoughtful analysis, and the discipline to consider all of the statutory sentencing factors before reaching a decision.

My experience has reinforced that public safety must always be the guiding principle. In cases involving violent offenses or individuals who present a continuing danger to the community, protecting the public is paramount, and the sentence imposed must reflect both the law and the seriousness of the offense. At the same time, not every case presents the same circumstances. Hence, reducing cases to numbers without considering humanity is a flawed practice.

California law recognizes that rehabilitation, treatment, and diversion may be appropriate for certain offenders and certain offenses. When those options are authorized by law and supported by the facts, they can reduce recidivism, promote accountability, and ultimately enhance public safety. Thus, in appropriate cases, especially involving juveniles, and if legally appropriate, it would be a disservice to society not to consider a diversionary sentence. Handling homicide and other serious felony cases has also taught me the importance of never viewing people as simply the charges they face. Every sentencing decision must be individualized, grounded in the facts of the case, and based on the law—not assumptions, emotion, or personal philosophy. It is how judges ensure both fairness and consistency.

You have experience in juvenile court and collaborative drug courts. Do you believe diversion and treatment programs are underutilized in Los Angeles County, and where do you believe they are appropriate?

My experience in juvenile court and collaborative drug courts has reinforced that diversion and treatment programs are valuable tools when they are used thoughtfully, consistently, and in accordance with the law. They are not appropriate for every case, but when they are available to the right individuals at the right time, they can improve outcomes for participants, reduce recidivism, and enhance public safety. There are equally as many success stories for every lack of success stories.

While there have been some great ideas and implementation of diversion programs, I do believe there are opportunities to make more effective use of diversion and treatment programs in Los Angeles County. One of the challenges is not simply the availability of programs which sometimes proves inadequate, but the coordination among the agencies responsible for delivering services. Courts, probation, behavioral health providers, substance use treatment programs, housing agencies, veterans' services, and community-based organizations often work toward the same goal, but too frequently they operate in separate systems. Better coordination and communication among these programs can improve access to services, reduce unnecessary delays, and help ensure participants receive the support they need to successfully complete their programs.

My experience in the juvenile drug collaborative court during my time as a supervisor at Eastlake Court has shown me that successful diversion depends on accountability as well as treatment. Participants benefit most when there are clear expectations, regular judicial oversight, timely information sharing among stakeholders, and appropriately-structured support services. A coordinated approach not only helps individuals address the underlying issues that contributed to their involvement in the justice system, but also makes the process more efficient for the court and more effective for the community.

As a judge, my responsibility would be to faithfully apply the law in determining eligibility for diversion while ensuring that public safety remains the paramount consideration. Diversion should never be viewed as avoiding accountability. When implemented effectively—with meaningful supervision, coordinated services, and measurable expectations—it is a form of accountability that can produce lasting behavioral change and stronger, safer communities.

Public confidence in the judiciary depends on impartiality and transparency. What principles would guide you when making unpopular decisions that may draw criticism from elected officials, advocacy groups, or the media?

Throughout my career, I have learned that doing what is right is not always the same as doing what is popular. As a public defender, I have routinely stood next to the most unpopular person in the courtroom—the defendant. The role required me to uphold the Constitution, protect due process, and ensure that every individual received the representation guaranteed by law, regardless of the allegations against them or the public sentiment surrounding the case. Those experiences taught me that the integrity of our justice system depends on professionals who are willing to make principled decisions even when they are unpopular.

That same principle has guided my leadership outside the courtroom. As President of several public defender associations, I have advocated for attorneys and the fair administration of justice, even when doing so required taking positions that were difficult or unpopular. Leadership means listening respectfully to differing viewpoints, making decisions grounded in principle rather than politics, and accepting criticism when necessary.

Those experiences have prepared me well for judicial service. A judge's obligation is not to satisfy public opinion, respond to political pressure, or follow the preferences of advocacy groups or the media. A judge's obligation is to faithfully apply the law, protect the constitutional rights of all parties, and decide each case based solely on the facts and the law presented in the courtroom.

When difficult or unpopular decisions are required, the principles that will guide me are independence, integrity, impartiality, and transparency. Independence means deciding cases free from outside influence. Integrity means applying the law consistently, even when the outcome is personally difficult or publicly criticized. Impartiality means treating every litigant with equal dignity and respect, regardless of who they are. Transparency means explaining my rulings clearly on the record so that the parties understand not only the outcome, but the legal reasoning behind it..

What distinguishes your candidacy from your runoff opponent, and why should voters choose your judicial philosophy over his?

Both my opponent and I have dedicated our careers to public defense, and I respect anyone who has devoted their professional life to serving indigent clients. Voters have a choice between an experienced attorney and a rounded, even more experienced, attorney. While our professional titles are similar, my record speaks to my more substantive qualifications.

What distinguishes my candidacy is the breadth, consistency, and depth of my experience over more than three decades. Throughout my career, I have consistently sought out the most demanding assignments in the Los Angeles County Public Defender's Office. Today, I serve in the Major Cases Unit, where I handle homicide cases with special circumstances—the most serious and complex cases in our criminal justice system. I have also served in juvenile court, collaborative drug court, supervised attorneys as a Deputy-in-Charge, and tried more than one hundred jury trials across courthouses throughout Los Angeles County. That broad range of experience has given me a comprehensive understanding of the issues judges face every day, from high-volume calendars to the most consequential felony cases.

My career has also been marked by sustained leadership and service to the legal profession and the community. I served for five years as President of the Public Defenders Association, advocating for professionalism, training, and the fair administration of justice.

Ultimately, I believe judicial service requires more than trial experience alone. It requires demonstrated leadership, sound judgment, unwavering integrity, and the courage to make difficult decisions fairly and independently. Judges are often called upon to make decisions that will be criticized by one side or the other. The measure of a judge is not whether those decisions are popular, but whether they faithfully apply the law and are made impartially, without fear, favor, or outside influence.

My judicial philosophy is straightforward: uphold the Constitution, apply the law fairly and consistently, treat every person with dignity and respect, and have the courage to do what is right—even when it is difficult.

Should judges consider broader social consequences when interpreting the law, or should they apply statutes strictly regardless of outcome?

This is an important philosophical question, and one that judges confront in different ways throughout their careers. The law governs human affairs, and human affairs are rarely simple. People's lives, relationships, and circumstances can be complicated, and the consequences of judicial decisions are often significant. That is precisely why judges must approach every case with humility, careful thought, and fidelity to the law.

A judge's primary responsibility is not to make policy or reach a preferred social outcome---that responsibility belongs to the Legislature. A judge's duty is to interpret and apply the Constitution, statutes, and binding precedent to the facts before the court. The rule of law depends on judges who are impartial and who resist the temptation to substitute their personal views for the law enacted by the people's elected representatives.

At the same time, the law itself often requires judges to exercise discretion and consider the real-world circumstances of the people who appear before them. Whether determining bail, sentencing, diversion eligibility, or fashioning an appropriate remedy, California law frequently directs judges to weigh multiple statutory factors. That is not policymaking—it is faithfully carrying out the responsibilities the Legislature has assigned to the judiciary.

A good judge listens carefully, understands the facts, applies the law faithfully, and takes the time to explain the reasoning behind the decision. Being mindful of the human consequences of a ruling does not mean allowing those consequences to override the law. It means recognizing that justice requires both legal discipline and sound judgment.

My guiding principle would be to faithfully apply the law as written, exercise judicial discretion where the law permits it, and ensure that every decision is grounded in the facts, the law, and the Constitution—not in personal philosophy or public opinion.

(Nick Antonicello is a thirty-three-year resident of the Westside who is covering the numerous judicial contests on the fall election ballot. A regular contributor to City Watch, he can be reached via e-mail at [email protected].)

این مدافع عمومی باسابقه شهرستان لسآنجلس و عضو پیشین کمیسیون تثبیت اجارهبهای بورلی هیلز، در انتخابات مقدماتی چهارنفره برای کرسی شماره ۱۳۱ دادگاه عالی بیشترین رأی را به دست آورد.

دونا تریفمن (Donna Tryfman)، مدافع عمومی باسابقه و عضو پیشین کمیسیون تثبیت اجارهبهای بورلی هیلز، پس از کسب رتبه نخست در انتخابات مقدماتی کرسی شماره ۱۳۱ دادگاه عالی شهرستان لسآنجلس، به انتخابات عمومی ماه نوامبر راه یافت.

بر اساس نتایج نهایی انتخابات شهرستان لسآنجلس، تریفمن ۶۱۲٬۸۵۸ رأی، معادل ۳۷٫۳۱ درصد، به دست آورد. دیوید راس (David Ross) با ۵۴۶٬۰۳۲ رأی، معادل ۳۳٫۲۴ درصد، در جایگاه دوم قرار گرفت. از آنجا که هیچ نامزدی بیش از ۵۰ درصد آرا را کسب نکرد، تریفمن و راس در دور دوم انتخابات روز ۳ نوامبر با یکدیگر رقابت خواهند کرد.

کارلوس دامایر (Carlos Dammeier) با ۲۴۵٬۹۶۹ رأی، معادل ۱۴٫۹۷ درصد، سوم شد و تروی اسلیتن (Troy Slaten) با ۲۳۷٬۸۹۴ رأی، معادل ۱۴٫۴۸ درصد، در جایگاه چهارم قرار گرفت.

تریفمن بیش از ۳۰ سال است که بهعنوان معاون مدافع عمومی شهرستان لسآنجلس فعالیت میکند. او در حال حاضر در بخش جرایم عمده این نهاد خدمت میکند و پروندههای قتل با شرایط ویژه را بر عهده دارد. تریفمن در طول دوران حرفهای خود بیش از ۱۰۰ محاکمه را به پایان رسانده و در پروندههای راهنمایی و رانندگی، دعاوی کوچک و تخلیه غیرقانونی نیز بهعنوان قاضی موقت خدمت کرده است.

سوابق حرفهای او همچنین شامل ریاست انجمن مدافعان عمومی، سرپرستی وکلای دادگاه اطفال و راهنمایی جوانان از طریق برنامههای «دادگاه نوجوانان» است. تریفمن در بورلی هیلز هم بهعنوان عضو و هم رئیس کمیسیون تثبیت اجارهبهای شهر خدمت کرده است.

تریفمن گفت کارزار انتخاباتی او همچنان بر تجربه حضور در دادگاه، منش قضایی، صداقت و استقلال متمرکز خواهد بود.

تریفمن گفت: «من نامزد نشدهام تا قاضی یک گروه خاص باشم. نامزد شدهام تا قاضی همه باشم. هر فردی که وارد دادگاه میشود، شایسته آن است که سخنش شنیده شود، با کرامت با او رفتار شود و مطابق قانون، عادلانه دربارهاش قضاوت شود.»

کارزار تریفمن حمایت سازمانهای کارگری، گروههای حقوقی، مقامهای منتخب و هیئتهای تحریریه روزنامهها را به دست آورده است. از جمله حامیانی که این کارزار معرفی کرده، میتوان به جسی گابریل (Jesse Gabriel)، عضو مجلس ایالتی، استیو کولی (Steve Cooley)، دادستان پیشین شهرستان لسآنجلس، انجمن معاونان دادستانهای شهرستان لسآنجلس، کانون وکلای مکزیکیتبار آمریکا و چندین باشگاه منطقهای حزب دموکرات اشاره کرد.

این کارزار همچنین حمایت شورای منطقهای نجاران ایالتهای غربی، شعبه ۱۱ اتحادیه UNITE HERE، شعبه ۱۱ اتحادیه IBEW و شعبه ۲۵ اتحادیه تیمسترز را اعلام کرده است. چندین هیئت تحریریه روزنامههای جنوب کالیفرنیا نیز در جریان انتخابات مقدماتی از تریفمن حمایت کردند؛ از جمله لسآنجلس دیلی نیوز، پاسادنا استار-نیوز، دیلی بریز و متروپولیتن نیوز-انترپرایز.

اسلیتن که در انتخابات مقدماتی چهارم شد و بهعنوان قاضی حقوق اداری کالیفرنیا خدمت میکند، از آن زمان حمایت خود را از تریفمن در دور دوم اعلام کرده است.

راس نیز وکیل مدافع باسابقهای است و بهعنوان معاون ارشد محاکمات در دفتر مدافع عمومی جایگزین شهرستان لسآنجلس فعالیت میکند. رقابت ماه نوامبر مشخص خواهد کرد چه کسی کرسی خالی این دادگاه را در اختیار میگیرد.

Trump's voter claim and Khanna's moment

Programming note: We’ll be off next week but will be back in your inboxes on July 27.

DRIVING THE DAY — California Democrats on Thursday evening forcefully rejected the Department of Homeland Security’s claim that 190,832 noncitizens are registered to vote in the state, arguing the administration offered no evidence to back up the explosive allegation.

Trump’s “latest election conspiracy is nothing but a political stunt built on sham numbers that no one should trust,” Alex Padilla, California’s senior senator and former secretary of state, said in a statement. “DHS hasn’t explained how it arrived at these figures, how it obtained the underlying data, or whether any of these individuals are actually noncitizens who actually cast a ballot.”

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said his agency found thousands of non-citizens on voter rolls in California and three other states during a preliminary review and drafted a press release making the claim, John Sakellariadis and Maggie Miller reported.

The press release, which did not say whether there was any evidence of voting by non-citizens or explain how DHS reached its finding, was circulated inside the agency ahead of Trump’s planned prime time speech in which he had promised to reveal “really big news” on election security.

The announcement immediately raised questions about what records DHS relied on. California has so far succeeded in stopping the Trump administration from accessing its voter rolls. A federal judge in January dismissed a lawsuit the Department of Justice filed against Secretary of State Shirley Weber after her agency wouldn’t turn over the records the administration requested.

The DOJ has appealed the decision, and oral arguments took place before the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals in May.

“The California Secretary of State has not sent the federal government our statewide voter registration list in any format,” said DeDee Verdin, a spokesperson for the Secretary of State’s Office, in an email. “We have successfully fought the U.S. DOJ’s unlawful demand for a copy of our entire [unredacted] statewide voter registration database.”

“Given that no court has ruled in favor of U.S. DOJ’s efforts to access states’ unredacted voter rolls out of 15 cases that have reached a decision, we are optimistic that the Ninth Circuit will uphold the State’s ability to protect the sensitive information of California’s 23 million registered voters,” Verdin added.

Trump alluded to that challenge in an address Thursday evening, claiming his administration’s estimate was likely an undercount because states had refused to hand over their voter rolls.

Padilla said DHS’ “lack of transparency also raises serious questions about whether it violated state law to obtain California’s voter registration records.”

A spokesperson for the Los Angeles County Registrar said in a statement that “we have not received or provided information to the federal government regarding non-citizens on the rolls in Los Angeles County.”

Asked for comment, a spokesperson for Gavin Newsom pointed to a social media statement from the governor noting that only citizens are legally allowed to vote in state and federal elections in California.

“Voter fraud is EXTREMELY RARE — and almost always committed by U.S. citizens,” Newsom wrote. “Donald Trump’s Administration has repeatedly pushed false and misleading claims about elections. They have provided NO evidence to support these new ‘claims.”’

Marc Berman, a Democratic state lawmaker whose 2021 legislation made universal vote-by-mail permanent, said the Department of Homeland Security should instead focus on Trump’s baseless theories about his 2020 election loss.

“If Secretary Mullin wants to investigate voter fraud in America, I suggest he start with his boss,” Berman said in a statement. “The only person who has been caught demanding that elections officials make up thousands of votes is President Donald J. Trump, who begged the Georgia Secretary of State to ‘find 11,780 votes’ to steal the 2020 presidential election.”

— with help from Lindsey Holden

RO-ING — In the span of a week, Ro Khanna went from recriminations over his support for Graham Platner to sparring with the Israeli government over his detention in the West Bank and back to endorsing a new progressive Senate candidate in Maine.

It was peak Khanna — so much so that, at one point, he referred to himself as a “long-shot presidential” candidate.

The Silicon Valley lawmaker, a likely presidential contender, has long been known on Capitol Hill for his progressive politics and outspoken style. But now Khanna is offering for broader viewership an early glimpse into how that 2028 campaign may play out: Take major, headline-grabbing swings, and always double down on the next news cycle.

Critics cast him as a publicity hound, and he’s become a regular target of criticism from President Donald Trump, trillionaire Elon Musk and Israel Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

But where they see showboating, Khanna argues he’s offering a playbook for a more aggressive kind of Democratic politics that progressive voters long for — embracing tough fights that challenge the status quo around wealth inequality and foreign policy.

“I’m willing to take on the elite power structures of this country,” Khanna told Playbook. “And I’m willing to do it at a risk. That’s a lesson for Democrats in the attention economy: Have guts, take bold, clear stands that aren’t a word salad.”

Khanna’s headline-snatching sprint started last week with the implosion of Platner’s campaign for the Senate in Maine after POLITICO reported an allegation of sexual assault against Platner, an allegation he denied. Khanna had been one of Platner’s most vocal defenders amid a swirl of earlier controversies.

Khanna, after withdrawing his support and saying he “should’ve listened to (his) wife” about Platner, swiftly waded back into the Maine Senate contest, endorsing former Maine state Senate President Troy Jackson, another progressive who’s also backed by Bernie Sanders.

Within days, Khanna was sparring with Netanyahu and top Israeli officials after he said he had feared for his life when he was detained by Israeli settlers and soldiers during a visit to the occupied West Bank.

The incident made international headlines and emboldened Khanna and other progressives who’ve pushed to stop military aid. Israeli officials disputed aspects of Khanna’s account, but he pushed back — and in spicy fashion.

“Free advice to the Israelis: It’s not a good idea to detain long-shot presidential candidates,” Khanna told The New York Times. “Not how you’re going to build good will with the next American president, whoever that is.”

U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee called “the whole thing a stunt,” and various Israeli and Republican officials accused Khanna of staging a publicity gimmick to boost his presidential odds. A prominent Jewish group in Khanna’s backyard, the Jewish Community Relations Council of the San Francisco Bay Area, accused him of “using the backs of the Jewish community to gain the limelight.”

It’s the latest in what’s been a punchy year for Khanna. Last fall, he was a key player in Congress’ effort to force the release of the Epstein files and he sparred with Silicon Valley titans over his support for California’s proposed billionaires’ tax. There was also his tweet showdown with Musk earlier this summer.

Khanna said he has no plans to temper himself, adding that he’s still considering running for president despite being an “underdog” in early polling.

“Traditionally, people look for charismatic big personalities to charm them and win them over with magnetism and sizzle,” he said. “My view is these times call for something different.”

PLACE YOUR BETS — The 2026 World Cup comes to its conclusion Sunday when Argentina faces off against Spain. Playbook asked some of California’s most dedicated tourney followers to share their predictions for what will transpire in the final:

Rob Bonta, California attorney general, former Yale soccer player and father to professional soccer player Reina Bonta: “The South American champs vs the European Champs. Messi vs Yamal. San Jose Mayor Matt Mahan: “Given San Jose’s Spanish roots as the first official pueblo in “Alta California,” I’m going to call it 2-1 for Spain with a late-match Argentinian surge that falls just short.”

Tom Steyer, Democratic megadonor, former California gubernatorial candidate and former Yale soccer player: Spain, 2-1.

Randy Villegas, a Bernie Sanders-backed progressive running against GOP Rep. David Valadao: Spain, 2-1.

State Sen. Ben Allen, chair of the Senate Special Committee on International Sporting Events: Could not comment because he was too devastated by England’s loss to Argentina.

FIRST IN PLAYBOOK: NEW WEALTH TAX FOES — More public safety organizations are joining the coalition against a proposed tax on billionaires’ assets, with the California Professional Firefighters and California State Sheriffs coming out against Proposition 40 today. California Professional Firefighters President Darrell Roberts assailed the initiative as risky and unproven, warning in a statement that “when you gamble with the finances of our state and local governments, you gamble with public safety.”

AND (MAYBE) ALLIES — Meanwhile, the measure’s backers sought to drum up support on Capitol Hill this week as they work to counter the formidable coalition fighting it. Jones, a venture capitalist, is vying to oust Thompson, a fellow Democrat, in the race for a House seat that encompasses much of Napa County. Thompson’s campaign declined to respond to Jones

On Wednesday, Thompson said he couldn’t support the amendment “because it is so poorly drafted and overly broad that it would defund our efforts to protect civilians and promote peace, taking us farther from our goals.”

He added, “At the same time, I stand firmly against Netanyahu’s conduct in Gaza and his efforts to drag us into conflict with Iran.”

WASHINGTON

FIRST IN PLAYBOOK: ANTI-AID — Gregg Phillips, who attracted controversy as a top FEMA official and once claimed to have teleportation powers, fought against approving an extension for housing assistance for California fire victims shortly before he was pushed out of the agency, according to three people familiar with the matter.

“He kind of went off the reservation and was not keen on approving it,” said a current DHS official who had direct knowledge of Phillips’ qualms about granting the aid. A former DHS official said there was tension between Phillips and acting FEMA administrator Bob Fenton over the California extension. Phillips was pushing back on approving the California aid the day before he left his FEMA role in late June, according to one of the three people.

The people were granted anonymity to discuss internal deliberations they were not authorized to share.

Phillips pushed colleagues at FEMA for independent audits and reviews for the California assistance extension to be consistent with Trump’s executive order on combating fraud, the three people said. Phillips told colleagues that any grant that required an extension needed such anti-fraud protections, according to the people.

Some 35,000 people in California have received a total of $177 million in housing aid through the main FEMA program for such disasters, and an additional 1,000 people have used another FEMA program for getting such aid. In late June, the agency granted FEMA’s request for a yearlong extension for fire victims, which was due to expire July 9.

Phillips declined to comment. A FEMA spokesperson said that the agency was “grateful for his significant contributions” and said Phillips had stabilized the Office of Response and Recovery. “FEMA remains committed to transparency and integrity in all personnel and program decisions,” the spokesperson said. The spokesperson did not address a question on Phillips’ maneuvering against the aid.

Trump has clashed for years with Newsom over disaster aid. And in 2018, Trump initially refused to give California disaster aid for a massive wildfire but changed his mind after White House aides told the president that the fire-damaged area had supported him in the 2016 election, POLITICO reported. — Daniel Lippman and Thomas Frank

SILICON VALLEY

LOOKING FORWARD— In his two terms as governor, Gavin Newsom has threaded the needle with California’s booming tech sector, an approach that could be put to the test in his final months in office.

Neither an unabashed ally nor outright antagonist to Silicon Valley, Newsom has given the industry wide berth to innovate and grow, a posture that’s helped fuel billions of tech tax dollars into Golden State coffers. In some cases, he’s stepped in to put guardrails on the tech industry, as fears have risen around social media and artificial intelligence.

Now, with bills on chatbots, social media and AI workforce issues moving toward his desk, Newsom faces a choice: Try to stick to the middle path or take a more decisive stand for or against the industry.

“August into September could be the most consequential period of his tenure,” John Bennett, executive director of the nonprofit California Initiative for Technology and Democracy, said in an interview. “What he accomplishes in 2026 [could] define him in the next two years.”

WILL BRAKE FOR FIREWORKS — San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie is asking state autonomous vehicles regulators for changes after numerous Waymos blocked traffic lanes, leading to gridlock for cars, buses and thousands of fireworks viewers in the city on July 4th.

In a letter Lurie asked Toks Omishakin, who leads the California State Transportation Agency, to ensure that AVs won’t break down or run out of battery in traffic lanes — and that AV companies are able to respond quickly and coordinate with local agencies during events and emergencies.

State agencies regulate autonomous vehicle operations in California, with municipalities exercising little official control over their operations.

Lurie, in the letter, acknowledged that Waymo agreed to geofence some areas of the city ahead of July 4th and assigned staff to the city’s Emergency Operations Center. But the mayor said “the events that followed demonstrated that voluntary coordination and pre-event planning alone are insufficient.”

“Manufacturers must be able to assess evolving conditions and rapidly adjust fleet operations in real time,” he wrote. The San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency has apologized for the traffic delays, saying the transit system could not absorb the massive crowds that came out for the fireworks.

The state transportation agency referred questions to the Department of Motor Vehicles, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for the California Public Utilities Commission, which regulates commercial autonomous ride-hailing operations, said the agency was reviewing the letter.

Some of the changes Lurie is asking for are reflected in a bill from South Bay state Sen. Dave Cortese. His bill, SB 1246, would require stricter safety and oversight rules for AV companies statewide, while also requiring remote operators to be based in the U.S. with a valid driver’s license, establishing new rules for coordinating with first responders, and creating fines for blocking an emergency response.

In an interview with Decoded, Cortese called the Independence Day situation “predictable.”

“I hope his letter has some influence on the governor so my bill doesn’t get vetoed,” he said.
— Chase DiFeliciantonio

CALIFORNIA CURRENTS

TO 2028 AND BEYOND — We’re still two years from the Olympic Games in Los Angeles, but transit and community groups are already thinking about whether climate progress will be part of the post-2028 legacy. This week, POLITICO’s Alex Nieves attended a two-day summit focused on leveraging the Olympics to accelerate clean energy and transportation. REPUBLICAN RICHES — Despite losing significant political leverage under California Democrats’ redistricting effort, California Republicans in remaining competitive House seats still beat their Democratic opponents in campaign cash, Maya C. Miller reports for CalMatters. Valadao of the Central Valley, Jim Desmond of San Diego and Republican-turned-independent Rep. Kevin Kiley of the Sacramento suburbs all boast millions in their campaign coffers, far more than their opponents. The Republican funding success is magnified by a recent Supreme Court decision eliminating coordinated spending between candidates and political parties, causing Democrats to reevaluate their own campaign spending.

COMMUNICATIONS CHAOS — An unpaid adviser for Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass handled her office communications while balancing a nearly $600,000 three-year contract with Los Angeles World Airports for months, reports Noah Goldberg for the Los Angeles Times.

Yusef Robb, who leads the firm tk/Communications, served as an unpaid spokesperson and adviser for Bass from February through the beginning of June. On June 19, he started working for Lineage Logistics, the company whose Boyle Heights warehouse burned for eight days last month. He continued to advise Bass for free until the Los Angeles Times and other outlets reported on his work for Lineage on Saturday, prompting conflict-of-interest concerns.

Former Foes Unite Behind Brian Goldsmith in SD 24 Race

July 16 2026

Written by Nick Antonicello.

WESTSIDE - In an attempt to consolidate a large bloc of votes behind his post primary efforts, moderate Democrat Brian Goldsmith added to his long list of endorsements by securing the support of former rivals Eric Alegria and Mike Newhouse.

Goldsmith is facing West Hollywood Councilmember John Erickson in this consolidated runoff to succeed retiring incumbent Ben Allen of Santa Monica who is running for California Insurance Commissioner.

Allen has endorsed Goldsmith as his successor in Sacramento.

Goldsmith announced the enthusiastic endorsement of Palos Verdes Peninsula School Board Member and former Rancho Palos Verdes City Councilmember Eric Alegria. With Alegria’s backing, Goldsmith has now earned the support of three former challengers, including former Los Angeles Planning Commission member Mike Newhouse and community advocate Ellen Evans.

This rapid consolidation serves as a testament to Goldsmith’s ability to build a broad, diverse coalition that can cut through the political noise in Sacramento and secure tangible results for residents of this affluent and coastal legislative district that stretches from the South Bay, the Beach Cities and due north to Malibu and the Pacific Palisades according to his campaign.

Alegria released the following statement:

“Throughout my years of public service as a School Board Member, City Councilmember, and Mayor, I have learned that meaningful progress comes from bringing people together, listening to our communities, and focusing on solutions rather than division.

That belief guided my campaign for State Senate, and it is why I believe Brian Goldsmith is the right leader for Senate District 24. At a time when our communities need unity and thoughtful leadership, Brian brings the integrity and collaborative approach necessary to deliver results.

I know the importance of leaders who listen, build partnerships, and follow through. Brian Goldsmith has demonstrated those qualities, and I am proud to offer him my full support for State Senate.”

Goldsmith responded in kind: “I am deeply honored to receive Eric’s endorsement. He has a proven record of delivering under pressure—whether navigating environmental crises, addressing local crime, or protecting thousands of entertainment industry jobs. I look forward to partnering with him and leaning on his deep experience to champion the unique needs of the South Bay."

Newhouse also offered a strong endorsement of this fellow, "common sense" Democrat. \

"I also believe that providing housing and services to save people from a life, and death, on the streets is not inconsistent with enforcing anti-camping laws that we can fully support, and public safety while standing up for our California values and the most vulnerable amongst us. Having gotten to know Brian Goldsmith over the last 14 months, he is a common sense, independent-minded and pragmatic leader who shares that vision and will work tirelessly to ensure California is a place where working families can afford to live and thrive. I’m proud to endorse him to be our next State Senator," offered the Venice homeowner, husband and father of two teenage sons. Newhouse is an attorney by profession, small business owner and longtime Los Angeles Neighborhood Council advocate.

Goldsmith also embraced his newfound support by Alegria. \

"Eric is an accomplished executive, educator, and South Bay policymaker. Currently serving on the Palos Verdes Peninsula Unified School District and as COO of the Wellness Equity Alliance, he possesses nearly twenty years of experience expanding healthcare access for underserved communities. His extensive public service includes tenure on the Rancho Palos Verdes City Council, where he successfully navigated the devastating Portuguese Bend Landslides, led the initiative to secure the city's ranking as the fourth safest in the state, and slashed small business license taxes to zero during the pandemic. A California Film Commissioner, small business owner, and holder of multiple advanced degrees from USC, LMU, and CGU, he combines deep analytical policy expertise with a pragmatic, independent approach to governance focused on lowering costs, protecting public safety, and defending the local economy," noted the candidate.

These latest endorsements could certainly sway the electoral math in Goldsmith's favor when you review the June 2nd Primary tallies.

While West Hollywood Councilmember Erickson led the fragmented field of 10 with 62,397, Goldsmith was right behind with 55,627. The two Republicans, G. Rick Marshall (53,350) and Kristina Irwin (42,939) finished third and fourth respectively with Santa Monica College Trustee Dr. Sion Roy rounding out the top five finishers with 41,956 votes.

With Newhouse finishing 6th with 13,824, Alegria 7th with 12,412 and Evans ninth with 9,024, a solid foundation of new support is brewing in favor of Goldsmith as he continues to reach out and construct a broad-based coalition of support both geographically and politically speaking.

That said, Roy's endorsement could be crucial as well.

He did tally nearly 42,000 votes (13.8%), and many of his supporters came from Santa Monica and the healthcare community, where he had built support as a practicing physician.

Observers say his supporters are more ideologically aligned with Erickson, given both candidates' Democratic affiliations and support from progressive and labor constituencies during the primary, although that does not necessarily mean Roy would endorse Erickson if he chose to endorse anyone at all.

If Roy does make an endorsement in the campaign, it could matter most in Santa Monica, Malibu, and portions of the Westside where he performed relatively well as he was the officially endorsed candidate of the California Democratic Party.

Running for the first time, Goldsmith has earned numerous endorsements from a broad spectrum of prominent Democratic officials, organizations, and community leaders including:

Secretary Hillary Rodham Clinton; Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi; Senator Barbara Boxer (ret.); Senator Henry Stern (SD-27); Senator Josh Becker (SD-13); Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (AD-46); Assemblymember Rick Chavez Zbur (AD-51); Assemblymember Jacqui Irwin (AD-42); Assemblymember Esmeralda Soria (AD-27); former US Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg; Bob Hertzberg, former California State Senate Majority Leader and Assembly Speaker; and Fran Pavley, former California State Senator and Assemblymember.

Goldsmith is a small business owner, award-winning journalist, and Democratic consultant. Through his business, he has advised candidates, nonprofits, and companies, and helped elect several prominent Democratic members of Congress. Brian also founded Scriber, a text-based subscription service, and co-founded Junction, an equity crowdfunding business.

A graduate of Harvard College and Stanford Law School. Goldsmith is a Los Angeles native, and he and his wife Claire, an educator, reside in Beverly Hills with their two young children, Eliza and Teddy.

The 24th Senate Legislative district includes the cities of Agoura Hills, Beverly Hills, Calabasas, El Segundo, Gardena, Hermosa Beach, Hidden Hills, Lomita, Malibu, Manhattan Beach, Palos Verdes Estates, Rancho Palos Verdes, Redondo Beach, Rolling Hills, Rolling Hills Estates, Santa Monica, Torrance, West Hollywood, and Westlake Village; the Los Angeles neighborhoods of Bel Air, Beverly Grove, Brentwood, Fairfax, Holmby Hills, Hollywood, Hollywood Hills, Little Holmby, Mid City West, Pacific Palisades, Playa del Rey, Sunset Hills, Venice, Westwood, and Westwood Village; and the unincorporated Los Angeles County communities of the Santa Monica Mountains and Marina Del Rey.

(Nick Antonicello is a thirty-three-year resident of the Westside and is a regular contributor to City Watch LA and is covering the race for this open senate seat. A former legislative aide to the New Jersey Senate and General Assembly, he can be reached via e-mail at [email protected])
