Recent History Series: The 20-Year Cold Call: How AIPAC’s Invisible Pipeline Recruits Your Politicians in College

Imagine you are a twenty-year-old college student. You just won your campus election to become Student Body President. You sit down in your dorm room, your flip phone buzzes, and a Washington, D.C. area code pops up.

The person on the other end is not selling a product. They are pitching you your own future.

This is not a conspiracy theory. It is the highly disciplined, multi-decade talent acquisition strategy of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC). For over thirty years, the organization has operated a quiet talent filter that targets campus leaders years before they ever run for public office. By looking at how this pipeline works, we can trace exactly how today’s political and corporate landscapes were shaped.

If you appreciate me digging into this stuff and calling it like I see it, please consider a paid subscription. It is just me over here doing the research and connecting the dots, and your support is what allows me to keep this totally independent. It really does make a difference in helping me keep the lights on while I try to get the truth out.

Upgrade to Paid: Helps me dedicate more time to these deep dives.

Share this post: Honestly, just sending this to one person who needs to see it is huge.

Subscribe on Youtube: This is the platform I most need help with.

The Logic of the College Pivot

In the late 1990s and early 2000s, AIPAC’s leadership development division, directed by Jonathan Kessler, pivoted to a highly strategic model. Instead of spending millions of dollars trying to persuade established, stubborn politicians to change their minds, the organization realized it was far more efficient to find future politicians while they were still in college.

The formula was simple. The organization actively monitored student body elections, particularly at top public universities, Ivy League schools, and Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs). If you won the student presidency, or if you were elected to lead the campus College Democrats or College Republicans, you were statistically the most likely person in your peer group to run for public office in twenty years.

Staffers would cold-call these student leaders within days of their election victories. They offered congratulations, invited them to elite leadership summits like the Saban National Political Leadership Training Seminar, and offered fully funded trips to Israel through initiatives like the Campus Allies Mission.

From Student Senate to Capitol Hill

For many of these students, this early outreach built the foundation of their future political careers.

  • Bakari Sellers: In 2004, Sellers was elected student body president of Morehouse College. Within a week, he received a call from AIPAC’s Jonathan Kessler. The organization flew him to national seminars, introduced him to donor networks, and eventually gave him a primetime speaking slot at their national policy conference. Sellers has explicitly credited this early exposure with building the financial and professional network that helped him become the youngest member of the South Carolina state legislature.

  • Senator Cory Booker (D-NJ): While Booker’s intensive Jewish text study began through a close personal friendship with Rabbi Shmuley Boteach during his Rhodes Scholar years at Oxford, his introduction to the broader pro-Israel donor network was deeply intertwined with these student-era relationships.

  • Representative Glenn Ivey (D-MD): Long before winning his seat in Congress, Ivey was actively engaged by pro-Israel student networks during his undergraduate years in student politics at Princeton University.

  • Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-CA): Gabriel was targeted and recruited while serving as the student body president of UC Berkeley. Alongside his classmate Daniel Frankenstein, Gabriel was heavily involved in student senate organizing, establishing a template for campus advocacy that he eventually carried into the California State Assembly.

  • Representative Nick Miccarelli (R-PA): Recruited during his undergraduate years while serving as a leader of the College Republicans, Miccarelli used the policy training and network from the Campus Allies program to transition directly into state-level electoral politics.

The Corporate and Media Off-Ramp

Not every college student who goes through a political pipeline ends up on a ballot. The true scale of this talent acquisition strategy is that it seeds pro-Israel advocates across all major sectors of American influence.

  • Venture Capital: Daniel Frankenstein, who partnered with Jesse Gabriel as student activists at UC Berkeley, used his campus network to eventually co-found JANVEST Capital Partners, a venture capital firm that invests exclusively in Israeli technology startups.

  • Political Strategy & Lobbying: Alex Schriver, who was recruited through the campus pipeline while serving as the National Chairman of the College Republican National Committee, used those connections to transition directly to Capitol Hill as Chief of Staff to U.S. Representative Bradley Byrne. Today, he operates as a senior public affairs executive and lobbyist.

  • Corporate Law & Presidential Campaigns: Micah Fielden was recruited immediately after completing his term as Student Body President of the University of Kentucky. He used the connections made on his campus trip to secure a role on Mitt Romney’s 2012 presidential campaign, eventually transitioning into a career at elite corporate law firms.

  • Media & National Journalism: The social networks built at these student summits also shaped media landscapes. For example, national journalist Erielle Reshef, who is married to Daniel Frankenstein, was also deeply involved in the same network of campus advocacy during her formative years.

The Invisible Infrastructure

At its peak, this campus initiative brought four hundred to five hundred college student leaders to Washington twice a year. This annual cohort typically included up to three hundred student body presidents and over one hundred leaders of College Democrats and College Republicans from across the nation.

Only a tiny fraction of these students ever run for Congress. Most of them become corporate lawyers, venture capitalists, public relations executives, or behind-the-scenes political consultants. They do not wear name tags identifying themselves as former campus recruits, and they do not list student leadership seminars on their professional resumes.

This is not a shadow government. It is simply a highly disciplined talent filter that understood how to play the long game. By investing in twenty-year-old student leaders, they built an invisible, bipartisan infrastructure that still defines American foreign policy and industry decades later.

Advocates want to require California to investigate ICE shootings

Kendra Hanna

Published July 15, 2026 at 7:29 PM PDT

After two men were shot and killed by ICE agents this month, advocates are renewing calls to require independent investigations into shootings by federal immigration officers in California.

Assembly Bill 1806 would have the state attorney general perform a thorough investigation into any shooting involving an immigration agent and a civilian.

“We have seen the federal government investigate itself,” said Bruno Huizar with the California Immigrant Policy Center, referencing what he called “unlawful killings.”

“Assembly Bill 1806 would require our state Attorney General to conduct an independent investigation,” Huizar told KCBX.

The bill, coauthored by Assemblymembers Juan Carrillo and Jesse Gabriel, was approved by the state Assembly in May. It’s currently in committee.

In a statement to KCBX, Assemblymember Gabriel said recent shootings in Maine and Texas “underscore the urgent need for legislation to hold ICE accountable.”

“California cannot and will not stand idly by in the face of the Trump Administration’s reckless immigration policies,” he wrote.

In January, after federal agents shot and killed two people in Minnesota, California Attorney General Rob Bonta said state law enforcement can investigate crimes committed by federal agents.

In a statement, Bonta wrote that federal and state law enforcement normally collaborate on investigations.

“...[U]nfortunately, as recent events in Minnesota have made clear, cooperation in the conduct of such investigations can no longer be expected from the federal government,” Bonta wrote.

Existing California law does require the state to investigate fatal shootings of unarmed people by law enforcement officers.

Huizar says that AB 1806 “clarifies” state law by explicitly referencing shootings by federal immigration agents.

In March, the Department of Justice announced that it was investigating a fatal shooting by a San Luis Obispo Police Department officer.

According to reporting from CalMatters, those investigations often stretch on for years — the Department of Justice hasn’t recommended charges against an officer since the program began.

The office of the Maine Attorney General has launched an investigation into the recent shooting by an ICE agent of 26-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero.

Local police in Biddeford, Maine told the the Portland Press Herald their role was limited to providing security at the scene of the shooting.

In Texas, the Attorney General hasn’t announced an investigation into the death of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, who was shot and killed by an ICE agent in Houston earlier this month.

However, local officials in Harris County have launched their own investigation, according to Houston Public Media.

미국내 초가공식품에 대한 소송과 비 초가공식품 인증제도-제이 리(Jay Lee)의 미국 통신(176)

  • Jay Lee
  • 승인 2026.07.14 07:42

AB 2244 ‘초가공식품 인증 법안’ 준비…하원 통과
아닐 땐 Non-UPF…유통업체 ‘골든 존’ 진열해야
소비자, 초가공식품 제조사에 10억 불 손해배상 소송
복합 성분 첨가제 많은 한국 식품 발 빠른 대응 필요

이종찬 대표(J&B Food Consulting)

"부모들이 아이에게 무엇을 먹이는지 이해하기 위해 화학 박사학위까지 딸 필요는 없다."

최근 미국 식품업계를 가장 뜨겁게 달구고 있는 캘리포니아주 하원의원 제시 가브리엘(Jesse Gabriel)이 던진 일침이다. 캘리포니아주 하원을 74 대 0이라는 압도적인 표차로 통과하고 현재 상원 심사를 거치고 있는 ‘AB 2244(초가공식품 인증 표준 법안)’의 핵심을 관통하는 대목이다.

현재 미국 식품 시장은 거대한 변곡점을 지나고 있다. 정부가 공인하는 '비(非)초가공식품(Non-UPF)' 인증 마크 도입이 코앞으로 다가온 한편, 법원에서는 대형 식품 기업들을 상대로 한 천문학적인 규모의 집단소송이 잇따르고 있다. 미국 시장을 무대로 삼는 글로벌 식품 기업, 특히 K-푸드 수출 기업들이 결코 지나쳐서는 안 될 규제와 사법 리스크의 양동작전이 시작된 것이다.

‘초가공식품(Ultra-Processed Foods, UPF)’은 식품의 보존성, 맛, 시각적 효과를 극대화하기 위해 감미료, 착색료, 유화제 등의 식품 첨가물을 넣고 산업적으로 재가공한 식품을 말한다. 미국인 성인 식단의 절반 이상을 차지할 만큼 보편화되어 있지만, 최근 암, 심혈관 질환, 제2형 당뇨와의 연관성이 잇따라 증명되며 소비자들의 불안감이 극에 달했다. 문제는 소비자가 제품 뒷면의 복잡한 원재료명을 보고 이것이 UPF인지 아닌지 구별하기가 불가능에 가깝다는 점이었다.

AB 2244 법안은 이 혼란을 단칼에 정리하겠다는 의도다. 마치 우리가 잘 아는 유기농 인증인 ‘USDA Organic’처럼, 캘리포니아 보건부(CDPH)의 감독 아래 독립적인 인증 기관을 두고 기준을 통과한 제품에 ‘Non-Ultraprocessed Certified’라는 주 정부 공인 인장을 찍어주겠다는 것이다. 포장 전면에 붙을 이 심플한 마크 하나가 복잡한 화학 용어 가득한 성분표를 대체하게 된다.

더욱이 이 법안은 대형 유통업체(리테일러)에 부과되는 '의무 진열 및 가시성 확보' 조항까지 담고 있다. 연 매출 1000만 달러 이상의 대형마트는 이 인증을 받은 제품들을 매대 전면, 계산대 주변 등 소비자의 눈길이 가장 잘 닿는 '골든 존'에 의무적으로 돋보이게 진열해야 한다. 제조사들 입장에서는 유통 경쟁력을 위해서라도 울며 겨자 먹기로 제품 성분을 재배합 (리포뮬레이션)해 인증을 따내야만 하는 강력한 유인이 작동하게 된다.

캘리포니아가 입법을 통해 식품 업계를 압박하고 있다면, 법원에서는 '사법적 단죄'를 요구하는 소비자들의 분노가 폭발하고 있다.

최근 샌프란시스코에서 촉발된 초가공식품 집단소송의 불길이 위스콘신 동부연방법원으로 옮겨붙었다. 소비자들은 크래프트하인즈, 펩시코, 몬델리즈, 네슬레USA, 제너럴밀스, 코카콜라 등 미국의 내노라하는 글로벌 식품 거인들을 상대로 무려 10억 달러(약 1조 3천억 원)에 달하는 대규모 손해배상 청구 소송을 제기했다.

한국제품의 취약점인 복합성분들의 첨가제가 많이 들어간 제품들은 발 빠른 대응이 필요할 때이다.

California lawmakers are moving to put a constitutional amendment on the November ballot that would let the state sock away more of its stock market windfall and keep those savings clear of existing spending caps. The plan would channel a larger share of boom-year revenue into California’s rainy-day accounts ahead of several anticipated artificial intelligence IPOs, with supporters arguing it will smooth out the capital gains highs and lows that have driven recent budget surpluses.

As outlined by the California Secretary of State, the constitutional amendment, ACA 20, known as the Save for California’s Future Act, has been certified for the November 3 ballot and would rewrite the state’s reserve and spending limit rules. The ballot measure would let lawmakers count certain deposits into reserves outside the state’s spending cap, a technical change backers say is needed so California can save more during flush years. Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, who authored ACA 20, has pitched it as a bipartisan safeguard for education, health care, and other core services, according to the Assembly Democratic Caucus.

Nonpartisan budget analysts say the recent revenue bump is driven largely by capital gains from AI-linked stocks and the prospect of several large tech IPOs, prompting lawmakers to try to bank the unusual windfall while markets are still hot, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office. Bloomberg first reported that lawmakers are moving to carve those reserve deposits out of the state’s spending limit ahead of what it called "hot" AI IPOs. The May budget revision projected higher income tax receipts that state leaders partly credit to a stock market rally centered on AI companies.

How the Amendment Would Work

The measure would change the formulas that trigger deposits into the Budget Stabilization Account and related reserves, including raising the cap on how much the state can hold there, according to the ballot language. CalMatters has reported that the amendment would require bigger deposits when capital gains revenues cross certain thresholds, including a provision that 150% of excess capital gains must be deposited into the Budget Stabilization Account when those gains exceed 10% of general fund revenues. The legal specifics are laid out in ACA 20, which supporters argue updates California’s aging fiscal guardrails for the AI era.

Politics and the Pitch

Governor Gavin Newsom and top legislative leaders folded the reserve proposal into this year’s budget deal, arguing that locking money away now is the best way to shield key programs when the economy cools. Senate leaders outlined the three-way agreement that pushed ACA 20 onto the ballot. The timing is no accident, lawmakers say, pointing to higher than expected revenues fueled by the stock rally and looming IPOs, while KCRA has broken down how the measure would tweak reserve calculations.

Analysts Urge Caution

Budget analysts warn that the current gains are heavily concentrated in capital gains tax receipts and could fade quickly if markets cool, leaving the state in a bind if leaders build long-term spending on short-term money. The Legislative Analyst's Office has repeatedly cautioned that counting on uninterrupted AI-fueled market growth is risky and that one-time windfalls should not be used to fund ongoing programs. Policy groups tracking the May revision have echoed that warning, noting that revenue assumptions tied to tech valuations are volatile and that beefed-up reserves only help if paired with restrained spending, according to the California Budget & Policy Center.

What Voters Will Decide

If voters approve ACA 20 on November 3, the state constitution would be amended to allow a larger share of excess capital gains revenue to be routed into reserves and to let some of those deposits sit outside the Gann spending limit. The California Secretary of State has already certified the measure for the ballot, and lawmakers will still need to hammer out implementing details. The changes would take effect only if voters sign off and would reshape how Sacramento prepares for the next downturn.

Backers cast the amendment as basic fiscal common sense. Skeptics counter that it could someday be used to gloss over tough decisions about spending, KCRA has reported. Voters will decide on November 3 whether to lock more of this AI-era windfall into a supersized rainy-day fund or keep California’s existing spending rules in place.

State permanently commits to $80M annually for nonprofit security

Niva Ashkenazi

California has committed to $80 million in annual funding to protect vulnerable sites, including Jewish congregations, schools and community centers, from extremist violence, ending the yearly budget fights over the state’s security grant program for nonprofits.

The commitment, included in the budget agreement that Gov. Gavin Newsom signed on June 29, marks the first time the California State Nonprofit Security Grant Program has permanent annual funding since it was created in 2015.

“This is a generational win,” said David Bocarsly, CEO of Jewish California, the statewide coalition of Jewish groups that pushed for the funding. “For the first time, our institutions have security funding they can rely on every single year, rather than a one-time appropriation we have to fight for from scratch. We are no longer starting at zero each year. We are building from a permanent foundation.”

Newsom and the state Legislature made the funding permanent despite heavy pressure on the state budget. The $352 billion spending plan for 2026-27 relies on an expected surge in tax revenue from the AI boom to close the multibillion dollar deficit the state faced. 

Jewish California said the win is the result of an advocacy alliance with other ethnic and religious groups, including the African Methodist Episcopal Church, the Muslim Public Affairs Council, the Hollywood Sikh Temple and the Hindu American Foundation.

The program funds security upgrades, such as cameras, fencing and trained guards, at nonprofits that are considered vulnerable to hate crimes, including Jewish institutions, houses of worship of all faiths, reproductive health clinics and LGTBQ centers. More than $300 million has been granted to some 1,600 nonprofits since the program’s inception, according to Jewish California. 

The permanence of the funding will bring relief and certainty to Jewish leaders tasked with planning for their organization’s security needs, according to Rudy Granados, senior director of community security at Jewish Federation Bay Area. 

“It helps with the anxiety for the organizations themselves, and it helps them plan out better what they’re going to need and where they can dedicate their resources,” Granados said.

Now, lawmakers with the California Legislative Jewish Caucus are seeking to expand the program. 

AB 1836, authored by Jewish caucus chair Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino) and caucus member Chris Ward (D-San Diego), is making its way through the Senate. It seeks an additional $100 million for the program and to extend eligibility to security for offsite events. 

The effort comes amid the continuing threat of antisemitic violence and as a parallel federal program for nonprofit security is resuming after a period of uncertainty and confusion. The federal Nonprofit Security Grant Program was stalled amid a wider political impasse in Congress that shut down the Department of Homeland Security from February through April. In late June, the federal grant program published a notice for 56 new awards totaling $300 million, with an application deadline on July 24. 

At least one program related to fighting hate-related violence didn’t make it into California’s new budget. The state allowed funding to expire for a hotline to report hate crimes. 

The California vs. Hate hotline, created in 2023, allowed callers to report hate crimes they experienced or witnessed and referred callers to trained professionals for assistance. 

Since its launch in May 2023, the hotline responded to over 6,800 calls, nearly 1,000 of which were made in 2025, according to the California Civil Rights Department (CRD), which housed the program. (As of July 1, the CRD was transferred to the California Housing and Homelessness Agency.)

The CRD confirmed it did not request new funding for the hotline this year but wouldn’t say why. 

As of July 1, the hotline features a recorded message that also appears on its website: “The CA vs. Hate Resource Line and Network is no longer operational due to funding constraints in the state budget. If you are in immediate danger, call 911. If you are not in immediate danger and are seeking resources or referrals to service organizations in your area, call 211.”

Several Jewish groups worked with the state officials on the hotline program, including the Anti-Defamation League, which said it laments its loss. 

The ADL worked with the hotline’s case managers to provide insights on antisemitism and trends of extremism, as well as tailored advice on how to respond to specific reports of antisemitic hate, according to ADL Central Pacific associate regional director Yuval Berenstein. 

“I always felt, when I was working with them, that our issues, our community was heard, and they were actively trying to make sure that they can help our community,” he said. “Without California vs. Hate, everyone is going to be less served, and it’s really a shame.”

California Lawmakers Defend New ‘Glock Ban’ in Face of Trump Lawsuit

Ayah Ali-Ahmad

The state “won’t back down in the face of threats from Donald Trump and the NRA,” said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, an author of a new law restricting pistols that can be converted into fully automatic machine guns.

Jul 2, 2026

Updated 4:42 pm PT

Instructor Tom Nguyen, middle, founder of L.A. Progressive Shooters, instructs Nikki Shrieves, 41, right, during a firearms education course in Norwalk, California, on Oct. 29, 2023. Nikki is holding a 9mm Glock. Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office says it will defend California’s gun safety laws in court after the Trump administration filed suit Wednesday.  (Francine Orr/ Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

The ban on Glock-style handguns, AB 1127, took effect Wednesday. It prohibits the sale of pistols with a specific trigger design that allows them to be converted into fully automatic weapons using a small device known as a “switch,” sometimes made on a 3D printer.

Lawmakers pointed to a 2022 mass shooting near the state Capitol in Sacramento, which killed six people and wounded a dozen more, as an example of the danger posed by converted weapons.

“California won’t back down in the face of threats from Donald Trump and the NRA,” Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, D-Encino, one of the bill’s authors, said in a statement on Wednesday. “As a parent and lawmaker, I refuse to stand idly by while our schools and communities are being threatened by illegal gun violence.”

Though the Glock brand is not directly named in the new law, the DOJ’s complaint argues the law amounts to a ban on the country’s most popular handgun, citing analyst estimates that Glock held nearly two-thirds of the U.S. handgun market as of 2020. The complaint compares the law to banning shotguns because they could be illegally sawed off, arguing that the ability to convert a legal weapon doesn’t justify banning it.

James Gibbons-Shapiro, an assistant district attorney of Santa Clara County who oversees the office’s victim services unit, said the law addresses a threat he’s seen up close. His team has responded to two mass shootings since 2019, which includes the 2021 shooting at a VTA rail yard in San José that killed nine people.

“You shouldn’t be able to sell a gun that can easily convert to a machine gun with a plastic insert,” Gibbons-Shapiro said. “It’s illegal to have a machine gun under federal law. Those are weapons of war.”

He said the law is part of a broader local effort — including gun violence restraining orders and prosecutions of people manufacturing untraceable “ghost guns” — aimed at preventing mass shootings before they happen.

“These laws do not prevent guns from being sold in California,” he said. “They are trying to make sure that people who buy guns buy guns that are safe.”

Adam Wilson, California director for Gun Owners of California, said his organization was “ecstatic” about the lawsuit, arguing the state is illegally banning a firearm in common use. He dismissed the argument that Glock-style pistols are uniquely dangerous simply because they can be illegally modified.

“If the state of California is going to argue potential for misuse on one of the most commonly owned handguns in America, they can argue potential for misuse for any weapon that’s ever existed,” Wilson said. “Even things that aren’t weapons, like cars.”

The DOJ’s lawsuit also revives a fight over the state’s handgun roster, and targets state requirements that new handguns include a chamber-load indicator and a mechanism that prevents firing when the magazine is removed. Those requirements have faced a separate legal challenge in Boland v. Bonta. In 2023, a federal judge struck down its safety standards, including a microstamping rule — where handguns transfer identifiers like make, model and serial number onto fired shell casings — the state has since delayed to 2028.

Wilson argued gun owners shouldn’t need government-mandated features on their weapons.

“Gun owners are generally very law-abiding and responsible citizens,” he said. “They don’t need the government to babysit what kind of features should or should not be on the weapons that they choose for self-defense.”

Adam Skaggs, chief counsel and vice president at Giffords Law Center, an anti-gun violence advocacy group led by former Rep. Gabby Giffords, D-Arizona, defended the law’s narrow scope.

“AB 1127 does not ban Glocks outright,” he said. “The law prohibits gun dealers from selling firearms that can be easily converted into illegal fully automatic weapons.”

Giffords’ analysis has pointed to Glock’s own response as evidence the approach is working: after the law passed, the company announced a redesign of some newer models intended to make them harder to convert, though it remains unclear whether the changes are effective enough to deter criminal use.

The lawsuit is the latest in a string of legal battles between the Trump administration and California, which has separately sued or been sued by the federal government over immigration enforcement and other policies in recent months.

Gibbons-Shapiro’s office has spent years responding to gun violence cases, and so he hopes the law will hold. “I hope the way this lawsuit shakes out is that everybody sees that these laws are reasonable for the safety of people in our community,” he said.

Gabriel’s gun law draws fed lawsuit – Horvath takes red tape off restaurant menu – Bass houses vets – Barger pushes SBA fire loan extensions

Los Angeles County Politics

Gabriel’s gun law draws fed lawsuit

Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D – Encino, Lake Balboa, Van Nuys) saw his legislation closing a machine gun conversion loophole take effect yesterday, only to face an immediate federal lawsuit from the Trump administration’s Department of Justice seeking to overturn it.

Assembly Bill 1127prohibits the sale of semi-automatic handguns in California that can be easily converted into fully automatic weapons using a small device known as a “switch.” Law enforcement agencies nationwide have reported a surge in recoveries of these conversion devices, and a 2022 shooting just blocks from the California State Capitol – which left six dead and a dozen wounded – involved one of these modified weapons.

“California won’t back down in the face of threats from Donald Trump and the NRA,” said Gabriel. “As a parent and lawmaker, I refuse to stand idly by while our schools and communities are being threatened by illegal gun violence. California is proud to be a national leader in enacting commonsense gun safety laws, and we will defend these life-saving laws from those who prioritize gun industry profits over the safety of our communities.”

Governor Gavin Newsom signed AB 1127 into law in October 2025. Following its passage, the National Rifle Association, Firearms Policy Coalition, and Second Amendment Foundation filed a legal challenge – but later voluntarily dismissed it.

The DOJ lawsuit filed yesterday represents a new and more formidable front in the fight over the law. Since California passed the bill, New York, Connecticut, and Maryland have enacted similar legislation.

Horvath takes red tape off restaurant menu

Los Angeles County Supervisor Lindsey P. Horvath (D – Western Los Angeles and San Fernando Valley, including Pacoima, Panorama City, Santa Monica, Beverly Hills, West Hollywood, Calabasas, Malibu, Sylmar) won Board approval this week for a motion strengthening support and resources for restaurant owners navigating the county’s permitting and plan check processes.

The action directs the Department of Public Health and the Department of Public Works to develop implementation plans for new state laws streamlining restaurant permitting and renovation processes, including expedited review timelines and greater operational flexibility.

The Department of Public Health was also directed to update restaurant permitting websites, checklists and toolkits to make them more user-friendly, conduct outreach to ensure operators understand new state policies, and explore expanding one-on-one concierge-style technical assistance for restaurant owners before plans are submitted.

“Every restaurant starts with someone sharing a piece of themselves – a family recipe, a cultural tradition, or a dream they’ve carried for years,” said Horvath. “Those dreams become the places where we celebrate birthdays, gather after long days, and connect with neighbors and new cultures. The people opening and operating restaurants are taking a chance on our communities, and we should meet that courage with clear guidance, meaningful support, and a path that makes it easier to bring those ideas to life.”

Restaurants support thousands of jobs and are a critical driver of tourism and local economic activity across LA County’s 88 cities and unincorporated areas.

Bass houses 1,000 vets

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass announced yesterday that more than 1,000 veterans have secured permanent housing through her administration’s House Our Vets initiative, marking a major milestone in the city’s effort to end veteran homelessness.

Speaking from the rooftop terrace of a newly constructed affordable housing complex north of downtown Los Angeles, Bass celebrated the milestone alongside veterans, nonprofit service providers and community members – including Kevina Mitchell, a former Army soldier who experienced years of housing instability following a medical discharge while managing health challenges. Mitchell, now the mother of a seven-month-old, signed her lease and received her keys at the event.

“I made a promise to this city that we would do everything in our power to bring unhoused Angelenos indoors,” said Bass. “Today, more than 1,000 veterans and their families have secured housing through the House Our Vets initiative. For generations, Americans have stepped forward to serve our nation. As our country prepares to celebrate its 250th birthday, there is no better way to honor that service than by making sure every veteran has a place to call home.”

Launched in early 2025, House Our Vets brought together city, federal and nonprofit partners to accelerate housing placements for veterans. To date the initiative has housed 1,094 veterans and their families.

Barger pushes SBA fire loan extensions

Los Angeles County Supervisor Kathryn Barger (R – Palmdale, Lancaster, Santa Clarita, San Marino, Pasadena, La Canada Flintridge, portions of the San Gabriel Valley) is urging residents and small business owners impacted by the Eaton Fire to take advantage of what the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) is calling its final extension of disaster loan disbursement deadlines.

Under the extension, borrowers approved for SBA Home Physical Disaster Loans and Business Physical Disaster Loans will have 24 months from the date of their loan authorization to draw down approved funds – recognizing that many survivors continue to face delays related to insurance claims and other rebuilding challenges.

“While that progress is making a real difference, many wildfire survivors continue to face challenges that are beyond their control,” said Barger. “This SBA extension provides much needed flexibility, giving families and small businesses additional time to access the recovery funding they’ve already been approved to receive. I encourage every eligible borrower to take advantage of this opportunity as they continue rebuilding their homes, businesses, and lives.”

Barger also flagged a significant financing gap she raised directly with SBA Administrator Kelly Loeffler this week. Under federal duplication of benefits requirements, the SBA may withhold portions of an approved disaster loan until insurance proceeds are finalized – but many insurance companies won’t release the full amount needed to rebuild until a home receives a Certificate of Occupancy.

That leaves some families without access to funds during construction, even though those resources have already been approved.

“I appreciate Administrator Loeffler’s willingness to examine this issue and work toward a solution so survivors can access the financing they need to keep rebuilding,” said Barger.

‘Nothing about us without us!’ | Disability rights advocates, seniors send a message to the next governor amid annual threats to their healthcare

Disability rights advocates welcomed the decision to avoid major health care cuts but said they are disappointed that some hard-won protections were weakened.

By Becca Habegger
Published 4:50 PM PDT July 2, 2026

SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Big cuts and changes to Medi-Cal and In-Home Supportive Services in earlier budget proposals this year were largely avoided in the final version, which lawmakers passed and the Governor signed on Monday.

Still—seniors, Californians with disabilities and chronic conditions, and those who support them - have had to come to the Capitol repeatedly in recent years to fight for funding and eligibility around their healthcare.

With a new Governor taking office next year, advocates have a message for state leaders.

“Nothing about us without us!” shouted Brittanie Hernandez-Wilson, leading others in a chant.

She is a member of a coalition called Long Term Supports and Services for All (LTSS4All), which gathered outside the Capitol Wednesday morning for a rally reacting to the final budget – and looking ahead.

“This is what communities refusing to be invisible looks like, and the Legislature heard us.” said Hernandez-Wilson, who is also lead California homecare organizer at Hand in Hand: The Domestic Employers Network. “The Legislature rejected every single proposed cut to In-Home Supportive Services.”

In his January budget draft, Governor Gavin Newsom proposed three changes to In-Home Supportive Services (IHSS): Cutting the IHSS Backup Provider System, ending a temporary care-stopgap practice when someone loses Medi-Cal eligibility, and shifting more costs to counties, which advocates worried would result in reduced hours of care someone can get.

All of these cuts were avoided in the final budget.

Not every accomplishment this legislative session, however, is seen as a win.

“Sure, yes, they’ve done better than the worst, but that’s not the same as doing right by us,” said Elizabette Guéçamburu, a disability rights advocate from Stanislaus County, who was born with a severe neuro-muscular disability and said she relies upon Medi-Cal and IHSS.

She points to something called the asset limit, also known as the asset test, which is a financial cap that seniors and Californians with disabilities must stay under in order to remain eligible for Medi-Cal and IHSS. The lower the cap, the harder to stay eligible.

It has fluctuated in recent years – and this latest budget dealt a blow to seniors and disabled Californians on Medi-Cal, though less of a blow than proposed earlier this year.

For decades, California’s asset test mirrored the federal resource limit for SSI (Supplemental Security Income) eligibility. That federal figure was last raised in 1989 to a cap of $2,000 for an individual, $3,000 for a couple – and has not been raised since then, not even for inflation.

What counts as one’s ‘assets’ includes how much money someone has in their checking and savings accounts at any given moment - though it does not include a retirement fund. It does not include someone’s primary vehicle but does count a secondary vehicle. Advocates say – the limit prevents people from saving for things like emergencies and medical expenses not covered by insurance and keeps families from having a second vehicle, which can impact employment and getting kids to school.

Advocates call the asset test an outdated limit that forces seniors and Californians with disabilities to live in a state of poverty just to keep their medical care. They point out the asset test is not applied to – and therefore is not a determinant of Medi-Cal eligibility – for people without disabilities under the age of 65.

The $2,000/$3,000 asset test was in place in California for years, and disability rights advocates fought it for years.

Then, Gov. Newsom agreed to raise the limit to $130,000 for an individual, $195,000 for a couple in 2022, as a transition to 2024, when the limit was erased completely.

But that win was short-lived. The move cost the government money, according to administration officials, who told state lawmakers last year the asset test’s elimination led to many more people enrolling in Medi-Cal than anticipated, which contributed to the state’s growing costs. Between 112,000 and 115,000 people newly enrolled, compared to early estimates of just 40,000, according to officials.

So in 2025, to save money, Newsom proposed fully reinstating the test to its $2,000/$3,000 level once again. Advocates and lawmakers pushed back on that, and a compromise was reached, with a return to the 2022 limit of $130,000/$195,000 starting in 2026.

Facing another looming budget deficit for Fiscal Year 2026-27, Gov. Newsom - in the May 2026 revision of his budget proposal – once again recommended a full return to the $2,000/$3,000 asset test, saying it would save the state an estimated $278.3 million in the 2026-27 budget and $495.6 million ongoing.

Advocates appealed to lawmakers to reject this proposal, which they did – in part.

The final budget landed on $21,000 for an individual, $31,000 for a couple, to become effective July 1, 2027 - or whenever after that date someone currently on Medi-Cal has their annual redetermination. The law also says the state will track, quarterly, "the number of Medi-Cal enrollees who lost eligibility due to the asset limit."

Guéçamburu calls the compromise “very bittersweet.”

“We’ve still lost here,” Guéçamburu said. “We’ve had to give up practically all of the gains we’ve made in the last two, three years, to get the asset limit completely eliminated.”

She said her services are now at risk because of the newly lowered asset limit, set to go into effect in a year, barring changes by lawmakers during 2027’s budget negotiations.

"A wheelchair van itself is – for a used van, $75,000, and new is $90,000. Let’s say you need to do a bathroom modification to make a bathroom accessible. You’re talking at least $15,000,” Guéçamburu said. “And these are disability-related expenses; this is not even talking about other stuff like a new washer and dryer. So how are we supposed to save for everyday disability-related expenses on only $21,000 in assets? It’s impossible—especially in California, with the cost of living here.”

This is the third time she has come to the Capitol in the last six weeks. She said disability rights advocates find themselves having to do this year after year, asking lawmakers not to cut their life-sustaining care.

“Repeated attacks on the programs that allow us to live and have freedom - are repeated attacks on us,” said Kate Laddish of Yolo County, who is president of the California In-Home Supportive Services Consumer Alliance.

Laddish said this advocacy comes at the cost of many people’s health. 

“And yet we cannot afford to stay silent. We have sustained injuries using the Capitol’s ramps, had flare-ups due to fatigue and so much more," Laddish said. "For others, coming to the Capitol is not even an option.”

The rally was held on July 1, which Laddish pointed out is the first day of Disability Pride Month.

Serving as emcee of Wednesday’s rally, she also thanked the many lawmakers who partnered with them to advocate for their healthcare, “for meeting with us, for hearing us and for a budget that protects our essential programs.”

She named Senate President pro Tem Monique Limón (D-Santa Barbara), Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas (D-Salinas), Senate Budget Chair John Laird (D-Monterey), Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), subcommittee leaders and members Sen. Caroline Menjivar (D-San Fernando Valley), Asm. Dawn Addis (D-Morro Bay), Asm. Dr. Corey Jackson (D-Moreno Valley), Asm. Mia Bonta (D-Oakland) and Asm. Pilar Schiavo (D-Santa Clarita) and Assembly Majority Leader Cecilia Aguiar-Curry (D-Woodland).

Her bipartisan list also included Asm. Jeff Gonzalez (R-Indio), who attended Wednesday’s rally and said this fight is personal; he has a son with severe disabilities.

“This asset limit is forced poverty,” Gonzalez said. “We cannot balance our budget on the backs of California's most vulnerable. Don’t be fooled, lowering the Medi-Cal asset limit to $21,000 tells seniors and Californians with disabilities they must spend nearly everything they've worked for before they can access the care they need. In California, $21,000 isn't even enough to purchase many reliable vehicles, yet we're telling families that's too much to have.”

Asm. Gonzalez said he plans on introducing legislation next year to completely do away with that asset limit.

Trump DOJ sues California over new gun conversion device law

Supporters say the measure will help keep convertible machine guns off the streets, while opponents call it unconstitutional.

By Jeannie Nguyen
Published 5:19 PM PDT July 2, 2026

CALIFORNIA, USA — California's new law restricting the sale of firearms that can be converted into makeshift machine guns is now in effect, and the Trump administration has already filed a lawsuit seeking to block it.

Supporters say Assembly Bill 1127 will help keep convertible machine guns off the streets, while opponents argue it violates the Second Amendment.

The lawsuit, filed by the U.S. Department of Justice, challenges the new law, which prohibits gun manufacturers from selling firearms that can be converted into makeshift machine guns through the use of a "switch."

"We're excited to see that the DOJ is taking the same stance as our organization and fighting back against California's unconstitutional gun laws," Alex Wilson of Gun Owners of California said.

Wilson argued the law targets one of the country's most popular handguns based on the possibility it could be converted into a machine gun.

"The author used, you know, potential for misuse to justify banning one of the most popular handguns circulated in America," Wilson said. "Based on the fact that they said it was machine gun convertible."

AB 1127, authored by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), prevents gun manufacturers from selling firearms that can be converted into makeshift machine guns with a switch. The law targets Glock-style handguns that can be modified with the device.

Gabriel was not available for an interview with ABC10 but has previously spoken about the dangers posed by the conversion devices.

"They're small devices. They're cheap devices. They can be bought for $25 or less. They can be 3D printed at home. They can be installed with a screwdriver," Gabriel said in August 2025. "And this tiny device, this switch, can turn something that is a pistol into a deadly lethal machine gun capable of firing hundreds of rounds in a mere matter of mere minutes."

The Justice Department's lawsuit argues California's new law is unlawful under the Second Amendment.

"The court said that Americans have the right to use arms that are in common use for self-defense and other lawful purposes," Barry Arrington, Acting Chief of the Justice Department's Second Amendment Section, said.

In response to the lawsuit, Gabriel said California would not back down in the face of threats from President Donald Trump.

Gavin Newsom also responded on social media, saying in part that the Trump administration is trying to dismantle California's "common-sense gun safety laws." He added that the laws save lives and that the state will continue defending them.

"Common sense gun safety laws work. That is something that California has proved," Gabriel said.

A spokesperson for Rob Bonta said the Attorney General's Office is reviewing the lawsuit and will defend what it called California's constitutional gun safety laws in court.

The law does not require people who already legally own Glock-style handguns to surrender them.

Federal lawsuit challenges California Glock‑style handgun ban

Noe Padilla Brian Day James Ward

USA TODAY NETWORK

July 1, 2026, 6:12 p.m. ET

California’s latest effort to restrict the sale of Glock-style handguns is facing a new legal challenge after the Trump administration’s Department of Justice sued the state on July 1, arguing the law violates the Second Amendment. The lawsuit escalates a growing battle over firearms regulation in a state long known for having some of the nation’s strictest gun laws.

At the center of the dispute is Assembly Bill 1127, a first-in-the-nation law that took effect July 1 and prohibits licensed firearms dealers from selling certain semiautomatic pistols that state lawmakers say can be easily converted into fully automatic weapons using illegal devices commonly known as “Glock switches.”

The federal lawsuit seeks to block enforcement of both AB 1127 and California’s handgun roster, which limits which handguns can be sold through licensed dealers in the state. Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said California lawmakers cannot ban what he described as “the most popular type of handgun in America.”

Gov. Gavin Newsom and state officials, however, argue the measure is a common-sense public safety law designed to curb the growing use of illegally modified firearms.

The federal lawsuit is likely to become the latest major test of California’s gun laws in the post-Bruen era, when courts increasingly scrutinize firearm restrictions under the Second Amendment.

With the DOJ, the NRA, the Firearms Policy Coalition and other gun-rights organizations all challenging aspects of California’s handgun regulations, the fight over AB 1127 appears headed for a lengthy court battle that could ultimately help define how far states can go in regulating firearms that remain legal elsewhere in the country.

For now, the law remains in effect, and licensed California firearms dealers are prohibited from selling affected Glock-style pistols while the legal challenges move through federal court

What is California's Glock ban?

AB 1127 does not specifically name Glock, but it targets semiautomatic handguns that use a cruciform trigger bar design and can be readily converted into fully automatic weapons through the installation of a conversion device.

Those devices, often called Glock switches, are already illegal under federal law and can transform a handgun into a machine gun capable of firing multiple rounds with a single pull of the trigger. Lawmakers behind the bill argued that manufacturers have known about the vulnerability for years but failed to redesign affected firearms.

Beginning July 1, licensed firearms dealers can no longer sell newly acquired Glock-style handguns that fall under the law. Existing owners may keep their weapons, and private-party transfers remain legal. Sales to law enforcement agencies are also exempt.

Why the Department of Justice is suing California

The Trump administration contends California's law bans commonly owned firearms based on the possibility that someone could illegally modify them.

In court filings and public statements, DOJ officials argue the state is prohibiting legal firearms because they could potentially be converted into illegal ones through the addition of a separate, already-banned device. They also challenge California’s handgun roster, saying it restricts access to firearms that are widely used for lawful purposes.

The lawsuit follows a June warning letter from Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, who accused California of violating the constitutional rights of residents seeking to purchase lawful firearms.

Gun-rights groups have also launched separate legal challenges, including the federal case Jaymes v. Bonta, arguing that the Supreme Court has repeatedly ruled that firearms in common use cannot be banned.

California says the law targets machine-gun conversions, not lawful gun owners

Supporters of AB 1127 say the measure targets a specific public safety threat rather than ordinary firearm ownership.

Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, a Democrat from Encino and one of the bill’s authors, has argued that California is closing a loophole that allows firearms to remain on the market despite their susceptibility to conversion into fully automatic weapons. Lawmakers say the law is intended to encourage manufacturers to redesign affected firearms rather than prohibit handgun ownership outright.

There are still hundreds of handguns available for purchase in California through the state’s handgun roster, and AB 1127 does not affect people who already own Glock pistols. Dealers who violate the law face escalating penalties, ranging from fines to license revocation and potential misdemeanor charges

Newsom points to falling crime and gun death rates

Newsom quickly pushed back on the federal lawsuit, calling it another attempt to dismantle California’s gun safety framework.

The governor said California is experiencing historically low crime and gun death rates and pledged to continue defending laws designed to keep dangerous weapons off the streets.

Those comments came as California Attorney General Rob Bonta released new criminal justice data showing the state’s homicide rate declined between 2024 and 2025. Even with that decrease, firearms remained the most commonly used weapon in California homicides, accounting for roughly two-thirds of killings statewide.

Supporters of AB 1127 argue those numbers underscore the need for stricter firearm safeguards, while opponents say constitutional rights should not be limited based on potential misuse by criminals.

High-profile crimes linked to Glock firearms in California

The debate over AB 1127 has been fueled in part by increasing concern among law enforcement agencies about Glock switches and other machine-gun conversion devices.

Supporters of AB 1127 argue that limiting future sales of easily convertible firearms could reduce the availability of weapons that can be unlawfully transformed into machine guns. Gun-rights advocates counter that existing laws already make conversion devices illegal and that banning firearm sales punishes lawful owners rather than criminals.

Federal officials have warned that small conversion devices can transform compatible semiautomatic pistols into fully automatic weapons capable of firing dozens of rounds in seconds. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives has reported recovering tens of thousands of machine-gun conversion devices nationwide in recent years.

California law enforcement agencies have repeatedly cited Glock-style handguns in investigations involving gang violence, organized crime and mass-casualty shootings. Public safety officials say the growing availability of conversion switches has increased concern about the firepower available to criminals.

In 2024 alone, ATF’s Los Angeles Field Division reported recovering over 31,000 machine gun conversion devices nationwide, with a significant portion linked to Glock models in California. These seizures often occur during raids targeting organized crime networks and drug trafficking operations, where Glock pistols are frequently discovered alongside narcotics and other illegal firearms.

Several headline-making cases underscore the role of Glock firearms in violent crimes. For example, in San Francisco, a Glock modified with a conversion switch was used in a drive-by shooting that left multiple victims injured. Similarly, in Sacramento, a Glock handgun was central to a mass shooting outside a nightclub, prompting renewed calls for stricter firearm regulations. Prosecutors have highlighted that the ability to convert these pistols into machine guns easily has made them a weapon of choice for criminals seeking maximum firepower, reinforcing the rationale behind California’s legislative crackdown.

Governor Newsom signs California's record $351.7 billion state budget

SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Governor Gavin Newsom signed California's $351.7 billion budget Monday, approving a balanced spending plan for the 2026-27 fiscal year. Newsom and state Democratic leaders emphasized their plan not only eliminates a deficit for this year but also the following.

State reserves total $28.8 billion, according to a spokesperson for the Department of Finance.

The budget takes effect Wednesday, July 1, the start of the state's new fiscal year. It is the final budget of Newsom's administration before he leaves office.

Lawmakers sent the spending plan for the governor’s desk Monday after weeks of negotiations between the governor's office, the state Senate and the Assembly. The agreement passed despite Republican opposition because Democrats hold a supermajority in the Legislature.

The Legislature also passed what’s called budget trailer bills — specific provisions on how the money allocated for state programs in the actually budget bill will and should be utilized.

Among notable deliverables, the final budget restores or delays several health care reductions Newsom initially proposed. Lawmakers rejected cuts to In-Home Supportive Services, delayed raising Medi-Cal premiums for undocumented immigrants and pushed back the full reinstatement of the Medi-Cal asset test for seniors and people with disabilities.

Legislative analyst Chris Micheli said lawmakers deferred some health care funding decisions until next year, leaving California's next governor to decide whether to implement those cuts.

Republicans critics described the delays as Newsom “kicking the can down the road.”

The budget also includes $900 million for the Homeless Housing, Assistance and Prevention program, about $400 million more than Newsom originally proposed. It provides more than $40 million for elections to increase staffing, expand voter outreach, educate voters and combat misinformation, as promised by Newsom both before and in the weeks following the June primary election.

According to the governor's office, the budget continues funding for child care, affordable housing, public schools, health care programs, wildfire resilience and public safety while preserving nearly $30 billion in state reserves.

Republicans criticized the budget, arguing California continues to spend more than it takes in. Indeed, while the 2026-2027 fiscal year budget reflects higher-than-anticipated revenues due to the stock market boom as a result of success with artificial intelligence, experts and analysts note such revenue is volatile.

Republicans also continue to object to new tax proposals, including a renewal of  the managed care organization tax — the tax rate will be higher for private insurers. Critics, as well as Democratic leaders themselves, acknowledge such a tax increase on health plans could increase monthly premiums for Californians. About $100 more annually per enrollee, estimates show.

There will also be an expansion of the state's sales tax to some software and digital products, starting next year. The base sales tax will be 7.25%, but local jurisdictions can add on.

Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel said lawmakers worked to protect vulnerable Californians from federal funding reductions.

“We heard from many members of the Democratic caucus that that was simply unacceptable and that we needed to step up to protect our vulnerable communities… A lot of the work we’re doing is to soften the blow of those federal cuts to protect families in California. Unfortunately, we’re not in a place to backfill every federal cut, but we do feel a responsibility to protect our communities,” Democrat Gabriel said.

Assembly Budget Vice Chair David Tangipa said the state's spending priorities remain misplaced despite record revenue.

“While the state has always talked about cuts coming from the federal administration, there’s nothing that looks like we’re actually running out of money. We have more money than we’ve ever had before. And yet, we believe that some of the priorities are off in this budget,” Tangipa, a Republican, said.

Newsom also signed several budget trailer bills Monday to implement the spending plan, including measures covering health care, education, taxation and human services.

Political Notebook: CA budget includes funds for LGBTQ services

  • by Matthew S. Bajko, Assistant Editor
  • Tuesday, June 30, 2026
Share this Post:

State Senator John Laird, left, and Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón looked on as Governor Gavin Newsom signed the state budget with Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas, second from right, and Assembly Budget Chair Jesse Gabriel.

Photo: Courtesy Governor’s Office

LGBTQ advocates notched a host of fiscal successes totaling more than $2 billion in the 2026-27 state budget and associated trailer bills that California Governor Gavin Newsom signed into law Monday. It marks the final budget for the outgoing Democratic leader, widely expected to seek to be his party’s presidential nominee in 2028, and the first time a state has established a statewide fund to support LGBTQ community centers.

Also among this year’s budget priorities for LGBTQ advocates were $26 million for a Gender-Affirming Care Fund to be used to ensure transgender, nonbinary, and gender-expansive people have access to the medically necessary care they need, and $30 million for the Uncompensated Care Fund, which is to be used to cover gender-affirming care alongside abortion and reproductive health services. The Legislature had included both in the budget they sent Newsom to sign.

“At a time when transgender youth and their families are facing unprecedented challenges across the country, California has chosen to stand as a beacon of hope, safety, and dignity,” stated California LGBTQ+ Health and Human Services Network Director Dannie Ceseña, who is Two-Spirit and Native. “We are deeply grateful to Governor Newsom and our state leaders for not just speaking about equality, but funding it. By protecting access to gender-affirming care and robustly supporting the Transgender Health Care Fund, California is actively saving lives and setting a powerful national standard.”

LGBTQ advocates in recent weeks had mounted an intense lobbying campaign to see legislators in Sacramento and the governor include the funding in the final $351.7 billion balanced state budget. State leaders also boosted California’s reserves to almost $29 billion in case of future fiscal shocks to the state’s finances.

In a video message his office posted about his signing the budget that begins on July 1, Newsom noted, "For decades, we've been told that government has to choose between balancing the books and investing in people. California proved that's a false choice. This budget reflects years of disciplined decisions that built historic reserves, paid down debt, strengthened our economy, and made transformational investments in education, healthcare, housing, infrastructure, and opportunity. We're leaving California stronger than we found it – and leaving the next generation a state that's fiscally sound, economically dominant, and ready for whatever comes next."

Helping oversee this year’s budget negotiations was gay state Senator John Laird (D-Santa Cruz) as chair of the Senate Budget and Fiscal Review Committee. Earlier in the month, after the Senate had approved several budget trailer bills that included the funding asks from LGBTQ advocates, Laird noted that they reflected “the same balanced approach that has guided budget negotiations this year. They provide additional revenues that help balance the budget over the next two years, reduce the structural deficit, maintain strong reserves, and avoid deeper cuts to services that Californians rely on every day.”

Acknowledging there was likely to be “debate about individual provisions, the alternative would have been more significant reductions to health care, education, housing, child care, public safety, and other essential programs,” added Laird. “This package represents another important step toward a final budget that protects Californians while strengthening the state’s long-term fiscal position.”

The money for gender-affirming care was a main focus of the inaugural TGI Youth Advocacy Day at the state Capitol. It took place June 23, a week prior to Newsom’s June 30 deadline to sign the budget bills. Equality California, the statewide LGBTQ advocacy organization, had also marshalled its members to contact the governor and legislators and urge them to back the Gender-Affirming Care Fund and other budgetary asks made by the community this year.

“At a time when the federal government continues attacking transgender people and undermining access to medically necessary health care, California is making a historic investment to ensure that our community can continue to access the care they need,” stated gay EQCA Executive Director Tony Hoang.

One of the fiscal priorities advocates secured is roughly $9 million for LGBTQ+ community centers and other LGBTQ+ serving organizations. Another $995,000 is to be directed to those LGBTQ service providers “in less resourced regions” of the state, according to the budget bill. Gay Los Angeles LGBT Center CEO Joe Hollendoner called the $10 million funding allocation “truly historic,” as it’s believed to be the nation's first statewide LGBTQ+ Community Center Fund.

"At a moment when LGBTQ+ communities across the country are under relentless attack and states are dismantling protections for our community, California has chosen a different path—one rooted in dignity, compassion, and action,” stated Hollendoner. “This is one of the most significant LGBTQ+ policy victories in our state's history. These investments will save lives, expand access to healthcare and housing, and strengthen the institutions our communities rely on to survive and thrive.”

LGBTQ advocates also secured $50 million to strengthen victim services through a Victims of Crime Act (VOCA) backfill. They were also successful in seeing $900 million be directed toward the state’s Homeless Housing, Assistance and Prevention (HHAP) Program.

Another priority was having state leaders designate nearly $1 billion over five years through the ADAP Rebate Fund expenditure plan to strengthen HIV prevention, treatment, care, and efforts to end the epidemics of HIV and other sexually transmitted infections. Lobbyist Ryan Souza, speaking Monday on behalf of the San Francisco AIDS Foundation, APLA Health based in Los Angeles, and the End the Epidemics Coalition at the Senate budget committee’s final hearing on the budget, thanked Newsom, the Legislative LGBTQ Caucus, and the Legislature for backing the ADAP spending plan.

Their “leadership, vision and collaboration allowed the ADAP Rebate Fund to be used in a truly generational investment in the effort to end the epidemic of HIV,” said Souza.

The budget also includes $15 million for the Chancellor’s Office of the California Community Colleges to distribute to community college districts so they can “provide additional funds to support LGBTQ+ students.”

The State Department of Education was also awarded $77,000 to continue its having a half-time position tasked with updating existing, and developing new, resources, strategies, and in-service teacher training to support LGBTQ and questioning students. The state agency also received $150,000 and a full-time position in its School Health and Safety Office “to support LGBTQ+ initiatives and best practices,” according to the budget bill.

California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed a nearly $352 billion state budget that delays healthcare cuts, expands childcare funding and provides new resources to speed up election vote counting ahead of November.

The spending plan is Newsom’s final budget before leaving office in January and comes as speculation grows that he could pursue a presidential campaign. The state’s financial decisions are likely to face renewed scrutiny if he seeks national office.

Newsom used the budget signing to highlight accomplishments from nearly eight years as governor, including free school meals, expanded internet access, renewable energy investments, and higher wages for fast-food and healthcare workers. He also pointed to the state’s reserves as evidence that California can balance major investments with fiscal responsibility.

“To every other state across our country — to Washington, D.C. — to anyone who’s been told that responsibility and ambition can’t share the same balance sheet: Come to California,” Newsom said, pushing back against criticism from Republicans, including President Donald Trump, who have frequently targeted the state’s spending and policies.

The budget avoids major tax increases but raises revenue through targeted measures, including changes to a healthcare provider tax, a new sales tax on some software products and limits on certain corporate tax breaks. Newsom has rejected broader proposals, including a one-time billionaire tax backed by a healthcare union.

Democrats who control the Legislature said the plan eliminates the state’s projected deficit and helps shield low-income residents from federal healthcare cuts. Assembly Budget Committee Chair Jesse Gabriel said the state worked to “protect vulnerable communities,” while acknowledging California could not fully replace lost federal funding.

Republicans argued the budget only delays difficult decisions. State Sen. Roger Niello said Newsom was leaving future leaders with the financial consequences of current spending.

California has faced repeated budget challenges in recent years, including projected multibillion-dollar shortfalls. A surge in tax revenue, fueled in part by strong stock market gains tied to artificial intelligence companies, gave lawmakers more flexibility and allowed them to reverse some planned cuts.

The budget delays reductions to Medi-Cal benefits, including cuts affecting low-income immigrants without legal status and proposed premiums for some recipients. A planned monthly premium increase was pushed to the next governor.

Childcare remains a priority for Newsom, with the budget funding nearly 23,000 new childcare spaces.

The spending plan also directs nearly $29 million to the secretary of state’s office for election staffing and technology upgrades, along with $10 million for voter education efforts. Another $1 million will go toward combating election misinformation.

The funding comes after years of criticism over California’s slow vote-counting process. Trump and other Republicans have claimed, without evidence, that delays contribute to election fraud concerns.

The November election will feature several closely watched races, including competitive congressional contests, ballot measures and the race to replace Newsom.

Lawmakers also postponed several major decisions, including how to spend future cap-and-trade revenue and whether to penalize large companies whose workers rely on Medi-Cal rather than employer-sponsored health insurance.

Democratic state Sen. María Elena Durazo criticized the delays, saying: “This is a budget that bought time: Medi-Cal delayed, not resolved, not restored.”

The budget also transfers more authority to the governor over the state Department of Education, a move Newsom says could help improve student outcomes.

Gov. Gavin Newsom signs state budget, granting UC $350 million funding increase

Gov. Gavin Newsom is pictured. He signed a state budget for the 2027-28 fiscal year Monday that includes a $350 million increase to the UC’s funding. (Daily Bruin file photo)

By Lauren Trautenberg

June 30, 2026 11:17 p.m.

Correction: The original version of this article incorrectly stated that California’s state budget for the upcoming fiscal year increased the UC’s funding to $350 million. In fact, it increased the UC's funding by $350 million.

This post was updated July 5 at 10:28 p.m.

Gov. Gavin Newsom signed California’s state budget for the upcoming fiscal year Monday, increasing the UC’s funding by $350 million.

The budget also preserves a nearly $130 million deferral to the University until the 2027-28 fiscal year. Both provisions were included in Newsom’s original budget proposal in January.

The funding increase upholds the UC and California State University systems’ compact, which promises the universities an annual 5% budget increase for five years in exchange for enrolling more California residents and improving graduation rates, according to EdSource.

The California State Legislature approved a state budget June 15 before entering negotiations with Newsom. Newsom’s deadline to sign the budget was Wednesday, which marked the start of a new fiscal year.

UC President James Milliken said in an emailed statement that the funding increase will help the University foster economic mobility and scientific growth across California.

“The 7% increase from the state goes a long way toward fulfilling the compact and providing the funding necessary to educate and invest in our students,” he said.

The funding increase is important due to recent federal funding cuts, Milliken added in the statement.

The Trump administration froze $584 million in UCLA’s research grants from the National Institutes of Health, National Science Foundation and United States Department of Energy in July. The federal government alleged that the university allowed antisemitism, affirmative action and “men to participate in women’s sports.”

A federal judge temporarily restored most of the grants in August and September. The judge separately ruled in November that the Trump administration could not freeze or threaten to freeze the UC’s research funding.

The state budget prioritizes healthcare and housing, said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, chair of the Assembly Budget Committee, in an emailed statement.

The budget lowers the asset threshold for Medi-Cal eligibility and increases funding for affordable housing programs, according to the Los Angeles Times.

“California is delivering a budget rooted in compassion, fiscal responsibility, and opportunity for all,” Gabriel said in the statement.

However, Scott Graves, the budget director of the California Budget and Policy Center, said in an emailed statement that he believes the budget does not fully address the affordability challenges Californians face.

“While the budget takes some steps toward ensuring corporations in California pay their fair share, it stops short of advancing the bold, sustainable revenue solutions needed to make investments that would help alleviate Californians’ affordability challenges,” he said in the statement.
