Katie Porter Fights Back, Antonio Hits Swalwell, Mahan in the News, and the Long-Game Described and Confirmed (a Prediction We Made Proved Out).

Let’s start with a California Power Lesson and end with a campaign lesson with a few tidbits in between.

I Called It

I am going to give an “I told you so” moment to demonstrate how Power works in Sacramento.

Last fall, under the radar, there was a spat regarding anti-semitism, and it is a major flashpoint with the far left of the Democratic Party. In the case of California, there was a bill which was fought over in the legislature. The bottom line was small, obscure, Jewish Political Action Committee (JPAC), a small organization not aligned with AIPAC, was able to muscle through a watered down anti-semitism bill in the legislature against the wishes of the California Faculty Association (CFA) among other groups. It was a minor skirmish in the bigger issues going in the Democratic Party. It also brought out some of the most venial language you use in politics.

First there was the threat made by the CFA (and therefore others) they would not endorse any candidate who took money from JPAC, AIPAC or other “dirty sources.” The message was clear, Jewish money which fought them would be considered “dirty” for the purposes of politics. They “tainted the well” with a clear anti-semitic trope, but it was not presented as such.

Then, after blowback, they back off a couple days later, but the message was clear. The base was upset. It was more about Power. JPAC is a small player in Sacramento. Education labor unions/associations? They own Sacramento. How did this happen? Sure there is the politics, but it is the raw Power involved. We said at the time, it is good JPAC had friends with butts in seats, and it was a lesson to learn.

Then, in November, we published another piece which used the episode as an example of the future battles of the Party.

I am going to quote the three paragraphs because they illustrate the point clearly.

“People are worn out and those in Power get it. That is the point. The wearing you out is exactly what they want. They want to keep their seats. They will keep coming. You might get a temporary reprieve, but the long-term trends, unless changed, leave you exposed. I said a great example was the JPAC situation with the California Faculty Association (CFA). JPAC, a Jewish Political Action Committee focused on matters in California (not to be confused with AIPAC, which is the boogie man to the far left). JPAC won some anti-Semitism reforms in education. Not hard to understand, one would expect such a cause from JPAC.

Well, the CFA opposed the bill. When they lost to little old JPAC, they tried to exact retribution. Any political candidate seeking the CFA’s endorsement, the announced with great fanfare, had to indicate their receipt of money from JPAC (along with oil, tobacco, and AIPAC). While you say, “who cares about the CFA,” the answer is if you do not seek their endorsement but you do from others, well, are you hiding something, and then what is that something? Others can silently boycott candidates supporting Jewish causes through the CFA’s filter.

The situation was resolved when the CFA apologized the next day. One wonders why? Scott Weiner and Jesse Gabriel are two of the most Powerful people in the Legislature. What happens when they are gone? The CFA just goes back at it. JPAC might think they won, and they may have won a battle but the game is a lot longer, and unless the status quo is changed, the CFA will come back, mark my words. They did not forget little JPAC beat them on anti-semitism, watered down as much as it was. Publicly apologizing for their “spat” was not something they will just walk away from. [Emphasis added]”

What do they do? They “lean.” They came back. From today’s Politico Playbook.

“CLEANUP DRAMA — Two groups behind a proposal to undo key provisions of a law aiming to clamp down on antisemitism in schools escalated their clash with Jewish groups that have been highly critical of the effort.

The California Faculty Association and Council on American-Islamic Relations sent a letter to lawmakers referring to the criticism as a “targeted misinformation campaign” and urging them to give the bill, which is expected to be contained in AB 2159, a hearing.

In the letter, the groups disputed claims from Jewish California, which sponsored AB 715 last year, that they were trying to “gut” the bill. The measure was pushed by the Legislature’s Jewish Caucus amid concerns about a rise in antisemitic incidents on school campuses.

David Bocarsly, executive director of Jewish California, said last month that the groups “have decided that their priority is to try to weaken civil rights laws protecting Jewish children,” calling it a “moral failure, and a dangerous precedent.” Read the full story in POLITICO Pro. — Eric He”

As predicted, they came back. And, they will come back again until they get what they want. It is about Power, plain and simple. JPAC (which is new Jewish California) won and needs to be taught a lesson. The CFA, and whoever else is behind the effort, are “docked” in the Power Game until this “episode” is “resolved.” On and on it goes. The Power Game.

The Gubernatorial

Ok, back to the happenings of the campaign.

We said earlier this week Katie Porter was starved of oxygen in her campaign as it was stuck. It seems she is starting to find that oxygen.

Politico had a piece this morning with a lot of tidbits in its California Playbook. The first being Porter “fighting” to get attention via a “leftward shift.” Will it succeed?

Well, she is getting press now.

Interesting timing as Swalwell is getting his own (not positive) press, along with Steyer (the painful article in the Los Angeles Times where he invoked a “Road to Damascus Moment,” while saying that he “donated the proceeds on investments in Corrections Corporation of America to charity,” after he made his billions).

Good week for Ms. Porter so far, especially as Matt Mahan is reeling after the $35 million challenge (leading some to think his campaign is falling apart).

In fact, Playbook quoted Swalwell supporters as pointing the finger to Porter regarding the whole situation about the sexual harassment rumors.

What is also happening is the “second tier” candidates are hitting at the Big 3. Tony Thrumond has been an effective “foil” to Tom Steyer, and Antonio Villaraigosa is now hitting on Swalwell with regularity.

Today he kept the negative story regarding Swalwell’s rumors going with a hit on him not showing up to a candidate forum because of his concern of facing reporters because of the allegations. Another negative cycle for Swalwell after a good couple weeks.

The “undercard” is an effective tool to “hit” the front runners in the race, softening them up, while there is oxygen in the other campaigns. It is a “heads I win tails you lose” situation. You stay in and hope you can catch fire, but meanwhile, you score points with whoever you are aligned with by landing blows which look “part of the game.”

See how long this goes. 30 more days for those campaigns could be very effective to keep the “front runners” from getting “too dirty.” Ah politics.

Mahan’s Struggles

Mahan’s campaign has been reeling over the last few days. First, he hit the “reset” button and shifted his campaign staff last week. Then there was the New York Times piece about the $35 million “challenge.” Then the “rebranding” of the campaign slogan from “Back to Basics.”

Per Politico this morning:

“BACK TO BASICS — San Jose Mayor Matt Mahan pushed back on The New York Times reporting that he briefed donors on a plan to move away from his “Back to Basics” motto as he seeks to gain traction in the field.

“I think we absolutely need to get California back to basics, so I don’t really know where that came from,” Mahan told Playbook, adding that a donor or donor’s “opinion on the call is not really material to me.”

Mahan projected confidence that he’d gain support without a messaging pivot now that he has hired new consultants. “We need to deliver our message aggressively across the state and have best-in-class creative to do so, and so you’re going to hear a lot more from us in the coming weeks.””

The press he is getting looks like the whole campaign has “too many cooks in the kitchen,” and no direction, and he is out of control. Whoever is leaking to the New York Times (twice this week now), is trying to force the issue inside. Silicon Valley is all about pivots. They are trying to find the pivot, but it looks like they are out of control. He is seemingly trying to wrest control from a faction of donors who are not in synch with where his campaign is going.

Bill Gross, a local tech entrepreneur here in Pasadena, has a good TED talk on why businesses succeed (start ups in his case). He said a business succeeds when three things line up. First you need the idea. Then you need the team. You can control (usually for the first two). The last is timing. You cannot control for that.

Mahan’s campaign is struggling with the three elements.

They have the idea, but it is falling flat because it is not sharp enough or too generic and poll tested. It needs “life.”

They have the team, but there are a lot of smart people involved, and sometimes that team does not click. How many USC football fans can point to a huge recruiting class and failing team though a lot go on to play professionally. Something is not aligned because he is having to send messages to those leaking to the New York Times that he has control over “the basics” of his own campaign theme (see what I did there).

The timing seems right, but maybe it is not exactly the time. The campaign is not catching on with the electorate which may be a cycle away (see my Virginia post yesterday). We need to get the words to better capture the timing frankly, and we allow the easy words being used to ill-define the moment.

Each has to be in synch, just right, to make it happen.

The hard part about politics is the compressed window.

You do not get to fail small and fail often in a 120 day campaign. Many founders spend years in a start up to get where they need to. Campaigns need to be done faster and cleaner to succeed in that moment. Maybe the mindset is this is a long-term project, and this election is a “pilot” or “test,” though the millions being raised are a lot for a pilot.

In a campaign, the roll out “is hard and fast-” you are “going to market” in the Silicon Valley parlance.

It has very small room to deliberate.

A lot of investors can cause “fog of war.”

Either, the candidate “gets it, or he doesn't.” You cannot change the “product,” which is the candidate during the campaign.

The campaign is promising “big things,” but we heard those words two weeks ago when they “parted ways” with the chief strategist. They are doing it again. We are beyond “big things in the coming weeks,” it is time to “put up or shut up.” Enough salesmanship, enough “tease,” get to it.

Want a contrast? Watch Josh Shapiro on All In this week. That is what a Governor and beyond looks like. See the jokes? See the self depreciation?

Mahan? Here is the All In Podcast. Big difference.

[미국] 캘리포니아주, ‘초가공식품 아님’ 인증 라벨 도입 검토

곡산 2026. 4. 8. 07:18

[미국] 캘리포니아주, ‘초가공식품 아님’ 인증 라벨 도입 검토

[규정/제도]

캘리포니아주가 ‘초가공식품이 아님’을 인증하는 식품 라벨 도입을 검토하고 있다. 식품업체가 자발적으로 참여할 수 있는 주 차원의 검증 프로그램으로, 도입될 경우 미국 내 첫 사례가 된다.

이번 논의는 캘리포니아가 지난해 가을 ‘초가공식품’에 대한 법적 정의를 처음으로 마련한 이후 본격화됐다. 제시 가브리엘 캘리포니아주 하원의원은 초가공식품이 아닌 제품에 부여하는 ‘캘리포니아 인증(California Certified)’ 라벨을 제안했다. 이 제도는 식품업체에는 선택사항이지만, 해당 인증을 받은 제품에 대해서는 대형 식료품점이 매대에서 눈에 띄게 진열해야 한다.

가브리엘 의원은 기자회견에서 “이 제도는 소비자들이 더 건강한 선택지를 쉽고 신뢰할 수 있는 방식으로 식별할 수 있도록 돕기 위한 것”이라며, 미국 농무부(USDA)의 유기농 인증 라벨을 본떠 구상했다고 설명했다. 그는 앞서 학교 급식에서 초가공식품을 금지하는 캘리포니아 법안도 주도한 바 있다.

그는 “이 법안은 초가공식품의 위험성에 대응하면서도 소비자 선택권을 강화하고, 업계의 혁신을 촉진하며, 어떤 제품도 금지하지 않은 채 식품 공급 전반에 걸쳐 더 건강한 선택지를 확대하는 방식”이라고 말했다.

캘리포니아는 포화지방, 첨가당, 나트륨 함량이 높고, 동시에 향료, 색소, 유화제, 점증제 같은 식품첨가물을 포함한 식품을 초가공식품으로 정의하고 있다.

펜실베이니아대 식품·영양정책센터의 앨리사 모런 부소장은 캘리포니아의 정의에 따르면 포장식품의 약 3분의 1가량이 ‘비초가공식품’에 해당할 수 있다고 추산했다.

모런 부소장은 “초가공식품이 없으면 먹을 것이 거의 없거나, 모든 음식을 처음부터 직접 조리해야 한다는 오해가 있다”며 “하지만 이는 사실과 거리가 멀다”고 말했다.

가공 원료와 첨가물에 대한 소비자 우려가 커지는 가운데, 해당 라벨은 구매 결정에 적지 않은 영향을 미칠 수 있을 것으로 보인다. 새 인증 프로그램은 식품기업들이 인증 요건을 충족하기 위해 첨가물을 줄이거나 지방·당 함량을 낮추도록 유도하는 효과도 노리고 있다.

이 법안은 4월 중 논의될 예정이며, 가브리엘 의원은 오는 9월까지 주지사에게 법안을 송부하는 것을 목표로 하고 있다고 밝혔다.

초가공식품 문제가 초당적 이슈로 떠오르면서 미국 여러 주에서도 특정 성분 금지나 초가공 여부 표시 의무화 같은 입법이 추진되고 있다. 다만 식품기업들이 관련 법안에 대해 법적 대응에 나서면서, 웨스트버지니아와 텍사스에서는 입법이 중단된 상태다.

가브리엘 의원은 캘리포니아가 중남미 여러 국가처럼 설탕이나 포화지방 함량이 높은 식품 전면에 검은 팔각형 경고 문구를 붙이는 방식도 검토했다고 밝혔다. 그러나 그는 “매대마다 검은 팔각형 표시가 가득하면 소비자들이 제품 간 차이를 구별하기 어려워질 수 있다”며, 경고보다는 ‘더 건강한 제품’을 인증하는 방식이 소비자에게 더 유익하다고 판단했다고 설명했다.

이어 “올바른 방향으로 제품을 만들고 있는 기업, 건강한 제품을 생산하는 기업을 인정해주는 편이 소비자에게 더 도움이 되는 정보라고 봤다”고 덧붙였다.

한편 캘리포니아가 자체 인증제 도입을 검토하는 가운데, 민간 인증기관들도 서로 다른 기준을 바탕으로 자발적 라벨을 내놓고 있다.

비GMO 프로젝트(Non-GMO Project)는 ‘비초가공식품 검증 기준(Non-UPF Verified Standard)’을 발표했으며, 스핀드리프트(SpinDrift), 에이미스 키친(Amy’s Kitchen) 등의 브랜드가 이를 적용할 예정이다. 이 기준은 원재료 자체보다는 식품이 산업적 제조 과정을 거치며 얼마나 가공됐는지, 또 그 과정에서 식품의 구조적 특성이 얼마나 변화했는지에 초점을 맞추고 있다.

Live updates: Family of man shot by ICE denies criminal ties. ‘He is not a gang member’

Graham Womack and Andrew Graham

*A man identified as Carlos Ivan Mendoza Hernandez has been hospitalized after a shooting that involved U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, acting ICE director Todd Lyons said in a statement Tuesday. Mendoza Hernandez’s condition has not been revealed. Our live coverage for the day has concluded. Click here for the latest on this developing story.*

7 p.m. Family of man who was shot responds

Patrick Kolasinski, a Modesto-based immigration attorney representing Mendoza Hernandez’s family, said that the man is in stable condition at Doctors Medical Center and that the family denies all allegations that Mendoza Hernandez was affiliated with gangs, as ICE asserted. “The biggest thing the family wants to get out right now is that he is not a gang member,” the attorney told The Modesto Bee. “He is a family man engaged to a U.S. citizen with a 2-year-old U.S. citizen daughter who was on his way to work in the Bay Area.”

3:30 p.m. Stanislaus County Sheriff: FBI primarily responsible for investigation

Stanislaus County Sheriff Jeff Dirkse said during a press conference that the Federal Bureau of Investigation was primarily responsible for investigating the ICE-involved shooting Tuesday of Carlos Ivan Mendoza Hernandez.

Dirkse then introduced Eugene Wu, a special agent for the FBI’s Sacramento office.

“This will take time as our agents conduct their investigation,” Wu said.

2 p.m. Valley Watch Network urges skepticism of ICE statement

Nora Zaragoza-Yáñez, a program manager for Valley Watch Network, which monitors ICE, said any statements from ICE should be viewed with skepticism given the agency’s history of issuing statements after shootings that are later found false. “We must question the accuracy of their statements,” Zaragoza-Yáñez told The Sacramento Bee. “We need an independent investigation and we need ICE out of our community.”

Zaragoza-Yáñez also said that shooting was “another example that ICE puts our community in danger.”

1:45 p.m. Assemblymember touts bill that would require AG to investigate ICE-involved shootings

California Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-LA) is one of six sponsors of AB 1806, which would require the state attorney general’s office to conduct an investigation into “any incident where a federal immigration enforcement officer shoots a civilian.”

“While we wait for additional details, incidents like these underscore the need for a thorough, transparent, and independent investigation of any shooting involving federal agents,” Gabriel said in a statement Tuesday. “Assembly Bill 1806 will ensure transparency and accountability.”

Sacramento Mayor Kevin McCarty, who authored similar legislation while serving in the state legislature, said in a Jan. 26 statement that he looked forward to working with Gabriel.

“We must ensure that our laws give the Attorney General clear authority to pursue independent investigations even when federal officers are involved,” said McCarty, who didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday afternoon. “Strengthening these powers would help guarantee transparency, build public trust, and ensure that all uses of force are thoroughly reviewed, no matter the agency involved.”

1 p.m. 36 ICE arrests in Stanislaus County since beginning of Trump’s second term

Carlos Ivan Mendoza Hernandez’s encounter with ICE on Tuesday morning was far from the first time the agency’s officers have crossed paths with people in Stanislaus County.

Data provided to The Modesto Bee by UC Berkeley Law School’s Data Deportation Project shows that ICE has arrested 36 people in Stanislaus County since the beginning of Donald Trump’s second presidential administration in January 2025. This includes 18 arrests in the past six months.

Fernanda Pereira, an attorney, told The Modesto Bee that ICE officers formerly could release individuals who were undocumented and weren’t perceived as public safety threats.

“At this point, we are not seeing an exercise of that discretion,” Pereira said.

12:45 p.m. Shooting is at least seventh of 2026 involving ICE or CBP officers

Tuesday’s shooting in Patterson was at least the seventh of the year involving officers of ICE or U.S. Customs and Border Protection Agency, which are both part of the Department of Homeland Security.

Of the other six shootings, the two most prominent have been in Minneapolis. Renee Good was fatally shot by ICE on Jan. 14, while a CBP officer fatally shot Alex Pretti 10 days later. Both shootings prompted mass protests.

12:30 p.m. Dashcam video shared on social media appears to show shooting

Dramatic dashcam footage posted on social media early Tuesday afternoon appeared to detail the traffic stop in Patterson that led to a shooting involving ICE.

The video, which is 23 seconds long, appears to show Carlos Ivan Mendoza Hernandez’s car by the side of the road, with what appears to be three agents near it. The car backs up and then quickly accelerates in the direction of an agent. An agent fires toward the vehicle as the car drives over a center embankment.

Multiple hubcaps come off from the car as it appears to veer slowly into opposing traffic. Mendoza Hernandez was hospitalized following the shooting. The Washington Post reported that Mendoza Hernandez was in critical condition, citing a spokesperson for the Stanislaus County Sheriff’s Office, which Patterson contracts with for police services. Authorities would not confirm that report.

It is not clear where the dashcam footage originated from.

12:15 p.m. Newsom briefed on incident

The press office for Gov. Gavin Newsom said in an X post that officials had briefed the governor on Tuesday’s shooting involving ICE.

“As is established practice, we expect our federal law enforcement partners to appropriately collaborate with state and local law enforcement as this matter is investigated,” the post read, from the account @GovPressOffice.

Newsom retweeted the post through his gubernatorial account but didn’t otherwise post about the incident from that account on X or his individual one.

Members of the FBI evidence response team conference on Sperry Avenue in Patterson on Tuesday. Andy Alfaro aalfaro@modbee.com

12 p.m. ICE issues statement

Lyons said in a written statement that officers conducted a traffic stop Tuesday in Patterson, which is about 80 miles south of Sacramento, “to arrest Carlos Ivan Mendoza Hernandez, an 18th Street Gang member wanted in El Salvador for questioning in connection to a murder.”

Lyons stated that when officers approached his car, Mendoza Hernandez “weaponized his vehicle in an attempt to run an officer over.” Officers then fired what Lyons described as defensive shots.

Mendoza Hernandez was subsequently hospitalized. It is unclear how many times he was shot or what his condition is currently. ICE declined to provide further information on Mendoza Hernandez, in response to a question by a reporter for The Sacramento Bee.

ICE agents have been involved in at least six other shootings this year.

12 p.m. FBI Sacramento on-scene

At about noon, an account for the Sacramento office of the Federal Bureau of Investigation posted on X that it was “responding to the scene of an ICE and CBP involved shooting in Patterson.”

“We are conducting a thorough investigation in partnership with the Stanislaus County Sheriff’s Office and are grateful for the Patterson community’s continued patience and support,” FBI Sacramento’s post noted. “As the investigation is in its early stages, we are unable to release additional information at this time.”

Where the incident took place

The shooting took place near Interstate 5 and Sperry Avenue in Patterson, an incorporated city of about 27,000 people. It is south of Tracy along I-5 and near Modesto. Patterson is around 70% Latino.

Patterson is part of Stanislaus County and contracts for police service with the Stanislaus County Sheriff’s Office. That office was assisting after the shooting on Tuesday but had no involvement with the incident, according to a Facebook post just before 10 a.m. Tuesday by the Stanislaus County Sheriff’s Office.

“The on and off ramps on I-5 and Sperry Ave are closed and they are expected to be closed for the remainder of the day,” the post noted. “Motorists should expect significant delays and avoid the area.”

California Certified: America’s Largest State Proposes Non-UPF Label for Food Producers & Supermarkets Anay Mridul . Anay Mridul.

4 Mins Read

California is considering a new bill seeking to create a non-ultraprocessed seal that food manufacturers can use on packaging, and grocery stores would be required to prominently display.

Taking a leaf out of the organic food playbook, California is stepping up its fight against ultra-processed foods (UPFs).

The state is now considering a bill that would create a ‘California Certified’ seal that food producers can label their packaging with if they meet certain criteria. It would also require supermarkets to display these accredited products in “prominent, high-traffic” areas of their stores.

The seal is modelled after the USDA Organic label and designed to “empower consumers with clear, trustworthy information and make it easier for them to locate healthier foods that are free from harmful additives”, said Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, who authored AB 2244.

“While Washington DC is paralysed by inaction, California is stepping up to protect our kids and confront the health risks associated with ultra-processed foods,” he said.

‘California Certified’ seal would follow state’s definition of ultraprocessed foods The bill builds on Gabriel’s AB 1264, which established a statutory definition of UPFs and initiated a phaseout of the most concerning ingredients from school meals in California. The first-of-a-kind legislation was signed into law by Governor Gavin Newsom last October.

It defines UPFs as products that contain certain stabilisers, thickeners, emulsifiers, flavouring and colouring agents, nonnutritive sweeteners and high amounts of saturated fat, sodium or added sugar. AB 2244 would establish a system overseen by the California Department of Public Health, where food manufacturers can apply to accredited certification agents to use the California Certified label on their packaging.

While the scheme is voluntary for food producers, it mandates that retailers with over $10M in annual sales and more than 25 non-UPF-certified products on offer display California Certified items at more visible points, including at checkout and store entrances. In addition, the state would maintain a publicly available list of these products, maintain audit certification records, and enforce standards for the seal.

It’s inspired by the USDA Organic label, for which companies pay to have their products certified by an independent agent.

California is the first and only state to create its own organic programme, which led Congress to introduce a federal standard for the term ‘organic’ in 1990.

The anti-UPF bill would allow companies to apply for the seal starting June 2028, and if they receive the certification, they’ll need to renew it every three years.

Given California’s efforts to clean up the food system and Gabriel’s contribution to them, the bill has legs. The assemblymember had passed into law two other bills, the California Food Safety Act in 2023 and the California School Food Safety Act in 2024, which his office says have “shaped federal policy and inspired similar legislation across more than 30 other states”.

In addition to UPFs, the state last year enacted laws that banned foods containing dyes like Red 40 from being sold in schools and products with chemicals like brominated vegetable oil from being sold anywhere in the state by 2027.

Policymakers rail against processed foods amid several non-UPF schemes First classified under the Nova system developed by Brazilian researchers in 2009, UPFs are described as those made with industrial formulations and techniques or containing cosmetic additives thought to be of little culinary use. Put simply, they’re thought of as foods you can’t make in your home kitchen.

Americans now get 55% of their calories from UPFs, and this rises to 67% for children. Many experts have linked these to a multitude of health ailments (and even premature death).

But there’s no standard definition of these products, and the Nova classification has been criticised by many as overly broad. Health experts have argued that processing levels shouldn’t be conflated with nutritional value, since many UPFs can actually be good for you.

That hasn’t stopped companies from disassociating themselves from UPFs, which now top Americans’ list of health concerns. Now, 72% of them are trying to avoid these products in their diets, and 79% feel they’re a “significant threat” to public health.

The anti-UPF rhetoric has pushed the US Food and Drug Administration to work on a definition of UPFs to encourage companies to label their offerings as ‘non-ultra-processed’ the same way products are marketed as sugar- or fat-free.

These efforts have magnified under the rise of the Make America Health Again (MAHA) movement, which attacked UPFs with a highly controversial Super Bowl ad with Mike Tyson, who has been convicted of rape (for which he served a three-year term in prison) and has a history of domestic violence.

US health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, the chief architect of the MAHA drive, has promised to act on a petition by former FDA chief David Kessler, who has asked the government to revoke the GRAS status of some UPFs. That said, he stopped short of promising that the agency will begin regulating these products.

The House of Representatives is also considering a bipartisan childhood diabetes bill that seeks to convene an expert panel to define UPFs, prohibit them from being advertised to children, and require them to carry front-of-pack warning labels Several other states have imposed restrictions on UPFs, including Arizona, Texas, Louisiana, and West Virginia. If California’s bill passes, it will join a host of non-UPF certifications launched over the last 18 months by the likes of the NonUPF Program, the Non-GMO Project, and Wisecode. *The Lempert Report — April 6, 2026*

When the Grandson Bites Back: How One Family’s Outrage Just Changed What’s Inside Your Reese’s

Just last week on April 1, 2026, The Hershey Company made an announcement that sounded like it had to be a joke. After weeks of viral outrage, media appearances, and a LinkedIn letter that shook one of America’s most beloved candy brands to its chocolate-coated core, Hershey declared it would reverse course and return all Reese’s products to their classic milk chocolate and peanut butter recipes. April Fools’ Day. You can’t make this up. Except this time, nobody was laughing — least of all the 70-year-old grandson of the man who invented the peanut butter cup, who spent six weeks watching a corporation scramble to protect a legacy it had been quietly dismantling one cheaper ingredient at a time. This is not a prank. This is a $12 billion company being brought to its knees by a single bite of a Valentine’s Day candy.

That man is Brad Reese. His grandfather, H.B. Reese, invented the peanut butter cup in 1928. On Valentine’s Day 2026, Brad picked up a bag of Reese’s Unwrapped Chocolate Peanut Butter Crème Mini Hearts — a seasonal product his family’s name is plastered across — took a bite, and threw the bag in the trash.

“It didn’t taste like milk chocolate,” he told NBC News. “It tasted cheap.”

He was right. What happened next is one of the most revealing food industry stories of the year — one that touches on skimpflation, consumer trust, the cost of cocoa, tariffs, and the price a brand pays when it quietly rewrites the recipe that built it.

Reading the Label That Changed Everything

When Brad Reese flipped over that Valentine’s bag and read the ingredient list, he wasn’t just a disappointed customer. He was a man confronting corporate math applied to his family’s legacy. What he found was “chocolate candy” and “peanut butter crème” — not the “milk chocolate” and “peanut butter” that defined his grandfather’s original recipe. That distinction is not just semantics. Under FDA standards, the term “milk chocolate” requires at least 10% chocolate liquor. If a product can’t legally use that term on the front of the package, guess what? It’s not milk chocolate.

On Valentine’s Day, Brad posted an open letter to Hershey’s corporate brand manager on LinkedIn. “My grandfather built Reese’s on a simple, enduring architecture: milk chocolate + peanut butter,” he wrote. “But today, Reese’s identity is being rewritten — not by storytellers, but by formulation decisions that replace milk chocolate with compound coatings and peanut butter with peanut butter-style crèmes across multiple Reese’s products.”

The post drew 97,000 likes and more than 7 million views on X, with thousands of comments — nearly all of them agreeing with him. “I got roasted last Halloween at work for saying they aren’t the same anymore and that I don’t even eat them now,” wrote one user. “Vindicated.”

I’ve been in the food industry for more than 30 years. I’ve watched hundreds of brands quietly reformulate their products — swapping real ingredients for cheaper alternatives, trimming an ounce here, replacing cocoa butter with PGPR there. And I’ve watched consumers absorb it, complain about it, and then move on. What’s different this time is that the complaint came from an insider.

The Ingredients We Should All Know

Let me be precise about what’s actually in a classic Reese’s Peanut Butter Cup, because this is where the story gets nuanced. The standard cup’s ingredients are: milk chocolate (sugar, cocoa butter, chocolate, skim milk, milk fat, lactose, lecithin (soy), PGPR), peanuts, sugar, dextrose, salt, and TBHQ & citric acid. Real chocolate is in there — but so is PGPR, a castor oil-derived emulsifier used to reduce the amount of expensive cocoa butter needed, and TBHQ, a chemical preservative. Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups once had 9 ingredients and contained no PGPR, TBHQ, or citric acid. Today’s version has 14.

TBHQ happens to be banned at Whole Foods, which cites it as “unacceptable in food.” That tells us something. And Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups have also gradually shrunk from 0.9 ounce in the 1980s to 0.75 ounce today — nearly a 17% reduction. It’s the classic playbook of shrinkflation.

The classic cup, for all its tweaks, still qualifies as real milk chocolate. But as Brad Reese correctly identified, certain seasonal and specialty Reese’s items are now labeled as “chocolate candy” with “peanut butter creme” rather than the brand’s original milk chocolate and peanut butter formula. Reese’s Mini Eggs sold for Easter — the ones your family may have just finished off yesterday — contain no milk chocolate. Reese’s Pieces has no milk chocolate either. These are products carrying the Reese’s name and orange branding that millions of consumers assume are true to the original classic.

The Business Pressure Behind the Decision

To understand why Hershey made these moves, you have to look at the numbers. And they are not pretty.

Hershey reported full-year 2025 net sales of $11.69 billion, up 4.4%, but reported net income fell more than 60% to $883.3 million. Sales up, profits down. The culprit was commodity costs — primarily cocoa. High cocoa prices have led Hershey and other manufacturers to reformulate by using less chocolate in recent years. The company’s Q4 gross margin declined 17 percentage points, with reported and adjusted gross margin declines reflecting higher commodity costs, incremental tariff expenses and lower volume. Hershey's chocolate and candy manufactured in Mexico and shipped to the U.S. should qualify for USMCA tariff-free treatment; the tariff impact on finished Reese's products from Mexico is likely minimal. However, the tariff squeeze on raw cocoa beans imported into the company’s U.S. factories is very real, which explains why Hershey's profit margins collapsed even as revenue grew, and why there's actually a financial incentive to manufacture MORE in Mexico, not less. That's a rich irony that the administration should take note of.

More broadly, inflation, cost-of-living pressures, and shifting consumer behaviors towards healthier eating are weighing on sales across the sweets category. As household budgets tighten, consumers are also trading down, buying less frequently, or switching to cheaper options.

On a conference call with investors, Hershey CFO Steven Voskuil said: “I would say in all the changes that we’ve made thus far, there has been no consumer impact whatsoever.” Guess he wasn’t told about the millions of people who clicked on Brad Reese’s post before he jumped on the call.

The Reversal

What the food industry almost never does is reverse course. Brands reformulate forward, not backward. So the April 1 announcement from Hershey is worth noting.

Hershey said it will use classic recipes for all Reese’s products starting next year. The company acknowledged that a small portion of Reese’s products — including those mini Easter eggs — are now made with a coating that contains less chocolate, and it is now committed to shifting those products to “their classic milk chocolate and dark chocolate recipes” in 2027. What about doing it before Halloween 2026? That is the biggest candy sales period of the year. Hershey also announced it will transition to natural colors across its sweets portfolio and enhance the Kit Kat recipe to make it creamier.

This is significant. It tells us that the consumer voice, amplified by social media and given credibility by a family name, can still move a $12 billion company. But it also tells us something we should sit with: Hershey knew these products had been reformulated. They did it as part of a plan. They called it “innovation,” naturally. And they described it as having no consumer impact — right up until the moment a 70-year-old man with the right last name made it impossible to ignore.

What This Means for Shoppers Right Now

Until 2027 arrives and those classic recipes are restored, here’s what Brad Reese himself advised consumers: look for “milk chocolate” and “peanut butter” in the ingredients list, not substitutes like “chocolate candy” and “peanut butter creme.” If the front of the package doesn’t say “milk chocolate,” the FDA doesn’t allow it to be there because it isn’t.

The lesson here is one I’ve been preaching for decades: read the label. Not the front panel with its warm orange branding and promises of the perfect peanut butter-chocolate ratio. The back. The ingredient list. The nutritional facts panel. That’s where the real story is, and in this case, it took a grandson’s heartbreak to remind an entire industry of that fact.

H.B. Reese built something remarkable. His family sold it to Hershey in 1963 for $23.5 million in stock — 666,316 shares of Hershey stock. After 63 years of stock splits, those original shares now represent 16 million shares valued at over $4.4 billion, and pay annual cash dividends of $29.9 million.

For decades, Hershey honored what H.B. Reese created. The question now is whether the reversal they announced on April 1, which is almost a year away and affects only a “small portion” of products, is genuine stewardship of a great American brand, or just a clever PR move in the face of a viral moment.

Let’s be clear about what happened. A 70-year-old man posted an open letter on LinkedIn, and within six weeks, he forced a $12 billion company to reverse course on one of the most iconic candy brands in American history. That is the power of consumer trust and the very real consequence of betraying it. But the victory is incomplete. Hershey’s reversal doesn’t take effect until 2027, and the hard economics haven’t changed: cocoa prices, packaging, labor, and distribution costs are all headed in one direction — up. The classic recipe is coming back. The question that should keep Hershey’s executives up at night is this: when it does, how much are they going to charge shoppers for it... and will they pay the price?

MAHA's Moment of Reckoning

The movement that helped elect Trump is now threatening to undo his coalition — and the food industry should pay close attention.

There’s a political earthquake rumbling beneath Washington right now, and its aftershocks are headed straight for every supermarket aisle, every food manufacturer’s boardroom, and every commodity board in America. Politico just dropped a bombshell poll, and as you’re in the food business, you need to read it carefully.

The POLITICO Poll, conducted between March 13 and 18 among more than 3,800 U.S. adults, reveals that 52 percent of Americans believe the Trump administration has not done enough to “Make America Healthy Again.” More than half the country says the movement that helped put RFK Jr. at the helm of HHS hasn’t delivered. And here’s the kicker: 41 percent of Trump’s own 2024 voters agree.

That’s not a small crack in the coalition. That’s the Grand Canyon.

The poll shows both broad frustration and dissatisfaction with the Trump administration on health priorities, and it reveals real opportunities for Democrats to make inroads with Kennedy’s MAHA supporters. Tony Lyons, president of MAHA Action, put it bluntly in a memo obtained by Politico: Republicans are only “renting MAHA voters” and have not yet “purchased” their loyalty.

For those of us who have tracked the food and grocery industry for decades, this political dynamic is not just fascinating — it’s consequential. Because MAHA voters aren’t a fringe. They’re the shoppers already reading ingredient labels, already asking about seed oils at the deli counter, already choosing brands that have pledged to go dye-free. They are, by and large, the most engaged food consumers in America we have ever witnessed.

The deregulatory instincts of the Trump administration keeps colliding with MAHA’s core demands for stricter rules. The most glaring example is the administration’s decision to let Bayer expand production of Roundup which has particularly angered MAHA voters, given Kennedy’s long history of fighting glyphosate and winning that landmark $289 million jury verdict against Monsanto.

Meanwhile, the food industry has been playing defense at a cost. Trade groups and major manufacturers have poured millions into K Street lobbying as the Trump administration has proved harder to access than in its first term. And the political math is working against them: the Politico poll found that roughly 3 in 10 voters believed the GOP was more susceptible to pressure from the pesticide industry, compared to 2 in 10 who say the same about Democrats — a perception problem that is only getting worse as MAHA voters drift.

Here’s what the food retail industry must understand right now. A separate Politico/Public First poll conducted in November 2025 found that nearly half of Americans now consider grocery prices the “most challenging” household expense, outranking housing and health care — and that creates a dangerous tension. Shoppers want cleaner food AND they want affordable food. They aren’t willing to choose. The brands and retailers who figure out how to deliver both will win.

More than a hundred bills targeting sugar, synthetic dyes, and chemical additives have been introduced across statehouses this year, nearly five times the number from last year. The federal government may be gridlocked, but the states are not waiting.

The clearest signal for food companies? MAHA supporters, the Politico Poll found, prioritize issues like combating infectious diseases, regulating “forever chemicals,” and expanding access to reproductive health care — positions that clearly cut across party lines.

The food industry’s window to get ahead of this both proactively and authentically is narrowing fast. The brands that treat MAHA as a political football to be managed will lose. The ones that treat it as a genuine signal from consumers about what they want to feed their families will lead.

This Politico poll isn’t just about midterm politics. It’s a roadmap for the food industry.

If you’re serious about in‑store foodservice, prepared foods, and the changing “grocerant” model, you need to be in Chicago May 16--19 at McCormick Place for the National Restaurant Association Show. What keeps me coming back to the National Restaurant Association Show is the community it is where operators, chefs, and partners actually meet face‑to‑face, share what’s working and what’s not, and build relationships that last far beyond the four days in Chicago. Go to nationalrestaurantshow.com, use my promo code PHIL26 to take $26 off your registration, and make sure you do it before May 7 --- because that offer is only valid online, only for operators, and it won’t work once onsite registration starts.

California Just Redrew the Map for Every Grocery Store, Manufacturer and State in America

Walk into any supermarket in the country today and roughly 70% of what you see on those shelves is, by most scientific measures, ultra-processed food. Not just the obvious stuff — the chips and the soda and the hot dogs. We’re talking about the breakfast cereals, the flavored yogurts, the packaged bread, the frozen meals, the snack bars we tell ourselves are healthy. U.S. adults on average receive 53% of their daily calories from ultra-processed foods, according to the CDC — and for children, that number climbs to 62%.

We’ve known about this for years. We have studied it, debated it, written about it, and largely done very little about it — until now.

What California Has Already Done — and What’s Coming Next

Last October, Governor Gavin Newsom signed AB 1264 into law — and with that signature, California became the first state in the nation to legally define ultra-processed food. The “Real Food, Healthy Kids Act” makes California the first state in the United States to define and ultimately phase out unhealthy ultra-processed foods from what’s projected to be over one billion meals served to California schoolchildren annually.

California’s new law broadly defines “ultra-processed food” as any food or beverage that contains one or more ingredients with specified technical effects — such as emulsifiers, stabilizers, colors, flavors, flavor enhancers, and non-nutritive sweeteners — and either contains high amounts of saturated fat, sodium, or added sugar, or contains a non-nutritive sweetener or certain other specified substances.

The timeline is deliberate. The law officially took effect January 1, 2026, with schools beginning to phase out restricted ultra-processed foods starting in 2029, with a full vendor prohibition by 2032 and full school implementation by 2035.

California didn’t stop there. On March 25, 2026, just a couple of weeks ago, Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel introduced AB 2244, and this bill goes further than schools.

AB 2244 would establish a first-of-its-kind “California Certified” seal that food manufacturers could place on products that meet clear standards for not being ultra-processed — modeled after the USDA Organic label. And here’s where it gets real for grocery retailers: grocery stores generating more than $10 million in annual revenue, and carrying at least 25 certified products, would be required to display those items prominently in high-traffic areas such as entrances or checkout zones. FMI–The Food Industry Association reports the average annual sales per supermarket in 2024 was $37,013,912.

California is telling grocery stores where to put food on their shelves — a move that should give every category manager in this country a splitting headache.

This Is Not Just a California Story

I’ve watched California reshape national food policy for over three decades. The organic certification movement. The food dye bans. The additive restrictions. Every single time, the same thing happens: California moves, the industry grumbles, adapts, and then the rest of the country follows. Lawmakers in other states watch what happens, consumers in other states demand the same, and manufacturers who don’t want to produce separate SKUs for California, versus everyone else, reformulates nationwide.

More than half the nation began working on food dye bans after California passed one in 2024. The same domino effect is already in motion for UPFs. Texas passed a law requiring warning labels on products containing any of 44 specific additives — a measure that the food industry challenged on First Amendment grounds, and a federal judge temporarily blocked. Louisiana and Wisconsin followed with their own versions. The legislative momentum is unmistakable.

Assemblymember Gabriel said it himself on a press call: “We would love to see Washington follow our lead. But until then, there’s no reason companies couldn’t use the California seal in grocery stores outside of California.”

He’s right. And companies will. Because the consumer demand is already there, the regulatory pressure is building, and the financial incentive of preferred shelf placement is not something manufacturers or retailers are going to ignore. And then there is California’s undeniable leadership in health and wellness — the state is consistently the largest organic food market in the country, and that gravitational pull on national consumer preferences is only growing.

What This Means for CPG

It is estimated that a third of packaged foods would be considered not ultra-processed under California’s definition, according to nutrition policy researcher Alyssa Moran of the University of Pennsylvania. That means roughly two-thirds of the packaged food supply — the products manufacturers have spent decades engineering for palatability, shelf life, and cost efficiency — are now in California’s crosshairs.

The California Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment is required to produce a more specific definition for UPFs by July 1, 2026. That definition, once finalized, becomes the compliance target. Manufacturers who want the “California Certified” seal will need to reformulate. Those who don’t will find their products relegated to wherever the store chooses to put them — which, under AB 2244, will not be the high-traffic entrance zones reserved for certified products.

What This Means for Grocery Retailers

The shelf-placement mandate in AB 2244 is the provision the grocery industry needs to pay the closest attention to right now. This is not a labeling requirement that affects manufacturers. This is a direct operational directive to retailers — telling them how to merchandise their stores, where to place products, and by implication, what their store layout should prioritize.

Think about what this actually means at store level. Entrances and checkout zones are prime real estate. Those placements are negotiated, paid for, and strategically managed. AB 2244 would effectively require retailers — once they carry a threshold number of certified products — to give that prime real estate to “California Certified” non-UPF foods. That is a fundamental shift in how category management works. It inverts the traditional pay-to-play model of retail placement.

For grocery retailers, this should be a wake-up moment. The risk is real: if you ignore it, wait for the law to pass, and then scramble to reorganize your store layout and renegotiate vendor relationships under regulatory pressure, you’ve already lost.

Consumer awareness of the “California Certified” designation will spread — just as USDA Organic spread far beyond the farmers’ markets where it first took hold.

What This Means for the Other 49 States

Here is the scenario I want every food retailer, manufacturer, and state legislator to sit with: it is 2028. The California definition of ultra-processed food is finalized. Hundreds of products carry the “California Certified” seal. Manufacturers have reformulated the products they want to sell into California schools and preferred shelf positions. Consumer awareness of the seal is growing.

That is how national change happens. Not through federal mandates. Through the quiet, powerful, relentless force of an informed consumer who has been given a new lens through which to evaluate what she’s buying.

UPFs have become a governance issue that sits awkwardly between public health, procurement rules, education policy, and corporate accountability.

Washington has been slow. The MAHA Commission’s final strategy report, released in September 2025, called for the government to “continue efforts” to define ultra-processed foods — falling well short of the decisive action many had hoped for. The FDA and USDA are still seeking public comment on how to define the category. While federal agencies deliberate, California is building compliance frameworks, certification programs, shelf-placement mandates, and ingredient disclosure databases.

My Take…

I’ve said for years that the future of food retail belongs to the store that helps consumers make better decisions — not just more decisions. California’s twin-track approach is to define what ultra-processed means, then reward the foods that don’t qualify. In my view, this is the most coherent food policy framework any U.S. government body has produced.

It’s not perfect. The scientific debate over UPF definitions is real, and there will be products that fall into gray areas. But imperfect action is better than perfect inaction — and California has been proving that in food policy for 30 years.

For CPG and store brands, the message is simple: the cost of reformulation today is far less than the cost of regulatory non-compliance tomorrow. For retailers, the message is equally clear: the stores that win the next decade will be the ones that made it easy for shoppers to find better food.

And the Reese’s and California stories are not separate. They are the same story — one told by a family name, the other told by a legislature. Both are forcing the food industry to answer a question it has spent decades avoiding: what, exactly, is in your food?

A word to those other 49 states: pay attention!

California just drew the map. The rest of the country will follow.

Phil Lempert is a food industry analyst, trend tracker, and founder of SupermarketGuru.com. Subscribe to The Lempert Report for weekly insights on food, retail, and the future of what America eats.

עמדו רגע מול מדף בסופרמרקט. נסו לקרוא את רשימת המרכיבים של דגני בוקר לילדים. בין השורות הקטנות מופיעים מונחים טכניים: אמולסיפיירים, מייצבים, צבעי מאכל סינתטיים, ממתיקים מלאכותיים וחומרי טעם וריח. עבור הורים רבים, המאמץ להבין מסתיים בוויתור.

על הרקע הזה מציג חבר האסיפה המחוקקת של מדינת קליפורניה, ג'סי גבריאל, הצעת חוק חדשה – מספר 2244 – שנועדה לפשט את הבחירה. "הורים לא צריכים תואר בכימיה כדי להבין מה הם מאכילים את ילדיהם", אמר. מהתסכול הזה נולד רעיון פשוט: סימון ברור למזון שאינו מעובד־יתר.

על הרקע הזה מציג חבר האסיפה המחוקקת של מדינת קליפורניה, ג'סי גבריאל, הצעת חוק חדשה – מספר 2244 – שנועדה לפשט את הבחירה. "הורים לא צריכים תואר בכימיה כדי להבין מה הם מאכילים את ילדיהם", אמר. מהתסכול הזה נולד רעיון פשוט: סימון ברור למזון שאינו מעובד־יתר.

לפי ההצעה, מוצרים שיעמדו בקריטריונים תזונתיים ומדעיים יקבלו חותמת “מאושר קליפורניה”. מדובר בתוכנית וולונטרית: יצרן שיבחר להגיש מוצר לבדיקה ויעמוד בתנאים, יוכל לציין זאת על גבי האריזה. אין איסור על מוצרים אחרים, ואין ענישה – אלא יצירת הבחנה נגישה לעין.

המודל נשען על הצלחת תווי סימון קודמים, ובראשם תווית “אורגני” של משרד החקלאות של ארצות הברית, שהפכה בעשורים האחרונים לאחד הסמלים המוכרים לצריכה בריאה. ההבדל הוא במוקד: לא “אורגני”, אלא “לא מעובד־יתר”.

בנוסף, ההצעה מחייבת רשתות שיווק גדולות להציב את המוצרים המסומנים במיקומים בולטים. המטרה היא להקל על צרכנים שמבצעים קנייה מהירה, ולאפשר להם לזהות חלופה בריאה מבלי לחפש.

הצורך במהלך נשען על נתונים מטרידים. לפי ארגוני בריאות וסביבה, מזון מעובד־יתר מהווה יותר משני שלישים מתזונת הילדים בארצות הברית, ויותר ממחצית מתזונת המבוגרים. מדובר במזון שעבר עיבוד תעשייתי משמעותי, כולל תוספים כימיים ורמות גבוהות של סוכר, מלח ושומן.

מחקרים שונים מצביעים על קשר בין צריכה גבוהה של מזון כזה לבין השמנה, סוכרת מסוג 2, מחלות לב ואף סוגים מסוימים של סרטן. חלק מהחוקרים אף מתארים אותו כבעל פוטנציאל ממכר.

גבריאל פועל בתחום זה כבר כמה שנים. מאז 2023 קידם שורה של חוקים: איסור על חומרים מסוימים במזון, הגבלות על צבעי מאכל סינתטיים במסגרות חינוך, והגדרה חוקית למונח “מזון מעובד־יתר” לצד יעד לצמצומו בבתי ספר. החקיקה זכתה לתמיכה רחבה במיוחד, כמעט מכל קצוות המפה הפוליטית.

הצעת החוק הנוכחית ממשיכה את הקו הזה – אך בוחרת בכלי רך יותר: לא לאסור, אלא להבליט. לא לכפות, אלא לכוון.

אחד ההיבטים המעניינים הוא התמיכה הרחבה שמתגבשת סביב המהלך. לצד ארגוני בריאות הציבור, מצטרפים גם גורמים שמזוהים עם יוזמות שמרניות הקוראות לשיפור בריאות הציבור. החיבור הזה מאפשר לקדם חקיקה שאינה נתפסת כהתערבות מוגזמת בשוק, אלא כהנגשת מידע.

ההשפעה האפשרית של המהלך חורגת מגבולות קליפורניה. מדובר בכלכלה עצומה, שמכתיבה לא פעם סטנדרטים לתעשיות שלמות. אם יצרני מזון ירצו לשווק מוצרים עם החותמת, הם עשויים לשנות את הרכבם – ושינויים כאלה נוטים להתפשט גם לשווקים אחרים בארצות הברית.

כך, גם מדינות שלא יאמצו חוק דומה עשויות ליהנות ממוצרים משופרים, פשוט משום שהיצרנים יעדיפו לייצר גרסה אחידה לכלל השוק.

ב־14 באפריל תידון ההצעה בוועדת הבריאות של האסיפה המחוקקת. אם תאושר, היא תמשיך במסלול החקיקה לקראת חתימת מושל המדינה. ייתכן שכבר בשנים הקרובות יופיע על מדפי הסופרמרקט סמל חדש – קטן, אך בעל משמעות רחבה.

לא מהפכה רועשת, אלא שינוי שקט בהרגלים. לפעמים, די בסימון אחד ברור כדי לשנות את מה שמונח בעגלת הקניות – ומה שמונח על שולחן האוכל.

Celebrating a New EV Shuttle for Warner Center - Valley News Group

VNG Desk

The Los Angeles Cleantech Incubator (LACI) and the Warner Center Association hosted a press conference and ribbon cutting Friday to formally launch an innovative microtransit pilot project at Warner Center in partnership with the Warner Center Association. The pilot, which is now operational in the Warner Center’s Transportation Technology Innovation Zone (TTIZ), will bring an all-electric shuttle service to the West San Fernando Valley.

The shuttles are provided by Circuit,  a LACI portfolio company and a leading provider of electric, on-demand microtransit services. 

Shuttles will be available for $1 per ride from 6 am to 8 pm on weekdays and 7 am to 9 pm on weekends within the geographic area of Warner Center. Theall-electric vehicle fleet includes GEM e6 six-seat electric shuttles, Volkswagen ID Buzz vans, and an ADA-accessible Ford E-Transit van.

“By launching this EV shuttle pilot here at Warner Center–a far reaching and bustling live-work community in the heart of the West San Fernando Valley–we have an opportunity to expand mobility access for the local residents, commuters, and visitors, while also showcasing the power of zero emissions solutions,” said Matt Petersen, President and CEO of LACI. “We are grateful for the support of Councilmember Blumenfield, Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, and Senator Henry Stern for securing the funding that has allowed us to work with the Warner Center Association to deploy this innovative pilot.”

“Warner Center is exactly the kind of community where microtransit can make a real difference, and we’re proud to finally be up and running for the people who live and work here,” said Daniel Kramer, Vice President of Business Development (West) at Circuit. “This is just the beginning, and we look forward to growing with the community as Warner Center continues to evolve.”

This shuttle service launch is the first of two planned LACI Innovation Pilots in the bustling live-work Warner Center community. 

Later this year, LACI will launch a second pilot that will deliver mobile EV charging robots provided by EV Safe Charge. These low-cost solutions will be available for residents, employees, commuters, and visitors alike–all while testing market-ready technologies ahead of wider rollouts.

During the launch event, local elected officials and community leaders voiced their support for this innovative solution:

“It’s not often that we have the opportunity to take a step together that has the potential to truly change the nature of our community,” said Brad Rosenheim, Chairperson of the Warner Center Association. “Today signifies one of those rare opportunities and I could not be more grateful to Councilmember Blumenfield, Supervisor Horvath, Assemblymember Gabriel, Sena-tor Stern, our partners at LACI and Circuit and the Warner Center Association Board of Directors for making this new transit opportunity possible.”

“As Warner Center has seen the largest growth in Los Angeles with residents, businesses, and visitors, this circulator is an exciting addition—making it easier, more affordable, and environmentally friendly for people to get where they need to go,” said Councilmember Bob Blumenfield.

“The Warner Center has been an important hub for innovation and economic growth in the West Valley,” Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel, Chair of the Assembly Budget Committee. “That’s why I’m proud to have secured $2 million in state funding to deliver clean, zero-emissions transportation options that will help reduce pollution and congestion in our community. I’m grateful to LACI and the Warner Center Association for their important partnership in this effort.”

The TTIZ serves as a hub for innovation where LACI seeks to invite zero emissions mobility, charging, and other solutions into a dedicated ‘innovation sandbox’ to better serve the needs of over 14,000 Angelenos who call Warner Center their home as well as the 45,000 people who work in the community. LACI and the Warner Center Association are piloting these transportation technologies in the TTIZ testbed following LACI’s merger with Urban Movement Labs in 2024.

The pilot is scheduled to run for an initial period of one year. Funding for the pilots comes from the State Legislature via the Governor’s Office of Business Development (GoBiz) and the Office of Councilmember Bob Blumenfield.

California Proposes Landmark Labeling Law Targeting UPFs

By Alexandra B. Cunningham and Jane G. Legris

California continues to lead the nation in efforts to regulate ultra-processed foods (“UPFs”).  On March 25, Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino) introduced Assembly Bill 2244 – The California Certified Food Standard Act. 

The bill proposes a first-of-its-kind labeling regime that would enable food and beverage manufacturers to display a “California Certified” seal on products that meet defined standards confirming the product is not classified as a UPF.  Modeled after the well-known “USDA Organic” label, the initiative aims to enhance consumer transparency and promote public health outcomes throughout the state. 

A central feature of AB 2244 is its reliance on forthcoming regulatory definitions.  The Real Food, Healthy Kids Act – which we have previously reported on – was signed into law by Governor Gavin Newsom in October 2025 and mandates a gradual phaseout of UPFs in California’s public schools.  It also requires the State Department of Public Health to adopt regulations by June 1, 2028, formally defining UPFs.  Under AB 2244, accredited certification agents would apply this forthcoming definition in determining product eligibility for the “California Certified” seal.   

In addition, AB 2244 would impose retail placement requirements on certain grocery stores.  Specifically, stores operating in California with annual sales exceeding $10 million would be required to display at least three “California Certified” products in prominent, high-traffic areas. 

As the legislative session advances, we will continue to monitor both the advancement of AB 2244 and the broader public response.  California’s continued focus on UPF regulation positions the state as a national leader in this evolving area of food law and policy, and its developments are likely to inform similar efforts across the country.

<div class="asset-content subscriber-premium" false="" id="article-body" itemprop="articleBody">
<meta content="false" itemprop="isAccessibleForFree"/>
<div class="subscriber-preview"><p dir="ltr"><span>LOS ANGELES — Brian Goldsmith, a Los Angeles native, former journalist, Democratic consultant, and first-time candidate, is running to represent California’s 24th State Senate District, a sprawling, diverse seat stretching from Agoura Hills and Calabasas through Beverly Hills, West Hollywood and the Pacific Palisades down to the South Bay beach cities.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-preview"><p dir="ltr"><span>The seat is being vacated by term-limited Sen. Ben Allen, and Goldsmith has emerged as the race’s leading fundraiser, raising more than $2 million and securing endorsements from figures such as former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, and businessman Rick Caruso. </span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr">A graduate of Harvard College and Stanford Law School who spent more than a decade as a political commentator at CBS News, Yahoo News, and CNN, Goldsmith says the January 2025 wildfires and what he describes as California’s pattern of “good intentions and bad governance,” compelled him to move from advising candidates to becoming one. The Westside Current sat down with Goldsmith to discuss his platform and vision for the district.</p></div><div class="tnt-ads-container text-center">
<div class="tnt-ads dfp-ad" id="fixed-big-ad-top-asset" style="min-height:250px; min-width:300px;">
<script>
                googletag.cmd.push(function() {
                        googletag.display('fixed-big-ad-top-asset');
                        
                });
            </script>
</div>
</div><div class="tncms-region hidden-print" id="tncms-region-article_instory_top"></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>At the top of the interview, Goldsmith emphasized that the issues most people talk about in their daily lives are state and local matters, not Washington, D.C., even though the press is far more focused on national politics. “You gotta look at these contests, these offices, because they actually have a profound effect on your daily life,” he said.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>Goldsmith described his path to candidacy as a gradual evolution. After covering politics at outlets including The Atlantic, Yahoo, and CBS News, where he served as Katie Couric’s political producer, he left journalism during the first Trump administration to focus on advocacy and helped his friend Pete Buttigieg’s presidential campaign. He also launched a startup, giving him firsthand experience with the regulatory and financial burdens facing California entrepreneurs.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>But he said two developments pushed him from advising to running. The first was the 2024 election, including not just the outcome but the way California became a central part of the case against Vice President Kamala Harris. “As much as I disagreed with a lot of people making that argument, we have to be honest enough to admit that the state has failed in a number of areas,” Goldsmith said, citing the cost of living, challenges facing small businesses and what he described as years of fraud and mismanagement in state government.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>The second catalyst was the January 2025 Palisades fire, which devastated communities within the district. Though he was not personally displaced, he and his wife took in a family of four who lost their home, and he said many friends and neighbors are still struggling to rebuild.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>“We now know that the Palisades fire was entirely preventable, and that it was mismanaged at every stage — before, during, and after — at all levels of government,” Goldsmith said. “I think we need more people in office who can take a fresh perspective, who can disagree with the people in power when they’re doing something wrong.”</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span style="text-decoration: underline;"><strong>The Toll of the Fires</strong></span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>Goldsmith pushed back against the perception that the fire’s impact was limited to the wealthy. He pointed to the trailer park in Malibu, to families who invested everything they had into homes that happened to sit on expensive land, and to the broad economic effects on domestic workers, landscapers and small businesses that depended on residents who are no longer there.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>“It’s a multidimensional failure, and the cast of victims is not just the stereotype that has been perpetuated,” he said. He noted that the absence of federal aid has compounded the pain, arguing that if the same disaster had occurred in another state, federal funds would have arrived far more quickly. Many fire survivors, he said, were “house rich” but not cash rich, and now face the challenge of fighting insurance companies, draining savings and confronting serious doubts about the safety of returning to their lots.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span style="text-decoration: underline;"><strong>Housing</strong></span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>On housing, Goldsmith said he would evaluate each piece of legislation on its merits and does not support a one-size-fits-all approach to density. He opposed SB 79, calling it “far too blunt of an instrument” that punished communities that had already done the hard work of local planning to meet their housing goals.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>Instead, he outlined a multi-pronged strategy: leveraging publicly owned land for below-market-rate housing development, converting empty commercial buildings to residential use, which he said is already being proven in Manhattan, and speeding up the state’s permitting and regulatory processes.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>“There’s no reason that the cost of building a unit of housing in California should cost twice what it does in Colorado,” Goldsmith said. “That’s not the land. That’s the cost of the house. A lot of that is embedded regulatory and permitting costs.”</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>He drew on his journalism background to make the case for deadlines. “As a journalist, one of the most powerful tools we had was, you had a deadline,” he said. “I think too much of construction is just open-ended.”</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>Goldsmith also advocated expanding manufactured and modular housing, which he said has improved dramatically in quality while offering significant cost and speed advantages. “We don’t do anything else the way we did 40 or 50 years ago. Why are we still building all houses the way we did 40 or 50 years ago?” he said.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>He noted that a colleague elected to the Santa Barbara County Board of Supervisors ordered an audit of publicly owned land that had been deemed environmentally sensitive, only to find that roughly half of it was not and included underutilized parking lots, office buildings and undeveloped industrial zones with existing infrastructure that could support housing.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span style="text-decoration: underline;"><strong>Homelessness</strong></span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>On homelessness, Goldsmith did not mince words. “In the richest state, in the richest country, that we have this many people who are unhoused — there is nothing progressive about allowing anyone to sleep on the street even for one night,” he said. He called the situation a “scandal” and cited LAUSD’s estimate that thousands of its students are functionally homeless and noted that four Angelenos die on the streets every day.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>Goldsmith said the state should stop managing the crisis and start solving it, with the goal of ending the era of encampments. He called for rapidly standing up dignified, clean shelter, rather than $800,000-per-unit permanent housing, and deploying proven drug treatment and mental health services through effective nonprofits. He highlighted organizations such as the Downtown Women’s Center and Hope the Mission as models of accountability.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>“Some of them won’t take public money because it comes with too many strings attached,” Goldsmith said. “If they’re doing great work on the ground and they won’t take Sacramento’s money, it’s not the groups that should have to change. It’s Sacramento that should have to change.”</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>He said that once sufficient shelter capacity is in place, anti-camping ordinances should be enforced, giving people multiple chances to accept services before being placed into programs. For those who are unable to make decisions for themselves, Goldsmith said the Care Courts established by Proposition 1 are a step in the right direction, but that the pathway into involuntary treatment is “far too restricted and narrow.”</span></p></div><div class="tnt-ads-container text-center">
<div class="tnt-ads dfp-ad" id="fixed-big-ad-middle-asset" style="min-height:250px; min-width:300px;">
<script>
                googletag.cmd.push(function() {
                        googletag.display('fixed-big-ad-middle-asset');
                        
                });
            </script>
</div>
</div><div class="tncms-region hidden-print" id="tncms-region-article_instory_middle"></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>“Sometimes people present a false choice between involuntary treatment and voluntary treatment,” he said. “In many of these cases, it’s a choice between involuntary treatment and folks literally dying on the streets.”</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>He pointed to the work done in San Francisco under Mayor Daniel Lurie and in San Jose under Mayor Matt Mahan as models that the state should replicate.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span style="text-decoration: underline;"><strong>Public Safety and Proposition 36</strong></span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>Goldsmith said he supported Proposition 36 at the time of the vote, not retroactively, and that he took criticism from fellow Democrats for doing so, just as he did for supporting Nathan Hochman for Los Angeles County District Attorney. He described both as answers that sought a middle ground between accountability for repeat offenders and pathways to rehabilitation for first-time, nonviolent offenders.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>“Prop 36 was about striking the right balance between holding folks more accountable and providing the care and the services that people need and also providing for the small businesses that were the target of repeated smash and grabs, seemingly without consequence,” Goldsmith said. He added that the challenge now is for the state to fund the measure’s full implementation.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span style="text-decoration: underline;"><strong>Entertainment Industry</strong></span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>Goldsmith called the entertainment industry a critical economic engine of the district and emphasized that it supports a broad ecosystem of middle-class jobs and small businesses, not only movie stars. He praised the bill authored by Sen. Ben Allen and Assemblymember Rick Zbur that dramatically expanded California’s film and television tax credit.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>“The film and TV tax credit that passed was a floor, not a ceiling,” Goldsmith said. “I think we ought to be doing more.”</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>He called for expanding the credit both above and below the line to remain competitive with other states and countries that are attracting California’s productions and jobs. He also stressed the importance of returning to legislation after it passes to evaluate what is working and what isn’t, a practice he said Speaker Robert Rivas has started through outcomes reviews.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>“In California, I think too much of our focus has been on how many billions of dollars are we spending, what are our good intentions — and not as much on outcomes and results,” Goldsmith said.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span style="text-decoration: underline;"><strong>Jewish Identity and AB 715</strong></span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>Goldsmith spoke openly about his Jewish identity and its role in his candidacy. His wife serves as vice president of Wilshire Boulevard Temple, and his son attends a Jewish day school. He said the 24th District likely has the largest concentration of Jewish voters outside New York, and that the community is facing record levels of antisemitism.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>“You can disagree with Prime Minister Netanyahu’s policies in Israel — that’s totally legitimate. Half of Israelis disagree with his policies,” Goldsmith said. “That’s not what we’re talking about. We’re talking about people being targeted in the United States based on who they are. And that is wrong.”</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>He said he was a strong supporter of AB 715, the antisemitism prevention legislation, and that he personally lobbied members of the state Legislature on its behalf. He drew a contrast with some of his opponents, saying he is “not ducking that issue” and is not “saying different things to different groups.”</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>Goldsmith pointed to his early work with Democratic Majority for Israel, which he described as focused on defeating antisemitism in the United States, and said his advocacy is one reason he has been endorsed by the Legislative Jewish Caucus and leaders such as former Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel and Julie Platt, the second woman in history to chair the Jewish Federations of North America. Former Sen. Barbara Boxer serves as the honorary chair of his campaign. He also noted the support of non-Jewish allies such as Rick Caruso.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span style="text-decoration: underline;"><strong>Personal Life and Closing</strong></span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>Goldsmith, who lives in the Beverly Hills–West Hollywood area with his wife and two children, said family is the center of his life. When he is not on the campaign trail, he tries to put the phone down and focus on his kids. The family frequents farmers markets around the district, enjoys cooking, and building Legos with his son.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>Goldsmith said he is the first in his family to run for office, though public service runs in the family. His father led an economy and jobs committee under Mayor Antonio Villaraigosa, and his mother has spent three decades working on behalf of foster children through the Alliance for Children’s Rights.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>He summarized his goals in four pillars: making it easier and more affordable to live in California, including for small businesses and families; taking on quality-of-life concerns around crime and homelessness with proven strategies; spending less time on performative politics and more time addressing the big challenges of the future, from disruptive technologies to climate resilience; and building coalitions in the state Legislature to pass bills and deliver results.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>“I’ve heard different politicians get cheap applause by saying, ‘I’m not going up there to make friends, I’m going up there to make a difference,’” Goldsmith said. “Well, you’re a legislator. You have to be able to build relationships and find common ground in order to pass bills and make a difference. And that’s what I would set out to do.”</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p dir="ltr"><span>The primary election for California’s 24th Senate District will take place on June 2, 2026.</span></p></div><div class="subscriber-only" style="display:none"><p><em>Editor's Note: <span id="docs-internal-guid-8813c076-7fff-1e88-c401-768e47a3bede">This story is part of an ongoing series of candidate profiles published by the Current as part of our coverage of the race for California’s 24th State Senate District. Our goal is to provide voters with clear, in-depth information about each candidate's background, platform and vision for the district.</span></em></p></div><div class="tnt-ads-container text-center">
