Jewish heirs of Holocaust victims and their representatives have filed two lawsuits in California staking their claims to Nazi-looted paintings that still hang on the walls of prominent museums in Los Angeles and Auschwitz.

The two lawsuits are the first to be filed after the recent passage of laws by California and Congress, which strengthen U.S.-based claims to artworks that were forcibly taken from Jewish families during World War II.

One lawsuit was filed in Los Angeles Superior Court on Monday by the Jewish Federation of Greater Los Angeles and its board chair Daniel Gryczman against Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena for the return of "Adam and Eve." These are two life-size oil-on-panel masterpieces created by Lucas Cranach the Elder in 1530.

The other lawsuit was filed in federal court in L.A. the same day by the daughters of the late Dinah Gottliebova Babbitt, a Holocaust survivor and California-based animator who was held in Auschwitz. It demanded the return of watercolors of fellow prisoners that the artist was forced to paint for Josef Mengele, a Nazi physician who had earned the nickname the "Angel of Death."

Spokespersons for both museums say the museums legally hold titles to the works and intend to continue displaying them to the public. The lawsuits don't specify the monetary value of the paintings.

The issue of Nazi-looted art is an emotional, legally and ethically charged topic that pits Jewish families that have suffered inter-generational trauma against museums that say they are trying to preserve a painful, yet important, chapter of history.

Between 1933 and 1945, the Nazi regime orchestrated the largest art theft in world history, seizing over 600,000 works of art across Europe from Jewish families, collectors and museums. Decades later, many of these masterpieces reside in prominent museums around the world, making the push for their recovery more complex than a simple property dispute.

Rabbi Noah Farkas is president and CEO of the Jewish Federation of Los Angeles, the organization to which Marei von Saher, sole heir of Dutch Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker, has signed over her rights. The paintings were seized from Goudstikker's collection by Hermann Göring, Adolf Hitler's second-in-command, and changed hands several times before being sold in the 1960s to the Pasadena Museum of Modern Art, which was renamed the Norton Simon Museum in honor of its benefactor.

Farkas said the federation plans to use most of the net proceeds from the recovered art to provide much-needed help to the about 2,500 Holocaust survivors living in the L.A. area.

"These are incredibly beautiful European masterpieces stolen from a Jewish family to enrich the Nazi party and fund the war and death machine against the people," he said. "It's our honor to take on this role on behalf of the community and use most of the proceeds to help these elderly survivors live out the last years of their lives in dignity, comfort and peace – something their family members were denied during the Holocaust."

Marei von Saher, in a statement, said she is grateful to the Jewish organization for taking up her family's cause.

"This effort represents a meaningful step toward justice for Holocaust survivors and victims of Nazi era atrocities," she said.

Democratic California Assemblyman Jesse Gabriel, who represents the Woodland Hills neighborhood of L.A., wrote Assembly Bill 2867, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom in September 2024, which requires that the state law must apply in lawsuits brought by California residents or their heirs to recover art seized during the Holocaust or during other acts of persecution. Gabriel, who co-chairs the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, introduced the legislation in response to a federal court ruling, which allowed the state-owned Thyssen-Bornemisza National Museum in Madrid to keep a multimillion-dollar Camille Pissarro impressionist masterpiece.

That painting had been taken by the Nazis from the Cassirer family in 1939. This case, which prompted this new law, is expected to be heard in federal court in California next month.

Gabriel said it's time for museums to "do some deep introspection on whether they want to be on the right side of history."

Norton Simon Museum released a statement pointing out that a federal court in 2018 unanimously determined that the museum had proper title to the Cranach paintings. In May 2019, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to get involved in the case, leaving in place lower court rulings.

They said the Cranach paintings, which originally belonged to the Stroganoff family, were put up for sale in 1931 by the Soviet Union in an illicit auction in Berlin where they were purchased by Goudstikker. After a complicated journey, the paintings were sold to the museum by a Stroganoff family descendant. The museum later restored and preserved the pieces.

"For nearly 50 years, they have been on view at the Norton Simon Museum and will continue to be accessible to the public for years to come," the statement said.

Pawel Sawicki, a spokesperson for the Auschwitz Memorial, said the watercolors of Roma victims that Gottliebova Babbitt was forced to paint by Mengele to document his horrendous experiments and racial research, "must remain in the Memorial" to document the man's crimes. He said these paintings must not be mischaracterized as "Nazi-looted art" because Gottliebova Babbitt painted them against her will as a prisoner and therefore didn't have ownership of the watercolors.

While he understands the family's sentiments, Sawicki said the portraits of Roma and Sinti victims are among the few remaining documents of Mengele's criminal experiments and should be treated as unique documents related to the history of the Auschwitz concentration camp.

"While fully respecting the rights of people who created some of the documents here, we are of the opinion that any loss in the collections of the Memorial will constitute irreparable harm," he said. "… The loss of even the smallest part of the documentation is an irreparable loss and blemish on the memory of the victims of Auschwitz."

California Democrats have a budget deal

By Yue Stella Yu, CalMatters

Davis Enterprise, The · 2026-06-15 · Section: News · 922 words

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California lawmakers adopted a $356 billion state budget late Monday that would largely avoid or delay billions of dollars in social service cuts Gov. Gavin Newsom proposed last month.

Then, the (real) budget negotiations can begin.

The vote was only a formality, because lawmakers are constitutionally required to pass a balanced budget by June 15 each year to continue collecting their pay. They have until the end of the month to strike a deal with Newsom before the new fiscal year starts July 1.

State lawmakers agreed with Newsom's plans to raise taxes on computer software, reduce tax credits to businesses and extend a tax on health care providers.

But in the next two weeks, legislators will also have to settle their differences with Newsom on healthcare cuts, funding for schools and homelessness and more.

Democratic leaders on Monday deemed their legislative spending plan a fiscally sound proposal that would reduce future budget deficits while maintaining some services for low-income Californians.

"We have talked in previous years and again this year about the balance between compassion and fiscal responsibility," said Assemblyman Jesse Gabriel, an Encino Democrat who chairs the Assembly budget committee, during a budget hearing Monday.

"That is at the center of our budget conversation."

Punt and soften healthcare cuts Faced with federal funding cuts under the tax and spending law President Donald Trump signed last year, Newsom proposed several measures to limit healthcare coverage for undocumented immigrants as well as refugees, asylees and human trafficking survivors.

Top legislative Democrats want to delay those cuts by a year while looking for alternatives to soften the impact.

Newsom also wants to raise the monthly Medi-Cal premium undocumented immigrants pay from $30 to $50. But lawmakers prefer waiting him out, proposing to leave the decision to the next governor.

"I don't think it's about Gavin Newsom," said Sen. John Laird, a Santa Cruz Democrat who chairs the budget committee. "It's really about trying to stretch as far as we can in the hope that we don't have to make those cuts."

The Legislature rebuked Newsom's proposal to reinstate stringent Medi-Cal asset tests for seniors and adults with disabilities by July, instead pitching a less restrictive limit to take effect in fiscal year 2027-28. With bipartisan support, the lawmakers also rejected Newsom's proposed cuts to the In-Home Supportive Services program.

They did, however, agree to Newsom's plan to spend $300 million to subsidize private healthcare for low-income Californians.

Restoring some child care, TK-12 money Democratic lawmakers want to add 22,000 state-funded child care slots over the next few years. They also rejected Newsom's proposed reduction of 6,800 state-supported spaces due to declining federal and state funding.

The new slots would prioritize children ages 3 and under. Advocates who applauded the proposal say it would address a gap left unfilled by Newsom's transitional kindergarten expansion to reach 4-year-olds.

Banking on a rosier revenue forecast, state lawmakers proposed $2.7 billion more in funding for TK-12 schools and community colleges than Newsom did in May.

Schools and educators were hoping for more. They wanted the Legislature to reject Newsom's proposal to withhold $3.9 billion in constitutionally guaranteed school money — an accounting mechanism to prevent overpaying schools in case the projected revenue doesn't materialize.

"We demand that the Legislature and the governor follow the law, stop with the gimmicks and the shell games, and fully fund our schools," said David Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association. "Our union is prepared to do whatever it takes to hold them accountable if they don't. Our students deserve no less."

More generous with counties The Legislature's spending plan would give counties more money to step up eligibility checks for Californians applying for food stamps and health care benefits, reviews that are now required under Trump's spending bill.

It would also allocate $125 million to help counties reestablish indigent care — a program serving low-income Californians that largely went away under Obamacare.

State lawmakers also want to set aside $900 million for the state's homelessness fund, whereas Newsom included just $500 million in his proposal.

More revenue, please Newsom proposed three new tax measures and lawmakers are on board with them:

* Applying a sales tax on most company software, like Slack and Microsoft Suites * Capping tax credits big corporations claim * Extending a tax on Medi-Cal health providers, which the state has relied on to qualify for more federal funding.

The proposals come at a time when California voters have rejected most local tax initiatives during the June primary. But Newsom's proposals require no voter approval — just the support of two-thirds of each legislative chamber.

There's still an appetite among lawmakers to make corporations pay up. Senate Democrats had proposed a monthly charge on big employers for having employees enrolled in Medi-Cal, but have now backed away from the plan, instead asking the next governor to pitch "fully viable options" next year.

Save more money for rainy days There's a consensus between the Legislature and the governor to raise the ceiling on the revenue the state can deposit into its rainy day fund. The question is how much. State leaders are constitutionally required to make deposits into the account each year, but the balance cannot exceed 10% of the state's general fund tax revenue

under current law.

Changing that amount would require voter approval. Lawmakers are considering placing a measure on the November ballot that would allow them to sock away more money for lean years. They have a tight deadline of June 25 to settle on what they want to put before voters.

applying for food stamps and health care benefits, reviews that are now required under Trump's spending bill. It would also allocate $125 million to help counties reestablish indigent care — a program serving low-income Californians that largely went away under Obamacare.

State lawmakers also want to set aside $900 million for the state's homelessness fund; Newsom included just $500 million in his proposal.

"For some of the most hard-hit Californians, we know that what we do tonight is going to make a difference in them eating and them sleeping in a home," said Assemblymember Sharon Quirk-Silva, D-Orange County.

State pushes 'first in the nation' grocery label for highlighting non-ultra-processed foods

Andrea Margolis

California consumers may soon see a new label on grocery shelves — one designed to highlight foods that are not ultra-processed.

Assemblyman Jesse Gabriel introduced the bill behind the proposal on Wednesday, according to a press release shared with Fox News Digital. 

The legislation, AB 2244, would establish a "California Certified" seal that manufacturers could place on products that meet standards for not being ultra-processed foods (UPFs).

The legislation would also require grocery stores to prominently display products bearing the seal in high-traffic areas, making it easier for consumers to find those items. 

Gabriel's office described the seal as a "first-in-the-nation" label.

Ultra-processed foods often contain preservatives, additives and flavor enhancers that can contribute to slower weight loss. (iStock)

Not only would the seal allow shoppers to make more informed decisions, but it may also put some pressure on manufacturers to reformulate their products to qualify.

The bill defines ultra-processed foods as those containing certain additives, such as emulsifiers and preservatives, along with high levels of sugar, salt or fat.

"Parents shouldn’t need a Ph.D. in chemistry to understand what they’re feeding their kids," Gabriel said in the release.

"While Washington, D.C., is paralyzed by inaction, California is stepping up to protect our kids and confront the health risks associated with ultra-processed foods."

Gabriel said he hopes to have the bill on Gov. Gavin Newsom's desk by late summer, according to STAT News.

"While Washington, D.C. is paralyzed by inaction, California is stepping up to protect our kids and confront the health risks associated with ultra-processed foods," said Gabriel, seen right. (PATRICK T. FALLON/AFP via Getty Images)

Speaking to Fox News Digital, Gabriel said the bill "provides a market-based solution to address the dangers of ultra-processed foods."

He added, "[It] strengthens consumer choice, drives innovation and promotes healthier options across the food supply – without banning any products."

Gabriel told Politico the bill is the "next logical step" in addressing ultra-processed foods in grocery stores.

"But we’re doing it in a way that strengthens consumer choice and encourages innovation," he added.

The proposed "California Certified" label under AB 2244 aims to give consumers a clearer way to distinguish non-ultra-processed foods while browsing grocery store shelves. (Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty Images)

Though the definition of UPFs is debated, they're generally understood to be foods that undergo multiple industrial processes.

These processes make them "stabilized for consumption," Dr. Jeffrey Kraft, a bariatric surgeon at Hackensack Meridian Palisades Medical Center in New Jersey, previously told Fox News Digital.

"Processed foods are not natural foods," he said. "They've gone through a factory or been chemically changed so they last longer on the shelf."

Kraft added, "They are almost always combined with other unhealthy things, like high fructose corn syrup, emulsifiers and hydrogenated oils."

The legislation seeks to balance consumer choice with industry innovation by keeping participation voluntary for manufacturers. (iStock)

The lack of a "clear universal standard" for what a UPF is "opens the door for bureaucrats to decide what's real," said California-based chef Andrew Gruel.

"I am all for transparency, and encourage it, but that should come from clear and honest ingredient labeling, not some pay-to-play subjective stamp that reduces foods into a government label," Gruel told Fox News Digital. 

He added, "I am confident this label will get hijacked by the large food manufacturers and Doritos will be considered a non-processed food by some weird definition, just like chips used to be labeled heart healthy."

Fox News Digital reached out to the Consumer Brands Association for comment.

加州推全美首个州级食品标签,食品业或迎来大洗牌

洛城24小时   旧金山快报   Monday 2026/09/28 19:58 PM

收藏

分享

Facebook

新浪微博

2026年9月28日，加州州长加文·纽森签署了由众议员Jesse Gabriel提出的AB 2244法案，创建了全美第一个州级“非超加工认证”（Non-Ultraprocessed Certified）印章。

KTLA截图


这个印章的灵感直接来自USDA Organic有机认证标签。正如Gabriel在声明中所说：“就像USDA有机标签一样，这个新印章将为消费者提供清晰、可信的信息，帮助他们更容易找到不含有害添加剂、更健康的食品。家长们不需要化学博士学位，就能搞懂自己给孩子吃的是什么。 ”

一、这个标签长什么样？怎么拿到？

AB 2244建立了一套由加州公共卫生部（CDPH）监管的认证流程。食品制造商需要通过CDPH认可的认证机构，才能在产品上使用“Non-Ultraprocessed Certified”印章。

具体时间表已经很明确：

2029年6月1日前，CDPH必须完成认证机构的认可工作，并建立认证产品的公开目录。

每三年至少重新认证一次，产品才能继续使用印章。

大型杂货零售商——定义为销售超过25种非超加工认证产品类型、年销售额超过1000万美元的零售商——必须通过标识牌、物理分区或其他视觉提示，在店内明确标示出认证产品。

二、什么算“超加工”？定义有讲究

这个标签的判定依据，是加州去年通过的另一部里程碑法律——AB 1264《真实食物健康儿童法案》所建立的“超加工食品”法定定义。

这一定义目前已编纂为加州健康与安全法典第104661条。它规定，任何含有以下成分的食品或饮料均属于超加工食品：表面活性剂、稳定剂和增稠剂、推进剂、充气剂和气体、色素、乳化剂等。

换句话说，含有染料、增味剂、非糖甜味剂和某些其他添加剂的产品，拿不到这个印章。

这套定义参考了国际营养学界广泛使用的NOVA分类体系，但加州的版本更为具体，包含了更多关于禁止使用的添加剂和营养平衡的细节。

印章可能的图样，图源：Jesse Gabriel办公室



三、为什么加州要这么做？数据触目惊心

超加工食品已经占据了美国人餐桌的半壁江山。根据美国公共卫生杂志（AJPH）2026年发表的研究，超加工食品提供了约53%的成年人能量摄入和62%的儿童能量摄入。

而超加工食品的危害，正在被越来越多的科学研究证实。

心血管和代谢风险。 同一项AJPH研究分析了1999至2018年间近48,000名成年人的数据，发现每增加10%的超加工食品能量摄入，就与更高的BMI、糖化血红蛋白、舒张压相关，代谢综合征风险增加7%，癌症风险增加5%，全因死亡率风险增加4%。即便在全面调整营养质量后，这些关联仍然显著。

痴呆风险翻倍。 哈佛大学2026年6月发表的研究追踪了5,370名老年人近九年，发现摄入超加工食品最多的人群，患痴呆症的风险比摄入最少的人群高出58%，认知障碍（非痴呆）的风险高出46%。

胃肠道癌症。 2026年6月发表在AACR期刊上的研究显示，超加工食品摄入与结直肠癌的关联最为一致，高摄入人群的风险增加10%至30%。

四、行业炸了：支持与反对激烈交锋

AB 2244在州参众两院获得了罕见的两党全票支持——参议院32票赞成、0票反对，众议院72票赞成、0票反对。

但行业内部并不平静。

支持者阵营包括环境工作组（EWG），该组织联合发起了AB 2244，称其为“开创性的法律”。加州移民政策中心等公共健康倡导者也力挺该法案。

反对者阵营则包括拥有独立认证项目的“Non-UPF Verified”组织，他们曾在法案签署前敦促纽森否决，理由是该法案的认证标准没有将加工方法纳入考量。

美国国家谷物食品协会（NCC）也表达了强烈担忧。他们认为，基于加工方式的分类系统——包括NOVA框架—— “在科学上存在缺陷且具有误导性” ，因为这些系统忽略了营养密度和蛋白质质量。NCC警告说，一块裹面包糠的鸡胸肉——富含优质完整蛋白质、铁、锌和B族维生素——仅仅因为达到了“加工”门槛，就被与糖果或汽水归为同一类。

法律和商业层面的担忧同样存在。Morrison Foerster律所的律师Brian Sylvester指出：“我们不确定消费者会如何回应这些标签。 ”还有专家警告，当各州各自建立不同的认证标准，而联邦层面仍在制定统一定义时，食品公司面临的合规复杂性将进一步增加。

五、写在最后

一个标签的力量，可能比一部法律更大。

USDA Organic用几十年时间，让“有机”从边缘概念变成了766亿美元的市场，改变了整个农业产业链。“非超加工认证”可能正在走同样的路。

纽森在签署声明中说得很清楚：“我们应该做的是医疗保健，而不是‘疾病护理’。预防疾病远比寻找和负担治疗更为可取。 ”

Gabriel的话更直接：“家长们不需要化学博士学位，就能搞懂自己给孩子吃的是什么。 ”

但对于食品行业来说，这不仅仅是一个标签的问题。这是一个关于重新定义什么是“食物”的问题。当科学证据越来越指向超加工食品与痴呆、癌症、心血管疾病的关联，当消费者开始用钱包投票，当各州和联邦政府竞相建立标准——食品行业面临的选择只有一个：要么重新配方，要么被市场淘汰。

2029年，第一批认证印章将出现在加州的货架上。到那时，你拿起一包零食，或许只需要扫一眼包装，就能知道它到底是不是“真食物”。

Nora LaTorre on why school lunch is the biggest lever for children's health

Show: American Dish

Episode: Nora LaTorre on why school lunch is the biggest lever for children's health

Date: 2026-04-29

Duration: 57:32

Hosts: Helena Bottemiller Evich

Guests: Nora La Torre

Episode description (names Gabriel)

Schools are the largest restaurant chain in America, bigger than Subway, Starbucks, and McDonald's combined. Nearly 100,000 locations, 30 million kids, and roughly 7 billion meals a year. Right now, the lion’s share of the calories served through this system are ultra-processed at a time when there’s growing concern about chronic diseases among children.

Nora LaTorre is the CEO of Eat Real, a nonprofit that's transforming school meals scale — certifying school districts against doctor-developed standards and helping food service leaders pivot to fresher, more local, more scratch-cooked food. Since 2019, the organization has grown from one district in one state to more than a million kids across 21 states. This expansion has put LaTorre and her organization at the center of an active debate about what the future of school meals should look like in the U.S.

Highlights:

– How Eat Real's certification model works and what the two-year journey looks like for school districts

– Why better food means more kids eat school lunch (which means more revenue)

– The story behind California's AB 1264, which passed with near-unanimous bipartisan support

– LaTorre’s take on how federal preemption is a serious threat to food policy progress

– What the MAHA moment means for school food

– What parents can do to support change at their local school

– The infrastructure gap: transforming school food nationally could require tens of billions in kitchen investment

Political Playback: California Capitol News You Might Have Missed

by California Black Media Jun 2, 2026Jun 2, 2026

By Bo Tefu and Antonio Ray Harvey, California Black Media 

No Taxes on Reparations Payments: Asm. Tina McKinnor’s Bill Moves Closer to Becoming State Law  

A California bill that would prevent reparations payments from being taxed by the state is moving closer to becoming law after advancing out of the Assembly with bipartisan support.

Assembly Bill (AB) 2186, introduced by Assemblymember Tina McKinnor (D-Inglewood), would exempt future reparations benefits from California personal income taxes if the payments are approved through federal, state or local reparations programs. The measure now heads to the California Senate for further consideration.

The bill would apply to taxable years beginning Jan. 1, 2027, through Jan. 1, 2032. Under the proposal, reparations benefits could include direct cash payments, grants, trust distributions, debt forgiveness and other forms of financial compensation tied to reparations efforts.

“For generations, descendants of formerly enslaved people have been denied both justice and economic opportunity,” McKinnor said in a statement announcing the bill. “Reparations are meant to repair harm, not be partially taken back through taxation.”

Supporters say the legislation is intended to ensure recipients receive the full value of any reparations payments approved in the future. Under current California law, some reparations-related payments could potentially be treated as taxable income.

The proposal comes as California continues examining recommendations from the state’s Reparations Task Force, which studied the lasting impacts of slavery and discrimination on Black Californians. The task force released recommendations in 2023 that included proposals related to housing discrimination, education, economic inequality and financial compensation.

McKinnor said California should prepare for future reparations programs by establishing tax protections ahead of time.

“California is actively preparing for the implementation of reparations programs,” McKinnor said. “We must ensure that recipients receive the full benefit of these efforts.”

The Assemblymember also framed the measure as part of a broader effort to provide tax relief for Californians facing economic pressures and high living costs.

The bill received bipartisan support on the Assembly Floor, passing with a 58-17 vote, before advancing to the Senate, where lawmakers will debate the proposal. 

If the Senate passes AB 2186, the bill will be sent to Gov. Gavin Newsom’s desk for final approval.

Gov. Newsom Signs Election Security Bill; Asm. Bryan Praises Move

Gov. Gavin Newsom signed legislation on May 29 aimed at strengthening protections for California elections, arguing that the measure is necessary to guard against voter intimidation, election interference and unauthorized access to voting systems.

The new law, Senate Bill (SB) 73, authored by state Sens. Sabrina Cervantes (D-Riverside) and Tom Umberg (D-Santa Ana), expands existing safeguards for election workers, ballots, voter rolls and election infrastructure. The legislation comes amid ongoing national debates over election administration and voting security.

“California will not allow our elections to be commandeered by political intimidation, abuse of power, or chaotic interference from extremists chasing conspiracy theories. This law protects voters, election workers, and the integrity of the democratic process from election-deniers who want to undermine democracy,” Newsom said.

Under SB 73, unauthorized access to voter rolls, voter lists and certified voting technology by law enforcement agencies — including federal authorities — is prohibited unless authorized by a court order or tied to a specific investigation under California election law. The measure also restricts peace officers from interfering with election administration except during public safety emergencies and requires the California Department of Justice to issue guidance to county election officials on responding to law enforcement requests involving ballot-processing locations.

Assemblymember Isaac Bryan (D-Ladera Heights), vice chair of the California Legislative Black Caucus (CLBC), praised Newsom for signing into law legislation that protects state elections, ballots, and election workers from political and federal interference.

“We have seen Republicans steal ballots and intimidate voters. Here in California, we believe in the power of the people, and voter suppression efforts will not work here. We will fight to protect Democracy at all costs,” Bryan told California Black Media (CBM).

The law further increases penalties for the unlawful removal or seizure of voted ballots. Individuals who knowingly take voted ballots from election officials can face fines, imprisonment, or both.

“Senate Bill 73 is a direct response to efforts by officials in the Trump Administration and local elected leaders to undermine our democracy piece by piece,” Cervantes said. “The enactment of SB 73 protects Californians’ sacred right to vote free from fear of intimidation or interference, and safeguards the essential integrity of elections in California.”

Supporters, including the League of Women Voters of California, praised the measure as a safeguard against federal interference in election administration. 

“This landmark law erects essential barriers against unauthorized federal access to voting systems, voter rolls, and polling places – protections that are more vital now than ever,” said Dora Rose, deputy director of the organization.

The legislation builds on a series of election-related measures California has enacted since 2019, including universal vote-by-mail, expanded protections against voter intimidation, and cybersecurity investments designed to protect election infrastructure.

In Wake of San Diego Shooting, Gov. Newson Announces $300 Million to Protect Non-Profits, Faith-Based Orgs

California is investing more than $300 million to help protect nonprofit organizations and places of worship from hate crimes and violent attacks, Gov. Gavin Newsom announced May 28. 

The new funding comes in the wake of the recent tragic shooting at the Islamic Center of San Diego.

The governor’s office said the state is awarding an additional $80 million through the California Nonprofit Security Grant Program to strengthen safety measures at 343 nonprofit organizations statewide, including 228 faith-based groups. The latest funding round brings California’s total investment in nonprofit and faith-based security programs to more than $300 million since the initiative launched in 2015.

The announcement comes after the May 18 shooting at the Islamic Center of San Diego, which prompted renewed concerns about rising threats targeting religious and community organizations across the country.

“Hate and violence have no place in California,” said Newsom in a statement. “By investing in critical security upgrades, we are leading the nation in protecting places of worship and high-risk communities, strengthening preparedness, and ensuring every Californian can gather safely and without fear.”

Most of the new funding, approximately $76 million, will go directly toward security improvements, including reinforced doors and gates, alarm systems, surveillance systems, high-intensity lighting and emergency preparedness enhancements. The remaining $4 million will support technical assistance and program administration through the California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services, known as Cal OES.

State officials said the grant program has expanded in recent years as nonprofits, cultural institutions and faith communities face increasing threats of hate-motivated violence. The program is now the largest grant initiative administered by Cal OES.

Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), who authored legislation establishing the program, said the grants are an important tool for protecting vulnerable communities.

“At a moment of rising threats, we are doubling down on our commitment to protect our most vulnerable communities,” Gabriel said.

California officials also announced victim support services for individuals and families impacted by the San Diego mosque shooting. The California Victim Compensation Board said eligible victims and witnesses may qualify for assistance covering medical costs, mental health treatment, lost wages and funeral expenses.

The state’s revised budget proposal also includes an additional $40 million to continue supporting organizations facing heightened threats and hate-related violence.

Asm. Isaac Bryan’s Environmental Reparations Bill Passes on Assembly Floor 

On May 26, the California State Assembly passed legislation aimed at providing direct financial assistance to families harmed by pollution tied to a major urban oil field in South Los Angeles.

Assembly Bill (AB) 1661, introduced by Assemblymember Isaac Bryan (D-Ladera Heights), cleared the Assembly floor with a 44-10 vote after lawmakers concluded debate on the measure.

The bill would direct money from a community repair fund toward families who suffered negative health effects from living near what Bryan described as the state’s largest toxic urban oil field. The repair fund was created under legislation approved two years ago that shut down the oil field and required polluters to contribute financially to community recovery efforts.

“All this bill does is allocate resources from that repair fund and direct cash assistance to families that have had negative health impacts as a result of living next to that oil field,” said Bryan during remarks on the Assembly floor.

Bryan called the proposal “the largest environmental reparations opportunity for South LA” and told lawmakers the bill had not received opposition during the legislative process.

The legislation is part of California’s broader push to address environmental justice concerns in communities historically exposed to industrial pollution. South Los Angeles residents and environmental advocates have long raised concerns about health risks linked to oil drilling operations located near homes, schools and parks.

Supporters say the measure represents a new approach to environmental accountability by ensuring that communities affected by pollution directly benefit from funds collected from responsible companies.

After debate concluded, Assembly leadership opened the roll call vote, and the measure passed with majority support from lawmakers.

AB 1661 now moves to the Senate for further review. 

Sen. Akilah Weber Pierson’s Bill to Label Sugary Drinks Passes Senate 

The California State Senate has passed legislation that would require chain restaurants to identify beverages containing high levels of added sugar, advancing a measure supporters say is aimed at improving consumer awareness and public health.

Senate Bill 869, introduced by Sen. Akilah Weber Pierson (D-San Diego), would require restaurants to clearly label drinks containing more than 50 percent of the recommended daily value of added sugars on menus and menu boards.

The bill now heads to the California Assembly for further consideration.

“Consumers deserve clear and honest information about what they are putting into their bodies,” said Weber Pierson in a statement following the Senate vote.

Weber Pierson, who is a medical doctor, said many sugary beverages contain excessive levels of added sugar that contribute to serious long-term health conditions, including diabetes, obesity and heart disease.

Supporters of the proposal say the labeling requirements would help customers make more informed decisions when ordering drinks at restaurants and fast-food establishments.

Public health advocates have increasingly focused on sugar-sweetened beverages as a major contributor to diet-related illnesses in the United States. Research has linked excessive sugar intake to higher risks of Type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, fatty liver disease and dental problems.

According to advocates backing the measure, some restaurant beverages contain more than an entire day’s recommended amount of added sugar in a single serving.

The legislation is sponsored by the Center for Science in the Public Interest (CSPI), which says states are increasingly stepping in to strengthen food safety and nutrition transparency policies as federal regulatory efforts slow.

“California lawmakers are continuing to lead on food safety and nutrition transparency,” said Dr. DeAnna Nara, campaign manager for CSPI. 

California Birth Rate Falls Below “Replacement Level”

California’s birth rate has fallen to its lowest level on record, dropping well below the threshold needed to maintain population growth and signaling a major demographic shift that could reshape the state’s economy, schools, workforce and political influence in the decades ahead.

A new report from the Public Policy Institute of California (PPIC) found that the state’s total fertility rate declined from 2.21 children per woman in 2007 to 1.48 in 2023 — far below the “replacement level” of 2.1 children per woman needed to sustain a population without migration.

“The significance of falling so far below replacement level cannot be overstated,” the report states. “It signals a fundamental shift in the state’s demographic trajectory.”

Researchers project that by 2038, deaths will outnumber births in California, ending a long period in which natural population growth helped drive the state’s expansion. Without increased immigration or a rebound in birth rates, population growth could stagnate or decline.
The report found that declining birth rates among younger women are largely responsible for the trend. Birth rates among women ages 20 to 24 fell by 54% between 2008 and 2023, while teen birth rates dropped nearly 90% since 1991. Researchers described the decline in teen births as a major public health success.

Birth rates declined across all racial and ethnic groups, with the steepest drops occurring among Latina women, particularly those born outside the United States.

The phenomenon is not unique to California. Birth rates have fallen in all 50 states, and every state now has fertility rates below replacement level.

“The decline in birth rates is one of the most important developments of recent decades and will structure policy debates for decades to come,” the report concludes.

Among the most immediate impacts could be shrinking school enrollment. PPIC projects California’s public school population will decline by roughly 630,000 students by 2038, while longer-term concerns include labor shortages, an aging population and the potential loss of congressional representation.

Es oficial: desde el 1° de julio en California entró en vigor la prohibición de las armas Glock

Redacción Clarín

Una ley prohíbe, desde el 1 de julio de 2026, la venta de armas cortas que cuenten con un dispositivo que permite convertirlas en “ametralladora”. La disposición abarca al estado de California y había sido firmada por el gobernador Gavin Newsom el año pasado.

Propuesta por el asambleísta Jesse Gabriel, la ley AB-1127 considera como “ametralladora” a cualquier arma que mediante un mecanismo conocido como Glock Switch o Pistol Converter puede transformarse en automática.

Según el texto legal ya no podrá venderse “cualquier pistola semiautomática que posea una barra de gatillo cruciforme y pueda cambiarse fácilmente a mano o con herramientas domésticas comunes en una ametralladora mediante la instalación o el acoplamiento que reemplace la placa posterior de la corredera”.

Esto afectará, en concreto a varios modelos de la pistola más popular del país, la Glock, como 17, 19, 26 y 48. Los modelos G18 y G18C, que también poseen el dispositivo, solo pueden entregarse a la policía y las fuerzas armadas.

Una tragedia como origen de la ley

El principal antecedente de la ley es una tragedia ocurrida en 2022, cuando Greg “Najee” Grimes fue asesinado en un club nocturno de Sacramento, por un tirador que utilizó una Glock modificada. Entonces, disparó once tiros rápidos contra la multitud, siete de los cuales impactaron en Grimes.

Algunos modelos de Glock pueden transformarse en "ametralladoras". Foto: Bloomberg.

La popularidad de las Glock ha sido comparada con las de los coches Honda Civic en un artículo del New York Post. Curiosamente, la exvicepresidente y excandidata demócrata Kamala Harris admitió en una entrevista, realizada en 2024, que tenía una Glock para uso personal, aunque, aclaró, no modificada.

De todas formas, Harris y otros propietarios de Glock quedan al margen de la legislación porque esta solo abarca a los futuros compradores. La ley también exige que los vendedores de armas de fuego también deberán realizar una capacitación integral, diseñada para ayudarlos a identificar a los clientes que podrían representar un peligro para sí mismos o para los demás.

El New York Post se pregunta “¿Qué constituye realmente un comportamiento sospechoso? ¿Quién determina el nivel de estabilidad mental en un mostrador de venta al público? ¿Qué protecciones existen para las personas comunes que son señaladas erróneamente debido a prejuicios personales?”.

El otro aspecto controvertido es que al aplicarse solo a las nuevas pistolas, y no prhobir la tenencia, millones de residentes de California podrán seguir utilizando este tipo de Glock sin ningún problema. Muchos de ellos, seguramente, se dedican a actividades delictivas o son personas potencialmente peligrosas.

En las Glock un pequeño dispositivo permite efectuar disparos de manera continua. Foto: AFP.

La publicación considera que California vuelve a convertirse en un “laboratorio” sobre las controvertidas leyes sobre tenencia de armas de fuego, algo sustentado en la 2ª Enmienda de la Constitución. Y afirma que si los demócratas obtienen mayoría en el Congreso podrían realizar un proyecto de ley similar, pero a nivel nacional.

When it comes to ultra-processed food, research shows that Black Americans pay a steeper health price. Now California is betting a simple label can help. Gov. Gavin Newsom signed Assembly Bill 2244 on Sept. 28, creating a first-in-the-nation label that marks foods as not ultra-processed, the governor’s office announced.

The seal is voluntary for manufacturers, but according to Food Dive, large grocery stores must prominently display items with the state label when they carry at least 25 products. Don’t look for it yet, though. The state health department will not even roll out phase one until June 2029. The bill’s author, Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), modeled it on the USDA Organic label.

“Parents shouldn’t need a Ph.D. in chemistry to understand what they’re feeding their kids,” Gabriel said in a statement released by the governor’s office.

Under California law, a food is generally considered ultraprocessed if it contains additives such as artificial flavors, colors, or emulsifiers and is high in saturated fat, sodium, or added sugar, or contains an artificial sweetener. Think soda, chips, sugary cereals and snack cakes.

In a large heart study published this year, ultraprocessed food made up 32% of daily food servings among Black participants, compared with 30% for white participants, TCTMD reports. For every 10% rise in ultraprocessed food intake, Black participants saw a 12.3% higher risk of cardiovascular disease, versus 7.9% for non-Black participants.

The heart study’s researchers pointed to two factors: food companies target more junk-food ads at Black communities, and many Black neighborhoods have fewer places to buy fresh, less-processed food. The ad part is well documented. A 2022 report from the Rudd Center at UConn found candy, sugary drinks, snacks, and cereals made up three-quarters of Black-targeted TV ad spending in 2021, up from about half in 2017.

Not everyone welcomed the seal. Food and manufacturing industry groups, including the Consumer Brands Association, which represents major packaged-food companies, opposed the bill. Navigating a grocery store has never been simple, but California just made it a little easier. Gov. Products that want to carry the seal must meet the state’s definition of non-ultra-processed.

California’s definition, which mirrors the one used in the state’s school lunch law, identifies a food as ultra-processed if it contains certain additives like emulsifiers, flavors, or preservatives and is also high in sugar, sodium, or fat, or contains non-nutritive sweeteners. Under that standard, about a third of packaged foods will qualify for the seal, according to University of Pennsylvania nutrition researcher Alyssa Moran.

How the “California Certified” Seal Actually Works

The certification process is modeled after the USDA Organic label. Under the new law, the California Department of Public Health will accredit agents to certify food products as non-ultra-processed no later than June 1, 2028, according to the LA Times. Manufacturers must apply to use the seal and renew that certification every three years, according to The Independent.

Grocery stores will also play a role under the new law. Newsom framed the signing as a move with reach beyond state lines, saying California was “clearing the way for the rest of the country to follow,” according to The Independent. Support for the law extends beyond California. A poll conducted by Politico and Public First found that more than 60 percent of Americans favor removing ultra-processed foods from store shelves, including 73 percent of Donald Trump voters and 66 percent of Kamala Harris voters, making it one of the rare health policy issues with strong backing on both sides of the aisle.

The health case behind the law is also significant. Ultra-processed foods are linked to chronic diseases including obesity, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and cancer. Nutrition researcher Alyssa Moran said during a press call that ultra-processed foods are contributing to roughly 1,400 American deaths each day. Among children specifically, ultra-processed foods account for roughly 62 percent of daily calories, Moran noted on the press call.

A new California law will lead to the expansion of organized sports programming as a form of rehabilitation for people incarcerated in state prisons.

The Second Chance Sports Act (AB 2204), authored by Assemblymembers Jesse Gabriel and Isaac Bryan, was signed into law by Gov. Gavin Newsom last month and takes effect on January 1, 2027. It will allow the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation (CDCR) to work with professional sports teams and leagues, the University of California and California State University systems, community colleges and private universities to expand sports programming in prisons.

“Structured sports programs can help build discipline, teamwork, and accountability,” said Assemblymember Gabriel. “It can potentially reduce disciplinary problems and recidivism and promote rehabilitation.” He went on to explain that those improvements would thereby support correctional staff, as well.

Assemblymember Bryan believes the new law will help reduce violence inside prisons and crime after people return to their communities: “Anyone who has played a team sport understands the positive impacts it can have on a person. It can reduce depression and anxiety and promote positive social interactions.”

Weightlifting used to be a staple of California prisons. Like many sports, studies show that weightlifting promotes health by reducing stress and violence, strengthening the heart and cardiovascular system and lowering risks of heart attack and stroke. It also boosts metabolism, helping to lower weight and control diabetes and other chronic ailments and can sharpen cognitive skills. During the 1970s, body building champions Lou Ferrigno and Arnold Schwarzenegger toured California prisons and youth facilities to promote the sport as a way for incarcerated people to cope with prisons and find purpose.

All of that came to an end in the mid-1990’s when the myth of the Superpredator, created by criminologist John DiIulio, began taking hold in the media and in public consciousness. It characterized a generation of young Black and brown men as unusually violent and remorseless. The myth led to devastating changes in criminal justice policy, including the federal Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act and California’s “Three Strikes and You’re Out” law, both passed in 1994.

By August of the same year, the California Senate passed Senate Bill 22, which aimed to remove weight training programs from the state’s prisons. Senator Steve Peace, one of the bill’s authors said, “Allowing prisoners to become body builders could create human weapons who might eventually harm police after release.” CDCR officially banned weightlifting programs in prison in 1998.

Weightlifting was not the only victim; the super predator myth led to a reduction of athletic programs throughout prisons, which contributed to a rising prison health care crisis that continues today.

When Schwarzenegger became Governor in 2004, he suggested bringing weightlifting back. “As you know, in the 1970s I used to go around and visit all the prisons and youth facilities in California to promote weight training for inmates,” he told the media. “But I don’t want to put them back if people don’t want them back, if that is not what people want.” The California Correctional Peace Officers Association (CCPOA) and crime victims were against it, so the Governor backed down.

Today, the CCPOA was one of the biggest supporters of AB 2204 According to CCPOA President Neil Flood, “California’s correctional officers see firsthand the difference that meaningful programming makes for the people in our facilities and for the safety of our communities. When incarcerated people have opportunities to develop discipline, self-esteem and teamwork, everyone benefits,” he said in an August 31, 2026 letter to the legislature.

Even the California Police Chiefs Association (CPCA) endorsed the bill. “This bill is about promoting what works to make communities safer. Structured sports can build discipline and skills and help reduce reoffending,” said CPCA President Sean Thuilliez.

Over the years, California has eased up on weightlifting bans, making exceptions for certain therapeutic, rehabilitative, and vocational circumstances. Weight training equipment, for example, is part of the training program for incarcerated people assigned to firefighting. Today, at least 31 states across the country, including New York, New Jersey, and Colorado, allow weightlifting in prisons.

Enhancing sports in prison by bringing back weightlifting could potentially reverse other harms caused by mass warehousing and the prison system’s broken health care system, marking a definitive end to an era of racist labeling of incarcerated Black and brown men.

Crime rates are down in California and recidivism rates are lower. The prison population has dipped below 90,000 for the first time in decades and is projected to drop further. And California is now on a trajectory to humanize its prisons.

The Second Chance Sports Act, with its rehabilitative mission, could eventually give everyone a second chance. Incarcerated individuals could improve their health, strengthening their bones and their hearts. Some could even get a second chance at freedom, participating with major league teams or becoming personal trainers. Politicians, including those who once believed in the myth of the superpredator, could also get a second chance to correct some of the harms from their racist past. They have paved the way to bring all sports programming back, including weight training, and to build community and camaraderie and support a healthier and more humane California prison system.

LA NACION

El gobernador Gavin Newsom firmó la AB 1807, una norma que impide utilizar propiedades y recursos estatales para preparar o ejecutar operativos de control migratorio federal. La legislación también establece mecanismos de identificación, señalización, documentación y reporte de posibles intervenciones.

Qué cambia con la AB 1807 en California

  • La legislación fue impulsada por los asambleístas Juan Carrillo y Jesse Gabriel y forma parte de un paquete de medidas firmado por Newsom.
  • La ley también contempla disposiciones relacionadas con centros privados de detención, procedimientos policiales y vehículos empleados durante arrestos o traslados.

Uno de los principales puntos de la AB 1807 es la obligación de identificar los inmuebles públicos que fueron utilizados o pueden ser empleados en el futuro para operaciones migratorias.

El Departamento de Servicios Generales (DGS, por sus siglas en inglés) y las distintas agencias estatales deberán coordinar esa tarea.

Una vez identificados esos espacios, las autoridades tendrán que implementar medidas para impedir accesos no autorizados.

Entre ellas se encuentran la colocación de barreras físicas y de carteles estandarizados que informen sobre las restricciones establecidas por la legislación.

La Oficina del Fiscal General de California tendrá a su cargo el diseño de la señalización correspondiente y deberá poner los modelos a disposición para su descarga gratuita.

De esta manera, las distintas dependencias podrán utilizar un formato común para informar sobre la prohibición.

“California toma medidas para fortalecer la transparencia, la rendición de cuentas y la supervisión en materia de control migratorio en nuestro estado”, dijo Newsom en un comunicado.

“Se trata de asumir la responsabilidad donde el gobierno federal ha fallado a nuestras comunidades”, agregó.

Las agencias deberán registrar posibles operativos migratorios

La AB 1807 también incorpora obligaciones de documentación, por lo que las agencias estatales deberán establecer procedimientos para dejar constancia escrita de cualquier intento o utilización efectiva de una propiedad estatal por parte de agentes federales vinculados con la aplicación de las leyes migratorias.

Los registros deberán incluir, cuando corresponda, fotografías o videos como evidencia. Además, las dependencias tendrán que informar de manera inmediata a la Oficina del Fiscal General sobre estos episodios, de acuerdo con los procedimientos establecidos por la nueva norma.

Otro componente de la legislación es la información sobre derechos; los empleados, inquilinos y trabajadores de seguridad de los recintos estatales tendrán que recibir materiales educativos que expliquen sus derechos frente al ingreso de agentes federales a esas instalaciones.

El paquete firmado por Gavin Newsom incluye otras medidas

La AB 1807 no es la única medida promulgada por Newsom. El paquete legislativo también establece un impuesto del 25% para los centros privados de detención que operen en California.

Otra disposición prohíbe que las fuerzas del orden utilicen guantes capaces de producir descargas eléctricas durante actividades de aplicación de la ley. Además, se establecen requisitos para identificar de forma clara los vehículos de alquiler empleados en arrestos o traslados.

Tras la firma del paquete, Newsom sostuvo que el Estado no puede determinar la política federal, pero sí establecer las condiciones bajo las cuales determinadas actividades se desarrollan dentro de su territorio.

Según su declaración, las nuevas leyes buscan que las actuaciones vinculadas con el control migratorio estén sujetas a las normas estatales y cuenten con mecanismos de supervisión.

“Se trata de dar un paso al frente; dar un paso al frente donde el gobierno federal le ha fallado a nuestras diversas comunidades”, dijo el gobernador.

“California continuará protegiendo a nuestra gente, haciendo cumplir el estado de derecho y dejando en claro que el gobierno federal debe operar en nuestro estado con la rendición de cuentas y la transparencia que todos merecemos”, reiteró.

California will prohibit stores and online sellers from selling over-the-counter diet pills and dietary supplements marketed for weight loss or muscle building to anyone under 18 without a prescription. Gov. Gavin Newsom signed the measure, Assembly Bill 2030, on Sept. 28 as part of a package of health bills that also created a state label for foods that are not ultra-processed.

The governor's office said nearly 1 in 10 adolescents have used these products and that young people who use over-the-counter diet pills are six times more likely than nonusers to be diagnosed with an eating disorder within three years. California is the second state to restrict these sales to minors, following New York, whose law took effect in April 2024, NutraIngredients reported.

The law does not remove these products from store shelves, and adults can still buy them.

Rules Stores and Online Sellers Must Follow

The law, written by Assemblymember Josh Lowenthal, a Long Beach Democrat, bars anyone from selling, offering to sell, or giving away as a promotion an over-the-counter diet pill or a dietary supplement for weight loss or muscle building to a person under 18 in California. Minors with a prescription for the product are exempt.

Stores must ask for valid identification when they cannot reasonably judge whether a buyer is under 18. Online and delivery sellers must confirm a buyer's age either by checking the buyer's name, birth date, and address against a commercially available database or by using a shipping method that requires an adult to sign for the package, according to the chaptered bill text for Assembly Bill 2030.

Businesses that break the law face civil penalties of up to $500 per violation. The state attorney general, county counsel, or city attorneys can go to court to stop violations. The penalties apply to sellers, not to young people who try to buy the products, and the law does not carry criminal penalties.

The governor's announcement did not list an effective date for AB 2030. Under California's standard rule, laws passed without an urgency clause take effect on Jan. 1 of the following year, which in this case is Jan. 1, 2027.

The same package included AB 2244, a separate law by Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel that creates a voluntary "Non-Ultraprocessed Certified" seal for qualifying foods, overseen by the California Department of Public Health.

Health Risks Behind the Ban

Dietary supplements do not need Food and Drug Administration approval before they are sold, and the FDA warns that products sold for weight loss and bodybuilding are among those most likely to contain hidden drug ingredients. The governor's office said these products can carry dangerous side effects, are often mislabeled, and may contain harmful substances such as steroids. Many weight-loss products contain stimulants, laxatives, or diuretics, which can cause a rapid heart rate, high blood pressure, dehydration, and digestive problems.

For teens, the larger concern is the link to disordered eating. Adolescence is a period of rapid growth, and restricting food can affect bone development, hormones, and heart health. Research has found that young people who use diet pills or laxatives for weight control are more likely to later be diagnosed with an eating disorder, though that research shows an association rather than proof that the products cause the disorders.

Muscle-building supplements raise separate concerns, especially for teen boys and young athletes who may take them to meet appearance or sports pressures.

Supporters and Industry Critics

Public health advocates praised the law. "Today, Newsom signed historic public health legislation banning the sale of certain over-the-counter supplements to minors," said Jensen Jose, senior regulatory counsel at the Center for Science in the Public Interest, according to Nutrition Insight.

The supplement industry opposed the measure. Steve Mister, president and CEO of the Council for Responsible Nutrition, said protecting young people from eating disorders "is an important objective that we share." He argued that the goal calls for policies "grounded in evidence" rather than "broad restrictions that cast suspicion on lawful products without establishing that those restrictions will address the problem."

Daniel Fabricant, president and CEO of the Natural Products Association, said that when states create their own restrictions for products already covered by federal rules, "the result is an increasingly unworkable patchwork of conflicting requirements for manufacturers, retailers and consumers."

Warning Signs and Help for Families

Teens who play sports with weight classes or who spend a lot of time on fitness and diet content online may see more marketing for these products.

Parents may notice empty pill bottles, packages from online supplement sellers, skipped meals, secretive eating, rapid weight changes, excessive exercise, or an intense focus on body size. Mood changes, dizziness, fainting, missed periods, or a racing heartbeat are reasons to see a doctor.

Calm, open conversations tend to work better than confrontation. Ask what your teen has seen online, and focus on health and energy rather than weight. Pediatricians can screen for eating disorders and check heart rate and blood pressure.

Help is available. The National Alliance for Eating Disorders offers referrals to care and free support groups through its helpline at 866-662-1235. Fainting, chest pain, confusion, or a very slow or irregular heartbeat requires emergency care.

Key Questions Answered

What does California's new law do?

It bans selling over-the-counter diet pills and dietary supplements for weight loss or muscle building to anyone under 18 without a prescription.

When does the law take effect?

The governor's office did not list a date. California laws without an urgency clause generally take effect on Jan. 1 of the following year, which would be Jan. 1, 2027.

Does the law apply to online sales?

Yes. Online and delivery sellers must verify a buyer's age through a commercial database check or require an adult's signature at delivery.

What are the penalties?

Sellers face civil penalties of up to $500 per violation. Teens who try to buy the products are not penalized.

Why are diet pills risky for teens?

They can cause heart, blood pressure, and digestive problems, and their use is associated with a higher chance of a later eating disorder diagnosis.

Where can families get help for eating disorders?

The National Alliance for Eating Disorders offers referrals and free support groups through its helpline at 866-662-1235, and pediatricians can screen teens for eating disorders.

같은 날 음료 당 표시·어린이 메뉴 기준도 서명

이날 서명된 법안에는 식생활 관련 법이 여럿 포함됐다. 주지사실 발표에 따르면 레스토랑 메뉴에 하루 권장량을 넘는 당이 든 음료를 표시하게 하는 법, 체인 레스토랑이 최소 영양 기준을 충족하는 어린이 메뉴를 하나 이상 내놓게 하는 법, 공공기관에 건강한 식품을 공급하는 '팜 투 포크' 사업을 만드는 법이 함께 서명됐다.

2026년 9월 28일 캘리포니아 주지사가 서명한 식품·영양 관련 법안(자료: 캘리포니아 주지사실)

뉴섬 주지사는 발표문에서 "우리는 '질병 관리'가 아니라 '건강 관리'를 해야 한다"며 "질병을 예방하는 것이 치료법을 찾고 그 비용을 감당하는 것보다 훨씬 낫다"고 말했다.

작년엔 '초가공식품' 법적 정의…학교 급식서 2035년까지 퇴출

이번 인증 제도는 캘리포니아가 지난해 만든 법의 연장선에 있다. 가브리엘 의원실에 따르면 2025년 10월 서명된 AB 1264 '진짜 음식, 건강한 아이들 법'은 미국 최초로 초가공식품을 법률로 정의하고, 주 보건부가 가장 해로운 초가공식품을 가려내 2035년까지 공립학교 급식에서 단계적으로 없애도록 했다. 이번 AB 2244는 학교 밖 일반 소비자가 매장에서 초가공식품이 아닌 제품을 고를 수 있도록 표시를 만든 것이다.

미국인의 초가공식품 섭취 비중은 여전히 높다. 미국 질병통제예방센터(CDC) 국립보건통계센터(NCHS)가 2025년 8월 발표한 조사(2021년 8월~2023년 8월)에서 1세 이상 미국인은 하루 섭취 열량의 55%를 초가공식품에서 얻었다. 청소년(1~18세)은 61.9%로 2017~2018년 조사 때 65.6%보다 3.7%포인트 낮아졌고, 성인(19세 이상)은 55.8%에서 53.0%로 2.8%포인트 낮아졌다.

다만 인증 표시는 자율 제도여서 실제로 얼마나 많은 제조사가 인증을 받을지는 인증기관 지정과 세부 기준이 나온 뒤에야 가늠할 수 있다. 인증기관 인가 기한이 2029년 6월인 만큼 매장에서 표시를 보게 되기까지는 시간이 걸릴 전망이다.

Bill Roundup: Sign/Veto Deadline Passes; What Are the New Laws?

Back to News

By

CSAC Staff

Date Published

October 1, 2026

Last week, we reported on notable legislation Governor Newsom had signed or vetoed since the Legislature adjourned on August 31. Now, with the September 30 deadline to act on new legislation behind us, we’re bringing you an update on some key bills that made it through before the cutoff, and some that didn’t. The measures below are of particular note to county governments and were either signed or vetoed in the final week before the Governor’s September 30 deadline to act on new legislation. 

Chaptered 

AB 762 (Irwin) (Chapter 717, Statutes of 2026) 
Disposable, battery-embedded vapor inhalation device: prohibition and penalties.
To help prevent fires caused by the improper disposal of single-use electronic devices that lack end-of-life management options, this bill prohibits the import or manufacturing of single-use/disposable nicotine vaping devices beginning January 1, 2027, and the sale or distribution of single-use/disposable nicotine vaping devices beginning January 1, 2028. This bill does not impact the availability of reusable nicotine vaping devices.
Read the coalition’s request for signature letter here.
Questions? Contact Jordan Wells at jwells@counties.org and Caitlin Loventhal at cloventhal@counties.org. 

AB 1331 (Elhawary) (Chapter 851, Statutes of 2026)
Workplace surveillance.
This bill was substantially narrowed to restrict the use of specific workplace surveillance tools in bathrooms. CSAC negotiated additional amendments to protect worker privacy and address our remaining security concerns.
Read the Governor’s signing message here.
Questions? Contact Eric Lawyer at elawyer@counties.org and Julissa Ceja Cardenas at jcejacardenas@counties.org. 

AB 1699 (Rogers) (Chapter 761, Statutes of 2026) 
Good Fire Act: Prescribed Fire Liability Pilot Program: burn bosses: California Environmental Quality Act. 
This bill establishes the Good Fire Act, largely codifying the Governor’s 2025 executive order to expand the use of tools for safely implementing beneficial fire projects. It also makes the Prescribed Fire Liability Program permanent and extends burn boss certifications from one year to three years, among other provisions.
Read CSAC’s request for signature letter here. 
Questions? Contact Jordan Wells at jwells@counties.org and Caitlin Loventhal at cloventhal@counties.org. 

AB 1811 (Rogers) (Chapter 549, Statutes of 2026)
Health professionals. 
This bill would preserve existing Health Professions Shortage Area designations, to ensure that programs to recruit and retain health professionals will continue to be available, even if the federal government withdraws current designations. 
Read the coalition’s request for signature letter. 
Questions? Contact Brendan McCarthy at bmccarthy@counties.org and Danielle Bradley at dbradley@counties.org. 

AB 1821 (Pacheco) (Chapter 899, Statutes of 2026)
California Public Records Act: agency response time.
This bill updates the California Public Records Act response timelines from “calendar days” to “business days,” aligning deadlines with actual working days instead of weekends and holidays.
Read the coalition request for signature here.
Questions? Contact Eric Lawyer at elawyer@counties.org and Julissa Ceja Cardenas at jcejacardenas@counties.org. 

AB 1883 (Bryan) (Chapter 853, Statutes of 2026)
Workplace surveillance tools.
This bill restricts  public agencies from using “workplace surveillance tools,” that include emotional recognition or neural data collection. Amendments offered by our coalition of local government advocates that would have fully addressed our concerns while preserving the purpose of the bill were not taken.
Read the coalition’s request for veto letter here and the Governor’s signing message here.
Questions? Contact Eric Lawyer at elawyer@counties.org and Julissa Ceja Cardenas at jcejacardenas@counties.org. 

AB 1924 (Gabriel) (Chapter 794, Statutes of 2026)
Statewide homelessness prevention strategy.
This bill requires the California Interagency Council on Homelessness (Cal ICH) to develop a statewide homelessness prevention strategy within Cal ICH’s Action Plan to Prevent and End Homelessness.
Read CSAC’s request for signature letter.
Questions? Contact Justin Garrett at jgarrett@counties.org and Danielle Bradley at dbradley@counties.org.  

AB 1934 (Bennett) (Chapter 763, Statutes of 2026)
State Fire Marshal: home hardening certification program implementation plan.
This bill requires the Office of the State Fire Marshal’s (OSFM) Wildfire Mitigation Advisory Committee, which CSAC serves on, to develop an implementation plan for a home hardening certification program by January 1, 2029.
Read the Coalition’s request for signature letter here.
Questions? Contact Jordan Wells at jwells@counties.org and Caitlin Loventhal at cloventhal@counties.org. 

AB 1964 (Bennett) (Chapter 765, Statutes of 2026)
State Fire Marshal: home hardening.
This bill directs the OSFM to develop home hardening standards by January 1, 2028, and compile a report by January 1, 2030 that estimates the number of homes in specified fire hazard severity zones that meet these standards or require additional home hardening.
Read CSAC’s request for signature letter here.
Questions? Contact Jordan Wells at jwells@counties.org and Caitlin Loventhal at cloventhal@counties.org. 

AB 1738 (Carrillo) (Chapter 271, Statutes of 2026)
State Housing Law: remote inspections. 
The bill requires cities and counties that meet specific population minimums to offer remote inspections for certain building-permit work in one- and two-family homes, while allowing local agencies to set procedures and apply existing immunities. Additionally, the bill allows building officials to deny remote inspections to applicants for willful misrepresentation for a specified period of time. The bill would require most California cities and counties to offer remote inspections for certain building-permit work in one- and two-family homes, while allowing local agencies to set procedures and apply existing immunities. The bill is set to take effect on January 1, 2028. 

AB 2051 (Wicks) (Chapter 575, Statutes of 2026) 
Public resources: coastal resources: Coastal Resilience Permitting Working Group.  
This bill directs the California Natural Resources Agency to convene an interagency Coastal Resilience Permitting Working Group to identify administrative improvements and develop a clear roadmap for streamlining permitting for coastal resilience projects. This measure would help accelerate critical climate adaptation projects while upholding California’s environmental protections, protecting coastal communities and ecosystems.
Read CSAC’s request for signature letter here.
Questions? Contact Charles Delgado at cdelgado@counties.org and Caitlin Loventhal at cloventhal@counties.org. 

AB 2478 (Schultz) (Chapter 611, Statutes of 2026)
Kinship family approval.
This bill implements a streamlined Kinship Family Approval (KFA) pathway and clarifies emergency placement rules so that children can be placed quickly and safely with people who already know their needs.
Read CSAC’s request for signature letter.
Questions? Contact Justin Garrett at jgarrett@counties.org and Danielle Bradley at dbradley@counties.org. 

AB 2513 (Petrie-Norris) (Chapter 768, Statutes of 2026)
Wildfire: Regional Forest and Fire Capacity Program: local assistance grant program: regional landscape grants.
Wildfire mitigation must be addressed at the parcel, community, and landscape scales. This bill amends various state grant programs to authorize administering agencies to directly award regional landscape grants to regional entities.
Read the request for signature letter here.
Questions? Contact Jordan Wells at jwells@counties.org and Caitlin Loventhal at cloventhal@counties.org. 

SB 299 (Cabaldon) (Chapter 413, Statutes of 2026)
California Environmental Quality Act: exemption: day care center: zoning. The bill exempts day care centers which meet certain criteria and are located in a residential area from CEQA review requirements. Read CSAC’s support and request for signature letter for this bill here. 

SB 577 (Laird) (Chapter 971, Statutes of 2026)
Public entities.
This bill addresses public agency liability due to AB 218 (Gonzalez, 2019), as well as general liability for cases when public agencies share a small portion of the fault. SB 577 includes provisions heightening evidence and knowledge standards for past claims brought by a claimant above age 40; improves joint and several liability, limiting public agency liability for economic damages to their share of fault, if their share of fault is fifteen percent or less; and includes a variety of provisions aimed at prevention. CSAC was neutral on the bill. 
Read the Governor’s signing message here. 

SB 894 (Allen) (Chapter 770, Statutes of 2026)
Wildfire resiliency: financial assistance.
This bill establishes the California Wildfire Resilience Loan Program and requires the California Alternative Energy and Advanced Transportation Financing Authority to administer a low-interest loan program to reduce upfront costs and incentivize home hardening and defensible space activities.
Read CSAC’s request for signature letter here.
Questions? Contact Jordan Wells at jwells@counties.org and Caitlin Loventhal at cloventhal@counties.org. 

SB 947 (McNerney) (Chapter 859, Statutes of 2026)
Employment: automated decision systems.
This bill regulates the use of automated decision-making systems, which include artificial intelligence and other routine tools used for everyday work, when making employment-related decisions. This bill is the successor to SB 7 (McNerney) that was vetoed by the Governor last year. CSAC opposed both bills because they complicate the routine work of local governments.  
Read the coalition’s request for veto letter here.
Questions? Contact Emma Jungwirth at ejungwirth@counties.org and Julissa Ceja Cardenas at jcejacardenas@counties.org. 

SB 973 (Becker) (Chapter 772, Statutes of 2026)
Wildfire County Coordinator Program.
This bill establishes the California Wildfire Preparedness Program and requires CAL FIRE to enter into an agreement with the California Fire Safe Council to administer and deliver the Wildfire County Coordinator Program.
Read the coalition’s request for signature letter here.
Questions? Contact Jordan Wells at jwells@counties.org and Caitlin Loventhal at cloventhal@counties.org. 

SB 1051 (Menjivar) (Chapter 1002, Statutes of 2026)
Foster care: childcare. 
This bill will ensure that there is no wrong door for eligible children and caregivers in accessing the Emergency Child Care Bridge Program for foster children.
Read CSAC’s request for signature letter. 
Questions? Contact Justin Garrett at jgarrett@counties.org and Danielle Bradley at dbradley@counties.org.  

SB 1370 (Stern) (Chapter 777, Statutes of 2026) 
Covered wildfire mitigation projects: consolidated and expedited review.
This bill builds on the success of the Governor’s 2025 executive order and establishes a consolidated and expediated review process for certain covered wildfire mitigation projects. The bill also requires the Board of Forestry and Fire Protection to adopt regulations to develop a Certified Regulatory Program for nontimber vegetation management
Read the coalition’s request for signature letter here.
Questions? Contact Jordan Wells at jwells@counties.org and Caitlin Loventhal at cloventhal@counties.org. 

Vetoed 

AB 1881 (Ramos) California Indian Freedom Act of 2026.
This bill would have established a private right of action, allowing tribes and individual tribal members to challenge state decisions involving state lands and waterways, thereby increasing potential litigation risk. The measure would have further prioritizes tribal governmental interests through a strict scrutiny standard and overlaps with, or conflicts with, existing state and federal frameworks that already govern tribal consultation and protections.
Read the coalition’s request for veto letter here and the Governor’s veto message here.
Questions? Contact Charles Delgado at cdelgado@counties.org and Caitlin Loventhal at cloventhal@counties.org. 

AB 2218 (Kalra) Water policy: California Native American tribes.
This bill sought to address longstanding inequities faced by California Native American Tribes due to the loss of access to and control over water resources. However, the bill’s policy statement and directive introduced substantial uncertainty into existing water management processes by establishing a broad policy framework without providing clear direction, safeguards, or limitations to ensure the continued reliability of water supplies. This measure would have also had unclear, but potentially far-reaching impacts on surface water rights. 
Read the coalition’s request for veto letter here and the Governor’s veto message here.
Questions? Contact Charles Delgado at cdelgado@counties.org and Caitlin Loventhal at cloventhal@counties.org. 

AB 2656 (Petrie-Norris) Public employees: notice: artificial intelligence performing service within scope of work.
This bill would have required public employers to provide 45-day written notice to union representatives before developing, purchasing, or requiring the use of any generative AI to perform a service that is within the scope of work of a represented job classification. CSAC had significant concerns regarding the burdensome, costly obligations for local agencies.
Read the coalition’s request for veto letter here and the Governor’s veto message here.
Questions? Contact Eric Lawyer at elawyer@counties.org and Julissa Ceja Cardenas at jcejacardenas@counties.org.

AB 2739 (Soria) Water: affordability and system stabilization.
This bill would have established the Water Affordability and System Stabilization Fund and the Community Water Affordability Program, which would have helped ensure that local jurisdictions have the necessary resources to ensure access to clean, affordable drinking water for all residents.
Read CSAC’s request for signature letter here and the Governor’s veto message here.
Questions? Contact Charles Delgado at cdelgado@counties.org and Caitlin Loventhal at cloventhal@counties.org. 

SB 872 (McNerney) Delta Levees and Canal Subsidence Fund.
This bill sought to protect the millions of water users in the state, communities reliant on safe, clean drinking water, and the environment by making long overdue investments in the State Water Project and the network of levees protecting the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta.  
Read CSAC’s request for signature letter here and the Governor’s veto message here.
Questions? Contact Charles Delgado at cdelgado@counties.org and Caitlin Loventhal at cloventhal@counties.org. 

SB 661 (Hurtado) Airports: financial assistance.
The bill sought to redirect a portion of jet fuel sales and use tax revenues into the Aeronautics Account and require those funds to be distributed among airports and aviation-related programs according to a set formula. Additionally, it would require annual transfers from the Retail Sales Tax Fund, reporting of jet fuel flowage by airports, and allocation of the money mainly to airports based on fuel use, with smaller shares for general aviation, aviation education, and certain grant programs. Notably, the bill would have redirected sales tax revenues from the Local Public Safety Fund and the Local Revenue Fund, which would have reduced county funding for public safety and health and human services programs. 

SB 1125 (Menjivar) Water Rate Assistance Program.
This bill would have established a water rate assistance program, upon appropriation by the Legislature, to provide rate assistance to low-income residents.
Read the coalition’s request for signature letter here and the Governor’s veto message here.
Questions? Contact Charles Delgado at cdelgado@counties.org and Caitlin Loventhal at cloventhal@counties.org. 

SB 1272 (Menjivar) Local ordinances: administrative fines or penalties.
This bill would have required county and city building officials to give at least six months to correct certain nonimmediate building, plumbing, electrical, or similar zoning violations on qualifying owner-occupied residential properties before imposing administrative fines or penalties. Specifically, it would have applied when the property has four or fewer units and the current owner files a sworn affidavit stating the owner did not cause the violation and did not know of it when acquiring the property. The bill would have allowed a six-month extension for a good faith effort to fix the problem and would have allowed for further extensions at the agency’s discretion. Read CSAC’s opposition and request for veto letter for this bill here.
