As the end of a two-year legislative session concludes, Governor Newsom continues to take action on bills that have advanced out of the Legislature and to his desk for consideration. Emphases on affordability and how newly signed legislation helps California households and communities is a consistent theme from Governor Newsom’s press office as bills are signed before the September 30 deadline.

Overshadowing the impacts of new legislation may be the fate of Proposition 1, the $11.25 billion Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026. The resources in Proposition 1 will have the most significant impact on affordable housing production for years to come, more than any other single piece of legislation. Still, many other measures just signed into law are significant, including:

Removing Development Barriers

  • AB 1815 (Wicks, D-Oakland): Supports factory-built housing by limiting local jurisdictions’ ability to impose building standards that exceed the states.
  • SB 677 (Wiener, D-San Francisco): Enhances streamlining to already approved housing projects.
  • SB 963 (Laird, D-Santa Cruz): Streamlines the Coastal Development Permit appeals process by establishing clear deadlines for the California Coastal Commission to request information and make final decisions on appealed projects, providing greater certainty for housing and other coastal development.
  • SB 1116 (Caballero, D-Merced): Expands and strengthens existing state law to make it easier to subdivide eligible urban lots and build smaller, lower-cost starter homes for homeownership, including townhomes and condominiums.

Reducing Development Cost

  • AB 2044 (Petrie-Norris, D-Irvine): Requires proposed state building standards to include a complete estimate of compliance costs and underlying assumptions before the California Building Standards Commission can approve them, increasing transparency around the cost impacts of new building regulations.
  • SB 1014 (Grayson, D-Orinda): Increases certainty for housing developers by requiring local governments to provide timely, upfront information about required onsite and offsite infrastructure improvements, helping prevent unexpected requirements and costs later in the permitting process.
  • SB 1117 (Cervantes, D-Riverside): Changes how jurisdictions calculate impact fees for ADUs, allowing fees only for units greater than 750 square feet.

Increasing Resources

  • SB 113 (Budget Trailer Bill): $94 million allocated to specific housing needs or projects in communities throughout the state.
  • AB-750 (Quirk-Silva, D-La Palma): Allows HCD to provide loans or grants to financially “challenged” affordable housing developments to rehabilitate properties, replenish operating reserves, and preserve their long-term affordability.
  • AB 2074 (Haney, D-San Francisco): Would create a new, lower-cost financing option for high-rise residential developments near major regional transit hubs through a new revolving loan fund.
  • SB 417 (Limón, D-Goleta/Cabaldon, D-West Sacramento): Places an $11.25 billion Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond on the November 2026 ballot to fund affordable rental housing, supportive housing, homeownership programs, and housing assistance for veterans.
  • SB 1091 (Caballero, D, Merced): Establishes the Community Anti-Displacement and Preservation Program for purposes of funding the acquisition and rehabilitation of unrestricted housing and attaching long-term affordability restrictions on the housing. This program would be funded out of proceeds from the passage of Proposition 1.
  • SB 1388 (Durazo, D-Los Angeles): Establishes an Affordable Housing Risk Reduction Program within HCD to provide technical assistance and resources to affordable housing providers to reduce portfolio risk and help them secure more affordable insurance coverage.

Streamlining Processes

  • AB 956 (Quirk-Silva, D-La Palma): Expands ADU development by requiring streamlined, ministerial approval of up to two detached ADUs on lots with an existing or proposed single-family home, increasing housing opportunities in single-family neighborhoods.
  • AB 1621 (Wilson, D-Suisun City): Reduces delays during the construction plan check process by streamlining post-entitlement building permit reviews and enforcing clear, predictable timelines once a housing project has been approved.
  • AB 1751 (Quirk-Silva, D-Fullerton): Establishes the Missing Middle Townhome Ownership Act, which creates a streamlined, ministerial approval process for townhome developments on residentially zoned lots.
  • AB 2089 (Ward, D-San Diego): Extends the sunset on provisions in the welfare exemption for affordable rental housing that received Low Income Housing Tax Credits to maintain eligibility when a tenant’s income increases to 140% of Area Median Income.
  • AB 2433 (Alvarez, D-Chula Vista): Streamlines approvals for projects that meet CEQA exemption and density bonus law.

Reforming the Housing Finance System

  • AB 179 (Budget Trailer Bill): Reforms and streamlines the state’s affordable housing finance system through a “one-stop shop” approach, reduces development costs and impact fees, extends homelessness funding and accountability measures, and supports investments including $500 million for state Low-Income Housing Tax Credits and $200 million for the Multifamily Housing Program.
  • AB 2020 (Gabriel, D-Encino): Allows affordable housing developers to move project reserves across their portfolios to stabilize projects under extreme financial pressure.
  • AB 2185 (Quirk-Silva, D-La Palma): Requires state housing and finance agencies to review and revise affordable housing program rules to remove barriers to and facilitate the use of factory-built housing, with the goal of lowering costs and accelerating affordable housing production.

Addressing Homelessness

  • AB 1556 (Haney, D-San Francisco): Establishes standards for state-funded recovery housing for people experiencing or at risk of homelessness, requiring programs to align with Housing First principles while supporting substance-use recovery, relapse protections, and overdose prevention.
  • AB 1924 (Gabriel, D-Encino): Requires the California Interagency Council on Homelessness to develop and publicly issue a statewide homelessness prevention strategy by July 1, 2028.
  • AB 2146 (Stefani, D-San Francisco): Requires the California Interagency Council on Homelessness to complete a statewide study of the Coordinated Entry System to identify barriers to connecting people with affordable housing by July 2028.

Supporting Student Housing

  • AB 1732 (Alvarez, D-Chula Vista): Expands an existing California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) statutory exemption for infill affordable housing to include qualifying public university and community college housing projects, allowing those projects to proceed without environmental review if they meet specified labor, location, and environmental standards.
  • AB 2480 (Ávila Farías, D-Concord): Requires a local government to provide an additional density bonus for student housing developments that meet a minimum affordability threshold and provide additional units for moderate-income students.

Newsom Signs First-in-Nation Non-Ultraprocessed Food Label Into Law

28 Sep 2026 2:45 p.m. · Source: California Governors Office

California Governor Gavin Newsom signed legislation creating a first-in-the-nation label for non-ultraprocessed foods, along with a package of health bills covering menu sugar warnings, diet pill sales to minors and tobacco and vape restrictions.

The bills, announced Monday, advance what the Governor's Office described as California's nation-leading holistic healthcare strategy, taking on ultra-processed foods, high-sugar content and Big Tobacco while making healthier foods and products easier to identify and access.

"We should be about healthcare, not sick-care, recognizing that preventing illnesses is far preferable to finding — and affording — treatments," Newsom said. "It's why California is focused on making whole, healthy foods as accessible as possible, why we're making healthier choices easier."

The non-ultraprocessed certification program, created by AB 2244 from Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino), gives manufacturers a voluntary standard and provides front-of-package information to consumers, with improved in-store placement of healthier options. The Governor's Office compared the approach to the USDA Organic label.

"Like the USDA Organic label, this new seal will provide consumers with clear, trustworthy information and make it easier for them to locate healthier foods that are free from harmful additives," Gabriel said. "Parents shouldn't need a Ph.D. in chemistry to understand what they're feeding their kids."

Other measures require chain restaurants to offer one children's meal meeting a minimum nutrition standard, require menus to flag drinks containing more than the recommended daily intake of sugar, and require diaper manufacturers to disclose the full list of ingredients used to make their products.

The package also bans the sale of over-the-counter diet pills and dietary supplements for weight loss or muscle building to anyone under 18. The Governor's Office said nearly 1 in 10 adolescents have used such products, and that young users are six times more likely to be diagnosed with an eating disorder within three years than nonusers.

On tobacco, the legislation requires retailers to display lung cancer screening awareness signage and bans single-use vapes and advertising of vape products designed to look like items marketed to minors, such as food or school supplies. It builds on California's flavored tobacco ban signed in 2022 and reaffirmed by voters' passage of Proposition 31.

First Partner Jennifer Siebel Newsom said California is committed to giving children the best start in life, citing two free school meals every day and the state's Farm to School program. A new program will seek locally based vendors to supply healthy foods to California public schools.

The Farm to School program has connected more than half of California's public school students with local, nutritious school meals, working alongside a universal school meals program that has served almost 3.5 billion free meals since 2021, according to the Governor's Office.

This is the first of a two-part story looking at efforts to lower recidivism rates in California prisons.

On August 1, 1974 a young Detroit Tigers outfielder named Ron LeFlore stepped up to the plate for the first time in the major leagues. Facing the Milwaukee Brewers’ hard-throwing right-hander Jim Slaton, LeFlore didn’t do much in that at-bat or any others that day. But that inauspicious debut hardly mattered.

Almost exactly 13 months to the day prior, LeFlore had been an inmate at Michigan State Prison in Jackson, Michigan. In and out of lock-ups since he was a kid, he had served just over three years of a five-to-fifteen-year sentence for armed robbery, a crime he had committed while high on heroin.

While in prison, LeFlore discovered baseball, a sport he had never played before. A natural, he quickly became the star of the prison baseball team, good enough to draw the attention of then-Tigers manager Billy Martin. Released on July 2, 1973, LeFlore signed with the Tigers almost immediately after the gates closed behind him.

His life had officially moved from one of getting high and stealing money to chasing down high fly balls and stealing bases for a living. He would play nine years in the majors with Detroit, Montreal and the Chicago White Sox before hanging them up with more than 1,200 hits and 455 stolen bases to his credit.

LeFlore’s story is admittedly one in a million (actually the name of the 1978 made-for-TV-movie about his life starring Sacramento-native LeVar Burton), but it is exactly the kind of hopeful one that sparked legislation (AB 2204) this year from Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (D-Encino) that requires the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation (CDCR) to adopt a comprehensive statewide policy to increase opportunities for inmates to participate in organized sports.

The measure, co-authored by Assemblymembers Isaac Bryan (D-Los Angeles) and Juan Alanis (R-Modesto), further allows CDCR to enter into partnerships with colleges, universities, and professional sports teams and leagues that want to support such programs.

Gov. Gavin Newsom signed the bill into law on September 30th.

Gabriel told Capitol Weekly he wasn’t familiar with LeFlore when he introduced the bill, but rather had been influenced by a New York Times piece about the history of baseball in San Quentin. (He says former Assemblymember and current Sacramento Mayor Kevin McCarty eventually brought him up to speed on LeFlore’s story.) He was so fascinated by the piece he sent it to his staff, presuming there was already some kind of statewide policy on sports programs in state lockups.

“And they said, ‘there is none.’”

Gabriel, Bryan and Alanis went about trying to change that, and it didn’t take long for them to gain strong bipartisan support in the Legislature and from groups outside of it that rarely agree on much.

“We had a bill that’s got the police chiefs, CCPOA and all the criminal justice reform groups on the same side. And they’re all saying the same thing, which was, “We think this is a really good idea. It’s going to be good for rehabilitation. It’s going to reduce violence inside of prisons. It’s going to make communities safer when people go home.”

The measure ultimately cleared both the Assembly and Senate without a single opposing vote.

For Jacob Brevard, Chief of Programs at the Anti-Recidivism Coalition, which works to keep people from re-offending and heading back to prison, Newsom’s signature was a watershed moment in the state’s efforts to reduce recidivism.

“I think it gives people hope. It inspires them, and it makes them more confident in who they are,” he said. Brevard agrees with supporters who believe it has a good chance to also reduce violence behind prison walls.

Brevard speaks from personal experience, having served 25 years behind bars after being convicted of first-degree murder at age 19. His mother’s passing while he was inside motivated him to change his life for the better. That yearning led him to join a football team at California’s Correctional Training Facility, better known to most as Soledad State Prison.

“We had a bill that’s got the police chiefs, CCPOA and all the criminal justice reform groups on the same side. And they’re all saying the same thing, which was, “We think this is a really good idea.”

He says what he experienced in that atmosphere was life-changing.

Not that it was always easy. The game itself was nothing new – he said he had played it his whole life – but never with quite the same circumstances or the same motivation.

“I felt weird interacting with different cultures and different people that I didn’t normally associate with,” he says. “It was multicultural. There were many different members from different gangs in there. But when we was on the field, none of that mattered. It wasn’t so and so from this neighborhood, so and so from that neighborhood. It was the team name. And we all fought together on that field to make it happen.”

Brevard says being part of the team helped him learn lessons that had missed him in his younger days.

“Conflict resolution for sure,” he says. “There was a lot of huge situations that I had to learn how to work through without becoming violent. The ability to compromise, the ability to work through problems, the ability to understand that we all have roles to play.”

All of which, Gabriel said, is exactly the point.

“Sports are about a lot of things: you’re building teamwork and discipline, you’re accountable to other people, and you have to think about how your actions affect others. You have to learn how to control your emotions in heated situations. And all of these things that sports teaches are actually life lessons.”

Critical life lessons, he said, given that most incarcerated people will eventually return to society.

“How important it is to help people as they’re going through this process of rehabilitation and prepare them to go back into their communities, because the overwhelming majority of folks that are in the system are gonna come home and they’re gonna be our neighbors, right?” he said.

Like all prison reform, the path forward is not without questions. AB 2204 included what Gabriel called “seed funding” in this year’s budget, and the plan is to encourage public-private partnerships similar to how the San Francisco Giants (And the Oakland Athletics before them) offer significant financial support for the San Quentin baseball team. Future state funding would be dependent on the governor and lawmakers allocating it in the budget every year. The law is also set to expire in 2036, leaving its long-term future up to future governors and lawmakers.

Gabriel is confident his colleagues will see the program as a valuable investment both in public safety and fiscal responsibility.

“The average cost of incarceration is north of $130,000 a year per person in the system,” he said. “So anything that we can do to cut down on recidivism, anything that we can do to cut down on crime in our communities, is obviously, first and foremost, going to protect folks. But it’s also going to result in huge savings for the state.”

Sports programs are only one of the many efforts being made in California state prisons to help the incarcerated to learn life and job skills that will help them reclaim a spot in society and not return to prison. In part II of this series, we will look at the impact of other non-sports programs in reducing recidivism.

A new “California Certified” label will soon be available for foods in the state that are not ultra-processed as a growing number of places take action on products linked to serious health outcomes.

The new label, to be released some time in the next two years, could be slapped on certified breads, canned goods, fruits and more, and those items displayed prominently on grocery store shelves.

Food manufacturers must apply to the state’s health department to use the seal by June 1, 2028, with recertification needed every three years, according to legislation signed this week by California Governor Gavin Newsom. The governor said it was part of the state’s efforts to improve people’s health through access to healthy food and that California was “clearing the way for the rest of the country to follow.”

Ultra-processed foods are made with ingredients that wouldn’t be found in a kitchen, such as chemical preservatives, sweeteners and artificial colors and flavors, according to Johns Hopkins, like brightly colored chips and candy and smoked meats.

These foods have been linked to increased risk of cancer, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, obesity and premature death, dozens of studies have found. Yet, more than half of Americans’ daily calories come from these foods, federal data shows.

California isn’t the only state targeting ultra-processed foods and is also phasing them out in schools over the next decade. Arizona banned ultra-processed foods in schools this year and New York City has eliminated processed meats and restricted artificial colors and sweeteners in school meals and in other city facilities.

The Golden State, however, is the first to come up with a label for non-ultra-processed foods.

“California Certified” labels are modeled after the Department of Agriculture’s “USDA Organic”, which means a product was made without pesticides or fertilizers.

The state has also taken action to ban additives in ultra-processed food while the City of San Francisco filed a lawsuit against some of the nation's top food manufacturers, arguing that health care costs tied to ultra-processed foods have become a burden for states.

Nearly half of states are considering or have introduced separate legislation to regulate ultra-processed foods, according to the non-profit Environmental Working Group.

The Trump administration has also made moves to tackle ultra-processed foods led by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr’s “Make America Health Again” agenda.

The Health Department has pushed companies to transition away from artificial dyes in ultra-processed foods. “These poisonous compounds offer no nutritional benefit and pose real, measurable dangers to our children’s health and development,” RFK Jr said last April.

However, the department’s efforts have reportedly met with resistance within the White House, according to a report earlier this week in The Wall Street Journal. During a discussion about the definition of ultra-processed foods, White House staffers were allegedly concerned it may cover most food in grocery stores, with negative impacts for companies.

But HHS pushed back on this characterization.

”The idea that the White House is blocking the MAHA food agenda is false,” Calley Means, senior advisor at HHS, told The Independent in email on Wednesday, citing efforts to overhaul dietary guidance and artificial dyes.

“Together, HHS, USDA and the White House are driving these reforms while ensuring policies - including our work on ultra-processed foods - are scientifically rigorous, legally durable and deliver lasting results for American families,” she said.
